alien-world-ground.alien planet base: Overlap sand paste, crackle and coarse grit, prime white, then flood turquoise, purple and magenta inks into each other while wet.
alien-world-ground.how do i make a weird alien world base: Mix sand paste, crackle and grit, add spare tentacles as plants, prime white and run bright inks together, then drybrush white and add bright tufts.
alien-world-ground.colourful otherworldly ground for sci fi: Prime the textured base white and flood turquoise, purple and magenta inks wet into each other so the colours run and mix.
alien-world-ground.base for xenos looking odd and bright: Use mixed textures flooded with bright inks over a white primer, with spare tentacles as odd plants and brightly coloured tufts.
alien-world-ground.strange alien plants on a base: Glue spare tentacles or tails upright in a cluster as an odd plant, then work a purple wash round them to separate them from the ground.
alien-world-ground.bright ink pools on a base: Prime white so the inks stay bright, then flood turquoise, purple and magenta into each other while wet so the colours run and mix.
alien-world-ground.make the ground look like another planet: Overlap sand paste, crackle and coarse grit, prime white, flood bright inks together, then drybrush white once the inks are fully dry.
alien-world-ground.alien basing ideas: Try cork for height, overlapping textures, spare tentacles as plants, bright inks over white, and brightly coloured tufts with their tips opened.
alien-world-ground.what tufts suit an alien world: Brightly coloured grass tufts, glued on last with their tips opened out using tweezers.
alien-world-ground.funky colorful base for monsters: Flood turquoise, purple and magenta inks wet into each other over a white primed texture, then drybrush white and varnish matt.

paving-and-cast-stone.cracked paving slabs on a base: Snap a plain plastic floor tile by hand or with pliers, glue the pieces down as one cracked slab and fill the gaps with sanded grout.
paving-and-cast-stone.broken concrete base: Snap a plastic floor tile for rough concrete edges, or spread grey texture paste unevenly with a spatula for cast concrete.
paving-and-cast-stone.how to make ruined pavement: Snap a plastic tile, glue the pieces as a cracked slab with some tilted up, press in gravel and fill the gaps with sanded grout.
paving-and-cast-stone.snapped tile for basing: Use a plain plastic floor tile with no sticky back; it breaks by hand or with pliers with rough edges much like concrete.
paving-and-cast-stone.urban rubble base with cracked slabs: Glue snapped tile down as cracked slabs, press in gravel, grout the gaps, then paint the slabs grey and the ground between dark brown.
paving-and-cast-stone.make the ground look like it shifted: Tilt some of the snapped tile pieces and prop them up as you glue them, so the slabs sit at different angles.
paving-and-cast-stone.city street base for my models: Glue snapped plastic tile down as cracked paving, grout the gaps, paint it mid grey, wash the cracks brown and drybrush light grey.
paving-and-cast-stone.cast concrete from filler paste: Spread grey texture paste unevenly with a spatula, not a brush; the grey paste already gives you the base colour.
paving-and-cast-stone.post apocalyptic road base: Use cracked, partly raised slabs of snapped tile with gravel and grout between, grimy brown cracks, and a little grass for an overgrown look.
paving-and-cast-stone.raised broken flagstones: Tilt and prop up some pieces of snapped plastic tile as you glue them, as if the ground has shifted.

foam-bushes-and-shrubs.make bushes from sponge: Tear fine sponge into crumbs, mix with white glue and thinned green paint into a thick paste, and press clumps onto the base.
foam-bushes-and-shrubs.cheap shrubs for bases: Crumbled sponge mixed with white glue and thinned paint makes bushes with real height.
foam-bushes-and-shrubs.tall bushes on a base: Build each bush up in clumps of sponge paste, as loose crumbs sprinkled on glue only lie flat.
foam-bushes-and-shrubs.foam clump foliage: Mix torn foam crumbs with white glue and thinned green paint into a paste that holds together, then press it into shape on the base.
foam-bushes-and-shrubs.how to make hedges for terrain: See: building bushes up in clumps of sponge, glue and paint paste, in this entry's steps 2 to 4.
foam-bushes-and-shrubs.bushes made from kitchen sponge: Tear the sponge into small crumbs rather than cutting it, so the edges look leafy, then bind it with white glue and paint.
foam-bushes-and-shrubs.leafy undergrowth on base: Press clumps of sponge crumb paste onto the base, drybrush mid green then yellow green on top, and sit a few tufts round them.
foam-bushes-and-shrubs.diy shrubbery for scenery: Mix torn sponge crumbs with white glue and well thinned green paint, then build bushes up clump by clump with a blunt brush handle.
foam-bushes-and-shrubs.bushes look like flat blobs: Build each bush up in clumps for height, as loose crumbs sprinkled on glue only lie flat.
foam-bushes-and-shrubs.add height to forest bases: Build sponge bushes up in clumps of crumb, glue and paint paste rather than sprinkling crumbs, which only lie flat.

paper-plants.laser cut paper plants: Pop them out gently, bend every plant so none sit flat, tint them with thin washes, then glue them in clumps.
paper-plants.how do i make paper ferns look real: Bend and twist each one, lift leaf sides with a blunt point, and wash it green or soft brown to hide the white cut edges.
paper-plants.paper leaves look too flat: Bend and twist every plant, run a blunt point down each leaf so its sides lift, and hold the shape with a little hair gel.
paper-plants.tint paper plants with paint: Wash live plants a well thinned leaf green and dead ones soft brown before gluing, then drybrush pale green over the edges.
paper-plants.ferns on a base: Shape and tint paper ferns, then glue them first, before larger leaves and tufts, letting them hide joins and spill over rocks.
paper-plants.glue plants in natural clumps: Glue ferns first, then larger leaves, then a few tufts, letting them hide joins and spill over rocks.
paper-plants.jungle foliage for bases: Use laser cut paper plants, bent so none sit flat, tinted green or brown, and glued in clumps of ferns, leaves and tufts.
paper-plants.bend paper plants so they dont look fake: Open healthy leaves out and let dead ones droop and curl; a blunt point lifts leaf sides and hair gel holds the shape.
paper-plants.colouring paper flowers and leaves: Use thin washes so the print still shows: leaf green on live plants, soft brown on dead ones and on a few live tips.
paper-plants.dead leaves drooping on base plants: Let dead leaves droop and curl, roll the tips to curl them, and wash them a soft brown before gluing.

sci-fi-deck-plates.spaceship floor base: Cut a plastic card disc, add panel lines, tube pipes and fine mesh, then prime black and drybrush grey with brown and black grime.
sci-fi-deck-plates.sci fi base from plasticard: Cut a disc of 1 mm card to the base's top face, add panel lines, tube pipes, frame offcut steps and mesh, then file ends flush.
sci-fi-deck-plates.how do i make metal deck plating bases: Pencil panel lines on plastic card, cut thin slivers between panels and deepen the lines with a file, then drill tiny bolt holes.
sci-fi-deck-plates.starship corridor base: Build a plastic card floor with pipes under fine mesh, prime black, and drybrush dark grey brightest just off centre like a spotlight.
sci-fi-deck-plates.grated floor with mesh: Lay fine steel mesh over tube pipes, short of the edges, and hide its cut edges under thin card strips; black primer keeps the pipes in shadow.
sci-fi-deck-plates.panel lines on a base: Pencil the lines, cut thin slivers out between panels, glue them down, and deepen the lines with a file.
sci-fi-deck-plates.industrial metal floor base: Plastic card plates with tube pipes, mesh and drilled bolts, primed black, drybrushed grey, grimed brown and black, with small rust patches.
sci-fi-deck-plates.plastic card base toppers: Measure the base's top face, which is smaller than its listed size, and cut a disc of plastic card to match with a compass cutter.
sci-fi-deck-plates.scifi bases diy: Cut a plastic card disc, add panel lines, tube pipes, frame offcut steps, mesh and drilled bolts, then prime black and drybrush grey.
sci-fi-deck-plates.tech floor base: Plastic card panels with tube pipes under fine mesh, primed black, heavily drybrushed dark grey, grimed, then edged in light grey.

tile-grout-ground.tile grout for bases: Spread a thin layer of sanded grout with a palette knife; it sticks without extra glue and dries in under an hour.
tile-grout-ground.cheap base texture: Sanded tile grout grips the base without glue and is a cheap texture.
tile-grout-ground.basing paste without glue: Tile grout spread thinly over the base sticks without any extra glue.
tile-grout-ground.sanded grout ground: Spread it thin with a palette knife, press in rocks, let it dry, then flood brown ink over it and drybrush the grains light tan.
tile-grout-ground.quick textured ground on bases: Spread a thin layer of tile grout, press in rocks, and it dries in under an hour; left plain it already reads as beach sand.
tile-grout-ground.diy texture paste for bases: Use sanded tile grout for grit, or unsanded for a smoother ground, spread on with a metal palette knife or old spoon.
tile-grout-ground.grout for terrain: See: grout used as base ground, spread thin, inked brown and drybrushed tan, in this entry's steps 1 to 5.
tile-grout-ground.texture that sticks to base without pva: Tile grout spread over the top of the base sticks without extra glue.
tile-grout-ground.fast drying base texture: A thin layer of tile grout dries in under an hour.
tile-grout-ground.budget alternative to texture paint: Cheap sanded tile grout grips the base without glue; flood it with brown ink and drybrush light tan.

aged-bronze.old bronze: Base dark bronze, wash black with a second coat on some panels, edge in brass, then glaze a thin pale blue green into the recesses.
aged-bronze.how do i paint aged bronze: Two thin coats of dark bronze, a black wash doubled on some panels, brass edges with silver points, and a pale blue green glaze in recesses.
aged-bronze.verdigris in the recesses: Thin a pale blue green right down and glaze it into recesses and panel edges, moving any pools so no tide marks form.
aged-bronze.green patina on bronze armour: Glaze a well thinned pale blue green into the recesses and panel edges over dark bronze, moving pools so no tide marks form.
aged-bronze.make bronze look ancient: Give some panels a second black wash for an uneven, aged look, then glaze pale blue green verdigris into the recesses.
aged-bronze.weathered brass trim: Base dark bronze, wash black, edge the main edges in brass with tiny silver points, and glaze pale blue green into recesses.
aged-bronze.bronze statue look: Dark bronze washed black unevenly, brass on the main edges, and pale blue green verdigris glazed into the recesses.
aged-bronze.dark bronze with green corrosion: Base dark bronze over black or grey primer, wash black, edge in brass, then glaze pale blue green into recesses and panel edges.
aged-bronze.tarnished bronze shield: Base dark bronze, wash black and add a second coat on some areas for unevenness, then brass edges and a pale blue green glaze in recesses.
aged-bronze.verdigris recipe: A pale blue green thinned to a glaze, worked into recesses and panel edges over dark bronze, with pools moved so no tide marks form.

black-gun-casing.black gun: Base off black in one thin coat, pick out metal parts in dark silver, wash black, then edge dark grey with pale grey dots on corners.
black-gun-casing.how to paint black weapons: Off black base, dark silver muzzle and small parts, an even black wash, then dark grey edge lines and pale grey corner dots.
black-gun-casing.black rifle casing: One thin coat of off black so detail stays crisp, a black wash, then dark grey on the edges and pale grey dots on corners.
black-gun-casing.gun looks like a black blob: Break it up with dark silver and bronze metal parts, then add dark grey edge lines and pale grey dots on the corners.
black-gun-casing.black plastic look on guns: Base off black, wash black evenly, then highlight with dark grey lines on edges and pale grey dots on corners.
black-gun-casing.paint black guns neatly: Use one thin coat of off black so detail stays crisp, take care around painted hands, and move the wash about so it does not pool.
black-gun-casing.off black weapon: Off black base, dark silver and bronze metal trim, a black wash, dark grey edges, pale grey corner dots and brighter silver on metal edges.
black-gun-casing.how to highlight a black gun: Dark grey lines along the edges, pale grey dots on the corners, and brighter silver on the metal edges.
black-gun-casing.black pistol: Base off black, pick out the muzzle in dark silver, wash black, then edge dark grey with pale grey dots on corners.
black-gun-casing.guns with metal trim: Pick out the muzzle and a few small parts in dark silver, some in bronze, over the off black casing, then edge them in brighter silver.

bog-zombie-skin.zombie skin: Base sandy tan, wash sepia all over, layer pale yellow bone with cold flesh on sharp features, then glaze sickly green round wounds.
bog-zombie-skin.rotting yellow flesh: A sepia wash over sandy tan pushes skin to rotten yellow; layer pale yellow bone up, then glaze thin green round wounds, eyes and mouth.
bog-zombie-skin.swamp corpse skin: Sandy tan base, sepia wash, pale yellow bone highlights, and a thin sickly green glaze around wounds, eyes and mouth.
bog-zombie-skin.sickly yellow skin with green: Wash sandy tan with sepia, layer pale yellow bone, then glaze a thin sickly green around wounds, eyes and mouth for rot.
bog-zombie-skin.undead flesh colour: A sickly yellow: sandy tan washed sepia, highlighted pale yellow bone and pale cold flesh, with green rot glazed in.
bog-zombie-skin.drowned body skin: Sandy tan base, sepia wash, pale yellow bone and cold flesh highlights, then a thin sickly green glaze for swamp rot.
bog-zombie-skin.diseased skin recipe: Base sandy tan, wash sepia, layer pale yellow bone then pale cold flesh, and glaze thin sickly green round wounds, eyes and mouth.
bog-zombie-skin.ghoul skin: See: sickly rotten yellow skin, sandy tan washed sepia with green rot glazed in, in this entry's steps 1 to 4.
bog-zombie-skin.plague zombie: Paint the skin sandy tan, wash sepia, highlight pale yellow bone and cold flesh, then glaze sickly green round wounds, eyes and mouth.
bog-zombie-skin.make skin look rotten and gross: Glaze a thin sickly green around wounds, eyes and mouth over sepia washed, yellowed skin.

brown-to-bone-cloth.bone coloured cloth: Block in deep brown, layer up mixes with more stone each step, finish pure stone on the highest folds, then stone with pale grey on the top edges.
brown-to-bone-cloth.how do i paint robes brown to bone: Base deep brown, layer brown stone mixes with more stone each step, pure stone on the highest folds, then a touch of stone and pale grey.
brown-to-bone-cloth.highlight brown cloth with bone: Mix stone into the deep brown in steps, making the first highlights bigger than you think, then pure stone on the highest folds.
brown-to-bone-cloth.mixing two colours for highlights: Add more of the lighter colour each step, make the first highlights bigger than you think, and finish with the pure light colour on top.
brown-to-bone-cloth.cream robes recipe: Deep brown base, layered brown stone mixes, pure stone on the highest folds, and stone with pale grey on the most raised folds.
brown-to-bone-cloth.tan cloth highlights: Layer brown stone mixes, adding more stone each step, then pure stone on the highest folds; look from above to see where light falls.
brown-to-bone-cloth.monk robes paint: Block in deep brown, layer up towards stone in steps, then a pale grey stone touch only on the most raised folds.
brown-to-bone-cloth.brown cloak to pale highlight: Base deep brown, layer brown stone mixes, pure stone on the highest folds, then stone with pale grey on the most raised folds.
brown-to-bone-cloth.layering cloth by mixing paints: Use two colours, adding more of the lighter one each step; make the first highlights bigger than you think and keep later ones smaller.
brown-to-bone-cloth.beige tabard: Block in deep brown, layer brown stone mixes up to pure stone on the high folds, then edge the most raised folds in pale grey stone.

dark-glossy-claws.glossy claws: Base a near black blue green, line teal along the top, edge pale teal towards the tips, dot pale flesh on the tips, then gloss varnish.
dark-glossy-claws.dark claws: Base a very dark blue green, add a teal line along the top of each claw, then finer pale teal towards the tips.
dark-glossy-claws.how to paint talons: Near black blue green base, a teal line along the top, finer pale teal towards the tips, tiny pale flesh dots, then gloss varnish.
dark-glossy-claws.shiny black claws: Use a near black blue green base with cool teal highlights and tiny pale flesh dots on the tips, then gloss varnish for a wet shine.
dark-glossy-claws.teal claws: Base a very dark blue green, layer teal along the top of each claw, then edge in pale teal towards the tips.
dark-glossy-claws.make claws look wet: Add tiny pale flesh dots on the very tips, then gloss varnish for a wet shine.
dark-glossy-claws.dark blue green nails: Base a very dark blue green, line teal along the top, edge pale teal near the tips and dot pale flesh on the tips.
dark-glossy-claws.monster talons: Very dark blue green base, teal along the top, pale teal edges towards the tips, pale flesh dots on the tips, and gloss varnish.
dark-glossy-claws.claws look dull: Add cool highlights, teal then finer pale teal towards the tips, tiny pale flesh dots on the tips, and gloss varnish for a wet shine.
dark-glossy-claws.paint glossy horns and claws: See: dark glossy claws, a near black blue green with teal highlights and gloss varnish, in this entry's steps 1 to 4.

fair-skin.pale skin: Drybrush pale cream over a cream undercoat, glaze a light flesh thinned half with water, repick the high points in cream, then glaze again.
fair-skin.quick fair skin over a cream undercoat: Drybrush pale cream, glaze light flesh thinned half with water, pick out knuckles, nose and cheeks in cream, then a thinner flesh glaze.
fair-skin.light skin tone for a human face: Pale cream over a cream undercoat, a light flesh glaze settling in recesses, cream on nose and cheeks, then a thinner flesh glaze.
fair-skin.how do i paint pale flesh fast: Drybrush pale cream over a cream undercoat, then glaze light flesh thinned half with water and let it settle in recesses.
fair-skin.easy skin for beginners: Drybrush pale cream over a cream undercoat, glaze a skin paint thinned half with water, then pick out the high points in cream.
fair-skin.peachy skin: Glaze a light flesh thinned half with water over pale cream, highlight in cream, then add a thinner second flesh glaze.
fair-skin.skin for rank and file soldiers: For quick skin, drybrush pale cream over a cream undercoat, then glaze a light flesh thinned half with water over it.
fair-skin.skin wash pooling in the face: Thin the flesh paint half with water and let it settle in recesses, then repick the highlights and add a thinner second coat.
fair-skin.light skin looks too orange: See: building fair skin from pale cream with thin flesh glazes, in this entry's steps 1 to 4.
fair-skin.fair skin highlights: Pick out knuckles, knees, collarbones, nose and cheeks in pale cream, then a thinner flesh glaze adds depth without hiding them.

gold-treasure.gold coins: Prime gold, wash a warm red brown with darker brown in the gaps, then drybrush light silver over the top.
gold-treasure.treasure pile paint: Gold spray, a warm red brown wash, a light silver drybrush, then a few scattered gems in bright colours finished with gloss.
gold-treasure.how do i paint a pile of gold: Spray it gold, wash it warm red brown with darker brown in the deepest gaps, then drybrush light silver over the coins.
gold-treasure.dragon hoard coins: Prime gold, wash warm red brown, drybrush light silver, and paint a few scattered bright gems finished with gloss.
gold-treasure.quick gold treasure chest: A gold spray makes treasure piles very quick; follow with a warm red brown wash and a light silver drybrush.
gold-treasure.gold coins look flat: Wash warm red brown with darker brown in the deepest gaps, then drybrush light silver, which gives more punch than a lighter gold.
gold-treasure.spray gold for treasure: Yes, a gold spray primer makes treasure piles very quick, then wash warm red brown and drybrush light silver.
gold-treasure.wash on gold coins: Use a warm red brown wash all over the coins, with a darker brown in the deepest gaps.
gold-treasure.loot pile painting: Prime gold, wash warm red brown, drybrush light silver, and add a few bright gems with gloss varnish.
gold-treasure.treasure base: See: a quick gold coin pile, gold spray, warm wash and silver drybrush, in this entry's steps 1 to 4.

grey-zombie-skin.zombie skin: Base mid grey, wash a warm flesh brown, layer light grey on raised areas, then edge pale khaki on nose, brow, cheekbones and joints.
grey-zombie-skin.dead grey skin: Mid grey base, a warm flesh brown wash for faint rotten warmth, light grey layers on raised areas, and pale khaki on the sharpest features.
grey-zombie-skin.how to paint undead flesh: Base mid grey, wash all over with warm flesh brown, layer light grey up the muscles, then pale khaki on nose, brow and joints.
grey-zombie-skin.corpse skin: Paint mid grey, wash warm flesh brown, layer light grey towards the tops of muscles, and edge pale khaki on the bony points.
grey-zombie-skin.rotting skin colour: A dried out mid grey, given a faintly rotten warmth with a warm flesh brown wash, highlighted light grey and pale khaki.
grey-zombie-skin.ghoul skin: See: dried out grey dead skin with a warm wash and khaki highlights, in this entry's steps 1 to 4.
grey-zombie-skin.dead looking flesh: Use a mid grey base with a warm flesh brown wash, then light grey layers and pale khaki edges on nose, brow, cheekbones and tendons.
grey-zombie-skin.grey skin for zombies: Two thin coats of mid grey, or a pale grey spray over dark green, then a warm flesh brown wash and light grey highlights.
grey-zombie-skin.pale grey dead skin: Base mid grey, wash warm flesh brown, layer light grey twice towards the muscle tops, then pale khaki on the sharpest points.
grey-zombie-skin.make skin look dead: Paint it a dried out grey and wash it with a warm flesh brown for a faintly rotten warmth, then highlight light grey and pale khaki.

magenta-energy-glow.pink glow: Base the glowing parts white, glaze saturated magenta over it, add a pale pink white core, then a thin fluorescent magenta glaze.
magenta-energy-glow.magenta energy: Paint the parts white, thicker in the centre, glaze saturated magenta twice, repaint a pale pink white core, then glaze fluorescent magenta.
magenta-energy-glow.hot pink weapon glow: White base, two see through magenta glazes, a small pale pink white patch in the centre for the hot core, then fluorescent magenta over it.
magenta-energy-glow.glowing pink plasma: Build it from white with see through magenta glazes, then a pale pink white hot core kept vivid with a thin fluorescent magenta coat.
magenta-energy-glow.pink glow on a gun: Base the glowing weapon parts white, glaze saturated magenta, add a pale pink white core, and finish with thin fluorescent magenta.
magenta-energy-glow.energy coils glowing pink: Cover the coils white, a little thicker in the centre, then glaze a bright see through magenta that colours without darkening.
magenta-energy-glow.how to paint a pink glow: Start from a white base, glaze a bright see through magenta over it twice, re add a pale pink white core, then a thin fluorescent magenta.
magenta-energy-glow.neon pink effect: Glaze a thin fluorescent magenta over a pale pink white core on a white base to keep it vivid.
magenta-energy-glow.pink glow over white: Yes: a bright see through magenta glaze colours the white without darkening it, giving a hot pink glow.
magenta-energy-glow.purple pink energy blade: See: a hot pink glow built from white and see through magentas, in this entry's steps 1 to 4.

orange-armour.orange armour: Base soft orange over light grey primer, layer bright orange, shade deep orange red into recesses, then edge pale yellow orange.
orange-armour.how do i paint bright orange: Thin coats of an opaque orange over light grey primer, a punchier orange on top, a deep orange red in recesses and pale yellow orange edges.
orange-armour.orange armor recipe: Soft orange base, bright orange layer, deep orange red shade in recesses, pale yellow orange edges and pale bone on the sharpest corners.
orange-armour.orange looks patchy: Use thin coats of an opaque orange over a light grey primer, as an opaque orange covers best.
orange-armour.orange over grey primer: Yes, use thin coats of an opaque soft orange over a light grey primer, then layer a punchier orange on top.
orange-armour.shade orange with red: Run a deep orange red neatly into the recesses only, for depth.
orange-armour.highlight orange towards yellow: Edge the main edges with the side of the brush in pale yellow orange, then pale bone on the sharpest corners.
orange-armour.punchy orange vehicle: Base a soft orange over light grey primer, layer a bright orange on top, shade deep orange red in recesses and edge pale yellow orange.
orange-armour.saturated orange paint job: Opaque soft orange over light primer, a bright orange layer, red shading kept to the recesses, and edges pushed towards yellow.
orange-armour.orange keeps going brown: Shade with a deep orange red run neatly into the recesses only, over a light grey primer, so the orange stays saturated.

pale-tinted-gold.pale gold trim: Base pale gold, wash purple or a colour matching your armour, layer pale gold back leaving the wash in recesses, then edge bright silver.
pale-tinted-gold.gold that goes with purple: Wash pale gold with purple for shade and a slight tint, layer pale gold back over most of it, then edge in bright silver.
pale-tinted-gold.how to tint gold: Wash it all over with a colour matched to your armour, such as purple, then layer the pale gold back, keeping the tint in recesses.
pale-tinted-gold.cool gold: Base pale gold, wash it purple or to match cool armour, layer pale gold back over most of it, then add fine bright silver edges.
pale-tinted-gold.gold trim on purple armour: Pale gold base, an all over purple wash, pale gold layered back leaving purple round rivets, and fine bright silver edges.
pale-tinted-gold.light gold: Base pale gold, wash for shade and tint, layer pale gold back, then edge in bright silver for a bright, white gold finish.
pale-tinted-gold.gold looks too yellow: Wash pale gold with a purple or armour matched wash for a slight tint, and finish with bright silver edges for a white gold look.
pale-tinted-gold.wash on gold: Wash pale gold all over in a colour matched to your armour, such as purple, then layer gold back keeping the wash in recesses.
pale-tinted-gold.shade gold to match armour: Match the wash to your armour: purple works for purple or cool armour, washed all over then kept in recesses and round rivets.
pale-tinted-gold.champagne gold: Pale gold washed with a slight purple tint, layered back up, then fine bright silver edges for a bright, white gold finish.

purple-armour.purple armour: Base rich purple over a light undercoat, shade deep plum into the shadows, edge pale pink purple, then glaze violet over it all.
purple-armour.purple armor recipe: Rich purple base, deep plum shade, pale pink purple edge highlights, then one or two thin violet glazes to tie it together.
purple-armour.deep purple plate: Base rich purple, shade deep plum into the shadows so they stay coloured, edge pale pink purple, then glaze violet.
purple-armour.how do i paint rich purple: Thin coats of rich purple over a light or pre highlighted undercoat, deep plum shadows, pink purple edges, and a thin violet glaze.
purple-armour.purple shadows going black: Shade with a deep plum instead, run into the shadows so they stay coloured, not black.
purple-armour.violet armour that pops: Keep the purple bright over a light undercoat, edge in mostly pink with a little purple, then glaze violet to tie it together.
purple-armour.royal purple knight: Rich purple over a light undercoat, deep plum shadows, pale pink purple edges and a thin violet glaze over everything.
purple-armour.plum shadows on armour: Run a deep plum shade into the shadows over the rich purple so they stay coloured rather than black.
purple-armour.pink edge highlights on purple: Mix mostly pink with a little purple and run it along top edges and raised areas, then a thin violet glaze ties it in.
purple-armour.my purple looks dull and grey: Use thin coats over a light or pre highlighted undercoat to keep it bright, shade with plum not black, and glaze violet over it.

rich-red-armour.rich red armour: Base strong mid red, glaze deep burgundy down panels and into lines, edge scarlet orange, then pale peach on the corners only.
rich-red-armour.how do i paint clean red armor: Thin coats of mid red over primer, or spray it smooth, then glaze burgundy, edge scarlet orange, and dot pale peach on corners.
rich-red-armour.red armour shaded burgundy: Glaze a deep burgundy, dark red with a touch of dark green, down each panel and into the lines over a strong mid red.
rich-red-armour.edge highlight red with orange: Run a chunky scarlet orange line on every edge, then a finer orange line inside it, with pale peach on the corners.
rich-red-armour.deep red knight: Strong mid red base, deep burgundy glazes down panels, scarlet orange edges, and pale peach only on the corners.
rich-red-armour.red armour recipe: Base a mid red, glaze deep burgundy into panels and lines, edge in scarlet orange, then pale peach on corners.
rich-red-armour.red looks pink when highlighted: Use peach rather than paler red on corners to keep red rich; a thin red glaze fixes edges that have gone pink.
rich-red-armour.glaze red panels: Glaze a deep burgundy, dark red with a touch of dark green, down each panel and into the lines, two thin coats.
rich-red-armour.glossy looking red armour: See: deep clean red glazed burgundy down each panel with orange and peach edges, in this entry's steps 1 to 4.
rich-red-armour.peach edge highlights on red: Put pale peach on corners only; peach keeps the red rich, and a thin red glaze fixes any edges gone pink.

turquoise-gem.blue gem: Base dark teal, pull a black wash to the top corner, paint a bright turquoise crescent low on the opposite side, then a white dot top corner.
turquoise-gem.turquoise gem: Dark teal base, black wash pulled to the top corner, a bright turquoise crescent in the lower opposite corner, and a white glint.
turquoise-gem.how to paint a blue gemstone: Fill it dark teal, darken the top corner with black wash, add a turquoise crescent low on the opposite side, then a white dot top corner.
turquoise-gem.sapphire: See: glassy blue gems with a dark corner, light crescent and white glint, in this entry's steps 1 to 4.
turquoise-gem.glassy blue jewel: A dark top corner, a light crescent in the lower opposite corner and a white glint in the dark corner make it look glassy.
turquoise-gem.gem crescent highlight: Paint a bright turquoise crescent in the lower corner opposite the dark side, then a finer, paler one tighter in.
turquoise-gem.blue gems on armour: Put the dark corner, the crescent and the white glint on the same side of every gem so they all read as lit from one direction.
turquoise-gem.aqua gem: Base dark teal, wash black towards the top corner, layer bright turquoise crescents in the lower corner, then a white dot.
turquoise-gem.how do i make gems look shiny: Add one white dot in the dark top corner, on the same side on every gem, over a dark corner and a light crescent.
turquoise-gem.sky blue jewel: Base dark teal, shade the top corner black, build bright turquoise crescents low on the opposite side, then a white glint.

white-and-pale-fur.white fur: Prime white, wash a warm off white into the hairs, glaze blue grey over back and tail, then a light pure white drybrush.
white-and-pale-fur.pale cream fur: Over white, wash warm off white, glaze sepia instead of blue grey over back and tail, then drybrush pure white.
white-and-pale-fur.white wolf pelt: White primer, a warm off white wash, a blue grey glaze over the back and tail, then a light pure white drybrush over everything.
white-and-pale-fur.snow beast fur: Prime white, wash warm off white, glaze blue grey over the back and tail for a cooler tone, then drybrush pure white.
white-and-pale-fur.how to shade white fur: Wash a warm off white straight over the textured fur so it sinks between hairs, then glaze blue grey over the back and tail.
white-and-pale-fur.fur cloak white: Prime white, wash warm off white, glaze blue grey on the deepest areas, then drybrush pure white to pick out the hairs.
white-and-pale-fur.drybrush white fur: Finish with a light pass of pure white over everything; it picks out the hairs and hides patchiness.
white-and-pale-fur.polar bear fur: See: clean white fur shaded with thin washes and a white drybrush, in this entry's steps 1 to 4.
white-and-pale-fur.white fur looks flat: Glaze blue grey over the back and tail for a cooler, deeper tone, then drybrush pure white to pick out the hairs.
white-and-pale-fur.wash white fur without it going dirty: Start from a bright white undercoat, use a thin warm off white wash, and finish with a pure white drybrush that hides patchiness.

acrylic-enamel-and-oil-paints.acrylic vs enamel: Acrylics thin with water and dry in seconds to minutes; enamels thin with a spirit thinner and stay workable for hours, so you can blend or wipe them off.
acrylic-enamel-and-oil-paints.difference between oils and acrylics: Acrylics are water based and dry fast; oils thin with white spirit and take a day or more to dry, which suits smooth blends, filters and washes.
acrylic-enamel-and-oil-paints.can i use oil paint on miniatures: Yes. Thin oils with white spirit over acrylic that is fully dry and gloss varnished, and use their long drying time for blends, filters and washes.
acrylic-enamel-and-oil-paints.what thins enamel paint: A spirit thinner, such as odourless white spirit. Never mix water into enamels.
acrylic-enamel-and-oil-paints.white spirit or water: Water for acrylics; white spirit for enamels and oils. Never mix water into enamels.
acrylic-enamel-and-oil-paints.why did my enamel wash lift my paint: Spirit thinner softens and lifts enamels and oils already on the model; gloss varnish fully dry acrylic before enamel goes over it.
acrylic-enamel-and-oil-paints.how long do oils take to dry: Oil paints take the longest to dry, often a day or more.
acrylic-enamel-and-oil-paints.types of paint base explained: Acrylics are water based and dry fast; enamels and oils thin with spirit, stay workable longer, and spirit lifts them but not dry acrylic.
acrylic-enamel-and-oil-paints.can i mix enamel and acrylic: Layer them rather than mixing: never add water to enamel. Gloss varnish acrylic before enamel goes on, and acrylic can go on last over dry enamel.
acrylic-enamel-and-oil-paints.odourless thinner for oils: Oils thin with white spirit, and odourless white spirit is one such spirit thinner.

airbrush-paint-thinning.thinning paint for airbrush: Thin it with airbrush thinner to about whole or semi skimmed milk with no lumps, then test on paper before the model.
airbrush-paint-thinning.how thin for airbrush: Like whole to semi skimmed milk: pulled up the side of the dish it should run straight back down. Go thinner, like ink, for fine detail.
airbrush-paint-thinning.airbrush keeps clogging: Thin the paint more, mix it in a dish and move it with a dropper to keep lumps out, and avoid stirring with a brush, as a bristle can block the nozzle.
airbrush-paint-thinning.what consistency should airbrush paint b: Whole to semi skimmed milk with no lumps; it should run straight back down the side of the dish.
airbrush-paint-thinning.milk consistency airbrush: Yes, aim for whole to semi skimmed milk, with no lumps, and thinner, like ink, for detail and small nozzles.
airbrush-paint-thinning.airbrush thinner ratio: There is no fixed ratio. Equal parts is a fair start for dropper paints, and thick pot paints may need two or three parts thinner.
airbrush-paint-thinning.can i spray normal paint through an airb: Not as it is: brush paint is far too thick and will clog the nozzle. Thin it to about the consistency of milk first.
airbrush-paint-thinning.airbrush paint too thick: Speckled, grainy or spattering spray means too thick or too little pressure: add thinner a few drops at a time rather than turning the pressure up.
airbrush-paint-thinning.airbrush thining: Thin with airbrush thinner or distilled water to about the consistency of milk, with no lumps, and test on paper first.
airbrush-paint-thinning.test spray on paper: Yes. Test on paper or your hand before the model, changing one thing at a time: pressure, distance or paint to thinner ratio.

all-over-wash.wash the whole model: Base coat everything, run one wash over the whole model with a large brush, move and lift pools with a damp brush, then layer raised areas back up.
all-over-wash.all over wash: Run a thin wash over the base coated model so it settles in every recess, lift pools, let it dry naturally, then layer the raised areas back up.
all-over-wash.dip method: See: washing a base coated model all over, then layering the raised areas back up, in this entry's steps 2 to 8.
all-over-wash.quick shading for a squad: Base coat each model, then run one wash over the whole thing so it settles in every recess, and layer the raised areas back once dry.
all-over-wash.one wash for everything: A warm brown ties earthy colours together and warms gold; a black wash suits clean silver. Test on a spare part first.
all-over-wash.shade a whole mini at once: Run one wash over the whole base coated model with a large brush, keeping it thin on flat panels, and hold it at one angle while it settles.
all-over-wash.wash left my model looking dirty: Layer each main colour back over the raised areas, leaving the darker tone only in creases and recesses, and shade only recesses on smooth panels.
all-over-wash.layer back up after a wash: Once dry, layer each main colour back over the raised areas, leaving some darker tone in creases; one clear step brighter is enough.
all-over-wash.speed painting with a wash: Base coat all the colours, wash the whole model with one wash, then layer each colour back one clear step brighter on the raised areas.
all-over-wash.tie colours together with one wash: A warm brown wash over cloth, leather, bone and metal ties earthy colours together; a black wash pulls mismatched touch ups together.

base-coating.base coat streaky: Thin to the feel of melted ice cream, stroke along the shapes, and let each coat dry however patchy it looks; brushing half dry paint makes texture.
base-coating.how do i get a smooth base coat: Use two or three thin coats, each left to dry fully, with paint thinned to the feel of melted ice cream so it dries flat with no ridges.
base-coating.brush marks in my first coat: Thin the paint so it flows to the end of the stroke and dries flat, lay each coat quickly and do not brush over half dry paint.
base-coating.how many coats of paint: Two or three thin coats, each left to dry fully; yellow and white need more, as do bright colours over black.
base-coating.basecoat patchy over black: Black dulls colours and bright ones can need three or four coats; let each thin coat dry fully, or prime white for brighter colours.
base-coating.first colour goes on blotchy: That is normal for one thin coat. Let it dry however patchy it looks, then add a second and third; too much water also makes it patchy.
base-coating.base coating tips for beginners: Thin paint to melted ice cream, use the largest brush you can control, stroke along shapes, and build two or three thin coats.
base-coating.bright colours wont cover black primer: Bright colours over black can need three or four thin coats; white primer makes colours brighter.
base-coating.basecoating over zenithal: Keep the base coat thin so some of the light and dark undercoat shows through for free contrast.
base-coating.solid even colour on a model: Build two or three thin coats, each dry before the next; it is done when the colour is even, with no primer showing or pooling in recesses.

battered-brass.battered brass: Base orange copper, overbrush brass, stipple brass and silver highlights, then wash brown heavily into recesses and thinly over everything.
battered-brass.worn copper: Base a strong orange copper, wash brown to kill the shine, and add a thin dark turquoise wash for age, keeping plenty of warm metal showing.
battered-brass.old pitted brass: Stipple highlights rather than blending, then dab brown wash on the lower shaded parts for texture and run dark brown ink round rivets and cuts.
battered-brass.how to make brass look old: Wash it brown to kill the shine, flatten some areas with thinned mid grey, and add a thin dark turquoise wash for a hint of age.
battered-brass.stippled metal wear: Dab brass with about a third silver on upper areas, then mostly silver on the very tops; texture is a good thing here.
battered-brass.weathered bronze armour: See: battered warm metal stippled and washed brown with a turquoise hint, in this entry's steps 1 to 7.
battered-brass.dirty brass pipes: Over a copper and brass base, wash brown heavily into recesses and thinly over everything, then dab brown onto the lower parts for texture.
battered-brass.grimy copper finish: Wash brown heavily into recesses and thinly over everything to kill the shine, and run very dark brown ink round rivets, cuts and holes.
battered-brass.brass looks too shiny: Wash brown thinly over everything to kill the shine, wash some areas with thinned mid grey, then coat it all with clear matt medium.
battered-brass.scratched brass: Stipple a silver heavy mix or specks of bright bronze onto the highest points over the dulled brass for broken bright edges.

blood-effects.blood splatter: Dab a dark see through red on with a torn sponge blotted almost dry, or flick thinned red off a stiff brush for finer spatter.
blood-effects.how to paint blood: Use a dark, see through glossy red with a touch of black, keep it loose and uneven, and gloss the wet areas.
blood-effects.fresh blood that looks wet: Fresh blood is glossy: use a clear gloss red with a touch of black, and add a little more on blades and edges for pooled spots.
blood-effects.bloody handprint: Paint an upside down L for the palm and thumb, then four short lines for fingers.
blood-effects.blood drips on a sword: Drag the paint along the blade in the direction of the swing, add short drips from marks and edges, and a little more on the edge.
blood-effects.blood looks like red paint: Use a dark, see through red with a touch of black instead; bright or opaque reds look like paint, and neat blood looks painted on.
blood-effects.make blood look old and dried: Add more black to the red and keep it matt, as old blood dries matt; a little dark brown helps where blood is older.
blood-effects.gore smears on armour: Put down a warm flesh coloured wash, then glaze a much thinned red on in uneven patches, adding a little dark brown where it is thicker.
blood-effects.splatter with a sponge: Hold a torn piece of sponge in tweezers, blot most of the paint off, and dab lightly, building it up gradually.
blood-effects.glossy blood effect: Use a clear gloss red with a touch of black, and put gloss over part of a matt deep red so it reads as fresh over old.

brush-control.shaky hands painting: Brace both hands: rest the model hand on the desk and the painting hand against it, hold the brush like a pen, and breathe out on fine strokes.
brush-control.how do i paint steadier: Brace both hands together on the desk, hold the brush near the bristles, pull with a small finger movement and breathe out slowly on the finest strokes.
brush-control.brush control tips: Brace your hands, use a size 2 to 4 brush with a sharp point, load the belly but draw the tip dry, use a light touch and plan each stroke.
brush-control.how to hold a paint brush: Like a pen, firm but relaxed: nearer the bristles for precision, further back for longer movements.
brush-control.keep paint off the wrong areas: Draw the excess off the tip before painting, as a blob on the tip floods off the edge, and use the lightest touch with the side near the tip.
brush-control.brace my hands while painting: Rest the hand holding the model on the desk, and rest the painting hand against the other hand.
brush-control.cant paint fine lines: Use the side near the tip of a sharp size 2 to 4 brush, touch down as lightly as you can, and draw the line in one planned stroke.
brush-control.steady hand for detail: Brace both hands, hold the brush near the bristles, turn the model so the stroke runs the way your hand pulls best, and breathe out slowly.
brush-control.how much paint on the brush: Load the belly so the tip stays wet along the line, then draw the excess off the tip on kitchen paper.
brush-control.hand shakes on small details: Brace the painting hand against the hand holding the model, rested on the desk, and pull with your fingers rather than the wrist.

bust-scale-faces.painting a bust face: Set a light to dark sketch from above, glaze colour zones across the face, build skin from many thin layers, and paint the eyes in full.
bust-scale-faces.bust skin: Build it from many thin glazes and layers, soft wet blends, and fine stippling in a slightly darker tone that reads as pores.
bust-scale-faces.how do i paint a face on a bust: Light it from above first, glaze yellow, red and grey colour zones, build skin in thin glazes, then add full eyes and small details.
bust-scale-faces.large scale face: At bust size use real anatomy, colour zones, skin texture and fully painted eyes, working from reference photos lit from one direction.
bust-scale-faces.realistic skin on busts: Glaze colour zones thinly: a yellowish forehead, warmer redder cheeks, nose and ears, and a cooler greyer jaw, then stipple pores.
bust-scale-faces.bust eyes: An off white greying to the corners, an iris with a dark rim and lighter flecks, the pupil, one reflection dot and a wet line on the lower lid.
bust-scale-faces.face on a big model looks fake: Realism comes from value and soft changes far more than tiny detail; check the light to dark pattern from across the room or in a photo.
bust-scale-faces.skin texture bust: Fine stippling in a slightly darker tone reads as pores at bust scale.
bust-scale-faces.bust portrait painting: Keep reference photos of real faces lit from one direction beside you, set the light first, then build skin and colour zones in thin glazes.
bust-scale-faces.lighting a bust face: Spray or paint a light to dark sketch from above, so the brow, nose, cheekbones and chin stand out and the eye sockets sit in shadow.

checking-values-in-greyscale.check contrast with a black and white ph: Light the model evenly, photograph it and turn saturation to zero; each main area should separate clearly from its neighbours.
checking-values-in-greyscale.model looks flat from a distance: Check it in a greyscale photo; if areas share the same grey, lighten one highlight or darken the area beside it.
checking-values-in-greyscale.colours merge at arms length: They likely share the same lightness. Lighten the highlight on one or darken its neighbour, using edge highlights and dark lining.
checking-values-in-greyscale.greyscale filter on my phone: Use the phone's mono filter, or set saturation to zero in any editor, on an evenly lit photo of the model.
checking-values-in-greyscale.how do i know if my contrast is good: Photograph it in greyscale: if it reads well there, it will nearly always work in colour.
checking-values-in-greyscale.values look the same: Lighten the highlight on one area or darken the area beside it, with edge highlights or dark lining, then check again.
checking-values-in-greyscale.grayscale check: Photograph the model under even light and drop saturation to zero; skin, cloth and metal should separate clearly in grey.
checking-values-in-greyscale.everything blends together: Check a greyscale photo, then separate merged areas by lightening one or darkening its neighbour; a value change does more than detail.
checking-values-in-greyscale.is my highlight light enough: Check in a greyscale photo; the brightest point and strongest contrast should sit where you want the eye, such as the face.
checking-values-in-greyscale.test values in mono: Photograph under even light with the mono filter, then shrink or blur it to mimic table distance and see if the big pattern still works.

choosing-highlight-colours.highlight colour: Lighten with a lighter neighbouring hue, a pastel, cream or bone rather than white, so the highlight stays vivid.
choosing-highlight-colours.highlights look chalky: Push them anyway, then pull the colour back with thin glazes of the mid colour or an ink, which also smooths the steps.
choosing-highlight-colours.red highlights turn pink: White turns red pink; lighten it with yellow or a warm orange instead, or about a third pink or light skin tone.
choosing-highlight-colours.what colour to highlight with: A lighter neighbour on the colour wheel: pale yellow, sand, ivory or light skin for warm colours, sky blue or mint for cool ones.
choosing-highlight-colours.dont use white to highlight: Right: white greys a colour. Lighten with a lighter neighbouring hue, a pastel, cream or bone, and keep pure white for a few specks.
choosing-highlight-colours.highlight blue without chalky: Use a lighter neighbouring hue such as sky blue or mint rather than white, then glaze the mid colour back over if it still looks chalky.
choosing-highlight-colours.lighten a colour without greying: Mix in a lighter neighbouring hue from the colour wheel rather than white, which lightens but also greys.
choosing-highlight-colours.what to mix for highlights: Pale yellow, sand, ivory or light skin tone for warm colours, sky blue or mint for cool ones, and a little cream or bone for the last step.
choosing-highlight-colours.my highlights look dull and grey: You are probably lightening with white; use a lighter neighbouring hue instead, such as yellow for red or pale blue for purple.
choosing-highlight-colours.best highlight for green: See: picking a lighter neighbouring hue, pastel or cream instead of white, in this entry's steps 2 and 3.

colour-harmony-by-mixing.colours dont go together: Mix a little of one mother colour into every mix, or borrow colours from other areas for shading, so every part shares a tint.
colour-harmony-by-mixing.how to make colours match: Add a little of a mood setting mother colour to every mix, and start every area from one shared dark and finish towards one shared light.
colour-harmony-by-mixing.mother colour: One colour that sets the mood, added in small amounts to every mix, including skin, metal and base, so the whole model belongs together.
colour-harmony-by-mixing.tie the scheme together: Use a mother colour in every mix, borrow one area's colour to shade another, and finish most materials with one shared pale highlight.
colour-harmony-by-mixing.model looks disjointed: Areas in unrelated colours cause that; shared tints fix it, such as one mother colour mixed into everything.
colour-harmony-by-mixing.mix a colour into everything: That is the mother colour method: a little of one mood colour in every mix, so even loud mixes look calm on the model.
colour-harmony-by-mixing.colour harmony mixing: Mix a mother colour or colours already on the model into the others, and shade one area with another's colour to link them.
colour-harmony-by-mixing.make the palette feel unified: Start every area from one shared dark and finish towards one shared light; the middle colours can then differ a lot and still belong.
colour-harmony-by-mixing.colours clash on my model: Mix one of the main colours into the clashing one, such as the leather brown into a turquoise cloth.
colour-harmony-by-mixing.shared tint: A touch of one area's colour in another's midtone, such as gold's warm brown in a green cloak, links them and calms a too bright colour.

colourful-underpainting.colourful underpainting: Smear bright, varied colours loosely over a rich dark base, paint the real mid tone very thin over them, then unify with glazes.
colourful-underpainting.sketch colours under the final layer: Dab varied colours on loosely, lighter where light lands, then paint the real mid tone thin from shadow to light so they show in the darks.
colourful-underpainting.bright smear underneath: Smear strong colours over a dark base with a brush, fingertip or airbrush; they set the mood of the shadows rather than the final colours.
colourful-underpainting.loose underpainting: Base a rich dark colour, dab varied colours on loosely with lighter ones where light lands, and squint to see the big shapes.
colourful-underpainting.mood through underlying colours: Lay down bright, varied colours first; they set the mood of the shadows once thin mid tones go over them.
colourful-underpainting.paint random colours first then glaze: Yes: smear varied colours over a dark base, paint the mid tone thin, then glaze one coat paint thinned with three or four parts medium.
colourful-underpainting.varied undercolours: Set strong pure colours out first, smear them on loosely over a dark base, then keep the mid tone thin so they show in the shadows.
colourful-underpainting.underpainting for interesting shadows: Paint the real mid tone very thin from shadow towards light over a colourful underpainting, so the colours show through in the darks.
colourful-underpainting.how to make my paint job less boring: Try a loose colourful underpainting: varied bright colours under thin mid tones give the shadows mood and variety.
colourful-underpainting.unify an underpainting with glazes: Glaze loose areas with a one coat paint thinned with three or four parts medium.

contrast-over-coloured-base.contrast over a base colour: Base a pale or mid version of the same colour first; the closer it is to the one coat colour, the smoother the result.
contrast-over-coloured-base.what colour under one coat paints: A pale or mid version of the same colour. Over black they barely show, especially yellows and light greens.
contrast-over-coloured-base.contrast over black doesnt show: One coat paints barely show over black. Base a pale or mid version of the same colour first and put the one coat paint over that.
contrast-over-coloured-base.richer contrast results: Put unthinned one coat paint over a pale tinted base for a vivid, almost luminous finish, or a thinned coat over a solid one for depth.
contrast-over-coloured-base.contrast over grey: See: picking the base colour under one coat paints, in this entry's steps 1 and 2.
contrast-over-coloured-base.one coat paint over matching base: Yes: the closer the base is to the one coat colour, the smoother it looks, and the top coat only has to add depth in the recesses.
contrast-over-coloured-base.smoother contrast finish: Base a colour close to the one coat paint, do not let it flood or pool, and finish with matt varnish to even out the sheen.
contrast-over-coloured-base.contrast yellow over black: Yellows barely show over black. Base a pale or mid yellow first, then put the one coat yellow over it.
contrast-over-coloured-base.base coat before contrast: Yes, especially on large flat areas: a normal paint of a similar colour first makes the one coat paint go on far more evenly.
contrast-over-coloured-base.contrast too dark over white: Mix in a normal paint of the same colour, or base a pale tint of it first so the top coat only adds depth in recesses.

custom-symbols-and-icons.design my own symbol: Keep a familiar icon shape, swap in one new element that fits your idea, and keep it bold and simple with few lines.
custom-symbols-and-icons.custom heraldry: Borrow shapes people already recognise, such as jaws, wings, skulls, stars or crossed blades, and swap in one element of your own.
custom-symbols-and-icons.make my own army badge: Keep one familiar element, replace the main object with your own idea, and keep it simple enough to paint dozens of times.
custom-symbols-and-icons.icon ideas: Start from shapes people already recognise, such as jaws, wings, skulls, stars or crossed blades, or combine shapes from two designs.
custom-symbols-and-icons.design a shield emblem: Sketch several bold, simple versions, then redraw the best one smaller until it is the real size of the shield and check it still reads.
custom-symbols-and-icons.homebrew faction symbol: Take a familiar icon shape and swap in one new element, or combine shapes from two designs, keeping it bold with few lines.
custom-symbols-and-icons.custom shoulder pad icon: Keep it bold and simple, as fine detail is lost on a small shoulder plate, and redraw it at real size to check it still reads.
custom-symbols-and-icons.how to design a logo for my army: See: building a badge from one familiar icon shape plus one new element, kept bold and simple, in this entry's steps 1 to 4.
custom-symbols-and-icons.simple bold symbols: Use few lines and clear shapes to colour; fine detail is lost at small sizes, and the design must be easy to repeat.
custom-symbols-and-icons.freehand emblem design: Paint a light outline before filling it in, then straighten wobbly edges by cutting back in with the base colour.

digital-sculpting.digital sculpting: Start with a tablet app that exports print files, set small practice goals, and cut detail deeper and bolder than looks necessary.
digital-sculpting.3d sculpting for printing: Make recesses and raised detail deeper than looks necessary, zoom out to near real size to check, then export an STL or OBJ to a slicer.
digital-sculpting.sculpt on an ipad: A tablet sculpting app that exports print files is an easy way in; try every tool in the first session, then set small goals.
digital-sculpting.how do i start sculpting my own minis: Use a tablet sculpting app, try every tool once, then build a simple creature from a few basic shapes with only a few brushes.
digital-sculpting.sculpting app for beginners: A tablet sculpting app that exports print files is an easy way in; desktop programs work but feel more complex at first.
digital-sculpting.design bases to print: For parts that must fit an exact size, such as bases, use a measuring CAD program and measure the real thing with calipers.
digital-sculpting.details too shallow after printing: Detail that looks sharp on screen can vanish at miniature scale; make recesses and raised detail deeper and bolder than looks needed.
digital-sculpting.make my own 3d models: Block out forms with spheres, cylinders and tubes, clone and flip them, push in masked areas, and save parts like horns to reuse.
digital-sculpting.learn digital sculpt: Little and often, about an hour a night; copying a real object with a reference image overlay teaches precision quickly.
digital-sculpting.sculpt files for a resin printer: Export an STL or OBJ file and open it in a slicer to scale and duplicate it across the build plate.

dry-fitting.dry fit: Fit parts together without glue first to find nubs, gaps, which way round parts go and where the glue needs to go.
dry-fitting.test fit before glue: Yes. It shows leftover nubs, gaps and orientation, and gaps you fix now need no filler later.
dry-fitting.parts dont line up: Look for a nub or mould line on the joining faces, and clip off locating pegs that force panels to bend.
dry-fitting.gaps after gluing: Dry fit first: gaps you find and fix before gluing need no filler later.
dry-fitting.which way round does this go: Dry fit the parts without glue; it shows which way round they go before you commit.
dry-fitting.paint parts separately then glue: Dry fit to see which parts block your brush, and leave those off for painting.
dry-fitting.subassemblies for painting: Dry fit to see what blocks your brush; for tight wraparound parts, glue one half against a dry fitted half so it slots back after painting.
dry-fitting.part wont sit flush: Look for a nub or mould line on the joining faces, or shave a little off tight parts rather than squeezing them in.
dry-fitting.dry fitting tips: Check for nubs and gaps, clip pegs that force bends, scratch joining faces for grip, and use sticky tack to check angles and poses.
dry-fitting.leave parts off to paint: Dry fit first to see which parts block the brush; glued wraparound halves can come off cleanly and slot back after painting.

drybrushing-metal.drybrush metal: Base dark, drybrush silver darkened with black, then add more pure silver each pass over smaller areas, ending near pure on the highest points.
drybrushing-metal.drybrushing silver: Use the tiniest amount on the bristle tips, brush across ridges, and build up in passes rather than loading more paint.
drybrushing-metal.quick metal: Drybrush silver freely over everything, then paint thinned black back into joints and soft areas.
drybrushing-metal.how to paint chainmail: See: drybrushing metal in steps over a dark base, then a wash in recesses, in this entry's steps 1 to 4 and 8.
drybrushing-metal.metal looks flat: Darken the first pass with black so recesses stay dark and matt, then build to near pure silver only on the most raised points.
drybrushing-metal.gunmetal drybrush: Prime black, drybrush dark gunmetal over everything, wash black, then drybrush a brighter steel on the raised parts.
drybrushing-metal.fast metallic armour: Drybrush silver freely over everything, then paint thinned black back into the joints and soft areas.
drybrushing-metal.silver over black: Yes: black underneath makes silver look its most silvery.
drybrushing-metal.drybrushed armour: Base dark, drybrush in a few passes from silver mixed with black up to near pure silver on the edges, then flow a thin wash into recesses.
drybrushing-metal.dry brushing metallics: Shake the paint very well, use the tiniest amount on the bristle tips, test first and repeat passes, as too much silver turns stark fast.

editing-model-photos.edit photos of my minis: Correct exposure and white balance, keep saturation gentle, clean dust with a healing brush, then crop and resize to about 1600 pixels.
editing-model-photos.fix white balance on model photos: Use the white balance picker on the white or grey backdrop, then tweak until the colours match the real model beside the screen.
editing-model-photos.fix the yellow tint on model photos: Click the white balance picker on the white or grey backdrop, then adjust until colours match the model held beside the screen.
editing-model-photos.model too dark in the photo: Raise exposure until the model is clear but highlights do not clip, and open the shadows a touch.
editing-model-photos.remove the background from a photo: Trace round the model by hand with a precise path tool, as one click selections leave fringes, then put a new backdrop on its own layer.
editing-model-photos.colours look wrong in pictures: Set white balance with the picker on the backdrop, then tweak until the colours match the real model beside the screen.
editing-model-photos.should i shoot raw: Yes, if the camera allows it; raw files keep far more room to correct light and colour.
editing-model-photos.photos look oversaturated: Go easy on saturation: pushing it destroys detail and changes your colours, so nudge it only slightly and aim for true colour.
editing-model-photos.add a black backdrop afterwards: Cut the model out by hand with a precise path tool, then put the new backdrop on its own layer underneath.
editing-model-photos.highlights blown out in photo: Turn on clipping warnings, keep exposure below where highlights clip, and pull the highlights in.

fantasy-hero-colours.colours for a knight: Let a mid steel grey lead, with one bold colour such as deep red or royal blue on the shield, tabard or plume.
fantasy-hero-colours.what colour should my wizard be: Pick one rich robe colour, such as deep purple or midnight blue, with pale cream trim, and save the brightest colour for the staff gem or spell.
fantasy-hero-colours.ranger colour scheme ideas: Earthy, muted greens and browns that differ in lightness, a dirtied cloak hem, and one small cool accent such as grey blue fletching.
fantasy-hero-colours.elf colour scheme: Cool pale skin, light cloth such as ivory or sea green, fine gold or silver trim, smooth blends, crisp edges and little grime.
fantasy-hero-colours.what colours suit a dwarf: Warm and heavy: ruddy skin, a rusty red, dark brown or grey white beard, and warm metals such as bronze.
fantasy-hero-colours.rpg hero colors: Pick one main colour, support it, and save one accent, kept close to the head; the face should get the brightest highlights.
fantasy-hero-colours.paladin colour ideas: See: the knight scheme, steel leading with one bold colour such as deep red or royal blue, in this entry's step 1.
fantasy-hero-colours.colour ideas for my tabletop rpg charact: Choose one main colour that fits the role, support it, and save one accent near the head; the props already tell the role.
fantasy-hero-colours.fantasy character palette: One main colour, supporting colours, and one saved accent; two colours plus steel looks noble on a knight, four looks like a jester.
fantasy-hero-colours.what colours go well on a hero mini: One main colour with support and a single accent kept close to the head, with a slightly brighter highlight on nose, brow and cheekbones.

finding-your-style.painting style: Style is the sum of your habits and choices; it grows from solid basics, lots of practice and noticing what you keep leaning towards.
finding-your-style.find my own style: Notice what you tend to do, such as hard contrast or soft blends, bright or grim colour, then lean into it and improve those parts on purpose.
finding-your-style.how do i develop a style: Learn the basics, copy methods to learn them, borrow single ideas you admire, then lean into the looks you keep coming back to.
finding-your-style.my models all look generic: Notice which looks you keep coming back to and lean into them, and spend effort on the parts you want noticed while keeping the rest simpler.
finding-your-style.personal painting style: It grows from solid basics, lots of practice and noticing your own habits; it cannot be forced, but you can lean into what you favour.
finding-your-style.copying other painters: It is a fine way to start. Later, borrow single ideas you admire, such as how someone shades cloth, rather than their whole look.
finding-your-style.what is a painting style: The sum of your habits and choices; two painters with the same model and colours still get different results.
finding-your-style.develop my style: Paint often, learn one new skill per project, notice what you keep leaning towards, and improve those parts on purpose.
finding-your-style.style vs technique: Style ties your techniques together and can matter more than polish, but sloppy brushwork or clashing colours are not a style.
finding-your-style.how do painters get a style: By learning the basics, practising a lot, and noticing and leaning into what they keep doing, such as soft blends or hard contrast.

fix-chalky-highlights.chalky highlights: They come from jumping to white too fast or overthinning; use smaller steps, make each layer cover solidly, and glaze colour back over.
fix-chalky-highlights.highlights look grainy: Patchy pale layers stacked on each other read as grainy; give each step enough thin coats to go solid before the next.
fix-chalky-highlights.white highlights too stark: Going from a mid tone to white is a bigger jump than it looks; add white in small amounts so each step is only slightly brighter.
fix-chalky-highlights.highlights look dusty: Glaze a saturated version of the colour over the area, then reapply the pale highlight over a smaller area.
fix-chalky-highlights.highlight patchy and speckled: Overthinned pale paint leaves specks; use enough thin coats for each step to go solid before moving on.
fix-chalky-highlights.skin went chalky: On skin, dot or stipple thin highlight paint, about half water, instead of stroking it, and glaze the colour back over chalky areas.
fix-chalky-highlights.jumped to white too fast: Glaze a saturated version of the colour back over it, then rebuild in smaller steps with only a little white added each time.
fix-chalky-highlights.highlights look like chalk: Pale layers that never fully cover cause it. Build each step solid in thin coats, and glaze colour back over areas that went chalky.
fix-chalky-highlights.grainy edge highlights: Give each pale step enough thin coats to go solid; overthinned pale paint leaves specks with darker colour between them.
fix-chalky-highlights.glaze colour back over pale highlights: Glaze a saturated version of the colour over the chalky area, then reapply the pale highlight over a smaller area.
fix-chalky-highlights.Why do my highlights look chalky?: Usually from jumping to white too fast or overthinning pale paint, so layers never fully cover and read as grainy.

fix-loose-joints.loose joints: Set the pose, run a small drop of superglue into each wobbly joint and hold it until it grabs.
fix-loose-joints.floppy joints on posable model: Fix them in place with a drop of superglue, or keep them movable by brushing a thin coat of varnish inside the joint.
fix-loose-joints.model keeps falling over: Superglue loose joints in the pose you want, and use a heavier base to support tall, top heavy figures.
fix-loose-joints.fix wobbly joints: Set the pose, run a small drop of superglue into each wobbly joint and hold it still until it grabs.
fix-loose-joints.posable kit wont hold pose: Superglue the joints in the pose you want, or a thin coat of varnish inside the joint can tighten it a little and keep it movable.
fix-loose-joints.loose arm joint: A small drop of superglue fixes it in place; to keep it movable, put a thin coat of varnish or nail varnish inside the joint.
fix-loose-joints.superglue joints: Set the pose, run a small drop into each wobbly joint, and hold it until it grabs. You lose the posing but gain a stable model.
fix-loose-joints.mech joints too loose: Glue them in pose with superglue, or tighten them a little with varnish inside the joint; paint in the joints also loosens poses.
fix-loose-joints.stop model toppling: Superglue the loose joints in pose, and give tall, top heavy figures a heavier base.
fix-loose-joints.fix loose legs on robot kit: Set the pose and run a drop of superglue into each loose joint, or varnish the inside of the joint to tighten it and keep it movable.

fix-wash-tide-marks.wash tide marks: Lift pools while wet with a damp brush and leave the wash alone to dry; if marks dry in, layer the base colour back over raised areas.
fix-wash-tide-marks.wash rings: Use enough wash to cover quickly, then leave it; brushing back into half dry wash leaves hard rings. Feather the edges towards shaded areas.
fix-wash-tide-marks.wash pooled: Touch a clean, only damp brush to the pool to wick the excess away, and move it into a recess that needs it.
fix-wash-tide-marks.coffee stain wash: Once dry, layer the base colour back over the raised areas; re washing will not match.
fix-wash-tide-marks.wash dried with lines: Let it dry, then layer the base colour back over the raised areas, avoiding the recesses; on texture, drybrush the base instead.
fix-wash-tide-marks.fix tide marks: Layer the base colour back over raised areas once dry, tinted slightly darker if the whole model was washed, or drybrush it on texture.
fix-wash-tide-marks.wash pooling on flat areas: Thin the wash with medium or add a drop of flow improver, apply two thin coats, and lay the part flat and still while it dries.
fix-wash-tide-marks.wash marks on cloak: Layer the base colour back over the raised folds, avoiding recesses; check the lower folds and bottom edge for pools while wet.
fix-wash-tide-marks.get rid of wash rings: Once dry, repaint the raised areas in the base colour, slightly darkened if the whole model was washed, rather than washing again.
fix-wash-tide-marks.wash left stains: Layer the base colour back over the stained raised areas, avoiding recesses, or drybrush the base on textured areas.
fix-wash-tide-marks.My wash dried in blotches and rings. How: Layer the base colour back over the raised areas, avoiding recesses; on texture, drybrush it on. Washing again will not match.

foliage-camouflage-on-vehicles.foliage on a tank: Glue small dry leafy sprigs with PVA to the turret sides, hull edges and front plate after painting, keeping hatches and gun clear.
foliage-camouflage-on-vehicles.leaves on a vehicle: Use small dry leafy sprigs kept to scale, glued on last with PVA where a crew would tie branches.
foliage-camouflage-on-vehicles.branches tucked into a tank: Glue scale sized sprigs with PVA to the turret sides, hull edges and front plate; a branch longer than a hatch looks wrong.
foliage-camouflage-on-vehicles.glue bushes on a tank: Use PVA on the finished vehicle, keep hatches, vision slits and the gun clear, and let the glue dry fully before handling.
foliage-camouflage-on-vehicles.natural camo with plants: Glue torn foliage clump or trimmed dried plant to the finished vehicle with PVA, varying the layout on each one.
foliage-camouflage-on-vehicles.sprigs of leaves on armour: Glue small dry sprigs with PVA where a crew would tie branches, and handle the model gently afterwards as they are fragile.
foliage-camouflage-on-vehicles.how to add foliage camouflage: Paint and weather the vehicle first, then glue small dry sprigs with PVA to turret sides, hull edges and the front plate.
foliage-camouflage-on-vehicles.vehicle hidden in hedges: See: gluing leafy sprigs to a finished vehicle as camouflage, in this entry's steps 2 and 3.
foliage-camouflage-on-vehicles.tank covered in branches: Glue scale sized leafy sprigs on with PVA, keep hatches, vision slits and gun clear, and vary the amount from tank to tank.
foliage-camouflage-on-vehicles.leafy camo for vehicles: Glue small dry leafy sprigs to the finished vehicle with PVA, vary them on each one, and handle it gently afterwards.

fuel-and-oil-stains.oil stains: Add one or two small, glossy dark brown black stains last, at fuel caps, engines and hubs, so they shine against matt dust.
fuel-and-oil-stains.fuel spills: Spilt fuel round a cap shows best as a slightly paler, see through ring, added last over the dust.
fuel-and-oil-stains.grease stains on engine: Dot a glossy dark brown black on the engine deck, pull a short drip down, and soften the edge with a brush barely damp with thinner.
fuel-and-oil-stains.wet oil look: Gloss against a matt, dusty surface sells it: use a dark brown black in oil, glossy enamel, or acrylic mixed with gloss varnish, added last.
fuel-and-oil-stains.fuel cap weathering: Paint a slightly paler, see through ring round the cap for spilt fuel, with a small fresh glossy mark over part of it.
fuel-and-oil-stains.glossy oil leaks: Dot glossy dark brown black at the source, pull a short run downwards, and keep the centre darkest and shiniest. Do not matt varnish over it.
fuel-and-oil-stains.dirty engine: See: placing glossy fuel and oil stains on engine decks and hubs, in this entry's steps 2 to 4.
fuel-and-oil-stains.how do i paint oil leaks: Dot a dark brown black at the source, pull a short drip downwards with a fine brush, and fade the outer edge with a barely damp thinner brush.
fuel-and-oil-stains.fresh oil effect: Fresh oil is dark and glossy; add it last, after dust and matt varnish, and keep the centre darkest and shiniest.
fuel-and-oil-stains.vehicle weathering oil: Add one or two glossy dark stains at fuel caps, engine decks, hubs and below hatches last, over matt dust; too many look messy.

glow-in-the-dark-and-uv-paints.glow in the dark paint: It soaks up light and gives it off in the dark. Use several thin coats over smooth solid white, on small areas such as eyes or runes.
glow-in-the-dark-and-uv-paints.uv paint on miniatures: UV paints glow under an ultraviolet lamp and look like normal bright colours in daylight; they work best over a smooth, solid white.
glow-in-the-dark-and-uv-paints.black light paint: UV reactive paint glows while an ultraviolet lamp shines on it; many fluorescent paints react too. Use it over a smooth, solid white.
glow-in-the-dark-and-uv-paints.does glow paint need a white base: Yes. Both glow and UV paints work best over a smooth, solid white; over dark colours the glow is weak or lost.
glow-in-the-dark-and-uv-paints.uv reactive paint: It glows only while an ultraviolet lamp shines on it, and looks like a normal bright colour in daylight, so it can be part of the scheme.
glow-in-the-dark-and-uv-paints.luminous paint: Glow in the dark paint shines after charging in light, fading over minutes to hours; it needs a smooth, solid white base.
glow-in-the-dark-and-uv-paints.my glow paint is not glowing: Put it over a smooth, solid white in several thin coats, charge it under a bright lamp for a few minutes, and test whether varnish dulls it.
glow-in-the-dark-and-uv-paints.model that glows under a uv torch: Use UV reactive or fluorescent paints over a smooth, solid white, painting the daylight look first in normal colours.
glow-in-the-dark-and-uv-paints.fluorescent paint under black light: Yes, many fluorescent paints react to UV, and they work best over a smooth, solid white.
glow-in-the-dark-and-uv-paints.glow in dark eyes: Paint the eyes smooth solid white, then stir the glow paint well and add several thin coats; charge it under a bright lamp.

gluing-models-to-bases.glue model to base: On a plain base, glue it down before texturing; on a finished base, scrape bare a patch under the feet and use a little super glue.
gluing-models-to-bases.base before or after painting: Plain bases: glue the model first so the ground blends into the feet. Detailed bases: paint both separately and join them at the end.
gluing-models-to-bases.model fell off its base: Glue holds poorly on paint, so scrape a small patch back to bare material where the feet sit, then re glue with a little super glue.
gluing-models-to-bases.feet blend into the base: Glue the model down before texturing, work paste round the feet with a small tool, then add a little ground colour up the feet as dust or mud.
gluing-models-to-bases.super glue on the base: Put a little on the feet, touch them on a mat to take off the excess, then press down; less glue means no shiny bulges.
gluing-models-to-bases.attach a mini to a base: Use super glue; on paint, scrape the spot bare first. A figure on its own small base needs just two small dots underneath.
gluing-models-to-bases.which glue for bases: Super glue, with the paint scraped back to bare material where the feet sit, as glue holds poorly on paint.
gluing-models-to-bases.when should i base a model: On a plain base, glue the model down first; on a detailed sculpted, resin or printed base, paint both separately and join at the end.
gluing-models-to-bases.paint model and base separately: Yes for detailed sculpted, resin or printed bases, so the brush reaches every bit of texture, then join them at the end.
