gluing-models-to-bases.wrong base size: Check which base size the model needs before gluing anything, so you never have to cut a figure off later.

grime-with-washes.grime: Work dark brown, black and dark olive washes into recesses and texture without rinsing between them, so they blend unevenly.
grime-with-washes.how do i make a model look grimy: Switch between brown, black and olive washes in the recesses without rinsing, leave flat panels mostly clean, then drybrush pale bone downward.
grime-with-washes.mix washes for dirt: Use dark brown, black and dark olive washes, each with a little water, and switch between them without rinsing; the uneven mix is the point.
grime-with-washes.filthy armour with washes: Work two or three washes into recesses and texture without rinsing, leave large flat panels mostly alone, and keep some clean bright accents.
grime-with-washes.oily dirt shade: Black and brown washes stirred together make one oily, dirty shade.
grime-with-washes.aged dirty look with washes: Work two or three washes into the same area without rinsing and let them blend unevenly, then drybrush pale bone downward for streaks.
grime-with-washes.brown and black wash together: Yes: stirred together they make one oily, dirty shade, or switch between them unrinsed in recesses for uneven grime.
grime-with-washes.make metal look grubby: Work brown, black and olive washes into the recesses unevenly, or cover with an oil wash and wipe the raised areas with a spirit damp sponge.
grime-with-washes.dirty recesses: Work a dark brown, black and dark olive wash into the recesses, switching without rinsing so the grime is uneven.
grime-with-washes.layering washes for grime: Switch between dark brown, black and dark olive washes in the same area without rinsing, and let them blend unevenly as they dry.

highlight-before-or-after-wash.highlight before wash: Do it for soft, smooth transitions; push the highlights brighter than looks right, as the wash pulls harsh spots back.
highlight-before-or-after-wash.highlight after wash: Do it for crisp, strong contrast, as a wash tones down every highlight it touches.
highlight-before-or-after-wash.do i wash first or highlight first: Highlight first for soft, unified transitions; wash first and highlight after for crisp, strong contrast.
highlight-before-or-after-wash.wash killed my highlights: The wash was too strong or thick. Once dry, lay the base colour or highlight back over the raised areas, and keep later washes to recesses.
highlight-before-or-after-wash.order of wash and highlight: Highlight then wash gives soft transitions; wash then highlight gives sharper contrast. Either way, bring back the brightest edges after.
highlight-before-or-after-wash.should i wash over highlights: Yes, if you want soft, unified transitions, but push the highlights brighter first and restore the brightest edges after.
highlight-before-or-after-wash.soft transitions with a wash: Highlight first and wash over the top; the wash pulls harsh highlights back into the rest for a smooth, unified look.
highlight-before-or-after-wash.wash then highlight: That order gives crisp, strong contrast, since the highlights go on after the wash has toned everything down.
highlight-before-or-after-wash.highlights look muted after shade: A wash tones down highlights. Bring back the brightest edges and points after it, or highlight after washing for stronger contrast.
highlight-before-or-after-wash.sharper contrast after wash: Wash first, then highlight after, for crisp, strong contrast.

hobby-kit-pets-and-kids.is paint safe around kids: Most hobby acrylics are low risk on skin but are not food, and some contain heavy metals or solvents, so keep all paint out of reach.
hobby-kit-pets-and-kids.cat knocked over my paints: Put lids back on pots and the rinse cup whenever you leave the desk; a cat drinking from a rinse pot means a trip to the vet.
hobby-kit-pets-and-kids.keep hobby knives away from children: Keep blades in a closed box up high or locked, never in an open caddy, and count blades back into their box after each session.
hobby-kit-pets-and-kids.dog ate a model part: Call a vet or poison line straight away and take the container so they can read the label; two swallowed magnets are especially dangerous.
hobby-kit-pets-and-kids.safe storage for superglue: Keep it with blades, solvents and resin in a closed box or cupboard, up high or locked, never in an open caddy on the desk.
hobby-kit-pets-and-kids.toddler and hobby desk: Lock away blades, glue, solvents and resin, keep small parts and magnets in sealed tubs, and sweep under the desk for dropped blades.
hobby-kit-pets-and-kids.are acrylics toxic: Most are low risk on skin but are not food; some pigments contain heavy metals, and metallics, inks and washes can contain solvents.
hobby-kit-pets-and-kids.small parts choking hazard: Yes. Keep small parts, bases and magnets in sealed tubs; two swallowed magnets can pinch through the gut.
hobby-kit-pets-and-kids.hobby room with pets: Close away dangerous kit, lid pots and the rinse cup when you leave, count blades back in, and keep the resin printer behind a closed door.
hobby-kit-pets-and-kids.lock away solvents and resin: Yes: keep blades, superglue, solvents, strippers, resin and spray cans in a closed box or cupboard, up high or locked.

improving-your-painting.how do i get better at painting: Pick one small, reachable goal per model, review each finished piece honestly against your last one, and practise the skill on spares.
improving-your-painting.improve my painting: Set one written goal for the next model, give that part extra time, and paint often in short sessions most days.
improving-your-painting.stuck at the same level: Painting the same way every time builds speed but little else; set one small new goal per model and review each finished piece.
improving-your-painting.painting not improving: Name what you dislike and its cause on your last model, set one goal for the next, and practise that skill on a spare part.
improving-your-painting.practice tips: Paint just one skill on a leftover blade or head for 10 or 15 minutes, note what went wrong, and try twice more.
improving-your-painting.set goals for painting: One small, reachable goal per model, written down, such as darker shadows or brighter highlights; the newer you are, the smaller the goal.
improving-your-painting.learn new techniques: Break a big skill into smaller ones, try one per model, and test it on spare parts first.
improving-your-painting.how to level up painting: Set one goal per model, practise it on spares, and now and then give one model far longer than usual and push every part.
improving-your-painting.review my finished models: Study it honestly for a few minutes, compare it with your last model, and name what you do not like and its cause.
improving-your-painting.small goals per model: Yes: good first goals are darker shadows, brighter highlights, or dark lining between areas to push contrast.

keeping-white-clean.white turned pink: Red in the rinse water or bristles tints white. Change to clean water, and rinse, dip in black and rinse again so any tint left is grey.
keeping-white-clean.white looks dirty: Use clean water and fresh paint, replace tinted white on the palette, and fix spills with a high coverage off white.
keeping-white-clean.keep white clean: Use clean water or a separate rinse pot, fresh paint and a clean palette, paint white areas last, and seal them with varnish.
keeping-white-clean.white tinted by other colours: Even a trace tints white: change to clean water, replace tinted palette white, and clear red from bristles with a dip in black then a rinse.
keeping-white-clean.rinse water tints white: Change to clean water before painting white, or keep a separate rinse pot just for it.
keeping-white-clean.should i paint white last: Yes, where you can, since mistakes on white are hard to fix.
keeping-white-clean.white areas look grey: See: correcting white with a high coverage off white and fresh paint, in this entry's steps 4 and 6.
keeping-white-clean.white cloak got stained: Cover the stain with a high coverage off white, which usually hides a dark spill in one coat, then seal the white with varnish.
keeping-white-clean.my white isnt white: Something tinted it: change to clean water, use fresh paint, clean the brush and palette, and paint over with a high coverage off white.
keeping-white-clean.separate water pot for white: Yes, keep a separate rinse pot for white, as you would for metallics, or change to clean water before painting it.

lengthening-and-shortening-weapons.make a sword longer: Cut the end off one copy and the start off another at the same slight angle, glue them with plastic glue, and scrape the seam once dry.
lengthening-and-shortening-weapons.shorten a barrel: Saw off the muzzle, cut the barrel near its base with a knife, trim the faces level and glue the muzzle back on.
lengthening-and-shortening-weapons.lengthen a spear: Join two copies: cut both at the same slight angle so details line up, glue them with plastic glue, and scrape the seam when dry.
lengthening-and-shortening-weapons.weapon too short: Lengthen it with a second copy, cut at a matching slight angle, glued and scraped smooth; test fit before gluing to the model.
lengthening-and-shortening-weapons.cut a gun barrel down: Saw off the muzzle end, cut a section out near the base with a knife, trim the faces level and straight, then glue the ends together.
lengthening-and-shortening-weapons.extend a weapon with two copies: Cut the end off one and the start off the other at the same slight angle, glue them straight with plastic glue, then scrape the seam.
lengthening-and-shortening-weapons.longer polearm conversion: Join two copies of the haft, cut at the same slight angle, with plastic glue, and test fit first as longer parts can clash.
lengthening-and-shortening-weapons.shorter rifle: Remove the muzzle, cut a section from the barrel near its base, trim the faces level and glue the muzzle back on.
lengthening-and-shortening-weapons.join two swords: Cut both at the same slight angle so details line up, glue with plastic glue run into the join, and scrape the seam when dry.
lengthening-and-shortening-weapons.resize a weapon: Lengthen by joining two copies cut at a matching angle, or shorten by cutting a section out of the barrel and regluing the muzzle.

maggots-and-grubs.maggots: Paint some creamy sand and others pink, highlight along the ridges, then give all the same pale flesh highlight on top.
maggots-and-grubs.how to paint maggots: Leave purple shade between them, paint some creamy sand and some pink, highlight the ridges, and finish all with one pale flesh highlight.
maggots-and-grubs.grubs crawling out of a wound: See: painting maggots in two colours with a shared pale highlight, in this entry's steps 2 to 4.
maggots-and-grubs.worms on a model: Paint them pale flesh, then stain the base half with thinned pink one coat paint and feather the edge so it fades out.
maggots-and-grubs.rotting flesh with maggots: Paint the maggots two colours, creamy sand and pink, with purple shade between, and keep them low key so the face stays the focus.
maggots-and-grubs.maggots look like one blob: Use two colours, creamy sand and pink, with purple shade left between them; two shades together look more natural.
maggots-and-grubs.paint wriggling grubs: Paint some creamy sand and some pink, highlight along the sculpted ridges, then add one pale flesh highlight to all.
maggots-and-grubs.plague monster maggots: Creamy sand and pink maggots over purple shade, highlighted along the ridges and finished with a shared pale flesh highlight.
maggots-and-grubs.what colour are maggots: Several colours; a creamy sand and a pink together look more natural than one uniform colour.
maggots-and-grubs.how to highlight worms: Highlight along the sculpted ridges, pale yellow on cream ones and pink with pale flesh on pink ones, then one pale flesh highlight on all.

material-contrast.materials look the same: Give touching areas clearly different colours or values, vary the finish, and add texture or scratches so each reads as its own material.
material-contrast.separate leather from cloth: Use clearly different colours or values, add scratches or texture to leather, and keep cloth matt with soft blends.
material-contrast.model looks like one blob: Give neighbouring areas clearly different colours or values; if it is mostly two materials, make one light and one dark.
material-contrast.how to make materials look different: Vary colour, value and finish: soft warm highlights on cloth, crisp cool ones on hard surfaces, and tiny bright highlights for shiny leather.
material-contrast.everything blends together: Give touching areas clearly different colours or values, and step back to check each part still reads at arm's length.
material-contrast.leather and metal look the same: Add small steel chips to the metal and leave leather plain, or give the leather scratches and texture so it reads differently.
material-contrast.colour separation: Neighbouring areas need clearly different colours or values; tint neutrals to suit the main colour and add a dark line where they meet.
material-contrast.tell cloth and armour apart: Start the cloth darker with warm soft highlights, give armour paler, cooler crisp edges, and keep cloth matt beside slightly glossier armour.
material-contrast.skin and shell same colour: Make one light and one dark, so the two materials separate clearly.
material-contrast.areas merge at arm's length: Similar neighbouring colours blur together; give touching areas clearly different colours or values and step back to check.

midtones-make-blending-easier.my colours wont blend together: The gap is probably too big; mix a few in between steps and paint them side by side first, or add a middle colour.
midtones-make-blending-easier.mix in between colours before blending: Mix two colours into a few steps, kept close to undiluted, and paint them side by side; band width sets how gradual the change is.
midtones-make-blending-easier.midtones: In between mixes of two colours, painted side by side before blending, so each gap is small and the blend is easier.
midtones-make-blending-easier.blend has a hard jump: Add a middle colour between the two, such as an orange between a pale skin and a red, and blend only the borders.
midtones-make-blending-easier.gap between colours too big: Add a middle colour; the smaller the gap between neighbouring colours, the easier the blend.
midtones-make-blending-easier.highlight with white wont blend: Whites tend to be thick and chalky; mid value colours like turquoise, orange or ochre flow better as top highlights.
midtones-make-blending-easier.easier wet blending: Lay midtone steps first and blend only the borders; if one colour overpowers, add a touch more of the weaker one while wet.
midtones-make-blending-easier.how many steps between shadow and highli: Enough that each gap is small; more steps do not slow you down if you mix small amounts on the brush tip.
midtones-make-blending-easier.blending looks stripy: See: laying midtone bands and blending only their borders, in this entry's steps 1 to 4.
midtones-make-blending-easier.why is blending so hard: Usually the colours are too far apart or the top highlight is a thick white; add midtones and use a mid value colour on top.

molten-metal.molten metal: Base bright red, glaze see through orange in many coats, then yellow nearer the hot point and a small spot of pale yellow and white at the hottest.
molten-metal.heated metal: Glaze from red through orange and yellow to white at the hottest point, with patchy cooler browns dotted along the edges.
molten-metal.glowing hot sword: Keep the spine hottest: red base, many thin orange glazes stopping short of the tip, yellow nearer the centre, and a little white at the hottest.
molten-metal.red hot metal: Base bright red, build a slow, wide orange zone with thin glazes, then small yellow and white at the hottest, thickest part.
molten-metal.lava blade: See: glazing a blade from red to white hot with uneven specks, in this entry's steps 1 to 5.
molten-metal.forge glowing metal: Thick, central parts stay hottest: glaze red to orange to yellow towards them, and dot red brown then darker brown along the cooler edges.
molten-metal.how do i paint heated metal: Plan the hottest spot, base red, glaze orange thinly in many coats, add yellow then a small white point, and dot browns on cool edges.
molten-metal.hot iron effect: Glaze orange, yellow and a small white point over red, using specks and dots rather than a perfect gradient, with brown on cooler edges.
molten-metal.glowing runes on blade: Treat the rune as the hottest point: glaze red through orange and yellow towards it, with pale yellow and white right on it.
molten-metal.white hot centre: Finish with pale yellow and then white right on the hottest spot, kept small; too much white and yellow looks less hot.

mud-on-vehicles.mud on tank: Pile textured mud on tracks and wheels, then flick light dry mud and darker wet mud, heaviest low down at the front and rear.
mud-on-vehicles.muddy wheels: Mix mud paste with a little fine sand and grass fibres; lighter dry mix higher up, darker coarser wet mix on the lower running gear.
mud-on-vehicles.mud splatter: Thin mud to runny honey, load a short stiff brush, hold it close and draw a toothpick across the bristles; practise on paper first.
mud-on-vehicles.dirty tracks: Brush a darker, coarser wet mud mix onto the lower running gear, piled most at the front and rear, and add glossy wet mud in recesses.
mud-on-vehicles.flick mud on a vehicle: Draw a toothpick across a stiff brush loaded with mud thinned like runny honey, tilting the model so spots land at an angle.
mud-on-vehicles.weather a tank with mud: Add mud last: textured mud on tracks and wheels, light dry splatter then a smaller, lower dark wet splatter, and a few glossy spots.
mud-on-vehicles.how to make a truck look muddy: Splatter a light, dry mud over the lower hull, mudguards and wheels, then a darker tone over a smaller, lower area.
mud-on-vehicles.tank tracks dirt: Mix mud paste with fine sand and short grass fibres, adding them slowly, and pile it on the tracks, darker and coarser low down.
mud-on-vehicles.mud weathering: Use at least two related tones, light for dried and dark for wet, applied last and heaviest low down; check it suits the setting.
mud-on-vehicles.splattered mud low down: Flick light mud over the lower hull first, then darker mud over a smaller, lower area, and lift any spots that land too high.

nmm-reflections.where do reflections go on painted metal: Where light bounces towards the viewer, so more on the front of a shoulder pad than its top, with parts of the same angle matching.
nmm-reflections.nmm reflections: Break painted metal into scattered, uneven light patches, add weaker counter reflections, and pick up colours from nearby objects.
nmm-reflections.non metallic metal looks flat: Place lighter steps in several small, uneven patches rather than a smooth gradient, with each new light spot well above its surroundings.
nmm-reflections.nmm sword reflections: Avoid neat stripes, make one face brighter than the other, push the main band slightly off centre, and use triangles of light on flats.
nmm-reflections.counter reflections: Dimmer reflections from bounced light, with a band of shadow between them and the main one; keep those underneath much darker.
nmm-reflections.reflect nearby colours in metal: Place them only where a straight line runs from the object to the metal, starting darker and greyer than the object.
nmm-reflections.painted metal doesnt look shiny: Scatter small uneven light patches two or three steps above their surroundings, add a few points of light near bright areas, and counter reflections.
nmm-reflections.scattered highlights on nmm armour: From the mid tone up, place each lighter step in several small, uneven patches, skipping spots, then feather only their edges.
nmm-reflections.fake chrome shine: Over white, paint a bent scene: a dark brown horizon, ground lightening to sand below, and blue sky fading to near white above.
nmm-reflections.how to place nmm highlights: Place them for the viewer, scattered in uneven patches; a black primed model under a lamp shows where reflections fall.

oil-subtractive-method.oil paint wipe off: Block oils over a light primed model, let the spirit evaporate about 30 minutes, then wipe raised areas with a makeup sponge.
oil-subtractive-method.subtractive oils: Coat a light primed model in oils, then wipe paint off the raised areas so the bright primer shows as highlights.
oil-subtractive-method.remove oil with brush: See: wiping oils off raised areas with a makeup sponge, in this entry's step 5.
oil-subtractive-method.oils over zenithal: Yes: prime a colour, spray lighter then white from above, let it cure, block in oils, then wipe the high points so the zenithal shows.
oil-subtractive-method.oil painting method miniatures: Thin oils with odourless mineral spirits, block colours in with a big brush, blend wet where they meet, then sponge the raised areas back.
oil-subtractive-method.highlight by wiping paint: Wipe oil off raised areas with a makeup sponge so a light primer shows through; with acrylics, wipe the high points straight away.
oil-subtractive-method.oil subtract technique: Prime light from above, block in oils thinned to layer consistency, wait about 30 minutes, then sponge paint off the raised areas.
oil-subtractive-method.oils on light primer: Let the primer cure fully, ideally overnight, then block in oils and wipe them off the raised areas so the light primer becomes the highlights.
oil-subtractive-method.how do i use oils subtractively: Block in oils over a zenithal primer, let the spirit evaporate until not slippery, then wipe raised areas with a makeup sponge.
oil-subtractive-method.oil wash removal: Use a makeup sponge rather than cotton buds or tissue, which leave fibres, after letting the spirit evaporate for about 30 minutes.

out-of-scale-details.details look the wrong scale: Remove, repurpose or repaint them: cut off what you cannot save, use giant parts on bigger models, or paint chunky details dark.
out-of-scale-details.parts too big: Cut them off and cover the scar with panels, pipes or rubble, or repurpose them for a bigger model.
out-of-scale-details.terrain looks like a toy: Oversized furniture or controls cause it; cut them off, repurpose them, or paint them as something else.
out-of-scale-details.oversized furniture: Repurpose it for a bigger model, such as an oversized chair for a large walker, or paint it as a machine with glowing lights.
out-of-scale-details.out of scale: Check parts next to your models, then remove, repurpose or repaint any that look too big or too small.
out-of-scale-details.scale problems: Check terrain beside the models you will use; cut off, repurpose or repaint anything that looks wrong.
out-of-scale-details.model looks toylike: Oversized details make a piece look like a toy; cut them off and cover the scar, or paint chunky parts dark so they recede.
out-of-scale-details.details too big for the model: Paint chunky details like huge buckles dark so they recede.
out-of-scale-details.fix oversized parts: Cut off what you cannot save and cover the scar with panels, pipes or rubble, or paint the part as something else.
out-of-scale-details.chain looks too chunky: Paint chunky details dark so they recede.

paint-drying-too-fast.paint dries too fast: Keep paint in compact blobs, use a wet palette, refresh it every few hours, and add a little retarder for blending or fine work.
paint-drying-too-fast.paint drying on the brush: Add a drop of flow improver or drying retarder; water does not slow drying. In heat, rinse the tip often and load small amounts.
paint-drying-too-fast.paint dries on my palette: Keep each colour in a tight blob rather than spread thin, put out more than a tiny dab, and use a wet palette.
paint-drying-too-fast.paint goes tacky while blending: Add a little retarder, which can double working time; too much leaves a sticky glossy film.
paint-drying-too-fast.paint dries before i can blend: Use retarder sparingly; it can double the working time for blending.
paint-drying-too-fast.paint skins over: Keep colours in compact blobs on a wet palette, and put out a fresh blob after about three hours.
paint-drying-too-fast.hot room paint drying: Heat speeds drying; rinse the tip often, reload small amounts, work in smaller sections, and leave the finest detail for a cooler time.
paint-drying-too-fast.paint drying in the brush tip: A drop of flow improver or drying retarder slows it; water does not.
paint-drying-too-fast.keep paint workable longer: Use a wet palette, keep paint in tight blobs, and add a little retarder; refresh paint after about three hours.
paint-drying-too-fast.paint dries too quick on palette: Keep each colour in a tight blob rather than spread thin or pulled into strings, and use a wet palette.

painted-metal-blades.nmm sword: Base a fairly light grey, paint curved or diagonal bands of light with one edge brighter than the other, then run pure white along the edges.
painted-metal-blades.non metallic blade: Curved bands of light, one edge brighter and swapped on the reverse, biased towards light greys, finished with white edges and a few glints.
painted-metal-blades.how do i paint an nmm sword: Base light grey, sketch bright curved bands, glaze back through darker tones, then run pure white along both edges and the centre ridge.
painted-metal-blades.painted reflections on a blade: Use a few long, stretched curved or diagonal bands rather than many small ones, keeping the brightest colour broad inside each.
painted-metal-blades.sword with white edge glints: Run pure white along both cutting edges and the ridge in one slow stroke, add a few short flicks to the edge, and a tiny dot where each meets it.
painted-metal-blades.where do reflections go on a blade: In curved or diagonal bands following the light, with one edge brighter, swapped on the other side; light gathers where an edge curves.
painted-metal-blades.nmm weapon tutorial: Black out the flat, base light grey, paint curved bands with one edge brighter, glaze until smooth, then add white edges and a few glints.
painted-metal-blades.curved bands of light on a sword: Sketch the bright band first, keep it broad with narrow midtones around it, then glaze back through the darker tones until it blends.
painted-metal-blades.blade looks flat not shiny without metal: Use the full range from near black to near white, bias it towards light greys, and finish with pure white edges and small glints.
painted-metal-blades.nmm axe head: See: painting non metallic blades with curved bands of light and white edges, in this entry's steps 2 to 4 and 8.

painting-boils-and-pus.boils: Dab a lighter skin tone on each boil, glaze bruised purple round the base, build red to magenta, add a mustard centre and a pale dot on top.
painting-boils-and-pus.pustules: Lighter skin on the bump, bruised purple and red around it, a mustard yellow centre, and a tiny pale bone dot on the very top.
painting-boils-and-pus.how do i paint pus: Paint a thin mustard yellow in the centre, glaze a cold yellow over it, and touch a pale bone dot on top; for burst boils, use glossy green yellow gloop.
painting-boils-and-pus.zits on a monster: Lighten each raised spot, ring it with thin red and purple, add a mustard yellow centre, and dot a pale bone on the very top.
painting-boils-and-pus.plague boils: Fade a thin purple or burgundy bruise round each boil, build red to magenta, paint a mustard centre, then a tiny pale dot on top.
painting-boils-and-pus.blisters about to burst: A tiny pale bone dot on the very top of each boil makes it look tight and full.
painting-boils-and-pus.infected skin: Ring a thinned red wash round the boil so the skin looks inflamed, with a thin purple or burgundy glaze faded in like bruising.
painting-boils-and-pus.paint pimples: Dab a lighter skin tone on each, ring it with thin red, paint a mustard yellow centre, and touch a tiny pale dot on top.
painting-boils-and-pus.pus filled spots: A thin mustard yellow strongest in the centre, a cold yellow glaze over the boil and nearby skin, then a tiny pale bone dot on top.
painting-boils-and-pus.make boils look gross and swollen: Build red to magenta towards the swollen part with small dots and glazes, and finish with a tiny pale dot so it looks tight and full.

painting-dark-skin.dark skin: Base deep brown flesh, wash warm brown into recesses and eyes, build up through lighter flesh to pale bone and yellow cream highlights.
painting-dark-skin.black skin tone: Base a deep brown flesh chosen to suit, shade warm browns into the eyes, and build up through lighter flesh to yellowish highlights.
painting-dark-skin.brown skin: Pick a base to suit, from deep umber to warm orange, shade warm browns, and highlight through lighter flesh to a pale yellow cream.
painting-dark-skin.deep skin tones: Keep highlights small and tight with more surface left dark; that reads deeper with the same paints.
painting-dark-skin.how to highlight dark skin: Mid flesh thinned half and half on brow and raised areas, then lighter flesh, pale bone and a pale yellow cream over smaller areas.
painting-dark-skin.dark skin looks grey: See: using yellow tinted highlights and warm brown and red glazes on dark skin, in this entry's steps 4 and 6.
painting-dark-skin.dark skin recipe: Deep brown flesh base, warm mid brown wash, reddish brown in the sockets, mid then light flesh, pale bone and yellow cream highlights.
painting-dark-skin.rich dark skin: Glaze thin warm browns over the steps, and thin red into the lips, under cheekbones and eyes so the face looks alive.
painting-dark-skin.dark skin highlights go ashy: Use yellow tinted highlights, such as a pale yellow cream, which look warmer and more natural than plain ivory, then glaze warm browns.
painting-dark-skin.warm brown flesh: Base deep brown flesh, wash warm mid brown, highlight up through lighter flesh to a pale yellow cream, and glaze warm browns and red.

painting-gems.gems: Paint the side facing the light dark and the far side glowing, then put a crisp white dot on the light facing side.
painting-gems.how do i paint a gem: Paint it near black, build colour towards the far side in smaller, brighter steps, glaze smooth, then add a white dot on the light facing side.
painting-gems.jewels on a crown: Keep every gem agreeing: dark towards the light, glowing on the far side, with a white dot on the light side, in one or two related colours.
painting-gems.gem looks like a blob of paint: It lacks contrast: darken the dark side further, push the bright side brighter, and keep the white dot small.
painting-gems.gemstone highlight: One crisp white or ivory dot on the light facing side, inside the dark area rather than on the very edge.
painting-gems.red ruby on a sword hilt: Place the glow by the model standing upright, not the gem; on an angled hilt the bright side may end up almost underneath.
painting-gems.green emerald effect: See: painting a gem dark towards the light and glowing on the far side, in this entry's steps 3 to 6.
painting-gems.painting jewelry stones: Base black, build colour to the far side in two or three brighter steps, glaze smooth, and add a white dot on the light facing side.
painting-gems.which side of a gem is light: The far side glows, as light passes through the gem; the side facing the light stays dark and gets the white dot.
painting-gems.white dot on gems: One crisp white or ivory dot on the light facing side, inside the dark area; trim a fat dot by pushing dark paint against it.

painting-joints-and-cables.joints: Paint them black after the armour, then a broad dark blue grey highlight, a thinner mid blue grey, and a fine pale grey towards the outside.
painting-joints-and-cables.cables: Paint them black, then skim one blue grey line along the side facing the light, usually the top.
painting-joints-and-cables.undersuit: Black base, broad dark blue grey highlight, then thinner mid blue grey and fine pale grey, brightest on the outer side of the limb.
painting-joints-and-cables.black joints on power armour: Paint black after the plates, then stacked blue grey highlights brightest on the outside; for speed, one thin blue grey line on the ridges.
painting-joints-and-cables.armour joints: Paint them after the armour, black with stacked blue grey highlights, touching only the middle of each raised rib.
painting-joints-and-cables.hoses and cables: Paint black and skim one blue grey line along the top; for glossy cables, jump straight to a tight pale blue line.
painting-joints-and-cables.how do i paint cables: Black base, then one line skimmed along the side facing the light, usually the top, since a round cable has no edge to follow.
painting-joints-and-cables.bodyglove: See: painting dark undersuits black with stacked blue grey highlights, in this entry's steps 3 and 4.
painting-joints-and-cables.dark undersuit highlights: A broad dark blue grey, a thinner mid blue grey, then a very fine pale grey, finer and lighter towards the outer side of the limb.
painting-joints-and-cables.flexible joints between armour plates: Line the brush up with each joint, use two thin coats stroked along the ribs, and touch only the middle of each rib with highlights.

painting-pale-cloth.white cloth: Paint the white first, shade it with a soft wash of darker ivory in clear medium, keep steps small, and save pure white for last.
painting-pale-cloth.cream cloth: Base cream or sand for worn white, shade the folds with sandy beige glazes, and build up in small steps to ivory on creases and hems.
painting-pale-cloth.white robe: Base it smooth in thin coats, shade folds with a soft ivory or bone wash in medium, build up in small steps, and add white last.
painting-pale-cloth.off white fabric: Shade with soft light washes or sandy beige glazes rather than a dark brown wash, and use ivory rather than pure white over a whole garment.
painting-pale-cloth.shade white cloth without it going muddy: Use a soft wash of darker ivory mixed with about four parts clear medium, or sandy beige glazes, never a dark brown wash.
painting-pale-cloth.brown wash on white went dirty: A dark brown wash over off white turns muddy; shade with ivory in clear medium or sandy beige glazes instead.
painting-pale-cloth.bone coloured robes: Brush a bone one coat paint mixed half and half with medium into the folds and leave it alone while wet, as overworking blotches.
painting-pale-cloth.white cloak: Use a size 4 or larger brush, shade with a soft ivory wash, build up in small steps, and keep the brightest tone for creases and hems.
painting-pale-cloth.cream robes: Base cream or sand, add darker colour on downward faces, build up in small steps, and finish with ivory on creases and hems.
painting-pale-cloth.pale cloth looks flat: Try tinted greys: a warm reddish grey for shadows and a cool pale green grey for highlights, with khaki brown in the deepest folds.

painting-sci-fi-terrain.sci fi terrain: Prime black, drybrush the main colour on heavily, pick out metal details, wash brown, drybrush lighter tones, then add a few glowing screens.
painting-sci-fi-terrain.how do i paint sci fi buildings: Prime black, heavy drybrush the main colour in rough circles, dark metal on vents and trims, a brown wash, then lighter drybrushes and pale bone.
painting-sci-fi-terrain.paint terrain fast: Prime black so missed corners read as shadow, drybrush the main colour heavily, wash brown, and keep each terrain type to a short set of colours.
painting-sci-fi-terrain.space station terrain: Black primer, a heavy drybrush of the main colour, dark metal details with silver worn edges, a brown wash, lighter drybrushes and lit screens.
painting-sci-fi-terrain.glowing screens on terrain: Paint the screens, then add tiny white lines as readouts.
painting-sci-fi-terrain.black primer terrain: Yes: on busy terrain any corner you miss just reads as shadow, and two heavy drybrush passes act as a base coat.
painting-sci-fi-terrain.corridor tiles painting: See: painting dark sci fi interiors with metal drybrushes and coloured washes, in this entry's steps 1 and 6.
painting-sci-fi-terrain.spaceship interior: Drybrush a warm dark metal all over, build up lighter metal passes, and add coloured washes in a few recesses for grime and variety.
painting-sci-fi-terrain.industrial bunker terrain: Prime black, drybrush the main colour heavily, wash brown with a second wash low down, and add one strong accent like yellow on hazard props.
painting-sci-fi-terrain.heavy drybrush on terrain: Load a big brush quite heavily and work in rough circles; two passes act as a base coat but leave black in the deepest corners.

painting-stone.painting stone: Base coat or spray, drybrush a sandy brown unevenly, catch edges in bone, and stipple or glaze colour shifts so it does not look like plastic.
painting-stone.how do i paint stone walls: Spray mid green then dust grey from one angle, drybrush sandy brown, catch edges in bone, and vary a few scattered stones.
painting-stone.stone looks flat: Add colour shifts: a thin blue grey glaze over the midtones, red in low spots, green for moss, and lighter or darker dabs on random stones.
painting-stone.drybrush rocks: Drybrush a sandy brown, heavier in places, then catch edges in bone; start with a fully dry brush and go lightly with pale tones.
painting-stone.grey stone ruins: Avoid a plain neutral grey: mix grey with dark brown, wash brown for natural stone or black for rubble, then drybrush sandy brown and bone.
painting-stone.castle walls: Drybrush stonework sandy brown, catch edges in bone, pin wash the mortar dark brown, and dab random stones lighter or darker.
painting-stone.mossy old stonework: Spray mid green, then dust grey over it from one angle while wet; the green left in the recesses looks like moss.
painting-stone.stone texture with stippling: Wipe most paint off a large brush and stab straight down, alternating a lighter stipple with a thin darkening wash for depth.
painting-stone.quick rocky terrain: Base, wash and drybrush: a brown wash makes grey stone natural, black reads as rubble, and green suggests moss.
painting-stone.make rocks look natural: Mix colour into the grey, wash brown, and add shifts like a cool blue grey glaze, red in low spots and green where moss would start.

painting-white.how do i paint white: Build up from a light or blue grey in greyish off whites covering less each time, or shade down from off white, and keep pure white for edges.
painting-white.white looks grey: A black wash straight from the pot turns white grey; cut it half and half with clear medium, and bring white back on raised areas.
painting-white.white is so hard: Treat it as a range of light greys and tints, thin it a lot or feather small dabs, and save pure white for a few edges.
painting-white.white coverage problems: Start from a grey or blue grey that covers better, or base off white in about three thin coats, each left to dry.
painting-white.bright white: Use cool blue greys for a crisp, clean white, and keep pure white for a few edges and shiny points.
painting-white.white looks flat: A large area of pure white has nowhere lighter to go; treat it as a range of light greys and tints, with only the top half truly white.
painting-white.white wont cover: Base an off white, which covers better, in about three thin coats; or paint mid blue first, then two parts white to one of blue.
painting-white.white goes chalky: Avoid normal layer thickness: thin white a lot and build coats, or place a small thick dab and feather its edge with a damp brush.
painting-white.build white from grey: Start from a mid, light or pale blue grey, then lay greyish off whites over all but the deepest areas, covering less each time.
painting-white.save pure white for last: Yes, keep it for a few edges and shiny points; many painters stop at a pale bone or blue grey.

paper-and-tape-cloth.masking tape cloak: Cut an oversize cloak from paper masking tape, stick it on and work in folds with tweezers, then prime or varnish and stiffen with thinned PVA.
paper-and-tape-cloth.how do i make a banner for a model: Cut paper, glue it round a brass wire pole and bend it into a droop while wet with varnish; or use foil, which bends to look windblown.
paper-and-tape-cloth.paper banner on a pole: Glue cut paper round a brass wire pole, then bend it into a droop while wet with varnish; bent dry, it creases.
paper-and-tape-cloth.make a cloak without sculpting: Use paper masking tape: cut it oversize, stick it on, work it into folds, then lock the shape with thinned PVA.
paper-and-tape-cloth.tape pennants on spears: Fold tape back on itself, leaving a loop to slide over the shaft, and cut a V in the free end.
paper-and-tape-cloth.thin paper flags: Soak thin paper in watered PVA so it drapes into flags that dry stiff.
paper-and-tape-cloth.cloak conversion with no putty: Paper masking tape works: cut a tapering shape with neck strips, fit it into folds, and brush on thinned PVA to make it rigid.
paper-and-tape-cloth.wrap a scarf from tape: Wrap strips about 4 to 5 mm wide, twisting them back on themselves each turn so they bunch like cloth.
paper-and-tape-cloth.my sculpted cloak is too thick: See: making thin cloaks from paper masking tape, in this entry's steps 1, 2 and 7.
paper-and-tape-cloth.cheap way to add a cape: Cut one from paper masking tape, stick it on, work it into folds, and prime or varnish it to kill the stickiness.

plain-sculpts-character.boring sculpt: The fix is usually in the paint: shift the skin colour, add mud on feet and hems, freehand war paint and paint eyebrows.
plain-sculpts-character.plain model: Add story with paint: skin colour shifts, grime where it would really collect, simple war paint and eyebrows.
plain-sculpts-character.model looks too clean: Add mud splatter on feet, legs and cloth hems, where the figure would really get dirty.
plain-sculpts-character.add character to a model: Shift the skin colour, add mud where it would collect, freehand war paint or tattoos, and paint eyebrows for expression.
plain-sculpts-character.bland face: Paint eyebrows to give expression, and shift the skin with hints of pink, purple or sickly green.
plain-sculpts-character.war paint on a face: Freehand simple war paint or tattoo shapes on bare skin, and make the leader's the most elaborate.
plain-sculpts-character.how do i make a dull model interesting: Use paint: cool and shift the skin, add mud on feet and hems, add war paint, and paint eyebrows, keeping what already works.
plain-sculpts-character.paint eyebrows: Yes, they give a face expression and stop it looking flat.
plain-sculpts-character.add story with grime: Put mud splatter on feet, legs and cloth hems, where the figure would really get dirty.
plain-sculpts-character.sculpt has no character: Add it in paint: skin colour shifts, grime, war paint and eyebrows, and only change the parts that help the story.

pre-highlighting.pre highlighting: Paint or drybrush light areas before a wash or see through paint, so the highlights show through it.
pre-highlighting.prehighlight before contrast: Drybrush pale sand over a light primer, heavier where it should stay light, then apply the see through colour over it.
pre-highlighting.drybrush before a wash: Yes: a pale drybrush underneath makes thin or see through colours over it look brighter and ready shaded.
pre-highlighting.why does my contrast paint look flat: See: pre highlighting under see through paints so the light shows through, in this entry's steps 1 to 3.
pre-highlighting.light first then shade: That is pre highlighting: put a pale layer where light falls, then thin or see through colour over it.
pre-highlighting.highlights show through see through pain: Yes, a pale layer underneath shows through, so drybrush or paint the light areas before the see through colour.
pre-highlighting.sand drybrush under washes: Drybrush pale sand all over a light primer, heavier where it should stay light, then apply colour thinned about half and half with water.
pre-highlighting.prehighlight for speed painting: Over a light primer, drybrush pale sand heavier where it should stay light, then apply thinned colour; it suits shaky hands.
pre-highlighting.zenithal then drybrush then tint: Over black, drybrush mid grey then white on the highest points, then put thinned or see through colour over that map of light.
pre-highlighting.put the light in first: Yes: paint or drybrush pale where the highlights go, then thin colour over it; you can paint white back and glaze at any stage.

protecting-painted-models.dust on my models: Keep finished models behind closed doors, and clear dust with a soft, dry makeup brush or a gentle puff of air.
protecting-painted-models.display cabinet for minis: Glass door cabinets suit whole armies; pick one whose doors close fully, and add extra glass shelves, as most figures fit in 13 to 15 cm.
protecting-painted-models.how do i protect painted miniatures: Keep them behind closed doors and out of strong sunlight and hot or cold cars, and varnish anything that gets handled.
protecting-painted-models.should i varnish models i handle: Yes. Models used for games wear where fingers touch, so varnish once painting is fully finished, including the base if you hold them there.
protecting-painted-models.keep finished models safe: Use a cabinet with fully closing doors, keep them out of sunlight and cars, and use magnets under bases in a metal lined case for transport.
protecting-painted-models.pet hair stuck on minis: Keep models behind closed doors, as open shelves gather pet hair, and lift it off with a soft, dry makeup brush or a puff of air.
protecting-painted-models.how to dust miniatures: Use a soft, dry makeup brush or a gentle puff of air; dusting by hand risks snapping parts.
protecting-painted-models.glass cabinet for an army: Pick one whose doors close fully, or add brush style draught strip, and fit extra glass shelves with one taller level for big models.
protecting-painted-models.paint rubbing off from handling: Varnish once painting is fully finished, paying attention to the base if that is where you hold the model.
protecting-painted-models.keep cat hair off my models: Keep them in a cabinet with fully closing doors, or add draught strip round the door edges, and clear hair with a soft dry brush.

real-chain-details.real chain: Use scale model or fine jewellery chain sized to the model, wrap or hang it, and lock it with thin super glue that wicks through the links.
real-chain-details.add chain to a model: Glue one end somewhere hidden, wrap it tightly in crossed X shapes, finish the end out of sight, then touch thin super glue along it.
real-chain-details.jewellery chain: Fine jewellery chain works if the link size suits the model; coarse chain looks out of scale. Cut it with old cutters.
real-chain-details.hanging chains: Pre shape them on oiled wax paper, touch thin super glue to each link, and pop them off once dry as fixed shapes.
real-chain-details.chain looks out of scale: Check the link size against the model before using it; coarse chain looks out of scale, so pick finer chain.
real-chain-details.glue chain on: Fix one end in a hidden spot with super glue, wrap it, then touch thin super glue along the chain so it wicks through and locks rigid.
real-chain-details.floating chain: Lay cut lengths in the bends you want on oiled wax paper, touch thin super glue to each link, then pop them off as stiff curved shapes.
real-chain-details.chains on a base: See: shaping and gluing fine chain so it holds its curve, in this entry's steps 1 and 6.
real-chain-details.wrap chain around a model: Glue one end in a hidden spot like an armpit, wrap tightly in crossed X shapes, and finish the other end out of sight.
real-chain-details.jewelry chain conversion: Use fine jewellery chain sized to the model, wrapped tightly and locked with thin super glue, with a small plate hung off it to hide a join.

replacing-snapped-parts.broken spear: Cut away the broken shaft and replace it with brass or steel rod of the same thickness, drilled and glued into the hand and spear head.
replacing-snapped-parts.snapped ankle: Drill up through the foot into the leg, add a pin, and fix the model to its base through that foot, ideally with a second pin in the other foot.
replacing-snapped-parts.my model broke: If the break is clean, pin it: drill both faces, glue in a short wire, then superglue the joint. Scrape paint off both faces first.
replacing-snapped-parts.pin a broken part back on: Drill a small hole into both faces, glue in a short length of wire, then superglue the joint; it is far stronger than glue alone.
replacing-snapped-parts.replace a spear with wire: Use brass or steel rod of the same thickness, drilled into the hand and spear head; next time it bends instead of snapping.
replacing-snapped-parts.brass rod for a staff: Match the rod to the old part by eye or with calipers, drill into the hand and head, glue it in, and wrap thin putty or thread for a grip.
replacing-snapped-parts.snapped thin parts keep breaking: Replace them with metal rod or wire so they bend instead of breaking, or pin clean breaks for a stronger joint.
replacing-snapped-parts.fix a broken lance: Cut away the broken shaft and swap in brass or steel rod of the same thickness, drilled into the hand and the head.
replacing-snapped-parts.model snapped at the feet: Pin up through the foot into the leg and fix it to the base through that foot, adding a second pin from the base into the other foot.
replacing-snapped-parts.stop thin parts breaking again: Swap them for metal rod or wire, which bends rather than snapping; wire suits parts that stick out and get knocked.

reviving-old-paint.old paint: Most just needs a hard shake or a little medium, but paint that has set into a solid layer or hard chunks cannot be saved.
reviving-old-paint.paint dried up in the pot: If it has set solid or into hard chunks, it will not mix back; replace it with a close colour.
reviving-old-paint.paint too thick: If it is still smooth, add a few drops of water or medium, stir well and check it on the palette.
reviving-old-paint.paint separated into water and goo: That is settled paint; shake hard for a good while, or open it and stir with an old brush. Mixing balls or a vortex mixer are faster.
reviving-old-paint.can i save old paints: Usually: shake hard or add a little medium. Paint that has set into a solid layer or hard chunks cannot be saved.
reviving-old-paint.paint gone gloopy like jam: If still smooth, add a few drops of water or medium and stir well; check it on the palette before use.
reviving-old-paint.lumps in my paint: Hard chunks will not mix back, so replace the pot; sludge under runny liquid just needs a long, hard shake or a stir.
reviving-old-paint.revive dried paint: Thickened but smooth paint takes a few drops of water or medium; paint set into chunks or a solid layer cannot be saved.
reviving-old-paint.paint gone stringy: See: thinning thickened paint with water or medium, or replacing set paint, in this entry's steps 1 and 7.
reviving-old-paint.should i throw away old paint: Only if it has set into a solid layer or hard chunks; otherwise a hard shake or a little medium usually brings it back.

sculpting-armatures.sculpting armature: Bend soft aluminium wire to a scale body drawing, bulk it with foil, cover it in a thin epoxy putty skin, and set the pose first.
sculpting-armatures.wire armature: Fold a long soft aluminium wire in half for head and spine, bend out the hips and legs, bind on arms, and lock joints with super glue.
sculpting-armatures.how do i build an armature: Bend soft wire over a body diagram at figure height, bind arms and hips, pose it, bulk with foil, then wrap in a thin skin of epoxy putty.
sculpting-armatures.how to start sculpting a figure from scr: Build a wire armature to a scale drawing first; for a first sculpt, a blob like creature is far kinder than a human.
sculpting-armatures.foil bulk under putty: Glue scrunched kitchen foil onto the chest and back of the skull, keep it slim if the design is not settled, and leave room for the face.
sculpting-armatures.armature wire size: See: the soft aluminium wire and thinner binding wire this entry uses, in steps 1 and 2.
sculpting-armatures.pose a sculpt before adding putty: Yes: add a gentle S curve to the spine, tilt shoulders and hips opposite ways, and decide the pose before pushing the legs into the cork.
sculpting-armatures.green stuff sculpt base frame: Cover the wire armature in a thin skin of two part epoxy putty, mixed until no streaks remain, so clay can grip it.
sculpting-armatures.scale drawing for sculpting: Print a body diagram at the exact figure height and bend the wire over it, marking shoulders and elbows from the drawing.
sculpting-armatures.skeleton for a sculpt: A soft aluminium wire armature bent to a scale drawing, bulked with foil and skinned in thin epoxy putty, with joints left bare to repose.

shading-metallics-with-ink.shade metallics with ink: Mix ink into the metallic, or glaze thinned ink over it; ink darkens while keeping the sheen, unlike black paint.
shading-metallics-with-ink.shade silver without going dull: Use a bluish black ink rather than black paint, which dilutes the shiny flakes; mix it in or glaze it thinly into recesses.
shading-metallics-with-ink.black ink on silver: A bluish black ink suits silver; mix it into the metallic for a range of tones, or glaze it heavily thinned into the recesses.
shading-metallics-with-ink.ink wash on metal: Glaze heavily thinned ink in several thin coats, kept to recesses so it does not pool, and do not scrub wet paint over it afterwards.
shading-metallics-with-ink.shading gold: Use a warm reddish brown ink, mixed into the gold or glazed thinly into recesses, then dot bright metal where light reflects most.
shading-metallics-with-ink.wash left tide marks on metal: Keep ink to the recesses and stop it pooling on flats, and keep the metal base to two smooth thin coats.
shading-metallics-with-ink.black paint makes metal dull: Black paint dilutes the shiny flakes; ink darkens metallics while keeping the sheen and mixes straight into them.
shading-metallics-with-ink.glaze ink over metallics: Thin the ink heavily and glaze it on in several thin coats like a wash; a dash of matt medium takes off its slight gloss.
shading-metallics-with-ink.how do i shade metal: Mix a range from mostly ink to pure metallic, cover in the darkest, layer lighter mixes where reflections go, and edge in pure metallic.
shading-metallics-with-ink.ink shading on armour: Mix ink into the metal and paint it into recesses and the lower part of each panel, adding more ink with each lower pass.

skin-blemishes-and-freckles.freckles: On finished skin, dot a soft dark brown, eased back with skin tone, in mixed sizes and uneven gaps, then glaze the skin tone over to blend.
skin-blemishes-and-freckles.age spots on an old face: Dot a soft dark, brown or blue with a little black eased back with skin tone, in varied sizes, some overlapping, then glaze skin tone over.
skin-blemishes-and-freckles.blemishes on skin: Add them last on finished skin: soft dark dots in mixed sizes and spacing, a few pale highlight dots for pores, and a thin skin glaze over all.
skin-blemishes-and-freckles.skin looks too smooth and perfect: Real skin is never even; dot freckles or spots in mixed sizes and tiny pale dots for pores on the lit areas, then glaze to blend.
skin-blemishes-and-freckles.pores and skin texture: Dab tiny dots of a pale skin highlight, mostly on the lit areas, so they catch the light like small bumps.
skin-blemishes-and-freckles.wrinkly old man skin detail: See: dotting age spots and pores onto finished skin, in this entry's steps 2 to 5.
skin-blemishes-and-freckles.how do i paint freckles: Mix a soft dark brown eased back with skin tone, dot it quickly in different sizes and uneven gaps, then blend with a thin skin glaze.
skin-blemishes-and-freckles.freckles look like a pattern: Break it up with a few more random dots, letting some overlap; dot quickly so your hand does not space them evenly.
skin-blemishes-and-freckles.moles and spots on a face: Dot a soft dark in mixed sizes, giving a few a lighter centre or a darker partner so they seem to sit at different depths.
skin-blemishes-and-freckles.make skin look more real: Add blemishes last: soft dark spots in mixed sizes, pale dots for pores on lit areas, then a thin glaze of the skin tone over them.

soot-and-scorch.soot on a gun barrel: Paint a heavily thinned warm brown on the barrel end, then once dry add thinned black over the very tip, fading back a little way.
soot-and-scorch.scorch marks: Use thin brown then black, a soft drybrush of off black in circles, or black pigment stippled on and fixed, heaviest at the source.
soot-and-scorch.burnt barrel tips: Thin warm brown on the end of the barrel, then thinned black over the very tip, and a dot of bright silver on the rim so the detail reads.
soot-and-scorch.exhaust stains: Base dark steel, give it three coats of a strong brown wash, then one of dark grey, and carry soot upward from the opening.
soot-and-scorch.how do i make a gun look like its been f: Paint thinned warm brown on the barrel end, add thinned black at the very tip once dry, or stipple black pigment around the muzzle.
soot-and-scorch.blackened exhaust pipes: Drybrush a little off black in soft circles at the tips with a small soft brush, carrying it upward and fading away from the source.
soot-and-scorch.heat staining on metal: Base dark steel and give it three coats of a strong brown wash, then one of dark grey.
soot-and-scorch.fire damage on a tank: See: soot, blast marks and scorching with thin paint, drybrushing and pigment, in this entry's steps 1 to 5.
soot-and-scorch.burn marks with pigment: Dab most black pigment off on tissue, stipple it on and build slowly, then fix it with pigment fixer touched on with an old brush.
soot-and-scorch.smoky muzzle: Stipple black pigment around the muzzle, building slowly, fix it, and dot bright silver on the rim of the nozzle.

spotlit-models.spotlight effect: Light only a small area, usually the head and shoulders, with a hard, bright pool that falls fast into deep dark.
spotlit-models.spotlit model: Prime black, spray or drybrush white only round the chosen centre from a narrow angle above, then paint full colour there and near black elsewhere.
spotlit-models.pool of light on a dark model: Use your full range of colour steps inside the pool and only the darkest two or three outside it, with a short, fairly hard edge.
spotlit-models.head and shoulders lit only: Spray or drybrush white only round the head and shoulders over black primer, from a narrow angle above, letting it fall off quickly.
spotlit-models.dramatic stage lighting: Choose the centre of the pool, prime black, light only that area, and keep the change from lit to dark short and fairly hard.
spotlit-models.model mostly in darkness: Use only the darkest two or three colour steps outside the lit pool, with a faint cold rim of colour so the shape still reads.
spotlit-models.how do i paint a spotlight: Pick the centre, prime black, spray white just round it from above, paint the pool in full colour and the rest close to black.
spotlit-models.hard light falling into shadow: Keep the change from lit to dark short and fairly hard, over a few millimetres, not a long soft fade.
spotlit-models.moody dark mini: See: lighting a small pool and dropping the rest into darkness, in this entry's steps 2 to 6.
spotlit-models.light just the face: Put a white dot on the face as a reminder, light only round it, and keep all highlights inside that pool.

starter-tool-kit.beginner tools: Clippers that cut flush, a hobby knife, fine sandpaper, tweezers, the right glues, a lamp, a few brushes, a palette, primer and a few colours.
starter-tool-kit.what do i need to start painting minis: A lamp, a heavy water pot, a few synthetic brushes including a size 1 or 2 round, a palette, paper towel, primer and a handful of colours.
starter-tool-kit.starter kit for a new hobbyist: Flush clippers, a hobby knife, sandpaper, tweezers, plastic glue, super glue, PVA, a desk lamp and a basic painting set.
starter-tool-kit.basic hobby tools list: Flush cutting clippers, a hobby knife, fine sandpaper or sanding sticks, tweezers, and a small hand drill with fine bits later.
starter-tool-kit.first time painting miniatures: Start with a handful of colours for the model in front of you, a few brushes, primer and a lamp; add tools as you add skills.
starter-tool-kit.which glue do i need: Plastic glue for plastic kits, super glue for metal and resin, and white PVA for basing and terrain.
starter-tool-kit.do i need a lamp to paint: Yes, a desk lamp close to the model; a daylight bulb saves your eyes.
starter-tool-kit.what brushes should a beginner get: A few synthetic brushes, including one pointed round around size 1 or 2, cleaned with brush soap after every session.
starter-tool-kit.new to the hobby what tools: Flush clippers, a hobby knife, sandpaper, tweezers, the right glues, a lamp and a basic painting set; everything else can wait.
starter-tool-kit.cheap tools to get started: Hardware and craft versions work as well as hobby branded ones, bulk scalpel blades cost far less, and an old tile makes a palette.
starter-tool-kit.I'm new. What do I need to start paintin: A lamp, a heavy water pot, a few brushes, a palette, paper towel, primer and a handful of colours for the model in front of you.

stringy-gore.drool strands: Take a blob of plain stringy contact or craft glue on a pin, touch one anchor point, pull away and touch the next.
stringy-gore.stringy blood: Use a stringy blood gel, or mix clear gloss red, a little dark brown ink and clear glue until it pulls strings, then stretch it between points.
stringy-gore.gore strings between teeth: Work from the back outwards, tongue to palate and gum to gum, touching each anchor two or three times so the strand holds.
stringy-gore.saliva strings: Pull plain stringy contact or craft glue between anchor points with a cocktail stick or pin, working fast before it thickens.
stringy-gore.drooling mouth: Pull clear glue strands from deep inside and the jaw corners outward, then gloss the inside of the mouth so it looks wet.
stringy-gore.blood strings on a sword: Mix clear gloss red, dark brown ink and clear glue until stringy, then touch one anchor, pull away and touch the next.
stringy-gore.slime strands: Use plain stringy contact or craft glue, pulled between anchor points on a cocktail stick or pin, and pick off strays once fully dry.
stringy-gore.how do i make strings of blood: Mix clear gloss red with a little dark brown ink and clear glue until it pulls strings, then stretch it between anchors with a pin.
stringy-gore.gory jaws: Pull blood strands from the back of the mouth outwards, gloss the inside of the mouth, and add a little splatter around it.
stringy-gore.spit hanging from fangs: Pull clear glue strands between the fangs, then dab gloss on a thick strand to form a hanging drop.

tentacles-and-suckers.tentacles: Base the darkest colour, work towards the tip in two or three lighter steps, smooth with glazes, then pick out suckers and gloss them.
tentacles-and-suckers.suckers: Paint each with a light rim in the pale colour, then drop a thin wash or a dark dot into the middle.
tentacles-and-suckers.octopus arms: Fade dark at the root to pale at the tip, use a paler colour on the sucker side, and finish with gloss to look wet.
tentacles-and-suckers.how do i paint tentacles: Base deep purple, work lighter towards the tip in steps, highlight along the top of each curve, pick out suckers, then gloss varnish.
tentacles-and-suckers.squid colours: A colour shift along the length, such as purple to pink to cream, with spots or stripes, suits sea creatures.
tentacles-and-suckers.kraken tentacles: See: fading tentacles dark to pale and picking out suckers, in this entry's steps 2 to 7.
tentacles-and-suckers.tentacle fade dark to pale: Base the darkest colour, then two or three lighter steps towards the tip, each covering less, smoothed with glazes or a drybrush from the tip.
tentacles-and-suckers.what colour are suckers: A paler, contrasting colour, such as a soft pink, with a light rim and a darker centre.
tentacles-and-suckers.tentacle monster: Fade each tentacle dark at the root to pale at the tip, pick out the suckers in a lighter colour, and gloss only the tentacles.
tentacles-and-suckers.tentacles look flat: Highlight along the top of each curve, use a paler colour underneath, and finish with gloss to make them look wet.

thinning-washes.wash too strong: Mix roughly equal parts wash and clear medium; if unsure add a little more medium, as you can always add a second coat.
thinning-washes.thin a wash with medium: Mix roughly equal parts wash and clear medium on the palette and stir well with a large brush.
thinning-washes.wash staining raised areas: Thin it with clear medium and brush it on one panel at a time from one spot; recesses still shade but raised areas stay lighter.
thinning-washes.wash left tide marks: Thin with medium rather than lots of water, which leaves crusty rings, and lift puddles with a clean brush dipped in pure medium.
thinning-washes.how do i dilute a wash: With clear medium, about equal parts; water is fine up to about half and half, but past that it breaks the paint.
thinning-washes.flow improver in washes: It thins a wash like medium; a tiny drop of washing up liquid or airbrush thinner also stops a wash beading on raised areas.
thinning-washes.water or medium to thin a wash: Medium. Water is fine up to about half and half, but more breaks the paint and leaves pale, crusty rings.
thinning-washes.lighter wash for shading: Thin it about half and half with clear medium; it still settles in recesses but leaves raised areas lighter.
thinning-washes.wash too dark: Thin it with clear medium, about equal parts, and build a second coat if you need it.
thinning-washes.the wash left rings: Overthinning with water breaks the paint and leaves rings; use medium instead, and lift puddles with a brush dipped in pure medium.

travel-painting-kit.painting on holiday: Pack a small, leak proof kit and a USB task lamp, cover the table, and clean up fully before you leave; expect to paint less than planned.
travel-painting-kit.portable painting kit: A few brushes in a tube, a handful of small paints, glue, brush soap, a small wet palette, tweezers and scissors, all in zip bags.
travel-painting-kit.painting away from home: Pack only the basics and a small lamp, protect the furniture with a mat, and clean the desk, sink and floor before you leave.
travel-painting-kit.painting in a hotel: Bring a small USB task lamp, as room lighting is dim and warm, cover the desk with a mat, and clean the sink and floor before leaving.
travel-painting-kit.what to pack for travel painting: A few brushes, small paints, glue, brush soap, a small wet palette, tweezers, scissors and a USB lamp; leave the airbrush and sprays home.
travel-painting-kit.painting at a friends house: Cover their desk with a mat, wipe brushes on paper towel, and clean the desk and sink and check the floor for paint flecks before you leave.
travel-painting-kit.leak proof paints for travel: Close every pot tightly and pack them in large zip bags, as paint leaks in transit; check travel rules before you fly.
travel-painting-kit.paint on the go: Keep the kit small: a few brushes, small paints, a small wet palette with its sponge damp not soaked, and a USB task lamp.
travel-painting-kit.small travel kit: A few brushes, a handful of small paints, glue, brush soap, a small wet palette, tweezers and scissors; brush on primer instead of spraying.
travel-painting-kit.protect the table when painting elsewher: Cover desks and counters with a mat, as knives, solvents and glue can mark furniture.

unclog-dropper-bottles.dropper bottle clogged: Push a thin metal pick, such as a pin or small metal toothpick, into the nozzle a couple of times, then squeeze gently.
unclog-dropper-bottles.paint wont come out: Dried paint has likely plugged the tip; push a pin into the nozzle a couple of times to break the plug, then squeeze gently.
unclog-dropper-bottles.unclog a dropper bottle: Push a thin, smooth metal pick about the size of the hole into the nozzle a couple of times, then squeeze gently.
unclog-dropper-bottles.dried paint in bottle tip: Break it up with a pin pushed into the nozzle a couple of times, then wipe the pick clean straight away.
unclog-dropper-bottles.blocked nozzle: Push a thin metal pick or pin into the nozzle a couple of times to break the plug, then squeeze gently.
unclog-dropper-bottles.nothing comes out when i squeeze: The tip is plugged with dried paint; clear it with a pin pushed in a couple of times, then squeeze gently.
unclog-dropper-bottles.clear a dropper tip: Use a thin metal pick about the size of the nozzle hole, push it in a couple of times, then squeeze gently.
unclog-dropper-bottles.pin to unblock a bottle: Yes, a pin works: push it into the nozzle a couple of times, squeeze gently, and wipe the pin clean straight away.
unclog-dropper-bottles.dropper blocked again: Wipe the nozzle and snap the cap shut after each use; that stops most plugs forming.
unclog-dropper-bottles.bottle tip crusted: Break the crust with a pin in the nozzle, and wipe the nozzle and close the cap after every use to prevent it.

using-stencils.stencils: Cut a simple design from masking film or vinyl, press every edge down, spray or dab thin coats, and let it set before lifting.
using-stencils.how do i use a stencil: Line it up against a tape guide, press every edge flat, dab or spray thin coats with paint only a little thinned, then let it set before peeling.
using-stencils.spray through a stencil: Spray thin coats of only slightly thinned paint; very runny paint creeps under the edge in spidery lines.
using-stencils.stencil numbers on a tank: Press the stencil flat into panel lines with a pick, dab or spray thin coats, and use light coverage for a worn look.
using-stencils.make my own stencil: Cut a simple, bold design from thin masking film or removable vinyl with a sharp knife or a cutting machine.
using-stencils.paint bled under the stencil: Press every edge down firmly and use paint only a little thinned; very runny paint creeps under the edge.
using-stencils.vinyl stencil for a logo: Cut it from removable vinyl, keep the design simple and bold, and use a decal instead on bumpy surfaces or for two or more colours.
using-stencils.cutting masking film: Use a sharp knife or a cutting machine, and keep the design simple and bold.
using-stencils.unit markings without freehand: Use a stencil for the main shapes: dab through it with a nearly dry sponge or spray thin coats, then finish small parts freehand.
using-stencils.stencil smudged when i lifted it: Let the paint set fully before peeling; lifting too soon pulls paint up and smears it.

very-small-models.painting tiny models: Block in bold colours with few layers, wash brown, push strong contrast, and pick out only what reads at arm's length.
very-small-models.how do i paint 10mm figures: Spray or batch the main colour, drybrush it, block in the rest roughly, wash brown, then tidy and add a few highlights on heads and shoulders.
very-small-models.6mm infantry: See: painting very small models with bold blocking, a brown wash and strong contrast, in this entry's steps 2 to 6.
very-small-models.very small minis: Prep and prime lightly, choose brighter colours than usual, use fewer steps with bigger jumps, and pick out shields, faces and spear tips.
very-small-models.small scale painting tips: Use brighter colours than usual, fewer steps with bigger jumps, thinner washes, and black lining between parts so shapes read.
very-small-models.micro scale tanks: Push contrast between neighbouring parts, such as dark metal on a bright vehicle, and thin washes more than usual so they do not flood grills and tracks.
very-small-models.how do i paint 15mm models: Block in bold, bright colours, wash everything brown, push strong contrast, and add edge highlights and a few highlights on heads.
very-small-models.tiny figures detail does not show: Nobody sees fine blends at arm's length; pick out shields, cloaks, plumes, faces and spear tips in brighter colours than usual.
very-small-models.bold colours for tiny scale: Choose a brighter version of each colour than usual so the shape reads at all, and push strong contrast between neighbouring parts.
very-small-models.what to pick out on small minis: Shields, cloaks, plumes, faces and spear tips; fine blends and small straps are not seen at arm's length.

washes-on-metallics.wash on metal: Keep washes to recesses, rivets and edges for bright metal, or wash all over and layer the metal back on raised areas.
washes-on-metallics.wash silver: Blue gives cold steel, black dark iron, brown or yellow oily or aged metal, and sepia warms it towards gold.
washes-on-metallics.wash gold: Purple looks rich, green looks aged or tarnished, and red or yellow deepen the warmth.
washes-on-metallics.blue wash over silver: Blue over silver gives cold steel; keep top highlights less blue so it still reads as steel.
washes-on-metallics.brown wash on gold: See: how each wash colour changes gold, in this entry's step 3.
washes-on-metallics.metal dull after wash: Every layer hides some flakes; layer the metal back on raised areas and add a brighter dot on the high points.
washes-on-metallics.tint metallics: Use a see through wash or heavily diluted ink, which keeps most of the shine; a one coat paint tints strongly but goes matt.
washes-on-metallics.which wash for steel: Blue for cold steel, black for dark iron, or black mixed half and half with a coloured wash for a tinted steel.
washes-on-metallics.aged oily metal: Wash silver with brown or yellow for an oily, aged look.
washes-on-metallics.wash on silver went flat: Layer silver back on the raised areas with a brighter dot on high points, and keep future washes to recesses, rivets and edges.

weathering-order.weathering order: Chips and scratches first, then streaks and grime, then soot and dust last, and stop early.
weathering-order.what order to weather a tank: Transfers, then chips and scratches, then rust streaks, oil stains and grime washes, then soot and finally dust rising from the ground.
weathering-order.chips before or after streaks: Chips first; they then guide where rust streaks and stains go.
weathering-order.when do i add dust: Last, with soot, as a light drybrush or pigment of dusty brown rising from the ground and fading upwards.
weathering-order.how much weathering is too much: Check from arm's length often and stop when you are happy, before it buries the paintwork; it is easy to add and hard to remove.
weathering-order.transfers before weathering: Yes, apply transfers before any weathering so they get chipped and dirtied with the rest.
weathering-order.weathering steps: Chips and scratches, then liquid effects like rust streaks, oil and grime washes, then soot and dust.
weathering-order.overdid the weathering: See: checking from arm's length and stopping early, in this entry's final step.
weathering-order.battle damage order: Damage in the paint comes first: sponge chips on corners and worn areas, then streaks and grime, then soot and dust.
weathering-order.weathering sequence vehicles: Transfers, chips and scratches, rust streaks and oil stains, grime washes low down, then soot and dust last.

wet-palette.wet palette: A tray of soaked paper towel under non waxed baking parchment keeps thinned paint fresh and the same consistency for hours.
wet-palette.diy wet palette: Fold about four layers of paper towel into a shallow tray, soak it until almost floating, then lay non waxed baking parchment flat on top.
wet-palette.paint drying on my palette: A wet palette keeps thinned paint workable for hours; keep paint in small, compact blobs.
wet-palette.how to make a wet palette: Soak about four layers of paper towel or a sponge in a shallow tray, then press non waxed baking parchment flat on top.
wet-palette.baking paper palette: Use non waxed baking parchment over soaked paper towel; wax paper will not work, as it blocks the moisture.
wet-palette.paint stays wet for hours: That is a wet palette: soaked towel under baking parchment, and with the lid on, paint often keeps for a day or more.
wet-palette.palette dries out too fast: Use plenty of water so it does not dry mid session, keep paint in compact blobs, and keep the lid on between sessions.
wet-palette.wet pallet: Soaked paper towel in a tray under non waxed baking parchment keeps thinned paint workable for hours.
wet-palette.do i need a wet palette: No. Any smooth, hard surface works; a wet palette just gives more working time for blending and glazing.
wet-palette.paint too watery on wet palette: Pour off water pooling on top; for sharp edge highlights, washes and inks, use a dry white tile instead.

white-armour.white armour: Base off white in thin coats, shade only the recesses with a warm brown or light grey wash, clean up, then edge brighter white and pure white.
white-armour.white armor: Off white base, recess shading in brown or grey, cleanup with the base colour, then edge highlights finishing in pure white on top edges.
white-armour.clean white plate: Shade only the recesses with a thin brush, clean any stray wash off the panels with the base colour, then add sharp pure white edges.
white-armour.white knight armour: Prime white or light grey, base off white, shade the recesses neatly, tidy with the base colour, and edge in brighter then pure white.
white-armour.how do i paint white armour: Base off white until smooth, shade only the recesses, clean up strays with the base colour, then edge highlight brighter white and pure white.
white-armour.white armour shading: Shade only the recesses with a warm brown or light grey wash; brown keeps white warm, blue grey keeps it cool.
white-armour.white armour edges: Edge highlight every edge in a brighter white, then a smaller final highlight of pure white on the top edges.
white-armour.white armour looks grey: Too dark a shadow all over makes it read as grey; keep shading to the recesses and clean the panels back with off white.
white-armour.white armour recipe: Off white base, a warm brown or grey recess shade, cleanup with the base colour, brighter white edges and pure white on top edges.
white-armour.clean white without going dirty: Keep the wash to the recesses, clean strays off the panels with the base colour, and plan for that cleanup step.

zenithal-priming.zenithal: Prime dark, then spray white or pale grey from above, so the model starts with its lighting already in place.
zenithal-priming.zenithal priming: Prime black or dark, then spray white or pale grey straight down from above, turning the model but keeping the spray overhead.
zenithal-priming.how do i zenithal prime: Prime the whole model dark, then spray white from straight overhead, turning the model so every upward surface gets some, and stop once tops are white.
zenithal-priming.spray white from above: Yes, over a dark prime; stop once the tops are white, as piling on coats leaves a chalky surface.
zenithal-priming.prime black then white: Prime black, then spray white from overhead so recesses and undersides stay dark and the model looks lit from above.
