zenithal-priming.zenithal undercoat: A dark prime with white or pale grey sprayed from above; thin paints and washes over it pick up the light and dark for free.
zenithal-priming.pre shading with primer: Spray dark, then light from above, or dark, mid and light shades of one colour, each from a higher angle.
zenithal-priming.zenithal with rattle can: Use a fresh, well shaken can in short bursts, as cans go speckled and grainy, especially when nearly empty.
zenithal-priming.what is zenithal highlight: Priming dark then spraying light from above, so recesses and undersides stay dark and the model already looks lit from above.
zenithal-priming.zenithal for contrast: Yes: thin one coat paints over a zenithal undercoat pick up the light and dark for free; a thin satin varnish first helps them flow evenly.

ash-wastes.grey ash base: Spread fine texture paste with sand over dark rocks and scrap, wash it a thin grey, then drybrush off white very lightly.
ash-wastes.ashy wasteland base: Glue down bark rocks and scrap, bank texture paste against them, wash the ground grey and paint the rocks near black.
ash-wastes.how do i make a burnt ground base: Try grey ash: texture paste washed dark grey with charcoal dotted into hollows, near black rocks, then a very light off white drybrush.
ash-wastes.post apocalyptic base with scrap: Glue small scrap such as canisters or pipes among bark rocks, then bank texture paste up against it so it sits half buried.
ash-wastes.base that looks like the aftermath of a: For a dead ash look, bank grey washed texture paste round near black rocks and dust it very lightly with off white.
ash-wastes.dead grey ground with dark rocks: Paint the rocks near black, wash the paste ground with a thin dark grey, dot charcoal into hollows and drybrush off white lightly.
ash-wastes.ash covered battlefield base: Bank texture paste against rocks and half buried scrap, sponge it into soft drifts, then wash it grey and drybrush off white.
ash-wastes.how to paint ash on a base: Wash the ground with grey thinned right down with water and a drop of matt varnish, dot charcoal into hollows, then dust off white lightly.
ash-wastes.scorched earth base idea: Try grey ash over near black rocks and half buried scrap, with charcoal dotted into the tracks and hollows while the grey is wet.
ash-wastes.gray dusty ruined ground with junk: Press sand and stones into thick texture paste around scrap bits, wash it dark grey and give it a very light off white drybrush.

cork-and-texture-gel.how do i make rocks out of cork: Tear coarse sheet cork by twisting pliers in it, trim each piece flat underneath, glue it down and gouge smooth faces with a pin.
cork-and-texture-gel.cork rocks look like cork not stone: Use coarse sheet cork with large, loose grains, as fine pressed cork looks like cork, and gouge any smooth faces with a pin.
cork-and-texture-gel.quick rocky ground for bases: Glue torn cork rocks down, spread coarse texture gel round them with grit pressed in, then base dark brown and drybrush up to light stone.
cork-and-texture-gel.cork board basing: Tear coarse sheet cork into rocks rather than using fine pressed cork, which looks like cork instead of stone.
cork-and-texture-gel.tearing cork for rocks: Twist pliers into coarse sheet cork to tear out rocks with natural edges, then trim each piece flat underneath before gluing.
cork-and-texture-gel.rocky base with texture paste: Glue cork rocks down, then spread coarse texture gel round them so it slopes to the base, pressing grit into it while wet.
cork-and-texture-gel.what's the cheapest way to make rocky te: Torn cork, even old bottle corks, under coarse texture gel gives quick rocky earth; prime it, then drybrush grey brown and light stone.
cork-and-texture-gel.make cork look like stone: Use coarse cork, gouge smooth faces with a pin, base dark brown, then drybrush grey brown and a light stone on the top edges.
cork-and-texture-gel.rubble and rocks on a base: Glue torn cork rocks down, spread coarse texture gel round them and press grit or small cork chips into it while it is wet.
cork-and-texture-gel.cliff base from cork: Tear coarse sheet cork into rocks with pliers, trim them flat underneath and glue them down, then blend them in with texture gel.

foam-hills.make hills for a display board: Spray expanding foam on a wooden board or stack cut foam board, carve the slopes, then cover it in fine filler and black tinted matt sealer.
foam-hills.carving expanding foam: Carve slopes and cliff faces with a long snap off blade in several passes, changing blades often.
foam-hills.spray foam cliffs: Spray less foam than you think, as it grows, carve cliff faces with a long blade, then slice cracks and widen them with a blunt tool.
foam-hills.how to build a cliff face for a diorama: Carve foam into cliff faces with a long blade in several passes, slice cracks with a fine knife, then fill and seal it before painting.
foam-hills.lightweight hills terrain: Use expanding foam or stacked foam board, carved into slopes, then covered in fine filler and matt sealer mixed with black.
foam-hills.foam board layered hill: Stack cut layers of extruded foam board, carve the steps into slopes, then smooth the steps over with fine surface filler.
foam-hills.cut insulation foam into rocks: Cut extruded foam board with a long blade in several passes, then slice cracks with a fine knife and widen them with a blunt tool.
foam-hills.expanding foam grew too much: Expanding foam grows, so use less than you think next time; carve the excess away with a long blade, changing blades often.
foam-hills.big rocky outcrop for display plinth: Carve foam into a cliff, cover it with filler and black tinted matt sealer, base dark grey brown and drybrush light stone grey.
foam-hills.how do i make a mountain for my scene: Build the bulk from expanding foam or stacked foam board, carve slopes and cliffs, fill and seal it, paint it, then add trees and tufts.

puddles-and-water.puddles on a base: Finish the ground first, then fill the dips in thin layers of thick gloss tinted with a single drop of paint.
puddles-and-water.how to make water on a base: Stir one drop of tinted paint into thick gloss and fill the low parts in thin layers; for deeper water, pour two part resin in layers.
puddles-and-water.water effects base: Use tinted gloss or water gel in the dips, resin for deeper water, and water gel dragged into rings round rocks for ripples.
puddles-and-water.muddy puddle: Darken the mud round each dip first, as wet earth is darker, then fill it with gloss tinted with a drop of yellow brown.
puddles-and-water.swamp water base: Darken the bottom of the dip with a murky green brown, then fill it with thick gloss tinted with a drop of yellow brown.
puddles-and-water.realistic rain puddles: Darken the mud round each dip, fill it with thin layers of tinted gloss, and pull a little out with a wet brush for damp ground.
puddles-and-water.gloss varnish puddle: Stir a single drop of tinted paint into thick gloss varnish and fill the dip in thin layers, popping bubbles with a toothpick.
puddles-and-water.how to use water gel: Drag thick water gel into rings round rocks for ripples, then gloss over it to level and clear the surface.
puddles-and-water.wet mud around a puddle: Darken the mud round the dip, as wet earth is darker, and pull a little of the gloss out onto it with a wet brush.
puddles-and-water.my puddle looks fake: Darken the ground round the dip, use only one drop of tint, gloss over any cloudy water, and add a fine pale blue shine line at the edge.

sea-waves.how do i make sea waves on a base: Press fast setting putty onto the base and push it into curling waves with quick, firm strokes, then base deep blue and drybrush lighter.
sea-waves.crashing surf on a rock: Glue a torn cork rock over two thirds of the base, sculpt putty waves against it and drybrush white where the foam hits the rock.
sea-waves.water effects for waves: Shape waves from putty or thick water gel, base midnight blue, drybrush icy blue then white, and gloss the water only.
sea-waves.ocean base with breaking waves: Sculpt curling putty waves round a cork rock, base deep midnight blue, drybrush icy blue up the wave faces, then white on the crests.
sea-waves.sculpting waves with putty: Knead the putty until the colour is even, press it on and push it into curling waves with quick, firm strokes, as it sets in minutes.
sea-waves.foamy white sea spray: Drybrush white only on the wave crests and where the foam hits the rock, over an icy light blue.
sea-waves.model standing on a rock in the sea: Glue a carved cork rock over about two thirds of the base, sculpt waves round it, and fix the figure on once everything is painted.
sea-waves.stormy sea basing: Push putty into curling waves against a cork rock, keep deep midnight blue in the hollows and drybrush white on the crests.
sea-waves.sea foam base: Drybrush up the wave faces in icy light blue, mixing lighter each pass, then white on the crests and where the water meets the rock.
sea-waves.wave base for a mermaid or sea monster: Sculpt curling putty waves round a cork rock, leaving flat room for the feet, then paint the water and gloss it so it looks wet.

tinted-moss-on-rocks.moss on rocks: Drop light green onto the tops and shaded sides of drybrushed rocks, push it round with a very wet brush, then add darker green patches.
tinted-moss-on-rocks.quick mossy stones: On a finished drybrushed base, drop light green onto the rocks and spread it with a very wet brush so it settles into the texture.
tinted-moss-on-rocks.how to add moss to a base: Tint drybrushed rocks with light then darker green using a very wet brush; for raised moss, glue fine scatter into the cracks.
tinted-moss-on-rocks.green tint for moss: Use a light green one coat paint pushed round with a very wet brush, then a darker green with a touch of brown in a few places.
tinted-moss-on-rocks.make rocks look damp and overgrown: Let light and deep green settle into the rock texture on the tops and shaded sides, then glue fine scatter into cracks for raised moss.
tinted-moss-on-rocks.mossy base fast: Drop light green onto a painted, drybrushed base, push it round with a wet brush, then drybrush pale bone very lightly once dry.
tinted-moss-on-rocks.lichen on base rocks: See: the tinted moss method here, light green dropped onto the rocks and spread with a very wet brush, in howto steps 2 and 3.
tinted-moss-on-rocks.green patches on grey rocks: Drop light green onto the tops and shaded sides, spread it with a very wet brush, then add a few darker green patches inside it.
tinted-moss-on-rocks.overgrown stone base: Glaze light and deep green moss into the rock texture, then glue fine scatter into cracks and dull it with brown ink for raised moss.
tinted-moss-on-rocks.add a bit of green to my rocky base: Drop a little light green onto the rocks and push it round with a very wet clean brush; it looks patchy until it dries.

aged-dirty-bone.bone colour: Base a dull olive brown, layer olive bone then pale grey bone, and wash it all with a green brown.
aged-dirty-bone.how to paint skulls: Base olive brown, layer olive bone, put pale grey bone on skull tops and raised points, then wash green brown, heavier in the sockets.
aged-dirty-bone.dirty old bones: Build up from olive brown to pale grey bone, then wash everything with brown and a touch of green, heavier in the cracks.
aged-dirty-bone.skeleton bone color: An olive brown base, an olive bone layer, pale grey bone highlights, then a green brown wash over all of it.
aged-dirty-bone.make bone look old and stained: Finish with a green brown wash over all the bone, left heavier in sockets and cracks, over an olive brown and bone build up.
aged-dirty-bone.skull pile: Base dull olive brown, layer olive bone, catch the skull tops with pale grey bone, then wash green brown into the sockets.
aged-dirty-bone.my bone looks too clean: Wash it with brown and a touch of green, left heavier in sockets and cracks, and start from an olive brown base rather than pale bone.
aged-dirty-bone.undead skeletons bone: Base a dull olive brown over a dark undercoat, layer olive bone and pale grey bone, then wash it all green brown.
aged-dirty-bone.aged yellowed bone: Start from a dull olive brown, build up olive bone and pale grey bone, then stain it with a green brown wash.
aged-dirty-bone.grimy bone recipe: Base olive brown, layer olive bone, highlight pale grey bone, then wash green brown, heavier in sockets and cracks.

black-leather.how do i paint black leather: Base black over black primer, layer a soft black on raised areas, then edge in dark grey and a light cool grey on the highest points.
black-leather.black leather jacket: Thin black base, soft black on raised areas, chunky dark grey lines on the main folds, then small light cool grey strokes on top.
black-leather.black boots and belts: Base black, layer soft black on raised areas, then edge highlight dark grey and dot light cool grey on the highest points.
black-leather.leather looks plastic: See: the highlight steps here; keep light grey to small strokes and dots, and add a little pink to the grey to soften it.
black-leather.grey highlights on black leather: Edge main folds with chunky dark grey lines, then add small light cool grey strokes and dots on the highest points.
black-leather.smart black leather with a sheen: A thin black coat over black primer keeps a soft sheen; then layer soft black on raised areas and edge in dark grey and cool grey.
black-leather.black gloves: Base black, soft black on raised areas, dark grey on the main folds, then tiny light cool grey dots on the highest points.
black-leather.clean black straps: Base black, edge the straps in dark grey, add light cool grey only on the highest points, and tidy wobbles with thinned black.
black-leather.black coat highlights: Leave the folds deepest, put chunky dark grey lines on main folds and edges, then small light cool grey strokes on the highest points.
black-leather.black leather armour: Base black, layer soft black on raised areas, edge highlight in dark grey, then light cool grey on the highest points.

bright-blue-armour.bright blue armour: Base a mid blue, line recesses with thinned dark navy, edge in a lighter blue, then pale blue grey on the sharpest edges.
bright-blue-armour.how do i paint blue armor: Mid blue base, dark navy lined into the recesses, lighter blue on every edge, then pale blue grey and dots on the corners.
bright-blue-armour.crisp mid blue power armour: Base an even mid blue, line it with thinned dark navy, then edge in lighter blue and finish the sharpest edges pale blue grey.
bright-blue-armour.blue armour edge highlights: Mix base with a brighter blue for every edge, go finer with pure bright blue, then pale blue grey on the sharpest edges only.
bright-blue-armour.dark lining on blue: Mix dark blue with black, two to one, thin it right down and line it into the recesses.
bright-blue-armour.clean vibrant blue plates: Even mid blue coats, thinned dark navy lining, then lighter blue edges and pale blue dots on the corners.
bright-blue-armour.light blue edges: Edge with base mixed with a brighter blue, then pure bright blue finer, and pale blue grey on the sharpest edges only.
bright-blue-armour.royal blue armour plates: Base a mid blue, line the recesses dark navy, and edge in lighter blue then pale blue grey on the sharpest edges.
bright-blue-armour.make blue armour pop: Line recesses with dark navy for contrast, edge every edge in lighter blue, then dot pale blue on the corners.
bright-blue-armour.blue armour recipe for a squad: Base mid blue by brush or airbrush, line dark navy into recesses, edge lighter blue, then pale blue grey on the sharpest edges.

candles.candles: Base pale greenish cream, blend up to near white on the rim and drips, then paint the flame orange with yellow and a white dot at its base.
candles.how to paint candles: Base pale greenish cream, blend softly to near white on the top rim and drip ends, then paint an orange flame with a white dot at its base.
candles.candle wax: Base pale greenish cream and blend up softly to near white on the top rim and drip ends; hard steps spoil the wax.
candles.candle flame: Fill the flame orange, add yellow dots near its base, then a tiny white dot at the bottom centre.
candles.melting candle drips: Blend the wax softly up to near white on the drip ends and the top rim, avoiding hard steps.
candles.candles look like plastic: Blend the wax up softly, as hard steps spoil it, and save the near white for the top rim and drip ends.
candles.candles on a shrine: Pale greenish cream wax blended to near white at the rim and drips, with orange flames that go yellow and white at their base.
candles.old dirty wax candle: Add a touch of green or black to the pale cream base coat for old candles, then blend up softly.
candles.tiny candle flame glow: Paint the flame orange, dot yellow near its base, then put a tiny white dot at the bottom centre where it is brightest.
candles.red wax candles: Base the wax a deep red instead of pale cream, then paint the flame orange with yellow dots and a white dot at its base.

dark-green-armour.quick dark green armour: Base dark green, wash black all over, drybrush dark green on flat panels, then flick bright green across the edges.
dark-green-armour.how do i batch paint green armour: Even dark green coats, a black wash all over, then a dark green drybrush and bright green flicked across the edges.
dark-green-armour.fast green army: Dark green base, black wash, dark green drybrush on flat panels, then bright green on edges and paler green on the sharpest.
dark-green-armour.dark green with a wash and drybrush: Wash black over dark green, lift pools on flat plates, let it dry fully, then drybrush dark green and flick bright green on edges.
dark-green-armour.speed painting green troops: Base dark green, wash black, then two drybrushes: dark green on the panels and bright green flicked across the edges.
dark-green-armour.green armour for a big horde: Use a dark green base, a black wash and two drybrushes, dark green then bright green, so the whole group goes quickly.
dark-green-armour.green armour plates quickly: Black wash over dark green, lifting pools on flat plates, then soft round drybrush strokes of dark green leaving recesses dark.
dark-green-armour.tabletop green plates: Base dark green, wash black, drybrush dark green on the panels and bright green on the edges, with paler green on the sharpest.
dark-green-armour.drybrush green armour: Use soft round strokes of dark green on flat panels, leaving recesses dark, then flick bright green across the edges.
dark-green-armour.easy green soldiers: Paint dark green, wash black all over, then drybrush dark green and flick bright green across the edges.

fiery-red-glow.lava glow: Paint the source, drybrush deep red outwards, glaze thin deep red over it, drybrush orange closer in, then touch yellow at the brightest point.
fiery-red-glow.red glowing cracks: Paint the crack, drybrush deep red outwards around it, then orange closer to it and a touch of yellow at the brightest point.
fiery-red-glow.how to paint fire coming from cracks: Drybrush deep red out from the crack, glaze it thin deep red, drybrush bright orange nearer the crack, and add yellow right at the hottest point.
fiery-red-glow.magma crack glow: Deep red drybrushed out from the crack, a thin deep red glaze, bright orange closer in, then a touch of yellow at the brightest point.
fiery-red-glow.hot red glow on the ground: Drybrush deep red outwards from the source, glaze thin deep red over the lit area, then drybrush orange nearer the source.
fiery-red-glow.orange glow near a source: Drybrush bright orange softer and closer to the source over a deep red glow, with yellow only at the brightest point.
fiery-red-glow.fiery runes glowing: See: this glow method, drybrushing deep red then orange outwards from a source with yellow at the brightest point.
fiery-red-glow.molten rock base: See: this recipe for glowing cracks: deep red drybrushed out from them, orange nearer, and yellow at the brightest point.
fiery-red-glow.glow looks chalky: Glaze a very thin deep red over the lit area to tint it and remove the chalkiness.
fiery-red-glow.red osl from a crack: Drybrush deep red outwards from the crack, glaze it thin deep red, add orange closer in and a touch of yellow at the brightest point.

graded-horns-and-tusks.horns: Base pale bone, wash sepia all over, then glaze red brown and finally very dark brown towards the root or tip, each coat stopping shorter.
graded-horns-and-tusks.how to paint horns: Base a pale bone, stain it with a sepia wash, then build red brown glazes towards the root or tip and finish the very end in dark brown.
graded-horns-and-tusks.tusks: Base pale bone, wash sepia to fill the ridges, then glaze red brown and very dark brown towards the root, each coat stopping shorter.
graded-horns-and-tusks.gradient horns: Glaze red brown over pale bone and sepia, stopping each coat shorter, then very dark brown on only the last part of the root or point.
graded-horns-and-tusks.ivory tusks: Cover a dark primer with a few thin coats of pale bone, wash sepia over it, then glaze red brown towards the root.
graded-horns-and-tusks.dark tipped horns: Over pale bone and sepia, glaze red brown towards the tip in coats that stop shorter each time, then very dark brown on the point only.
graded-horns-and-tusks.ram horns: Base pale bone, or warm brown for darker horns, wash sepia into the ridges, then glaze red brown and very dark brown towards one end.
graded-horns-and-tusks.horn colour: A pale bone base stained with sepia, grading through red brown to a very dark brown at the root or tip.
graded-horns-and-tusks.blend horns from dark to light: Build the dark end with glazes that each stop shorter than the last: red brown first, then very dark brown on the last part only.
graded-horns-and-tusks.tusks look flat: Wash sepia over the whole tusk to fill the ridges, then glaze red brown and very dark brown towards the root so it grades in tone.

grimy-olive-armour.olive drab: Base pale olive green over black, glaze a thinned green brown on lower panels, line dark brown green between panels, then edge khaki.
grimy-olive-armour.military green armour: Pale olive green base, green brown glazes on the lower panels, dark brown green lining, then pale olive and khaki edges.
grimy-olive-armour.grimy dirty green armour: Glaze a green brown shade, thinned half with water, over pale olive on the lower panels, then line the panel gaps in dark brown green.
grimy-olive-armour.how do i paint muddy olive green: Base a pale olive green, build up a half thinned green brown glaze on lower panels, line dark brown green, and edge in khaki.
grimy-olive-armour.khaki highlights on green: Edge all the edges in pale olive, then sharp khaki, with white on the top corners only.
grimy-olive-armour.worn army green: Base pale olive green, glaze green brown on lower panels, line dark brown green between panels, then pale olive and khaki edges.
grimy-olive-armour.drab green for infantry: Pale olive green over black primer, a thinned green brown glaze low down, dark brown green lining and khaki edge highlights.
grimy-olive-armour.olive green tank: Airbrush pale olive green over black, build a green brown glaze on lower panels, line the panels dark brown green, then edge khaki.
grimy-olive-armour.dirty green weathered look: Build up a green brown shade thinned half with water on the lower panels, so the olive gets grimier towards the ground.
grimy-olive-armour.camo green: See: grimy olive armour, a pale olive green with green brown glazes, dark lining and khaki edges, in steps 1 to 4.

metallic-blue.candy blue: Paint two smooth coats of bright silver, then see through blue grey and then an even strong blue over it, and edge in silver.
metallic-blue.metallic blue armour: Silver base, see through blue grey panel by panel, an even coat of see through strong blue, then fine silver on the sharpest edges.
metallic-blue.shiny blue metal: Lay down smooth bright silver, then see through blue over it so the shine shows through, and pick the sharpest edges in silver.
metallic-blue.blue over silver: Over two smooth coats of silver, coat see through blue grey one panel at a time, then an even see through strong blue.
metallic-blue.how to paint candy paint: Put down smooth bright silver, then coat see through colour over it evenly; the shine shows through everything on top.
metallic-blue.tinted metallic: Base bright silver, then build see through colour over it, blue grey first and strong blue on top, and edge in silver.
metallic-blue.glossy blue metal look: Two smooth coats of bright silver, then see through blue grey and strong blue over the top, with fine silver edge highlights.
metallic-blue.blue ink over silver: See: candy metallic blue, see through blue over smooth silver, in steps 1 to 3.
metallic-blue.coloured metal armour: Base smooth silver and coat see through colour over it, or use a coloured metallic paint over black instead.
metallic-blue.jewel blue metallic: Smooth silver, see through blue grey for depth, an even see through strong blue, then fine bright silver lines on the sharpest edges.

orange-flames.fire: Base warm yellow orange over black, glaze yellows at the base and oranges up, red on the tips, then white deep at the base.
orange-flames.flames: Over black, base yellow orange, glaze yellow low and orange high, deep red on the tips, white in the base and a smoky grey tip line.
orange-flames.how to paint fire: Base warm yellow orange in thin coats over black, glaze yellow at the base, orange up and deep red at the tips, then white at the root.
orange-flames.flame effect: Grade from white and yellow at the base through orange to deep red tips, finishing with a smoky grey line on the very tips.
orange-flames.torch flame: Base warm yellow orange, glaze yellow at the base and orange upwards, red only on the tips, then white deep in the base recesses.
orange-flames.fire looks flat: Put white deep in the base recesses, keep orange in the middle, darken only the tips with red then red and black, and add a smoky grey tip line.
orange-flames.burning: Paint flames over black: yellow orange base, yellow low, orange up, deep red tips, white at the root and smoky grey on the very tips.
orange-flames.flamer flames: Base yellow orange over black, glaze yellow at the base and orange towards the tips, then red and red with black on the tips only.
orange-flames.smoky flame tips: Glaze red, then red with black, on the tips only, and finish with a smoky grey line on the very tips.
orange-flames.paint fire over black: Use thin, fast coats of warm yellow orange over black so the surface stays smooth, then glaze yellows low and oranges high.

pearl-white-metal.pearl white metal: Prime white, airbrush very pale silver in two or three coats, wash white mixed with dark metallic wash into recesses, then tidy in pale silver.
pearl-white-metal.white metallic armour: Over white primer, build two or three thin coats of very pale silver, then flood a grey wash loosely into the recesses.
pearl-white-metal.pale silver over white: Prime white, as it helps a pale metallic cover far better, then build up two or three thin coats of very pale silver.
pearl-white-metal.how do i get pearly armour: Very pale silver over white primer, a mid grey wash of white and dark metallic wash in the recesses, then pale silver over any heavy pools.
pearl-white-metal.metallic white: Prime white and airbrush or brush two or three coats of very pale silver, then shade with a loose mid grey wash.
pearl-white-metal.silver looks grey over black: Prime white instead; a white primer helps a pale metallic cover far better than black.
pearl-white-metal.shiny white armour: Build very pale silver over white primer, wash mid grey into the recesses, then tidy heavy pools with pale silver once dry.
pearl-white-metal.pearlescent finish: Over a white primer, build up two or three thin coats of very pale silver, then shade with a mid grey wash.
pearl-white-metal.pale shimmering metal: Very pale silver in two or three thin coats over white primer, shaded with a loose wash of white mixed with dark metallic wash.
pearl-white-metal.white primer under silver: Yes for pale metals: a white primer helps a pale metallic cover far better, so the silver builds up in two or three coats.

quick-bright-gem.quick gems: Base near black, paint a white crescent on the side away from the light, glaze the gem colour over it, then dot white on the lit side.
quick-bright-gem.how do i paint gems fast: Near black base, a solid white crescent away from the light, any gem colour glazed over, and a small white dot facing the light.
quick-bright-gem.bright gemstone: Paint a white crescent on the side away from the light first, so the colour glazed over it glows against the black.
quick-bright-gem.jewel painting: Base the jewel near black, add a white crescent opposite the light, glaze your colour over it, then a white dot on the lit side.
quick-bright-gem.white under gem colour: Paint a solid white crescent on the side away from the light, then glaze the gem colour over it so it glows and blends into the black.
quick-bright-gem.easy gem: Black, a white crescent away from the light, a colour glaze over everything, then one white dot facing the light.
quick-bright-gem.make gems glow: Put a white patch under the colour on the side away from the light, so the glaze over it glows bright.
quick-bright-gem.red gem on a sword pommel: Base it near black, paint a white crescent away from the light, glaze red over it, then dot white on the side facing the light.
quick-bright-gem.gem looks dull: Paint a solid white crescent under the colour on the side away from the light, glaze over it, and add a small white dot facing the light.
quick-bright-gem.painting a crystal on a staff: See: quick bright gem, a near black base, white crescent and colour glaze, which suits any gem; steps 1 to 4.

silver-tipped-gold.gold: Base warm gold, glaze warm brown into the shadows, line dark brown in the deepest gaps, then edge with gold mixed with more silver each stage.
silver-tipped-gold.how to paint gold: Two thin coats of warm gold, brown ink glazed into the shadows, brown and black in the deepest gaps, then gold edges brightened with silver.
silver-tipped-gold.gold trim: Base warm gold, or a gold and silver mix for brighter trim, shade with brown, then edge with pale gold and pure silver on the sharpest points.
silver-tipped-gold.gold looks yellow and flat: Shade it with thin brown or red brown glazes, line the deepest gaps with brown and black, then edge it with gold and silver.
silver-tipped-gold.shading gold: Glaze thin brown or red brown ink into the shadows, dragged down to the darkest point, then brown with black in the deepest gaps.
silver-tipped-gold.gold armour: Warm gold base, brown glazes in the shadows, dark brown lining, gold laid back on raised parts, then silvery edge highlights.
silver-tipped-gold.brighter gold trim: Mix gold and silver for the base coat, and add more silver to the gold at each highlight stage.
silver-tipped-gold.metallic gold edges: Edge with gold mixed with more silver each stage, finishing with pure silver on the sharpest points.
silver-tipped-gold.gold with silver edge highlights: Add more silver to the gold at each highlight stage, then use pure silver on only the sharpest points.
silver-tipped-gold.golden trim on armor: Base warm gold in thin coats, shade with brown glazes and brown black lining, then edge pale gold and pure silver on the sharpest points.

turquoise-lenses.turquoise lenses: Base dark turquoise leaving a black ring in the recess, layer bright turquoise towards the middle, then a pale turquoise dot or line.
turquoise-lenses.teal glowing lenses: Dark turquoise base with a black ring left round it, bright turquoise towards the centre, and a fine pale turquoise centre highlight.
turquoise-lenses.how do i paint a glowing lens: Make it glow from the middle out: dark base with a black ring, a brighter layer towards the centre, then a pale dot in the middle.
turquoise-lenses.cyan eye lenses: Base dark turquoise leaving a black ring, layer bright turquoise towards the middle, then one pale turquoise dot.
turquoise-lenses.blue green helmet eyes: Dark turquoise with a black ring in the recess, bright turquoise towards the centre, then a pale turquoise line or dot.
turquoise-lenses.glowing gem in teal: See: turquoise lenses, which glow from the middle out over a dark ring, in steps 1 to 3.
turquoise-lenses.lens with dark ring: Leave a black ring in the recess when you base the lens dark turquoise, then brighten it towards the middle.
turquoise-lenses.helmet lenses: Base dark turquoise leaving a black ring, layer bright turquoise towards the middle, and finish with a fine pale centre line or dot.
turquoise-lenses.turquoise glow: Grade from dark turquoise at the rim to bright turquoise in the middle, with one pale turquoise dot or fine line in the centre.
turquoise-lenses.aqua lenses: Dark turquoise base with a black ring kept in the recess, bright turquoise towards the middle, then a pale turquoise dot.

wine-purple-cloth.burgundy cloth: Base pink purple and deep red, three to one, with black for cloth, glaze darker low down, then edge dusky pink and pale pink.
wine-purple-cloth.wine coloured robes: Mix pink purple and deep red three to one, add black for cloth, glaze it darker on the lower half, then edge with bone added.
wine-purple-cloth.deep purple cloak: Base a pinkish burgundy darkened with black, glaze dark burgundy towards the lower half, then edge in dusky pink and pale pink.
wine-purple-cloth.how to paint maroon: See: wine purple cloth, a pink purple and deep red mix darkened with black, in steps 1 and 2.
wine-purple-cloth.purple shield: Base pink purple and deep red three to one, glaze darker towards the lower half, then edge dusky pink and pale pink on the corners.
wine-purple-cloth.rich red purple: Mix pink purple with deep red, three to one, and glaze a darker version towards the lower half.
wine-purple-cloth.plum coloured fabric: Base pinkish burgundy with a little black, glaze dark burgundy low down, then highlight with bone added to the base and pale pink corners.
wine-purple-cloth.dark purple cloth recipe: Pinkish burgundy with black for the base, a dark burgundy glaze, dusky pink edges and pale pink on the sharpest corners.
wine-purple-cloth.mixing burgundy: Mix pink purple and deep red, three to one, and add black when it is for cloth.
wine-purple-cloth.claret cloak: Base pink purple and deep red with black, glaze dark burgundy towards the hem, then edge in dusky pink and pale pink corners.

added-panel-lines.panel lines: Paint each new panel line thin and near black with a fine brush, then run a fine pale line along the side facing the light.
added-panel-lines.add more detail to plain armour: Add painted panel lines with a pale edge on the lit side, plus a few small markings, numbers or warning stripes.
added-panel-lines.freehand panel lines: Use well thinned near black and a fine brush, pull the line from a rivet as a guide, and add a fine pale line on the lit side.
added-panel-lines.tank looks too plain: Paint in extra panel lines with a fine pale edge, and add a few small, thin markings, numbers or warning stripes.
added-panel-lines.vehicle markings: Keep markings small and thin, use an opaque paint, and paint the pale colour first, as dark covers pale more easily.
added-panel-lines.make a plain vehicle look detailed: Add dark panel lines with a fine pale edge on the lit side, plus a few small markings; small markings make a big machine look bigger.
added-panel-lines.big empty panels look boring: Break them up with painted panel lines and a few small markings or stripes, taking positions from a more detailed version of the design.
added-panel-lines.paint lines on a smooth hull: Paint thin near black lines with a fine brush, using a rivet as a guide, then add a fine pale line along the side facing the light.
added-panel-lines.fake panel lines: A thin near black line with a fine pale line beside it, on the side facing the light, reads as a cut groove, not a drawn line.
added-panel-lines.plain armour: Add painted panel lines with a pale edge and a few small markings, then shade and edge highlight them like the rest of the surface.

airbrush-priming.priming with an airbrush: Use airbrush primer, mix three or four drops to one of thinner, and spray short light passes at about 18 to 20 psi in two thin coats.
airbrush-priming.airbrush primer psi: Around 18 to 20 psi for most primer; white primer is chalkier and goes better at about 35 to 40 psi.
airbrush-priming.airbrush primer clogs: Use a 0.3 mm or larger nozzle, put thinner in the cup before the primer, and rinse the cup every few minutes so rim flakes cannot form.
airbrush-priming.how do i prime through an airbrush: Thin primer three or four drops to one, spray short sweeping bursts at about 18 to 20 psi, and build two thin satin coats.
airbrush-priming.what pressure to prime at: Around 18 to 20 psi, or about 35 to 40 psi for chalky white primer; large models can take more pressure.
airbrush-priming.thinning primer for airbrush: Mix about three or four drops of primer to one of thinner; a droplet dragged up the cup wall should slowly slide down, not run.
airbrush-priming.primer dried in the nozzle: Put a few drops of thinner in the cup before the primer so it wets the nozzle, and clean with a few drops of isopropyl alcohol.
airbrush-priming.airbrush undercoat: Spray two thin coats of thinned primer at about 18 to 20 psi, keep it looking satin, and let it dry for about an hour before painting.
airbrush-priming.primer too thin runs: Use less thinner: about three or four drops of primer to one; a droplet that runs down the cup wall is too thin.
airbrush-priming.spray primer without a can: Prime through an airbrush with a primer made for it, thinned slightly, sprayed in short light passes at around 18 to 20 psi.

angular-surfaces.highlighting robots: Treat each flat face as its own light level: faces turned to the light clearly lighter, faces turned away clearly darker, crisp edges.
angular-surfaces.how to highlight a vehicle: Pick a light direction, make faces turned to it clearly lighter and those turned away darker, then finish corners with crisp edge highlights.
angular-surfaces.blocky armour highlights: Give each flat face its own brightness and exaggerate the step between neighbouring faces, then edge the corners crisply.
angular-surfaces.tank looks flat: Push the difference between faces: lighter on those turned to the light, darker on those turned away, with bold steps at each corner.
angular-surfaces.flat panels highlighting: On big flat faces, a gradient from one corner to the opposite one gives a polished, crystal like sheen.
angular-surfaces.light on hard edges and planes: On hard shapes light changes at each corner, not gradually, so make each face a clear step lighter or darker.
angular-surfaces.highlight square shapes: Make each face one light level, exaggerate the step between neighbours more than feels natural, and finish corners with crisp edges.
angular-surfaces.mech painting light: Decide where the light comes from, then light the faces turned towards it and darken those turned away, in bold clean steps.
angular-surfaces.boxy model shading: Shade by face, not by curve: faces turned away from the light go clearly darker, with a clean step at each corner.
angular-surfaces.each face different brightness: Yes: give each flat face its own light level based on the light direction, and push the difference more than feels natural.

base-colours-for-weathering.model too dark after weathering: Washes, oils and grime darken what is underneath, so start base colours a step lighter and a little greyer than the finish you want.
base-colours-for-weathering.colours went dull after oils and washes: Weathering mutes and darkens colour, so base a step lighter and greyer, over a bright white zenithal, and glaze strength back later.
base-colours-for-weathering.what base colour before weathering: One a step lighter and a little greyer than the finish you want; if your range has graded shades, base with the lighter one.
base-colours-for-weathering.start lighter for weathering: Yes: choose base colours a step lighter and a little greyer than the finish, as washes, filters and oils all darken them.
base-colours-for-weathering.weathering swamped my paint job: Start paler and greyer next time, over black primer with a heavy white zenithal, and keep a big value gap between nearby light and dark areas.
base-colours-for-weathering.heavily weathered tank colours: Base colours a step lighter and greyer than the finish, over a strong white zenithal, then add strength back with a glaze if needed.
base-colours-for-weathering.pick paler colours for grime: Yes: grime, oils and filters darken and mute the paint, so pick base colours a step paler and a little greyer than the finish.
base-colours-for-weathering.everything looks muddy after weathering: Start brighter, with a heavy white zenithal and paler, greyer bases, and keep a big value gap between light and dark areas placed close together.
base-colours-for-weathering.base coat for a rusty dirty vehicle: Prime black, add a heavy white zenithal from above, then base a step lighter and greyer than you want, as dirt only reads over a bright start.
base-colours-for-weathering.why is my tank so dark after washes: Washes, filters, oils and grime all darken what is underneath, and small models already look darker, so start base colours a step lighter.

battle-worn-blades.chipped sword: Paint small dark chips running in from the cutting edge, larger at the main point of impact, each with a fine light highlight on its edge side.
battle-worn-blades.how do i paint battle damage on a blade: Paint dark chips in from the cutting edge, tip and teeth, bigger where blows land and finer further away, each with a fine light lip.
battle-worn-blades.worn axe edge: Start the damage at the cutting edge, larger at the main impact point, and run bright silver along the whole outer edge.
battle-worn-blades.nicks in a sword: On a dark silver blade washed dark, paint short silver strokes from the cutting edge inwards, then repeat a few in bright silver.
battle-worn-blades.battle damaged weapon: Put the chips where it takes hits: the cutting edge, tip and teeth, larger at the main impact and finer as they spread away.
battle-worn-blades.chips on a blade: Paint small dark chips in from the edge, all in the same general direction, and add a fine light highlight on the edge facing side of each.
battle-worn-blades.make a sword look used: Paint short silver nicks from the cutting edge inwards on a dark washed silver blade, a few in bright silver, and line the whole edge bright.
battle-worn-blades.damaged knife edge: Paint small dark chips in from the cutting edge, slightly random but in one general direction, larger where it would take the most hits.
battle-worn-blades.weathered weapons: Chip the cutting edge, tip and teeth, larger at the main impact point, and keep the flat of the blade mostly clean.
battle-worn-blades.old battered sword: Dark silver washed dark, short silver nicks from the cutting edge inwards, a few in bright silver, and bright silver along the whole edge.

bone-coloured-armour.bone armour: Prime light, base cream in thin coats, line every panel with dark brown thinned half and half, then edge with base mixed half and half with white.
bone-coloured-armour.cream armour: Over light grey or white primer, base cream in several thin coats, shade the recesses, line dark brown and add one edge highlight.
bone-coloured-armour.how to paint bone colour armor: Prime light, base cream, glaze a darker warm mix or sepia wash into recesses, line panels dark brown, then one half white edge highlight.
bone-coloured-armour.cream wont cover black primer: Prime light grey or white instead; cream over black needs coat after coat and seldom ends up smooth.
bone-coloured-armour.off white armour plates: Base cream over a light primer, shade the lower part of each panel, line the panel lines dark brown and edge with base and white.
bone-coloured-armour.bone coloured power armour: Base cream over light grey or white primer, line every panel line dark brown thinned half and half with water, then one pale edge highlight.
bone-coloured-armour.smooth cream base coat: Prime light grey or white and build cream up in several thin coats; an airbrush makes it fast, with crevices touched up by brush.
bone-coloured-armour.shading cream armour: Glaze a slightly darker, warmer mix into recesses and lower panels, or push a thin sepia wash into the shadows and layer cream back.
bone-coloured-armour.ivory armour: Base cream in thin coats over a light primer, shade with a warm glaze or sepia wash, line dark brown, then edge with cream and white.
bone-coloured-armour.bone armor looks patchy: Prime light rather than black, build cream in several thin coats, then smooth rough joins with a glaze of the base colour.

brush-priming.brush on primer: Use a large, soft brush, dab primer into every recess, roll the brush to spread pools, and leave it alone once it starts to skin.
brush-priming.prime without spray: Brush on thin coats of primer with a large soft brush, dabbing it into recesses, and stop working it once a film starts to form.
brush-priming.no spray can how to prime: Brush primer on with a large soft brush, neat or with a tiny drop of water, dabbing it into recesses and leaving it once it skins.
brush-priming.brush primer: Shake it well, let the bubbles settle, use it neat or with a tiny drop of water, and dab it on with a large soft brush.
brush-priming.priming indoors: Brush bottled primer on with a large soft brush instead of spraying, letting it dry 10 to 30 minutes until fully matt.
brush-priming.do i need to prime: Yes, always prime, even if the plastic is already the right colour; an undercoat gives later paint something to grip.
brush-priming.primer pooling in recesses: Roll the brush with light pressure to spread pools; if it pools before skinning, wipe it off with a damp brush and redo it.
brush-priming.primer beading on plastic: Wash the parts in lukewarm soapy water first, as leftover release agent makes primer bead and pool.
brush-priming.too cold to spray prime: Brush on bottled primer instead: thin coats with a large soft brush, dabbed into recesses and left alone once it skins.
brush-priming.prime by hand: Dab primer on with a large soft brush, poking it into every recess, then let it dry 10 to 30 minutes until fully matt.

busts-and-large-scale-workflow.painting a bust: Prep every seam carefully, plan one main light, work long smooth fades a section at a time, and use five to eight steps from shadow to highlight.
busts-and-large-scale-workflow.how do i paint large scale models: Prep carefully, light from one main source, blend smoothly, add texture on purpose and use more colour steps than at small scale.
busts-and-large-scale-workflow.big model looks rough: Clean every seam and mould line, fill gaps and sand smooth, then blend big areas with long, smooth fades.
busts-and-large-scale-workflow.bust painting tips: Prep thoroughly, plan one high front light, blend in five to eight steps, add deliberate texture, and fix it to a plinth or holder early.
busts-and-large-scale-workflow.large scale blending: Use long, smooth fades by airbrush, wet blending or many thin glazes, working one small section at a time as thin paint dries fast.
busts-and-large-scale-workflow.75mm figures: Big models show everything, so prep carefully, plan one main light, blend smoothly and use five to eight steps from shadow to highlight.
busts-and-large-scale-workflow.prep for big models: Clean every seam and mould line, fill gaps with putty and sand smooth; a scratch you would miss on a small model is plain on a bust.
busts-and-large-scale-workflow.painting a big monster with smooth blend: Work big areas in long fades by airbrush, wet blending or thin glazes, one small section at a time, then add some texture so it is not plastic.
busts-and-large-scale-workflow.busts show every mistake: Prep more carefully than usual: clean seams and mould lines, fill gaps and sand smooth, and add texture so large surfaces do not look plastic.
busts-and-large-scale-workflow.display bust workflow: Prep, fix it to a plinth, map one light with a zenithal or value sketch, blend each area fully before moving on, face when your hand is steadiest.

chests-and-crates.treasure chest: Over brush the wood mid brown, vary the metal fittings, wash it all brown, then dry brush a dusty beige lightly over everything.
chests-and-crates.wooden crates: Over brush mid brown, dry brush the edges lighter brown, wash brown, then a light dusty beige dry brush over everything.
chests-and-crates.how to paint a chest: Mid brown wood with lighter brown edges, metal bands in iron, silver or gold, a brown wash all over, then a light dusty beige dry brush.
chests-and-crates.crates and barrels scatter: Base brown, wash brown, dry brush dusty beige over wood and metal alike, and tint a few with thin green or another brown so they differ.
chests-and-crates.metal bands on a chest: Vary the bands and fittings between dark iron, silver and gold, then wash and dry brush them along with the wood.
chests-and-crates.loot box wood: Over brush the wood mid brown, dry brush lighter brown on the edges, wash brown, then dry brush dusty beige.
chests-and-crates.supply crates terrain: Base mid brown, wash brown, and dry brush a dusty beige lightly over everything; tint a few crates so the group looks varied.
chests-and-crates.wooden box with iron fittings: Mid brown wood dry brushed lighter, dark iron fittings, a brown wash over both, then a light dusty beige dry brush.
chests-and-crates.quick scatter terrain painting: Over brush mid brown, wash everything brown, then one light dusty beige dry brush, which highlights wood and metal together.
chests-and-crates.dusty crates: Finish with a dusty beige dry brushed lightly over everything after a brown wash.

choosing-paints.which paints should i get: Most ranges are fine: start with the colours your current models need, and look for strong pigment and a white that covers well.
choosing-paints.best paint range for beginners: Almost no range is truly bad; pick one that is easy to get hold of, check it flows and covers, and learn how it behaves.
choosing-paints.what paint brand is best: The differences between ranges are small; strong pigment matters most, and a good brush with a sharp point matters more than the range.
choosing-paints.acrylic paints for miniatures: Water based hobby ranges are all fine and mix together; choose strongly pigmented paint that covers in few coats.
choosing-paints.can i use craft paint: Not ideally: craft paint is made for paper, and on models it covers and grips poorly, dries slowly and smears when handled.
choosing-paints.dropper bottles or pots: Dropper bottles are easy to dose and often slightly thinned; pots are fine but dry out faster and need thinning.
choosing-paints.paint that covers well: Look for strong pigment: it covers in fewer coats, so the finish stays smooth instead of muddy.
choosing-paints.which white paint covers best: Whites vary a lot between ranges, so test them; one that covers black in one thin coat is worth seeking out.
choosing-paints.hobby paints worth it: Yes over craft paint, which grips poorly and smears, but between hobby ranges the differences are small.
choosing-paints.starting paint collection: Start with the colours your current models need and add a paint only when a project calls for it.

colour-modulation.colour modulation: Light each vehicle panel on its own, dark at one end and light at the other, building three to five tones over a dark shadow mix.
colour-modulation.how do i paint a tank so it isn't flat: Modulate it: spray each panel darker at one end and lighter at the other, and set a panel's brightest part beside its neighbour's darkest.
colour-modulation.vehicle panels look boring: Treat every panel as its own surface, lighter at the top or one end and darker at the other, and exaggerate the contrast on purpose.
colour-modulation.modulation on vehicles: Spray a dark shadow mix all over, then the main colour on the upper part of each panel, then paler mixes over smaller areas inside it.
colour-modulation.lighting each panel: Tilt the model so the spray only catches the edge you want lighter, or mask the neighbours with tape, paper or putty.
colour-modulation.tank looks one colour: Give each panel its own fade from a dark shadow mix up to pale mixes of the main colour, in three to five tones.
colour-modulation.shading big flat panels: Fade each panel dark at one end to light at the other; on flat tops, push the light towards the front or back.
colour-modulation.airbrush tank panels: Spray a shadow mix overall, then the main colour on the upper part of each panel, largest first, then smaller areas of paler mixes.
colour-modulation.color modulation: Light each vehicle panel on its own, dark at one end and light at the other, so big flat panels look lit at arm's length.
colour-modulation.make vehicle look lit: Build three to five tones on each panel from a dark shadow mix to pale highlights, then brush the lightest mix onto rivets, hatches and top edges.

combining-techniques.which technique should i use: Ask what effect each area needs: fast methods like dry brushing and washes for the bulk, careful layering where it shows.
combining-techniques.mixing techniques on one model: Work broad first with dry brushing or washes, then refine with lining, edge highlights or layering where it matters most.
combining-techniques.drybrush and layer together: Dry brush the bulk quickly, then layer or edge highlight by hand on the head, arms, chest, weapon and upper edges.
combining-techniques.speed and quality balance: Use quick methods for the bulk and save careful work for the head, arms, chest, weapon and upper edges; the back and feet can stay dry brushed.
combining-techniques.when to wash vs layer: Wash or dry brush the bulk of the model quickly, then layer or edge highlight by hand where it matters most.
combining-techniques.fast bulk careful details: Yes: dry brush or wash the bulk, add lining where parts need separation, then edge highlight or layer the focal areas by hand.
combining-techniques.combining wash drybrush and highlights: Wash or dry brush the bulk first, line or wash where parts need separation, then edge highlight the key areas and glaze rough patches.
combining-techniques.what technique for each area: Decide what effect each area needs and what the brush has to do to get it, rather than using one method for the whole model.
combining-techniques.how to plan the painting steps: Go broad first, then refine: bulk methods, then lining, then hand highlights where it matters, then glazes and an optional overall filter.
combining-techniques.using different methods on one mini: Mix smooth areas with texture from lines, dots and stippling, so the model does not look samey and soft.

contrast-paint-order.what order do i do one coat paints: Over a pale primer, paint the light, weak colours first and the strong dark ones last, then details in normal opaque paint.
contrast-paint-order.which colours first with contrast paints: The pale, weak ones such as flesh, joints and pale weapons first, then the strong, dark colours last.
contrast-paint-order.contrast paint over a pale primer: Prime off white or pale bone so the colours stay bright, then work from the weakest, palest colours to the strongest, darkest ones.
contrast-paint-order.contrast paints running into each other: Paint pale colours first, clean slips with paint in the primer colour, then do dark colours last with a small brush so they cover slips.
contrast-paint-order.dark contrast stained my skin colour: Do dark colours last; to fix a slip on a pale area, tidy it with a pot of paint in the primer colour, as see through paint cannot cover it.
contrast-paint-order.one coat paints messy overlaps: Work light to dark: pale colours first, slips tidied with primer colour paint, then strong dark colours with a small brush to cover the rest.
contrast-paint-order.paint light colours first or last: First: paint the pale, weak colours first and the strong, dark ones last, as the dark colours cover slips from earlier ones.
contrast-paint-order.speed painting order of work: Pale primer, weak light colours first, small bits next, dark colours last with a small brush, then eyes and teeth in opaque paint.
contrast-paint-order.bone undercoat for contrast: Yes, prime off white or pale bone so the one coat colours stay bright.
contrast-paint-order.should i do flesh before the dark cloth: Yes: flesh and other pale, weak colours first, then the strong dark colours, which cover any slips.

cutting-and-sealing-foam.how do i cut foam for terrain: Use a long snap off blade with a fresh section and a steel ruler, in two or three light passes, or a hot wire cutter for smooth curves.
cutting-and-sealing-foam.xps foam board: Use dense, fine celled insulation foam board: it cuts cleanly and holds pressed detail, unlike coarse, beady packing foam.
cutting-and-sealing-foam.hot wire cutter foam: Go slowly, keep the wire at the lowest heat that cuts, work in a well aired room and keep your face out of the fumes.
cutting-and-sealing-foam.spray paint melted my foam: The solvent in many spray cans melts foam, so seal it first with two coats of thinned white glue, glue and paint, or wall paint.
cutting-and-sealing-foam.sealing foam before painting: Brush on two coats of thinned white glue, a glue and paint mix, or acrylic wall paint, and let it dry fully before priming.
cutting-and-sealing-foam.brick texture in foam: Draw the lines in with a ballpoint pen or blunt pencil, press crumpled foil or a rough rock over it, and push a few corners down for wear.
cutting-and-sealing-foam.foam crumbles when cut: Use dense, fine celled insulation foam and a fresh blade in light passes; coarse packing foam crumbles and a dull blade tears.
cutting-and-sealing-foam.insulation foam terrain: Cut dense insulation foam with a sharp blade or hot wire, press in texture, then seal it with thinned glue or wall paint before any spray.
cutting-and-sealing-foam.pressing stone texture into foam: Press a ball of crumpled foil or a rough rock over the surface, after drawing the stone lines in with a pen or blunt pencil.
cutting-and-sealing-foam.styrofoam scenery: Coarse, beady packing foam crumbles and is poor for terrain; use dense, fine celled insulation foam board instead.

dip-method.dip method: Base coat a step lighter, dunk the model in a tinted varnish dip, flick off the excess, lift out pools, then matte varnish it after a day.
dip-method.dipping miniatures: Hold the model by its base in old pliers, swirl it in the stirred dip for 10 to 20 seconds, then flick off the excess firmly.
dip-method.dipping in tinted varnish: Base coat neatly a step lighter than the final look, dip for 10 to 20 seconds, throw off the excess, and matte varnish once fully dry.
dip-method.speed paint with varnish dip: Prime light, base coat every area a step lighter, dip, flick off the excess, lift out puddles, then matte varnish and pick a few highlights.
dip-method.dunk the model in stain: Swirl it in the dip for 10 to 20 seconds, flick it hard over kitchen towel, and stand it on a non absorbent surface for 5 to 10 minutes.
dip-method.fast army painting dip: Base coat everything a step lighter, dip in one tone across the whole army, matte varnish, then repaint a few raised areas for highlights.
dip-method.dip too shiny: Dip dries very glossy, so finish with a matte varnish in dry air after a full day of drying; test the spray first.
dip-method.pools after dipping: Check collars and under arms and lift puddles out with an old brush or a dab of make up sponge before they set; never use tissue.
dip-method.dip then matte varnish: Yes: leave the dip a full day somewhere still and dust free, then matte varnish in dry air, as damp air can frost it.
dip-method.wood stain on minis: See: speed painting with a dip, a coloured varnish the whole model is plunged into, in this entry's steps 2 to 7.

dry-palette.dry palette: Any non absorbent surface works; glazed ceramic with small wells is easiest, and it gives exact control of paint thickness, though paint dries faster.
dry-palette.ceramic palette: Glazed ceramic with small wells is the easiest dry palette, as it keeps colours apart and holds thin mixes, and dried paint soaks off.
dry-palette.wet palette vs dry palette: A wet palette keeps paint open for hours but slowly thins it; a dry one gives exact, repeatable thickness but dries faster. Many keep both.
dry-palette.tile palette: A tile works as a dry palette and costs little, but it is small and paint dries quickly on it.
dry-palette.paint dries too fast on my palette: Put out small amounts, plan colours and work briskly; a drop of drying retarder keeps a mix usable longer, or use a wet palette.
dry-palette.what palette for inks and glazes: A dry palette: inks, glaze mediums, oils and oil washes need a solid dry surface, ideally glazed ceramic with wells.
dry-palette.glass palette for painting: A glass sheet is big and tough, but paint dries fast on it, thin mixes run about and it can break.
dry-palette.palette for oil paints: Use a dry palette, such as glazed ceramic, as oils and oil washes need a solid dry surface.
dry-palette.can i use an old plate as a palette: Yes, any surface that does not soak up paint works, though plates are small and paint dries quickly on them.
dry-palette.palette with wells: Glazed ceramic with small wells is the easiest dry palette to live with: it keeps colours apart and holds thin mixes.

drybrushing-strokes.drybrush leaves blobs: Hold the brush further back and loosely, and test each pass on your thumb for smears before touching the model.
drybrushing-strokes.how hard do i press when drybrushing: Lightly where it should stay darker, firmer where colour should build up; hold the brush loosely so you do not press too hard.
drybrushing-strokes.dry brushing technique: Flick one way across edges for clean highlights, use round strokes for texture, and test every pass on your thumb first.
drybrushing-strokes.drybrush direction: Brush across the detail you want to catch, at a right angle to edges, from both sides; directional for plates, circles for fur and rocks.
drybrushing-strokes.drybrushing edges only: Use light, grazing flicks across the edge at a right angle, coming from both sides; dragging along its length smears.
drybrushing-strokes.drybrush looks chalky and messy: Buff the area softly with the current colour before stepping up to a much paler one, and test each pass on your thumb.
drybrushing-strokes.how to drybrush properly: Use normal paint on a dry layer, test on your thumb, flick across edges or circle on texture, and clean the brush between colours.
drybrushing-strokes.circular drybrush strokes: Circles suit fur, rough skin, rocks and terrain, where texture faces every way; heavier round strokes also cover flat panels.
drybrushing-strokes.drybrush smears: Flick across edges instead of dragging along them, test on your thumb first, and let the layer underneath dry fully.
drybrushing-strokes.too much paint on drybrush: Test each pass on your thumb for smears before the model; heavier loads are only for covering flat panels after a wash.

enamel-streaks.enamel streaks: Varnish first, place enamel round rivets and recesses, let it set about five minutes, then pull it down with a flat brush damp with spirit.
enamel-streaks.rust streaks: Dot light orange rust enamel round rivets, wait about five minutes, then drag it down with a spirit damp flat brush and soften the sides.
enamel-streaks.how to do rain marks: Paint thin lines of unthinned grime where rain would run, then pull them upwards from the bottom with a clean dry brush.
enamel-streaks.white spirit weathering: Over varnished paint, place enamel, let it set, then pull it into streaks or fades with a brush or bud damp with clean spirit.
enamel-streaks.streaking grime: Start each line at a rivet, chip or top edge on vertical faces, mixing rust, pale rain marks and dark grime, then pull them down with spirit.
enamel-streaks.mud weathering on tanks: Work a mud coloured enamel onto the lower parts, then dab spirit on to fade it upwards.
enamel-streaks.enamel washes: Varnish the acrylic first so spirit cannot lift it, use brushes kept for enamels, and seal with matte varnish between enamel layers.
enamel-streaks.rust running down: Dot light orange rust enamel at rivets and recesses, let it set, then pull it downwards with a spirit damp flat brush, building up in repeats.
enamel-streaks.weathering with enamels: Varnish first, place enamel, let it set, then streak or fade it with a spirit damp brush or bud, and varnish before the next layer.
enamel-streaks.soft fade with spirit: Dab thinned enamel around details, then fade its outer edge with spirit so the stain stays tight to the detail.

fantasy-skin-colours.blue skin: Highlight it with flesh mixed into a cool grey, so it feels organic but icy, and keep a warm red undertone in the deepest shadows.
fantasy-skin-colours.purple skin: Put a warm flesh note in the top highlight; for a quick lilac, paint purple one coat over bone, then layer mixes of purple and pale flesh.
fantasy-skin-colours.grey skin: Charcoal or stone grey skin is a black one coat paint over a lighter grey, with a warm flesh note in the top highlight.
fantasy-skin-colours.alien skin: Any colour works as skin if a warm flesh note sits in the top highlight or the deepest shadows.
fantasy-skin-colours.unnatural skin colour: Mix a warm tan or flesh into the final highlight on nose, cheeks, brow and knuckles, and keep warmth in the deepest shadows.
fantasy-skin-colours.fantasy skin tones: Blue, red, purple or grey skin reads as living flesh mainly because of a warm flesh note in the final highlight.
fantasy-skin-colours.make blue skin look alive: Mix flesh with a cool grey for the highlights, underpaint a warm berry red in the recesses, and add a purple or thin magenta flush.
fantasy-skin-colours.red skin looks dead: Dull the shadows slightly, highlight with a warm ivory, and add a soft red or pink flush on the cheeks, lips and knuckles.
fantasy-skin-colours.green skinned monster: See: green skin, which has its own entry; this one covers blue, red, purple and grey skin.
fantasy-skin-colours.how to paint skin that isnt human colour: Use any colour, but put a warm flesh note in the top highlight or deepest shadows, and add a flush where skin is thin.

finishing-an-army.how do i finish an army: Choose a simple, repeatable scheme with a small palette, time a test model honestly, set a realistic deadline and stick to the plan.
finishing-an-army.never finish painting: Simplify the scheme until the timed test model is quick enough to repeat, then set a tight but realistic deadline and follow the plan.
finishing-an-army.pile of shame: See: actually finishing an army, a small palette, a timed test model and a realistic deadline, in this entry's steps 1 to 7.
finishing-an-army.too many unpainted models: Paint one test model, time it, and if it is too slow to repeat, change the style rather than the goal.
finishing-an-army.painting an army fast: Use a simple scheme, a small palette and one or two universal highlight colours, and spend time only on armour, faces, weapons and bases.
finishing-an-army.simple scheme for a big army: A small palette with one or two strong accents and one or two universal highlight colours used on every area.
finishing-an-army.how long to paint an army: Paint one test model in the planned style, note honestly how long it took, and multiply; if it is too slow, simplify the style.
finishing-an-army.staying on track painting an army: Follow the written plan, treat the group like one model, and touch up the first models at the end instead of changing course.
finishing-an-army.batch painting plan: Any workflow can work: one at a time, batches of five or ten, or one colour across everything; write the steps down in order.
finishing-an-army.army taking forever: Simplify: one tone with a quick highlight for belts and pouches, time on armour, faces, weapons and bases only, and a firm deadline.

fix-chalky-white-paint.chalky white: Mix opaque white about one to one with a high flow white, or add flow improver, instead of water, and lay it on a light primer in thin coats.
fix-chalky-white-paint.grainy white paint: Smooth it with a high flow white or a drop of flow improver instead of water, stir often, and check for ridges on dark card.
fix-chalky-white-paint.white paint clumps: Stir often as the pigment settles, and loosen it with high flow white or flow improver rather than using it straight from the pot.
fix-chalky-white-paint.white wont go smooth: Use a smooth, light primer, a white loosened with high flow white or flow improver, and two or three thin coats, each left to dry.
fix-chalky-white-paint.white streaky: Water tends to leave streaks in white, so thin it with a high flow white, flow improver or white ink instead.
fix-chalky-white-paint.white covers badly: Work over a light primer or pale tint, climb from tinted mixes to pure white, and lay two or three thin coats; a see through first coat is normal.
fix-chalky-white-paint.lumpy white: Avoid white straight from the pot; mix it with a high flow white or flow improver and lay thin, smooth passes without scrubbing.
fix-chalky-white-paint.flow improver white: A drop of flow improver or white ink smooths white without diluting the pigment, unlike water, which tends to streak.
fix-chalky-white-paint.white paint looks gritty: Mix it about one to one with a high flow, ink like white, or half and half with gloss varnish, and fix any rough primer first.
fix-chalky-white-paint.how to paint white without chalk: Use a light primer, a white smoothed with flow improver or high flow white, and two or three thin coats, judging it only once dry.

fix-messy-edge-highlights.messy edge highlights: Once dry, paint the colour underneath from the middle of the panel up to the line to trim it thinner.
fix-messy-edge-highlights.wobbly edge highlight: Trim it with the colour underneath, starting each stroke well inside the panel and pulling towards the highlight.
fix-messy-edge-highlights.edge highlights too thick: Thin the paint so it glides, wipe excess off the brush, and trim fat lines back with the colour underneath once dry.
fix-messy-edge-highlights.how to fix edge highlights: Finish the whole highlight first, then once dry pull the colour underneath from mid panel up to the line, creeping closer to trim it.
fix-messy-edge-highlights.edge highlighting mistakes: Finish the pass first, lift wet blobs off with a rinsed brush, then trim dry lines with the colour underneath.
fix-messy-edge-highlights.shaky lines on edges: Trim wobbles with the colour underneath once dry; on long edges, run the side of the bristles along the edge instead of the tip.
fix-messy-edge-highlights.clean up edge highlights: Paint the colour underneath up to the line from inside the panel, or push a thinned shade against the inside of a fat line to slim it.
fix-messy-edge-highlights.tidy up edges: Load the colour underneath and pull it from mid panel towards the edge line, trimming it thinner; dot wash back into any filled recesses.
fix-messy-edge-highlights.blob of highlight on a flat panel: If it is still wet, rinse the brush and lift it off at once; if dry, paint over it with the panel colour.
fix-messy-edge-highlights.edges look chunky: Trim them back with the colour underneath, and next time thin the paint, wipe off excess and use the side of the bristles on long edges.

fix-wet-blending.wet blending patchy: Lay a solid coat of the midtone first, then while it is wet blend the darker tone into one end and the lighter into the other.
fix-wet-blending.wet blend not working: Use creamy rather than watery paint, work small sections quickly, stop when it drags, and let it dry before another pass.
fix-wet-blending.base coat shows through blend: Paint a solid midtone over the whole area first, as few paints cover in one coat, then blend the dark and light into it while wet.
fix-wet-blending.paint dries too fast to blend: Work small sections at a steady pace and add a little drying retarder or flow improver; too much leaves a thick, glossy film.
fix-wet-blending.retarder for blending: A small amount of drying retarder or flow improver extends working time; too much leaves a thick, glossy film.
fix-wet-blending.how do i wet blend: Lay a solid midtone, then while it is wet blend darker into one end and lighter into the other, pulling the brush tip towards its loaded colour.
fix-wet-blending.blend looks streaky: Pull rather than push, with the tip pointing towards the colour on the brush, and lay creamy paint thinly so it is not scraped into stripes.
fix-wet-blending.wet blending cloak: Lay the midtone over the whole cloak, blend dark into one end and light into the other while wet, and expect two or three passes.
fix-wet-blending.blending wet on wet: Blend darker and lighter tones into a wet midtone, working small sections fast and stopping as soon as the paint starts to drag.
fix-wet-blending.blending acrylic dries too fast: Acrylics dry fast, so work small sections, spread paint quickly, and add a little retarder or flow improver for more working time.

following-tutorials.followed a tutorial but looks different: Paint thickness, step order, number of glaze passes and method change the result far more than the exact colours do.
following-tutorials.copying a painting guide: Treat it as a starting point: read it all first, match the method and paint thickness, not just the colours, and expect to adjust.
following-tutorials.why doesnt mine look like the video: How the paint goes on, its thickness, the step order and the method, matters far more than the exact paints used.
following-tutorials.same paints different result: The same paints look different thick, glazed, wet blended or feathered, and neighbouring colours change how each one reads.
following-tutorials.tutorial didnt work: Read the whole guide first, match the method and paint thickness, and expect to adjust; brush control comes from practice.
following-tutorials.recipe looks wrong: Neighbouring colours change how a colour reads, so a recipe copied onto a different scheme can look wrong; adjust to suit.
following-tutorials.how to follow a painting guide: Read it all the way through first, check you have every colour or close matches, zoom in on pictures to see where highlights sit.
following-tutorials.mine looks nothing like the picture: Compare thickness, step order and glaze passes rather than colours, zoom in to see where highlights sit, and keep practising.
following-tutorials.tutorial colours wrong: For an ordinary red or blue, any similar colour gets you close; exact paints matter most for special effects and technical products.
following-tutorials.results differ from the video: Method, paint thickness and step order change the result more than the exact colours, and still pictures do not show how strokes are made.

gap-filling.gaps between parts: Pick the filler by gap size: plastic glue for hairlines, super glue for small gaps, paste filler under 1 mm, two part putty for big ones.
gap-filling.gap filling: Let the glue set overnight, fill by gap size, overfill slightly as most fillers shrink, then sand smooth before priming.
gap-filling.join lines show after painting: Run thinned base coat into a hairline gap again and again until it fills, then repaint.
gap-filling.green stuff for gaps: For larger gaps, knead two part epoxy putty to one even colour, press a thin sausage in and smooth it with a wet tool.
gap-filling.seams: Brush plastic glue on both faces and squeeze so softened plastic beads out, then once hard scrape the ridge off and sand flush.
gap-filling.fill gaps: Dab super glue into small gaps, use paste filler under about 1 mm and two part putty for larger ones, then sand smooth.
gap-filling.gap between arm and body: Fill a small gap with super glue or paste filler, or a larger one with two part putty, then shave flush and sand before priming.
gap-filling.putty for gaps: Two part epoxy putty for larger gaps, smoothed with a wet tool; solvent tube putty only on small seams, as it shrinks and smells strongly.
gap-filling.hairline seam: Squeeze plastic glue so softened plastic beads out of the join, then scrape and sand flush once hard; paste filler also suits it.
gap-filling.sand join smooth: Let the filler cure, ideally overnight, shave flush with light knife passes, then sand from about 400 to 1000 grit.

glow-on-surroundings.osl: Glaze the glow colour onto surfaces that face the source, strongest close to it and fading away, never as bright as the source itself.
glow-on-surroundings.object source lighting: Finish the source, keep the model a little darker, then glaze mid strength glow colour onto facing surfaces, stronger nearer the source.
glow-on-surroundings.glow on nearby armour: Highlight the edges facing the source pale blue grey or white, then glaze the glow colour over them, pulling strokes towards the source.
glow-on-surroundings.light spill: Only surfaces that can see the source catch it: glaze them thinly in the glow colour, building brighter closer in.
glow-on-surroundings.how do i paint light from a lantern: Paint the lantern first, then glaze its colour thinly onto facing surfaces, building brighter coats over smaller areas closer to it.
glow-on-surroundings.glow from a sword onto face: Glaze the glow onto the face and chest facing the blade, including small undersides like brows, lips and knuckles.
glow-on-surroundings.torch light on model: Glaze dark red, then orange, then yellow onto surfaces facing the flame, each kept closer to the source.
glow-on-surroundings.glow effect on surroundings: Glaze the glow colour thinly onto facing surfaces, strongest near the source, and keep a dark band between it and normally lit areas.
glow-on-surroundings.lighting effects: A glow only reads against darkness: keep the model a little darker and use mid strength mixes, saving the brightest for the source.
glow-on-surroundings.glowing weapon reflecting: Light only the surfaces facing the weapon, the face and chest above it included, with thin glazes that fade with distance.

gluing-painted-parts.glue wont hold on painted parts: Glue only holds as well as the paint does, so scrape paint and primer off both contact points to bare plastic, then use super glue.
gluing-painted-parts.arm keeps falling off: Scrape the paint off both contact points so you glue bare plastic, use a little super glue, and add a pin for heavy parts.
gluing-painted-parts.gluing after painting: Scrape the contact points back to bare plastic and join them with a very small amount of super glue, holding still while it sets.
gluing-painted-parts.scrape paint before gluing: Yes: scrape paint and primer off both contact points with a file, knife or metal pick until bare plastic shows.
gluing-painted-parts.weapon snapped off painted model: Scrape the paint off both contact points, reglue with a little super glue, and pin it if it is heavy.
gluing-painted-parts.attach painted arms: Clear paint from both contact points, including a ring inside any socket, then use a very small amount of super glue.
