gluing-painted-parts.super glue on painted surface: It only holds as well as the paint, so scrape back to bare plastic at the contact points first; super glue is safer than plastic glue here.
gluing-painted-parts.paint then assemble: Keep the contact points free of paint when painting in sub assemblies, then join them with a little super glue.
gluing-painted-parts.glue bare plastic contact points: Yes: scrape to bare plastic, apply a very small amount of glue to the contact points only, and touch the part on a mat first to remove excess.
gluing-painted-parts.reattach broken painted part: Scrape both contact points back to bare plastic, use a little super glue, and add a pin if the part is heavy.

grimy-metal.dirty metal: Dull it with heavy washes or ink, such as brown then black, then bring the shine back only on edges and worn points.
grimy-metal.grimy steel: Over a steel base, slap on a dark brown black wash, then run bright silver on the flat of the brush along a few edges.
grimy-metal.metal too shiny: Real worn metal has little shine: wash it heavily with brown then black, and keep bright silver to a few edges and rubbed points.
grimy-metal.make metal look dirty: Wash brown, then black, dab small patches of sepia, green or orange wash, and add thinned rust brown round bolts.
grimy-metal.old iron: Wash a brown first and black after so it looks old rather than just dark, then add silver only on a few edges.
grimy-metal.worn industrial metal: Silver base, black wash, brass on caps and joints, an all over dark brown wash for oil, then a silver drybrush.
grimy-metal.dull dirty gun metal: Drybrush silver mixed with plenty of black and a touch of blue over a dark brown base, or ink a dark silver with deep brown.
grimy-metal.how do i make silver look used and grubb: Cover it with a thick deep brown ink and re edge the raised parts, or wash it brown then black, with silver only on edges.
grimy-metal.rusty dirty chainsaw blade: See: grimy metal, heavy dark washes with rust brown round bolts and silver on edges, in this entry's steps 2 to 7.
grimy-metal.metal looks like new: Dull it with heavy washes, dab patches of different coloured washes for a used look, and add a glossy dark oil spot on joints.

highlighting-black.highlighting black: Use small, sharp steps of grey or tinted colour, each smaller than the last, and leave most of the surface dark so it still reads black.
highlighting-black.how do i highlight black: Chunky very dark grey on main folds and edges, a finer mid grey line on the highest parts, then light grey only on the sharpest edges.
highlighting-black.black looks grey: The highlights cover too much: trim them back with thinned black and leave more black between; changing the tint rarely fixes it.
highlighting-black.black armour: Use cool blue greys in small shrinking stages, then a few dots of light grey with a touch of white on the corners.
highlighting-black.black cloak highlights: Tint the greys with a touch of pink, cream or pale yellow for cloth, and keep each stage smaller than the one below.
highlighting-black.black looks flat: Add a mid step or a lighter top edge, and make edges facing the light brighter than those in shadow.
highlighting-black.grey highlights on black: Very dark grey first on main folds, then mid grey finer, then light grey only on the sharpest edges, leaving plenty of black.
highlighting-black.blue highlights on black: Cool blue greys suit hard shiny armour and black beside red; on smooth panels, slip blue between the highlight and the black.
highlighting-black.black robes: Highlight with black plus a touch of pink, cream or pale yellow, which reads as light rather than dust, in small tight stages.
highlighting-black.keep black looking black: Keep most of the surface dark, make each highlight stage smaller than the last, and stop before pale grey on a dull, dark model.

hobby-on-a-budget.painting on a budget: Get only the colours the scheme needs, mix your own washes, use cheap synthetics for rough work, and put out less paint.
hobby-on-a-budget.save money painting: Mix washes from matt varnish, flow aid and water, avoid duplicate paints, and base with sand, grit, cork and twigs.
hobby-on-a-budget.hobby is expensive: Cut costs with a small core set plus mixing, home made washes, cheap brushes for rough jobs and less wasted paint.
hobby-on-a-budget.cheap washes: Mix matt varnish, a drop of flow aid and water, tinted with any paint you already have.
hobby-on-a-budget.make my own wash: Use matt varnish, a drop of flow aid and water, tinted with paint; match the paint to the base, such as oil paint in oil washes.
hobby-on-a-budget.cheap alternatives: Home made washes from varnish, flow aid and water, and basing from sand, grit, cork, twigs and kitchen spices.
hobby-on-a-budget.do i need all these paints: No: a small core set plus mixing covers a lot; get only what the current scheme needs.
hobby-on-a-budget.stop wasting paint: Put out small amounts, keep lids closed, and use a wet palette so mixes stay usable between sessions.
hobby-on-a-budget.hobby costs too much: Avoid doubles by keeping paints visible in a rack, save good brushes for detail, and use household materials for bases.
hobby-on-a-budget.budget friendly painting: Use cheap synthetic brushes for priming, base coats and drybrushing, mix your own washes, and only get colours a project needs.

inverted-edge-highlights.inverted edge highlights: Paint a fine light line along the lower lip of grooves and indents, and along the panel right under a trim.
inverted-edge-highlights.highlight grooves: Run a fine light line along the lower lip of each groove, where light would catch the inner edge.
inverted-edge-highlights.big plain panels: Add fine light lines along the lower lip of grooves and under trims, so the plate reads brighter and more detailed.
inverted-edge-highlights.edge highlight recess: Paint a fine light line on the lower lip of the recess, thinner and dimmer than the main edge highlights.
inverted-edge-highlights.lower lip highlight: Paint a fine light line along the lower lip of grooves and indents, kept thinner and dimmer than the raised edge highlights.
inverted-edge-highlights.trim blending in: Paint a fine light line on the panel right under the trim; it can be a different colour, such as warm brown beside green trim.
inverted-edge-highlights.panels look empty: Highlight the lower lip of grooves and the inner edge beside trims as well as the raised edges.
inverted-edge-highlights.separate trim from armour: Run a thin line along the panel just under the trim, perhaps in a different colour, such as warm brown on black beside green.
inverted-edge-highlights.fine line under trim: Yes: a fine light line on the panel right under a trim separates the two and makes the area read brighter.
inverted-edge-highlights.highlight inside edge: Paint a fine line where light catches the inner edge of grooves, thinner and dimmer than the main edges so those read first.

kitbashing.kitbashing: Start from a core model with a strong pose, swap parts that match its scale and style, and change the outline with a new head or arms.
kitbashing.kit bash: Combine parts from different kits by starting with a strong pose, dry fitting spares with tacky putty, and changing the outline.
kitbashing.conversions: Swap heads, hands and weapons, change the outline, and blend joins with putty so add ons look built in.
kitbashing.how do i convert a model: Start simple with a head or weapon swap; for bigger builds, dry fit spares with tacky putty before assembling and change the outline.
kitbashing.head swap: A head swap alone makes a big difference; kits from the same maker and scale often share neck joints, so heads swap with no cutting.
kitbashing.mixing parts from different kits: Pick parts that match the core model's scale, style and level of detail; parts from much bigger or smaller kits look wrong.
kitbashing.making a custom character: Let the model's story steer the parts: list a few visual signs of its theme, and spread small themed details over the whole model.
kitbashing.weapon swap: Remove the old weapon bit by bit with clippers, knife and file, slice the joint flat, and pin a wrong hand weapon at the hilt.
kitbashing.converting a spear to a staff: Trim the head off the spear to make a staff.
kitbashing.unique model from spare bits: Dry fit spares with tacky putty until ideas come, change the head, helmet or shoulder shape, and avoid neat symmetry.

light-and-magnification.painting lamp: Use diffused daylight lamps of about 5000 to 6500K, CRI 90 or more and 800 to 1000 lumens, ideally two, one over each shoulder.
light-and-magnification.daylight bulb: Pick about 5000 to 6500K with a colour rendering of 90 or more, and use the same bulbs in every lamp.
light-and-magnification.magnifier for painting: About 2 to 3 times suits most work; try an inexpensive visor or glasses first, and glass lenses are less tiring than plastic.
light-and-magnification.colours look different in the morning: Paint under even daylight bulbs, all the same colour temperature; warm bulbs tint everything orange.
light-and-magnification.cant see fine detail: Use a magnifying visor, reading glasses or a magnifying lamp at about 2 to 3 times, plus bright, diffused daylight lamps.
light-and-magnification.best light for painting: Diffused, flicker free daylight LED at about 5000 to 6500K, CRI 90 or more, placed so your hand does not shadow the model.
light-and-magnification.eye strain painting: Avoid flickering old fluorescent tubes and bare glare; use steady, diffused LED daylight lamps, and glass magnifier lenses.
light-and-magnification.magnifying glass: About 2 to 3 times magnification suits most work; stronger lenses shorten the gap to the model and blur anything that moves.
light-and-magnification.lighting for painting at night: A basic daylight lamp is far better than room lighting, and it matters most in the evening; diffuse it and match every bulb.
light-and-magnification.head magnifier: A visor must sit firmly without tilting your head; about 2 to 3 times suits most work, with glass lenses clearer than plastic.

magnetising.magnets: Small magnets in joints let one model swap heads, weapons and options; magnetise only what you will really swap.
magnetising.magnetize weapons: Drill a hole sized to the magnet so it sits flush, glue the body magnet first, then match each weapon magnet to it and mark its face.
magnetising.swap weapons on one model: Magnetise the weapon joints, keeping magnet size and polarity the same on every mount so any weapon fits any mount.
magnetising.how to magnetise arms: Cut the ball joint flush and glue a magnet there, or drill a small ball, then set the matching magnet in each arm by sticking it to the first.
magnetising.what size magnets: Heavy weapons need big magnets: going from 1 mm to 1.5 mm thick discs in load bearing joints makes a big difference.
magnetising.magnetise heads: Magnetise the neck before the halves go together, sizing the hole so the magnet sits flush, and keep polarity the same across heads.
magnetising.drill holes for magnets: Drill each hole to the magnet's size so it sits flush; thicken thin solid parts with plastic sheet first, as they split.
magnetising.magnetize a tank turret: Set a large magnet flush into solid plastic, and key the joint with a short slot or square tube so it cannot spin.
magnetising.build one model with all the options: Plan magnets before the main halves go together, keep sizes and polarity matching on every mount, and paint the options separately.
magnetising.is magnetising worth it: For parts you will really swap, usually heads and weapon hands, yes; if a part never changes, glue it.

membrane-wings.dragon wings: Base the skin with strokes along the stretch, drybrush or stipple lighter towards the centre of each panel, then line veins and corners dark.
membrane-wings.bat wings: Pull every stroke the way the skin hangs, fade the skin tone lighter to the panel centres, and run undiluted shadow over the veins.
membrane-wings.how do i paint wings: Streak the base along the stretch, build a soft gradient to each panel's centre by drybrushing or stippling, then line the veins dark.
membrane-wings.wing membrane: Paint thinned coats from the bones downwards so faint streaks read as stretched skin, then lighten the middle of each panel.
membrane-wings.veins on wings: Run the shadow colour, undiluted, over the veins and into the corners where membrane meets bone, after the highlights.
membrane-wings.demon wings: Drybrush the skin tone fading towards the bones, line veins in undiluted shadow, and finish with one thin glaze over the whole wing.
membrane-wings.wings look flat: Work more paint into the middle of each panel with a paler tone on the centres, re line veins dark, and edge torn ends lightly.
membrane-wings.painting wyvern wing: Stroke along the stretch, stipple from the brightest spot outwards with a very dry stiff brush, then outline the veins dark.
membrane-wings.leathery wings: Stipple with a small stiff brush wiped very dry, starting at the brightest spot and spreading outwards, for a leathery texture.
membrane-wings.stretched skin wings: Pull each stroke the way the skin hangs, usually from the bones downwards; the faint streaks read as stretched skin.

mixing-colour-steps.mixing highlights: Mix the base half and half with a lighter paint of the same family; pale bone, cream or ivory keep steps warmer than white.
mixing-colour-steps.make shade colour: Darken the base with a little of a deeper related colour or a brown, or mix it half and half with black, added in tiny amounts.
mixing-colour-steps.mix my own colours: Mix steps by parts from paints you own, three to one, two to one, one to one, and write the ratios down.
mixing-colour-steps.darken a colour: Add a little of a deeper related colour or a brown; black overpowers fast, so add it in tiny amounts.
mixing-colour-steps.lighten without white: Use pale bone, cream or ivory, which keep steps warm, or for red a skin tone or orange so it does not turn pink.
mixing-colour-steps.highlight colour mixing: Mix the base with a lighter paint of the same family, half and half, for the cleanest step; bone or cream keep it warm.
mixing-colour-steps.dont have the right paint: Take the closest paint and add tiny amounts of a second colour, testing swatches against the reference; close is good enough.
mixing-colour-steps.mix layer steps: Mix a ladder in separate pools, three to one, two to one, one to one, and if two steps look too far apart, mix a little of each.
mixing-colour-steps.paint ratios: A part is any equal blob of paint; with dropper bottles, count drops and write the ratio down so you can mix it again.
mixing-colour-steps.make a darker version: Mix the base with a little deeper related colour or brown, or half and half with black as a shade.

moss-and-rot.moss: Blotch thin dark green round joints and fittings, wash yellow green into the centres, then stipple a few dabs of yellow green for texture.
moss-and-rot.moss on stone: Place it where water sits and light is low, blotch on thinned dark green, brighten the centres with yellow green and stipple texture.
moss-and-rot.moss on wood: Rotting wood moss is often a warm yellowish green: blotch dark green round fittings, then yellow green in the centres.
moss-and-rot.rotting wood: Blotch thinned dark green round fittings and at the bottom of uprights, wash yellow green into the centres, and stipple a little texture.
moss-and-rot.damp rot: Put it where water sits and light is low: round metal fittings, joints, the bottom of uprights and the shaded side.
moss-and-rot.how to paint moss on a model: Thin a mid dark green to a semi wash and blob it on in uneven patches, wash yellow green inside them, then stipple tiny dabs.
moss-and-rot.mossy statue: Blotch thin dark green where water would sit and on the shaded side, brighten the centres with yellow green, and stipple a little texture.
moss-and-rot.green moss texture: Stipple tiny, slightly thicker dabs of yellow green inside the patches, or use a textured moss effect paint on a warmed, damp surface.
moss-and-rot.make wood look old and rotten: Blotch thin dark green round fittings and joints, wash warm yellow green into the centres, and add gloss if it should look wet.
moss-and-rot.moss around rivets and joints: Blob a semi wash of mid dark green round the rivets and joints, then wash yellow green inside, strongest at the centre.

multi-colour-drybrushing.drybrushing looks chalky: Use three to five steps from a dark version of the colour, keep colour in the highlights, and go back with a saturated drybrush if it greys.
multi-colour-drybrushing.drybrush looks grey: Going straight to pale bone washes it out; step up through lighter tones of the colour itself, then a saturated drybrush if needed.
multi-colour-drybrushing.multiple drybrush colours: Lay the steps out in order and move to each lighter colour without rinsing, each covering less with lighter pressure.
multi-colour-drybrushing.how do i drybrush a monster: Prime in the skin colour, drybrush a heavy mid tone, then three to five lighter steps of the colour, aiming the last from the light.
multi-colour-drybrushing.drybrushing layers: Start from a dark two coat base, drybrush a mid tone, then each lighter colour on less area with lighter pressure.
multi-colour-drybrushing.drybrush washed out: Push the top highlight up in colour, such as red to orange and yellow, rather than to pale bone, and use satin paints.
multi-colour-drybrushing.drybrush big creatures: Prime in the skin colour, leave more paint on the brush for the first pass, then lighter steps over shrinking areas.
multi-colour-drybrushing.colourful drybrushing: Drybrush each zone with lighter tones of its own colour, then a very light pale bone over everything to tie them together.
multi-colour-drybrushing.stop drybrush going grey: Keep colour in the highlights with three to five steps of the colour itself, and re saturate with a stronger colour if it greys.
multi-colour-drybrushing.drybrushing a big model: Prime in the main colour, make a heavy first pass, then lighter colours over less area, smudging dark into shadows before the last pale pass.

nmm-shapes.nmm: Break each part into a flat, cylinder or dome and place the painted light and dark bands to suit that shape.
nmm-shapes.non metallic metal for beginners: Ask what simple shape each part is, flat, cylinder or dome, and place light and dark bands by that shape, darkening the darks first.
nmm-shapes.where do the highlights go on nmm: On cylinders a bright band with dark beside it, on domes an off centre hotspot facing you, and flats kept mostly dark.
nmm-shapes.painting metal without metallic paint: Paint light and dark bands by shape: light, dark and light again on cylinders, an off centre hotspot on domes, flats mostly dark.
nmm-shapes.nmm on a round shoulder pad: Put a bright hotspot slightly off centre facing the viewer, fade it outwards, and add a weaker reflection on the opposite lower side.
nmm-shapes.reflections on a cylinder: Show light, dark and light again: on a lying tube a sharp bright line about the middle, darkest just below, soft reflected light underneath.
nmm-shapes.how to place light on a dome helmet: Place a bright hotspot slightly off centre facing the viewer, not on the very top, fade it out, and add a smaller lower reflection.
nmm-shapes.my nmm looks like grey paint: Avoid bands of equal width: vary and taper them, keep flats mostly dark, and darken the darks first so the pale tones read brighter.
nmm-shapes.nmm sword blade: Treat it as a flat: keep it mostly dark and run a shaft of light that spreads like a triangle, broad at one end and narrow at the other.
nmm-shapes.painted chrome on curved armour: Read each part as a cylinder or dome: bright and dark bands on cylinders, an off centre hotspot on domes, tapered rather than even.

oil-washes.oil wash: Mix oil paint with mineral spirit until smooth, flood it on gently, let the spirit evaporate, then wipe the raised areas clean.
oil-washes.enamel wash: See: oil washes, oil paint thinned with mineral spirit, flooded on and wiped back once the spirit evaporates.
oil-washes.panel line wash with oils: Brush the oil wash on gently, ending each stroke in a recess, then wipe the raised areas with a makeup sponge once the spirit evaporates.
oil-washes.oil paint wash: Thin artist oil with odourless mineral spirit or white spirit, about like skim milk for shading, testing it on paper towel.
oil-washes.white spirit wash: Mix oil paint with white spirit until no lumps remain, about like skim milk for shading or equal parts for a strong wash.
oil-washes.oil wash on a tank: Gloss varnish first to help it flow, brush the wash on, let it settle, then wipe raised areas with a sponge and matte varnish once dry.
oil-washes.wipe off oil wash: Once the spirit evaporates, wipe raised areas with a small makeup sponge, pressing lightly and turning to a clean side often.
oil-washes.mineral spirits with oils: Yes, odourless mineral spirit thins oil paint into a wash, and it does not dissolve acrylic underneath, though scrubbing can lift it.
oil-washes.can i thin oils with water: No, never thin oils with water; use odourless mineral spirit or white spirit.
oil-washes.oil wash for recesses: Flood the wash on with a big soft brush, ending each stroke in a recess; it flows in evenly and dries without tide marks.

over-highlight-then-glaze.over highlight then glaze: Push highlights brighter than needed, then glaze the base colour back over about three quarters of each shape, repeating until smooth.
over-highlight-then-glaze.highlights not bright enough: Take them brighter and further than you think they should go, then glaze the base colour back over to tie them in.
over-highlight-then-glaze.too little contrast: Too little highlight is the hardest to fix, so overshoot the highlights, then glaze the base back over them to smooth it.
over-highlight-then-glaze.glaze back highlights: Thin the area's own colour or a close mid tone into a glaze and brush it over about three quarters of each shape, off the top highlights.
over-highlight-then-glaze.how do i get smoother blends: Over highlight with rough layers, then glaze the base colour back over in several thin passes until the transition is smooth.
over-highlight-then-glaze.blend too bright: That is the easy problem: glaze the original colour thinly over most of the area, letting each coat dry, until it ties back in.
over-highlight-then-glaze.contrast too low: Push the highlights further than feels right, then glaze back; darkening a blend takes a few glazes, lightening one takes many passes.
over-highlight-then-glaze.glazing over highlights: Glaze about three quarters of each shape, keeping off the top highlights, and avoid washes, which spread and stain.
over-highlight-then-glaze.push highlights further: Yes: going too bright is the easiest contrast problem to fix, as a few thin glazes of the base colour pull it back.
over-highlight-then-glaze.model looks dull: Push highlights brighter than you need, glaze the base colours back over them, then dot the brightest mix on the sharpest points.

paint-hidden-areas-first.what order should i paint in: Hard to reach inner parts first, then layers in the order they sit on the body: skin or bone, clothing, armour, then cloaks.
paint-hidden-areas-first.paint inside first: Yes: paint the innermost parts first so slips land on areas you have not painted yet, not on finished work.
paint-hidden-areas-first.hard to reach parts: Paint them first, turning the model and coming in from several angles; parts unreachable once glued are best painted off the model.
paint-hidden-areas-first.painting under a cloak: Do the area under the cloak first, getting its dark shades in, so you never reach over finished work.
paint-hidden-areas-first.inside to outside painting: Work from the innermost layer out: skin or bone, then clothing, then armour, then cloaks, so slips land on unpainted areas.
paint-hidden-areas-first.keep hitting finished areas: Paint the hidden, hard to reach areas first; reaching over finished armour to paint cloth beneath is how most slips happen.
paint-hidden-areas-first.slips on painted bits: Change the order: do inner, framed and hard to reach areas first, so mistakes land on parts that still need painting.
paint-hidden-areas-first.how to paint behind a held weapon: Paint the chest behind it first, and if you catch the weapon in front, leave it, as it gets painted later.
paint-hidden-areas-first.inside wings first: Yes, start with places the brush struggles to reach, such as inside wings, and get their dark shades in first.
paint-hidden-areas-first.awkward recesses: Paint them first; over white primer, paint deep undercuts matt black early so any missed gap does not glint white.

painting-animals.horse: Vary coat colours, white face marks and socks across a unit, keep a pale belly, and use quick black manes and tails for contrast.
painting-animals.dog: Check reference for markings, keep the top of the muzzle bright, filter yellow brown into fur shadows, and dot gloss on the nose.
painting-animals.wolf: Filter a thin yellow brown onto the lower side of each muscle so grey fur is not dull, then a light drybrush for texture.
painting-animals.how to paint animals: Paint a paler belly, warm the fur shadows with a thin yellow brown filter, keep a glossy nose, and use reference for markings.
painting-animals.beast: Lighter underside, warm filters in the fur shadows, short lines in the direction hair grows, and pink scars and gums.
painting-animals.horse markings: Vary white face marks of different shapes and white socks from a thin band at the hoof to half the leg on one to four legs.
painting-animals.animal nose: Noses are damp, so add tiny dots of a pale colour along them for a glossy reflection.
painting-animals.cavalry horse: Keep the mount simple so the rider leads: a couple of brown drybrushes, black tack and pale hooves, with varied coats across the unit.
painting-animals.hound: Paint the belly paler than the back, keep the top of the muzzle bright, filter warm brown into fur shadows and dot gloss on the nose.
painting-animals.make animals look alive: Warm filters in the fur shadows, a glossy nose and lips, a tiny off white dot in each eye, and pink on scars and gums.

painting-bone.bone: Base sandy beige, layer bone leaving sand in the recesses, highlight pale yellow cream, dot white on tips, and shade only the deepest recesses.
painting-bone.skulls: Over a bone base, brush on a brown one coat paint, lift it off the tops before it dries, then highlight the crown.
painting-bone.how do i paint bone: Sandy base in two thin coats, a bone layer, pale cream highlights, white dots on the highest points, then brown in the deepest recesses.
painting-bone.skeleton: Paint bone first, before armour and cloth, wash with dark brown one coat paint thinned with medium, then highlight brightest on the skull.
painting-bone.how do i paint skulls: Base bone, brush a brown one coat paint over, lift it off the tops with a damp brush or fingertip, then highlight the crown.
painting-bone.bone colour: A sandy beige base built through bone to pale yellow cream; a greenish tan middle reads grimy, a cool grey white reads bleached.
painting-bone.bone looks chalky: Base a sandy beige or medium bone rather than pale bone, and satin varnish first so a wash flows evenly.
painting-bone.skeleton army: Spray bone primer, wash with dark brown one coat paint thinned with about ten parts medium, then one highlight or drybrush on each bone.
painting-bone.horns: See: the horns and tusks recipe; this entry covers bone and skulls, though its sandy to pale cream layering suits pale horn too.
painting-bone.teeth and tusks: Use very little paint and the flat of the brush on tiny teeth, tidy afterwards, and dot white on the tooth tips.

painting-different-materials.make different materials look different: Vary the highlight: narrow, bright and contrasty for shiny things, broad and soft for matt ones, and change the brush marks.
painting-different-materials.how to paint leather vs cloth: Leather takes irregular broken strokes, cloth takes cross hatching or dots, and matt cloth never reaches pure white or black.
painting-different-materials.silk looks like plastic: Keep silk smooth with fine parallel lines for its sheen, and give it its own highlight shape rather than copying another part.
painting-different-materials.metal vs cloth highlights: Metal gets narrow, bright bands with strong contrast; cloth gets broad, soft transitions that never reach pure white or black.
painting-different-materials.everything looks the same material: Ask how each surface catches light: shiny ones get sharp, narrow highlights, matt ones soft broad ones, with different brush textures.
painting-different-materials.brush stroke texture: Cross hatching reads as coarse wool, fine parallel lines as satin, small dots as felted cloth, broken strokes as leather.
painting-different-materials.shiny vs matt surfaces: Shiny surfaces take narrow, bright highlights with strong contrast; matt ones take broad, soft transitions without pure white.
painting-different-materials.make cloth look like velvet: See: the matt cloth notes here; broad, soft transitions that never reach pure white or pure black, in body point 3.
painting-different-materials.satin sheen: Use fine parallel brush lines; satin surfaces like skin and hair take bright but softer highlights than shiny ones.
painting-different-materials.how sharp should highlights be: Sharp and narrow on shiny things like metal and gems, broad and soft on matt wool, skin and leather, and weak on rough bark.

painting-glass.glass: Give it a dark edge, a strong gradient from dark to bright across it, a sharp white glint near the opposite corner, then gloss varnish.
painting-glass.potion vials: Paint the liquid line level whatever the angle, fill solid below, highlight the top and one side, dot bubbles in lines, then gloss.
painting-glass.how do i paint glass: Base very dark, build a bright L into the lower corner with thin glazes, blend the middle, then dot white in the opposite corner and gloss.
painting-glass.lenses and gems on a helmet: Paint each as a dark to bright gradient with a dark edge and a crisp white glint near the opposite corner, then gloss it.
painting-glass.window panes on a building: Prime and paint them: a very dark base, a bright L glazed into the lower corner, a white dot top opposite, then gloss.
painting-glass.clear parts paint or leave: Paint them: primed clear parts save painting the interior, and a painted gradient often looks better than clear plastic.
painting-glass.glass bottle looks flat: Push the contrast: a dark edge, a strong dark to bright gradient, and a small sharp white glint, then gloss the glass only.
painting-glass.make glass look shiny: Finish with gloss varnish on the glass only, over a strong gradient and a crisp white glint.
painting-glass.white glint on glass: Put a small, sharp white glint near the corner opposite the bright gradient.
painting-glass.lantern glass: For a glowing pane, paint white where brightest and a mid tone elsewhere, add two thin fluorescent coats, then a soft glow nearby.

painting-lava.lava: Over white, tint yellow, orange then transparent red, leaving yellow in the recesses, then add black cooled plates with glowing cracks.
painting-lava.glowing cracks: Draw thin, wandering pale ivory yellow lines, glaze orange over each and a little either side, then edge red near the hottest parts.
painting-lava.how do i paint lava: Work bright to dark over white: yellow, orange, transparent red, then black plates grown from small shapes so cracks glow between them.
painting-lava.magma: Keep the blending rough and borders jagged: yellow in the hottest recesses, orange and red outwards, black cooled plates on top.
painting-lava.lava base: Crackle paint over gritty texture, prime white, tint yellow then orange, drybrush red on the crust and stipple black on top.
painting-lava.molten rock: Paint black cooled plates in rough five and six sided shapes over a yellow to red glow, edging each plate red, then orange near the heat.
painting-lava.cracked glowing ground: Use crackle paint over texture, prime white, tint yellow and orange, then red and black on the raised crust so the cracks glow.
painting-lava.volcano base: See: the lava base method here, crackle paint tinted yellow and orange, then red and black crust, ringed with blackened ground and grey ash.
painting-lava.lava flow: Keep it rough and jagged, never a smooth gradient, brightest yellow where hottest and red at the edges, with dark crust plates.
painting-lava.fire cracks: Paint thin pale ivory yellow lines of varied thickness, glaze orange over and beside them so the dark nearby picks up a tint.

painting-pink.painting pink: Paint it over a white or pale undercoat, and it covers clean in one or two thin coats; shade with deeper pink or magenta.
painting-pink.pink looks patchy: Fix the undercoat, not the paint: lay white, ivory or a pale pink first, and the pink goes on clean.
painting-pink.pink wont cover: Most pinks are fairly see through, so lay down white, ivory or a pale flesh first rather than piling on coats.
painting-pink.pink over grey primer: Over grey or dark primer pink looks patchy and dull even after several coats; put white or ivory down first.
painting-pink.fluorescent pink: Fluorescent pinks are even more see through, so paint them over a white or pale undercoat.
painting-pink.pink armour: Undercoat white or pale pink, apply one or two thin coats, and shade with deeper pink, magenta or dark red purple, not brown or black.
painting-pink.how do i get a bright pink: Use a white or pale undercoat and keep shading clean with deeper pink or magenta; a chalky pastel pink loses the brightness.
painting-pink.pink needs ten coats: Change the undercoat instead: white, ivory or a pale pink underneath lets pink cover in one or two thin coats.
painting-pink.pastel pink cloth: A pastel pink covers better but loses the clean, bright look; a clean pink over a white undercoat avoids that.
painting-pink.best undercoat for pink: White, ivory, or a pale pink or light flesh; pink also sits happily over a cool, bluish gradient.

painting-scratches.scratches: Paint a thin pale line catching the light, then a thinner dark brown line tight along its upper side as the shadow inside the gouge.
painting-scratches.how to paint scratches: Use a sharp fine brush and flowing paint: a pale line in one quick stroke, then a thinner dark line along its upper side.
painting-scratches.battle damage scratches: Put short scratches where things get knocked, edges, corners and lower areas, keeping a similar direction as if from the same blows.
painting-scratches.scratches on armour: Paint a pale line a step lighter than the surface, or silver for bare metal, with a thin dark brown line on its upper side.
painting-scratches.scratched metal: Paint a few bright silver scratches, then age them with a very thin red brown filter, or a turquoise tint on brass.
painting-scratches.fine scratch marks: Roll a fine brush to a point, test beside the model, and paint each scratch as one quick stroke of thinned paint.
painting-scratches.claw marks on armour: See: painting scratches; keep strokes in a similar direction, as if from the same blows, with a dark line on each pale one's upper side.
painting-scratches.scratches look like random lines: Keep one direction across a part, vary length, avoid pairs and even spacing, and use fewer; a photo reference helps.
painting-scratches.realistic scratches with a fine brush: Pale line first, dark line tight against its upper side, and match light: darker scratches in shadow, paler ones in lit areas.
painting-scratches.worn scratched paint: Scratch painted stripes with the colour underneath as if worn back, then add a smaller dark line inside each one.

painting-tank-tracks.tank tracks: Stipple dark silver and flat brown, wash dark or red brown, rub graphite on the raised links, and save bright silver for the sharpest edges.
painting-tank-tracks.how do i paint tracks: Stipple a thick dark silver and brown mix, wash red brown, wipe the flats back, then rub soft pencil graphite on raised links and edges.
painting-tank-tracks.tracks on a vehicle: Treat them like basing: pick colours that suit the model and its ground, starting from a rough dark metal base and a brown wash.
painting-tank-tracks.what colour are tank treads: A dull, grimy cast iron: dark silver mixed with flat brown, washed brown, with colours chosen to suit the ground it stands on.
painting-tank-tracks.muddy dusty tracks: Brush soil coloured pigment thinned with white spirit over tracks and lower wheels, or dab mud texture paste on and flick wet mud last.
painting-tank-tracks.worn shiny edges on tracks: Rub soft pencil graphite onto raised links and edges with a fingertip, and save bright silver for the very sharpest edges.
painting-tank-tracks.cast iron look: Stipple a thick mix of dark silver and flat brown with an old drybrush in two coats for a slightly rough, cast surface.
painting-tank-tracks.tracks look like plastic: Stipple a rough dark silver and brown base, wash it red brown, and rub graphite on the raised links for a dull, worn sheen.
painting-tank-tracks.should i paint tracks before gluing: Yes, paint them before fitting if the kit allows.
painting-tank-tracks.tread weathering: Wash dark brown, wipe the flats with a spirit damp sponge, add graphite on worn edges and pigment dust, and hold back so it does not look fake.

painting-with-children.painting with kids: Pick a big, simple, expressive model, teach only loading the brush and rinsing, and praise their choices rather than neatness.
painting-with-children.getting my child into painting: Start with a large model with a big face and fun pose, talk about how colours tell a story, and keep it about fun.
painting-with-children.my kid wants to paint minis: Avoid small, detailed armoured figures; give them something large with a big face and eyes, or a primed plastic toy.
painting-with-children.first model for a child: Something large with a big face, big eyes and a fun pose; tiny lenses and fine trim make it easy to feel they have failed.
painting-with-children.painting with my son: Let him colour a line drawing of the model first, teach only brush loading and rinsing, and ask about the figure's name and story.
painting-with-children.painting with my daughter: Choose a big, expressive model, let her pick the colours, praise her choices rather than neatness, and do one part per session.
painting-with-children.how to keep it fun for kids: Talk about the figure's story, praise choices over neatness, keep sessions short, like just the face, and never push them to show it.
painting-with-children.child gets frustrated painting: Use a bigger, simpler model, paint one part per session, and praise their choices rather than how neat it is.
painting-with-children.what model for a seven year old: A large model with a big face, big eyes and a fun pose, or a primed plastic toy, rather than a small detailed figure.
painting-with-children.should i correct my kids painting: No, praise their choices rather than the neatness, and teach only how to load the brush and rinse between colours.

parchment-and-scrolls.parchment: Base sandy tan, layer paler bone, highlight the folds pale cream, age it with thin sepia at edges and creases, then add dark brown squiggles.
parchment-and-scrolls.scrolls: Sandy base, paler bone layer, pale cream on raised folds, sepia in creases and nicks, white along curled ends, then fake text in dark brown.
parchment-and-scrolls.how to paint paper scrolls: Base sandy tan in two coats, highlight across the strip in the fold direction, age with thin sepia and add tiny dark brown squiggles.
parchment-and-scrolls.old paper colour: A pale sand suits most models, aged with a thin orange brown sepia; use a cool light grey next to lots of warm cream or bone.
parchment-and-scrolls.aged parchment: Run a thin orange brown sepia along the top edge, down the creases and into any nicks.
parchment-and-scrolls.scroll looks too yellow: Try a cool light grey base instead, shaded with a thin blue grey, especially next to lots of warm cream or bone.
parchment-and-scrolls.fake writing on parchment: Paint tiny thin squiggles, dots and dashes in dark brown last; glaze parchment colour over it in places if it looks stuck on.
parchment-and-scrolls.parchment strips on armour: Base pale brown, highlight raised parts and curled edges pale cream, then wash it brown so it ages into the folds.
parchment-and-scrolls.make paper look old: Wash a thin orange brown sepia into the top edge, creases and nicks, and write in dark brown rather than black.
parchment-and-scrolls.sepia wash on scrolls: Apply it thinly at the top edge, down the creases and in nicks; on cool parchment use a thin blue grey instead.

planning-a-diorama.diorama: Sketch the scene first, test the layout with sticky tack, pick one main viewing angle and light source, then paint the centrepiece first.
planning-a-diorama.how do i plan a diorama: Start with the scenery, sketch it even with stick figures, then hold models on with sticky tack and photograph layouts you like.
planning-a-diorama.diorama layout: Balance it: if one side is high, raise the other so the eye travels round, and keep the background simple.
planning-a-diorama.scene with lots of figures: Let the space decide how many fit, try placements and heights with sticky tack, and keep hard to reach figures separate till the end.
planning-a-diorama.composition for a diorama: Choose one main viewing angle where the story reads at a glance, a believable light source, and balance high and low sides.
planning-a-diorama.arranging figures on a big base: Hold them on with sticky tack, try different placements and heights, and photograph a layout you like before gluing.
planning-a-diorama.which viewing angle for a scene: Pick one main angle where the whole story reads at a glance, and turn figures so their faces show to the viewer.
planning-a-diorama.sketching a scene before building: Yes: sketch backdrop, figures, roads and focal point on paper, even with stick figures; it is quicker than building.
planning-a-diorama.where do i start with a diorama: With the scenery, since the space decides how many figures fit; sketch it, then dry fit figures with sticky tack.
planning-a-diorama.vignette or diorama layout: Pick one main viewing angle, a believable light source and a balanced layout, and in two figure scenes avoid both facing side on.

pre-mixing-colours.premix paint: Mix a larger batch once, counting drops for an exact ratio, and keep it in a spare lidded bottle with the ratio written on it.
pre-mixing-colours.mixing a batch of custom colour: Count drops from dropper bottles for an exact ratio, mix thoroughly, and keep it in a lidded bottle with a mixing ball.
pre-mixing-colours.keep a mixed colour for later: Keep it in an empty dropper bottle or lidded pot with a mixing ball, and write the ratio on it so you can make more.
pre-mixing-colours.colours dont match between models: Mix a batch of the colour once and keep it, rather than remixing each session, so every model matches.
pre-mixing-colours.my mix came out different this time: Count drops for exact ratios, write them down, and keep a dried dab of each step on card to match against.
pre-mixing-colours.put mixed paint in a dropper bottle: Yes: an empty dropper bottle with a small mixing ball inside keeps it mixed, with the ratio written on the bottle.
pre-mixing-colours.count drops to mix paint: Yes, counting drops from dropper bottles makes the ratio exact; note it even for small mixes such as two to one.
pre-mixing-colours.matching colour across an army: Premix one batch of each custom colour and keep it in a labelled bottle, so no model ends up slightly different.
pre-mixing-colours.save a custom mix: Keep it in a lidded dropper bottle or pot with a mixing bead, labelled with the ratio, plus a dried dab on card.
pre-mixing-colours.mix once use for whole army: Yes: mix a larger amount once, keep it labelled, and mix washes in batches too, as they drift in strength when made fresh.

pushing-contrast.more contrast: Push highlights brighter and shadows deeper than feels right, two or three times, and glaze the base back over if you overshoot.
pushing-contrast.model looks washed out: Deepen the down facing areas with the base mixed with deep blue, purple or black, then push the highlights further.
pushing-contrast.model looks flat from a distance: Judge it at arm's length in normal room light and exaggerate light and dark, as small features cannot cast real shadows.
pushing-contrast.push highlights: When they look right, push them brighter again two or three times; a bold jump to a stark final highlight on the sharpest points reads well.
pushing-contrast.darker shadows: Mix the base with a deep blue, purple or black for the down facing areas; highlights look brighter next to them.
pushing-contrast.model doesnt pop: Add edge highlights and dark lining, deepen the shadows, and put the brightest highlights around the face.
pushing-contrast.low contrast: Exaggerate more the smaller the model: deeper shadows, brighter highlights, edge highlights and dark lining in recesses.
pushing-contrast.how to make my model stand out: Push contrast further than feels natural, and put the brightest highlights around the face to pull the eye there.
pushing-contrast.highlights too subtle: Make a bold jump to a stark final highlight on the sharpest points, rather than adding many small steps near the top.
pushing-contrast.extreme highlights: Try one cheap model with shadows to black and highlights to white; it grabs attention across a room and resets your sense of normal.

rebasing-models.rebasing: Cut the model free in small bites, protect the feet, and super glue it firmly to the new base, filling gaps under the feet.
rebasing-models.how do i rebase a model: Clip away chunks of the old base well clear of the feet, nibble in close, trim the soles flat with a knife, then super glue it down.
rebasing-models.removing a model from its base: Slide an old blade under the basing first, then nibble the base away, holding the model by its sturdiest area.
rebasing-models.cutting off a cast on base: Never try one big snip: clip chunks well clear of the feet, nibble small bites around each foot, then score flat with a knife.
rebasing-models.move model to a bigger base: Saw most of the old base off leaving a thin slab, glue it to the new base centre, blend the step with putty and texture it all.
rebasing-models.rebase old models: Use old blades and clippers, as grit ruins good tools, slide under the basing first, then nibble the old base away.
rebasing-models.scenic base looks the same on every mode: Cut the model off its cast on base in small bites, keeping the feet intact, and fix it to a new base of your own.
rebasing-models.cut feet free without breaking them: Clip away chunks well clear of the feet, then nibble small bites towards and around each foot, and score along the sole.
rebasing-models.pin model to new base: Super glue it, as feet give only small contact points, and fill gaps under the feet with slate, a rock or a slab of the old base.
rebasing-models.base size changed: Saw away most of the old base, glue the remaining slab to the new base, and blend the step with epoxy putty.

reposing-models.reposing a model: Cut limbs at the joints with a fine saw, trim the faces to the new angle, pin larger joints, then reglue and fill gaps with putty.
reposing-models.change the pose of a mini: Decide the new pose, cut at knees, hips, elbows or shoulders, trim the cut faces until it pivots, then pin and reglue.
reposing-models.cut and reposition limbs: Use a fine razor saw or sharp knife rather than clippers, keep cut faces flat, and trim them until the part sits at the new angle.
reposing-models.make a model sit down: Cut at the hips and knees, trim the faces to the new angles, pin and reglue, then fill gaps with epoxy putty and sculpt folds.
reposing-models.repose an arm: Cut at the elbow or shoulder, trim the faces to pivot, then pin it; a bent paper clip wire core can angle or lengthen it.
reposing-models.repose legs: Work from the ground up, cutting at the knees or hips, and check from every side that the feet sit flat and the stance is balanced.
reposing-models.how do i change how a model stands: Cut at the joints, trim the faces to the new angle, test with poster putty, then pin and glue so the feet sit flat.
reposing-models.more dynamic pose: Small cuts go a long way: turning a foot at the ankle or lifting the arms forward changes the whole feel.
reposing-models.conversion with a new pose: Cut at the joints, trim to the new angle, pin and reglue, swap hands from other kits if needed, and hide joins with cloth or cables.
reposing-models.every model has the same pose: Repose a few: cut limbs at the joints, trim the cut faces to new angles and reglue them, filling gaps with putty.

rinse-water-habits.rinse water: Change it before smooth stages, never let the pot dry out, and keep a second clean pot for thinning paint.
rinse-water-habits.fluff stuck in my paint: Flick it off the wet paint with the brush tip, or lift it with a blade once dry and touch up; change dusty rinse water.
rinse-water-habits.bits and grit on the model: Floating dust and sludge in rinse water end up in the paint; change it, and never let the pot dry out with paint in it.
rinse-water-habits.how often should i change my water: Check it before every smooth stage, such as base coating, glazing or stippling, and change it if it looks dusty.
rinse-water-habits.dust in a smooth finish: Change the rinse water before smooth stages, as floating dust and fluff end up stuck in the finish.
rinse-water-habits.water pot dried out: Empty and wash it, as the crust loosens bits into your brush; soak a crusted plastic pot in household degreaser.
rinse-water-habits.dirty rinse water ruins glazes: Colour in the water does no harm, but dust and sludge do: change it before glazing and keep a clean pot for thinning.
rinse-water-habits.two water pots: Yes: one for rinsing and one kept clean for thinning and wetting the brush, plus a separate rinse for metallics.
rinse-water-habits.specks in my base coat: Change dusty rinse water before base coating, and wash the pot regularly so no crust forms on the bottom.
rinse-water-habits.does dirty water matter: A little colour does no harm; floating dust, fluff and loose sludge are the problem, as they stick in smooth finishes.

sculpting-cloth.sculpting cloth: Roll putty thin on a wet tile, half cure it for clean cuts, and press in folds that follow how the cloth would hang.
sculpting-cloth.green stuff cloak: Lay a thin sheet of two part putty on the model while soft and press in folds with a rounded tool, following how it hangs from the shoulders.
sculpting-cloth.how do i sculpt a banner: Roll putty flat, leave it one to two hours to half cure, cut it by pressing a wet blade straight down, and fold the top over for a pole sleeve.
sculpting-cloth.putty cloak: Lay a thin, soft sheet over the shoulders, press folds in with a rounded tool, and add overlapping folds as further layers once each cures.
sculpting-cloth.sculpting folds: Press folds in with a rounded tool following how the fabric hangs and gathers, and let each layer cure before adding the next.
sculpting-cloth.rolling putty flat: Roll it on a wet tile with a wet brush handle, with two thin rails such as toothpicks either side to keep the sheet even.
sculpting-cloth.sculpt a tabard: Roll a thin sheet, half cure it, cut the edges square by pressing a wet blade straight down, then add a seam line with the blade back.
sculpting-cloth.putty too sticky to cut: Leave the sheet one to two hours to half cure, then press a wet loose blade straight down rather than dragging it.
sculpting-cloth.sculpt a loincloth: Cut a half cured putty strip, nick small triangles out for a ragged hem, and press folds that follow how it would hang.
sculpting-cloth.how to make cloth hang naturally: Press folds that follow how the fabric would hang from the shoulders and gather where it is caught, then sand cured edges thinner.

shading-with-contrast-paints.contrast as a wash: Cover the whole area with the one coat paint, not just recesses, ending each stroke in a recess so it shades without wash rings.
shading-with-contrast-paints.shading with contrast: Base the midtone, cover the area with the one coat paint, and push it into recesses and downward faces, lifting off there.
shading-with-contrast-paints.contrast over base colour: Base each area in its midtone, then coat it fully with the one coat paint so it dries lighter on raised areas and darker in recesses.
shading-with-contrast-paints.contrast over metal: Pick a light, weak tone so it tints rather than covers: warm flesh over gold, grey over silver.
shading-with-contrast-paints.tint with contrast: Thin the one coat paint with its medium, about two parts paint to one, to shade more softly and shift the hue.
shading-with-contrast-paints.speed paint over silver: Use a light, weak one coat paint such as grey over silver, so it tints the metal and stains textured areas evenly.
shading-with-contrast-paints.contrast as a glaze: Thin it with its medium about two to one, or sandwich it: coat, relayer the lighter colour on raised areas, then a thinner second coat.
shading-with-contrast-paints.smooth shading fast: Coat a midtone base fully with a one coat paint, push it into recesses, wipe bright areas with pure medium, and soak up pools.
shading-with-contrast-paints.one coat paint shading: Cover the whole area, end strokes in recesses where pigment collects, and lay the model on its side to dry so it does not pool at hems.
shading-with-contrast-paints.white primer for contrast: Yes, a white primer keeps bright colours strong under one coat paints.

skin-by-layering.layering skin: Base a warm mid brown, then step lighter mixes onto smaller raised areas, ending near white on the highest points, then glaze in colour.
skin-by-layering.skin from a brown base: Brown covers black primer well and missed spots read as shadow; mix it half with mid skin for the first broad layer.
skin-by-layering.skin highlights: Step towards a pale yellow cream on brow, nose ridge, cheekbones, upper lip and chin, with near white only on the highest points.
skin-by-layering.build up skin in layers: Base dark, keep the first layers broad, then each lighter mix on smaller areas where light lands, glazing back if it gets stark.
skin-by-layering.skin over black primer: Base a warm mid brown in a few thin coats; it covers black far better than a flesh tone does.
skin-by-layering.flesh tone wont cover black: Base in a warm mid brown or your darkest skin tone first, then layer the flesh mixes over it.
skin-by-layering.how to layer flesh: Mix half base and half mid skin for most of the face, then lighter mixes on smaller areas, two thin coats each, judged dry.
skin-by-layering.skin on a big model: Layer from a brown base through lighter mixes on smaller raised areas, alternating highlights and glazes, keeping it smooth over contrasty.
skin-by-layering.smooth skin layers: Skin is not shiny, so smoothness beats contrast: glaze the previous stage over anything too stark, alternating with highlights.
skin-by-layering.skin step by step: Brown base, half and half mid layer, lighter steps on smaller areas, pale cream top, then dark brown lines, purple and pink glazes.

speed-painting.speed painting: Limit yourself to about five colours, prime dark with a light dusting from above, use one coat paints or drybrushing, and work while things dry.
speed-painting.how do i paint faster: Use fewer colours, a zenithal primer for free shading, one coat paints, the biggest brush you can control, and do each step across the batch.
speed-painting.paint a model in 30 minutes: Pick about three main areas and five colours, prime with a light zenithal, use one coat paints, and spend saved time on the head and chest.
speed-painting.quick paint job: Prime dark, dust white from above, one coat paints or drybrush, block in parts while big areas dry, then eyes and a neat base rim.
speed-painting.fast painting: Do not base coat everything: one pass of colour on raised volumes, primer left in recesses, and neat work only on focal areas.
speed-painting.limited palette: Around five colours is plenty, with one very dark and one very bright for quick contrast, and let one colour do several jobs.
speed-painting.quick tabletop: Stop rank and file once table ready, take only leaders further, and do each step on every model before the next.
speed-painting.one coat paints: Use them over a zenithal primer, as they shade and highlight in one go, and soak up pools at hems before they dry as rings.
speed-painting.painting takes too long: Cut to about three main areas and five colours, skip full base coats, and spend the time on the head, shoulders and chest.

spots-and-markings.spots on creature skin: Make them random: blotches of different sizes, some broken apart, with stray dots, larger near the spine and smaller further away.
spots-and-markings.animal stripes: Paint stripes in a thinned dark one coat paint over the finished fur, then drybrush the whole area again so they read as one material.
spots-and-markings.leopard spots: Dot irregular blobs of thin dark paint, wait about half a minute, then touch a clean, dry brush to each centre so the edge dries darker.
spots-and-markings.how to paint creature markings: Lay out a random, uneven pattern that follows the body, then shade and highlight it with the same light as the skin underneath.
spots-and-markings.tiger stripes on a beast: Paint thinned dark stripes over the finished fur, narrowing where the body pinches, then drybrush the whole area again.
spots-and-markings.markings look stencilled: Avoid even spacing: vary sizes and shapes, break some apart, add stray dots, and glaze the skin shade over to tie them in.
spots-and-markings.random blotches on hide: Use blotches of different sizes and shapes, some broken apart, with stray dots near the main patches, fading out from the spine.
spots-and-markings.frog patterns on skin: Mark the pattern out in a pale neutral first so a bright colour goes on crisp, then build each blotch deep with a lighter centre.
spots-and-markings.make spots look natural: Keep them uneven, follow the body's form, and shade and highlight them with the same light as the skin so they do not look stuck on.
spots-and-markings.patterned skin on a lizard: Make larger, overlapping spots near the spine or plates and smaller, sparser ones further away, narrowing where plates pinch together.

staying-motivated.lost motivation: Do not wait to feel it: keep your kit set up, paint in a regular short slot, and set small goals such as one colour across a squad.
staying-motivated.hobby burnout: If you sense it coming, switch to something simpler for a while; that is looking after the hobby, not giving up.
staying-motivated.pile of shame: Start with the model that excites you, set small regular goals, and tick groups of work off on a list to see progress.
staying-motivated.how to finish a big army: Split it into stages and tick them off, accept the standard you set at the start, mix in a vehicle or monster, and set a target date.
staying-motivated.hobby slump: Most projects slump about two thirds through, so save a favourite job such as basing for then, and keep a favourite model as the finale.
staying-motivated.set painting goals: Set small goals you can meet, like one model or one colour across a squad, and raise them as you go.
staying-motivated.track painting progress: Split the project into groups such as cloth, leather and metal, tick them off a list, and take photos of finished models.
staying-motivated.bored of painting the same model: Swap in a vehicle or monster between infantry, keep a simple model on the go, and paint a standout model as a reward after each batch.
staying-motivated.too many unpainted models: Sort a stalled unit by stage, bring the least finished up to the next stage, then carry on as one batch.
staying-motivated.big project feels endless: Get primer, base coats and a drybrush on first so it looks like a unit, then add detail, ticking off stages as you go.

stripping-paint.stripping paint: Soak the model in a stripper that suits its material, scrub the paint off with an old toothbrush, wash it in soapy water, then reprime.
stripping-paint.how do i strip a model: Soak it in a lidded jar or squeezed zip bag of suitable stripper, scrub with an old toothbrush, clear recesses, then wash and dry.
stripping-paint.paint stripper safe for plastic: Hobby paint strippers are made to be safe on plastic, resin and metal; acetone can soften or melt plastic, so keep it for metal.
stripping-paint.remove paint and start again: Soak in a suitable stripper, scrub with an old toothbrush over tissue, wash in soapy water, let it dry fully and prime again.
stripping-paint.primer went on grainy and thick: Stripping is the cleanest fix: soak it, scrub the primer off, wash and dry it, then prime again.
stripping-paint.detail clogged with paint: Strip it, then clear stubborn recesses with isopropyl alcohol on cotton buds or the blunt back of a knife; never sand it.
stripping-paint.strip second hand models: Wear gloves, as very old metal may contain lead, and clip awkward joints rather than prising, since stripper softens old glue.
stripping-paint.soaking models in alcohol: Isopropyl alcohol on cotton buds clears stubborn recesses; for a full soak, use a stripper that suits the material, tested on a hidden spot.
stripping-paint.redo a bad paint job: Strip it: soak in a stripper suited to the material, scrub, wash and reprime; only paint over old paint that is sound and firm.
stripping-paint.get old paint off resin: Use a hobby stripper made safe for resin, not acetone, and test a hidden spot first; resin is the hardest to strip cleanly.

terrain-colour-choices.terrain colours: Mostly greys, dull metals and browns, with one muted accent such as mustard yellow or faded red, so models stand out.
terrain-colour-choices.what colour for terrain: Warm light greys suit most boards, with browns and dull metals, and one restrained accent colour that suits the setting.
terrain-colour-choices.scenery colours: Keep scenery dull, in greys, dull metals and browns, since it is a backdrop, and add one muted accent.
terrain-colour-choices.terrain too bright: Pull it back to greys, dull metals and browns, keeping only one restrained accent, so it does not fight bright models.
terrain-colour-choices.dull terrain: Yes, keep it dull; break up large plain areas with one masked stripe or a few pipes picked out in copper.
terrain-colour-choices.terrain accent colour: One muted accent suited to the setting: mustard yellow, faded red, cool green moss for temperate boards or orange rust for hot ones.
terrain-colour-choices.board colours: Warm light greys suit most boards and sit well beside bright models; choose one look for the whole table.
terrain-colour-choices.terrain stands out too much: Mute it to greys, dull metals and browns with one restrained accent; scenery is the backdrop, not the subject.
terrain-colour-choices.should terrain match my army: For a display or diorama, repeat the figures' patterns and palette on walls, flags and props; on a table, keep scenery dull.
terrain-colour-choices.models dont stand out on the table: Keep the scenery dull, in greys, browns and dull metals with one muted accent, so the models become the subject.

tinted-metallics.candy paint: Base smoothly in silver or gold, then apply a thin coloured one coat paint, ink or glaze over it one panel at a time.
tinted-metallics.tinted metal: Put a thinned deep ink or one coat paint over a smooth metallic base, panel by panel, leaving it alone while it dries.
tinted-metallics.coloured metal: Tint a smooth silver or gold base with thin ink or one coat paint; one silver can serve every metal on the model.
tinted-metallics.metallic red: Glaze red over silver for a candy red, or over gold for a warmer metallic red, letting some metal show through.
tinted-metallics.metal glaze: Thin a deep ink or one coat paint with a little water or medium and colour in one panel at a time, then leave it alone.
tinted-metallics.candy apple red: Base a shiny silver, tint it red one panel at a time, add a second coat for depth, then restore shine on edges with bright metal.
tinted-metallics.shiny green metal: Glaze green over a smooth silver base, shade with a matching green wash rather than black, and edge in bright metal.
tinted-metallics.colored metallic armour: Base smooth silver, drybrush brighter metal on raised areas, tint each panel with thin coloured ink, then a second coat for richness.
tinted-metallics.ink over silver: Yes: thin ink over silver, one panel at a time, gives a candy finish, or mix a little ink into the metallic for coloured steel.
tinted-metallics.contrast over silver: A thinned deep one coat paint over silver works, applied panel by panel and left alone; over spray metal, brush a coat of metal first.

true-metal-technique.true metallic metal: Place light and dark metallic mixes as reflections, like painted metal: steel and black bands for shadows, stippled silver on top.
true-metal-technique.tmm: Mix steel with matt black for fixed shadows, stipple steel and silver as the lights, and put the brightest dot on a tip or corner.
true-metal-technique.high contrast metallic: Copy polished steel: near white highlights right beside very deep shadows, with pure black fine in the deepest recesses.
true-metal-technique.how do i make metal look reflective: Paint bands of steel and black along cylinders and the lower parts of round shapes, then stipple silver on the upper areas.
true-metal-technique.metallic paint reflections: Place them as you would for painted metal: dark mixes in fixed bands, bright silver on upper areas, a midtone between.
true-metal-technique.polished steel look: Near white highlights next to very deep shadows, the light end of one plate beside the dark end of the next, and faint coloured glazes.
true-metal-technique.mirror shine on armour: Push contrast hard: black steel mixes in shadow bands, bright silver stippled on top, and a light touch on prominent upward edges.
true-metal-technique.chrome effect: See: this method's high contrast placement, near white highlights beside very deep shadows, in body points 1, 3 and 5.
true-metal-technique.metallics look flat and grey: Place dark and light mixes as reflections, avoid washes, which kill shine, and add faint blue, purple or warm yellow glazes.
true-metal-technique.black in recesses of metal: Yes, pure black is fine in the deepest recesses; real polished steel has very deep shadows beside near white highlights.

undead-and-sickly-skin.undead skin: Drain a normal flesh with grey or pale grey green, highlight with pale grey, khaki or bone, and keep thin crimson or purple in the recesses.
undead-and-sickly-skin.zombie skin: Mix green into the shadows and midtones, cold yellow into the highlights, and stipple rather than smooth; stain shadows turquoise for rot.
undead-and-sickly-skin.pale sick skin: Drain flesh with grey or pale grey green, leave out the orange, and highlight with pale grey, khaki or bone instead of warm yellow.
undead-and-sickly-skin.corpse skin: Drain flesh with grey, keep a little warmth in the deepest shadows, and vary the highlight: pale khaki green for rotting, icy blue for long dead.
undead-and-sickly-skin.rotting flesh: Stain the natural shadows with thin turquoise, then a thin magenta more selectively once dry, with a pale khaki green highlight.
undead-and-sickly-skin.ghoul skin colour: Base dark plum and layer up with more and more green, always keeping a little purple, with pure pale green on the highest points.
undead-and-sickly-skin.pale vampire skin: Keep pinks out of cheeks and lips for a bloodless look, highlight cold with pale violet and pale blue, and set it against red and black.
undead-and-sickly-skin.how do i make skin look dead: Drain a normal flesh with grey, black or pale grey green, then highlight with pale grey, khaki or bone rather than white or warm yellow.
undead-and-sickly-skin.sickly green skin: Add green to the shadow and midtone mixes and a cold yellow to the highlights, and stipple and dab for a rough texture.
undead-and-sickly-skin.how to make skin look ill: Mix green into the shadows, cold yellow into highlights, stipple roughly, and run thin crimson around wounds and under the eyes.

using-value.value: Value is how light or dark a colour is, and it does more to make a model read than the choice of hue.
using-value.light and dark: Make neighbouring areas differ in value, not just hue: light next to mid, dark next to either, never dark against dark.
using-value.value scheme: Use one scheme colour at different values on different areas: dark on the cloak, mid on the armour, light on the trim.
using-value.greyscale test: Take a black and white photo; if two neighbouring areas look the same grey, change one.
using-value.value contrast: Place light next to mid and dark next to either, never dark against dark, and let the face reach the brightest values.
using-value.model reads badly: Check it in a black and white photo; neighbouring areas the same grey merge from a distance, so change one.
using-value.how important is value: Very: it does more to make a model read than hue, and a model painted only in greys still shows light, shadow and material.
using-value.tonal contrast: Vary neighbouring areas in value, let important areas like the face reach the brightest values, and keep less important areas darker.
using-value.value study: A model painted only in greys still shows light, shadow and material; check your values with a black and white photo.
using-value.one colour at different values: Yes: one colour at several values, dark cloak, mid armour, light trim, reads as one scheme without repeating.

vignette-bases.vignette base: Paint the outer base very dark into a black rim, work lighter tones in towards the feet, and highlight only details near the middle.
vignette-bases.dark rim light middle: Paint the outer area very dark so it blends into a black rim, then work lighter tones in towards the centre under the feet.
vignette-bases.how do i fade a base to black: Paint the outer area very dark so it blends into a black rim, getting lighter towards the centre under the model.
vignette-bases.base fade: Fade from dark at the rim to light under the feet, with the strongest highlights only on detail tops near the middle.
vignette-bases.display base gradient: Dark outer area into a black rim, lighter tones towards the feet, in cool tones for a cool figure or a warm glow for a warm one.
vignette-bases.base distracts from model: Vignette it: dark at the rim, lighter under the feet, so the eye is pulled onto the model.
vignette-bases.dark edges on base: Paint the outer area very dark so it blends into a black rim, then lighten towards the centre.
vignette-bases.spotlight effect on base: Work lighter tones in towards the centre under the feet, and put the strongest highlights only on detail tops near the middle.
vignette-bases.pull the eye to the model: Fade the base from dark at the rim to light under the feet; the eye follows the light onto the model.
vignette-bases.base lighter under feet: Yes: work lighter tones in towards the centre, under the feet, from a very dark outer area and black rim.

watercolour-gouache-washes.watercolour wash: Gloss varnish first, brush runny watercolour or gouache into recesses, let it dry, then wipe the raised areas clean with a damp brush or bud.
watercolour-gouache-washes.gouache wash: Water down black or dark brown gouache until runny and brush it into recesses over gloss varnish; it gives stronger lines than watercolour.
watercolour-gouache-washes.wash i can wipe off: Use a runny gouache or watercolour wash over gloss varnish; once dry, a damp brush, bud or finger lifts it off the raised areas.
watercolour-gouache-washes.removable wash: Gouache or watercolour over gloss varnish stays workable: water wakes it up, so you can wipe it off and redo it.
watercolour-gouache-washes.wash over gloss varnish: Gloss protects the paint and lets a gouache or watercolour wash wipe clean off the raised areas once dry.
watercolour-gouache-washes.how do i undo a wash: With a gouache or watercolour wash over gloss, wet it again and wipe it off; water wakes the paint up.
watercolour-gouache-washes.watercolour on minis: Over a gloss varnish, watercolour works as a soft tint that wipes back off the raised areas; seal it with spray varnish when done.
watercolour-gouache-washes.gouache on minis: Thin it runny over gloss varnish, brush it into recesses, wipe the raised areas once dry, then seal with a sprayed varnish.
watercolour-gouache-washes.panel lining with gouache: Brush runny black or dark brown gouache into panel lines over gloss, let it dry, then wipe the surface clean so only the lines stay dark.
watercolour-gouache-washes.wash mistakes easy to fix: Use gouache or watercolour over gloss: until you seal it with spray varnish, water lifts it so you can wipe off and redo anything.

weathering-pencils.weathering pencils: Dampen the tip with a wet brush, draw on rust, chips or dust, then streak, fade or lift it with a clean damp brush.
weathering-pencils.watercolour pencils: Wet the tip so it becomes a thick paste, draw on the weathering, then shape or remove it with a damp brush.
weathering-pencils.rust pencil: Draw rust on with a damp tip, blend several rust tones together on the surface with a clean damp brush, and varnish if handled a lot.
weathering-pencils.chips with a pencil: Dampen the pencil and draw chips on boldly; a sharp dry point is fine for small markings, and a damp brush lifts mistakes.
weathering-pencils.pencil weathering: Draw rust, chips, verdigris or dust with a dampened pencil tip, then streak, fade or erase it with a clean damp brush.
weathering-pencils.watercolor pencils: Touch the tip with a wet brush first, then draw; it goes on as a bold paste and stays workable when wet again.
weathering-pencils.pencil dust: Pale dusty colours show best on black items; draw them on with a damp tip and fade them with a damp brush.
weathering-pencils.how to use weathering pencils: Dampen the tip, draw on rust, chips or grime, shape it with a clean damp brush, and varnish if the piece will be handled a lot.
weathering-pencils.pencil marks look dusty: Dampen the tip first by touching it with a wet brush; used dry, it leaves dusty, patchy lines.
weathering-pencils.pencil chipping: Draw chips with a damp pencil tip, or a sharp dry point for small marks, and lift any overdone ones with a damp brush.

wet-palette-problems.wet palette: Use baking paper cut smaller than the sponge, keep water level with the sponge top, blot droplets, and clean it weekly.
wet-palette-problems.wet palette paper curls: Cut the paper smaller than the sponge so it cannot lift at the edges, soak both sides and smooth out bubbles and creases.
wet-palette-problems.paint too watery on palette: The sponge is too wet: squeeze some out, blot stray droplets, and vent the lid slightly if paint goes runny overnight.
wet-palette-problems.mould in palette: Use distilled or boiled water with a drop of washing up liquid or hydrogen peroxide, and clean tray, lid and sponge weekly.
wet-palette-problems.wet palette smells: Empty the water, bin the paper, wash tray and lid in hot soapy water, and deep clean the sponge in boiling water or vinegar and water.
wet-palette-problems.how do i fix my wet palette: Keep water level with the sponge top, blot droplets, use baking paper cut smaller than the sponge, and clean it once a week.
wet-palette-problems.best paper for wet palette: Baking paper works well; some supplied membranes are not porous enough for hobby paints. Replace it often.
wet-palette-problems.wet palette mold: Use distilled or boiled and cooled water plus a drop of washing up liquid, peroxide or an anti mould additive, and clean it weekly.
wet-palette-problems.paint going runny: Squeeze water out of an overwet sponge, blot droplets on top, and vent the lid slightly if paint soaks up water overnight.
wet-palette-problems.how wet should the sponge be: Keep the water level with the top of the sponge; if paint turns watery it is too wet, if it dries fast the sponge has dried.

whole-model-colour-gradient.colour gradient across the whole model: Give each armour plate its own flat colour, shifting step by step, such as deep red at the boots to orange yellow on the helmet.
whole-model-colour-gradient.red at the feet to yellow at the head: Deep red on the boots, orange in the middle and orange yellow on the shoulders and helmet, each plate one flat colour.
whole-model-colour-gradient.gradient armour: Paint each plate one flat colour and shift it plate by plate; the steps between plates make the gradient, so no wet blending is needed.
whole-model-colour-gradient.colour shift across armour plates: Mix the in between colours from their neighbours, such as red with orange, so each plate's step looks related.
whole-model-colour-gradient.fade colour across a model: Shift the colour plate by plate, putting the brightest, warmest colour at the head and shoulders to draw the eye to the face.
whole-model-colour-gradient.ombre armour: Paint each plate a flat colour stepping from deep red to orange yellow, mixing the in betweens from their neighbours.
whole-model-colour-gradient.transition from one colour to another: Mix the in between colours from their neighbours so each step looks related, giving each plate one of them.
whole-model-colour-gradient.plate by plate gradient: Give each plate its own flat colour; because each is distinct, the steps from plate to plate make the gradient.
whole-model-colour-gradient.colour change from boots to helmet: Deep red at the boots, orange in the middle, orange yellow at the top, with a pale undercoat under the yellow plates.
whole-model-colour-gradient.how do i do a gradient scheme: Step the colour plate by plate, brightest at the head, mixing in betweens from neighbours, then one shared highlight to tie it together.

bark-rocks.bark as rocks on bases: Break garden or cork bark into pieces of different sizes and super glue them down; the flaky layers read like wind worn rock.
bark-rocks.cork bark rocks: Cork bark breaks into flaky, layered pieces that look like wind worn rock. Glue them down, base near black and drybrush up to pale stone.
bark-rocks.how do i make cheap rocks for my bases: Use garden bark chips: break them into different sizes, super glue them down, base near black, then drybrush grey brown and pale stone.
bark-rocks.garden bark chips for basing: Garden bark chips make layered, wind worn rocks. Plan them while building so the feet still fit, then super glue them down.
bark-rocks.layered rock look on a base: Break bark so its flaky layers show and glue it down. Base near black, drybrush mid grey brown, then a light pale stone on top edges only.
bark-rocks.rocky outcrop for a model to stand on: Glue down a large bark chunk and pin through foot, rock and base, as glue alone can snap. Plan it while building so the feet still fit.
bark-rocks.make a riverbed with rocks: Roll leftover epoxy putty into smooth pebbles, scatter fine sand between them, and fill any awkward gaps with small rocks before priming.
