bark-rocks.what can i use for big rocks on a base: Garden bark chips or real cork bark. Break them into pieces of different sizes; the flaky layers read like wind worn rock.
bark-rocks.flaky stone cliffs from bark: Break bark so the flaky layers show. Base near black right into every layer, then drybrush grey brown and a light pale stone on top edges.
bark-rocks.wind worn rocks diy: Bark chips do it: their flaky layers read like wind worn rock. Break them up, super glue them down, then base dark and drybrush lighter.

crackle-earth.cracked earth base: Lay crackle paint over a thin sandy coat, blend it into the sand with a damp brush, let it dry fully, then seal it before any washes.
crackle-earth.dry desert ground with cracks: Blend crackle paint into sand, base pale sandy yellow, wash the cracks dull red brown, and drybrush pale bone in many light passes.
crackle-earth.sun baked mud base: Crackle paint blended into sand gives sun baked cracked ground. Seal it once dry, then paint it pale sandy yellow with red brown in the cracks.
crackle-earth.crackle paint on bases: Put a thin sandy or brown coat down first, add crackle with a little grit, blend it into the sand with a damp brush, dry fully, then seal.
crackle-earth.how to make a dried up riverbed base: Use crackle paint for the cracked mud: lay it over a thin sandy coat, blend it into the sand, push rocks into the sandy parts and seal it dry.
crackle-earth.drought cracked soil: Crackle texture paint, mixed with a little grit and blended into sand, cracks as it dries. Seal it, then wash the cracks a dull red brown.
crackle-earth.cracks too small on my base: Mix a little grit into the crackle and lay it thicker for bigger cracks, but not too thick or it chips off.
crackle-earth.crackle chipping off base: It is probably laid too thick. Once dry, seal it with varnish or thinned white glue so washes do not loosen it and chunks stay put.
crackle-earth.craquelure ground effect: Use crackle paint over a thin sandy coat. For crisper cracks, press a very thin sheet of putty over a bumpy base and crack it with a brush end.
crackle-earth.parched wasteland base: Crackle paint blended into sand, painted pale sandy yellow, washed red brown in the cracks, drybrushed pale bone, with dry beige tufts.

forest-floor.woodland base: Build height with putty, glue bark or rocks big to small, add a twig as a fallen branch, then soil, leaf litter, and moss and tufts once painted.
forest-floor.how to make a forest floor base: Press putty on for height, glue bark and stones big to small, scatter soil and leaf litter, lock it with thin super glue, then add moss.
forest-floor.leaf litter on a base: Scatter crumbled dried leaves, birch seeds or tea leaves, or set single leaves with tweezers, then lock it all with thin super glue.
forest-floor.bark and moss basing: Glue bark pieces first, then smaller stones and soil. Once painted, add moss clumps with white glue against rocks and in hollows.
forest-floor.base for elves in a forest: Build a forest floor: putty for height, bark and rocks, a twig as a fallen branch, soil and leaf litter, then moss and tufts in clusters.
forest-floor.make my base look like woods: Add height with putty, half bury bark and rocks, lay a twig as a fallen branch, scatter soil and leaves, then cluster moss and tufts.
forest-floor.height on a base with rocks and roots: Press epoxy putty onto the base and shape it with wet fingers, pushing bark or rocks in to half bury them before it sets.
forest-floor.fallen leaves and moss on the ground: Scatter crumbled dried leaves and lock them with thin super glue. After painting, add moss clumps with white glue in hollows and against rocks.
forest-floor.forest basing with sticks and soil: Glue a twig across one side as a fallen branch and settle it in, then scatter dried soil and leaf litter and lock it with thin super glue.
forest-floor.what order do i glue basing bits: Always big to small: the biggest bark or rocks first, then smaller stones, then soil and leaf litter, with moss and tufts after painting.

real-soil-bases.using real dirt on bases: Dry garden soil right through, grind it fine, sift it through a stocking, then dip the base into it over thinned white glue.
real-soil-bases.garden soil for basing: Garden soil works once dried fully, ground fine, picked clean of stones and twigs, and sifted through a nylon stocking.
real-soil-bases.sand looks like boulders on small bases: Coarse grains read as boulders at that scale. Use sifted garden soil instead, and keep a tub of only the finest dirt.
real-soil-bases.how fine should basing grit be: For small bases, fine enough to pass through a nylon stocking; coarse grains look like boulders.
real-soil-bases.sift soil for bases: Dry it fully so it does not clump, grind it in an old blender or mortar, pick out stones and twigs, then sift it through a nylon stocking.
real-soil-bases.can i use dirt from outside on my models: Yes, if it is dried right through, ground fine and sifted. Glue it with thinned white glue, and seal it with thin super glue to paint at once.
real-soil-bases.fine texture for small bases: Use sifted garden soil from a tub of only the finest dirt, over thinned white glue that does not pool into sculpted detail.
real-soil-bases.base texture too coarse: Switch to dried garden soil ground fine and sifted through a stocking; coarse grains look like boulders on small bases.
real-soil-bases.realistic earth ground: Sifted real soil over thinned white glue, based dark earth brown, drybrushed mid earth, then a very light pale tan on the highest grains.
real-soil-bases.does real soil work for basing: Yes. Dried, ground and sifted garden soil keeps small or sculpted bases crisp where coarser grit would look like boulders.

slate-shards.broken slate on base: Glue broken slate shards angled upward as if the ground burst open, then blend the gaps with paste or putty and sprinkle soil on while wet.
slate-shards.ground bursting open base: Glue sharp slate shards so they angle upward, blend paste or putty round them, and pile soil against the shards while it is wet.
slate-shards.jagged rocks sticking up: Use real slate shards glued at an upward angle, with paste or putty blended round them and soil piled up against them.
slate-shards.cork vs slate for rocks: See: slate breaks into sharp shards suited to burst, broken ground; this entry covers slate only.
slate-shards.shattered earth base: Angle slate shards upward, blend the gaps with paste, add soil, then base blue black, wash muddy blue brown and drybrush slate grey on the edges.
slate-shards.how to break slate for bases: Wrap a natural slate tile in a cloth before you hit it with a hammer, then pick out the best sharp shards.
slate-shards.rocks pushing through ground: Glue slate shards angled upward and pile soil against them while the paste is still wet, so they look like they burst through.
slate-shards.earthquake cracked base: Set broken slate shards at upward angles as if the ground has burst open, blend round them with paste or putty, then add soil.
slate-shards.sharp stone shards on base: Break slate in a cloth with a hammer, pick the sharpest shards, glue them angled upward and drybrush slate grey on the split edges.
slate-shards.real slate for basing: Break a natural slate tile in a cloth, glue the shards angled upward, blend with earth paste, lock loose soil with thinned white glue.

trees-from-twigs.model trees from twigs: Glue dry roots and twigs one branch at a time with super glue and accelerator, then press putty into the joins and drag a tool along the grain.
trees-from-twigs.how do i make trees for a base: Build them from dry roots and twigs glued with super glue and accelerator, hide the joins with putty, then add clump foliage or sea moss.
trees-from-twigs.use roots and sticks as trees: Yes. Collect far more than you need, pick a main tree that towers over the figure, and glue it a branch at a time, letting each set.
trees-from-twigs.hide joins on twig trees: Press epoxy putty into the gaps and joins, curing each layer, then drag a tool along the grain so it reads as bark. Base it all dark brown.
trees-from-twigs.dead tree on a display base: Use a gnarled dry root, glued with super glue and accelerator, putty the joins as bark, base dark brown and drybrush grey brown and pale grey.
trees-from-twigs.framing a figure with trees: Place the largest tree first, then smaller ones either side of the figure, with one running past the top.
trees-from-twigs.scratch build trees cheaply: Collect dry roots and twigs, glue them with super glue and accelerator, and blend the joins with epoxy putty textured along the grain.
trees-from-twigs.spooky gnarled tree from a root: Use a dry root as the trunk, putty its joins and texture them as bark, base dark bark brown, then drybrush grey brown and pale grey.
trees-from-twigs.tree on a diorama: Build the tree from roots and twigs, glue it a branch at a time, putty the joins, and pin the figure so it always refits.
trees-from-twigs.putty to blend branches together: Press two part epoxy putty into the gaps, curing each layer, then drag a sculpting tool along the grain so it reads as bark.

albino-scaly-skin.albino lizard skin: Pale bone over light grey primer, a thin pinkish grey contrast built towards the spine, flesh pink glazes in folds, pink tinted ivory edges.
albino-scaly-skin.pale pink reptile skin: Base pale bone, build a thin pink and grey purple one coat paint towards the spine, glaze flesh pink into creases, edge in pink tinted ivory.
albino-scaly-skin.how do i paint white scales: Start very pale: bone over a light grey primer, then thin pinkish grey coats, pink glazes in the folds, and ivory edges near the face.
albino-scaly-skin.pale scaly skin: Pale bone base, thin coats of pinkish grey one coat paint, flesh pink glazed into folds, then pink tinted ivory on the scales by the face.
albino-scaly-skin.albino snake: Base pale bone over light grey primer, build pinkish grey in thin coats towards the spine, glaze pink into folds, edge in pink tinted ivory.
albino-scaly-skin.pinkish grey skin: Mix pink and grey purple one coat paints evenly and build them in thin coats over a pale bone base, darker towards the spine.
albino-scaly-skin.light scales on a dinosaur: Pale bone base, thin pinkish grey built up towards the spine, flesh pink in the creases, and pink tinted ivory edges near the face.
albino-scaly-skin.pale lizard folk skin: Bone over light grey primer, thin pinkish grey coats towards the spine, flesh pink glazes in knuckles and folds, pink tinted ivory edges.
albino-scaly-skin.washed out pale reptile: Keep the start very pale, bone over light grey, then add colour only in thin pinkish grey coats and very thin flesh pink glazes.
albino-scaly-skin.how to paint pale scales without it look: See: this recipe keeps it pale with thin coats of pinkish grey over bone, adding pink glazes in folds rather than more white.

black-scaly-hide.black dragon skin: Prime black, stipple a very dark grey heavily for scale texture, then a finer dark grey on raised areas, with neutral grey nicks and scratches.
black-scaly-hide.paint a black dragon: Black primer as the shadow, a heavy very dark grey stipple, a lighter dark grey stipple on raised areas, then small neutral grey highlights.
black-scaly-hide.dark scaly monster hide: Prime black, stab on very dark grey to fake scales, stipple dark grey finer on the raised areas, then nick in neutral grey scratches.
black-scaly-hide.near black skin for big monsters: Keep black primer as the deepest shadow and stipple up through very dark grey and dark grey, breaking flat areas with grey scratches.
black-scaly-hide.black scales without looking flat: Stipple texture on with very dark then dark grey, and break large flat areas with small neutral grey nicks, scratches and knee highlights.
black-scaly-hide.stipple texture on smooth skin: Stab a very dark grey on heavily over smooth hide to fake a scaly texture, then stipple a lighter grey more finely on raised areas.
black-scaly-hide.black lizard skin: Black primer, a heavy very dark grey stipple, a finer dark grey stipple on raised areas, then small neutral grey highlights.
black-scaly-hide.dark reptile hide: Prime black, stipple very dark grey for texture, then dark grey on the raised areas, with neutral grey nicks to break it up.
black-scaly-hide.how to highlight black scales: Stipple up with very dark grey then dark grey on raised areas, and finish with small neutral grey nicks, scratches and knee highlights.
black-scaly-hide.black wyvern: Prime black, stipple very dark grey heavily for scales, a finer dark grey on raised areas, then neutral grey nicks on the big flat areas.

bright-bronze.bright bronze: Base a saturated bronze, wash amber brown without pooling, line dark brown into recesses, then edge with bronze and silver.
bright-bronze.warm bronze that pops: Use a saturated bronze, or silver mixed with an orange brown one coat paint, then an amber brown wash, dark brown lining and pale bronze edges.
bright-bronze.bronze stands out against dark colours: A saturated warm bronze stands out against cold dark colours: bright bronze base, amber brown wash, dark brown lining, pale bronze edges.
bright-bronze.shiny saturated bronze trim: Base bright bronze in smooth coats, wash amber brown all over, line dark brown round each detail, then edge in bronze mixed with silver.
bright-bronze.mix silver and orange for bronze: Yes: silver mixed with an orange brown one coat paint makes a bright bronze base. Follow with an amber brown wash and pale bronze edges.
bright-bronze.how to paint bright bronze armour: Bright bronze base, amber brown wash all over, dark brown mixed with black lined into recesses, then relayer bronze and edge with silver.
bright-bronze.bronze pooling in recesses: Wash amber brown all over but do not let it pool. Put the depth back by lining dark brown and black into the recesses instead.
bright-bronze.golden bronze weapons: Base a bright bronze, wash amber brown, line dark brown round details, then relayer bronze on raised parts and edge in bronze and silver.
bright-bronze.make bronze look rich not dull: Start with a saturated bronze, not a dull one, add an amber brown wash, line the recesses dark brown, and edge in bronze mixed with silver.
bright-bronze.bronze recipe for cold schemes: Bright bronze base, amber brown wash, dark brown lining and pale bronze edges; the warm saturation stands out against cold dark colours.

clean-bone-armour.bone armour: Pale cream over a light primer, a warm sand glaze on lower panels, thinned dark brown lined into recesses, near white on the edges.
clean-bone-armour.how do i paint bone white armour: Base pale cream in thin coats, glaze warm sand low down, line dark brown into recesses only, then edge with the cream mixed half with white.
clean-bone-armour.off white armour: Pale cream base, bone and sandy brown glazed on the lower panels, dark brown lining in recesses, and a near white edge highlight.
clean-bone-armour.clean bone colour: Keep it clean by lining thinned dark brown only into recesses, tidying overflow with the cream base, then edging in near white.
clean-bone-armour.ivory armour plates: Pale cream base, warm sand glaze on the lower panels, dark brown lines in the recesses, then cream mixed half with white on the edges.
clean-bone-armour.bone white looks chalky: See: this recipe glazes a warm sand onto the lower panels and lines recesses in dark brown, which adds the warmth and contrast bone needs.
clean-bone-armour.paint bone with brown lines: Thin dark brown half and half with water and line it into recesses only, then tidy any overflow with the pale cream base.
clean-bone-armour.cream armour: Pale cream over a light or bone primer, warm sand glazed on lower panels, dark brown lining, then a near white edge highlight.
clean-bone-armour.bone coloured shoulder pads: Base pale cream, glaze two parts bone to one sandy brown low on the pad, line the recesses dark brown, and edge in near white.
clean-bone-armour.high contrast bone: Clean pale cream with dark brown lined into the recesses and near white edges gives high contrast; tidy overflow with the base colour.

dark-iron.gunmetal colour: Gunmetal mixed half and half with black, a dark wash with a little gloss medium, then a lighter grey metal on raised parts and silver edges.
dark-iron.dark iron weapons: Base very dark metal, wash brown black into recesses, layer a dull grey metal on raised parts, then bright silver on sharp edges only.
dark-iron.dull dark metal: Darken silver or gunmetal with black for the base, wash brown black, layer a dull grey metal on raised parts, and keep silver to the edges.
dark-iron.paint gun barrels dark metal: Base gunmetal mixed half and half with black, wash brown black into recesses, layer dull grey metal on top, silver on the sharp edges.
dark-iron.blackened steel: Silver darkened with black, a brown black wash with a little gloss medium, a dull grey metal on raised parts, bright silver on edges only.
dark-iron.dark metal for small parts: Very dark metal base, any dark wash into recesses, a dull grey metal layer on raised parts, and bright silver on sharp edges.
dark-iron.iron that isnt shiny: Base gunmetal mixed half with black so it stays dark, then keep bright silver to the sharp edges only.
dark-iron.gunmetal grey: Mix gunmetal half and half with black, wash it brown black, then layer two parts base to one light grey on raised parts.
dark-iron.wash on dark metal went flat: Add a little gloss medium to the dark wash; it keeps the metal from going flat.
dark-iron.black iron recipe: Very dark metal base, brown black wash with gloss medium, dull grey metal layer, bright silver edges, and warm brown in rivets for rust.

frost-and-ice-weapons.ice sword: Base a vivid blue, dab many thin crisscrossed white coats for facets, glaze pale icy blue all over, then dab white chips on the edges.
frost-and-ice-weapons.how do i paint an ice blade: Start with a strong saturated blue, build thin dabbed whites to suggest facets, leaving some blue, glaze icy blue, then chip white on edges.
frost-and-ice-weapons.frozen weapon effect: Vivid blue base, many thin dabbed whites for facets, a pale icy blue glaze with a little turquoise in patches, and white chips on the ridges.
frost-and-ice-weapons.glassy ice axe: Base a strong blue, crisscross thin whites for a faceted, glassy look while leaving some blue, glaze pale icy blue, and chip white on edges.
frost-and-ice-weapons.frost weapon looks like plain blue: Build many thin dabbed, crisscrossed whites over the blue to suggest facets, then dab white chips along edges rather than a smooth line.
frost-and-ice-weapons.crystal blade faceted look: Dab and crisscross many thin white coats over a vivid blue to suggest facets, leaving some blue showing.
frost-and-ice-weapons.icy blue sword recipe: Vivid blue base, thin dabbed whites for facets, a pale icy blue glaze with patches of turquoise, then white chips on edges and ridges.
frost-and-ice-weapons.make a weapon look frozen: Over a vivid blue, dab thin whites in crisscross strokes, glaze pale icy blue all over, then dab white chips along the edges.
frost-and-ice-weapons.frost magic blade: Strong blue base, faceted thin whites, a pale icy blue glaze touched with turquoise, and white chips along the edges and ridges.
frost-and-ice-weapons.ice spear paint: Base the head a vivid blue, dab thin crisscrossed whites for facets, glaze pale icy blue, then chip white along the edges.

green-glowing-lenses.green glowing eyes: Paint the lens and nearby glow area white, thin a bright green contrast over both, add pale green on the lens, and a white dot at the back.
green-glowing-lenses.glowing lenses: White over the lens and glow area, thinned bright green contrast on top, pale green on the lens itself, then one white reflection dot.
green-glowing-lenses.how do i make eye lenses glow: Paint the lens and the area around it white, then thinned bright green over both so it tints the surroundings, and pale green on the lens.
green-glowing-lenses.light spill from lenses: Paint the nearby area that will catch the glow white along with the lens, then tint it with thinned bright green.
green-glowing-lenses.glowing visor: White over the visor and nearby glow area, thinned bright green contrast over both, pale green on the visor, and a white reflection dot.
green-glowing-lenses.green eye lenses on a helmet: Base the lens and surrounding area white, glaze thinned bright green over it, layer pale green on the lens and dot white at the back.
green-glowing-lenses.make lenses look glassy: Layer green mixed with white on the lens, then put one white dot at the back of the lens as a reflection.
green-glowing-lenses.glow effect around eyes: Paint the area round the eyes white along with them, then thin a bright green with medium over it so it gathers in the recesses.
green-glowing-lenses.robot glowing eyes: White base on the eyes and the area around them, thinned bright green contrast over both, pale green on the eyes, white reflection dot.
green-glowing-lenses.lense glow: White over the lens and glow area, bright green contrast thinned with medium, pale green on the lens and one white reflection dot.

grimy-steel.grimy metal: Base a dark steel that barely shines, brown black wash into recesses, then short scratchy silver strokes on edges only.
grimy-steel.dirty steel: Silver mixed with black and brown as a base, a thinned brown black shade in recesses, and scratchy bright silver on the edges.
grimy-steel.quick dark metal for a horde: Dark steel base, brown black shade lifted off high spots with a damp brush, then a light silver drybrush or scratchy edges.
grimy-steel.speed paint metal: Three steps: a dark steel base, a thinned brown black shade in the recesses, then scratchy silver edges or a light silver drybrush.
grimy-steel.worn steel for squads: Dark steel base, brown black thinned into recesses, then short scratchy silver strokes on edges, keeping the rest dark.
grimy-steel.dull dirty weapons: Base dark steel that barely shines, shade brown black into recesses, and add only short scratchy silver strokes on the edges.
grimy-steel.metal for a big army fast: Base a ready thinned dark steel, shade brown black, and finish with a light silver drybrush; quick enough for a whole group.
grimy-steel.grubby armour: Dark steel base, thinned brown black in the recesses with excess lifted off the high spots, and scratchy silver edges.
grimy-steel.fast metal batch painting: Dark steel base, brown black shade, then a light silver drybrush or scratchy edges, keeping most of it dark.
grimy-steel.dark steel that barely shines: Mix silver with black and brown, or use a ready thinned dark steel, then shade brown black and keep silver to the edges.

metallic-red.metallic red: Drybrush light silver over black, then two thin coats of cherry red one coat paint or ink, deep red in the recesses and bright red edges.
metallic-red.candy red armour: Prime black, drybrush light silver so raised areas shine, then two thin coats of cherry red one coat paint or ink barely thinned.
metallic-red.shiny red metal effect: Drybrush silver over a black primer, glaze two thin cherry red coats over it, shade deep red into recesses and lift edges bright red.
metallic-red.how to paint metallic red: Prime black, drybrush light silver, add two thin coats of red one coat paint or ink, then deep red in recesses and bright red edges.
metallic-red.red over silver drybrush: Yes: drybrush light silver so the raised areas shine, then two thin coats of cherry red thinned with only a touch of water.
metallic-red.red paint over metallic: Use red one coat paint or ink over a silver drybrush or pale silver base, in two thin coats with only a touch of water.
metallic-red.glossy metallic red car: Black primer, light silver drybrush, two thin cherry red coats of one coat paint or ink, deep red shading and bright red edges.
metallic-red.red armour that shines: Silver drybrushed over black makes the raised areas shine through two thin coats of cherry red; shade deep red, edge bright red.
metallic-red.candy apple red miniature: Silver drybrushed over black, then two thin coats of cherry red ink or one coat paint, with deep red in the recesses.
metallic-red.red with gold underneath: Drybrush gold underneath instead of silver for a warmer red, then two thin coats of cherry red over it.

painted-copper-and-bronze.copper without metallic paint: Start a very dark, slightly pink red brown, layer rusty orange brown reflections, push warm orange yellow into lit areas, then ivory edges.
painted-copper-and-bronze.nmm bronze: Deep red brown base, rusty orange brown reflections on upper planes, warm orange yellow in the lit areas, pale ivory on exposed edges only.
painted-copper-and-bronze.how to paint non metallic copper: Base a dark, slightly pink red brown, glaze rusty orange brown reflections, cover less each time with orange yellow, then ivory points.
painted-copper-and-bronze.painted bronze: Deep red brown, then rusty orange brown and warm orange yellow layers over less area each time, with pale ivory on the most exposed edges.
painted-copper-and-bronze.fake metal copper: Very dark red brown base, broad rusty orange brown reflections glazed smooth, warm orange yellow in the lit areas, then pale ivory edges.
painted-copper-and-bronze.bronze statue look: See: this entry paints bronze from deep red brown up through rusty orange and orange yellow to pale ivory edges, without metallic paint.
painted-copper-and-bronze.nmm copper: A slightly pink deep red brown base, rusty orange brown reflections, warm orange yellow in lit areas, and pale ivory beside dark brown.
painted-copper-and-bronze.red brown metal effect: Start very dark with a pinkish red brown, then layer rusty orange brown and warm orange yellow before small pale ivory edges.
painted-copper-and-bronze.copper with no metallics: Deep red brown base, layered rusty orange brown and warm orange yellow, with pale ivory on edges and dark brown beside them for contrast.
painted-copper-and-bronze.non metalic bronze: Dark red brown up to rusty orange brown, then warm orange yellow in lit areas before any white, and pale ivory on exposed points.

pink-and-magenta-cloth.pink cloth: Base deep plum magenta, stroke bright magenta along raised folds, tip with pale pink, then glaze milk thin plum over it all to blend.
pink-and-magenta-cloth.how do i highlight pink without it going: Use pale yellow instead of white on the sharpest tips, then glaze milk thin deep plum over everything to blend the steps.
pink-and-magenta-cloth.magenta robes: Thinned deep plum magenta base, bright magenta strokes along raised folds, pale pink on the sharpest tips, and a milk thin plum glaze.
pink-and-magenta-cloth.bright pink cloak: Deep plum magenta base, bright magenta following the sweep of the folds, pale pink tips, then a thin plum glaze to blend.
pink-and-magenta-cloth.pink fabric looks washed out: Keep it saturated: highlight the tips with pale pink mixed using pale yellow rather than white, and glaze milk thin plum back over it.
pink-and-magenta-cloth.hot pink dress folds: Base deep plum magenta, layer bright magenta along the raised folds only, tip in pale pink, and use blue violet in the shadows.
pink-and-magenta-cloth.fuchsia cloth recipe: Deep plum magenta base, bright magenta on raised folds, pale pink on the sharpest tips, then a milk thin deep plum glaze over everything.
pink-and-magenta-cloth.keep pink saturated: Highlight with pale yellow instead of white so the pink stays rich, and glaze deep plum back over to blend.
pink-and-magenta-cloth.pink sash on a model: Two thin coats of deep plum magenta, bright magenta strokes on the raised folds, pale pink tips, then a thin plum glaze.
pink-and-magenta-cloth.glaze pink back with plum: Thin deep plum to the feel of milk and glaze it over everything to blend the highlight steps; blue violet suits the shadows.

quick-skin.quick skin: Base a warm pale bone, flow a warm flesh one coat paint straight over it unthinned, let it settle, then optionally drybrush pale bone.
quick-skin.fast skin for tabletop: Warm pale bone base or primer, then an unthinned warm flesh one coat paint; rank and file models can stop there.
quick-skin.how to paint skin quickly: Over a warm pale bone base, apply a warm flesh one coat paint without thinning and let it settle. Add light pale bone flicks if you like.
quick-skin.two paint skin: A warm pale bone base, then a warm flesh one coat paint straight over the skin. A light pale bone drybrush is optional.
quick-skin.easy flesh tone: Base a warm pale bone, avoiding cold greys, then let an unthinned warm flesh one coat paint settle over it.
quick-skin.skin with contrast paint: Put a warm flesh one coat paint straight over a warm pale bone base without thinning, and let it settle into the recesses.
quick-skin.simple skin recipe for beginners: Two paints: a warm pale bone base, then a warm flesh one coat paint on top. Finish with light pale bone flicks on top edges if you like.
quick-skin.warm skin fast: Use a warm pale bone base, not cold grey, then an unthinned warm flesh one coat paint over it.
quick-skin.flesh paint over bone primer: Yes: a bone primer can stand in for the base. Apply the warm flesh one coat paint straight over without thinning and let it settle.
quick-skin.skin for a whole unit: Bone primer, then a warm flesh one coat paint unthinned; rank and file can stop there, leaders get light pale bone drybrush flicks.

spider-webs.spider webs: Prime the webbing bone, settle a mid grey one coat paint thinned half with medium between strands, then line the tops in white.
spider-webs.cobwebs: Bone or off white primer over the webs, a mid grey wash left between strands, then thin white lines along the tops.
spider-webs.how do i paint webbing: Prime it bone, shade with grey one coat paint thinned half with medium, then run thin white lines along the strand tops with a fine brush.
spider-webs.white web strands: Over a bone primer, settle a thinned mid grey between strands, then edge the tops of the strands in white with a fine brush.
spider-webs.web on a spider base: Prime the sculpted web bone, wash it mid grey thinned half with medium, then pick out the tops of the strands in thin white lines.
spider-webs.paint cobwebs: Off white or bone primer, a mid grey one coat paint thinned half with medium, then fine white lines on top of the strands.
spider-webs.shading thin strands: Thin a grey one coat paint half with medium and let it settle between the strands, then line the tops in white.
spider-webs.spider lair: See: this entry covers painting sculpted webs: bone primer, a mid grey wash between strands, and thin white edges.
spider-webs.web looks messy: Keep it to three steps: bone primer, a thinned grey left to settle between strands, then thin white lines only along the tops.
spider-webs.off white webs: Prime bone or off white, shade with grey thinned half with medium, then edge the strand tops in white.

two-colour-primer-blend.two colour zenithal: Prime black, spray deep purple from many angles leaving only deep recesses black, then bright pink from above only.
two-colour-primer-blend.purple to pink spray over black: Black all over, deep purple from many angles so only the deepest recesses stay black, then bright pink sprayed from above only.
two-colour-primer-blend.coloured zenithal priming: Over black, spray a deep colour such as purple from many angles, then a brighter one such as pink from above only.
two-colour-primer-blend.spray two colours for a glow: Prime black, then deep purple from many angles, then bright pink from above only; pink then bright blue gives a neon look.
two-colour-primer-blend.rattle can gradient on a model: Black primer, a deep purple sprayed from many angles, then a bright pink from directly above for the gradient.
two-colour-primer-blend.how do i get a glow from primer alone: Spray black, then deep purple from all angles, then bright pink only from above. For neon, use pink then a bright blue.
two-colour-primer-blend.colour fade with spray cans: Black first, a deep purple from many angles leaving the deepest recesses black, then bright pink sprayed from above.
two-colour-primer-blend.coloured primer over black: Spray black all over, then a deep colour from many angles and a bright colour from above, so recesses stay dark.
two-colour-primer-blend.undercoat that already looks lit: Black all over, deep purple from many angles, then bright pink from above only, so the light reads as coming down.
two-colour-primer-blend.zenithal with coloured sprays: Black base, deep purple from many angles, bright pink from above only; pink then bright blue gives a neon version.

woodland-camo.woodland camo: Olive green base, fairly large dark grey green blotches, smaller pale greenish cream shapes, then a dark brown wash to tie it together.
woodland-camo.how do i paint camouflage: Base olive green, add large dark grey green blotches, then smaller pale cream shapes leaving both showing, and wash it all dark brown.
woodland-camo.olive camo on vehicles: Two coats of olive green, big dark grey green blotches, smaller pale greenish cream shapes, then one part dark brown wash to two of water.
woodland-camo.sponge camo: Over a light beige or olive base, sponge dark grey green speckles with most paint dabbed off, then smaller cream shapes and a brown wash.
woodland-camo.green camo pattern: Olive green, then dark grey green blotches, then smaller pale greenish cream shapes, all tied together with a thinned dark brown wash.
woodland-camo.camo blotches: Make the dark grey green blotches fairly large, then the pale cream shapes smaller so both other colours still show.
woodland-camo.tank camouflage: Olive green base, large dark grey green blotches or sponged speckles, small pale cream shapes, then a thinned dark brown wash overall.
woodland-camo.camo on soldiers: Base olive green, add dark grey green blotches, then small pale greenish cream shapes, and wash dark brown thinned with two parts water.
woodland-camo.how to tie camo together: Wash the whole pattern with one part dark brown wash to two parts water.
woodland-camo.military camo scheme: Olive green base, dark grey green blotches, smaller pale greenish cream shapes, and a thinned dark brown wash over the pattern.

aged-dirty-white.dirty white: Finish the white with its grey shading, then wash sepia or light brown over it, stipple shade glazes along the bottom and add brown streaks.
aged-dirty-white.aged white cloth: Paint the white with grey shading as usual, then a sepia or light brown wash to tint it towards a worn yellow.
aged-dirty-white.how to make white look old: Wash finished white with sepia or light brown, stipple glazes along the bottom edge, and pull fine light brown streaks down from rivets.
aged-dirty-white.grimy white armour: Over finished white, use a blue grey wash half and half with water, then pick raised edges back out in white, and add chips and streaks.
aged-dirty-white.yellowed white: Apply a sepia or light brown wash over finished white; it tints it towards a worn yellow.
aged-dirty-white.stained white robes: Wash the finished white sepia or light brown, then stipple thin glazes of the shade colours along the bottom edge for muddy staining.
aged-dirty-white.white looks too clean: Wash it sepia or light brown for age, or blue grey for cool grime, then stipple dirt along the bottom and pull brown streaks from rivets.
aged-dirty-white.weathered white tank: Shade pale warm grey with grey brown towards the bottom and round rivets, add white chips with a brown dot, and light brown streaks.
aged-dirty-white.old dirty bandages: Paint the white with grey shading, then a sepia or light brown wash, and stipple thin shade glazes along the bottom edge.
aged-dirty-white.white with dirt streaks: Pull fine downward streaks of light brown from rivets and edges, after a sepia or blue grey wash over the finished white.

airbrush-safety.do i need a mask to airbrush: Yes. Wear a respirator with filters rated for paint particles every time, plus carbon filters for solvent paints, primers and varnishes.
airbrush-safety.respirator for paint: Use filters rated for paint particles, and activated carbon ones for solvents. Check the seal each time and replace filters as advised.
airbrush-safety.airbrush ventilation: Spray into a booth, ideally one venting outside. Otherwise ventilate well; an open window alone is not enough and a fan must push air outside.
airbrush-safety.is airbrushing water based paint safe: Not without a mask. Water based paint still makes a fine mist that can irritate your airways, so wear a respirator even for short jobs.
airbrush-safety.breathing in paint mist: Avoid it: airbrushing puts a fine paint mist in the air even with water based paint, so wear a respirator rated for paint particles.
airbrush-safety.is a dust mask enough: No. A simple dust mask does nothing against fumes; you need a respirator with paint particle filters, and carbon filters for solvents.
airbrush-safety.airbrushing in a bedroom: Only with a respirator and a booth, ideally venting outside. An open window alone is not enough, and a fan helps only if it blows outside.
airbrush-safety.fumes from airbrush cleaner: Cleaners and strippers are harsher than acrylic paint, so keep the mask on while cleaning, flush into a cleaning pot and keep lids on.
airbrush-safety.non toxic paint safe to spray: No. Non toxic means it will not poison you if swallowed, not that it is safe to breathe as a spray. Wear a respirator.
airbrush-safety.spray booth or open window: A booth, ideally with a hose venting outside. An open window alone is not enough ventilation for airbrushing.

applying-contrast-paints.contrast paint streaky: Work one panel at a time, flowing it across to a natural edge, and never brush back into half dry paint. Keep the model still while it dries.
applying-contrast-paints.how do i apply contrast: Over a light primer, load the brush full, flow it across one panel at a time to a natural edge, then leave it alone once it starts to dry.
applying-contrast-paints.contrast paint pooling: Press a clean, damp brush into the pool to soak it up while it is wet, and check low corners such as under shoulder plates.
applying-contrast-paints.one coat paint tide marks: Flow each panel to a natural edge and slightly over it, keep the model the same way up, and never touch it again once it starts drying.
applying-contrast-paints.contrast looks blotchy: Big smooth panels tend to go blotchy. A light drybrush of a brighter colour fixes mild blotches; use opaque paint on large panels.
applying-contrast-paints.best primer for contrast: White, bone or light grey, or a light drybrush; the paint is see through, so what is underneath sets how bright it ends up.
applying-contrast-paints.contrast paint tips: Light primer, light colours before dark, one panel at a time, soak up pools with a damp brush, and leave it alone once it starts to dry.
applying-contrast-paints.speed painting with one coat paints: Prime light, flow the paint one panel at a time, coat one model then move to the next, and seal with thin matt varnish as it rubs off.
applying-contrast-paints.contrast on flat panels: Big smooth panels tend to go blotchy with one coat paint, so use opaque paint and painted highlights there instead.
applying-contrast-paints.why is my contrast paint patchy: Usually from brushing back into half dry paint, which tears its skin. Work one panel at a time and leave it alone once it starts drying.

base-colours-to-suit-model.what colour should my base be: A different colour family from the model's main colour, such as sand or earth under grey, slightly darker and duller than the figure.
base-colours-to-suit-model.model disappears on its base: The base shares the model's main colour. Pick a different family, such as sand or earth under grey armour, or cold blue ground under red.
base-colours-to-suit-model.base colour clashes with the model: Echo the model's colours on the base a little less strongly, with glazed patches on stones, and paint the base from one related palette.
base-colours-to-suit-model.choosing base colours: Keep the model's main colour off the base, echo its colours there more softly, and keep the base a little darker, duller and less busy.
base-colours-to-suit-model.grey model on grey base: A grey figure on grey rubble disappears. Use sand or earth under grey instead, or glaze the model's colours onto the stones.
base-colours-to-suit-model.base that complements the miniature: Use a colour opposite the model's main one, such as orange dust in the recesses under blue armour, kept less strong than the model.
base-colours-to-suit-model.how to tie the base to the model: Thin the model's main colours to glazes and touch them in random patches on stones, and echo its colours in tufts, pigments or the rim.
base-colours-to-suit-model.base too busy: Keep it slightly darker, duller and less busy than the model. Knock a loud base back with a wash or a duller drybrush.
base-colours-to-suit-model.best base colour for blue armour: A warm contrast works well, such as orange dust in the recesses under blue armour, kept a little less strong than the model.
base-colours-to-suit-model.match base to the figure: Match the model's overall level of colour and echo its colours on the base, a little less strong, while keeping its main colour off the ground.

beating-perfectionism.scared to ruin my model: Paint can be stripped, and a model saved forever is a model never started. Accept imperfect results and finish it.
beating-perfectionism.perfectionism: Accept imperfect results and finish models; finishing, reviewing what went wrong and starting the next teaches more than extra polishing.
beating-perfectionism.i never finish anything: Set one realistic goal per model, and when more tidying risks spoiling the work, stop and call it done.
beating-perfectionism.afraid to paint an expensive model: Paint can be stripped, and the special model will feel less special once something new arrives. Saving it forever means never starting.
beating-perfectionism.unhappy with every model i paint: That is normal: you learn while painting, so by the end it already looks behind your skill. Compare it with your own earlier work.
beating-perfectionism.keep stripping and starting again: Stop redoing old models; you never finish anything that way. Keep older work as a record of progress and move on to the next one.
beating-perfectionism.how do i stop obsessing over tiny mistak: Judge the model at arm's length, where it is usually seen and most faults disappear, and stop when more tidying risks spoiling it.
beating-perfectionism.model looks bad close up: Every model shows faults close up. At arm's length, where it is usually seen, most of them disappear, so judge it from there.
beating-perfectionism.fear of messing up: Paint can be stripped, so nothing is ruined for good. Name the fear, set one realistic goal for the model, and finish it.
beating-perfectionism.how to get faster at finishing minis: Set one realistic goal per model, call it done when tidying risks spoiling it, and move on; finishing teaches more than polishing.

breaking-up-large-areas.big flat areas look boring: Break them up with bands, markings, chips or a gentle colour shift, such as warmer at one end and cooler at the other.
breaking-up-large-areas.how do i make a cloak more interesting: Paint bands or patterns through it, add a gentle warm to cool colour shift, or stipple highlight texture that follows the light.
breaking-up-large-areas.dragon wing looks plain: Paint lines or bands through the membrane, such as cool blue built up to pale ice blue against a warm main colour, as veins or markings.
breaking-up-large-areas.large panels look dull: Add small chips in the highlight colour, a gentle colour shift across the panel, or bands and markings to break it up.
breaking-up-large-areas.patterns on wing membranes: Paint lines or bands through them as veins, energy or natural markings; a cool blue up to pale ice blue contrasts with a warm main colour.
breaking-up-large-areas.add stripes to a big cloak: Paint bands or patterns through it, and knock them back with thin glazes of the base colour if the result is too strong.
breaking-up-large-areas.monster carapace looks flat: Paint thin parallel striations or blended colour markings near the edges, or pick out one band, such as the belly, in another colour.
breaking-up-large-areas.break up a large surface: Use bands, markings, chips, a warm to cool colour shift, or sponge stippled texture, then tie it together with very thin glazes.
breaking-up-large-areas.what to do with big empty panels: Add small chips and marks in the highlight colour, or on a squad paint one panel per model in a contrasting colour like black.
breaking-up-large-areas.shell looks one colour and boring: Paint thin parallel striations or blended colour markings near the edges, and mix in a related hue rather than only lighter and darker.

brush-size.what brush size: Size 2 or 3 for a normal infantry figure, 3 or 4 for larger figures and 4 to 6 for big monsters, as long as it keeps a sharp point.
brush-size.which brush should i use: The biggest brush that still keeps a sharp point; it holds more paint, stays wet longer and works faster.
brush-size.is a size 0 brush good: For eyes, yes: a size 0 is big enough not to dry out and small enough not to flood the socket. For most other work go bigger.
brush-size.tiny brushes for detail: Not needed: a larger brush with a good tip paints fine detail and dries out less. Drop to a small brush only for tight corners.
brush-size.bigger brush better: Usually, if it keeps a sharp point. It holds more paint, dries on the tip less, and covers a panel in one smooth stroke.
brush-size.brush size for details: The point matters more than the size; a large brush with a good tip can still paint fine detail.
brush-size.why use a big brush: It holds more paint, dries on the tip less and covers a panel in one stroke, so there is less chance of dragging half dry paint.
brush-size.what size brush for eyes: A size 0: big enough not to dry out, small enough not to flood the socket. With anything tinier, go straight from palette to model.
brush-size.best brush for beginners: See: this entry advises the biggest brush that keeps a sharp point, around size 2 or 3 for a normal infantry figure.
brush-size.brush point vs size: The point matters more. Judge a brush by its tip, not its number; a large brush with a good tip still paints fine detail.

camouflage-patterns.camo: Pick three or four clearly different tones from one colour family, shade the base first, then block in bold, ragged shapes of varied size.
camouflage-patterns.how to paint camouflage: Shade and highlight the base colour, then outline and fill bold, ragged patches in thinned paint, adding lighter tones and leaving gaps.
camouflage-patterns.desert camo on a tank: Use sands and warm browns in three or four clearly stepped tones, carry patches across the turret join and tracks, and vary each vehicle.
camouflage-patterns.woodland camo uniform: Greens and browns in three or four clearly stepped tones, kept to one part of the figure, such as the smock or trousers.
camouflage-patterns.urban camo greys: Warm greys, three or four tones each clearly darker than the last so no two read as one.
camouflage-patterns.camo colours blend into each other: Make each tone clearly darker than the last, or two will read as one. A very thin dark outline also crisps patches at small scale.
camouflage-patterns.camo pattern on a helmet: On troops, keeping camo to one part such as the helmet stops it hiding the figure's shape; at small scale use fewer tones and simpler shapes.
camouflage-patterns.disruptive pattern on a vehicle: Spray the first colour, mask what stays with putty, tape or liquid mask, spray the next and peel gently for crisp, hard edges.
camouflage-patterns.camoflage for soldiers: Keep it to one part, such as the helmet, smock or trousers, as camo over the whole figure hides its shape.
camouflage-patterns.which colours for camo: Match the bases and setting: sands and warm browns for desert, warm greys for urban, greens and browns for woodland, in three or four tones.

chip-colours.chipping colours: Dark chips on light surfaces, light or warm chips on black, and a mix of light scuffs and dark deeper damage on mid colours.
chip-colours.what colour for chips: It depends on the surface: dark brown or charcoal on light colours, highlight grey or warm brown on black, both light and dark on mid colours.
chip-colours.paint chips on white armour: Use a single dark brown or charcoal, dabbed with the side of the brush in an uneven pattern along the edges.
chip-colours.chips on black armor: A darker chip barely shows, so use the highlight grey, a warm primer like brown, or metallic paint for bare metal, in one step.
chip-colours.battle damage colour: Dark chips on light colours, light or warm chips on black, a mix on mid colours, and metal in the deepest scratches for bare metal.
chip-colours.scratches on yellow vehicle: Chip yellow with a single dark brown or charcoal, dabbed unevenly along the edges with the side of the brush.
chip-colours.dark or light chipping: Dark on light surfaces, light on dark ones, and both on mid to bright colours: light for scuffs, dark for deeper damage.
chip-colours.chip colour on red armour: Red is a mid to bright colour, so combine light scuffs with dark chips; a near black brown suits red well.
chip-colours.how do i choose chip colours: Go against the surface: dark on light, light on dark, and play temperature, such as a warm reddish brown on cool blue armour.
chip-colours.edge chips: Dab chips unevenly along edges, adding a fine light line on the lower edge of each dark chip where the new edge catches the light.

choosing-primer-colour.what colour primer: Prime in the colour that covers most of the model, or let the hardest colour decide; grey is the safe choice if you are unsure.
choosing-primer-colour.white or black primer: White for bright, saturated schemes and one coat paints; black for instant shadow, metals and hard to reach recesses. Grey sits between.
choosing-primer-colour.grey primer: Grey is the safe choice if unsure. It does not shift the colours on top and shows at a glance where a thin coat has not covered.
choosing-primer-colour.should i prime: Always. Paint on bare plastic or metal rubs and scratches off; primer is what makes paint grip.
choosing-primer-colour.which undercoat to use: Match what covers most of the model, or let the fiddliest colour decide. White suits bright colours, black suits metal, grey is safe.
choosing-primer-colour.do i need primer: Yes. Paint on bare plastic or metal rubs and scratches off, and a matt primer grips better than a glossy one.
choosing-primer-colour.coloured primer: Prime in the colour that covers most of the model, such as silver for full plate or sandy beige for cloth; it cuts out a base coat.
choosing-primer-colour.best primer for beginners: Grey if unsure, or white or very light grey, which shows clearly what each wash does while you learn.
choosing-primer-colour.paint rubbing off bare plastic: Prime first. Primer is what makes paint grip, and a matt primer gives more grip than a glossy one.
choosing-primer-colour.priming colour choice: Pick by what covers most of the model and how you will paint it: white for bright schemes, black for metal and shadow, grey if unsure.
choosing-primer-colour.Do I need to prime, and what colour shou: Always prime, as paint rubs off bare plastic. Use the colour covering most of the model, or grey if unsure.

colour-of-light.warm light vs cold light: Warm light gives warm highlights with shadows leaning cool; a strong coloured source recolours everything in its reach towards its colour.
colour-of-light.what colour should highlights be: Tinted by the light: warm light gives warm highlights. Decide where the light comes from and how warm or cool it is before you highlight.
colour-of-light.sunset lighting on a model: Sunset is warm light, so give highlights a warm tint and let the shadows lean cool; skin that looks pale in office light reads tanned.
colour-of-light.moonlight colour scheme: See: a cool or coloured light tints every colour it falls on, so push highlights towards that colour across skin, metal and cloth alike.
colour-of-light.does light change the colour: Yes. There is no single true colour for an object; warm, cold or coloured light tints every colour it falls on.
colour-of-light.highlight with yellow or blue: It depends on the light you choose: warm light gives warm highlights, a blue glow turns everything blue where it falls.
colour-of-light.decide light direction before highlighti: Yes. Pick where the light comes from and how warm or cool it is first; a desk lamp and a photo give a ready made map.
colour-of-light.cool highlights warm shadows: Under warm light it is the reverse: warm highlights and shadows that lean cool. Cool highlights suit a cool or blue light.
colour-of-light.colour temperature on miniatures: Warm light gives warm highlights and cooler shadows; a cool glow from below with warm light above looks striking, with dark between.
colour-of-light.colored light on a mini: A strong coloured source recolours everything in its reach: skin, metal, bone and cloth all turn towards that colour where it falls.

comfort-in-long-sessions.back hurts painting: Sit upright with firm lower back support, feet flat, and lift the model towards your face instead of bending over it. Move often.
comfort-in-long-sessions.best chair for painting: One that supports sitting straight or leaning slightly forward, with height adjustment and firm lower back support, not a reclining chair.
comfort-in-long-sessions.eye strain while painting: Take regular breaks looking across the room or out of a window, not at a phone, and use bright, diffuse, daylight balanced light.
comfort-in-long-sessions.neck ache from hobby: Lift the model towards your face rather than bending over it, let your shoulders drop, and try a raised work surface near eye level.
comfort-in-long-sessions.how to paint for hours: Sit upright with good support, rest your eyes, move often and loosen your grip; shorter sessions over more days are easier to keep up.
comfort-in-long-sessions.posture at the painting desk: Back straight, feet flat on the floor or a footrest, shoulders dropped, and lift the model towards your face instead of bending over.
comfort-in-long-sessions.wrist hurts from painting: Do not press your wrist or forearms hard on a thick desk edge, which can cause numbness, and loosen your grip on the brush.
comfort-in-long-sessions.taking breaks while painting: Change position, stretch and move every so often, and rest your eyes by looking across the room or out of a window.
comfort-in-long-sessions.sore hand from gripping brush: Squeezing hard while concentrating causes cramps and shake. Notice your grip from time to time and loosen it.
comfort-in-long-sessions.comfortable painting setup: A supportive upright chair, a raised work surface, bright diffuse daylight lighting, magnification if needed, and quiet music.

controlling-saturation.colour too bright: Dull it with a neutral grey, a touch of black, a pale highlight colour or a little of its opposite; too much opposite shifts the hue.
controlling-saturation.too saturated: Add a little grey or the colour's opposite, or finish the top edges with a pale, cool grey to pull the area back towards neutral.
controlling-saturation.how to dull a colour: Add a neutral grey, a touch of black, a pale highlight colour, or a little of its opposite. Too much of the opposite shifts the hue.
controlling-saturation.colour looks garish: Bright colours that suit small figures can look garish on busts and large models; a drop of grey makes them look natural.
controlling-saturation.tone down a colour: Mix in a neutral grey, a touch of black, a pale highlight colour or a little of its opposite; mixing more colours moves it towards grey.
controlling-saturation.saturation explained: Saturation is how strong a colour is, how far from grey; brightness is how light or dark. Pink is a lighter red, not a stronger one.
controlling-saturation.colour looks neon: Grey it down with a neutral grey or a little of its opposite, or finish with a pale, cool grey on the top edges only.
controlling-saturation.make colours less vivid: Mix them: two bright colours give a duller result, and adding grey, black or the opposite colour dulls it further.
controlling-saturation.desaturate paint: Add a neutral grey, a touch of black, a pale highlight colour or a little of the colour's opposite.
controlling-saturation.red is way too strong: Add a little grey or a touch of its opposite to the red, or finish the top edges with a pale, cool grey to pull it back.

cutting-kit-parts.how to cut plastic parts: Slice thin joints with a very sharp blade in several small strokes away from you, saw thick parts, and keep fingers out of the blade's path.
cutting-kit-parts.cut a model in half for a conversion: Use a fine saw with many small teeth and short, light strokes, leave about a millimetre spare, then shave it back with a knife.
cutting-kit-parts.cutting thick plastic: Use a fine saw with many small teeth and short, light strokes, letting the saw do the work; a coarse blade removes too much and wanders.
cutting-kit-parts.razor saw for models: A fine saw with many small teeth suits thick parts such as a torso. Use short, light strokes and leave a millimetre spare to shave back.
cutting-kit-parts.safe way to use a hobby knife: Lay the part flat or brace it, keep fingers out of the line of the blade, cut away from your body, and change blades often.
cutting-kit-parts.cut a head off: For a thin joint, slide a very sharp blade through in several small strokes away from you; saw thicker necks and shave back to fit.
cutting-kit-parts.clippers vs knife: Use a sharp knife for thin joints and side cutters to nibble big armour pieces down, leaving a little to file smooth.
cutting-kit-parts.cutting resin parts: See: this entry covers sharp blades for thin joints, fine saws for thick parts, and changing blades often, more so on soft metal.
cutting-kit-parts.slipped and cut myself: See: to avoid slips, brace the part flat, keep fingers out of the blade's line, cut away from you and use a sharp blade.
cutting-kit-parts.chop up a kit for kitbashing: Knife thin joints, saw thick parts with a fine saw, nibble big pieces with side cutters, then clean the faces and dry fit after each change.

directional-edge-highlights.edge highlights look fake: The same bright line on every edge looks graphic. Pick one light direction and highlight up facing edges strongest, downward ones dim or not at all.
directional-edge-highlights.where to put edge highlights: Strongest on edges facing up or towards you: head, shoulders, tops of arms, hands, knees and toes. Softer or none facing down.
directional-edge-highlights.light direction highlights: Pick one light direction, usually above and slightly in front, and keep every highlight consistent with it.
directional-edge-highlights.should i highlight every edge: Not for a believable look; as a beginner, highlighting about a third of the edges is a good start. Lining every edge is a valid stylised choice.
directional-edge-highlights.edge highlighting from above: Light from above and slightly in front makes up facing edges brightest, while edges facing down get a softer, darker highlight or none.
directional-edge-highlights.edge highlights look too graphic: Vary brightness and width by light direction, skip edges beside bright surfaces, and use broken dashes or a slightly warm or cool tone.
directional-edge-highlights.realistic edge highlights: Brightest on edges facing the light, fading along curves, with downward edges dim and the strongest lines kept near the focal point.
directional-edge-highlights.focal point highlights: Keep most lines a little muted and push the brightest ones around the face or focal point to draw the eye there.
directional-edge-highlights.which edges get highlighted: Those facing up or towards you get the strongest; downward edges get a softer, darker highlight or none, and edges beside bright areas can be skipped.
directional-edge-highlights.edging every panel: It looks graphic rather than believable, though valid if stylised on purpose. Otherwise follow one light direction and skip downward edges.

drybrush-care.drybrush care: Load only the tip, clean it before paint dries, swirl or press straight down when washing, and wipe on kitchen roll or microfibre.
drybrush-care.drybrush gone flat: Scrubbing sideways flattens it. Wash by swirling or pressing straight down, and dry clean by sweeping outwards while twisting.
drybrush-care.clean a drybrush: Clean it between steps before paint dries, swirling or pressing straight down so it stays round; a little gentle soap lifts colour.
drybrush-care.splayed drybrush: A flat, splayed tip leaves streaks. Keep it domed by washing straight down rather than sideways and never pressing towards the collar.
drybrush-care.drybrush streaks: A flat or splayed tip leaves streaks; a domed tip gives soft, even drybrushing. Also check it is dry enough on a painted scrap first.
drybrush-care.best drybrush shape: A rounded, domed tip. It leaves soft, even drybrushing and fine stipple dots, where a flat, splayed tip leaves streaks.
drybrush-care.looking after makeup brushes for drybrus: See: keep any drybrush domed, load only the tip, wash it by swirling or pressing straight down, and wipe it on a lint free surface.
drybrush-care.domed brush: A domed tip gives soft, even drybrushing and fine stipple dots. Keep it round by swirling or pressing straight down when washing.
drybrush-care.drybrush leaves fibres: Toilet tissue sheds fibres onto the model. Wipe on proper kitchen roll, a microfibre cloth, bare wood or a cork tile instead.
drybrush-care.dry brush maintenance: Load only the tip so paint stays out of the collar, clean before it dries, wash straight down, and flick out dust before use.

drying-retarder.retarder: Retarder slows acrylic drying so you have longer to blend on the model. Use very little: dip a damp brush in a drop, then pick up paint.
drying-retarder.slow down paint drying: Add a tiny amount of retarder, use a wet palette, or work in a cooler room.
drying-retarder.how much retarder: Very little: you only need to roughly double the working time. Dip a damp brush in a drop of retarder, then pick up paint.
drying-retarder.blending paint dries too fast: Add a touch of retarder, enough to roughly double the working time, and use a wet palette or a cooler room.
drying-retarder.drying retarder made paint blotchy: That is too much retarder; it thins the paint so far it goes blotchy and takes ages to dry. Use only a drop on a damp brush.
drying-retarder.retarder gel: Gel retarders vary: some work poorly, others add time without making paint runny. Test a new one before relying on it; liquid is easier to dose.
drying-retarder.keep paint wet longer for blending: Dip a damp brush in a drop of retarder before picking up paint, and use a wet palette in a cooler room.
drying-retarder.too much retarder: It thins the paint so far it goes blotchy instead of blending, and takes ages to dry. You only need to roughly double working time.
drying-retarder.extend working time acrylics: A small amount of liquid retarder roughly doubles working time; a wet palette and a cooler room help too.
drying-retarder.retarder vs medium: Separate retarder, flow improver and thinning medium let you control exactly what you add, unlike vague all in one mediums.

enamel-washes.enamel wash: Varnish the acrylics first, coat the model in a dark enamel wash, let it lose its shine, then wipe it off raised areas with spirit.
enamel-washes.oil wash wipe off: Thinned black oil paint works the same way as enamel: brush it over a varnished model, let it set, then wipe it back with spirit.
enamel-washes.how to use enamel washes: Seal with two coats of acrylic varnish, brush on a slightly thinned enamel wash, wait 20 to 30 minutes, then wipe downwards with spirit.
enamel-washes.grime wash with spirit: Over varnish, coat in dark brown or grey enamel wash, and once it loses its wet shine wipe it off raised areas with a spirit dampened bud.
enamel-washes.panel line wash on vehicles: Over gloss varnish an enamel wash runs into recesses and wipes off cleanly. Wipe raised areas with a bud dampened in white spirit.
enamel-washes.wipe off wash technique: Let the enamel lose its wet shine, then wipe downwards with a bud dampened in odourless white spirit and rolled on tissue first.
enamel-washes.enamel lifted my paint: Spirit lifts unprotected paint, and heavy scrubbing eats through varnish. Seal with two coats of acrylic varnish first and go easy.
enamel-washes.gloss varnish before wash: Yes: a gloss coat lets the enamel run into recesses and wipe off cleanly, where matt leaves more tint behind.
enamel-washes.fast dirty vehicle: Varnish it, coat it all in dark enamel grime wash, then wipe it downwards off raised surfaces with spirit, leaving it in the recesses.
enamel-washes.removing excess wash with thinner: Use a cotton bud or makeup sponge dampened in odourless white spirit, rolled on tissue, wiping downwards; proper enamel thinner is gentler.

fast-terrain-painting.paint terrain fast: Prime black, dust a lighter colour from above, drybrush roughly with big brushes, then wash once. Set a short deadline and fixed steps.
fast-terrain-painting.quick terrain: Black primer, a lighter grey or sand dusted from above, rough drybrushing dark to pale, and one dirty brown wash in the recesses.
fast-terrain-painting.how to paint scenery quickly: Use craft paint and big brushes, prime black and dust a lighter colour from above, then drybrush and wash. Do each step across every piece.
fast-terrain-painting.terrain painting tips: Fix a few steps and a deadline, use cheap paint and big old brushes, let a wash fill the cracks, and match the colours and tufts to your bases.
fast-terrain-painting.drybrush terrain: Overbrush roughly with plenty of paint, dark to pale, covering less each time; press harder on top edges and lighter lower down.
fast-terrain-painting.paint a lot of terrain: Line the pieces up and do each step across all of them: dark primer, a lighter colour from above, rough drybrushing, then one wash.
fast-terrain-painting.table ready terrain: Prime dark, dust lighter from above, drybrush roughly, wash once, add a few spot colours and paint cut edges black.
fast-terrain-painting.quick scenery painting: Prime black and dust grey or sand from above so the dark stays in recesses, then drybrush roughly and let one wash fill the cracks.
fast-terrain-painting.cheap craft paint for terrain: Yes: craft acrylics or household sample pots are fine for terrain. Keep fine model paints for small effects such as a glowing rune.
fast-terrain-painting.terrain never gets finished: Extra steps are usually why. Give yourself a short deadline and a fixed few steps, and favour the effect across the table over tidy edges.

finishing-touches.how do i make my model look finished: Paint the eyes, finish the base and its rim, add a little grime round the feet, and look it over at arm's length.
finishing-touches.model looks incomplete: Check the eyes are painted and the base and rim are finished; a bare base reads as an unfinished model.
finishing-touches.last details on a character: Push highlights a little further near the face, add one or two tiny contrasting accents, and line where areas meet in a neat dark line.
finishing-touches.paint the eyes to finish: Yes: painted eyes make a model look complete, and a tiny pale dot in each pupil as a reflection makes them look alive.
finishing-touches.tiny dot of light in the eye: A tiny pale dot in each pupil reads as a reflection and makes the eyes look alive.
finishing-touches.base left bare: A bare base reads as an unfinished model. Finish it and paint the rim; black always looks neat.
finishing-touches.what colour for the base rim: If unsure, black: it always looks neat and frames the model.
finishing-touches.final look over before varnish: Check at arm's length that glows read bright and metal shiny, tidy slips with the nearby colour, then matt varnish evens shiny patches.
finishing-touches.add a little grime at the end: A thin brown grey wash round the feet adds grime and ties the model to its base; put transfers on before it.
finishing-touches.nearly done what else should i add: Painted eyes with a pale dot, a finished base rim, a thin grime wash round the feet, and one or two tiny accents in a contrasting colour.

fix-clogged-airbrush.airbrush clogged: Wipe dried paint off the needle tip, then spray cleaner, flow improver or isopropyl alcohol through. Do not turn the pressure up.
fix-clogged-airbrush.airbrush spitting: Usually dried paint on the needle tip. Wipe it off often and spray a short burst away from the model before every pass.
fix-clogged-airbrush.airbrush stopped spraying: Check the needle tip and nozzle first and wipe off dried paint. If it keeps stopping, the paint is most likely too thick.
fix-clogged-airbrush.dried paint on needle: Wipe it off with a soft brush or cloth. In warm weather it dries within minutes, so wipe often; a little airbrush retarder helps.
fix-clogged-airbrush.tip dry: Paint drying on the needle tip. Wipe it often, spray a short burst away from the model before each pass, and add a little airbrush retarder.
fix-clogged-airbrush.airbrush splatters: Check the needle tip and nozzle for dried paint and wipe it off, rather than turning up the pressure, which spits blobs.
fix-clogged-airbrush.how do i unclog my airbrush: Wipe the needle tip, spray cleaner or isopropyl alcohol through, and as a last resort ease the needle back and forth with air flowing.
fix-clogged-airbrush.airbrush sputtering: Dried paint on the needle tip or nozzle is the usual cause; wipe it, flush cleaner through, and thin the paint if it keeps happening.
fix-clogged-airbrush.clean airbrush between colours: Spray out, add cleaner, work the needle back and forth, and repeat until it runs clear.
fix-clogged-airbrush.airbrush wont spray: Check the needle tip and nozzle for dried paint, flush cleaner through, and check the paint is not too thick or a brush on metallic.

fix-priming-problems.primer grainy: You sprayed from too far away, so it dried in the air. Hold the can at a steady 20 to 30 cm, and buff rough areas with a dry toothbrush.
fix-priming-problems.rough primer: Usually too far away, damp air or cold. Spray on a mild, dry day at 20 to 30 cm, and buff rough spots with an old dry toothbrush.
fix-priming-problems.primer gritty: Sprayed from too far, so it dried before landing. Buff the rough areas with an old dry toothbrush; you rarely need to strip.
fix-priming-problems.primer sticky: It has not cured, usually from an old or badly shaken can. Strip the model and prime again from a fresh, well shaken can.
fix-priming-problems.primer clogging detail: Spraying too close or too long in one spot floods detail. Use short, light, moving passes from 20 to 30 cm, one or two thin coats.
fix-priming-problems.spray primer orange peel: Damp air clumps the droplets into orange peel; bad orange peel can also mean an old can. Spray under about 60 percent humidity.
fix-priming-problems.primer went fuzzy: Sprayed from too far away, so it dried in the air. Buff it smooth with an old dry toothbrush, then hold the can at 20 to 30 cm.
fix-priming-problems.humid weather priming: Damp air causes a bumpy orange peel surface. Wait, run a dehumidifier, or use brush on primer or an airbrush indoors.
fix-priming-problems.frosted primer: See: fuzzy or rough primer usually comes from spraying too far away, damp air or cold. Spray on a mild, dry day from 20 to 30 cm.
fix-priming-problems.primer too thick: One coat, or two thin ones at most, is enough. Use short, light passes that keep moving rather than a heavy blast.
fix-priming-problems.Why did my spray primer come out rough o: You likely sprayed from too far, so it dried in the air, or in damp or cold weather. Hold the can at 20 to 30 cm on a mild, dry day.

fix-wet-paint-mistakes.slip of the brush: Act while it is wet: wipe it off an open surface with a fingertip or cloth, or loosen it in a recess with a clean damp brush and soak it up.
fix-wet-paint-mistakes.paint went where i didnt want: Lift it at once while wet: wipe open surfaces with a fingertip or lint free cloth, or sponge it out of recesses with a clean damp brush.
fix-wet-paint-mistakes.wash flooded the model: Soak up as much as you can with a large dry brush, then add a little clean water and soak it up again to lift more pigment.
fix-wet-paint-mistakes.wipe off wet paint: On an open surface, wipe it straight off with a fingertip or a lint free cloth before it dries.
fix-wet-paint-mistakes.lift paint before it dries: Run a clean damp brush over the spot to loosen it, use the brush like a sponge to soak it up, wipe it on tissue, rinse and repeat.
fix-wet-paint-mistakes.oops i painted over the eye: While wet, loosen it with a clean damp brush and soak it up; a little saliva on the brush often lifts it. Repaint any faint mark once dry.
fix-wet-paint-mistakes.fix a mistake straight away: Keep a clean damp brush, water and a lint free cloth beside you, and lift the slip at once; these fixes only work while it is wet.
fix-wet-paint-mistakes.got paint on the wrong part: Wipe it off open surfaces with a fingertip, or sponge it out of recesses with a damp brush, then repaint any faint mark once dry.
fix-wet-paint-mistakes.quick fix with a damp brush: Run the clean damp brush over the wet slip to loosen it, use it like a sponge to soak the paint up, wipe on tissue, rinse and repeat.
fix-wet-paint-mistakes.wash spilled everywhere: Soak up as much as you can with a large dry brush, add a little clean water, and soak it up again to lift more pigment.

freehand-flames.freehand flames: Paint thin S shaped curves rising from the bottom edge, widen each into a tongue, build solid colour, then cut back with the background.
freehand-flames.how do i paint flames: Thinned orange or dark red S curves of different heights, broadened into tongues, deep red at the tips and yellow low down, then cut back sharp.
freehand-flames.fire pattern on a cloak: Paint it at base coat stage: S curves widened into tongues, red tips, orange body, yellow at the base, then sharpen with the background colour.
freehand-flames.flame designs: Start each flame as a thin S curve of varied height, broaden it into a tongue with a few sparks above, and cut it back with the background.
freehand-flames.hot rod flames: Set the height with a central line, add S curves from the bottom edge, widen them into tongues, then cut back sharp with the background colour.
freehand-flames.paint fire on armour: Freehand at base coat stage: S curves into tongues, deep red tips, orange body, yellow low down, then cut back and glaze thin yellow over it.
freehand-flames.flame freehand tips: Paint before shading, build coats until solid, keep the hottest colours low, cut back with the background, and varnish between stages.
freehand-flames.flames on a tank: Set the height with one line up the panel, add S curved tongues from the bottom edge, colour them red to yellow, then cut back sharp.
freehand-flames.s curve flames: Paint a few S curves of different heights rising from the bottom edge, then widen each into a tongue, broader at the bottom.
freehand-flames.flames look blobby: Cut back into the flames with the background colour to sharpen the shapes, restoring with the flame colour if you cut too far.

ghostly-ethereal-spirits.ghost: Base white and build many thin glazes of a bright colour, deepening lower down, or drybrush white over a dusty purple. Finish top edges white.
ghostly-ethereal-spirits.how do i paint ghosts: Base white, glaze a bright colour mixed half with glaze medium all over, then lower and lower glazes so it deepens towards the bottom.
ghostly-ethereal-spirits.glowing see through spirit: Many thin glazes over white: light on top, colour deepening lower down and in recesses, with neat colour only on the bottom edge.
ghostly-ethereal-spirits.banshee colours: See: spirits read best pale on top with colour deepening lower down, glazed over white or drybrushed white over a dusty purple.
ghostly-ethereal-spirits.spectral glow on a wraith: Base white, glaze a translucent bright colour half with medium, add lower glazes so it deepens downwards, then white on the top edges.
ghostly-ethereal-spirits.ghostly green robes: Base white, glaze green mixed half with glaze medium all over, then lower glazes to deepen it towards the hem, neat only on the bottom edge.
ghostly-ethereal-spirits.make a model look translucent: Build many thin glazes over white rather than one heavy coat, keeping it light on top and deepening the colour lower down.
ghostly-ethereal-spirits.pale glowing spirit: White base, then thin glazes of a bright colour, each starting lower down, finished with slightly thinned white on faces and top edges.
ghostly-ethereal-spirits.ethereal ghost effect: Many thin glazes over white, darkest low down and in recesses, then pick out faces, knuckles and top edges in thinned white.
ghostly-ethereal-spirits.spirit host painting: Spray dark purple mixed with white, white from above, glaze purple and violet into recesses, then drybrush white with a soft brush.

glowing-energy-blades.energy sword: Base the glow colour in smooth thin coats, glaze alternating light and dark zones down the blade, then add stacked bright edges and white glints.
glowing-energy-blades.glowing blade: Plot alternating light and dark zones, build them with heavily thinned glazes, keep white only on the hottest spots, and glaze glow onto the hilt.
glowing-energy-blades.lightning sword: Base it near black, sketch bolts in the glow colour, glaze the whole blade, trace thin white inside the bolts, and line both edges off white.
glowing-energy-blades.glowing weapon blade: Base the glow colour smoothly, glaze light zones alternating side to side with dark between, then finer bright edges and white at the tip.
glowing-energy-blades.turquoise glow on a sword: Base a mid turquoise in thin smooth coats, glaze paler light zones and darker zones down the blade, and spill a little glow onto the hilt.
glowing-energy-blades.how to paint a glowing sword: Base the glow colour, glaze alternating light and dark zones, smooth the steps, stack fine bright edges and keep white to the hottest spots.
glowing-energy-blades.plasma blade: See: glowing blades are based in a vivid glow colour, glazed into alternating light and dark zones, and finished with white only on hot spots.
glowing-energy-blades.laser sword: Quick version: paint the blade white, glaze an icy blue one coat paint over it with more coats towards the darker end, and lay it flat to dry.
glowing-energy-blades.energy blade looks flat: Put deep darks right beside bright lights, with alternating light and dark zones down the blade; contrast is what sells the glow.
glowing-energy-blades.glowing axe head: Base it in a vivid glow colour, plot light and dark zones, build them with thin glazes, and keep white only on the hottest edges.

gluing-small-parts.how do i glue tiny parts: Put a drop of super glue on scrap card and apply a tiny amount to the contact point only with the tip of a pin or straightened paper clip.
