gluing-small-parts.superglue flooded the joint: Wick away a little excess with a cotton bud corner, but not a big puddle. Next time apply a thin film with a pin from a drop on scrap.
gluing-small-parts.glue left a white fog: Extra glue sets slower and can fog nearby detail. Use only a thin film, applied with a pin to the contact point.
gluing-small-parts.too much superglue: Only a thin film is needed. Put a drop on scrap card and touch a tiny amount to the joint with a pin tip.
gluing-small-parts.apply super glue with a pin: Put a drop on scrap plastic card, pick up a tiny amount on the pin tip, and touch it to the contact point only.
gluing-small-parts.gluing small bits neatly: Apply glue from a drop on scrap with a pin, pick up tiny parts on a knife tip or tweezers, and shave sprue nubs so they sit flush.
gluing-small-parts.tiny parts falling off my model: Shave sprue nubs so they sit flush; if a tiny part still will not stay put, a dab of UV curing resin set with a UV torch locks it in.
gluing-small-parts.cotton bud to wick glue: Use the corner of a bud to wick a little excess only; never mop a big puddle, as soaked cotton can get hot and smoke.
gluing-small-parts.glue on fiddly bits: Spear tiny parts lightly on a craft knife tip or hold them with tweezers, and touch them into glue placed with a pin.
gluing-small-parts.small detail wont stick: For plastic glue, scrape primer off the contact point. If it still will not stay, lock it in with a dab of UV curing resin.

gritty-dark-style.grimdark style: Muted, desaturated colours, deep shadows with a few sharp highlights, heavy wear and varied texture, with one stronger accent colour.
gritty-dark-style.gritty war torn look: Knock a clean base back with earthy washes, add chips, cuts and frayed cloth, then finish with grime, mud and gore where they would gather.
gritty-dark-style.dark weathered style: Muted palette, hard contrast, earthy glazes over a bright base, damage, then weathering powders and grime placed for a reason.
gritty-dark-style.how do i make a model look bleak: Use dull greens, browns, greys and off whites, deep shadows with few highlights, and heavy wear that tells a harsh story.
gritty-dark-style.muddy dirty soldiers: Finish with weathering powders, mud and grime placed low down, in folds and round joints, where it really gathers.
gritty-dark-style.make a model look grim: Keep the palette muted, push deep shadows against a few sharp highlights, and add damage and grime with a reason behind each mark.
gritty-dark-style.muted desaturated scheme: Dull greens, browns, greys and off whites, with one stronger colour saved for a small accent.
gritty-dark-style.battle worn look: Add chips and scratches on armour, cuts on skin and frayed cloth, then grime, mud and gore low down and in folds.
gritty-dark-style.colours too bright and cheerful: Knock them back with earthy layers, washes or glazes; a clean base dulled this way looks worn and dirty almost at once.
gritty-dark-style.grim dark painting style: Muted colours, strong contrast, earthy glazes, damage, oil washes in recesses, and grime placed so the model has survived something harsh.

highlighting-curves.highlight a rounded helmet: Paint each lighter layer as a smaller circle centred on the dome, then pull the light toward the brim and run the brush side along the rim.
highlighting-curves.no edges to highlight: Build a gradient instead: glaze heavily thinned highlight onto the highest part of the curve, each stage smaller, then one bright point on top.
highlighting-curves.edge highlights look wrong on curves: Rounded parts have no edge to catch a line, so glaze a soft gradient onto the highest part of the curve instead.
highlighting-curves.how to highlight a dome: Glaze lighter layers as smaller and smaller circles centred on the dome, finish with one small bright point, and soften the join with mid colour.
highlighting-curves.shiny shell highlight: On a shiny sphere the brightest light sits as a band near the edge, so build a halo round the side and keep the middle a little darker.
highlighting-curves.highlight a belly: Build heavily thinned highlight on the highest part of the curve, each stage over a smaller area, with strokes that follow the form.
highlighting-curves.soft highlight on round armour: Glaze thinned highlight onto the top of the curve over shrinking areas, finish with a small bright point, and glaze mid colour round it.
highlighting-curves.beetle shell carapace: Break the highlight into short, choppy strokes along ridges and upper edges, and touch the brightest point with a pale bone.
highlighting-curves.orb or gem curved highlight: On a shiny or glowing sphere, build a halo of light round the side near the edge and keep the middle a little darker.
highlighting-curves.organic shapes without edges: Glaze soft highlights onto the highest part of each curve, letting strokes follow the form from shadow into light.

hobby-paint-types.what types of paint: Base, layer, wash, one coat, dry, technical and air paints, plus inks. They are all acrylics made thicker or thinner for different jobs.
hobby-paint-types.base vs layer paint: Base paints are thick and opaque, covering in one or two coats. Layer paints are thinner, for building highlights in smooth steps.
hobby-paint-types.what is a wash: A very thin, see through paint, also called a shade, that runs into recesses.
hobby-paint-types.what is technical paint: Paint for special effects, such as base texture, crackle, rust, blood, gloss for gems and clear glowing liquid.
hobby-paint-types.dry paint vs normal: Dry paints are thick and paste like, made for drybrushing texture, where normal paints flow and thin with water.
hobby-paint-types.air paint: Paint thinned ready for the airbrush. By brush it works as a glaze or a smooth thin layer.
hobby-paint-types.different hobby paints explained: All are acrylics: base covers, layer builds highlights, washes run into recesses, dry paints drybrush, technical ones make effects.
hobby-paint-types.which paint do i need: Not every type: a few base colours, a wash or two and a good white go a long way. Thick paint can be thinned; thin paint is hard to make cover.
hobby-paint-types.are all paints acrylic: Most hobby paints are. The labels mostly describe thickness and pigment, and they all mix with each other and thin with water.
hobby-paint-types.beginner paint types: Start with a few base colours, a wash or two and a good white. Thick base paint can always be thinned for layering.

iridescent-colour-shift.iridescent: Base a colour between two shift hues, drybrush one from above and the other from below, then finish both with the same pale highlight.
iridescent-colour-shift.colour shift effect: Light the part in one hue from above and a neighbouring hue from below, over a base that sits between them, tied with one pale highlight.
iridescent-colour-shift.shimmering insect wings: Base a rich purple, drybrush pink purple from the top, deep blue to turquoise from below, and finish both with a small pale yellow.
iridescent-colour-shift.beetle shell shine: Pick two neighbouring colours on the wheel, drybrush each from its own light direction over a base between them, then one shared pale highlight.
iridescent-colour-shift.pearly scales: Drybrush pinks from above and blues to turquoise from below over a rich purple base, then the same pale yellow on both, kept small.
iridescent-colour-shift.oil slick colours: Base between two neighbouring hues, light one from above and the other from below, and keep the shared pale highlight small.
iridescent-colour-shift.how do i paint colorshift: Base a rich purple, drybrush pink purple from the top side, deep blue then turquoise from the other, and finish both with pale yellow.
iridescent-colour-shift.wing changes colour: Give each of two neighbouring colours its own light direction: pinks from above, blues and turquoise from below, over a purple base.
iridescent-colour-shift.multi colour shimmer: Drybrush two neighbouring hues from opposite directions over a base between them, keeping colours big and the pale highlight small.
iridescent-colour-shift.iridescent dragon scales: Base a rich purple, drybrush pinks from above in small circles, blues and turquoise from below, then one shared pale yellow highlight.

kitbashing-terrain.terrain from junk: Old toys, packaging and spare kits make good starting shapes; hide their old look under kit parts and plastic panels, then prime one colour.
kitbashing-terrain.kitbash terrain: Lay pieces out dry, build on a flat braced base, swap plain parts for detailed kit parts, cover blank areas with plastic card, then prime.
kitbashing-terrain.toys into terrain: Wash the toy, cover its plain, toy looking parts with detailed kit parts and thin plastic panels, then prime the whole piece one colour.
kitbashing-terrain.packaging scenery: Packaging makes good starting shapes; cover blank areas with thin plastic panels and kit parts, and prime it one colour so it reads as one object.
kitbashing-terrain.make terrain from rubbish: Use old toys, packaging and spare kit parts, hide the old shapes under detail, run cables over the joins, and prime it all one colour.
kitbashing-terrain.recycle old toys for terrain: Wash them in warm soapy water, replace toy looking parts with kit parts, add cables and texture, then prime and paint like your other terrain.
kitbashing-terrain.cheap scenery ideas: Old toys, playsets, packaging, wooden blocks and spare kits from charity stalls, built on a braced base with hot glue and primed one colour.
kitbashing-terrain.spare parts box terrain: Empty it and look for new jobs: a tank becomes a boiler, floor panels a deck, a gun barrel a chimney, and sprue makes supports and ladders.
kitbashing-terrain.turn a toy into a building: Cover plain parts with detailed kit parts and thin plastic panels, fit them upside down if needed to hide wrong details, then prime one colour.
kitbashing-terrain.bits box scenery: Lay out your spares and find shapes for new jobs, such as a gun barrel as a chimney or cleaned sprue as ladder sides with card rungs.

light-and-volume-sketch.sketch light: With a large brush, block in each volume quickly, darker away from the light and brighter where it hits, then refine between them.
light-and-volume-sketch.block in light and dark: Over a midtone base, set the deepest shadow and brightest highlight early with well covering paint, working from largest areas to smallest.
light-and-volume-sketch.volume sketch: A quick block in of dark and light tones and the light direction before detail, so you can test and move lights cheaply.
light-and-volume-sketch.light first approach: Light and shape matter more than small details, so get them down first; no careful refining saves a model with the light placed wrong.
light-and-volume-sketch.how do i plan light on a model: Do a rough sketch: block in darker areas away from the light and brighter ones where it hits, and move lights that look wrong now.
light-and-volume-sketch.zenithal sketch: With an airbrush, spray white ink or each light colour over black from the light's direction; the sprayed zones mark where highlights go.
light-and-volume-sketch.rough in shadows and highlights: Block in each volume with a big brush, then mix half steps between the sketch colours and glaze dark down and light up to refine.
light-and-volume-sketch.model looks flat overall: Get light and shape down first: block in darks away from the light and brights where it hits, and push contrast beyond real life.
light-and-volume-sketch.big brush sketch: Use a large brush and covering paint over a midtone, treating busy parts as one simple shape and working from largest areas to smallest.
light-and-volume-sketch.light direction first: Yes: placing the light and volumes first means everything else is quicker to fill in, and changing your mind costs minutes, not a repaint.

making-barbed-wire.barbed wire: Twist two lengths of thin soft wire into a tight strand, knot short barbs on every few millimetres, then glue it to posts and paint it.
making-barbed-wire.make barbed wire: Clamp two thin wires at one end and twist them evenly under gentle tension, then knot short pieces round the strand as barbs.
making-barbed-wire.barbed wire for bases: Twist fine craft or florist wire into a strand, add knotted barbs, let it sag between posts, glue it at the posts and paint it dark metal.
making-barbed-wire.razor wire: See: this entry makes barbed wire from twisted fine wire with knotted barbs, run along posts and wall tops.
making-barbed-wire.wire fence on base: Wrap twisted wire round fence posts and stumps, letting it sag a little between them, and fix it at each post with a dot of super glue.
making-barbed-wire.twisted wire barbs: Knot a short piece of wire round the strand every few millimetres and snip the ends short, tightening each knot with pliers, not fingers.
making-barbed-wire.trench barbed wire: Twist thin wire into a strand, add knotted barbs, let it sag between posts, then paint it dark metal with a brown wash for rust.
making-barbed-wire.diy barbed wire: Twist two fine wires into a tight strand with a hand drill or by hand, keeping gentle tension, then knot short barbs on with pliers.
making-barbed-wire.barb wire: Twist thin soft wire into a strand and knot short barbs round it every few millimetres; at table distance the strand alone also works.
making-barbed-wire.battlefield wire on posts: Wrap it round the posts with a little sag between them, fix it with a dot of super glue, then paint dark metal with brown or orange rust.

metal-powder-paints.metal pigment powder: Stir loose metal powder into gloss medium or gloss varnish to make your own metallic paint; it covers in one smooth, tough coat.
metal-powder-paints.make my own metallic paint: Mix loose metal pigment powder very thoroughly into a gloss medium or gloss varnish, a small amount at a time.
metal-powder-paints.smooth metallics: Metal powder mixed into gloss medium covers in one very smooth coat, even over white. Mix thoroughly so no dry powder is left.
metal-powder-paints.powder in gloss medium: Yes: stirred into gloss medium or gloss varnish it makes a smooth, shiny, tough metallic. Mix small amounts very thoroughly.
metal-powder-paints.mirror shiny metal: See: loose metal powder in gloss medium makes very smooth, shiny metallics that cover in one coat, even over white.
metal-powder-paints.grainy metallic paint: Try loose metal powder stirred into gloss medium; it covers in one smooth coat. Mix very thoroughly so no dry powder is left.
metal-powder-paints.mix metal pigments: Stir powder into gloss medium for the base, into plenty of brown ink for a shade, and add a few drops of bright silver paint for a highlight.
metal-powder-paints.chrome effect from powder: See: this entry mixes metal powder into gloss medium for very smooth, shiny metallics, brightened with a few drops of silver paint.
metal-powder-paints.pigment metals: Loose metal powder in gloss medium makes smooth metallic paint. It is not safe to swallow or breathe, so mix gently and wash your hands.
metal-powder-paints.homemade gold paint: Stir gold powder into gloss medium; mix it with brown ink for a deep shade and add a few drops of bright silver paint for a highlight.

mixing-coloured-blacks.tinted black: Mix a little colour, such as purple, dark green or turquoise, into black, or mix dark blue with dark brown for a richer black.
mixing-coloured-blacks.mixing black with colour: Put small blobs of black on the palette, mix a different colour into each, hold them next to the model and keep the one that suits it.
mixing-coloured-blacks.rich black: A dark blue mixed with a dark brown makes a richer black than black paint alone.
mixing-coloured-blacks.black looks flat: Tint it with a little colour or mix it from dark blue and dark brown, but not too close to the main colour, which can look flat.
mixing-coloured-blacks.black with blue: Mix a little blue into black, or dark blue with dark brown, which gives a richer black than black paint alone.
mixing-coloured-blacks.black with purple: Mix a little purple into a blob of black; strong colours need only a little. Hold it next to the model to check it suits.
mixing-coloured-blacks.colourful black: Mix small amounts of purple, dark green or turquoise into separate blobs of black and keep the one that suits the model.
mixing-coloured-blacks.how do i make black more interesting: Tint it with a little colour, or mix it from dark blue and dark brown, then highlight gently, for example with a little ivory.
mixing-coloured-blacks.black ties scheme together: Yes: black mixed with a little of another colour on the model looks richer and ties that part to the rest of the scheme.
mixing-coloured-blacks.coloured black mix: A small amount of a strong colour in black, or dark blue with dark brown. Paint it thinly and judge again after any wash.

mottled-and-veiny-skin.veins: Paint a wiggly tapered line across light and dark areas, then push a little shade along its underside.
mottled-and-veiny-skin.bruised skin: Brush thinned purple and red washes onto pale skin a small area at a time, let them mix, then dab with a damp cotton bud for blotchy texture.
mottled-and-veiny-skin.mottled skin: Thin a slightly lighter skin tone to a glaze and dab it on with the brush tip instead of stroking.
mottled-and-veiny-skin.blotchy natural skin: Dab a glaze of a slightly lighter skin tone on with the brush tip, and add small touches of pink purple and red brown low on muscles.
mottled-and-veiny-skin.veiny muscles: Paint wiggly tapered lines across light and dark areas, shade along their undersides, and pick out tendons last in thin pale paint.
mottled-and-veiny-skin.how do i paint veins: Paint a wiggly, tapered line across both light and dark areas, then push a little shade along its underside.
mottled-and-veiny-skin.purple veins on a monster: Paint wiggly tapered lines in purple across light and dark areas, shade their undersides, and start on the back where slips are hidden.
mottled-and-veiny-skin.skin bruises: Thinned purple and red washes on pale skin, one small area at a time, mixed together and dabbed with a damp cotton bud.
mottled-and-veiny-skin.realistic skin texture: Dab a lighter skin glaze for mottling, sponge faint pale dots or flick tiny strokes for leathery skin, then glaze the main colour over.
mottled-and-veiny-skin.skin looks too even: Dab a glaze of a slightly lighter skin tone on with the brush tip, and add pink purple and red brown touches at the bottoms of muscles.

muted-support-colours.model looks too busy: Decide which part leads, give it the vivid colours, and paint gear, wood and the rest of the cloth in dull grey, olive, brown or black.
muted-support-colours.colours fighting each other: Change the brightness, saturation or amount of one; mostly red with small green lenses reads far better than half and half.
muted-support-colours.how do i make one colour pop: Keep most of the model muted or desaturated and give only that part the vivid, pure colour, painted over white for full brightness.
muted-support-colours.too many bright colours: Pick one part to lead and mute the rest: grey, olive, blue grey, dull brown or black for gear, wood and secondary cloth.
muted-support-colours.muted colours for gear: Paint bags, wood and gear in dull natural tones such as grey, olive, blue grey, dull brown or black, or toned down scheme colours.
muted-support-colours.desaturated scheme with an accent: Keep most areas muted, then add a few pops of pure colour on gems, orbs or weapons, painted over white for full brightness.
muted-support-colours.colour scheme looks chaotic: Strong colours side by side compete. Use one main colour, its complement in smaller areas, and everything else grey, black or metal.
muted-support-colours.calm down a busy model: Grey down secondary areas, swap a main metal for flat grey, and push areas that should recede, like shield backs, to dark brown.
muted-support-colours.make the focal point stand out: Give that part the vivid, pure colours and keep the rest of the model muted, so it is the only thing that pops.
muted-support-colours.everything stands out so nothing does: Decide which part should lead, give it the vivid colours, and tone the rest down to dull natural tones and neutrals.

nmm-steel.nmm steel: Paint white reflections over black, cover them nine parts white to one dark blue, band three midtones across the joins, glaze smooth, then white.
nmm-steel.non metallic steel armour: Mix a grey ladder with a touch of blue, place white reflections, band midtones from light to dark, glaze them smooth, then counter reflections.
nmm-steel.how do i paint nmm silver: Over black, paint main reflections white, cover them with near white blue grey, band three midtones across the joins and glaze smooth.
nmm-steel.steel with grey and blue: Mix a ladder from white and a dark blue, about nine to one, seven to three, half and half and three to seven, then pure dark blue.
nmm-steel.nmm plate armour: Study photos of polished plate, place white reflections over black, band midtones across each join, glaze smooth and add counter reflections.
nmm-steel.white reflections on steel: Paint the main reflections in several thin coats of white over black first, and finish with pure white on the strongest reflections.
nmm-steel.nmm silver recipe: Black, white reflections, nine parts white to one dark blue on them, three blended midtones, dark blue shadows, then pure white points.
nmm-steel.smooth nmm bands: Glaze each midtone gently over its transitions, ending dark glazes in shadow and pale ones on the highlight, following the shape.
nmm-steel.polished steel look: High contrast bands from black and muted blue to pure white reflections, with counter reflections and one key item shinier than the rest.
nmm-steel.grey ladder for nmm: Mix it before you start: white and dark blue at nine to one, seven to three, one to one and three to seven, with a tiny touch of blue.

order-of-painting.what order to paint: Big to small and messy to neat: the biggest colour or any drybrushing first, then smaller, neater areas that tidy the slips before.
order-of-painting.order of painting: Work big to small and messy to neat, pale colours before dark, top down and centre out, so each step tidies the one before.
order-of-painting.which part first: The biggest, messiest step: the colour covering most of the model, or any drybrushing or sponging, painted quickly over everything nearby.
order-of-painting.paint inside out: Work from the top down and the centre out, doing the hardest to reach parts first so the brush never reaches past finished areas.
order-of-painting.messy to neat: Yes: start with the messiest step, then smaller, neater areas, each covering the slips of the one before.
order-of-painting.should i paint skin first: See: paint pale colours and poor coverers before dark, strong ones, and the hardest to reach parts first.
order-of-painting.where to start painting: With the colour that covers most of the model, or any drybrushing or sponging, painted quickly over everything nearby.
order-of-painting.what to paint first: The biggest, messiest step: the colour covering most of the model, or drybrushing, before smaller and neater areas.
order-of-painting.paint order for a model: Main colour or drybrushing first, then smaller neat areas, pale before dark, top down and centre out, grouping details that share a wash.
order-of-painting.drybrush first then details: Yes: drybrushing is messy, so do it first over everything, and let later neater steps cover the overspill.

over-shade-then-tidy.shading hands: Shade hands generously so plenty of colour gets between the fingers, then once dry tidy the raised parts with the base colour.
over-shade-then-tidy.how to shade fingers: Wash heavily so colour gets into the tight gaps between fingers, let it dry, then go back over the raised parts with the base colour.
over-shade-then-tidy.wash on hands looks messy: That is fine: once it dries, tidy the raised parts of the fingers with the base colour, leaving the shade in the gaps.
over-shade-then-tidy.shade belts and pouches: Shade crowded areas like belts generously on purpose, then clean up the raised parts with the base colour once dry.
over-shade-then-tidy.tight spots hard to shade: Do not aim precisely. Shade heavily so colour gets into the gaps, then tidy the raised parts with the base colour.
over-shade-then-tidy.hands look flat: Shade them heavily so dark colour fills the gaps between fingers, then tidy the raised parts back with the base colour.
over-shade-then-tidy.shade heavily then clean up: Yes: it is quicker than being exact in fiddly areas. Shade generously, let it dry, then tidy raised parts with the base colour.
over-shade-then-tidy.shading small fiddly areas: Overshade on purpose so colour reaches the tight gaps, then restore the raised parts with the base colour once dry.
over-shade-then-tidy.wash between fingers: Wash generously so plenty gets into the gaps between the fingers, then tidy the raised parts with the base colour when dry.
over-shade-then-tidy.get shade into tight gaps: Shade generously rather than precisely, then go back with the base colour and tidy the raised parts once it is dry.

paint-markers.paint markers: Felt tip markers filled with one coat paint, used like colouring in. Prime light first and prime the nib by pressing it down on scrap.
paint-markers.paint pens for models: They hold one coat paint, so prime light. They give good control on mail, helmets and straps and are quick on tunics and base rims.
paint-markers.how do i use a paint marker: Shake it, press the nib on scrap until paint soaks in, then colour in over a light primer with light pressure, letting each coat dry.
paint-markers.felt tip paint for miniatures: Markers holding one coat paint work like colouring in over a light primer, with fine control on mail, helmets and straps.
paint-markers.my paint marker wont flow: Shake it well, then press the nib down repeatedly on scrap or the upturned cap until paint soaks in. A dried nib reloads the same way.
paint-markers.colouring in models with pens: Prime white or light, then colour in with paint markers using light pressure; fill tight gaps from a pot with a brush.
paint-markers.how to prime a paint pen: Shake it well, then press the felt tip down repeatedly on scrap or the upturned cap until paint soaks in, away from finished work.
paint-markers.contrast markers: They hold a one coat paint, so prime white or light first. Thin coats on the model with a damp brush for softer results.
paint-markers.are paint markers good for beginners: Often: holding a pen feels familiar, so many people get more control than with a brush on mail, helmets and straps.
paint-markers.paint pen tips for small details: The nib is not very fine, so keep stripes broad and fill tight gaps with the same colour from a pot and a brush.

painting-armies-efficiently.paint an army fast: Build, prime and base first, cut brushed base coats with sprays or one coat paints, work stages across the batch, and focus on faces.
painting-armies-efficiently.batch painting: Work each stage across the whole batch from a written step list, rather than finishing one model at a time.
painting-armies-efficiently.how do i paint lots of models quickly: Spray the main colour, use one coat paints, group areas sharing a wash, and spend time only on faces and focal areas.
painting-armies-efficiently.speed up army painting: Cut base coats with sprays or primer close to the main colour, base in the shadow colour then highlight, and reuse each brushload.
painting-armies-efficiently.army takes forever to paint: Brushed base coats are the biggest time sink. Use a sprayed main colour or one coat paints, and save blending for leaders.
painting-armies-efficiently.assembly line painting: Follow a written step list from a finished test model and work each stage across the whole batch: do, do not think.
painting-armies-efficiently.paint efficiently for tabletop: Spend time on face, head, shoulders and chest; secondary areas get one coat and one highlight, and skip what nobody sees.
painting-armies-efficiently.tips to finish a whole army: Set a standard early, track every unit by stage, give each a time budget, and save blending and glows for centrepieces.
painting-armies-efficiently.painting a horde of troops: Prime close to the main colour, use one coat paints, and judge the unit not one model; back rows can stop at faces and weapons.
painting-armies-efficiently.too many models not enough time: Highlight only the colour that shows on every figure, then the most eye catching one, and stop back row models at faces and weapons.
painting-armies-efficiently.How can I paint a whole army faster?: Prep everything first, spray the main colour, work stages across the batch, and spend effort only on faces and focal areas.

painting-chainmail.chainmail: Base silver or drybrush dark gunmetal over black, wash dark brown or black, then drybrush with downward strokes only so ring tops catch light.
painting-chainmail.chain mail: Silver base, a dark wash poked into the links, then drybrush top to bottom only, brighter each pass, with a fine silver line on the top edge.
painting-chainmail.how do i paint chainmail: Base it silver, wash dark brown or black, then drybrush a metal mix from top to bottom only, repeating with a brighter mix.
painting-chainmail.drybrush chainmail: Load lightly, wipe most off, and stroke from top to bottom only, never back up, so the top of each ring catches the light.
painting-chainmail.chainmail looks messy: Drybrush downwards only rather than buffing in circles, which loses the lit from above look, and soak up wash so the links do not clog.
painting-chainmail.wash chainmail: Use a dark brown or black wash, poking the brush into the links to clear air bubbles, and soak up excess so they do not clog.
painting-chainmail.chainmail links filled with paint: Soak up excess wash as you go so the links do not clog, and keep the drybrush lightly loaded with most wiped off.
painting-chainmail.mail shirt on a knight: Block it in silver early, paint the cloth around it after, wash dark, drybrush downwards, then a fine bright silver line along the top edge.
painting-chainmail.ring mail: Silver or dark gunmetal over black, a dark brown or black wash, then downward only drybrushing so each ring top catches the light.
painting-chainmail.chainmail too shiny: Wash it dark brown or black first, keep later drybrush passes light and downward only, and save bright silver for one fine top line.

painting-eyes.painting eyes: Dark socket, off white eyeball leaving a dark rim, then a pupil touching both lids. Paint them after the face shade but before highlights.
painting-eyes.how do i paint eyes: Fill the socket black brown, paint an off white eyeball leaving a dark rim, then a short dark pupil line touching both lids.
painting-eyes.eye dots on a face: Quick version: a white dot in each corner of the eye, leaving a black line between them as the pupil, the same width in both eyes.
painting-eyes.where do the pupils go: Touching both lids, roughly above the corners of the mouth, with both eyes looking the same way.
painting-eyes.eyes look scary and staring: A floating pupil dot ringed in white looks startled. Make the pupil touch both lids, or let the upper lid cover part of it.
painting-eyes.eye white and pupil: Use ivory or off white with a touch of skin, never pure white, leaving a dark rim, then a short dark pupil touching both lids.
painting-eyes.glint in the eye: On bigger faces, add one tiny pale dot on the side facing the light, in the same place in both eyes.
painting-eyes.best brush for eyes: A size 0 or similar with a sharp point and short bristles; the point matters more than the size.
painting-eyes.iris colour on a big face: Ring a bright saturated iris inside the dark, lighter on the side away from the light, then a tiny pale dot on the side facing it.
painting-eyes.paint eyes on 28mm: Black brown socket, off white eyeball with a dark rim, then a pupil touching both lids. On rank and file a shaded socket will do.
painting-eyes.How do I paint eyes without them looking: Use off white, not pure white, keep a dark rim, and make pupils touch both lids with both eyes looking the same way.

painting-gun-barrels.gun barrel: Paint a neat dot of matt black with a touch of dark brown in the muzzle, run a thin dark wash round it, and highlight the top rim.
painting-gun-barrels.barrel holes: A neat dot of matt black mixed with a touch of brown makes an undrilled barrel end read as a hole.
painting-gun-barrels.undrilled barrels: Paint the muzzle end in matt black with a touch of dark brown, from the centre out to the rim, so it reads as a hole.
painting-gun-barrels.gun muzzle: Dot thinned black brown from the centre of the muzzle out to the rim, add a thin dark wash round it, then highlight the top rim.
painting-gun-barrels.paint barrel ends: Thin matt black with a touch of dark brown so it flows but covers, and paint from the centre of the muzzle outwards to the rim.
painting-gun-barrels.fake barrel hole: Matt black with a touch of dark brown, painted from the centre outwards; pure black draws attention to the cheat.
painting-gun-barrels.muzzle black dot: Mix in a touch of dark brown rather than pure black, and dab it with a brush or a blunt dampened toothpick from the centre out.
painting-gun-barrels.dont want to drill barrels: Paint a neat dot of matt black with a touch of brown in the muzzle instead; it reads as a hole.
painting-gun-barrels.how to make a barrel look hollow: A neat dot of black brown from the centre to the rim, a thin dark wash round the muzzle, and a highlight on the top rim.
painting-gun-barrels.rifle end looks solid: Paint a neat dot of matt black with a touch of dark brown in the muzzle, turning the model so your hand stays steady at the edge.

painting-leather.leather: Dark cool brown base, black wash or glaze in the recesses, glazed khaki along each strap, then sharp sand edges and tiny cracks.
painting-leather.brown leather straps: Line with thinned black, base dark cool brown, shade black into recesses, glaze khaki along the middle, and edge in sand or pale bone.
painting-leather.how do i paint leather: Base a dark cool brown, shade with thinned black, glaze khaki towards the centre of each strap, then thin sand edges and a few cracks.
painting-leather.worn leather: Use a rough, broken edge highlight in sand or pale bone, plus short diagonal strokes, tiny lines and dots of sand as cracks and scuffs.
painting-leather.leather belt: Line it black, base dark cool brown, shade black into recesses, glaze khaki along the middle, then edge thinly in sandy khaki and sand.
painting-leather.cracks in leather: Add a few short diagonal strokes, tiny lines and dots of the sand highlight colour as cracks and scuffs.
painting-leather.leather armour: Dark brown base, black shade in the recesses, khaki glazes, sand edges where it would rub, and a crack texture distinct from the cloth.
painting-leather.leather pouches: Dark brown base, black shade, khaki glaze, sand edges; highlight each pouch's edges and flap so neighbours do not merge.
painting-leather.leather boots: Base boots darker, edge them in a lighter brown or sand, and add a few dots on toe caps and corners to finish them.
painting-leather.leather looks like plastic: Give it texture: a rough, broken sand edge, short diagonal cracks and scuffs, and a texture different from the cloth.

painting-purple.purple: Shade with deep violet or dark red purple instead of black, and highlight with warm pink, magenta or a creamy ivory rather than pure white.
painting-purple.how do i paint purple: Shade with a deeper violet or red purple, then highlight by adding warm pink, magenta or ivory, keeping the palest mixes small.
painting-purple.purple looks grey: Black removes colour as it darkens, so purple shadows go grey. Shade with deep violet or dark red purple instead.
painting-purple.how to shade purple: Use a deeper violet or a dark red purple rather than black; if you use black, a tiny amount in the very deepest spot only.
painting-purple.how to highlight purple: Add warm pink or magenta, or creamy ivory at about two parts purple to one, rather than pure white, which turns it chalky lilac.
painting-purple.purple armour recipe: Purple base, deep violet or red purple shade, then pink or ivory mixed in for highlights, with a thin purple glaze to pull them together.
painting-purple.purple robes: Shade the folds with deep violet, highlight with purple mixed with warm pink or ivory, and glaze base purple over any drifting highlights.
painting-purple.violet goes chalky: Too much white pushes it towards cold lilac. Add white in small amounts, or highlight with pink, magenta or ivory instead.
painting-purple.rich purple not dull: Shade with deeper violets and red purples instead of black, and highlight with warm pinks so it stays rich.
painting-purple.black wash ruined my purple: Black removes colour as well as darkening, turning purple grey. Glaze the base purple back over and shade with deep violet instead.

painting-sheer-cloth.sheer cloth: Paint the skin underneath first as if bare, paint the cloth solid where thick or folded, then glaze very thin cloth colour over the skin.
painting-sheer-cloth.see through fabric: Paint what is underneath first, then glaze thin cloth colour over it, building more passes near solid folds so it fades to see through.
painting-sheer-cloth.transparent cloth: Paint the skin as bare first, then glaze very thin cloth colour over it, drying between passes; more passes make it less sheer.
painting-sheer-cloth.how do i paint a veil: Paint the face underneath first, keep thick folds solid, then glaze thin veil colour over the covered skin, building more near the folds.
painting-sheer-cloth.translucent fabric: Layer it in real life order: the skin first, then thin glazes of cloth colour, with more passes in the shadows and beside solid folds.
painting-sheer-cloth.thin silk showing skin: Paint the skin fully, then glaze the silk colour very thinly over it; the number of passes sets how sheer it looks.
painting-sheer-cloth.sheer dress: Paint the body underneath as bare, the dress solid where folded or hanging free, then thin glazes of the dress colour over the skin.
painting-sheer-cloth.see through sleeves: Paint the arm first, the sleeve solid where it folds or pulls away, then glaze thin sleeve colour over the covered arm.
painting-sheer-cloth.paint skin under cloth: Paint it as if the cloth were not there, then glaze very thin cloth colour over it. If it goes too dark, repaint the strongest lights.
painting-sheer-cloth.lace veil: See: this entry paints sheer veils by painting the skin first and glazing thin cloth colour over it, solid where folded.

painting-tartan.tartan: Space guide lines evenly round the cloth, paint crossing stripes between them, then shade and highlight the whole pattern together.
painting-tartan.plaid: Base the cloth, place evenly spaced upright lines, add a second colour and cross lines, put small squares where lines cross, then shade.
painting-tartan.kilt: Paint upright lines front, back and sides, halve the gaps, then cross lines from the hem upward, and shade the whole kilt over the pattern.
painting-tartan.tartan pattern: Stripes about a millimetre wide and a couple apart, in a darker shade or thin contrasting colour, crossing, with small squares where they meet.
painting-tartan.how do i paint tartan: Base it, set evenly spaced upright lines, add a second colour and the cross lines, then shade and highlight it all as one.
painting-tartan.tartan cloak: On a curved cloak, let the gaps widen slightly towards the hem and paint cross lines parallel to the hem, following the folds.
painting-tartan.checked fabric: Space lines evenly by halving the gaps, cross them, and mark crossings with a small square of a third colour, then shade over it.
painting-tartan.plaid pattern: Upright lines spaced by halving, a second colour beside them, cross lines worked up from the hem, then shade the cloth over it.
painting-tartan.tartan stripes crossing: Where lines cross, a small square of a third colour sells the weave. Tidy wobbles with the colour underneath.
painting-tartan.tartan blanket: Base in thin coats, space the lines evenly, paint crossing stripes with small squares where they meet, then shade the whole pattern.

painting-with-others.painting club: Look for hobby clubs, gaming groups, craft nights and local hobby venues; many welcome beginners and people who only paint.
painting-with-others.painting groups: Clubs, gaming groups, community craft nights and online groups or forums give feedback, motivation and new ideas.
painting-with-others.paint with friends: Meet up, or paint along on a call. Bring one model and a modest goal; busy rooms suit base coats and washes more than delicate blending.
painting-with-others.hobby night: Bring a small kit and one model with a modest goal, ask questions and offer help, and clean up fully before you leave.
painting-with-others.online painting community: Online groups and forums help when there is nothing nearby: share work in progress or join a monthly painting challenge.
painting-with-others.find other painters: Try hobby clubs, gaming groups, library or community centre craft nights, local hobby venues, and online groups and forums.
painting-with-others.travel paint kit: A few brushes, paints for one model, a lidded water pot, a palette, paper towel, a lamp and a mat to protect the table.
painting-with-others.painting meetup: Take a small kit and one model, keep to base coats and washes in a busy room, ask questions and offer help.
painting-with-others.get feedback on my painting: Paint with others, in person or online; share work in progress in groups and forums for feedback and new ideas.
painting-with-others.is it worth joining a club: Yes: seeing how others hold a brush, thin paint or pick colours speeds up learning in ways photos alone cannot.

pearl-and-shell.pearl: Start from a soft mid grey, shade towards cool purple blue, highlight towards pale green yellow, and blend the tints with thin glazes.
pearl-and-shell.pearly sheen: Shade a pale grey towards purple blue and highlight towards green yellow, keeping the shifts smooth with thin glazes.
pearl-and-shell.mother of pearl: Soft mid or silver grey, shaded towards cool purple blue and highlighted towards pale green yellow, with the very top near white.
pearl-and-shell.seashell: See: pearly shell sheen comes from a mid grey shaded towards purple blue and highlighted towards pale green yellow.
pearl-and-shell.how do i paint pearls: Mid grey base, cool purple blue shading, pale green yellow highlights with a near white top point, smoothed with thin glazes.
pearl-and-shell.pearl necklace: Base each pearl soft grey, shade towards purple blue, highlight towards pale green yellow, and keep the top point near white.
pearl-and-shell.shell looks plain grey: Shade towards cool purple blue rather than black or grey, and highlight towards pale green yellow rather than plain white.
pearl-and-shell.nacre effect: Mid grey shaded towards purple blue and highlighted towards green yellow; the smooth, shifting colour is what sells it.
pearl-and-shell.pearl white armour shimmer: Shade the pale grey towards purple blue and highlight towards green yellow with smooth glazes, keeping the very top near white.
pearl-and-shell.oyster shell: Soft grey shaded towards cool purple blue and highlighted towards pale green yellow, blended with thin glazes.

planning-a-kitbash.how do i plan a conversion: Gather reference, pick one core kit as an anchor, list what must change, sketch it front and back, then dry fit with tacky putty.
planning-a-kitbash.where do i start with a kitbash: With a picture or short story for the character, then one core kit whose size and pose suit it, and a list of parts to change.
planning-a-kitbash.dry fit parts before gluing: Hold parts with tacky putty, look from all sides and try flipping a part. Leave arms on the frame and trim pegs so they turn freely.
planning-a-kitbash.sketch a conversion idea: Sketch the finished figure front and back, especially the areas you will rebuild; it is quicker than building and helps you decide.
planning-a-kitbash.make a unique character from kits: Start from a story and reference, anchor on one core kit, swap head, hands, weapons and pack, and fit the head last.
planning-a-kitbash.tacky putty to test poses: Hold parts in place with tacky putty, view from all sides, try flipping parts, and choose what keeps the face visible.
planning-a-kitbash.which parts should i swap: List what must change, usually head, hands, weapons and pack. Kits where these fit the usual way are easiest to swap.
planning-a-kitbash.my conversion looks like a mess of bits: Keep new parts in the same style, get big shapes right before extras, and use a single coat of grey primer to see it as one piece.
planning-a-kitbash.pick a base kit for a conversion: Pick one core kit whose size and pose suit the idea, ideally one where arms, head and pack fit the usual way.
planning-a-kitbash.custom hero from spare parts: Judge spare parts by shape, not original job, keep to one maker for scale, dry fit with tacky putty, and fit the head last.

prep-check-before-priming.wash models before priming: Scrub with a drop of washing up liquid in warm water and an old toothbrush, rinse, and let it dry fully, ideally overnight.
prep-check-before-priming.what to check before primer: Under a bright lamp with something white behind, turn the model slowly looking for mould lines, gaps, flash and undrilled barrels.
prep-check-before-priming.release agent on new models: New models carry release agent that makes primer bead or slide off. Scrub it off with washing up liquid in warm water.
prep-check-before-priming.primer wont stick: Release agent and skin oil make it bead. Wash the model, let it dry, and wipe large surfaces with isopropyl alcohol just before priming.
prep-check-before-priming.mould lines only show after priming: Normal: one colour primer reveals flaws. Scrape the lines now, then brush primer over just that spot before painting.
prep-check-before-priming.gaps show up after undercoat: Fill them now, before paint: plastic shavings dissolved in plastic glue make a filler that hardens in minutes. Then spot prime.
prep-check-before-priming.prep steps before painting: Clip and clean parts, wash them, assemble, fill gaps, then prime, and fix anything priming reveals before paint goes on.
prep-check-before-priming.clean resin before paint: See: wash models in warm water with washing up liquid and an old toothbrush, or an ultrasonic cleaner, to remove release agent.
prep-check-before-priming.greasy model: Scrub it in warm soapy water with an old toothbrush, dry fully, hold it by the base after, and wipe with isopropyl alcohol before priming.
prep-check-before-priming.should i wash my minis first: Yes. Release agent and handling oils make primer and paint bead or slide off; wash in warm soapy water and dry fully.
prep-check-before-priming.How do I stop paint rubbing off my model: Wash off release agent and oils, prime first, and avoid very thin first coats, which grip poorly.

quartered-designs.quartered shield: Find the centre from a seam or emblem, mark it with small dots in a cross, paint the darker colour first, then bring the pale one up to it.
quartered-designs.halved uniform: Split along natural lines such as a belt or chest plate edge, painting the darker colour first and the lighter one up to it.
quartered-designs.split colours: Decide the layout at base coat stage, paint the darker colour first, bring the paler one up to it, then cut back to straighten the line.
quartered-designs.quartered heraldry: Mark the centre with dots in a cross, paint the dark quarters first, then the pale ones up to them, and repeat the split on smaller shields.
quartered-designs.straight line between two colours: Slow down near the line and pull the brush downwards in one smooth motion, creeping closer each pass, or mask with thin tape.
quartered-designs.half and half shield: Find the centre from a seam or emblem, paint the darker half first, then bring the lighter half up to it and cut back any wobbles.
quartered-designs.how do i paint a quartered design: Plan the layout, do metals first, paint the darker colour, bring the paler one up to meet it, cut back wobbles, then shade each colour.
quartered-designs.checker quarters: See: quartered designs are painted dark colour first with the pale colour brought up to meet it, using dots in a cross to find the centre.
quartered-designs.dividing line looks wobbly: Cut back into each colour with the other to straighten it. Later chipping and weathering hide small wobbles too.
quartered-designs.two colour split scheme: Decide halves or quarters early, paint the darker colour first, follow natural lines like a belt, and alternate colours on trim and pennants.

recess-shading.recess shading: Thin a wash about one to four with water, touch a sharp brush tip into the recess and let it run along the line, keeping flat areas clean.
recess-shading.lining by hand: Use a small sharp brush with well thinned shade, wipe off the excess, touch the tip into the recess and let the paint run along it.
recess-shading.shade only in the recesses: Touch a well thinned wash into creases, joins and panel lines with a fine tip, and clean any spill straight away while wet.
recess-shading.wash stains the flat areas: Shade only the recesses by hand instead; keep all over washes for textured parts like fur, mail and rough cloth.
recess-shading.clean shading without an all over wash: Recess shade: run thinned dark paint only into creases, joins and panel lines, starting where definition matters most.
recess-shading.panel lining with a brush: Thin the shade about one part to four of water, touch a sharp tip into the panel line and let it run, fixing slips once dry.
recess-shading.wash dulls my bright colours: An all over wash dulls bright colours. Put the shade only into recesses by hand for a cleaner finish.
recess-shading.black lining: Prefer each surface's own darkest tone where two meet; a black line looks like a cartoon outline.
recess-shading.pin shading recesses: Touch a well thinned dark shade into the recess with a sharp brush tip and let it run along the line; shade deep creases more.
recess-shading.neater than a wash: Yes: recess shading puts dark only into creases and joins, so you do not spend time repainting stained flat areas.

researching-historical-colours.historical uniform colours: Use period photos, surviving garments and history books, and allow for variation: real cloth varied by dye batch, fading and wear.
researching-historical-colours.how do i research a uniform: Gather period photos of the real uniform and kit, look at surviving garments or museums, and read about the unit and its conditions.
researching-historical-colours.what colour was the uniform really: There is no single exact colour; cloth varied between dye batches and faded with sun and wear, so pick a paint that looks right to you.
researching-historical-colours.period accurate colours: Use photos of surviving garments or museum visits over painted illustrations, which often drift in colour, and lighten a touch for scale.
researching-historical-colours.museum reference for painting: Surviving garments and museum visits are more reliable than painted illustrations, which often drift in colour.
researching-historical-colours.reference photos of real uniforms: Photos of surviving garments are more reliable than illustrations; military history books and online collections help too.
researching-historical-colours.napoleonic coat colours: See: for any period, use photos of surviving garments and books, and allow for dye, fading and wear varying the real colour.
researching-historical-colours.ww2 uniform colour: Many later uniforms sit in greens, olives and browns; for a grey field uniform a greenish grey works. Lighten it a touch for scale.
researching-historical-colours.uniforms faded and varied in real life: Yes: dye batches varied, and cloth faded in the sun and wore with use, so there is no single exact colour.
researching-historical-colours.historical accuracy for figures: Research period photos, surviving garments and books on the unit, then lighten the reference a touch, as small models look darker.

rubbed-edge-wear.worn edges: Over finished metal, paint the panel colour but stop just short of the edges, varying the gap so the metal rim looks like worn paint.
rubbed-edge-wear.paint rubbed off the edges: Paint wears from edges and corners first. Stop the colour short of the edges over metal, or drag half dry grey brown along them.
rubbed-edge-wear.edge wear on armour: Finish the metal, then paint the panel colour stopping short of the edges, varying the gap, and add a few silver scratches.
rubbed-edge-wear.scuffed corners: Run a grey mixed with a little brown along the edges, and as it dries on the brush drag it across nearby surfaces to leave specks.
rubbed-edge-wear.how do i make paint look worn on edges: Leave metal showing round the rim by stopping the colour short of edges, or drag a half dry grey brown along them.
rubbed-edge-wear.paint worn back to metal: Finish the metal first, then paint the coloured panel but stop just short of the edges so the metal shows like worn paint.
rubbed-edge-wear.old used armour edges: Stop the colour unevenly short of the edges over metal, smudge a few edges with a fingertip while wet, and add silver scratches.
rubbed-edge-wear.rubbed paint on a tank: Dark metal base, black wash, light steel drybrush, then two coats of the panel colour kept off the edges; patchy coverage reads as faded.
rubbed-edge-wear.weathered edges with grey: Mix grey with a little brown, run it along the edges, then drag and rub it across nearby surfaces as it dries on the brush.
rubbed-edge-wear.make shield rims look worn: Paint the shield colour stopping just short of a finished metal rim, varying the gap, then pick out a few silver scratches.

sculpting-organic-texture.sculpt pustules: Glue half round craft beads in mixed sizes, or slice putty from a 1 mm sausage, then blend their bases with thick water based filler.
sculpting-organic-texture.boils on a model: Place half round craft beads on dots of super glue with tweezers, blend the bases in with thick filler, and wipe the tops clean.
sculpting-organic-texture.fleshy bumpy texture: Paint thick water based filler onto the area and stipple it with a damp drybrush while wet, or push putty into bulges and ripples.
sculpting-organic-texture.diseased skin bumps: Half beads or putty balls in varied sizes for boils, filler stippled for rough skin, with some smooth areas left between clusters.
sculpting-organic-texture.craft beads as boils: Half round craft beads in mixed sizes make convincing boils. Glue them with tweezers and blend the bases with a thick filler.
sculpting-organic-texture.rough organic skin texture: Paint thick, water based filler onto the area and stipple it with a damp drybrush while it is still wet.
sculpting-organic-texture.stipple filler for texture: Brush thick water based filler on with an old brush, then stipple it with a damp drybrush while wet for rough organic skin.
sculpting-organic-texture.gross plague flesh sculpt: Push small amounts of putty into bulges and ripples with a wet tool, let it firm, then add growths, boils and burst boils on top.
sculpting-organic-texture.blister and pustule conversion: Use craft half beads or sliced putty balls glued with a pin dot of super glue; open a burst boil with a needle in small circles.
sculpting-organic-texture.make skin look lumpy: Push small amounts of putty into bulges and ripples with a wet tool, let it firm an hour or two, then shape growths on top.

shading-without-black.shading without black: Shade with a deeper neighbouring hue, such as orange or red under yellow, purple under blue, or a little of the opposite colour.
shading-without-black.black wash makes everything dull: Black drains saturation. Shade with rich dark colours such as deep blue, purple, deep red or dark green instead.
shading-without-black.shade with the complementary colour: Yes, in small amounts: a touch of red darkens bright green and a thin dark green glaze deepens red. Too much turns it brown.
shading-without-black.what do i shade red with: A thin dark green glaze deepens red without going grey, in small amounts; too much turns the mix brown.
shading-without-black.my shadows look grey and dirty: Black and grey drain saturation. Shade with a deeper neighbour on the colour wheel, one to three steps round, instead.
shading-without-black.shade yellow without it going green: Shade yellow with orange or red, its deeper neighbours on the colour wheel, rather than black.
shading-without-black.colourful shadows: Use a rich dark hue: purple under blue or warm orange, orange or red under yellow, or the middle colour of your scheme.
shading-without-black.should i shade with black: Only for the very deepest gaps or a deliberately grim, ashy look; otherwise it dulls colours.
shading-without-black.rich deep shadows: Shade with deep blue, purple, deep red or dark green rather than black, which drains saturation.
shading-without-black.shadow colour for green cloth: A touch of red darkens a bright green without greying it; yellow green also shades well with turquoise or blue.

skin-from-one-undercoat.different skin tones: Prime mid flesh, drybrush light then pale flesh, then pick the tint: warm flesh shade for standard, ochre for olive, brown for darker skin.
skin-from-one-undercoat.dark skin: Over a mid flesh undercoat drybrushed light, build a brown one coat paint in more coats.
skin-from-one-undercoat.olive skin: Use an ochre one coat paint over a mid flesh undercoat drybrushed with light and pale flesh.
skin-from-one-undercoat.pale skin: See: this entry builds skin from a mid flesh undercoat with light and pale flesh drybrushes, then a warm flesh shade for a standard tone.
skin-from-one-undercoat.how to paint dark skin: Prime mid flesh, drybrush light flesh then pale bony flesh, then build a brown one coat paint over it in more coats.
skin-from-one-undercoat.variety of skin tones in a squad: Use one flesh undercoat and drybrush for all, then vary the tint: warm flesh shade, ochre one coat paint or brown one coat paint.
skin-from-one-undercoat.quick skin tones: Mid flesh primer, a light then pale flesh drybrush, and one tint: warm flesh shade, ochre for olive, or brown for darker skin.
skin-from-one-undercoat.flesh primer skin: Prime mid flesh in two light coats, drybrush light and pale flesh, then wash with a warm flesh shade or a one coat paint.
skin-from-one-undercoat.one undercoat lots of skin colours: Yes: same flesh undercoat and drybrush, then a different wash or one coat paint for each tone, and swap highlights between recipes.
skin-from-one-undercoat.skin tones with washes: Warm flesh shade for standard skin, in two thin coats; if one swamps the skin, layer the drybrush tone back over raised areas.

speeding-up-drying.hair dryer on paint: Yes, on a low heat or cool setting, kept moving and held well back so it does not warp plastic or blow wet paint around.
speeding-up-drying.speed up drying: A short blast from a hair dryer on a gentle setting, kept moving, or simply work on another model while one dries.
speeding-up-drying.dry paint faster: Use a hair dryer on low or cool, kept moving and held well back from fresh paint. Too much heat can warp plastic.
speeding-up-drying.can a hairdryer warp plastic: Yes, too much heat can soften or warp plastic, and resin softens sooner. Use low heat, keep it moving and do not linger.
speeding-up-drying.dry layers between coats fast: A short, moving blast of a hair dryer on low, then let the model cool before the next glaze, wash or one coat paint.
speeding-up-drying.waiting forever for paint to dry: Dry thin layers with a hair dryer on a gentle setting, or work on another model or part while one dries.
speeding-up-drying.dry glazes quickly: Dry each glaze with a short, gentle hair dryer blast, and judge it only once dry, since wet paint looks darker.
speeding-up-drying.heat to dry a wash: Let the wash settle into the recesses first, then dry it, and let the model cool before the next wash to avoid tide marks.
speeding-up-drying.how long to wait between layers: Until the layer is fully dry, or glazing lifts the one below. A gentle hair dryer blast speeds that up.
speeding-up-drying.dry thin coats quickly: A short blast from a hair dryer on low or cool, kept moving and well back from the model, dries each thin layer fast.

spray-booth.spray booth: A hood with a fan and filters that pulls overspray and fumes away from you. Vent its hose out of a window and keep the filter clean.
spray-booth.how can i spray paint indoors: With a spray booth whose fan and filters pull overspray and fumes away, ideally venting out of a window through an adapter.
spray-booth.airbrush fumes in my room: Use a spray booth with its exhaust hose run to a window adapter, and leave the fan running at least 10 minutes after you stop.
spray-booth.when to change the spray booth filter: When a tissue strip at the front no longer snaps towards it after washing, or every two to three months with heavy use.
spray-booth.do i need a spray booth for airbrushing: It lets you spray indoors by pulling overspray and fumes away from you; vent it outside, or use filters alone for light use.
spray-booth.vent fumes out of a window: Run the booth's exhaust hose to a window adapter so fumes go outside.
spray-booth.overspray gets everywhere: Spray inside a booth with the fan on, nozzle inside and face outside, aiming at the back filter rather than the side walls.
spray-booth.setting up a spray booth: Vent the hose to a window, add a turntable and good light inside, fan on before you start, and do not crowd the booth.
spray-booth.spray booth fan not pulling: Clean the filter: soak it about an hour in warm soapy water, rinse, dry and refit. If a clean filter barely pulls, the fan may be failing.
spray-booth.airbrushing in a small flat: A spray booth vented to a window pulls fumes outside; with no window, its filters alone may do for light use.

steady-hands.shaky hands: Brace forearms or elbows on the desk, let the hand holding the model touch the brush hand, and move only your fingers.
steady-hands.how do i stop my hand shaking: Brace your arms on the desk, join both hands into one unit, relax, breathe normally, and avoid caffeine and an empty stomach before fine work.
steady-hands.wobbly lines: Pull the brush towards you, turn the model rather than your hand, keep strokes short, and brace both hands together.
steady-hands.brace hands when painting: Rest forearms or elbows on the desk and wrists on the desk, and let the hand holding the model touch the hand holding the brush.
steady-hands.hand tremor painting: Brace close to the fingertips, join both hands, work in short spells and stop when your hand starts to shake.
steady-hands.rest elbows on the desk: Yes: arms floating in mid air shake most. Rest forearms or elbows on the desk, wrists too, as close to your fingertips as you can.
steady-hands.steady brush for eyes: Brace elbows and hands together, rest a fingertip on the model, move only your fingers, and let the tip touch before the stroke starts.
steady-hands.lines wobble on edge highlights: Turn the model so you run along the edge rather than trace round it, pull the brush towards you, and keep strokes short.
steady-hands.hold the model steady: Rest a little finger on the holder or let both hands touch so they form one rigid unit, with arms braced on the desk.
steady-hands.jittery brush: Relax everything but your fingers, breathe normally, brace your arms, and plan fine work away from caffeine and recent exercise.

stubble-and-wrinkles.stubble: Glaze four parts skin to one blue grey, wicked almost dry, over the chin, jaw, cheeks and top lip in two or three thin coats.
stubble-and-wrinkles.five oclock shadow: Mix skin with a little blue grey, thin it to a glaze, wick the brush almost dry and build two or three thin coats where hair grows.
stubble-and-wrinkles.wrinkles on a face: Use the final pale highlight to paint fine lines at the outer eye corners, across the forehead and beside the mouth, kept gentle.
stubble-and-wrinkles.beard shadow: Glaze a skin and blue grey mix over chin, jaw, cheeks and top lip in several thin coats, keeping it off cheekbones and nose.
stubble-and-wrinkles.old man face: Fine pale lines at the eye corners, forehead and beside the mouth for wrinkles, plus a very thin dark red on nose and cheeks.
stubble-and-wrinkles.expression lines: Paint fine lines in the final pale highlight beside the mouth, across the forehead and at the outer corners of the eyes, with gentle contrast.
stubble-and-wrinkles.shaved head stubble: Glaze a mix of four parts skin to one blue grey over the scalp in two or three thin coats, then rehighlight the raised areas.
stubble-and-wrinkles.stubble effect on a chin: Thin a skin and blue grey mix to a glaze, wick it almost dry, and build it up in thin coats. Quick option: thinned black ink dabbed with a finger.
stubble-and-wrinkles.wrinkled face: After the skin is finished, add fine lines in the final pale highlight at eye corners, forehead and mouth, as soft shifts not hard lines.
stubble-and-wrinkles.crows feet: Paint fine lines at the outer corners of the eyes with the final pale highlight, keeping the contrast gentle.

testing-colour-schemes.test colours before painting: Paint stripes or a swatch grid over your undercoat colour, try a spare part with the full scheme, or colour over a photo of the primed model.
testing-colour-schemes.how do i pick a colour scheme: See: test candidate schemes as swatches, on a spare part, or as a quick digital mock up over a photo of the primed model.
testing-colour-schemes.swatches for a scheme: Paint each base colour with a few mixed steps from dark to light beside it, over your undercoat colour, and check them against a grey scale.
testing-colour-schemes.try colours on a spare part: Paint a spare part, old model or cheap figure with the full scheme first; a spare head on a cork makes a small test bust.
testing-colour-schemes.digital mock up of a scheme: Photograph the primed model and colour over it with a soft, low opacity brush in any free drawing program; ten schemes take half an hour.
testing-colour-schemes.will these colours work together: Test them: swatch them over your undercoat colour, or paint a spare part or a quick digital mock up before committing.
testing-colour-schemes.colour scheme looks wrong: If the test looks dark and muddy, restart from a brighter, more saturated base and keep coloured steps over larger areas before highlights.
testing-colour-schemes.value scale check: Hold a grey value scale next to your swatches to check there is enough light and dark, and change any steps too similar or too far apart.
testing-colour-schemes.plan a scheme before starting: Swatch the colours over your undercoat, test on a spare part or a printed photo, and keep the card beside you while you paint.
testing-colour-schemes.colour test strips: Paint small stripes of each colour, pure and thinned, over the same colour as your undercoat; thinning reveals hidden tints.

tinted-neutrals.tint white: Lean it towards a colour used elsewhere on the model: a little brown for warm white, a little blue for cold white.
tinted-neutrals.warm grey: Add a little brown to the grey; it gives a natural, warm tone like fur or old cloth.
tinted-neutrals.cool grey: Add a little blue to the grey, and add white to that tinted mix for each lighter step so every step shares the tint.
tinted-neutrals.tinted black: Lean black slightly towards a hue, ideally one used elsewhere on the model, so it feels tied to the scheme rather than flat.
tinted-neutrals.warm white: A little brown in the greys gives a natural, warm white; a thin sepia filter softens a stark white into off white.
tinted-neutrals.blue black: Lean black slightly towards blue for a cold neutral, ideally a blue used elsewhere on the model.
tinted-neutrals.grey looks flat and dead: Tint it slightly towards a hue used elsewhere on the model, such as brown for warmth or blue for cold.
tinted-neutrals.how do i make black more interesting: Lean it towards a colour used elsewhere on the model, and reuse the main armour's highlight colour on it so it shares the light.
tinted-neutrals.colourful greys: Tint greys towards a hue in the scheme, keep the tinted base on the palette, and add white to it for each lighter step.
tinted-neutrals.off white tinted: Thin a sepia or light brown wash into a filter and brush it over the whole white to turn it into a softer off white.

two-light-sources.two light sources: Place them at clearly different angles, make one noticeably brighter, paint one at a time, and keep a dark band where their shadows meet.
two-light-sources.moonlight and fire on one model: Cool moonlight from low on one side, firelight from high on the other, one clearly stronger, with a band of shadow left between.
two-light-sources.lit from two sides: Mix each light colour into the base and step up over smaller areas, one side at a time, leaving a dark band where the shadows meet.
two-light-sources.dual lighting: Two lights roughly opposite each other, one dominant, built one at a time, with a band of shadow between so neither merges into mush.
two-light-sources.two coloured lights: Mix each light colour into the base and step up in brightness over smaller areas, one light at a time, with dark left between.
two-light-sources.how do i paint two glows: Decide which dominates, paint one light at a time stepping up over smaller areas, and keep a dark band where the two shadows meet.
two-light-sources.fire on one side cold on the other: Over black, paint a warm colour from one side and a dark sea blue over the other, then build each side up, covering less each step.
two-light-sources.two osl sources: Make one clearly stronger so they do not compete, place them roughly opposite, and keep a dark band where the two shadows meet.
two-light-sources.which light should be stronger: Decide and make it noticeably brighter: a close fire overwhelms everything, while dying embers give only a faint warm tint.
two-light-sources.model lit by two lamps: Place the lights at clearly different angles, one brighter, paint each separately, and leave a band of shadow between them.

understanding-scale.what scale is this: See: millimetre scales are rough figure heights and makers measure differently; stand a figure by a door to check fit.
understanding-scale.28mm vs 32mm: 28mm is about 1:56 and 32mm about 1:48. Both are rough heights, and two makers' figures can still look mismatched.
understanding-scale.what does 1:56 mean: A true reduction: the real thing is 56 times bigger than the model. It roughly matches 28mm figures.
understanding-scale.miniature scales explained: Millimetre scales like 28mm are rough figure heights, often to the eye; ratios like 1:56 are true reductions of the real size.
understanding-scale.will this terrain fit: Stand a based figure by a door: around 35 to 37mm tall lets 28mm figures through, while a 28mm door looks too small.
understanding-scale.heroic scale: Heroic scale figures have chunky heads, hands and weapons; true scale figures are realistically proportioned.
understanding-scale.does this model fit with my others: Figures have grown over the years, so old and new ranges or two makers' 28mm can mismatch. Match new models to what you have.
understanding-scale.scale for doorways: A 2 m door at 1:56 is about 36mm; doors around 35 to 37mm tall let based 28mm figures through.
understanding-scale.15mm vs 28mm: 15mm is about 1:100 and 28mm about 1:56, so 28mm figures are close to twice the size.
understanding-scale.figure height scale: Millimetre scales describe rough height, often foot to eye; a 28mm figure is often 32 to 35mm tall overall.

varnish-changes-colour.varnish changed my colours: Sheen changes colour: gloss makes colours darker and richer, matt makes them flatter and muted. Pick the sheen that keeps your look.
varnish-changes-colour.matt varnish made it dull: Matt flattens and mutes colour. A light satin coat lifts a dull, over matt model; about four parts matt to one gloss gives a satin.
varnish-changes-colour.gloss darkens colours: Yes, gloss makes colours darker and richer, and can make pale armour look muddy. Finish with satin or matt to bring highlights back.
varnish-changes-colour.colours look different after varnish: Varnish gives every paint the same sheen, and sheen changes colour, most of all if you mixed paints with different finishes.
varnish-changes-colour.model looks shiny after varnish: Finish with satin or matt over gloss to bring the highlights back; roughly four parts matt to one part gloss gives a satin.
varnish-changes-colour.matt varnish washed it out: Matt makes colours flatter and more muted; skip very flat matt on bright reds and use a satin coat to lift a dull finish.
varnish-changes-colour.which varnish keeps the colours: Satin is a middle ground: gloss darkens and matt dulls. Test a new varnish on a spare painted part first.
varnish-changes-colour.does varnish change how paint looks: Yes. Gloss makes colours darker and richer; matt makes them flatter and more muted.
varnish-changes-colour.my blends vanished after varnishing: See: matt varnish flattens and mutes colours; a light satin coat brings back depth, and testing on a spare part first avoids surprises.
varnish-changes-colour.colours went flat after spraying varnish: Matt varnish flattens colour. Bring depth back with a light satin coat, and give metallics a brushed gloss coat to keep them bright.

volumetric-highlights.volumetric highlights: Decide the light direction and paint light and shadow across each whole surface by its form, not just its edges, so the model looks solid.
volumetric-highlights.model looks flat even with edge highligh: Light whole shapes, not just edges: cover the top of each bulging form with an opaque lighter layer and leave undersides dark.
volumetric-highlights.highlight the whole shape: Treat parts as simple shapes, shoulders as spheres and limbs as cylinders, and light each one as that shape from one direction.
volumetric-highlights.make it look solid: Paint light and shadow across each surface by its form: tops of bulges lighter, grooves and undersides dark, brightest on the highest points.
volumetric-highlights.light direction on forms: Pick where the light comes from; up facing sides catch it and down facing or low parts go darker, even within one groove.
volumetric-highlights.beyond edge highlighting: Highlight whole raised shapes by form and direction, then add smaller, brighter highlights on the highest points.
volumetric-highlights.3d look on armour: Light plates as boxes and shoulders as spheres from one direction, covering their tops lighter and leaving undersides dark.
volumetric-highlights.volume highlights: Cover the top of each bulging shape with an opaque lighter layer, leave grooves and undersides dark, then add brighter points on top.
volumetric-highlights.highlight top of a groove: Yes: one side of a groove faces up and should be brighter, the other faces down. A wash follows gravity, not light.
volumetric-highlights.form lighting: Light each part as a simple shape: a cylinder catches a line along its length, a sphere is brightest near its top.

wax-seals.wax seals: Base deep red, burgundy or pinkish purple, define the centre with a dark wash, dot brighter highlights on the blobs, then a tiny pale bone shine.
wax-seals.how do i paint wax seals: Two coats of deep red, a dark brown black wash in the centre, brighter red on rim and blobs, then mixed with bone, and a tiny bone dot.
wax-seals.red wax on armour: Deep red base, a dark wash in the stamped centre, brighter red dotted on the raised blobs, and a tiny pale bone reflection on top.
wax-seals.seal with scroll on a model: Paint the seal deep red or plum, wash the centre dark, dot highlights onto the blobs, add a pale shine point and gloss it if the rest is matt.
wax-seals.glossy wax look: Small, sharp highlights make wax look glossy: a tiny pale bone dot at the top, plus gloss varnish if the rest is matt.
wax-seals.wax seal looks flat: Add small, sharp dotted highlights on the raised blobs and a tiny pale bone dot as a reflection, then gloss varnish the seal.
wax-seals.highlight a wax seal: Skim a brighter red round the rim and dot it on the blobs, then that colour mixed half with pale bone on the tops, leaving shade round the centre.
wax-seals.parchment and seal: See: for the seal, base deep red or plum, dot highlights onto the blobs, add a tiny pale bone shine point and gloss it.
wax-seals.burgundy wax colour: On a dark burgundy, a little pale blue grey in the highlight mix gives a cooler, dusty highlight.
wax-seals.paper scroll with a seal: See: paint the seal deep red, burgundy or pinkish purple with dotted highlights and a tiny pale shine, glossed if the rest is matt.

weathering-pigments.weathering pigments: Finish painting first, then stipple dry pigment on lower legs, tracks and edges, or brush it on as a wet paste, and fix it.
weathering-pigments.weathering powder: Dry pigment powder for dust, mud, rust and dirt, stippled on dry or brushed on wet, then fixed by touching fixer beside it.
weathering-pigments.pigment dust on tracks: Work a little pigment into an old brush, dab most off, and stipple it on tracks and edges, heavier near the ground.
weathering-pigments.rust pigment: Dab it on round rivets and touch isopropyl alcohol to it; it flows into place and dries fairly tough.
weathering-pigments.how do i fix pigments: Touch fixer, thinner or alcohol next to the pigment so it wicks in rather than brushing it. Never brush varnish over it.
weathering-pigments.dust on a tank: Stipple a pigment close to your base colour on lower hulls, tracks and edges, heavier near the ground, starting with less than you think.
weathering-pigments.powder came off when i touched it: Loose pigment rubs off, so fix it: touch fixer, thinner or alcohol beside it so it wicks in, then add a light dusting if it fades.
weathering-pigments.dirt pigment paste: Mix pigment with water to a paste and brush it into recesses, tracks and wheels; wait until it is powdery again before judging.
weathering-pigments.how to use pigments: Finish painting, stipple pigment dry or brush it as a wet paste, wipe it off raised areas with a damp bud, then fix it by wicking.
weathering-pigments.pigment mud on wheels: Brush a pigment paste or wash into wheels and lower hulls; for textured mud, sprinkle pigment, drip fixer on and sprinkle again.

wet-palette-setup.wet palette: Keep the water level with the sponge top, cover it with paper towel and paper cut a centimetre or two smaller, and keep paint dots compact.
wet-palette-setup.wet palette setup: Fill water level with the sponge, add two or three sheets of paper towel, then paper cut smaller than the sponge, smoothed of bubbles.
wet-palette-setup.wet palette too wet: Wrinkles, bubbles and running paint mean too much water. Blot stray drops off the paper and keep water just level with the sponge.
wet-palette-setup.which paper for a wet palette: Plain baking parchment works; in a humid room a slightly waxy paper lets less water through and stops paint going runny.
