wet-palette-setup.paint too runny on wet palette: Too much water. Blot the paper, and in a humid room use a slightly waxy paper that lets less water through.
wet-palette-setup.mould on my wet palette: Swap the paper often and rinse or replace the sponge regularly to stop mould.
wet-palette-setup.diy wet palette: A sponge with water level to its top, two or three sheets of paper towel, and baking parchment cut smaller than the sponge.
wet-palette-setup.wet palette drying out: Top up water through the edge of the sponge, add paper towel layers to pass water up, keep paper off the walls, and close the lid on breaks.
wet-palette-setup.sponge in a wet palette: Water level with or just above its top; a sponge alone can hold water back, so lay paper towel over it. Rinse it regularly.
wet-palette-setup.paint spreading on wet palette: That points to too much water. Blot stray drops off, keep the water level with the sponge, and keep paint in compact dots.

why-metallics-look-flat.metallics look flat: Metallic paint reflects real light at miniature scale, so its shine looks small. Shade and highlight it strongly: dark recesses, bright edges.
why-metallics-look-flat.why is my metal so flat: Its shine relies on real light, which falls on a model as if it were tiny. Add strong shading and bright edges and dots.
why-metallics-look-flat.silver looks like a toy: At miniature scale real shine looks small and toy like. Shade the recesses dark and add bright edges and dots for contrast.
why-metallics-look-flat.metallic paint looks plastic: Shade and highlight the metal strongly, with dark recesses and bright edges and dots; that contrast is what sells metal.
why-metallics-look-flat.metal not shiny enough: Push the contrast: dark recesses against bright edges and dots. A metallic that is evenly bright from every angle reads flat.
why-metallics-look-flat.make metallics look real: Shade and highlight strongly, and compare paints on black card under a lamp; the dark reflections matter as much as the bright ones.
why-metallics-look-flat.metallics need shading: Yes. Metallic paint relies on real light, which reads as tiny at this scale, so dark recesses and bright edges make it read as metal.
why-metallics-look-flat.gold looks flat: Shade the recesses dark and add bright edges and dots, as metallic shine alone looks small and toy like at miniature scale.
why-metallics-look-flat.why do metallics look fake: Real light falls on a miniature as if it were tiny, so metallic shine looks toy like without strong painted shading and highlights.
why-metallics-look-flat.metal looks dull under lamp: A metallic that stays evenly bright from every angle reads flat, like grey paint; use it as a base under a brighter metallic and shade it.

beach-shoreline.how do i make a beach base: Glue fine sand in rough patches, add half buried driftwood and shells, paint it warm sand, wash brown, drybrush cream, then add clear water gel at the low edge.
beach-shoreline.sandy shore with shells: Dip a glued base in fine sand, then super glue tiny shells and driftwood in so they look half buried, and keep the props few.
beach-shoreline.driftwood on a base: Use small pieces of driftwood or twigs, glued in so they look half buried in the sand, then pick them out in a grey driftwood colour.
beach-shoreline.sand ripples like wind blown dunes: Before the sand, drag a flat shaper through a thin layer of putty in wavy, crossing lines, then drybrush from one side so the ripples catch it.
beach-shoreline.coastal base for a pirate model: Make a beach: sand over glue, half buried driftwood and shells, a soft sea blue glaze on the low side, and clear water gel for lapping surf.
beach-shoreline.what can i use for tiny sea shells on a: Tiny shells, bottles or crabs work, glued in with super glue so they sit half buried, and picked out after the sand is painted.
beach-shoreline.seaside basing ideas: A sandy shore with driftwood and tiny shells half buried, plus clear water gel along the lowest edge for lapping surf.
beach-shoreline.make sand look like a real beach: Base it warm sand, wash soft brown into the gaps, then drybrush pale cream lightly from one side so ripples catch the light.
beach-shoreline.beach base with sand and stones: Glue sand in rough patches and leave some ground bare, then add props so they look half buried. Keep the base darker and the props few.
beach-shoreline.basing a model on the shore: Build a sandy patch with driftwood and shells, glaze the low side soft sea blue, and run clear water gel along the lowest edge for surf.

crystal-and-ice-shards.ice spikes on a base: Cut clear frame plastic or rod into strips with sharp angled ends, shave the sides unevenly, and glue them in leaning clusters of mixed sizes.
crystal-and-ice-shards.how to make crystals for bases: Cut clear plastic into pointed strips, shave the sides with a knife, and glue them in leaning clusters. Leave bare for glassy crystal.
crystal-and-ice-shards.crystal shards from clear sprue: Cut the clear frame into strips, cut both ends at sharp angles so each comes to a point, and shave the sides unevenly before gluing.
crystal-and-ice-shards.frozen shards sticking out of the ground: Glue pointed clear plastic shards in leaning clusters, texture the ground, paint white and tint blue, then pile snow round each foot.
crystal-and-ice-shards.make magic crystals cheaply: Use clear frame offcuts: cut them into strips with sharp pointed ends, shave the sides, and glue them in clusters of mixed sizes.
crystal-and-ice-shards.clear plastic ice chunks: Cut clear frame or rod into angled shards, leave them bare for glassy crystal or paint them white and tint them blue for solid ice.
crystal-and-ice-shards.glowing crystal cluster scenery: Glue pointed clear shards in leaning clusters, then wash pale icy blue over them and dot deep blue into the middle of each shard.
crystal-and-ice-shards.jagged ice on winter base: Cut clear plastic shards with sharp angled ends, shave them unevenly, glue them leaning together, and pile snow round each foot.
crystal-and-ice-shards.what can i use for ice crystals: Clear plastic frame offcuts or clear acrylic rod, cut to points, plus hot glue pulled to a point on parchment for icicles.
crystal-and-ice-shards.crystal growth basing idea: Clusters of jagged clear shards in mixed sizes, leaning out of crackle textured ground, tinted icy blue with deep blue cores.

glowing-sewer.sewer base: Blue grey sewer stone with rusty grates and glowing green sludge: prime black, glaze blue black, stipple teal, then paint the sludge over white.
glowing-sewer.glowing green sludge in a drain: Paint the sludge white first, then fluorescent green with a touch of yellow over it so it stays bright.
glowing-sewer.rusty grate on a base: Paint the grate steel, add small orange rust dabs on rivets and edges, then rub rust pigment into cracks and along the metal.
glowing-sewer.underground tunnel base: Use stone or brick sewer toppers: prime black, glaze blue black, stipple teal, oil wash dark, and add glowing green sludge.
glowing-sewer.blue grey brick floor: Prime black, dust white from above, line the joints with a dark wash, glaze see through blue black, then stipple teal with a wiped brush.
glowing-sewer.toxic sewer basing: Blue grey stone, rusty steel grates, and sludge painted white then fluorescent green with a little yellow so it glows.
glowing-sewer.how do i paint sewer stone: Glaze blue black over a black and white primed base, stipple teal on, oil wash it dark, wipe the tops, then stipple teal again.
glowing-sewer.glowing slime between the bricks: Paint the slime white first, then fluorescent green with a touch of yellow over it. The white keeps the green bright.
glowing-sewer.city sewer theme base: Sewer stone in blue grey and teal, steel grates with rust dabs and rust pigment, and glowing green sludge painted over white.
glowing-sewer.grimy drain cover: Paint it steel, dab orange rust on rivets and edges, then rub rust pigment into the cracks and along the metal.

red-desert.red sand desert base: Base the sand and rocks dark red brown, wash warm red brown, then drybrush up through orange tan and ochre to a dusty bone.
red-desert.martian red ground base: Dark red brown base, a warm red brown wash, then drybrush orange tan, ochre and a light touch of dusty bone on the edges.
red-desert.how do i paint a red dusty base: Base dark red brown, wash warm red brown, then drybrush orange tan, ochre and dusty bone, and finish with earth pigment.
red-desert.red rocks drybrushed: Base the rocks dark red brown, then drybrush orange tan, ochre mostly on the rocks, and a very light dusty bone on the highest edges.
red-desert.alien planet basing in red: Cork and slate rocks, sand and cracked ground, based dark red brown and drybrushed up through orange tan and ochre to bone.
red-desert.red desert with slate rocks: Super glue cork and slate on, add sand round them, crackle the bare patches, then base dark red brown and drybrush up to bone.
red-desert.orange red rocky ground: Base dark red brown, wash warm red brown, and drybrush orange tan over everything before lighter ochre on the rocks.
red-desert.drybrush red earth to bone: Go dark red brown, orange tan, ochre, then dusty bone, without fully cleaning the brush between them, each lighter and lighter.
red-desert.base for a desert planet: Red desert: cork and slate rocks, sand, and crackle paint, based dark red brown and drybrushed up to a dusty bone.
red-desert.red dirt basing: Base dark red brown, wash a warm red brown that shades without killing the red, then drybrush orange tan, ochre and bone.

snow-bases.snowy base: Paint the ground blue black and drybrush it cold blues, then dab snow paste into cracks and drifts and sprinkle snow powder over it while wet.
snow-bases.how to do snow on bases: Dab snow paste into cracks and against rocks, thick in drifts and thin at the edges, and sprinkle snow powder on while wet.
snow-bases.winter base with snow drifts: Paint and tuft the ground first, then pile snow paste thick in drifts against rocks and feather it thin at the edges.
snow-bases.snow drift on rocks: Dab paste against the rocks, thick in the drift and feathered thin at the edges, and push the rock edges brighter than feels right.
snow-bases.cold blue ground under snow: Base blue black, drybrush slate grey, then pale icy blue on bare ground under thin snow, not grey.
snow-bases.making snow look gritty not fluffy: Use a gritty or textured paste, then sprinkle fine snow powder and a pinch of pearly sparkle over it while wet.
snow-bases.my snow looks like icing sugar: Use less than you think, keep it in cracks and drifts feathered thin, and glaze soft cold blue into the drift undersides.
snow-bases.frozen tundra base: Cork and rocks under texture paste, drybrushed cold blues, tufts added first, then snow paste in drifts with snow powder.
snow-bases.snow and tufts winter basing: Glue the tufts in before any snow, after drybrushing the ground, so they show through the snow in the shadows.
snow-bases.what to use for fake snow: Snow paste or textured modelling paste with snow powder, or white glue thickened with baking soda and a drop of white.

urban-ruins.ruined city base: Build one focal pile of beams and bricks, lay broken slabs round it, fill gaps with rubble, then stain, wash and drybrush grey.
urban-ruins.rubble base: Fill cracks with chopped frame plastic or crushed rubble and the rest with texture paste, then wash for grime and drybrush grey.
urban-ruins.urban basing: Broken slabs, bricks and rubble round one focal pile, stained grey brown, drybrushed grey, with a few warm bricks and rust.
urban-ruins.broken paving slabs: Use broken floor slabs or small slate pieces laid round a focal pile, with cracks filled with rubble and texture paste.
urban-ruins.bricks and debris on a base: Cut frame offcuts into bricks, planks and rubble, lean them in one focal pile, and pick out a few bricks in warm tones.
urban-ruins.bombed out street base: Lean beams and bricks in one pile on broken slabs, wash brown and olive for grime, then dust pale pigment over the ground.
urban-ruins.how to make rubble for bases: Chop plastic frame offcuts into bricks, planks and rubble, or use crushed rubble, and fill the rest with texture paste.
urban-ruins.grey city ground base: Stain it thin grey brown, wash brown and olive for grime, drybrush the concrete mid grey, then a light pale bone over all.
urban-ruins.ruins basing for sci fi: Slabs, beams and rubble in grimy grey, with rust on the metal, red brick dust on bricks and pale dust fixed with matt varnish.
urban-ruins.base with broken beams and bricks: Lean beams and bricks together in one focal pile, dry fitting the model so the feet sit firm, then paint the beams rust brown.

banded-fur.how do i paint wolf fur: Wet blend ivory at the tips into a mid warm brown and then dark brown at the roots, then wash soft black over the dark end.
banded-fur.fur with light tips and dark roots: Lay ivory thick at the tip end, stroke warm brown into it while wet, pull dark brown to the roots, then deepen the roots with a black wash.
banded-fur.striped fur pelt: Blend each band from ivory through mid warm brown to dark brown while wet, then soften the joins with a clean damp brush.
banded-fur.fur fading from cream to black: Wet blend ivory into mid warm brown and dark brown, then wash soft black over the dark end only to deepen the roots.
banded-fur.paint a fur cloak: Work fast with wet blending: ivory at the bright end, warm brown in the middle, dark brown at the far end, then a soft black wash at the roots.
banded-fur.wet blend fur: Put ivory on fairly thick, stroke warm brown into it with some ivory still in the brush, pull dark brown on, then soften joins with a damp brush.
banded-fur.animal pelt looks flat: Give it bands: ivory tips, a mid warm brown, dark brown roots, then a soft black wash blended out over the dark end.
banded-fur.realistic fur on a beast: Fade it from ivory tips through brown to a near black base with wet blending, and deepen the roots with a soft black wash.
banded-fur.brown and ivory fur: Wet blend ivory into a mid warm brown and then a dark brown, softening the joins with a clean damp brush.
banded-fur.furry hide painting: Blend ivory, mid warm brown and dark brown while wet along the fur, then wash soft black over the dark end for depth.

blonde-hair.blonde hair: Base light tan brown, wash sepia into the strands, layer sandy bone along them, then edge the ends in pale cream.
blonde-hair.how to paint blond hair: Two thin coats of light tan brown, a sepia wash in the strands, fine sandy bone strokes, and pale cream on the strand ends.
blonde-hair.blond beard: Base light tan brown, keep a sepia wash off the face, layer sandy bone along the strands, and tip the ends in pale cream.
blonde-hair.sandy hair colour: Base a light tan brown, shade with sepia, then layer a sandy bone along the strands.
blonde-hair.straw coloured hair: Start from a pale bone base for a whiter blonde, shade with sepia, then lift it with sandy bone and pale cream.
blonde-hair.golden blonde dwarf beard: Base light tan brown, wash sepia, layer sandy bone with fine strokes or a near dry brush, then pale cream on the lightest bands.
blonde-hair.make yellow hair not look like custard: Avoid lemon yellow. Use warm tan, a sepia wash, sandy bone and pale cream highlights instead.
blonde-hair.pale blonde braids: Base pale bone for a whiter blonde, let sepia wash sit in the strands, then highlight sandy bone and pale cream.
blonde-hair.light hair on a mini: Base light tan brown, sepia wash in the strands, sandy bone layer, and pale cream on strand ends only.
blonde-hair.fair hair recipe: Light tan brown base, sepia brown wash, sandy bone layer along the strands, pale cream edge on the lightest bands.

bright-green-armour.bright green armour: Base a bright mid green over grey, wash deep green, re layer the flat panels mid green, then edge every edge in yellow green.
bright-green-armour.green armor: Bright mid green base, deep green wash, fresh mid green on the panels, and yellow green edge highlights.
bright-green-armour.lime green armour: Base bright mid green over grey primer, shade deep green, re layer, then edge in yellow green with a paler mix on sharp corners.
bright-green-armour.how to paint green power armour: Thin coats of bright mid green over grey, a deep green wash, re layer the panels, then edge highlight in yellow green.
bright-green-armour.my green armour looks dull: After the wash, re layer the flat panels in a fresh mid green and edge every edge yellow green, paler on the sharpest corners.
bright-green-armour.vivid green plates: Base bright mid green over a grey primer until even, wash deep green, and re layer the panels stopping short of recesses.
bright-green-armour.yellow edge highlight on green: Run yellow green along every edge, with a paler mix on the sharpest corners, after re layering the panels.
bright-green-armour.green knight armour: Bright mid green base, deep green wash, fresh mid green re layer on flat panels, then yellow green edges.
bright-green-armour.neon green armor: See: this entry gives a bright green over grey, shaded deep green and edged in yellow green, not a neon finish.
bright-green-armour.green shoulder pads: Base bright mid green, wash deep green or run it into the recesses, re layer the flat areas, and edge in yellow green.

cold-blue-skin.blue skin: Base a mid blue, layer a lighter blue on raised areas, highlight with a cool grey tan, then glaze deep purple on cheeks and eyes.
cold-blue-skin.how do i paint blue skinned aliens: Mid blue base, lighter blue on raised muscles, a tan and blue grey mix on nose and brow, and a thin deep purple glaze.
cold-blue-skin.cold dead blue flesh: Base mid blue, layer lighter blue on raised areas, highlight cool grey tan, and glaze deep purple thinly in recesses.
cold-blue-skin.blue skin highlights: Layer lighter blue on raised features, then highlight with tan mixed with blue grey on the nose, brow and tops of muscles.
cold-blue-skin.frost giant skin: Mid blue base, lighter blue on the muscles, a cool grey tan highlight, and a very thin purple glaze round the eyes.
cold-blue-skin.undead blue skin tone: Base mid blue, layer lighter blue, edge with cool grey tan, then glaze deep purple very thin on cheeks and in recesses.
cold-blue-skin.ice elf skin: Mid blue base, lighter blue on features, a cool grey tan on nose and brow, and a thin purple flush round the eyes.
cold-blue-skin.blue skin looks streaky: Use thin coats for the mid blue base: too thin beats thick and streaky, so just add another coat.
cold-blue-skin.purple flush on blue skin: Glaze deep purple very thin on the cheeks, around the eyes and in some recesses after the highlights.
cold-blue-skin.blue flesh for a demon: Base mid blue, layer lighter blue on raised muscles, highlight cool grey tan, then glaze deep purple in the recesses.

dark-weathered-wood.dark wood: Base dark brown, wash thinned black over it, paint mid brown grain lines, then edge in a pale grey brown.
dark-weathered-wood.old weathered wood: Dark brown base, a near black wash, wobbly mid brown grain lines, and a pale grey brown on outer edges.
dark-weathered-wood.how to paint wood grain: Over a dark base and black wash, paint broad then finer wobbly grain lines in mid brown, each one lighter.
dark-weathered-wood.dark brown planks: Base dark brown, wash thinned black, add mid brown grain lines, then edge the planks pale grey brown.
dark-weathered-wood.wooden shield: Dark brown base, near black wash, mid brown grain in wobbly lines, and a pale grey brown on the outer edges.
dark-weathered-wood.spear shaft wood: Base the shaft dark brown, wash thinned black, add fine mid brown grain lines and a pale grey brown edge.
dark-weathered-wood.aged timber: Cool dark brown with painted grain: dark brown, black wash, mid brown grain lines, then a pale grey brown edge.
dark-weathered-wood.painted wood grain lines: Paint broad then finer wobbly lines in mid brown, each one lighter, then put pale grey brown inside a few thicker lines.
dark-weathered-wood.wooden haft colour: A cool dark brown, washed near black, grained in mid brown, with a pale grey brown edge.
dark-weathered-wood.weather beaten wooden boards: Dark brown base, near black wash, wobbly mid brown grain, then pale grey brown on outer edges and a few grain lines.

glossy-flesh.brain: Over white, two coats of purple contrast in every crevice, then dusky pink and pale pink on the raised folds, then gloss varnish.
glossy-flesh.exposed brain: Purple contrast over white primer, dusky pink on the folds, pale pink towards the top, and gloss varnish so it looks wet.
glossy-flesh.fleshy growth: Purple contrast into every crevice over white, layer dusky pink then pale pink on the raised folds, and finish in gloss.
glossy-flesh.gross flesh tentacles: Work purple contrast into the crevices, layer dusky pink and pale pink on the raised parts, then gloss varnish it.
glossy-flesh.wet looking guts: Paint them purple, then dusky and pale pink on the raised folds, and finish with clear gloss varnish to look wet.
glossy-flesh.pink purple flesh: Purple contrast over white primer, then pink, purple and pale yellow mixed to a dusky pink on raised folds, lifted to pale pink.
glossy-flesh.organic growths: Purple contrast over white, dusky pink and pale pink layers towards the top, then a gloss varnish for a wet look.
glossy-flesh.how to make flesh look wet: Put clear gloss varnish over the finished flesh so it looks wet.
glossy-flesh.glossy gore: Paint the gore purple into pink, then finish with a clear gloss varnish so it looks wet.
glossy-flesh.mutated flesh: Purple contrast over white in every crevice, layer dusky and pale pink on the folds, then gloss varnish.

green-scales.green scales: Base deep teal green, wash black between scales, layer mid green on each scale top, then edge pale grey green and dot pale flesh.
green-scales.how do i paint lizard skin: Deep teal green base, black wash in the gaps, mid green on scale tops, pale grey green edges, and tiny pale flesh dots.
green-scales.scaly green hide: Base deep teal green, wash thinned black between scales, then highlight the tops mid green and the edges pale grey green.
green-scales.dragon scales green: Deep teal green base, black wash in the gaps, mid green on top of each scale, and pale grey green on the edges.
green-scales.reptile skin: Base deep teal green, run a thinned black wash between scales, then highlight each scale mid green and pale grey green.
green-scales.highlighting each scale: Put mid green on the top of each scale, then a pale grey green on the edges, and tiny pale dots on the most prominent ones.
green-scales.snake skin: See: a deep green scaled skin, based teal green, washed black between scales and highlighted mid and pale grey green.
green-scales.crocodile skin: See: a deep green scaly hide, teal green washed black in the gaps, with mid green and pale grey green highlights.
green-scales.wash between scales: After a few coats of deep teal green, run a thinned black wash into the gaps between the scales.
green-scales.lizard man skin: Deep teal green base, black wash between scales, mid green on scale tops, then pale grey green edges and pale flesh dots.

heat-stained-metal.heat discolouration on gun barrels: Over a mid silver, wash a dark blue band at the muzzle, purple a little further back, then sepia fading out along the barrel.
heat-stained-metal.burnt metal: Base mid silver, then wash bands of dark blue, purple and sepia back from the hot end, with a touch of black to scorch the tip.
heat-stained-metal.blue purple heat bands: Wash dark blue at the muzzle, feathered back with a damp brush, then purple overlapping it and smudged while wet.
heat-stained-metal.hot barrel effect: Mid silver base, a dark blue wash band at the muzzle, purple further back, then sepia fading along the barrel.
heat-stained-metal.exhaust pipe heat stain: See: the same banding works anywhere: dark blue at the hot end, then purple, then sepia, over a light silver.
heat-stained-metal.scorched muzzle: Add a touch of black to the dark blue wash at the very tip of the muzzle to scorch it.
heat-stained-metal.how to make metal look overheated: Over a light silver, wash bands of dark blue, purple and sepia, fading back from the hot end and smudged while wet.
heat-stained-metal.rainbow heat tint on steel: Wash overlapping bands of dark blue, purple and sepia over mid silver. Heat colours need a light metal under them.
heat-stained-metal.burned exhaust: See: wash dark blue at the hot end with a touch of black, then purple, then sepia fading back, all over a mid silver.
heat-stained-metal.gun barrel colours from heat: Dark blue at the muzzle, purple a little further back, then sepia fading out along the barrel, all over silver.

navy-blue-cloth.navy blue: Mix blue and black equally for the base, line it thin black, then layer dark navy in broad steps and edge in a dusty blue.
navy-blue-cloth.dark blue cloth: Base navy black, shade very thin black, lift the folds in broad dark navy steps, and edge the most exposed bits dusty blue.
navy-blue-cloth.navy uniform: Equal blue and black base, thin black lining between garments, broad dark navy layers, and dusty blue edges.
navy-blue-cloth.dark blue coat: Base blue and black in equal parts, line round pockets with thin black, then lift raised folds with dark navy.
navy-blue-cloth.highlight navy blue: Use broad steps on raised folds, adding blue each time, then edge in pure blue or blue with a little pale sand.
navy-blue-cloth.dark blue jacket: Navy black base, thin black shade round pockets, broad dark navy layers, dusty blue on the most exposed edges.
navy-blue-cloth.naval officer coat: Base navy black from blue and black, shade thin black, layer dark navy on folds, and edge highlight dusty blue.
navy-blue-cloth.very dark blue fabric: Mix blue and black evenly as the base, then lift it in broad steps of blue so it still reads as blue.
navy-blue-cloth.navy blue looks black: Make the highlight steps broad, adding blue each time. Small ones leave it looking black.
navy-blue-cloth.blue trousers: See: this entry covers navy cloth: blue and black base, thin black lining, broad dark navy steps and dusty blue edges.

painted-gold.gold without metallic paint: Base a very dark red brown, layer up through orange brown and warm yellow, then edge a pale icy yellow.
painted-gold.how do i paint non metallic gold: Start very dark red brown, step up through orange brown and warm yellow, each covering less, then a pale icy yellow edge.
painted-gold.fake gold with normal paints: Go from a near black red brown through orange brown and warm yellow to a pale icy yellow, edges first.
painted-gold.nmm gold quick: Dark red brown base, orange brown layer, warm yellow layer, a thin warm yellow glaze to smooth the jumps, pale icy yellow edge.
painted-gold.gold from brown to yellow: Mix orange brown into the dark base in steps, then warm yellow, each covering less, then a pale icy yellow last.
painted-gold.painted gold trim: Base very dark red brown, step up to orange brown and warm yellow, edges first, then a pale icy yellow highlight.
painted-gold.yellow gold highlights: Keep stepping up in warm yellow, each covering less, then finish with a pale icy yellow. Skip white.
painted-gold.gold looks green: A khaki and black base gives a greenish gold. Use black with a deep red, or a dark brown, for warm gold.
painted-gold.non metalic gold recipe: Very dark red brown, then orange brown, warm yellow and a pale icy yellow edge, with a thin warm yellow glaze to smooth it.
painted-gold.gold armour without metallics: Base very dark red brown, step up through orange brown and warm yellow, glaze warm yellow, then edge pale icy yellow.

pink-tails-and-bare-skin.rat tails: Base deep pinkish flesh, layer pale pink along the top half, glaze bright pink at the tip, then edge each ring pale pinky ivory.
pink-tails-and-bare-skin.pink tail: Deep pinkish flesh base, pale pink on the top half, two bright pink glazes toward the tip, and ivory on top of the rings.
pink-tails-and-bare-skin.how to paint ratmen skin: Base the bare skin deep pinkish flesh, layer pale pink, glaze bright pink on noses and tips, then edge pale pinky ivory.
pink-tails-and-bare-skin.pinky skin on rats: Use a deep pinkish flesh on noses, ears, paws and tails so they match, then lift with pale pink.
pink-tails-and-bare-skin.rat noses ears and paws: Paint them the same deep pinkish flesh as the tail so they match, and glaze bright pink on the nose.
pink-tails-and-bare-skin.fleshy tail: Deep pinkish flesh base, a pale pink layer with a little off white on the top half, then pale ivory on each ring.
pink-tails-and-bare-skin.vermin bare skin: Base deep pinkish flesh, layer pale pink, glaze bright pink toward the tips, and highlight knuckles in pale pinky ivory.
pink-tails-and-bare-skin.pink rat feet: Base them deep pinkish flesh like the tail, then pick out the knuckles in pale pinky ivory after any glaze dries.
pink-tails-and-bare-skin.rat skin colour: A deep pinkish flesh, lifted with pale pink and glazed bright pink toward the nose and tail tip.
pink-tails-and-bare-skin.pink glaze on tail tip: Glaze bright pink on the tail tip end in two passes, feathering the edge out with clean medium.

red-demon-skin.red skin: Base dark red, layer bright red on raised areas, mix tan into the red for the tips, then glaze milky thin red over all.
red-demon-skin.demon skin: Dark red base, bright red on raised areas, a red tan on the tips so it looks fleshy, and a thin red glaze to smooth it.
red-demon-skin.red devil skin: Base dark red, layer bright red, tip with red mixed with tan, then glaze thin red over everything.
red-demon-skin.fleshy red: Mix tan into the red for the top highlights so it looks fleshy, not pink, then glaze thin red over all.
red-demon-skin.how to paint red skin: Smooth dark red base, bright red on raised areas, red tan on the tips, and a milky thin red glaze over everything.
red-demon-skin.red skin looks like plastic: Mix tan into the red for the highest points so it looks fleshy, then glaze thin red to smooth the steps.
red-demon-skin.daemon skin red: Base dark red, layer bright red, highlight with red and tan, then pull it back together with a thin red glaze.
red-demon-skin.red monster: Dark red base, bright red layer on raised areas, a red tan on the tips, and a milky thin red glaze over all.
red-demon-skin.red skin glaze: A milky thin red glaze over everything smooths the steps and pulls the highlights back to red.
red-demon-skin.crimson skin: Base dark red, layer bright red, tip with a red tan so it stays fleshy, then glaze thin red over the lot.

tanned-skin.tanned skin: Drybrush warm flesh over a peach or pink undercoat, apply a flesh contrast, layer warm flesh back up, then edge in light amber.
tanned-skin.how do i paint a warm skin tone: Over a peach or pink undercoat, drybrush warm flesh, coat in flesh contrast, then bring the raised areas back up.
tanned-skin.medium skin tone: A warm medium tone: warm flesh drybrush, flesh contrast over it, warm flesh layer, and light amber highlights.
tanned-skin.skin wash too dark: Soak up pools as you go, since a heavy coat turns the skin too dark, then layer warm flesh back on the raised areas.
tanned-skin.sun tanned flesh: Drybrush warm flesh heavily over peach, apply a flesh contrast, re layer warm flesh, and edge with a light amber skin.
tanned-skin.skin over peach undercoat: Drybrush warm flesh fairly heavily over the peach undercoat, then apply a flesh contrast over all the skin.
tanned-skin.warm pale skin: See: this is a warm medium tone. For lighter results, soak up the contrast pools and lift more with warm flesh.
tanned-skin.easy skin with a wash: Drybrush warm flesh, apply a flesh contrast over all the skin, then bring cheeks, nose and muscles back up.
tanned-skin.olive tan skin: See: this entry gives a warm medium tan from warm flesh, a flesh contrast, and light amber highlights.
tanned-skin.warm brown skin wash: Apply a flesh contrast over a warm flesh drybrush, soaking up pools so it does not go too dark.

urban-camo.urban camo: Base blue grey, wash brown, re layer, paint jagged near black blocks, then outline each in ivory and edge the armour light grey.
urban-camo.city camouflage: A blue grey base with sharp black and ivory shapes, painted as jagged angular blocks like rubble.
urban-camo.grey camo pattern: Base blue grey, wash brown for dust, re layer the base, then add jagged near black blocks outlined in ivory.
urban-camo.how to paint camouflage: Base the colour neatly, wash, re layer, paint jagged near black shapes, then line each one neatly in ivory.
urban-camo.black and white camo shapes: Paint jagged, angular near black blocks like rubble, then a neat ivory line around each black shape.
urban-camo.blue grey camo: Two coats of blue grey, a brown wash, re layer on raised areas, then black blocks with ivory outlines.
urban-camo.camo on armour: Base blue grey neatly, wash brown, re layer, paint near black blocks, outline them ivory, and edge all armour light grey.
urban-camo.digital urban camouflage: See: this entry uses jagged angular black blocks with ivory outlines on blue grey, not a square pixel pattern.
urban-camo.sharp edged camo: Paint jagged, angular near black blocks like rubble, then run a neat ivory line around each to keep edges sharp.
urban-camo.camo on a tank: Base the panels blue grey, wash brown for dust, then add near black angular blocks outlined in ivory.

worn-black-armour.black armour: Prime black, drybrush dark blue grey down across the edges, wash warm brown into rivets, then chip light grey on corners.
worn-black-armour.battered black armor: Black primer, a rough dark blue grey drybrush, a warm brown wash in chips, and small jagged light grey chips.
worn-black-armour.worn black plates: Drybrush dark blue grey down across every edge over black, wash dark brown into chips, then add light grey chips.
worn-black-armour.highlight black armour: Drybrush dark blue grey across the edges, then edge highlight small jagged light grey chips where light would catch.
worn-black-armour.chipped black: Add small jagged light grey chips on corners and rivets, with a dark warm brown wash run into the chips.
worn-black-armour.black armour looks flat: Drybrush dark blue grey down across every edge, then add light grey chips on corners where light catches.
worn-black-armour.rusty black armour: Run a dark warm brown wash into rivets and chips over the black and blue grey for rusty brown wear.
worn-black-armour.scratched black plate: Edge highlight small jagged chips in light grey on corners and rivets, over a rough dark blue grey drybrush.
worn-black-armour.black knight: Prime black, drybrush dark blue grey, wash warm brown into rivets, and chip light grey on the corners.
worn-black-armour.edge highlight black: Use light grey in small jagged chips on corners and rivets, where light would catch.

airbrush-basics.how do i use an airbrush: Thin paint about half and half, start around 25 psi, spray short bursts about a fist's width away, and turn the model, not the airbrush.
airbrush-basics.airbrush for beginners: Learn to strip and rebuild it first, practise with air, then water, then paint, and start on priming and big base coats.
airbrush-basics.airbrush thinning ratio: About half and half with airbrush thinner for most work, and around one part paint to ten of thinner for close detail.
airbrush-basics.how much do i thin paint for airbrush: Roughly half and half with airbrush thinner, putting the thinner in the cup first. Close detail needs about one paint to ten thinner.
airbrush-basics.airbrush distance and pressure: Most work sits at 20 to 30 psi, starting around 25. Spray a fist's width away for base coats and about three fingers for highlights.
airbrush-basics.first time airbrushing: Practise with air only, then water on card, then paint, and start with priming and big base coats where slips do not show.
airbrush-basics.airbrush cleaning and taking apart: Learn to strip and reassemble it before anything else. Tighten parts by hand, not with tools, and never clean it with a wire brush.
airbrush-basics.getting thin even coats with airbrush: Work in short bursts so each pass dries fast and stays thin, keep the airbrush steady, and rotate the model under it.
airbrush-basics.airbrush trigger control: Push down for air, draw back for paint, and let it spring forward. Start the air before the paint and stop the paint before the air.
airbrush-basics.airbrsuh tips: Thin it half and half, spray in short bursts around 25 psi, start air before paint, and rotate the model rather than the airbrush.

airbrush-setup.which airbrush should i get: A gravity fed, dual action airbrush with a nozzle of about 0.3 to 0.4 mm, whose spare needles, nozzles and seals are easy to get.
airbrush-setup.airbrush for beginners: A low cost gravity fed, dual action airbrush sprays well and survives cleaning mistakes. Spend the extra on the compressor.
airbrush-setup.compressor with tank: A tank lets the motor fill it and rest, so it runs quieter, steadier and lasts longer. It also needs a regulator and moisture trap.
airbrush-setup.dual action airbrush: Pressing the trigger down releases air and pulling it back adds paint, more the further back. A rear stop screw helps while learning.
airbrush-setup.gravity feed or siphon: Gravity fed, with the cup on top, suits the small amounts of paint used on miniatures and needs less pressure.
airbrush-setup.airbrush pressure regulator: The compressor must have one. Set about 20 to 30 psi for most work, 15 to 20 for detail and glazes, up to about 40 for priming.
airbrush-setup.what do i need to start airbrushing: A dual action gravity fed airbrush, a compressor with tank, regulator and moisture trap, thinner, cleaner, a cleaning pot and a respirator.
airbrush-setup.single or double action: Choose dual action: down for air, back for paint, and the further back the more paint.
airbrush-setup.airbrush kit setup: Gravity fed dual action airbrush, a tank compressor with regulator and moisture trap, a hose that fits, plus thinner, cleaner and a cleaning pot.
airbrush-setup.air compressor for minis: Get one with a tank, a pressure regulator and a moisture trap. Tiny battery or USB units cannot hold steady pressure and spatter.

applying-transfers.decals: Gloss the area, soak the transfer until it slides, slide it on with a soft brush, soften it into place, then seal with gloss and matt.
applying-transfers.transfers: Gloss varnish the panel, soak the transfer 20 to 60 seconds, slide it into place, add softener, then gloss and matt varnish over it.
applying-transfers.how to apply decals: On a cured gloss coat, slide the soaked transfer off with a soft brush, press the water out, brush on softener, then seal and matt.
applying-transfers.waterslide: Soak it in clean water or on damp tissue for 20 to 60 seconds until it slides on its backing, then slide it onto a wetted, glossed surface.
applying-transfers.decal softener: Brush softening solution on once the transfer is positioned and leave it for about fifteen minutes. It looks wrinkled at first, then pulls down.
applying-transfers.transfer setting solution: Brush a little setting solution onto the model, slide the transfer onto it and nudge it into place. Flat areas need only setting solution.
applying-transfers.where to put transfers: Plan where they go before painting, and paint a light patch under any that need a bright background, since they are see through.
applying-transfers.decals on a curved surface: Cut a small slit into the film so it can bend, then soften and press it with a damp cotton bud a few times until it settles.
applying-transfers.shoulder pad decal: Soften and press it a few times on the curve. If a fold will not settle on a round shoulder, paint it over as a scratch or chip.
applying-transfers.when do i put decals on: Part way through painting, before weathering, on a gloss coat left to cure, ideally overnight.

base-lighting.lighting the base: Light the base from the same direction and in the same colours as the model, drybrushing only from the lit side.
base-lighting.base doesn't match the model's lighting: Drybrush the base in one direction only, from the light's side, using the model's highlight colours, and keep shadow under the feet.
base-lighting.how do i paint light on the ground: Drybrush from the light's side with the model's highlight colours, add pale pigment on the lit side, and dark pigment in shadowed recesses.
base-lighting.directional drybrush base: Drybrush only from the side the light comes from, using the highlight colours already on your palette for each side.
base-lighting.osl on the base: If light hits the model in a colour, it hits the ground too: drybrush the base from that side in the same light colours.
base-lighting.base colour matches light source: Use the same highlight colours on the base as the model, and glaze raised edges on the lit side thinly pale.
base-lighting.diorama lighting: Light the ground from the same direction and colours as the figures, including tufts and stones, so the scene holds together.
base-lighting.light from one side on the base: Drybrush from that side only, work pale pigment into the lit side, dark pigment into the shadow side, and pale up the lit tufts.
base-lighting.base looks flat compared to model: A flat, evenly lit base clashes with directional light on the model. Drybrush it from the light's side and keep shadow under the feet.
base-lighting.shadow under feet: Keep the shadow colour under and between the feet when you drybrush the base from the light's direction.

black-lining.black lining: Paint thin dark lines where two colours or parts meet, using a fine brush and paint thinned to flow like ink.
black-lining.lining between colours: Run thin, inky dark paint into the join between two colours, then tidy any spread with the neighbouring colour.
black-lining.colours look muddy where they meet: Line the join with a thin dark line. Without that shadow, boundaries look muddy, especially after drybrushing or airbrushing.
black-lining.how to separate parts with dark lines: With a sharp fine brush and inky thin dark paint, run a line into each gap where plates overlap or cloth meets armour.
black-lining.line the joins: Run thin dark paint into gaps where parts meet and round bolts and rivets, or touch a strong dark wash into the corner.
black-lining.comic book outline style: See: black lining works like inking a comic, but keep the lines thin or it reads as a cartoon outline.
black-lining.parts blend into each other: Add a thin dark line where each part meets the next. On small models this stops skin, cloth and kit blurring together.
black-lining.dark line between armour and cloth: Run a thin, inky dark line into the gap where cloth meets armour; very dark brown is softer on warm colours.
black-lining.black lines in the gaps: Use thinned dark paint on a sharp fine brush, or a strong dark wash touched right into the corner without dragging it.
black-lining.tidy the borders between areas: As a last pass, run a thin dark line along the border, then go back with the neighbouring colour until only a sharp line is left.

breaking-up-metal-models.all metal model looks boring: Paint some parts as other materials, use two metals with one bright and focal, and add one or two small spots of strong colour.
breaking-up-metal-models.robot model all silver: Use a mid steel and a darker metal, paint joints and hoses black, some plates flat colour, and add a red valve or lights.
breaking-up-metal-models.metal model looks like a blob: Pick some parts to be other materials, vary the metals' tone and finish, and paint flexible joints and seals black.
breaking-up-metal-models.how to paint a fully armoured knight: Use two metals with one bright, paint some plates as flat colour, and add a small spot of strong colour to break it up.
breaking-up-metal-models.too much metal: Turn some parts into other materials, like black joints or off white plates, and tone down all but one focal metal.
breaking-up-metal-models.break up a silver model: Wash it all dark brown, repaint the cleaner parts, then wash black, so you get two tones from one silver.
breaking-up-metal-models.two different metals on one model: Use a mid steel for the main parts and a darker metal for others, or vary the finish, such as cool clean steel and warm oily iron.
breaking-up-metal-models.make metal armour more interesting: Vary undertone and finish, paint some plates flat colour, and add one strongly contrasted accent like a painted symbol.
breaking-up-metal-models.iron golem looks flat: Shade strongly with black and brown, add a second darker metal, and pick out joints black with one bright accent colour.
breaking-up-metal-models.mixing steel and brass: See: this entry suggests pairing metals such as copper trim with bronze panels, with one metal bright and the others toned down.

brushes-for-rough-jobs.what to do with old brushes: Move them down to jobs that would wreck a good brush: drybrushing, stippling, spreading glue, texture paste, pigment and solvents.
brushes-for-rough-jobs.brush lost its point: Do not throw it away. Keep it for drybrushing, stippling, glue or texture paste, and label it so it stays off detail work.
brushes-for-rough-jobs.brush for drybrushing: A slightly worn small brush suits controlled overbrushing on edges, and a worn medium one gives a bolder drybrush. Make sure it is fully dry.
brushes-for-rough-jobs.which brush for glue: An old brush, labelled as the glue brush, for PVA. Never put super glue on bristles; apply it with the handle end instead.
brushes-for-rough-jobs.use old brushes for texture paste: Yes. Spoon texture paste or snow with an old brush; a cheap flat covers terrain fast and a small round reaches round feet.
brushes-for-rough-jobs.split brush tip: When the hairs fork, retire it to rough jobs like drybrushing, stippling, glue and texture paste, and mark it so it stays there.
brushes-for-rough-jobs.make my good brushes last: Keep drybrushing, stippling, glue, texture paste and solvents to old brushes, and never stir clean pots with dirty bristles.
brushes-for-rough-jobs.cheap drybrush: A worn brush or a soft make up brush is a cheap drybrush. A worn medium brush gives a bolder result than a soft one.
brushes-for-rough-jobs.makeup brush drybrushing: Soft make up brushes are a cheap alternative for drybrushing and also suit stippling.
brushes-for-rough-jobs.ruined brush: Give it a second life on rough jobs, trim it flat for stippling, or use its handle to shape putty or hold tiny parts.

card-modelling.paper terrain: Print templates on heavy card, back them with cereal box card, score every fold, and super glue the tabs.
card-modelling.card models: Print on heavy card, around 300 gsm, glue to cereal box card for stiffness, score the folds, then glue the tabs and seal before painting.
card-modelling.printable terrain templates: Print them on heavy card around 300 gsm, then cut, score every fold line, and glue the tabs.
card-modelling.cheap vehicles from card: Glue heavy card printouts to cereal box card, score and fold, glue the tabs, and add layered card panels for depth.
card-modelling.cereal box terrain: Glue cereal box card to the back of printed parts with a glue stick; it adds weight and stiffness.
card-modelling.papercraft scenery: Print on heavy card, cut with slightly long tabs, score each fold, glue the tabs, and seal with thin varnish or watered PVA before painting.
card-modelling.scoring card folds: Score every fold line with a craft knife, through the print and partly into the backing but never right through, for crisp folds.
card-modelling.building with cardboard: Back printed card with cereal box card, score and fold it, super glue the tabs, and use thicker card for large flat tops.
card-modelling.free print and fold buildings: See: print templates on heavy card, score every fold, glue the tabs, and seal the card before painting.
card-modelling.card tank for gaming: Back the printed parts with cereal box card, layer on extra card plates, and use a washer and magnet for a turning turret.

choosing-a-colour-scheme.choose a colour scheme: Decide the setting or mood first, give one main colour about 70 percent and a contrasting one about 30, and alternate warm and cool.
choosing-a-colour-scheme.what colours should i paint my model: Start from a one line story or two or three mood words, then pick a main colour and its opposite on the wheel at similar strength.
choosing-a-colour-scheme.colour scheme ideas: Try opposites at similar strength: blue with orange, red with green, purple with yellow, with one main and one smaller colour.
choosing-a-colour-scheme.pick colours for a single figure: Decide setting, mood and key part first, then alternate warm and cool areas around it, with the head drawing the eye.
choosing-a-colour-scheme.warm and cool colours: Alternate warm and cool areas around the model, and put a little of the opposite temperature into each area's shading.
choosing-a-colour-scheme.how to plan a paint scheme: Pick a story or mood words, a main colour about 70 percent and a contrast about 30, then check for a light, dark, bright and dull.
choosing-a-colour-scheme.color scheme help: Use one main colour for most areas and its opposite on the wheel for the rest, and look at all base coats together before washing.
choosing-a-colour-scheme.mood colours for a grim model: Write mood words such as grim and pick colours that carry them, with a light, dark, bright and dull in the set.
choosing-a-colour-scheme.i cant decide colours: Paint one focal part first, such as the face or a mask, and let it guide the rest.
choosing-a-colour-scheme.scheme for a display piece: Build it from a story or setting, use a 70 to 30 split with opposites, and keep light tones near the head so the eye goes there.
choosing-a-colour-scheme.How do I pick colours that look good tog: Pair a colour with its opposite on the wheel at similar strength, such as blue with orange, and give one about 70 percent.

clean-crisp-painting.my models look messy: Keep paint off neighbouring areas, line the joins dark, and edge highlight thinly, then tidy spills with the neighbouring colour.
clean-crisp-painting.how do i paint neater: Thin paint to about half and half so it flows where you put it, base coat each area opaque, and tidy spills at the end.
clean-crisp-painting.model looks blurry: Add definition: dark lines between parts, shaded recesses, and thin edge highlights where two areas meet.
clean-crisp-painting.clean paint job: Opaque base coats, paint thinned about half and half, dark lines between parts, thin edge highlights, and tidied spills.
clean-crisp-painting.crisp looking model: Separate every part with an even dark line and a sharp edge highlight, and keep the brightest highlight to corners and peaks.
clean-crisp-painting.painting looks sloppy: Use enough thin coats to remove patchiness, keep a dark line between parts, and tidy spills with the neighbouring colour.
clean-crisp-painting.getting clean lines between colours: Keep a dark line in the join and put a thin light edge where two areas meet so they do not merge.
clean-crisp-painting.tidy painting: At the end, tidy spills with the neighbouring colour and trim highlights that came out thick.
clean-crisp-painting.model lacks definition: Paint dark into the recesses, edge highlight every sharp edge, and add a thin light edge where two areas meet.
clean-crisp-painting.why don't my models look sharp: Usually stray paint and no definition. Keep dark lines between parts and thin, sharp edge highlights.

colour-scheme-from-reference.how do i pick a colour scheme: Pick artwork or a photo whose colours you like, pull out about five main colours, and paint the whole model from that palette.
colour-scheme-from-reference.colour scheme ideas: Lift palettes from a ship, a sunset, an animal, a historical uniform or a fashion photo, and keep a folder of ones you like.
colour-scheme-from-reference.palette from a photo: Use a colour picker on a digital copy to pull about five main colours, nudged towards pure tones, then find the closest paints.
colour-scheme-from-reference.inspiration for colours: Illustrations, film stills or photos of anything work. They often give less obvious palettes than other painted models.
colour-scheme-from-reference.choosing colours for my army: See: pull a small palette from artwork or a photo you like, and copy where its dominant colour and accents sit.
colour-scheme-from-reference.colour scheme from art: Pull about five main colours from the art, then copy its rules: the dominant colour and where the accents sit.
colour-scheme-from-reference.use a painting as reference: Keep it large and in view, hold the model beside it now and then, and glaze a strong colour over areas that look dull next to it.
colour-scheme-from-reference.i cant decide on colours: Start from one loud colour you rarely use, such as a hot pink, and build round it with one colour that suits it plus black and white.
colour-scheme-from-reference.colour palette from a film: Pick a film still you like, colour pick about five main colours, and match them to the closest paints you have.
colour-scheme-from-reference.scheme from one colour i like: Build around it with one colour that suits it, set against black and white, and give the focal area the strongest contrast.

comic-style-painting.comic book style: Paint flat colour blocks with two or three hard edged tones, no blending, then outline the main shapes in bold dark lines.
comic-style-painting.cel shading: Give each colour a shadow, mid tone and light with sharp edges between them and no blending, placed for strong contrast.
comic-style-painting.cartoon style: Think simple shapes, flat colour, a few hard edged tones and bold dark outlines, not smooth gradients.
comic-style-painting.make a model look like a drawing: Flat colour blocks, hard steps between light and shadow, and bold dark outlines, heavier round faces and weapon edges.
comic-style-painting.black outlines on a mini: Use black acrylic ink, which flows better than paint, in two passes: by eye, then under magnification for fine lines.
comic-style-painting.2d style painting: Paint each part flat, add two or three hard edged tones, outline in black ink, and add crisp edge highlights.
comic-style-painting.anime style miniature: See: the cel shaded approach applies: flat colours, hard edged tones, bold dark outlines and crisp highlights.
comic-style-painting.hard edged shading: Use only a shadow, a mid tone and a light per colour, with sharp edges between them and no blending.
comic-style-painting.comic style lines: Outline main shapes in dark ink, and add groups of three or four parallel diagonal lines on panels or glass for comic shine.
comic-style-painting.cel shaded figure: Flat base colours, two or three hard edged tones each, bold ink outlines, then crisp edge highlights in a lighter tone.

corroded-metal.corroded metal: Base mid steel, wash dark brown black then brown to dull it, dab rust orange and turquoise patches, then add broken bright edges.
corroded-metal.pitted rusty metal: Dab texture paste into sheltered spots before painting, then dab thinned rust orange on with the brush tip for mottled pitting.
corroded-metal.how do i paint corrosion: Dull a steel base with dark washes, then dab on paint thinned about four water to one paint: rust orange on steel, turquoise on copper.
corroded-metal.verdigris and rust: Put warm rust browns and oranges in some patches and cool greens in others, with plain metal between, built in shrinking layers.
corroded-metal.rotting metal for plague models: Texture the corroded areas, base mid steel, dull it with dark washes, then dab warm rust and cool green patches on.
corroded-metal.rust texture: Dab crackle or fine texture paste where corrosion should be and wipe it off raised parts so it stays in sheltered spots.
corroded-metal.green corrosion: Dab turquoise thinned about four water to one paint onto copper and brass, building a few shrinking layers.
corroded-metal.crackle paste for rust: Dab crackle or fine texture paste on the corroded areas before painting, and wipe it off the raised parts.
corroded-metal.heavily weathered armour: Dull the metal with dark brown washes, dab rust and green patches with the brush tip, and finish with broken bright edges.
corroded-metal.old decaying metal: Wash steel dark brown black then brown so it loses its sheen, dab on rust and green patches, and add rough bright dots on edges.

cutting-plastic-card.cutting plasticard: Use a fresh blade and a steel ruler on a cutting mat, and score lightly several times rather than one hard cut.
cutting-plastic-card.how to cut styrene sheet: Score it lightly along a steel ruler with a fresh blade in several passes until it goes through, or snap it along a deep score.
cutting-plastic-card.plastic card snapping: Score deeply along a steel ruler, then bend the card and it snaps cleanly along the line.
cutting-plastic-card.razor saw: A fine toothed razor saw cuts thick plastic cleanly. Line it up, start gently, then saw with light, even strokes.
cutting-plastic-card.score and snap: Score along a steel ruler with a fresh blade in light passes, bend, and snap along the score.
cutting-plastic-card.thick plastic cutting: Use a fine toothed razor saw, not clippers, which crush thick scenery plastic. Saw with light, even strokes.
cutting-plastic-card.straight cuts in plastic sheet: Hold a steel ruler on a pencilled line and score lightly several times with a fresh blade. A knife bites into plastic rulers.
cutting-plastic-card.blade slipped cut myself: Fit a fresh blade. A blunt one needs more force, and that is when it slips. Score in light passes, never one hard cut.
cutting-plastic-card.cutting mat and steel ruler: Work on a cutting mat and hold a steel ruler on the line, as a knife bites into plastic rulers.
cutting-plastic-card.plasticard cutting tips: Fresh blade, steel ruler, light repeated scores, cut round parts long and file flush, and use a razor saw for thick plastic.

dirty-cloth-hems.dirty hems: Glaze a thin khaki brown up from the hem several times, strongest at the bottom and fading higher, then a pale sand right at the edge.
dirty-cloth-hems.muddy robes: Glaze khaki brown up from the hem, push darker dirt to the very bottom, and flick thinned dark brown for splashes landing mostly low.
dirty-cloth-hems.dusty bottom of a cloak: Drybrush or stipple a sandy brown that matches the base lightly round the hem, fading up, then a thin pale sand at the very bottom.
dirty-cloth-hems.make a cloak look used and worn: Build grime up from the hem in thin glazes, heaviest at the bottom, and add a few small light nicks near the hem.
dirty-cloth-hems.mud splashes on cloak: Flick thinned dark brown at the hem so most spots land low and fewer reach higher.
dirty-cloth-hems.weathered cloth: Glaze khaki brown up from the hem in thin passes, vary it patch to patch, and finish with pale sand dust at the very bottom.
dirty-cloth-hems.dirty robe edges: Push thinned black or dark brown down so it gathers at the edge. A dragging hem can go almost black.
dirty-cloth-hems.travel worn clothing: Grime the hem with khaki brown glazes fading upwards, add pale dust at the bottom, and a few small nicks.
dirty-cloth-hems.grime fading up a robe: Glaze thin khaki brown up from the hem several times, pulling each stroke down to the hem, strongest low and fading higher.
dirty-cloth-hems.how to weather cloth: Build a soft damp stain higher up and darker dirt lower down with thin glazes, then pale dust at the very bottom.

drybrushed-carapace.drybrushing a shell: Press a half black mix straight down onto each plate, scrub a mid tone on in circles, dust a lighter tone, then flick pale on points.
drybrushed-carapace.carapace painting fast: A dark base that doubles as shade, then three drybrushes, each lighter in tone and touch, and gloss for an insect sheen.
drybrushed-carapace.bug armour drybrush: Mix the shell colour half and half with black as base and shade, then drybrush a mid, a lighter and a very pale tone on points.
drybrushed-carapace.insect shell: Drybrush up from a very dark mix in three lighter steps, then gloss varnish the shell for an insect like sheen.
drybrushed-carapace.how do i paint chitin quickly: Drybrush a half black mix as base and shade in one, then mid tone, lighter tone and a very pale flick on spines.
drybrushed-carapace.alien carapace: Dark mix of shell colour and black drybrushed on, then three drybrushes getting lighter, with pale only on points and blades.
drybrushed-carapace.beetle shell: Drybrush up from a very dark base in three steps, then a gloss varnish for an insect like sheen.
drybrushed-carapace.skip the wash with a dark base: Mix the shell colour about half and half with black. It replaces both base coat and wash.
drybrushed-carapace.quick crab shell: Dark drybrushed base of shell colour and black, a mid tone in circles, a lighter dust on edges, and pale on spikes.
drybrushed-carapace.armoured plates on monsters drybrush: Press the dark mix down so undersides stay black, then drybrush mid, lighter and very pale tones, each with a lighter touch.

dust-on-legs.dusty boots: Stipple the darker base colour onto the feet with a near dry brush, fading out by mid shin, then lightly drybrush the paler base colour.
dust-on-legs.muddy feet: Stipple light crusty mud higher up, dark glossy wet mud low down, and dab a thinned mid mud where they meet.
dust-on-legs.dirt on legs: Use the base's own colours: stipple the darker one on the feet fading up the shin, then drybrush the paler one over it.
dust-on-legs.model looks like it walked through mud: Glaze thinned khaki brown down over feet and lower legs, repeat until dirty enough, then add darker brown at the very bottom.
dust-on-legs.match feet to base: Finish the base first, then stipple and drybrush the same base colours onto the feet and lower legs.
dust-on-legs.weathering boots: Stipple the darker base colour on, drybrush the paler one over it, and keep it desaturated, as real dust is chalky and dull.
dust-on-legs.dirty hem of robe: See: this entry covers feet and legs. Stipple base colours low and fade them up, the same way you would a hem.
dust-on-legs.mud splatter on legs: See: stipple crusty light mud high and dark glossy mud low, with a thinned mid mud dabbed between them.
dust-on-legs.pigment dust on feet: See: this entry uses stippled base paints, or enamel or oil dirt blended with white spirit, rather than pigment.
dust-on-legs.dusty trousers: Stipple the darker base colour on the lower legs, fading out around mid shin, then drybrush the paler one lightly over it.

essential-first-colours.first paints to get: Black, white, a warm red, mid blue, golden yellow, two browns, pale bone, mid green, mid grey, skin, silver, gold and two washes.
essential-first-colours.starter colours: About fifteen: black, white, three primaries, mid and dark brown, bone, green, grey, a skin tone, silver, gold, brown and black washes.
essential-first-colours.which colours do i need to start: Black, white, red, blue and yellow, earth browns and bone, green, grey, skin, silver and gold, plus a brown and black wash.
essential-first-colours.basic paint set: Around fifteen colours cover a first army, including black, white, three primaries, earths, two metals and two washes.
essential-first-colours.how many paints do i need: About fifteen, plus the main colour of your scheme. Mix the rest from those.
essential-first-colours.beginner paints list: White, black, warm red, mid blue, golden yellow, mid and dark brown, bone, mid green, mid grey, warm skin, silver, gold, two washes.
essential-first-colours.essential paints for a first army: About fifteen colours, then your scheme's main colour with a darker and lighter step if you would rather not mix them.
essential-first-colours.must have colours: A strong white and soft black first, then three clean mixing primaries, earth browns, a silver, a gold and brown and black washes.
essential-first-colours.do i need lots of paints: No. About fifteen colours cover a first army, and a short set teaches you more about colour than a wall of pots.
essential-first-colours.starting palette for miniatures: Black, white, red, blue, yellow, two browns, bone, green, grey, a skin tone, silver, gold and a brown and black wash.

fast-white-armour.easy white armour: Prime white, paint the other parts loosely, tidy slips with matt white, then shade with one thin grey or light brown wash.
fast-white-armour.how do i paint white quickly: Use a matt white primer as your main colour, paint everything else, tidy with white, and finish with one grey or brown wash.
fast-white-armour.white primer as base colour: Yes. Prime with a matt white spray and it is your main colour already, then tidy slips later with matching matt white.
fast-white-armour.white over black takes forever: It does, so prime white instead. The primer becomes the main colour and you skip the many coats.
fast-white-armour.white armour with a grey wash: Glaze a thin grey wash towards the lower part of each panel and let it wick along the panel lines. Lift any pools on flat panels.
fast-white-armour.speed paint white troops: Prime white, paint the other parts loosely, tidy once with white, shade with one wash, and drybrush white on raised areas.
fast-white-armour.white is so hard to paint: Prime white so the primer does the work, then shade it with a thin grey or light brown wash on a soft brush.
fast-white-armour.white sci fi troopers: Prime white, paint joints and weapons, tidy with white, wash grey along the panel lines, and line them with darker brown or grey.
fast-white-armour.quick white army: White primer, other colours painted loosely, one tidy pass in matt white, then one thin grey or brown wash over everything.
fast-white-armour.white models patchy: Apply the wash with a soft brush to avoid blotches and lift any pools on flat panels. It looks dark wet but dries paler.

first-model-steps.first model: Prime grey, base coat the main colour, wash and drybrush it, then block in and wash the details and add a few highlights.
first-model-steps.how do i start painting: Pick a simple model, clean and glue it, prime grey, then base coat, wash, drybrush, and do the small details last.
first-model-steps.beginner painting steps: Prime, base coat in two thin coats, wash, drybrush back up, block in and wash the details, add a highlight, then varnish.
first-model-steps.never painted before: Start with a simple model: prime grey, base coat the main colour, wash it, drybrush it, then do the small details.
first-model-steps.what order to paint a mini: Main colour first, then wash and drybrush while messiness does not matter, then small details, highlights, the base, and varnish.
first-model-steps.first miniature tips: Aim for a base, a shade and one highlight per area, change rinse water after metallics, and stop once you like how it looks.
first-model-steps.simple painting method: Base coat, wash, drybrush the base colour back on with a lighter tone on edges, then block in and wash the details.
first-model-steps.newbie guide: Prime grey, base coat in thin coats, wash, drybrush, block in details, add one highlight per area, paint the base and varnish.
first-model-steps.i just got my first mini: Clip parts with flush cutters, scrape mould lines, glue it, add sand to the base, then prime grey from about 30 cm.
first-model-steps.step by step first paint job: Prime, base coat, wash for about 45 minutes, drybrush, block in and wash details, highlight, paint the base, then matt varnish.

fix-dry-paint-mistakes.fix mistakes: Let the slip dry fully, then paint the original colour back over it in thin coats, dabbing irregular patches across its edge.
fix-dry-paint-mistakes.paint on the wrong part: Once dry, paint the right colour back over it in thin coats. For a strong colour, stipple matching greys first to kill it.
fix-dry-paint-mistakes.paint slip on dry paint: Paint the original colour back over it in thin coats, dabbing irregular patches across the edge rather than tracing along it.
fix-dry-paint-mistakes.how do i fix a mistake: Let it dry, then cover it with the original colour in thin coats. Repairs show mainly because of a hard, straight edge, so break that up.
fix-dry-paint-mistakes.messed up my model: Let it dry, repaint the affected area in thin coats of matched colour, and turn any remaining trace into wear marks.
fix-dry-paint-mistakes.touch up mistakes: Match the colour, including any wash on it, test on a small spot, then dab thin irregular patches over the mistake.
fix-dry-paint-mistakes.ruined my blend: Mix tones matching the surface next to the mark and rebuild them in thin layers, dark to light, on a wet palette.
fix-dry-paint-mistakes.paint went over the line: Let it dry, then paint the neighbouring colour back over the slip in thin coats until it covers.
fix-dry-paint-mistakes.accidentally painted the face: Let it dry, stipple matching greys over a strong slip to kill the colour, then rebuild with the original colours thinly.
fix-dry-paint-mistakes.hide a mistake as weathering: Add dots, scratches, freckles or a few dark chips across the trace so it reads as wear, but keep chips sparse.

fix-rough-paint-texture.paint looks rough: Usually thick paint or brushing over paint that has started to dry. Thin it, spread it quickly, and leave tacky areas alone.
fix-rough-paint-texture.ridges in my paint: They come from thick paint or going back over tacky paint. Thin it, and once an area goes tacky, leave it until fully dry.
fix-rough-paint-texture.paint looks like jam: It is too thick. Thin it so it flows and covers in two or three passes, and use fresh paint, not paint thickening on the palette.
fix-rough-paint-texture.brush strokes showing: Thin the paint, spread it quickly without going back over it, and cover patchiness with another thin coat once dry.
fix-rough-paint-texture.paint drying lumpy: Lumps usually come from dust or dried flakes off a dirty brush, palette or water pot. Shave them off with a new blade.
fix-rough-paint-texture.ring marks in paint: They come from brushing over drying paint. Once it goes tacky, often within about 15 seconds, move on and return when dry.
fix-rough-paint-texture.paint too thick: Thin it so it flows and covers in two or three passes. Thick paint leaves ridges and buries detail.
fix-rough-paint-texture.lost detail with paint: Thick paint and heavy coats bury detail. Use thinned paint in two or three passes instead.
fix-rough-paint-texture.paint goes tacky and drags: Acrylic starts drying as soon as it leaves the brush. Once tacky, leave it and come back when fully dry.
fix-rough-paint-texture.bumpy paint finish: Shave bumps with a new hobby blade or sand dry ridges gently with very fine sandpaper, then repaint thinly with a clean brush.

fixing-a-leaning-model.model leans forward: Raise one foot on a rock, step or rubble so the body tilts back upright. Test the angle on the base before gluing.
fixing-a-leaning-model.mini leaning too much: Put one foot up on a rock or piece of rubble so the model stands upright, then blend it into the base.
fixing-a-leaning-model.fix a model that tips forward: Raise one foot on a rock or step so it tilts back. If pinned, bend or re drill the pin to correct the angle.
fixing-a-leaning-model.raise one foot on a rock: Yes. A rock, step or rubble under one foot tilts the body back upright. Blend it in with texture or putty and paint it as one.
fixing-a-leaning-model.model falls over: See: if it leans too far, raise one foot on a rock or rubble so the body sits upright over the base.
fixing-a-leaning-model.posing on base: Test the angle on the base before gluing, and raise one foot on a rock or step if the model leans too far forward.
fixing-a-leaning-model.angle on base: Dry test the angle first, raise one foot on a rock to tilt it upright, or bend or re drill the pin if it is pinned.
fixing-a-leaning-model.upright model: Raise one foot on a rock, step or rubble so the body tilts back upright, then blend the piece into the base.
fixing-a-leaning-model.rock under foot: Glue a rock or rubble under one foot to tilt a leaning model upright, then blend it in with texture or putty.
fixing-a-leaning-model.model looks like its falling: Raise one foot on a rock or step so the body tilts back upright. Test the angle before gluing anything.

freehand-lettering.freehand lettering: Plan the word on paper, paint the middle letter first, then the first and last, and fill in between as thin skeletons.
freehand-lettering.writing on a scroll: Paint the middle letter faintly at the centre, then the end letters, fill in thin skeletons, and thicken them afterwards.
freehand-lettering.text on a banner: Pick a word that fits, count the letters, and place the middle one first so you do not run out of space.
freehand-lettering.how to paint letters: Place every letter as a thin skeleton, then thicken them with slightly thicker paint, straight strokes first, then curves.
freehand-lettering.tiny writing: Paint straight, evenly spaced rows of short marks in thinned black and dark brown, breaking each row at irregular points.
freehand-lettering.paint words on a sign: Mask a clean box for the text rather than following the boards, then place the middle letter first and work outwards.
freehand-lettering.freehand text: Plan it on paper, centre the middle letter, place the ends, then fill in as thin skeletons before thickening.
freehand-lettering.sign painting: Mask a clean box on the planks, plan the word on paper, and use plain capitals placed from the middle outwards.
freehand-lettering.lettering looks wonky: Tidy thick or wobbly letters with the background colour, and keep to plain capitals rather than fussy script.
freehand-lettering.fake writing on scrolls: Use rows of short broken marks in thinned black and dark brown, plus a red first capital, then glaze pale cream over the folds.

glaze-stroke-direction.glazing direction: Start each stroke where colour should be faintest and lift off where it should be strongest, as pigment gathers where the brush lifts.
glaze-stroke-direction.which way to glaze: For shading, pull from inside the panel towards the recess and lift off there. For highlights, pull towards the centre of the lit area.
glaze-stroke-direction.glaze leaves a hard edge: Feather a visible glaze edge out with a damp brush while wet, and start each coat a little further from the edge so the steps stagger.
glaze-stroke-direction.how do i glaze: Thin it until it pools on the palette, soak most off the brush, start where you want least colour and lift off where you want most.
glaze-stroke-direction.pigment pools at end of stroke: That is expected: most pigment is left where the brush lifts. So finish strokes where you want the strongest colour.
glaze-stroke-direction.brush stroke direction for shading: Start a little way into the panel and pull towards the bottom edge, recess or underside, lifting off there.
glaze-stroke-direction.glazes look blotchy: Put less on to begin with, soak blobs up with a clean brush tip, and smooth by glazing the midtone the opposite way over the middle.
glaze-stroke-direction.where to start a glaze: Start where you want the least colour, and finish where you want the most.
glaze-stroke-direction.glazing tips: Thin until it pools, unload on tissue, hold the brush low, pull towards you, turn the model, and repeat coats until the gradient appears.
glaze-stroke-direction.lift off with glaze: Lift the brush off where you want the most colour, since that is where most pigment is left.

glowing-eye-lenses.eye lenses: Over black, paint dark to light towards the front and bottom of the lens, keep a thin dark outline, and add one tiny white dot top corner.
glowing-eye-lenses.how to paint lenses: Paint each lighter colour over a smaller area towards the front, then a single tiny white dot in the dark upper corner as a reflection.
glowing-eye-lenses.glowing eyes on a helmet: Build from a deep red through bright red, orange and yellow to a pale yellow dot, then glaze a little glow onto the helmet below.
glowing-eye-lenses.visor lenses: Paint them dark at the back to bright at the front with a thin dark outline and one tiny white reflection dot.
glowing-eye-lenses.eye lens gem style: Start over black, leave black in the back corner, paint smaller lighter areas towards the front, and add one tiny white dot.
glowing-eye-lenses.red eyes glowing: Deep red base, then bright red, orange red, orange and yellow, with a pale yellow dot in the middle and a soft red glaze round it.
glowing-eye-lenses.helmet eyes: Paint the lenses before the helmet, dark at the back to bright at the front, add a white dot, and check from the normal viewing angle.
glowing-eye-lenses.lens with white dot: Put one tiny white or pale grey dot in the dark upper corner. It does most of the work of looking like glass; keep it tiny.
glowing-eye-lenses.green glowing lenses: Paint them white, cover with a strong see through or fluorescent green, brighten the inner corner, and add the white dot.
glowing-eye-lenses.glow around eye lenses: Glaze thin darker glow colours onto the helmet just below the eye, then tiny brighter touches right under the middle.

gluing-strong-joints.glue: Use plastic glue for plastic to plastic, super glue for metal, resin and mixed parts, a little on one face only, and let it fully cure.
gluing-strong-joints.strong joint: Dry fit, clean and roughen the faces, use a little glue on one face, hold it still, and let it fully cure before stressing it.
gluing-strong-joints.parts falling off: Clean off dust, oil and paint, score nicks across both faces, use a little glue, and wait for full cure before handling.
gluing-strong-joints.super glue: Use it for metal, resin and mixed materials, a small amount on one face only. Too much sets slowly and turns brittle.
gluing-strong-joints.plastic glue: Use it for plastic to plastic, as it welds the parts. A little on one face only, since too much melts detail.
gluing-strong-joints.glue not holding: Make the faces meet flush, clean them, scrape off paint, and score small nicks so the glue has something to grip.
gluing-strong-joints.gluing metal: Wash it in warm soapy water, score nicks across both faces, and use a little super glue. Smooth metal faces hold poorly otherwise.
gluing-strong-joints.gluing resin: Wash resin in warm soapy water, let it dry, score both faces with a knife, and use a small amount of super glue.
gluing-strong-joints.arm keeps snapping off: File it so the faces meet flush, scrape off paint, score both faces, glue, and do not pose or stress it until fully cured.
gluing-strong-joints.messy glue: Use a small amount on one face only, and wipe super glue ooze away before it sets. Thin plastic glue ooze can melt into the seam.

hairline-transition.where hair meets skin: Use the darkest skin shade on the face side and the darkest hair shade on the hair side, not a black line.
hairline-transition.hairline: Separate hair from skin with each area's own darkest tone, and keep the hairline dark even on fair hair.
hairline-transition.black line around face: A hard black line looks drawn on. Use the darkest skin shade and darkest hair shade side by side instead.
hairline-transition.how do i separate hair from skin: Run the darkest skin shade round the face and the darkest hair shade on the hair side, then glaze thin hair colour at the line.
