hairline-transition.hair looks painted on: Drop the black line and use the two areas' darkest tones. For bright hair, base neutral grey brown first so it does not look like a wig.
hairline-transition.framing the face: Keep the hairline dark, even on fair hair, so it frames the face, and save the strongest hair highlights for the top of the head.
hairline-transition.forehead and hair: Shade the forehead edge with the darkest skin tone and the hair edge with the darkest hair tone for a soft break.
hairline-transition.beard meets skin: See: the same rule as the hairline: darkest skin shade on the skin side, darkest hair shade on the hair side, no black line.
hairline-transition.lining hair: Do not line it black. Use the hair colour with a touch of black on the hair side and the darkest skin shade on the face side.
hairline-transition.hair edge on face: Glaze thin hair colour on the skin right at the hairline to soften the join between the two dark tones.

highlighting-metallics.highlight metal: Put bright silver only where light really catches, such as a helmet dome, rather than edge highlighting every plate.
highlighting-metallics.silver highlights: Turn the part under your lamp and stab bright silver just where the light catches. Keep the brightest to tiny dots.
highlighting-metallics.metal looks flat: Start dark and make a big jump to a bright silver highlight on the raised curves. Big jumps read shinier than close steps.
highlighting-metallics.how to make metal look shiny: Start from a dark mix of silver and black, then jump to bright silver only where the light catches.
highlighting-metallics.edge highlight metallics: Drag the side of the tip along the edge with thin, fine pigment metallic, and edge only a few plates and rivets.
highlighting-metallics.steel armour highlights: After the wash, dab gunmetal back on the raised curves, then stab bright silver at the top of each dome or shoulder.
highlighting-metallics.metallic highlight placement: Where light catches: the dome of a helmet, the top of a shoulder plate, the top of each chain link, a round spot on studs.
highlighting-metallics.cold steel: Mix silver with black, a deep blue or a green for a cold base, then add more silver in each step.
highlighting-metallics.make silver pop: Use a big jump from dark base to bright silver, keep the brightest silver to tiny dots, and do not edge every plate.
highlighting-metallics.chrome look: See: start very dark and make one big jump to bright silver where the light catches, as big jumps read shinier.

hobby-safety.is airbrushing safe: With precautions: spray outdoors or in a spray booth, and wear a sealed respirator, since paper masks do nothing against fumes.
hobby-safety.fumes: Work with good airflow and take breaks, keep solvent lids on, and wear a sealed respirator with an A2 vapour filter.
hobby-safety.respirator: Use one that seals to your face with a combined A2 vapour and top class particle filter. Resin needs B2 or higher as well.
hobby-safety.mask for spraying: A sealed respirator with combined filters, not a paper dust mask, which only stops particles and does nothing against fumes.
hobby-safety.is resin toxic: Uncured resin needs care: nitrile gloves, a filter also covering inorganic vapours (B2 or higher), and more than just ventilation.
hobby-safety.safety with thinners: Enamel thinners and white spirit are toxic to breathe, so keep lids on, and keep rubbing alcohol away from heat.
hobby-safety.should i lick my brush: No. A non toxic label covers normal use, not swallowing paint. Point the brush on the palette or a damp cloth instead.
hobby-safety.ventilation: Open a window or keep good airflow, and spray outdoors or in a booth that pulls mist out of the room.
hobby-safety.sanding resin dust: Wear a sealed respirator with a top class particle filter when sanding resin, with good airflow.
hobby-safety.spray paint indoors safe: Spray cans belong outdoors or in a spray booth that pulls the mist out of the room, with a respirator on.

is-an-airbrush-worth-it.do i need an airbrush: No. Everything it does can be done by brush, only slower. It pays off for fast base coats and priming when much of a model is one colour.
is-an-airbrush-worth-it.is an airbrush worth it: It is when roughly 40 percent or more of each model is one colour or smooth surface, such as armies, vehicles and big armoured models.
is-an-airbrush-worth-it.airbrush vs brush: A brush can do everything an airbrush does, only slower, but not the reverse. Faces, lining and edge highlights still need a brush.
is-an-airbrush-worth-it.should i get an airbrush: Get one if you paint armies, vehicles or large smooth models. Busy models with many small colour areas suit a brush.
is-an-airbrush-worth-it.can i paint without airbrush: Yes. Everything an airbrush does can be done by brush, only slower, and brush skills make the airbrush easier to learn later.
is-an-airbrush-worth-it.airbrush beginner worth it: You do not need one to paint well. If you get one, a budget airbrush and small compressor are enough, and practise pre shading.
is-an-airbrush-worth-it.what does an airbrush do: Fast, smooth base coats and priming in any colour, quick pre shading, smooth fades and glows, filters, masking and varnish.
is-an-airbrush-worth-it.airbrush necessary: Not necessary. It mainly speeds up base coats and priming, while fine detail, lining and highlights still need a brush.
is-an-airbrush-worth-it.benefits of an airbrush: Smooth base coats in any mixable colour, around two minutes versus five to ten by brush for white, plus easy fades and glows.
is-an-airbrush-worth-it.airbrush or rattle can: Spray cans come in only a few colours. An airbrush primes and base coats in any colour you can mix.

knowing-when-to-stop.when to stop painting: Stop when the next step risks spoiling what already works, and judge from arm's length whether more is worth it.
knowing-when-to-stop.overworking a model: If you are going round in circles correcting an area, it is done. Extra correction layers clog detail.
knowing-when-to-stop.is it finished: Look at it at arm's length, not in a zoomed photo. If the next step feels likely to go wrong, stop.
knowing-when-to-stop.table ready: A good base, a shading wash and re layered raised areas are already table ready for troops. Edge highlights are an extra.
knowing-when-to-stop.good enough: For tabletop, get the colours down with clear contrast and move on. For display, keep going to the top of your current skill.
knowing-when-to-stop.keep fiddling: If you keep correcting the same area, it is done. Note small flaws and do better on the next model.
knowing-when-to-stop.too many highlights: A clean base and one neat highlight often read better than several edges on every area.
knowing-when-to-stop.ruined it by adding more: More layers are not always better. Stop when the next step risks spoiling what works; you can always add more later.
knowing-when-to-stop.how much detail is enough: Judge from table distance, where many fine details vanish. Save slow extras for leaders and centrepieces.
knowing-when-to-stop.arms length quality: Yes, judge from arm's length, not a zoomed photo. Many fine details vanish at table distance, and units are seen together.

light-spots-on-armour.light bands: Glaze a thin stripe of each highlight colour down a curved plate, in different sizes with one dominant, all lit from one direction.
light-spots-on-armour.shiny armour: Glaze bands of light down curved plates and soft spots on round ones, then a few tiny pale dots on the sharpest corners.
light-spots-on-armour.glossy armour look: Add light bands down curves and spots on round parts, which suggest a shiny surface. Leave them off for matt armour.
light-spots-on-armour.curved plates look flat: Edge highlights alone leave them flat. Glaze a band of light down the curve to show its shape.
light-spots-on-armour.highlight curved armour: Glaze a thin stripe of each highlight colour down the curve, or block bands in thickly and wet blend the borders for a smoother look.
light-spots-on-armour.light spots: On round parts, place thin paint, draw it towards the centre and lift off so it gathers in the middle, then repeat once dry.
light-spots-on-armour.reflection on armour: Use light bands of different sizes with one dominant, darkest colour left between, and a few tiny pale dots in the spots.
light-spots-on-armour.dark armour shape: Glaze bands of light down curved plates and soft spots on round ones so dark armour shows its shape.
light-spots-on-armour.highlight shin: Glaze a thin stripe of each highlight colour down the shin and onto the foot.
light-spots-on-armour.spot highlight on helmet: Place thin paint, draw it towards the centre and lift off so it gathers there, repeat once dry, then add a tiny pale dot.

making-casualty-models.casualty markers: Pose spare bodies lying down with limp arms and the head turned to rest on the ground, built only for the view from above.
making-casualty-models.dead body models: Use spare bodies with bent knees, cut away anything that stops them lying flat, fit relaxed arms, and turn the head to one side.
making-casualty-models.fallen soldier: Pick a spare body with a bent knee, cut away parts that stop it lying flat, add loose arms, and turn the head against the ground.
making-casualty-models.how do i make a model lying down: Cut away arm parts or shoulders that stop it lying flat, even if it looks wrong from below. It is only seen from above.
making-casualty-models.corpse on a base: Pose a spare body lying down, fill gaps under it with super glue and accelerator or filler, and hide joins with sand or texture.
making-casualty-models.dead models for objective markers: Yes, casualties make good markers for objectives and wounded figures. Pose spare bodies lying down with limp arms.
making-casualty-models.wounded markers: Casualty models suit this: spare bodies posed lying with relaxed arms and the head turned to one side.
making-casualty-models.slain models: Cut the head off and reattach it turned to one side so it rests on the ground, and use relaxed, loose arms.
making-casualty-models.bodies on the battlefield: Pose spare bodies lying on their front or side, cut for the view from above, and blend gaps with sand or texture.
making-casualty-models.pose a dead model: Choose a body with a bent knee, cut away what stops it lying flat, try loose arms, and turn the head to rest on the ground.

metal-primer-speed-method.metallic primer: Prime in the armour metal, a mid silver or gold, so the metal is done in one step, then block in other colours and shade all at once.
metal-primer-speed-method.silver spray primer: A mid silver, neither too dark nor too bright. Block in the other parts, wash it all dark, then lightly drybrush bright silver.
metal-primer-speed-method.speed paint armour: Spray a metal primer, block in non metal parts, wash the whole model dark, then one light drybrush of bright silver.
metal-primer-speed-method.fast metal armour: Prime silver or gold, block in cloth and leather, shade everything with one dark wash or oil, then a light silver drybrush.
metal-primer-speed-method.knights in armour quickly: Prime mid silver, pick out trim in bronze, block in cloth and leather, wash dark grey or brown, then drybrush bright silver.
metal-primer-speed-method.prime silver then wash: Yes. Wash the whole model dark grey or brown, soaking up pools, then one very light drybrush of bright silver.
metal-primer-speed-method.armoured army fast: Prime in the armour metal, block in the rest, shade with one wash or a dark oil, and drybrush silver lightly.
metal-primer-speed-method.gold spray primer: Prime gold, add steel trim, then shade it. A purple wash gives gold a rich, warm depth.
metal-primer-speed-method.oil wash over metal: Gloss varnish first, then slap on near black oil thinned with odourless thinner, cure overnight, and clean the flats.
metal-primer-speed-method.quick chainmail army: See: prime silver, wash dark grey or brown over everything, then one very light drybrush of bright silver.

mixing-greys-and-browns.mix grey from colours: Mix opposite colours close to even and add white. A little more blue gives a cool grey, a little more orange a warm grey.
mixing-greys-and-browns.how to mix brown: Start with orange and add a little blue. More blue gives a cooler, darker brown, more red or yellow a warmer one.
mixing-greys-and-browns.complementary colours: Opposites on the wheel: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and purple. Mixed together they cancel into browns and greys.
mixing-greys-and-browns.opposite colours on the colour wheel: Each secondary sits opposite the primary it leaves out: green opposite red, orange opposite blue, purple opposite yellow.
mixing-greys-and-browns.shade without black: Add a little of the opposite colour, such as a drop of green in a red shadow. It stays rich instead of dirty.
mixing-greys-and-browns.how do i make a colour duller: Add a little of its opposite colour. It dulls more gently than black.
mixing-greys-and-browns.colour theory for painting: Red, yellow and blue make the secondaries, and mixing a colour with its opposite cancels it into browns and greys.
mixing-greys-and-browns.mix red and green: Red and green are opposites, so they cancel into a brown or grey depending on the balance.
mixing-greys-and-browns.desaturate a colour: Mix in a little of its opposite on the colour wheel, and test on the palette first, since real paints vary.
mixing-greys-and-browns.why is black shading so dull: Black dirties a colour. A little of the opposite colour shades and dulls more gently and keeps it rich.

mottled-textured-armour.mottled armour: Blob a thin dark wash on at random and let the tide marks dry, repeat in the shadows, then dab lighter tones on top higher up.
mottled-textured-armour.pitted organic armour: Base in thin coats, blob a very dark wash on at random so tide marks form, then dab thinned base and warmer mixes over the highlights.
mottled-textured-armour.tide marks texture: Blob thin wash on with the brush tip and let it dry with tide marks. They are the texture, so do not smooth them.
mottled-textured-armour.how do i make armour look textured: Blob thinned dark colour on at random, bigger and heavier low down, let tide marks dry, then dab lighter tones on top.
mottled-textured-armour.blotchy organic surface: Random blobs of thin dark wash left to dry with tide marks, then smaller, controlled dabs of lighter, warmer mixes higher up.
mottled-textured-armour.mottled skin: See: the same blob and dab method works: random dark wash blobs left to dry, then lighter dabs where you would highlight.
mottled-textured-armour.random wash blobs: Blob the dark wash on with the brush tip, heavier and bigger low down, smaller and fewer up top, and let them dry with tide marks.
mottled-textured-armour.alien armour texture: Base a cool blue green, wash very dark, blob more dark wash at random, then dab lighter, warmer mixes over the highlights.
mottled-textured-armour.pitted surface: Blob thinned dark wash at random and let the tide marks dry, then black in the lowest gaps and lighter dabs on top.
mottled-textured-armour.spotty texture: Blob thin washes on at random, keep the tide marks, and soften harsh dabs with a very thin glaze of the top colour.

muzzle-flash.muzzle flash: Paint rough, scratchy white rings round the barrel end, then glaze yellow and then orange over them, brightest in the centre.
muzzle-flash.gun firing effect: Paint rough concentric white circles round the barrel end and glaze yellow, then orange, with inks or thinned one coat paints.
muzzle-flash.firing glow: Glaze yellow and then orange over rough white rings round the barrel, keeping the centre brightest and fading outward.
muzzle-flash.barrel glow: Paint scratchy white rings around the barrel end, glaze yellow then orange over them, and let the colour fade outward.
muzzle-flash.shooting effect: Rough white rings at the barrel end glazed yellow then orange. On a clear flash part, satin varnish, wash orange, then glaze inks.
muzzle-flash.flamethrower glow: See: paint rough white rings at the nozzle, glaze yellow then orange over them, and keep the centre brightest.
muzzle-flash.how to paint a gun firing: Paint rough concentric white circles round the barrel end, glaze yellow then orange, brightest at the centre.
muzzle-flash.white rings on barrel: Paint them rough and scratchy round the barrel end, then glaze yellow and orange over them for a firing glow.
muzzle-flash.glow on gun end: Glaze yellow then orange inks over rough white rings round the barrel, fading outward from a bright centre.
muzzle-flash.osl from a gun: Paint rough white rings round the barrel end and glaze yellow, then orange, keeping the centre brightest and fading out.

oil-blending.oil blending: Dab dark, mid and light oils where shadow and light fall, then pull them together with a clean, completely dry brush.
oil-blending.blend with oil paints: Place all the dabs first, then fuzz over each border with a dry brush, wiping it on a lint free cloth after every stroke.
oil-blending.oils on minis: Base in acrylic, ideally satin or gloss, place oil tones where light and shadow fall, then blend with a dry brush.
oil-blending.smooth blend with oils: Use a large soft synthetic brush, completely dry, and pull from light into dark, wiping it after each stroke. Never rinse mid blend.
oil-blending.oil paint on skin: Dab light, mid and dark oils in place and blend with a dry brush. Use strong blues and magentas in tiny amounts, or a softer shadow.
oil-blending.oils on a cloak: Place light, mid and dark oils, then blend along the folds with a dry brush wiped after every stroke.
oil-blending.artist oils for miniatures: Mid grade artist oils are much easier to work than very cheap ones. Mix them on a plain, non absorbent palette.
oil-blending.how long do oils take to blend: Let an area set for 10 to 30 minutes until tacky before adding colour on top, and work elsewhere meanwhile.
oil-blending.oils over acrylic: Yes. Base in acrylic a little brighter than the mid tone. It only needs to be dry, and satin or gloss lets oils move more.
oil-blending.wet blending is too hard try oils: Oils stay workable: dab the tones in place, then blend them with a dry brush. Do not rush, or they go muddy.

organising-the-hobby-space.hobby desk setup: A strong light, painting handle, comfortable chair, a made up wet palette, clean water, and your most used paints within arm's reach.
organising-the-hobby-space.paint organisation: Use nail varnish wall racks for dropper bottles by colour and shallow spice racks for inks, in offset stepped rows.
organising-the-hobby-space.how do i organise my paints: Rack dropper bottles by colour, keep a small desk rack for the current project's paints, and dab colour on tube caps.
organising-the-hobby-space.hobby space: Set it up so you can be painting within a minute or two. A spot left set up beats packing away each time.
organising-the-hobby-space.painting station: Light, handle, chair, a few tools, a wet palette and clean water, with the paints you use most within arm's reach.
organising-the-hobby-space.paint rack: Wall racks meant for nail varnish hold dropper bottles neatly. Measure first: about 28 mm slots for droppers, 36 mm for wide pots.
organising-the-hobby-space.small painting area: A desk corner or a portable box works if a room is not possible. Keep only the tools you really use out.
organising-the-hobby-space.desk setup for painting: Keep the desk clear with a strong light, a few tools, wet palette and water. Never stack bottles, as they tip and spill.
organising-the-hobby-space.organizing hobby space: Most used paints in reach, bits sorted in labelled bead boxes, frames in magazine holders, and kits stood on their side.
organising-the-hobby-space.hobby room ideas: Separate gluing and sanding from painting, give unfinished models a shelf, finished ones a closed case, and use a whiteboard for projects.

overbrushing.overbrushing: Load a soft brush, wipe some paint off but leave it wetter than a drybrush, press the bristles flat and skim over the texture.
overbrushing.drybrush leaves chalky dust: Try overbrushing: a soft brush with more paint left in, pressed flat. It gives cleaner, stronger coverage than a dry, stiff brush.
overbrushing.makeup brush for drybrushing: A makeup brush or soft round leaves no streaks. Load it, wipe some off, and press it flat over the raised texture.
overbrushing.softer cleaner drybrush: Use a larger soft brush, slightly loaded, pressed flat and skimmed gently over the texture.
overbrushing.drybrush keeps flicking paint everywhere: Stiff drybrushes flick paint. Swap to a soft round or makeup brush, a little wetter, pressed flat.
overbrushing.stronger coverage on texture: Overbrush: a soft brush with paint neither watery nor thick, pressed flat and skimmed over sand, foliage or trim.
overbrushing.over brushing vs dry brushing: Overbrushing uses a soft, wetter brush pressed flat for cleaner, stronger coverage. A quick light drybrush on top finishes it.
overbrushing.drybrush too subtle: Overbrush instead, leaving more paint on a soft brush. Make each pass a clearly lighter colour than the one beneath.
overbrushing.wetter drybrush technique: Load a soft brush, wipe some off but leave it wetter than for drybrushing, press it flat and skim the raised texture.
overbrushing.how do i get a smoother drybrush on fur: Use a soft round or makeup brush, slightly loaded, pressed flat and skimmed gently over the fur texture.

paint-mediums.flow improver: It breaks surface tension so paint leaves the brush easily. Dilute about one to ten with water, then add less than a drop at a time.
paint-mediums.glaze medium: Binder and water with no pigment. It makes paint see through but even, so it suits glazes and is safe in fairly large amounts.
paint-mediums.mediums explained: Glaze medium thins paint without breaking it down; flow improver helps paint leave the brush. Use both sparingly.
paint-mediums.thinning paint: Water is fine to start. Glaze medium thins without breaking paint into blotches and gives the same result every time.
paint-mediums.thinners: Most named glaze and thinner products are mainly plain acrylic medium. A large art bottle costs far less.
paint-mediums.medium vs water: Water can break weak paint into blotches and rings; medium keeps it even but leaves a thin film. Try both.
paint-mediums.how much medium: Glaze medium is safe in fairly large amounts. Flow improver is strong: dilute it one to ten, then less than a drop at a time.
paint-mediums.paint mediums: Use glaze medium for glazes and blends, and a little flow improver for fine lines, but keep both out of first base coats.
paint-mediums.retarder: See: this entry covers glaze medium and flow improver, not drying retarder.
paint-mediums.should i use flow improver: A little helps fine lines, eyes, freehand and edge highlights. Too much stops paint setting, so it runs and stains.

painting-base-rims.base rim: Paint it last, after texture and drybrushing but before tufts, in a dark colour, with thinned paint and an angled stroke.
painting-base-rims.what colour base edge: Black is the safe choice and suits every scheme. Brown steps down to most boards, and grey suits ruins, concrete and ash.
painting-base-rims.black base rim: Black suits every scheme. A satin black levels more smoothly than matt and covers faster, in two or three thin coats.
painting-base-rims.how do i paint the edge of the base: Thin the paint to flow, stroke along the side at a slight angle so it stops cleanly at the top edge, and start and finish at the back.
painting-base-rims.base rims messy: Clean sand off the edge first, use two or three thin coats instead of one, and hold the model on a holder so fingers stay off.
painting-base-rims.base edge colour: Black suits everything, brown gives a natural step to most boards, grey suits ruins, or use a darker version of the ground.
painting-base-rims.brown base rim: Brown gives a natural step down to most gaming boards. Pick one rim style for the whole army and keep to it.
painting-base-rims.painting rim of base: Use thinned paint, an angled stroke or the brush held bristles up from underneath, and two or three thin coats.
painting-base-rims.clean base edge: Clean texture off the edge first, then stroke at a slight angle so colour stops at the top. On black primer, alcohol wipes it back.
painting-base-rims.rim before tufts: Yes. Paint the rim after drybrushing but before grass or tufts, which stick in wet paint.

painting-chips-and-scratches.chipping: Dab a small dark chip on edges and corners, then paint a fine line of the armour highlight along its lower edge. Keep them small.
painting-chips-and-scratches.paint chips on armour: Dab a dark colour on edges, corners and exposed parts, with a light line under each chip so it reads as a dented lip.
painting-chips-and-scratches.scratches on a vehicle: Keep them small and tight on edges and where knocks land. Long harsh scratches make a big object look small.
painting-chips-and-scratches.how to paint battle damage: Sponge or brush small dark chips onto edges and exposed parts, add a light line under each, and put silver in larger ones.
painting-chips-and-scratches.chipped edges: Dot along edges with a slight wobble and join a few speckles into bigger ragged chips, like little islands on a map.
painting-chips-and-scratches.sponge chipping looks like dots: Dab most paint off the torn foam first, or switch to a fine brush and join speckles into bigger ragged chips.
painting-chips-and-scratches.worn paint on edges: Tap and scuff a broken edge along the panels instead of a clean line, adding silver into some chips.
painting-chips-and-scratches.chips look like random blobs: Give them ragged outlines and a fine light line along the lower edge, and keep them to edges and exposed parts.
painting-chips-and-scratches.too many chips: Stop early, since adding more is easy. Keep chips small, random and mostly on edges, with only a few on flats.
painting-chips-and-scratches.scratched and worn tank: Sponge dark chips on panel edges, hatches and corners, add a highlight line under each, and dot silver in the larger ones.

painting-faces.face: Base a warm mid skin, wash warm chestnut brown, then layer thin skin on the raised areas and highlight nose, brow and cheekbones.
painting-faces.how to paint faces: Warm skin base, warm brown wash as a shadow map, thin layers on raised areas, then paler highlights on brow, nose and cheekbones.
painting-faces.face painting: Base warm skin thinly, wash warm chestnut, layer up from recess to high point, highlight, then glaze for depth.
painting-faces.human face: Warm mid skin base, chestnut wash, thin mid skin layers on raised areas, paler highlights, then thin blue and red brown glazes.
painting-faces.face wash: Use a warm chestnut brown. A cold brown makes skin look dead. The wash shows where the shadows go.
painting-faces.face highlights: Nose tip, brow, cheekbones, top lip and jaw, plus the folds from nose to mouth, with the upper face lighter than the lower.
painting-faces.face looks bad: Usually too much paint on the brush or fiddling. Stop once it looks right, and frame it by blacking out the hood or helmet.
painting-faces.skin on the face: Thin coats of warm mid skin, stroked along features, a warm chestnut wash, then thin layers from recess up to each high point.
painting-faces.face looks dead and grey: Use a warm chestnut wash, not a cold brown, and glaze a thin deep red brown on the cheeks and lower lip for warmth.
painting-faces.where to highlight a face: Nose tip, brow, cheekbones, top lip, jaw and the folds from nose to mouth, as light comes from above.
painting-faces.How do I paint skin and faces?: Base warm skin, wash warm chestnut, layer the raised areas thinly, highlight the high points, and glaze for depth and warmth.

painting-hair.hair: Highlight hair in a band round the crown and the side facing the light, and build texture with many thin, varied strands.
painting-hair.how do i paint hair: Block tones into zones, then paint thin lines along the flow from light to dark, each step covering less with varied lengths.
painting-hair.blonde hair: Avoid lemon or sun yellows. Build from sepia, rusty brown and ochre, then jump to ivory or a pale cream.
painting-hair.brown hair: See: block each tone into its zone, highlight round the crown in thin, varied strands, and mix a few greys into brown beards.
painting-hair.hair highlights: Picture a ring of light on the head: highlight round the crown and the lit side, and let it fall away fast as hair turns under.
painting-hair.hair looks like helmet: Highlight only where a ring of light would touch, vary strand lengths so bands never end straight, and keep bright bands narrow.
painting-hair.long hair: Block tones in by zone, then paint thin strands following the flow, light into dark, with varied lengths.
painting-hair.hair strands: Use sharp, thin lines that follow the flow, two or three passes per colour, each lighter step covering less.
painting-hair.ponytail: See: highlight where the ring of light catches and let it fall away as the hair turns down, with thin strands following the flow.
painting-hair.shiny hair: Hair has a sheen, so concentrate the highlights in a narrow band round the crown and let them fall away fast.

painting-leaves.painting leaves: Base mid green, wash darker, dab a darker colour in each leaf, outline pale then bright yellow green, and line between leaves dark.
painting-leaves.foliage colours: A mid green base, a darker wash, a bright yellow green over a pale outline, and deep purple or very dark green lines between leaves.
painting-leaves.tree leaves: Base, wash dark, hash a darker colour into each leaf's middle, edge in bright yellow green over pale, and vary each leaf a little.
painting-leaves.plants on a base: Base mid green, wash darker, edge each leaf bright yellow green over a pale underlayer, and line between overlaps very dark.
painting-leaves.autumn leaves: Base the leaves warm brown or orange instead of green, then wash darker and work up the same way.
painting-leaves.jungle foliage: See: base mid green, wash darker, add bright yellow green edges over pale, and separate leaves with very dark lines.
painting-leaves.leaves look like one blob: Paint thin deep purple or very dark green lines between overlapping leaves and in the recesses to separate them.
painting-leaves.hedge and bushes: Mid green base, darker wash, rough darker dabs in each leaf, bright yellow green edges, and dark lines between leaves.
painting-leaves.ivy on a wall: See: base mid green, wash darker, edge each leaf bright yellow green over pale, and line dark between overlaps.
painting-leaves.how do i paint sculpted leaves: Base, wash, dab darker into each leaf, outline pale then bright yellow green, and line between leaves with a deep purple.

painting-red.how to paint red: Build it in thin coats, shade with burgundy or dark green instead of black, highlight in small steps, and finish with a red glaze.
painting-red.red covers badly: It does. Thin it and build two or three thin coats, letting each dry, ideally over a white or pale undercoat.
painting-red.red looks patchy: Use two or three thin coats, letting each dry, over a pale undercoat. It looks much brighter over white than grey or black.
painting-red.red armour: Thin coats over a pale undercoat, burgundy shadows, small highlight steps up to orange red edges, then a deep red glaze over all.
painting-red.red cloak: Shade with a deep red wash cut with medium, highlight in small steps, top with pale peach, then glaze deep red over everything.
painting-red.shading red without black: Mix very dark green, blue green or deep purple into the red for a rich burgundy shadow, or use a violet wash.
painting-red.red shadows look brown: Black and brown washes make red muddy. Shade with a deep red wash or mix dark green or purple into the red.
painting-red.red highlights turn pink: Too much white causes it. Use pale peach, mid skin or bone for top highlights, then glaze deep red over the area.
painting-red.bright red over black primer: Red looks much brighter over a white or pale undercoat than over grey or black, so build thin coats over a pale base.
painting-red.what to shade red with: A very dark green, blue green or deep purple mixed into the red, or a deep red wash cut with medium. Save black for the deepest gaps.

painting-shields.shields: Paint them off the model, layer lighter rings towards the rim, and outline metal rims and bosses in watery black before painting them.
painting-shields.how do i paint a shield: Stick it to a pot lid, prime black, paint the main face colour, layer lighter rings towards the rim, then do rim, boss and back.
painting-shields.metal rim and boss on a shield: Run a fine line of watery black along every metal part first, then paint inside it: silver for iron, gold and brown for bronze.
painting-shields.should i paint shields off the model: Yes, where you can. Stick each to a pot lid or cork with tack putty, paint it, then glue it on at the end.
painting-shields.round wooden shield: Layer highlights in rings, each lighter ring nearer the rim, and paint the back brown with wood grain.
painting-shields.shield face looks flat: Layer highlights in rings that get lighter towards the rim, and add small light touches where two colours meet.
painting-shields.red shield over black primer is patchy: Put a red brown under the red first. Over black, a bright colour goes on far faster over a darker related base.
painting-shields.painting a whole unit of shields: Stick them all to pot lids or corks, prime black, and paint them off the models, leaving the backs for last.
painting-shields.shield with a metal edge: Outline the rim in watery black, paint inside it, then darken the recesses with thin black lines for iron.
painting-shields.holding shields while painting: Stick each shield to a pot lid or cork with tack putty, so you can reach the face and paint the back last.

painting-tattoos.tattoos: Mix a mid blue with a little black and some skin colour, paint the core of each shape small, then glaze thin skin over it.
painting-tattoos.how to paint tattoos: Finish the skin, paint a thinned blue, black and skin mix starting small and building out, then glaze a thin skin mix over it.
painting-tattoos.tattoo ink colour: A mid blue with a little black and some of the skin colour. Blue gives the faded look of real ink.
painting-tattoos.tattoo looks painted on top of skin: Mix some skin colour into the ink, and once dry glaze a thin skin mix over it so it sits in the skin.
painting-tattoos.tribal tattoos on arms: Keep to simple bands, dots or zigzags, run them right up to a sleeve or strap edge, and glaze skin over them.
painting-tattoos.faded blue tattoo: Use mid blue with a little black and skin colour, then glaze over it. A stronger glaze makes it look older.
painting-tattoos.tattoo on a shaved head: Pick the smooth side of the head, paint a simple design in the blue, black and skin mix, then glaze skin over it.
painting-tattoos.make a tattoo sit under the skin: Mix skin colour into the ink, let it dry or varnish it, then glaze a thin skin mix over it, with highlights faded over the top.
painting-tattoos.chest tattoo design: Keep it simple: bands, dots, zigzags or a simple symbol read well at this scale. Paint the core small and build it out.
painting-tattoos.what colour mix for tattoos: Mid blue, a little black and some of the skin colour, thinned with a drop of flow improver. Go darker or paler on dark or green skin.

painting-wood-grain.wood grain: Base dark brown, wash dark, paint broad loose lines in the base brown, then finer lighter wobbly lines, and edge pale grey brown.
painting-wood-grain.how to paint wood: Dark brown base and wash, broad loose grain lines, finer lighter ones inside them, then a pale grey brown edge highlight.
painting-wood-grain.wooden planks: Paint loose broad grain along each plank, then finer lighter lines, and filter a few planks reddish or greenish for variety.
painting-wood-grain.wooden shield: Base dark brown, wash black, add broad then finer lighter grain lines, and gather the brightest near the edges.
painting-wood-grain.spear shaft: Dark brown base and wash, loose lines along the length, finer lighter ones inside, and a pale grey brown edge with the brush side.
painting-wood-grain.axe handle: Grain it in broad then finer lighter lines, edge it pale grey brown, add small light chips for wear, and line black where it meets metal.
painting-wood-grain.wooden barrel: On smooth barrels, pull long, slightly wavy lines of inky dark brown along each plank, breaking some off.
painting-wood-grain.wood looks flat brown: Add grain: broad loose lines, then finer, lighter, wobbly lines inside them, brightest near edges and ends.
painting-wood-grain.wooden door: Paint broad loose grain along each plank, then finer lighter lines with the odd knot, and a pale edge. Do not highlight every line.
painting-wood-grain.freehand wood grain: Where none is sculpted, pull long, slightly wavy lines of inky dark brown along each plank, breaking some off.

photo-check-for-mistakes.take a photo to check my painting: Take a close photo in even light and zoom in on the phone. It shows missed spots and stray marks your eye skips.
photo-check-for-mistakes.spotting mistakes: Photograph the model close in even light and zoom in. Blobs, uneven lines and stuck fibres stand out at once.
photo-check-for-mistakes.phone camera shows every flaw: That is useful: your eye fills in gaps on a model you have stared at. Fix only what the photo shows, then decide whether to stop.
photo-check-for-mistakes.missed spots i can't see: Take a close phone photo and zoom in, especially on recesses and undersides. Gaps in base coat or drybrush show clearly.
photo-check-for-mistakes.looks fine in hand but bad in photos: Your eye fills in gaps the camera does not. Fix what the photo shows, but good enough on an army model usually is.
photo-check-for-mistakes.why do my photos show mistakes: Your eye fills in gaps on a model you have stared at for hours. A close, zoomed photo shows what is really there.
photo-check-for-mistakes.check painting with phone zoom: Photograph close in even light after fine detail like eyes or symbols, then zoom in to find blobs and uneven lines.
photo-check-for-mistakes.finding stray marks: A zoomed phone photo shows them. To hide a stray brush line, stipple either side of it rather than brushing over again.
photo-check-for-mistakes.fibres stuck in the paint: A close, zoomed phone photo makes stuck fibres stand out at once, so you can fix them before moving on.
photo-check-for-mistakes.eyes look wonky in photos: Photograph after painting eyes and zoom in. Fix only what the photo shows, as repainting a tiny area again fills in detail.

planning-large-models.big model: Write out the stages, build in sub assemblies, paint the biggest areas first, and do each shared colour on every part at once.
planning-large-models.large model project: Plan the stages in writing, including the base, leave riders and plates off, and finish the base before final assembly.
planning-large-models.how do i plan a big kit: Write the stages in order, pick the build option before cutting, note the methods for each stage, and check you have enough paint.
planning-large-models.subassemblies: Leave riders, crew, cloaks and large plates off the main body so every surface is reachable, and prime each in its closest colour.
planning-large-models.huge model feels overwhelming: Paint the biggest areas through to highlights first. Once done, the model is more than half finished, which keeps you going.
planning-large-models.where to start on a giant monster: Write out the stages, then paint the biggest areas first, through to highlights, before the figures and small details.
planning-large-models.planning stages for a centrepiece: Clean and build, sub assemblies, paint each part, the base, then final assembly, with the methods noted under each stage.
planning-large-models.paint big model in parts: Leave riders, cloaks and large plates off, paint them separately, then join the painted parts with super glue.
planning-large-models.paint all the same colour at once: Yes. Do each shared colour, such as a glow or a metal, on all parts in one sitting so they match.
planning-large-models.big dragon project: Prime the wings and body in colours near their finish, paint the largest areas first, and finish the base before final assembly.

preparing-3d-prints.3d print cleanup: Clip supports, slice the nubs flush, smooth with a fine file, clean off all residue, then prime in two or three thin coats.
preparing-3d-prints.remove supports: Clip them off with flush cutters, slice the leftover nubs level with a sharp craft knife, and smooth with a fine emery board.
preparing-3d-prints.support marks on prints: Slice nubs level with a sharp knife, cutting away from yourself, then smooth the spots with a fine sanding stick.
preparing-3d-prints.how to prep a resin print: Wash in isopropyl alcohol, cure fully under UV, trim and sand supports, wipe off residue, then prime in thin coats.
preparing-3d-prints.wash and cure resin: Wash in isopropyl alcohol, or water for water washable resin, then cure fully under UV as the resin's instructions say.
preparing-3d-prints.prime a 3d print: Clean off all residue first, then prime in two or three thin coats. Thick filler primer buries fine detail on small figures.
preparing-3d-prints.resin print sticky: See: wash it in isopropyl alcohol and cure it fully under UV as the resin's instructions say, wearing gloves until cured.
preparing-3d-prints.3d printed mini prep: Wash and cure, trim and sand the support nubs, wipe off every trace of residue, and prime in thin coats.
preparing-3d-prints.file off support nubs: Slice them level with a sharp craft knife first, then smooth with a fine emery board or sanding stick.
preparing-3d-prints.print came out the wrong size: Check the figure's own height in the slicer against your target scale. It is easy to scale by the wrong axis.

quick-faces.quick faces: Base a midtone skin, wash the whole face, layer the midtone back on brow, nose, cheeks and chin, and keep the eye sockets dark.
quick-faces.easy faces: Midtone skin, an all over wash, the midtone back on the raised parts, one lighter step with ivory, and simple dark eyes.
quick-faces.how do i paint faces fast: Set a few colours out first, base, wash, layer back the raised parts, and use a hair dryer between layers.
quick-faces.tabletop faces: Midtone base, all over wash, midtone on brow, nose, cheeks and chin, one pale step, and solid dark eye sockets.
quick-faces.simple face for a small model: Keep it to a few colours: midtone, a wash, the midtone back on raised parts, and one lighter step with pale ivory added.
quick-faces.faces for a whole squad: One coat of a one coat skin paint over a light primer, then a light drybrush of a matching skin tone, is enough.
quick-faces.face wash pooling: Lift any wash that pools on flat areas with a clean, damp brush.
quick-faces.faces look messy: Use fewer tones, since too many on a tiny face look messy, and leave the darker base as thin lines around the features.
quick-faces.easy eyes on tiny faces: Keep the sockets dark. Solid dark eyes look fine on most tabletop heads, or paint near white with a dark rim and pupil.
quick-faces.face in five minutes: See: midtone, an all over wash, the midtone back on raised parts and dark eyes is the fastest route this entry gives.

recording-your-recipes.write down my painting recipe: List each step in order: area, colour, paint, how thin, and technique, plus mix ratios and the primer colour.
recording-your-recipes.remember what paints i used: Write the recipe down once a scheme works, with a photo of the test model, the pots and the mix ratios.
recording-your-recipes.forgot which colours i used: Next time, record each step with the area, paint, thinning and technique, and keep it with a photo of the finished test model.
recording-your-recipes.painting notes: Note what changes the result, not every stroke: paints, mix ratios, primer, which wash went where, and the order of steps.
recording-your-recipes.repeat a scheme across an army: Follow your written recipe on every later model so the whole army matches, and update it when you find a better step.
recording-your-recipes.keep track of mixes and steps: Record mix ratios as well as pots, and the order of steps, in one place with a photo of the finished test model.
recording-your-recipes.painting log: A searchable notes app, a photo of pots in order, or a notebook with a dab of each colour all work. Date each entry.
recording-your-recipes.how to record a scheme: Write the steps in order with area, colour, paint, thinning and technique, and note what went wrong.
recording-your-recipes.recipe card for my army: List the primer, each area's paints and mixes, which wash goes where, and the step order, with a photo of the test model.
recording-your-recipes.pick up where i left off: With the recipe in front of you there is nothing to decide: do one step across a batch in twenty minutes and put it away.

resin-or-filament-printing.resin or filament: Resin for figures, as it prints the fine detail they need. Filament for terrain, or if you have nowhere to vent fumes.
resin-or-filament-printing.which 3d printer: Pick resin for figures and filament for terrain. Many hobbyists end up with one of each.
resin-or-filament-printing.resin printer for minis: Resin gives the fine detail minis need, but it needs a well aired room, gloves, eye protection, a wash bath and curing.
resin-or-filament-printing.fdm printer terrain: Filament suits buildings, scenery, bases and trays: large prints are cheap, the plastic is tough, and printers build larger.
resin-or-filament-printing.filament printer miniatures: Layer lines show on small figures and fine detail goes soft, so filament suits terrain better than figures.
resin-or-filament-printing.should i get a resin printer: If you print figures and have a well aired spare room, garage or shed to work in, yes. Otherwise filament is easier.
resin-or-filament-printing.is resin printing messy: Yes. It needs gloves, eye protection, a wash bath, curing and careful waste handling, and the fumes need extraction.
resin-or-filament-printing.best printer for terrain: Filament: it builds larger, prints are cheap, the plastic is tough, and it suits hills and buildings.
resin-or-filament-printing.3d printer for beginners: Choose by use: resin for figures, filament for terrain. Either way, expect a few weekends to get prints right.
resin-or-filament-printing.layer lines on minis: Resin layer lines are almost invisible at this scale, while filament layer lines show on small figures.

scale-mail.scale mail: Base metal, wash so the gaps go dark, layer metal on each scale's middle, flick a bright line along the lower edges, and dot the top.
scale-mail.how do i paint scale mail: Wash the gaps dark, light the whole panel as if flat, then shape the scales within it, finishing with a tiny dot on each.
scale-mail.scale armour: Keep the gaps dark through every step, flick a bright line along each scale's lower edge, and dot its top centre.
scale-mail.armour scales look flat: Do not highlight every scale the same. Light the panel as one broad area first, with the brightest on a few central scales.
scale-mail.lamellar armour: See: for rows of metal scales, keep the gaps dark, flick bright lines along lower edges, and light the panel as a whole.
scale-mail.fish scale armour: Dark gaps, the base metal back on each scale's middle, a thin bright line along the lower edges, and a tiny top dot.
scale-mail.metal scales shiny: Keep the gaps dark. Dark right beside bright is what makes the scales look shiny.
scale-mail.overlapping armour scales: Turn the model and paint downwards along each row's lower edge, flicking a thin bright line in one short stroke per scale.
scale-mail.dot on each scale: Put a tiny dot of the brightest tone at the top centre of each scale, toned down with base colour in the shadow areas.
scale-mail.wash between metal scales: Wash the base metal so the gaps go dark, and keep those gaps dark through every later step.

sculpting-over-damage.hide a gap: If it is too awkward to sand flat, cover it with a sculpted scarf, cloak edge, fur collar or belt so it looks deliberate.
sculpting-over-damage.gap too big to fill: Fill the deepest part with putty and let it cure, then lay a thin sheet of fresh putty over the join and shape it into cloth or fur.
sculpting-over-damage.sculpt a scarf over a join: Drape a thin flattened strip of putty over the join, press folds in the way gravity pulls, and thin the edge with a wet blade.
sculpting-over-damage.cover a break with fur: Lay a thin putty layer and drag a pointed tool in short strokes one way, overlapping like roof tiles, with varied lengths.
sculpting-over-damage.neck gap: Cover an angled neck join with a sculpted scarf or fur collar, filling the deepest part with putty first.
sculpting-over-damage.waist join gap: Hide it under a sculpted belt, cloak edge or cloth, after filling the deepest part of the gap and letting it cure.
sculpting-over-damage.rebuild broken part: Rebuild it around a small wire pin: bulk out the shape, let it cure, then add the fine shape in a second thin layer.
sculpting-over-damage.wire core for sculpting: Use a small wire pin as the core for a missing nose, hand guard or horn tip, bulking the shape out in two layers.
sculpting-over-damage.hide a bad join: Cover it with a sculpted scarf, cloak edge, fur or belt that matches the nearby sculpt, so it looks deliberate.
sculpting-over-damage.cant sand this gap flat: Cover it instead: fill the deepest part, then sculpt a thin layer of cloth or fur over the join.

shading-without-washes.shading without a wash: Glaze a thinned darker colour into the recesses and folds in several thin coats, or start dark and build only up.
shading-without-washes.how to shade without washes: Thin a darker mix of the base, wick most off, and glaze it into the folds in several dry coats, then highlight.
shading-without-washes.hand shading with layers: Paint a darker layer into the recesses and glaze over its edge to blend it into the base colour.
shading-without-washes.glaze the shadows: Thin a darker colour, add a little matt medium to keep it in place, and glaze it into recesses in several thin coats.
shading-without-washes.washes leave tide marks on my cloak: Wide flat areas like cloaks do not hold a wash well. Glaze thinned darker paint into the folds instead.
shading-without-washes.wash pools on smooth areas: Smooth rounded shapes and wide flats dry in patches and rings. Shade them by glazing thinned darker paint by hand.
shading-without-washes.smooth shading on a cloak: Glaze a darker mix into the folds in several thin coats, or wet blend a darker mix and the base together in each crease.
shading-without-washes.darker paint in the folds: Paint a darker layer into the folds and glaze over its edge, or wet blend it with the base while both are wet.
shading-without-washes.shade by layering: Base dark and build the light up, leaving the dark in the recesses, or paint a darker layer and glaze its edge.
shading-without-washes.is a wash necessary: No. Washes suit speed painting and heavy texture. Hand shading with thinned paint gives cleaner colour and more control.

slime-and-goo.slime: Paint the drips pale bone first, then flow on an unthinned glossy translucent green slime effect paint thickly, and keep nearby areas matt.
slime-and-goo.goo: Apply a glossy slime effect paint unthinned and generously over a pale base, with a second coat on the fattest drips once dry.
slime-and-goo.how do i paint slime: Base the drips a light bone, then put on an unthinned glossy green slime effect paint thickly so it stays shiny.
slime-and-goo.ooze dripping: Build thick, unthinned slime effect paint on the drips over a pale base, adding a second coat at the lowest point of each.
slime-and-goo.dripping slime: For a hanging drip, fix a fine thread or wire and brush gloss varnish along it in thin dried layers, like dipping a candle.
slime-and-goo.snot: See: paint it pale, then flow on a glossy translucent slime effect paint unthinned, and keep the skin round it matt.
slime-and-goo.acid drips: See: paint the drips pale, then thick unthinned glossy slime paint, with a second coat on the fattest drips.
slime-and-goo.wet looking slime: Thickness and gloss sell the wet look. Apply slime paint generously, unthinned, and keep the surrounding areas matt.
slime-and-goo.glossy slime: Use a glossy, translucent green slime effect paint straight from the pot over a pale base, built up thick on the drips.
slime-and-goo.toxic sludge: For a pool, fill a hollow with white glue, paint it, add several gloss coats, and glaze thin green on nearby metal for a glow.

spend-time-where-it-shows.where to spend time on a model: On the head, hands, chest and weapons, plus the main colour. Keep low and hidden parts to one coat.
spend-time-where-it-shows.what to prioritise: The face first, then weapons, hands and chest, and the main colour that covers most of the model.
spend-time-where-it-shows.face first: Yes. People look at the head first, then weapons, hands and chest. Let effort and highlights build towards the head.
spend-time-where-it-shows.dont waste time on feet: Right, almost nobody inspects the feet. Spend less time on each area as you work down and away from the face.
spend-time-where-it-shows.focal point: The head gets most attention, along with the parts the model is about. A small detail near the face adds a lot for little time.
spend-time-where-it-shows.which parts matter most: Head, weapons, hands and chest, plus the main colour covering most of the model, which can take half your time or more.
spend-time-where-it-shows.where people look on a mini: The head first, then weapons, hands and chest. Almost nobody inspects the feet.
spend-time-where-it-shows.speed up by skipping hidden bits: Yes. Low and hidden areas get one coat, deep shadows can stay dark, and if you must turn it upside down to find a spot, leave it.
spend-time-where-it-shows.focus on the head and weapon: Yes. Build the highlights towards the head and give themed parts, like a weapon, your best work.
spend-time-where-it-shows.is it worth detailing the back: Usually not. The back can often keep its base colours, while the front and head get the effort.

spray-priming.spray primer: Warm and shake the can well, then spray short sweeping bursts from about 15 to 30 cm, stopping at two thin coats.
spray-priming.rattle can priming: Shake for a minute or two, spray in short passes starting beside the model and releasing past it, from all sides and angles.
spray-priming.how to spray prime: Fix the model to a stick, spray the back first, sweep short light passes from 15 to 30 cm, and do two thin coats.
spray-priming.fuzzy primer: Usually spraying too far away or in cold, damp air. Scrub it off with isopropyl alcohol and an old toothbrush and re prime.
spray-priming.grainy primer finish: Paint dried in the air before landing, from spraying too far or in humid air. It will not improve; strip it and re prime.
spray-priming.primer too thick lost detail: Leave a thick coat to dry, as it often shrinks back. Next time spray two light coats from further away.
spray-priming.how far away to spray: About 15 to 30 cm, following the can's advice. Closer in hot, dry air, a little further in humid air.
spray-priming.warm the can: Stand it in warm, not hot, water for a few minutes, then shake it for at least a minute or two.
spray-priming.primer sputtering: A can that sputters or loses pressure usually just needs warming and shaking again.
spray-priming.spray priming in cold weather: Avoid it. Spray on mild, dry days of roughly 10 to 27 C, as cold or damp air gives fuzzy or grainy results.

stippling-texture.stippling: Wipe most paint off an old splayed brush and tap the tip straight down, never dragging, so tiny dots build a rough texture.
stippling-texture.how do i stipple: Load the brush, wipe most off, tap the tip straight down, and turn it between dabs so the dots do not repeat.
stippling-texture.dabbing paint for texture: Tap a nearly dry brush straight down so each tap leaves a cluster of dots, and vary the spacing to avoid patterns.
stippling-texture.grainy rough texture on cloth: Stipple with slightly thicker paint, which leaves grain that suits rough fabric, lighter colours over smaller areas.
stippling-texture.stippled cloak highlights: Block in rough shading first, then stipple lighter colours over smaller areas, more solidly near the top and sparse at the bottom.
stippling-texture.which brush for stippling: An old brush with splayed or trimmed bristles, as stippling wears brushes fast. A small narrow drybrush suits tight areas.
stippling-texture.make stone look rough: Stipple with thicker paint, which leaves a grain that suits stone, then a sparse pale stipple on the sharpest edges.
stippling-texture.tapping the brush for dots: Tap the side of the tip straight down, never drag, and re splay the bristles as they pull together.
stippling-texture.rough leather texture: Stipple with thicker paint for grain, then add a sparse pale stipple on edges; dots read rougher than lines.
stippling-texture.stipple a big cloak with a sponge: Yes. A scrap of sponge dabbed the same way is quicker on large cloaks.

sun-faded-paint.sun faded paint: Add grey or pale sand to each colour, glaze or drybrush a pale warm grey over top surfaces, then tie it in with a pale filter.
sun-faded-paint.bleached paint effect: Lighten and grey the tops most, keep undersides closer to the first colour, filter it all pale sand, and finish matt.
sun-faded-paint.faded paint: Start the scheme slightly dull, fade the upward surfaces with a pale warm grey, and unify with a thin filter.
sun-faded-paint.desert faded vehicle: Mix grey or pale sand into each colour, drag pale oil dots down big panels, add a dusty filter, and a few bright fresh chips.
sun-faded-paint.old faded paint job: Lighten and grey each colour, most on top surfaces, filter the whole model, add a few sharp newer chips, and finish matt.
sun-faded-paint.sun bleached tank: Drybrush or glaze a pale warm grey over upward faces, drag pale oil dots down flat panels, then a pale sand filter.
sun-faded-paint.faded armour: Plan each faded colour: reds go pinkish, blues and greens go grey and chalky, black becomes dusty grey.
sun-faded-paint.make colours look weathered and old: Add grey or pale sand to each colour before painting, fade the tops more, and mute it all with a thin filter.
sun-faded-paint.filter to tie in fading: Put a thin pale sand or dusty grey filter over the whole model to mute everything together.
sun-faded-paint.paint faded by weather: Fade the surfaces the sun hits most, tops and upper edges, lighter and greyer, and keep recesses closer to the first colour.

texture-as-highlight.texture as highlight: Put lighter scratches, lines and dots where highlights belong and keep shadows smooth, so texture and light build together.
texture-as-highlight.scratchy highlights: Use lighter, denser marks for brighter areas and sparse ones for darker, each lighter step smaller, with a glaze between.
texture-as-highlight.dots for texture: Place dots where the light catches. Denser, lighter dots read brighter and sparse ones read darker.
texture-as-highlight.texture marks: Start them with the first layer after the base coat, not at the end, or they look stuck on.
texture-as-highlight.sketchy texture style: Build texture with lighter marks from the first layer, each step smaller, glazing towards the light between steps.
texture-as-highlight.painterly texture: Use scratches, lines and dots as both wear and highlight, and keep a few smooth areas for contrast.
texture-as-highlight.texture and light together: Put texture marks only where highlights go and keep shadows smooth, so the busy lit areas stand out.
texture-as-highlight.stippling texture: See: stippling is one of the marks used here. Stipple where light falls, with denser, lighter dots reading brighter.
texture-as-highlight.wear marks in the highlights: Dab broken, uneven marks along worn edges, varying thickness and thinning out where there is less wear.
texture-as-highlight.make leather look textured: Drag the brush tip loosely over areas you want lighter, mix in some stippling, and add a few crack lines.

tiny-shine-points.shine points: A few very small, very bright dots and lines with a dark colour right beside them make things read as shiny.
tiny-shine-points.tiny bright dots: Put them on eyes, lenses, gems, blade edges and corners where light catches. Use only a few, and do it last.
tiny-shine-points.glint on a blade: Add short thin bright lines and dots on the corners and edges of the blade where light would catch.
tiny-shine-points.how do i make things look shiny: Shine comes from contrast, not area. Keep the brightest colour to tiny spots with dark right beside them.
tiny-shine-points.white dot in the eye: Put a tiny bright dot on the side facing the light, using near white or pure white, and only a few on the model.
tiny-shine-points.reflection dot on a gem: Add a tiny bright dot on the side facing the light, with the dark of the gem right beside it.
tiny-shine-points.specular highlight: A tiny spot of near white with a dark colour right beside it. Shiny things have few midtones and a sudden jump.
tiny-shine-points.lens pop with a white dot: Paint the lens white, then a strong colour over it, then a white dot in one corner.
tiny-shine-points.armour not looking glossy: Add short bright lines and tiny dots on corners and edges, and a dot where edges change angle, with dark beside them.
tiny-shine-points.make slime look wet with a highlight: Put a tiny bright dot on the side facing the light. Shiny things jump suddenly from dark to light.

two-part-putty.green stuff: Two part epoxy putty: cut roughly equal amounts, knead until no streaks remain, and keep tools lightly wet so it does not stick.
two-part-putty.epoxy putty: It hardens once its two parts are mixed. Hard kinds suit gap filling and plates; softer kinds suit faces, cloth and organic shapes.
two-part-putty.two part putty: Mix roughly equal parts until the colour is even, discarding the strip where they touched, and keep fingers and tools damp.
two-part-putty.putty too sticky: Wet tools lightly or rub on hand cream, and wait: it firms up over time. Extra soft part stays tacky; extra hardener sets firmer.
two-part-putty.mixing putty: Cut roughly equal amounts, discard the strip where the parts touched and any crusty bits, and knead until no streaks are left.
two-part-putty.gap filling putty: Use a hard, sandable kind for gap filling, and leave it to cure fully, ideally overnight, before sanding.
two-part-putty.sculpting putty: Softer, springy kinds suit faces, cloth and organic shapes. Rough the shape out soft and come back every half hour or so.
two-part-putty.putty ratio: Roughly equal parts. Extra of the soft part holds finer detail but cures slower; extra hardener sets faster with crisper edges.
two-part-putty.putty sticks to my tools: Wet fingers and tools lightly with water, or a little hand cream. Keep them damp, not dripping, or the surface turns slimy.
two-part-putty.how long to mix putty: Knead until there are no streaks left, and longer if both parts are a similar colour.

unify-army-colours.army colours: Repeat one vivid spot colour, a small shared set of paints and the same shadow tone on every model so the army reads as one.
unify-army-colours.cohesive army: Use one spot colour on every model, the same paints and recipes across units, and a shared shadow and top highlight tint.
unify-army-colours.tie army together: Put one contrasting spot colour on lenses, gems or buttons of every model, and share the shadow colour throughout.
unify-army-colours.spot colour: Choose one vivid colour that contrasts with the main scheme, such as glowing blue on red, and put it on every model.
unify-army-colours.army scheme: Keep a small set of paints across all units, use the same recipe wherever a colour appears, and base every model the same way.
unify-army-colours.army looks mismatched: Share the shadow tone and mix one tint into every final highlight. That ties old and new batches together too.
unify-army-colours.make different units look like one army: Carry the army colour onto small areas like a tabard or seal, and keep the same paints, shadows and bases.
unify-army-colours.accent colour on every model: Yes. One vivid spot colour on lenses, lights, gems or buttons of every model ties the army together.
unify-army-colours.matching army: Use the same recipe wherever a colour appears, base every model alike, and note the colours so later figures match.
unify-army-colours.consistent shadows across army: Use one shadow colour, such as a dark magenta, in the recesses of every model, weapon and base.

varnishing.varnish: It protects paint and sets the finish. For a tough coat, use slightly thinned gloss first, then matt or satin over it.
varnishing.how do i varnish: Once fully dry and dusted, brush it on like an all over wash, or spray thin passes from 20 to 30 cm. Gloss first, then matt.
varnishing.matt varnish: Matt is flat and suits cloth and skin but can deaden metals. Over gloss it usually needs two thin coats.
varnishing.gloss varnish: Gloss is shiny and hardest wearing, and suits metal and wet looks. Use it under matt, or brush it back on gems and eyes.
varnishing.protect paint from chipping: Varnish models you game with, base included: slightly thinned gloss for toughness, then matt or satin on top.
varnishing.satin varnish: Satin sits between gloss and matt. About three parts very flat matt to one part satin is tougher than pure matt and looks flat.
varnishing.model too shiny: Finish with matt, which over gloss usually needs two thin coats, then brush gloss back onto gems, eyes and wet effects.
varnishing.should i varnish my models: If you game with them, yes, as handling rubs paint off edges. Display pieces are often left bare.
varnishing.gloss then matt: Yes, that gives a tough finish: a slightly thinned gloss coat, then two thin coats of matt or satin over it.
varnishing.paint rubbing off edges when gaming: Varnish the model, base included: a gloss coat for toughness, then matt or satin, and leave it a day before heavy handling.
varnishing.Should I varnish my models, and how?: If you game with them, yes. Once paint is fully dry, apply thinned gloss, then matt or satin, by brush, spray or airbrush.

warm-cool-balance.warm and cool colours: Give a warm main colour cool details and a cool one warm details, including the base, so the parts stand apart.
warm-cool-balance.colour temperature: Warm colours seem to come forward and cool ones sit back. Changing temperature between materials tells the eye they differ.
warm-cool-balance.warm cool balance: Pair a warm main colour with cooler details, or a cool one with warm metals and leather, kept smaller and less bright.
warm-cool-balance.colours blend together: Change temperature between parts: add a touch of blue to minor details on a warm model, or warm metals on a cool one.
warm-cool-balance.warm vs cool: Warm seems to come forward and feels lively or harsh; cool sits back and feels calm or eerie.
warm-cool-balance.cool details on warm model: Add a touch of blue to the mixes for straps and leather, or add a small blue green prop, algae or verdigris.
warm-cool-balance.temperature contrast: Set warm against cool between main colour and details, and on the base, such as cool grey rocks on warm sandy ground.
warm-cool-balance.should the base be warm or cool: Contrast within it: cool grey rocks on warm sandy ground, or warm stone on cool grey ground.
warm-cool-balance.orange skin with blue straps: Yes. On warm orange skin, a touch of blue in the strap and leather mixes keeps the details from blurring in.
warm-cool-balance.parts dont stand apart: Shift their temperature: cool details on a warm model, warm ones on a cool model, and keep accents smaller than the main colour.

weapon-swaps.weapon swap: Cut at an existing band or ridge, file both faces smooth, fit the new weapon straight, and hide the join with putty or a colour change.
weapon-swaps.swap weapons: Cut at a bar, ring or notch so the join looks designed, test the fit as you file, and check it is straight before the glue sets.
weapon-swaps.conversion: See: for weapon swaps, cut at an existing band, file the faces, pin or glue the new part straight, and paint a colour change at the join.
weapon-swaps.kitbash: See: when swapping weapons, cut at a ring or cuff, fit the new part straight, and hide the join with putty or a thin rod ring.
weapon-swaps.hand swap: Cut along a cuff, bracer or glove edge so the seam reads as the edge of the clothing.
weapon-swaps.new weapon: If it will not sit in the hand, file a little plastic away behind it, test, and repeat. Small cuts can be added to.
weapon-swaps.weapon conversion: Cut at a band, drill and pin new blades to hafts with a short piece of paper clip, and put a colour change at the join.
weapon-swaps.cut weapon off: Cut at an existing bar, ring or notch so the new part lines up, then file the cut face smooth.
weapon-swaps.how to swap a sword: Cut the old one out, drill through the fist slightly oversize, slide the new one through at the right angle, and fill with putty.
weapon-swaps.hide the join: Fill it with putty, add a thin ring of plastic rod round the shaft, or paint a colour change right at the join.

weathering-transfers.weathering transfers: Apply transfers before weathering, chip and scratch their edges with the colour underneath, then shade and grime them with the panel.
weathering-transfers.decals look stuck on: Weather them with the surface: paint small chips into their edges, carry panel scratches across, and drag the same grime over them.
weathering-transfers.chipping decals: Paint small sparse chips with the colour underneath, or dab a nearly dry sponge of the background colour over them.
weathering-transfers.weather decals: Chip their edges, line up scratch directions with the panel, then shade, glaze and filter over them as you did the panel.
weathering-transfers.how do i weather transfers: Put them on before weathering, chip with the underlying colour or scrape with a toothpick, then wash and stain across them.
weathering-transfers.transfers too clean: Glaze a thin reddish brown over bright ones, or a brown wash so white ones are not pure white, and drag grime across them.
weathering-transfers.scratches across a decal: Paint them with the colour underneath, thinned, on a sharp brush, and line their direction up with scratches on the panel.
weathering-transfers.dirty decal: Drag the same grime washes and stains across it as the panel, and fade it towards the bottom with a thin dark glaze.
weathering-transfers.decal looks like a sticker: Give it a broken outline with chips in the colour underneath, then shade and filter it along with the panel around it.
weathering-transfers.transfer chips: Scrape small nicks off the dry transfer with a toothpick, fine needle or blade tip, gently, or paint them in the panel colour.

what-is-acrylic-paint.what is acrylic paint: Pigment for colour, acrylic binder that sets into a tough film, and water as the solvent.
what-is-acrylic-paint.what is binder: Acrylic medium. It sets into a tough film as the water evaporates and holds the pigment together.
what-is-acrylic-paint.too much water in paint: There is then not enough binder to hold the pigment, which gives tide marks, blotches and coffee ring stains.
what-is-acrylic-paint.tide marks: They come from too much water breaking the binder. For very thin mixes, use some medium instead of only water.
what-is-acrylic-paint.overthinned paint: Too much water leaves too little binder to hold the pigment, so it breaks up. Add medium for very thin mixes.
what-is-acrylic-paint.paint breaks up and goes blotchy: It is overthinned with water. Use some medium so the binder keeps up with the pigment.
what-is-acrylic-paint.pigment and binder: Pigment gives the colour; binder, acrylic medium, sets into a film that holds it as the water evaporates.
what-is-acrylic-paint.acrylic medium: It is the binder in acrylic paint. Adding some to very thin mixes keeps the binder up with the pigment.
what-is-acrylic-paint.why does paint dry so fast: The binder sets into a film as the water evaporates, so acrylics dry fast.
what-is-acrylic-paint.can i rewet dried acrylic: No. Once the binder has set into a film, acrylic cannot be rewetted.

wire-details.wire: Thin, soft wire makes lightning bolts, energy arcs and tiny candles to add life to a model or scene.
wire-details.lightning bolt: Bend short pieces of thin, soft wire into random zigzags, glue the main one into a drilled hole, then add branches.
wire-details.energy arc: Bend thin wire into zigzags, glue them branching from the source, paint white at the core fading to a bright colour, and add glow.
wire-details.wire candle: Cut 1 to 1.5 mm wire into 3 to 6 mm pieces of different heights, add white glue drips, paint off white with an orange yellow tip.
wire-details.wire effect: Bend thin wire into zigzags for lightning or cut short pieces for candles, then paint them and add a glow nearby.
wire-details.magic lightning: Glue zigzags of thin wire into a drilled hole, paint white at the core fading to a bright colour, and glow nearby surfaces.
wire-details.zigzag wire: Bend short pieces of thin, soft wire into random zigzags. The thinner the wire, the more convincing the bolt.
wire-details.arc: Bend thin wire into random zigzags, glue them in branching, and paint white at the core fading to a bright colour.
wire-details.spell lightning: Drill where the bolt starts, glue in thin wire zigzags, paint white fading to a bright colour, and glow the nearby surfaces.
wire-details.lightning from a staff: Drill a small hole in the staff tip, glue the main wire in, add more zigzags to branch, and paint white to a bright colour.

blending-base-textures.base looks like a flat sheet of sand: Mix in rocks and at least two textures, such as sand and crackle, with grit of three sizes in overlapping patches so it stops reading as one flat sheet.
blending-base-textures.how to make ground look natural on a bas: Glue rocks at random, lay two textures with three grit sizes, feather the joins, then paint one colour over all of it and wash and drybrush.
blending-base-textures.mix rocks and sand on base: Glue the rocks at random first, then add sand and grit of three sizes around them, and shade the foot of each rock with thinned dark brown.
blending-base-textures.bases look too uniform and boring: Vary it: random rocks, a tiny root on a bank, two textures and three grit sizes in overlapping patches, all tied together with one base colour.
blending-base-textures.rocks in a neat ring around the feet: Plan where the feet go, then glue the rocks at random rather than in a neat ring, adding a tiny root on any bank.
blending-base-textures.combine cracked earth and gravel: Lay crackle and gravel in overlapping patches, add the second while the first is wet or feather the join with a damp brush so no line shows.
blending-base-textures.realistic mixed terrain base: Random rocks, sand and crackle with three grit sizes, then a mid earth brown over all, a dark brown wash and drybrushes of light tan and pale bone.
blending-base-textures.different grit sizes on a base: Use fine, medium and coarse grit in overlapping patches rather than one size, so the ground reads as natural.
blending-base-textures.natural looking ground for skirmish mode: Mix random rocks, sand and crackle, base it all mid earth brown, wash dark brown, then drybrush light tan and pale bone on the high points.
blending-base-textures.how do i make my bases look less fake: Avoid neat rings and single textures: scatter rocks at random, mix textures and grit sizes, feather the joins, and paint one colour over all of it.

dirt-roads.muddy track base: Lay putty in a road, press in track links and ruts while soft, then paint it earth brown, wash the ruts dark and dust pigment over it.
dirt-roads.how do i make tank tracks in mud on a ba: Press spare track links along soft putty or texture paste, then run a dark brown wash along the track marks once painted.
dirt-roads.wheel ruts on a base: Scratch thin wheel ruts into the soft putty with a toothpick, then wash them dark brown and push darker pigment into them.
dirt-roads.dirt road basing: Lay putty as a road with low banks, press in tracks and ruts, rough the banks with earth and glue, then paint and dust it with pigment.
dirt-roads.make a road across my base: Lay putty in a road across the base with low banks on either side, keeping it below the rim.
dirt-roads.track marks pressed into putty: Press spare track links along the putty while it is still soft, then scratch wheel ruts beside them with a toothpick.
dirt-roads.dusty dirt path for vehicles: Base mid earth brown, wash the ruts dark brown, drybrush dusty tan, then brush pale dust pigment over the road, fix it and dust again.
dirt-roads.pigment on a dirt road base: Brush dry pigment over the painted road, wet it with white spirit or fixer, then dust on a second layer and push darker pigment into the ruts.
dirt-roads.rutted mud for a tank base: Press track links and toothpick ruts into soft putty, then wash the ruts dark brown and push darker pigment into them.
dirt-roads.country lane base for soldiers: Make a putty road with low banks, scratch in wheel ruts, rough up the banks, and set shrubs in uneven numbers along the sides.

grey-rocky-ground.grey rocky base: Texture with stones and sand, base near black, drybrush dark grey, then mid blue grey on the rocks and pale grey on the sharpest edges.
grey-rocky-ground.quick stone and gravel base: Glue stones, then fine sand on thinned white glue, base it black and drybrush up through two or three greys.
grey-rocky-ground.how to paint a rocky ground base: Base the texture black or dark brown into every gap, then drybrush dark grey all over and paler greys in stages on the raised rocks.
grey-rocky-ground.drybrush grey base: Drybrush dark grey over a black base, then a lighter mid blue grey on the raised rocks and a very light pale grey on the sharpest edges.
grey-rocky-ground.sand and stones on a base: Put the stones down first, then fine sand on thinned white glue, keeping clear of the feet.
grey-rocky-ground.base looks flat and boring: Wash one part of the base black and another brown, then drybrush the pale grey back over it for variety.
grey-rocky-ground.rubble ground with a bit of rust: Work a little rust pigment in around the rocks after drybrushing the base up from black to pale grey.
grey-rocky-ground.dark base drybrushed up to light grey: Base near black, then drybrush dark grey, a lighter mid blue grey on the rocks, and pale grey only on the sharpest edges.
grey-rocky-ground.simple rocky basing for beginners: Texture with paste or sand and stones, base it black, drybrush up through two or three greys, then add a few tufts.
grey-rocky-ground.grey gravel bases for a whole army: Base all the texture near black, then drybrush dark grey, mid blue grey and pale grey in stages, which works well in a big batch.

red-toadstools.red mushrooms on base: Paint white stems and deep red caps, wash it all dark brown, then drybrush the caps bright pink red and pale pink on top.
