making-your-own-transfers.white decal paper: White backed sheet suits dark surfaces; put the design on a simple shape, as cutting a complex outline leaves white edges.
making-your-own-transfers.inkjet decals run: Inkjet ink runs in water unless sealed, usually with a sprayed decal film; a matt varnish may not be enough.
making-your-own-transfers.diy decals: Print on waterslide decal paper, seal inkjet ink before use, then apply over gloss varnish with setting solution.
making-your-own-transfers.print my own emblems: Clean up a transparent background image, repeat it on waterslide paper, print, seal the ink, and apply over gloss.
making-your-own-transfers.decal ink smears in water: Inkjet ink runs unless sealed, so spray the sheet with decal film as its instructions say before use.

metallic-blades.metal sword: Keep the flat darker and the cutting edge brighter, brighten the tip, then add fine edge lines so it looks honed.
metallic-blades.sharp looking blade: Make the flat dark and run a brighter silver strip along the cutting edge only; the contrast reads as sharpened.
metallic-blades.how do i paint a sword: Base dark silver hilt to tip, wash it black, relayer mid silver on the cutting edge, glaze the tip bright, and line the edges.
metallic-blades.silver blade looks flat: Wash the flat black for darker reflections, then layer mid silver along the cutting edge bevel only.
metallic-blades.honed edge: Layer mid silver along the cutting edge bevel only, beside a darker flat, then line the edge with the side of the brush.
metallic-blades.metallic weapon edge: Keep the flat darker and the cutting edge bevel brighter, then pull a fine bright line along the edge.
metallic-blades.blade looks dull: Wash the flat black, keep it dark, and put a bright strip and fine lines along the cutting edge.
metallic-blades.knife blade paint: Dark silver base, black wash, mid silver on the cutting edge bevel, a bright tip and fine edge lines.
metallic-blades.axe blade metallic: Keep the flat of the axe dark with a black wash and the cutting edge bright, with fine edge lines.
metallic-blades.black wash on blade: Wash the blade black over a dark silver base, working it into the nicks; a second wash on the flat deepens it.

mixing-one-coat-paints.mixing contrast paints: They mix like normal paint; blend a couple to make a custom colour, or mix in thick white for a bright colour that covers.
mixing-one-coat-paints.mix contrast with white: Mix in a thick white for a bright colour that covers black in about three thin layers.
mixing-one-coat-paints.custom contrast colour: Mix two or more one coat paints like normal paint, tinting the one that flows best with a little of another.
mixing-one-coat-paints.contrast too dark: Mix in a more transparent one coat paint, or add medium, so more of the undercoat shows through.
mixing-one-coat-paints.one coat paint mixing: Mix them like normal paint, pairing a transparent one with a strong one to set coverage, and test in a hidden spot.
mixing-one-coat-paints.blend two contrast paints: Yes: they mix like normal paint; a transparent one with a strong one sets how much undercoat shows through.
mixing-one-coat-paints.make contrast cover better: Mix in a thick white, or use one with a pale deposit settled in the pot, as those usually cover more.
mixing-one-coat-paints.can i mix contrast paints together: Yes: one coat contrast style paints mix with each other like normal paint.
mixing-one-coat-paints.make a custom orange from contrasts: Blend a couple of yellows and reds, then test it in a hidden spot and mix enough for the whole batch.
mixing-one-coat-paints.contrast plus white: Mixing in a thick white gives a bright colour that covers black in about three thin layers.

mould-line-removal.mould lines: Find the thin ridge where the mould halves met, then scrape, file or sand it off before priming.
mould-line-removal.mold lines: Follow the ridge round the part under good light, then scrape it with the knife edge held steeply across it, or sand it.
mould-line-removal.how do i remove mould lines: Hold the knife edge steeply across the line and scrape in light strokes towards you, or use a sanding stick on curves.
mould-line-removal.seam line down the side of the model: That is the mould line; scrape it with a steep knife edge or sand it with a foam backed stick before priming.
mould-line-removal.ridge visible after priming: Scrape it and touch up the primer; next time follow the line all the way round under good light before priming.
mould-line-removal.scrape lines off with a knife: Hold the edge steeply across the line and scrape lightly towards you, using the part near the handle; do not slice.
mould-line-removal.file or sand mould lines: Files suit resin and metal but can scratch plastic; sanding sponges flex round curves, finishing with fine grits.
mould-line-removal.clean up a model before painting: Scrape or sand off the mould lines, brush thin plastic glue on fuzzy patches, and check under strong light.
mould-line-removal.mold line on a cloak: Scrape it with the knife edge, or pull narrow strips of sanding sponge across the rounded folds.
mould-line-removal.prep minis before priming: Remove the mould lines by scraping or sanding, smooth fuzzy patches with thin plastic glue, then brush the parts clean.

nmm-basics.nmm: Non metallic metal means painting the metal shine with ordinary paint, through light placement and very strong contrast.
nmm-basics.non metallic metal: Painting reflections with ordinary paint, so it reads as metal through light placement and strong contrast.
nmm-basics.what is nmm: Non metallic metal: metal painted with ordinary paint, so you decide where the shine goes.
nmm-basics.nmm vs metallic paint: Metallic paint is quicker and suits gritty pieces and big batches; painted metal gives controllable reflections without glare.
nmm-basics.painted metal effect: Painted metal reads as metal through where you place the light and very strong contrast, not smooth blending.
nmm-basics.how does nmm work: It sells metal through strong contrast, the right light shape per part, how much is lit, and a weaker bounce light.
nmm-basics.nmm for beginners: Learn on a small part like a blade, push contrast hard, use about three big highlight steps, and stop once it reads as metal.
nmm-basics.should i use nmm: Use it when you want controllable reflections and matching hand painted light; metallic paint is quicker for big batches.
nmm-basics.fake metal with normal paint: Sketch hard patches of dark and light over black, put the darkest dark against the brightest light, then add bounce light.
nmm-basics.high contrast metal: Shiny metal jumps from near black to near white over a short distance, so keep little of the surface in the midtones.

oil-filters.oil filter: Thin an oil tint with white spirit until very see through and brush it over the area to unify, warm or dirty it.
oil-filters.dot filter: Dot small spots of a few oils over a panel, then pull a barely damp flat brush through them in one direction.
oil-filters.oil dot filtering: Dot a few oils at random over a panel and drag them together with a blotted brush into soft streaks.
oil-filters.tint with oil paint: Thin oil paint with white spirit until very see through, and brush it on area by area rather than flooding it.
oil-filters.warm up a cold scheme: Thin a red brown oil with white spirit into a see through filter and brush it over the cold scheme.
oil-filters.fade colours with oils: Dot oils on a panel and pull a blotted brush through them in one direction until they fade into soft streaks.
oil-filters.oils to dirty a tank: Use a thin dark brown filter, dots of thicker oil near the edges, or a red brown blended out on sand panels.
oil-filters.how do i filter with oils: Thin oil with white spirit until very see through but not separating, and brush it on area by area.
oil-filters.oil wash over a vehicle: Thin dark brown oil, brushed slightly thicker into the recesses as a wash, then repaint a few highlights once dry.
oil-filters.unify colours with oils: Brush a very thin oil tint over the whole area; it ties the colours together and tones down a too bright scheme.

osl-basics.osl: Painted light follows simple rules: the source is brightest, light fades with distance, moves straight, and is blocked.
osl-basics.object source lighting: Make the lantern near white at its core, then cast fading light on nearby surfaces, crisp near the source and softer further off.
osl-basics.how do i paint light from a lantern: Make the torch the brightest thing, near white at its core, and light nearby surfaces in its mid tone, fading with distance.
osl-basics.torch glow on a model: See: the source is brightest near its core, and light on nearby surfaces fades with distance and is blocked.
osl-basics.candle light effect: Light fades with distance: close surfaces get strong, crisp light, further ones get less and softer, with edges catching a little.
osl-basics.light falloff rules: Keep the source brightest, fade light with distance, keep surfaces facing away dark, and keep the surroundings dark.
osl-basics.osl for beginners: Use the mid tone of the glow colour on nearby surfaces, strongest and crispest close to the fire and fading with distance.
osl-basics.light from a fire on nearby surfaces: Make the staff near white at its core, then light nearby surfaces in the glow's mid tone, fading with distance.
osl-basics.glow from a magic staff: It travels in straight lines, so surfaces facing the source catch it and recesses and surfaces facing away stay dark.
osl-basics.where does the light go: Light travels in straight lines and fades with distance, so it lands on surfaces facing the source and not behind objects.

paint-a-test-model.test model: Paint one model from the army start to finish at the level you mean to repeat, and note every paint, mix and step.
paint-a-test-model.try a scheme on one model first: Paint one model from the army start to finish first, note what works, and make every mistake once instead of across a unit.
paint-a-test-model.should i paint a test mini before the ar: Yes: paint one model start to finish at the level you mean to repeat, so you make every mistake once.
paint-a-test-model.test a colour scheme on one figure: Paint one model start to finish and judge it at table distance under ordinary light before doing the rest.
paint-a-test-model.practice model before a whole unit: Paint one model from the unit start to finish first, writing down every paint, mix and step to repeat.
paint-a-test-model.dont want to ruin a whole squad: Paint one test model first; thin paint lets you prime over or move anything that does not work.
paint-a-test-model.how do i plan an army scheme: Paint one test model, keep it to two or three main colours plus neutrals, and write down every step.
paint-a-test-model.first model in a new army: Make it a test model: paint it fully, photograph each step, and write down every paint, mix and step.
paint-a-test-model.paint one model then do the rest: Yes: paint one model start to finish, write the steps down, then follow the list on the rest.
paint-a-test-model.make mistakes on one model not ten: Paint one test model start to finish first, so every mistake happens once instead of across the unit.

paint-on-clothes.paint on clothes: Rinse it out with cold water straight away, working from the back of the fabric; heat sets acrylic.
paint-on-clothes.paint on shirt: Rinse it with cold water as soon as you can, from the back of the fabric, with a little washing up liquid.
paint-on-clothes.acrylic on fabric: Acrylic sets into fabric when heated, so rinse it out with cold water straight away while it is wet.
paint-on-clothes.get paint out of clothes: Rinse with cold water from the back of the fabric straight away, with a little washing up liquid, and avoid heat.
paint-on-clothes.spilled paint on jeans: Rinse cold water through from the back of the fabric straight away, and keep them out of a hot wash or dryer.
paint-on-clothes.paint stain: Rinse with cold water while still wet, adding a little washing up liquid; once dry it is very hard to remove.
paint-on-clothes.remove acrylic from clothes: Rinse it with cold water straight away while still wet, and keep it out of a hot wash until the paint is gone.
paint-on-clothes.cold or hot water for paint stains: Cold water; warm water and heat set acrylic into fabric.
paint-on-clothes.paint on carpet: See: acrylic on fabric comes out best with cold water and a little washing up liquid while still wet.
paint-on-clothes.paint on clothing: Rinse with cold water straight away, working from the back of the fabric, and do not use warm water.

painting-bases-with-inks.ink bases: Prime black, add white from one side, then use thin strong inks so the undercoat shows through as shading.
painting-bases-with-inks.quick bases with inks: Over a black and white undercoat, paint thin inks, darker colours where black shows and brighter ones on the white.
painting-bases-with-inks.inks over a black and white undercoat: Use darker inks where the black shows and brighter ones where it is white, blending wet colours with a damp brush.
painting-bases-with-inks.shaded bases fast: Prime black, add white from one side, and the inks pick up the light and shade from the undercoat.
painting-bases-with-inks.colourful bases: Inks over a black and white undercoat give rich colour; blend neighbouring colours while wet with a damp brush.
painting-bases-with-inks.rich looking ground in minutes: Use strong, thin inks over a black and white undercoat, letting the undercoat show through as shading.
painting-bases-with-inks.ink over zenithal on a base: Inks over a black primer with white from one side let the undercoat show through, so light and shade are already there.
painting-bases-with-inks.base looks dull: Use strong thin inks over a black and white undercoat for rich colour, highlighting with a little ink in pale paint.
painting-bases-with-inks.how do i paint bases quickly: Glue sand and grit, then drop two or three drops of earth brown ink with flow improver and let it wick through.
painting-bases-with-inks.desert base with inks: See: thin inks over a black and white undercoat give rich, shaded bases quickly.

painting-cloth.cloth folds: Shade the hollows and light the whole upward side of each fold, with soft transitions and sharp lines only at hems.
painting-cloth.how do i paint folds: Glaze darker tones into the recesses and lower parts, then light the whole upward facing side of each fold.
painting-cloth.robes look flat: Lay invented soft highlights where the cloth would bulge, or grade it from darker at the top to lightest at the hem.
painting-cloth.how to highlight cloth: Light the whole upward facing side of each fold, not just the ridge, then a smaller brighter step on the biggest folds.
painting-cloth.cloak highlights look like stripes: Do not just line the top ridge; light the whole upward side of each fold and blend it softly.
painting-cloth.fabric folds shading: Glaze darker tones into the hollows and lower parts, then light the whole upward side of each fold.
painting-cloth.shading clothing realistically: Shade the recesses and downward sides, light the upward sides, and keep deep darkness where cloth tucks under.
painting-cloth.how to paint a cape: Shade the hollows, light the whole upward side of each fold, and grade a plain cape from darker top to lighter hem.
painting-cloth.cloth looks like armour: Cloth reads through broad shapes of light and dark; keep transitions soft and sharp lines only on hems and seams.
painting-cloth.tabard folds highlights: Light the whole upward side of each fold, softly, with sharp lines only on hems and seams.

painting-feathers.feathers: Keep the base of each feather light and the tip dark, add thin hatched lines for texture, and darken the wing tips.
painting-feathers.feathered wings: Light feather bases, dark tips, thin hatched lines towards each tip, and grey then black on the outer wing tips.
painting-feathers.bird wings: Drybrush pale colour over a dark undercoat, run thinned white into each overlap, and darken the wing tips.
painting-feathers.how do i paint feathers: Light base and dark tip on each feather, a line down the spine and round the edge, and thin hatched lines for texture.
painting-feathers.eagle feathers: Base dark brown grey, drybrush mid brown then light tan, edge the front feathers pale tan, and vary the lower rows.
painting-feathers.feather texture: Paint thin hatched lines angled out towards each tip, or skim a nearly dry brush along the sculpted vanes.
painting-feathers.owl feathers: Base dark brown grey, drybrush mid brown and light tan, add pale tan edges, and give the lower rows a different tone.
painting-feathers.angel wings: Base pale grey and paint each feather in slightly thinned white, leaving grey between them; expect two coats.
painting-feathers.griffin wing: Keep the base of each feather light and its tip dark, add hatched lines, and darken the wing tips.
painting-feathers.wings look flat: Make the base of each feather light and its tip dark, and fade the outer wing tips to black.

painting-handles.painting handle: Grip the model by a handle so your fingers stay off wet paint, such as a spring clamp, cork, dowel or paint cap.
painting-handles.how do i hold the model: Fix its base to a handle and grip that rather than the model, with elbows braced on the desk.
painting-handles.fingers smudging wet paint: Use a handle so your fingers stay off the model; varnish any area you must hold.
painting-handles.cork holder: Glue a cork to a heavy spare base, push a straightened paper clip in, and fix the part on the wire with super glue.
painting-handles.make a painting handle: Fix the base to a cork, dowel, old paint cap or spray can lid with double sided foam mounting tape.
painting-handles.grip the model while painting: Fix it to a handle, brace your elbows on the desk and rest your hands against each other.
painting-handles.dowel handle: Fix the model's base to a short length of dowel with foam mounting tape or tacky putty.
painting-handles.hold a mini without touching it: Fix it to a handle such as a cork, dowel or spring clamp holder, and wear a thin glove if you must touch it.
painting-handles.diy painting holder: Use a cork, dowel, old paint cap or spray can lid, or glue a cork to a heavy base and add a paper clip.
painting-handles.stick a mini to a cork: Pin paper clips into the feet and push them into the cork, or use foam mounting tape on the base.

painting-marble.marble: Stipple lighter colours through a stretched wipe, or paint fine wandering veins, then gloss it so it reads as polished.
painting-marble.how do i paint marble: Stipple lighter colours through a stretched wipe taped over the panel, or drag thin wandering veins with a fine brush, then gloss.
painting-marble.marble effect: Stretch a baby wipe tight over the panel and stipple lighter colours through it, then finish with gloss or satin varnish.
painting-marble.marble veins look fake: Use thinned grey or khaki rather than black, wag the brush so veins wander and taper, and avoid criss crossing.
painting-marble.white marble statue: Buff pale bone then ivory, drag thinned grey or khaki veins that wander and taper, and finish with gloss.
painting-marble.polished marble look: Marble is polished, so finish with a gloss or satin varnish in thin coats so it does not pool.
painting-marble.veins in stone: Thin grey or khaki until inky and drag a fine brush across while twisting it, so the line wanders, splits and tapers.
painting-marble.marble floor tiles: Start fresh veins on each separate block so they do not run smoothly across a join, then gloss varnish.
painting-marble.black marble plinth: Base the plinth a dark colour, stipple lighter colours through a stretched wipe, then gloss it.
painting-marble.marble pillar paint: Buff pale bone and ivory, add thinned grey or khaki veins that wander and branch, then gloss or satin varnish.

painting-rope.rope: Base it light sandy beige, wash brown into the twists, then highlight each twist in short dashes and a finer pale cream top.
painting-rope.how do i paint rope: Base light sandy beige, wash brown, highlight back with the base in short dashes along each twist, then pale cream tops.
painting-rope.painting rope and cord: Base light, wash brown so it runs into the twists, then highlight along each twist with a finer pale top.
painting-rope.rope looks flat: Wash brown into the twists, then highlight back along each twist in short dashes with a finer pale cream top.
painting-rope.beige rope: Base light sandy beige, wash brown, then highlight back with the beige and finish with pale yellow cream on each twist.
painting-rope.rope on a ship: Base light sandy beige, wash brown into the twists, then highlight each twist with beige and a pale cream top.
painting-rope.sandy rope: Base light sandy beige so the wash has something to darken, wash brown, then highlight each twist.
painting-rope.rope with a brown wash: Base light sandy beige, wash brown into the twists, then highlight back with the base colour in short dashes.
painting-rope.twisted rope highlight: Highlight back with the base colour in short dashes along each twist, then pale yellow cream on just the top of each.
painting-rope.noose: Base light sandy beige, or mid brown for darker rope, wash brown, and highlight along each twist.

painting-small-eyes.eyes too big: Skip the eyeball: a dark warm brown in the socket reads as eyes in shadow, and slightly wrong eyes look worse than none.
painting-small-eyes.paint eyes: Dark socket, off white instead of pure white, and a short upright dark line touching top and bottom for the pupil.
painting-small-eyes.small eyes: Run a dark line into the socket, or fill it with off white and add a short upright pupil line.
painting-small-eyes.googly eyes: Avoid a round dot floating in the white; use a short upright dark line touching top and bottom instead.
painting-small-eyes.eyes on tabletop models: Keep them simple: a dark socket with soft off white and a near black pupil line, never stark black and white.
painting-small-eyes.eyes look wrong: Avoid a floating round dot, use off white and near black, and check both eyes look the same way from several angles.
painting-small-eyes.easy eyes for beginners: Paint a dark warm brown in the socket and skip the eyeball; it reads as eyes in shadow.
painting-small-eyes.eyes look staring: A floating round pupil makes the figure look startled; use a short upright dark line touching top and bottom.
painting-small-eyes.skip the eyeball: A dark warm brown in the socket reads as eyes in shadow, and slightly wrong eyes look worse than none.
painting-small-eyes.dark socket eyes: Fill the socket with a dark warm brown; it reads as eyes in shadow, and one dark line per eye is plenty under a helmet.

painting-teeth.teeth: Base sandy brown, paint the upper two thirds bone, then add white for the tips only, so they look set in the gums.
painting-teeth.how do i paint teeth: Sandy brown at the root, bone on the upper two thirds, then off white tips only.
painting-teeth.fangs: Paint a few root to tip growth lines, paler near the tip, then an ivory dot on the point.
painting-teeth.monster teeth look fake: Avoid pure white all over; build from sandy brown at the root to off white tips, darker further back.
painting-teeth.yellow rotten teeth: Base dark brown or grey brown for dirtier, older teeth, then bone and paler tips.
painting-teeth.teeth look like a white strip: Avoid pure white all over; keep the roots darker and only the tips near white.
painting-teeth.gums and mouth: Paint the mouth, tongue and gums before the final tooth layers, using the skin's dark shadow inside the mouth.
painting-teeth.dirty old teeth: Base a dark brown or grey brown, then bone on the upper part and paler tips.
painting-teeth.sharp teeth on a beast: Sandy brown roots, bone on the upper two thirds, white tips, growth lines on fangs and an ivory dot on each point.
painting-teeth.what colour are teeth: Sandy brown at the root shading up to off white at the tips, never pure white all over.

painting-yellow.painting yellow: Use a pale or warm undercoat and shade with warm oranges and browns, never black or grey.
painting-yellow.yellow looks green: Black or grey shading makes yellow green; glaze thin reddish orange over the lower areas, as red cancels green.
painting-yellow.yellow over black: Block it in with light grey, thinned off white or a dense yellow first, then paint the bright yellow over.
painting-yellow.how do i paint yellow: Prime white, bone, pink or yellow, shade with deeper golden yellow and warm brown, and highlight cream or paler yellow.
painting-yellow.yellow is see through: It is see through; use a pale or warm undercoat, or block in light grey first over black.
painting-yellow.what do i shade yellow with: A deeper golden or ochre yellow, then sepia or warm brown in the recesses and mid brown in the deepest gaps.
painting-yellow.yellow armour: Prime pale, shade with golden yellow and warm brown, highlight with cream, and paint any black up to it last.
painting-yellow.yellow covers badly: A dense, slightly ochre yellow covers far faster; over black, block in light grey or off white first.
painting-yellow.yellow goes dirty with black wash: Black wash makes yellow green and dirty; shade with deeper golden yellow and warm brown instead.
painting-yellow.best undercoat for yellow: White, bone, pink or yellow, sprayed in short light bursts so detail does not clog.

photographing-models.my photos are blurry: Use a tripod and the self timer so the camera stays steady, and avoid digital zoom.
photographing-models.photos look yellow: Use daylight LED bulbs, all the same colour, turn off yellow household lights, and set a custom white balance.
photographing-models.how do i photograph my minis: Soft front light, a plain matt backdrop and a steady camera on a tripod matter far more than the camera itself.
photographing-models.best background for model photos: A plain matt backdrop in white, mid grey or black, curved from wall to floor; black velvet gives clean black.
photographing-models.lighting for mini photos: Daylight LED bulbs, about 5000 to 6500K, lit from the front and slightly above, two lamps at about 45 degrees.
photographing-models.phone photos of models: Tripod about 30 cm away, self timer, tap to focus on the face, then drag the exposure down until highlights are not blown.
photographing-models.photo box setup: Curve paper from the wall down under the model, light it from the front with daylight bulbs and diffuse them with parchment.
photographing-models.model looks dark in photos: Against a white backdrop auto exposure darkens it; expose for the model so the backdrop looks slightly grey.
photographing-models.what light bulbs for photography: Daylight LED bulbs, roughly 5000 to 6500K, rated for good colour rendering, all the same colour.
photographing-models.shadows in my photos: Light from the front, not overhead, with a white card bouncing light into the shadow side and the flash off.

plinth-backdrops.plinth backdrop: Glue a torn card shape to the back wall, paint it as parchment, and draw a picture on it in thin dark brown.
plinth-backdrops.back wall on a display base: Use the flat back wall for a small painted picture or built scene, kept quieter than the model so it supports it.
plinth-backdrops.painted scene behind a model: Paint a small picture or scene on the plinth's back wall, with fewer colours and less contrast than the model.
plinth-backdrops.add a story to a display piece: Add a backdrop on the plinth's back wall, with a small red mark pointing to the model to tie the two together.
plinth-backdrops.backdrop picture for a bust: Glue torn card to the back wall, paint it as old parchment, sketch a picture in thin dark brown, and keep it quieter than the bust.
plinth-backdrops.plinth with a flat back: Use the flat back wall for a backdrop picture or a built scene that adds story or setting.
plinth-backdrops.card backdrop torn paper: Cut thick card into a torn paper shape, glue it on, and paint it pale tan with darker, browner edges.
plinth-backdrops.diorama back wall: Cut a floor and back wall from thick plastic sheet, cut and back the doors and windows, then add vents, tiles and junk.
plinth-backdrops.show the setting behind a figure: Add a backdrop on the plinth's back wall, either a painted picture or a small built scene of floor and wall.
plinth-backdrops.painted landscape on a plinth: See: a painted picture on a plinth back wall, kept quieter than the model with fewer colours and less contrast.

preparing-metal-models.metal models: Clean up flash and mould lines, use super glue and pins on heavy joints, and varnish to stop chipping.
preparing-metal-models.metal minis: Clip flash, file mould lines, wash in warm soapy water, use super glue and pins, and seal with matt varnish.
preparing-metal-models.prep a metal miniature: Check for miscasts, clip flash, file mould lines, wash in warm soapy water, and dry fully before gluing and priming.
preparing-metal-models.pinning metal parts: Pin heavy arms and weapons, as glue alone will not hold them for long.
preparing-metal-models.what glue for metal: Plastic glue does not work on metal; use a strong super glue, and file contact faces so the parts meet snugly.
preparing-metal-models.paint chipping off metal: Paint chips off metal much more easily than plastic; seal the whole model with a matt varnish.
preparing-metal-models.old metal miniatures: Check for miscasts, clean flash and mould lines, wash them, super glue and pin heavy parts, and varnish them.
preparing-metal-models.pewter models: Clean flash and mould lines with a file or knife, wash, super glue and pin the joints, and finish with matt varnish.
preparing-metal-models.miscast metal model: Makers usually replace a badly miscast part; small missing areas can be rebuilt with two part epoxy putty.
preparing-metal-models.clean mould lines on metal: Clip the flash away, then clean the lines with a needle file or a sharp knife, starting on long thin parts.

quick-highlights.quick highlights for speed painting: Add a few fast thin lines and dots on upward facing edges and the head; that may be enough.
quick-highlights.make a speed paint look finished: Highlight only the upward facing edges and the head with single thin lines and a few dots.
quick-highlights.fast highlights on a squad: Mix each highlight from the colour in use plus your palest colour, and do only upward edges, face and main colour.
quick-highlights.highlight only the top edges: Highlight head, shoulders, knees, feet and the top of any pack, as the edges that face up may be enough.
quick-highlights.few dots and lines to finish: Single thin lines on the upward edges, then a lighter colour on a short section where your lamp hits.
quick-highlights.speed paint looks unfinished: Add a few fast lines and dots on upward edges and the head, keeping the recesses dark.
quick-highlights.what to highlight when short on time: Do the face and the main colour first, on upward facing edges only; on a big army those two are often enough.
quick-highlights.quick edge highlights on helmets: Use the side of the bristles for one thin line along the top edges, then a short brighter touch where the light hits.
quick-highlights.finish a tabletop mini fast: Highlight only the upward edges and the head, aiming for about a minute of highlights per model.
quick-highlights.one highlight is enough: Often yes: one thin highlight on the upward facing edges may be enough.

red-armour.red over black primer: Prime black, base mid red in three or four thin coats, shade darker red, and highlight with brighter reds, not white.
red-armour.my red goes orange: Highlight with redder, brighter reds instead of yellow; keep orange to tiny touches on points and corners.
red-armour.red looks pink when i highlight: Highlight with brighter reds rather than white, or add a warm flesh tone for a lighter edge mix.
red-armour.how do i paint red armour over black: Base strong mid red in three or four thin coats, shade with darker red, then highlight with brighter reds.
red-armour.red needs so many coats: Expect three or four thin coats over black; a light spray of white from above first brightens it in fewer coats.
red-armour.red is patchy: Use thin paint and fast strokes in three or four coats, or spray white lightly from above first.
red-armour.deep red armour: Mid red base, darker red shading, very thin black or dark brown in the deepest lines, and brighter reds for highlights.
red-armour.red armor that stays red: Shade with darker reds and highlight with brighter reds, never white or yellow, and keep clear dark joins.
red-armour.red wont cover: Paint thin coats, three or four over black, or dust white from above first so it covers in fewer.
red-armour.rich red on a vehicle: Base strong mid red, shade darker red, highlight with brighter reds, and gloss sponged red for a wet look.

resin-printer-care.resin printer maintenance: Check the vat film, clear failed print scraps, keep the plate level, and soften cured resin off the screen with alcohol.
resin-printer-care.hole in the vat film: Replace it; even a pinhole lets resin through onto the screen.
resin-printer-care.failed print stuck in the vat: Cure a thin skin across the film with tank cleaning mode or a blank layer, then peel it out with the bits using a plastic tool.
resin-printer-care.how do i level the build plate: Loosen the plate bolts, lay the levelling card or paper on the screen, lower the plate onto it, and tighten with it pressed flat.
resin-printer-care.cured resin on the printer screen: Lay a cloth soaked in isopropyl alcohol over it, wait until it softens, then rub it away gently.
resin-printer-care.prints keep failing: Check for a slack, scratched or holed vat film and for cured flakes floating in the vat.
resin-printer-care.clean resin printer screen: Soften cured resin under a cloth soaked in isopropyl alcohol and rub it gently; never scrape it with anything hard.
resin-printer-care.fep film scratched: A scratched or slack film spoils prints; replace it over the alignment pegs and tighten the bolts evenly.
resin-printer-care.looking after my 3d printer: Check the vat film, clear failed print scraps, level the plate and keep the screen clean.
resin-printer-care.vat film slack: A slack film spoils prints; fit a new one over the pegs and tighten the bolts evenly.

scratch-building-details.scratch build details: Make armour plates, belts, wheels and handles from plastic tube, card, rod and spare bases.
scratch-building-details.make armour plates from plastic card: Cut thick plastic card and shave the edges at random angles for rough plates, or halve plastic tube for curved ones.
scratch-building-details.make wheels from scratch: Glue a small solid round base onto a slightly wider clear flying base with super glue for a flanged wheel.
scratch-building-details.plastic tube details: Halved tube makes curved plates, a narrower length with bevelled ends makes a band, and paper round tube makes shrouds.
scratch-building-details.make handles and belts: Use brass rod filed flat on two sides for a handle, and thin plastic card strips about 1 mm wide for belts.
scratch-building-details.diy details from spare bits: Spare bases make wheels, plastic tube makes plates and bands, and brass rod and card make handles and straps.
scratch-building-details.scratchbuild a banded pipe: Slide a short length of narrower tube with bevelled ends over the pipe as a band.
scratch-building-details.use spare bases as wheels: Glue a small solid round base onto a slightly wider clear flying base with super glue.
scratch-building-details.plasticard armour plates: Cut thick plastic card and shave the edges at random angles, or score thin sheet and bend it along the lines.
scratch-building-details.add details to a conversion: Add plates, bands, straps, rivets and pipes from card, tube, rod and wire, focusing on the most recognisable shapes.

sculpting-with-putty.green stuff: Mix the two parts until the colour is even, block in a rough shape, then refine it with small fine tools kept wet.
sculpting-with-putty.how do i sculpt with putty: Mix it evenly, keep fingers and tools wet, block in a simple shape, then refine it with small fine tools.
sculpting-with-putty.mixing two part epoxy putty: Mix the two parts until the colour is completely even, and discard the strip where they touched in the packet.
sculpting-with-putty.putty sticks to my tools: Keep tools wet or lightly coated in hand cream or petroleum jelly, and keep them spotless, as old cured putty tears fresh putty.
sculpting-with-putty.what tools do i need for sculpting: Small, fine tools beat big sets: a small bent blade, a firm rubber tipped shaper, a needle and a ball tool.
sculpting-with-putty.sculpt fur or a cloak on a model: For fur, dig the tool's edge in and flick away in the direction it grows; for a hood, drape a thin rolled sheet.
sculpting-with-putty.putty has streaks of colour in it: Keep mixing until the colour is completely even, with no streaks.
sculpting-with-putty.beginner sculpting tips: Take less than you think, keep tools wet, sculpt the deepest layers first, and let each stage cure before working beside it.
sculpting-with-putty.putty wont set hard: Mix the two parts until the colour is completely even, and leave it at least four hours, ideally overnight.
sculpting-with-putty.how much putty should i mix: Take less than you think you need, and mix the two parts until the colour is completely even.

silk-and-satin.silk: Paint it like polished metal: very dark base, strong contrast to near white, built from fine parallel hatched lines.
silk-and-satin.satin dress: Base very dark, build fine parallel hatched lines along the folds, each step smaller, and push the top highlight near white.
silk-and-satin.shiny fabric: Very dark base and a big jump to near white, built from many thin parallel lines, like polished metal.
silk-and-satin.how do i paint silk: Base a very dark version of the colour, then hatch fine parallel lines along the folds up to almost white.
silk-and-satin.silky robes: Paint them like polished metal: very dark base, fine hatched lines, each step smaller, up to near white.
silk-and-satin.shiny cloak: Base very dark, then strong contrast up to almost white in thin parallel lines, lined up with the light elsewhere.
silk-and-satin.satin sheen: Use strong contrast from very dark to near white, built from fine parallel lines along the folds.
silk-and-satin.fabric looks like metal: Yes: paint silk like polished metal, with strong contrast and fine parallel lines, like brushed steel.
silk-and-satin.strong contrast cloth: See: shiny fabric needs a big jump from very dark to near white, built in fine lines.
silk-and-satin.hatching on silk: Build up with many very thin parallel hatched lines along the folds, each lighter step covering a smaller area.

smooth-blends-on-large-areas.smooth blend on a big cloak: Use a larger brush and wet blend while the paint is wet, going over the blend more than once.
smooth-blends-on-large-areas.no airbrush smooth gradient: Use a larger brush and wet blending, or many soft drybrush passes, then glaze over the joins.
smooth-blends-on-large-areas.big areas look streaky: Small brushes leave streaks on big surfaces; switch to a larger brush.
smooth-blends-on-large-areas.blend large flat areas by brush: Switch to a larger brush, lay layers short of the last, wet blend while wet, and glaze over the joins.
smooth-blends-on-large-areas.airbrush look with a brush: Use a big soft drybrush and build colour over many very light passes.
smooth-blends-on-large-areas.smooth fade on a dragon wing: Wet blend with a larger brush, one area at a time, going over the blend more than once.
smooth-blends-on-large-areas.wet blend a large cloak: Work one area at a time with a larger brush while the paint is wet, and expect to go over it more than once.
smooth-blends-on-large-areas.streaks on big surfaces: Switch to a larger brush; small ones leave streaks on big areas whether you glaze or wet blend.
smooth-blends-on-large-areas.how do i blend a big area: Use a larger brush, lay layers stopping short of the last, wet blend or drybrush softly, and glaze the joins.
smooth-blends-on-large-areas.soft gradient on a tank panel: Use a larger brush, build many light soft drybrush passes, then finish with a couple of glazes over the joins.

splicing-kits.splicing kits: Cut both models at clean lines in small bites, file the faces flat, test fit often, and hide any gaps.
splicing-kits.how do i combine two models: Cut each at a clean line, avoiding detail across the join, file both faces flat, test fit often, and fill gaps.
splicing-kits.cut a model in half: Clip well away from the line, creep closer in small bites, then file or sand the face flat.
splicing-kits.kitbash two kits: Cut above or below belts and pouches, file both faces flat, test fit often, and fill gaps with putty.
splicing-kits.join a torso to different legs: Cut above or below any belts, file both faces flat, and watch proportions: about two parts legs to one part torso.
splicing-kits.gap after cutting models: Hide small gaps behind pouches or badges, and fill larger ones with putty pressed to match the texture.
splicing-kits.conversion cutting tips: Clip well away from the line, creep closer in small bites, file flat, and test fit after each adjustment.
splicing-kits.where to cut when converting: Cut above or below detail such as belts or pouches that runs across the join, not through it.
splicing-kits.file cut faces flat: Finish with a file or sanding stick so both faces meet flat, test fitting after each small adjustment.
splicing-kits.frankenstein conversion: Cut at clean lines in small bites, file flat, test fit, and fill gaps with putty or hide them behind spare parts.

sprue-goo.sprue goo: Plastic frame offcuts dissolved in plastic glue, left overnight to two days, make a paste that glues and fills gaps.
sprue-goo.liquid sprue: Chop frame offcuts into a jar of plastic glue up to just below the liquid level, and leave it until it becomes a thick paste.
sprue-goo.dissolve sprue in glue: Drop chopped plastic frame into a half full bottle of plastic glue and leave it overnight to two days.
sprue-goo.fill gaps with plastic glue: Use dissolved frame paste, spread on both faces so some squeezes out, then brush thin glue over to level it.
sprue-goo.how do i fill gaps between parts: Spread plastic paste generously on both faces, then brush thin plastic glue over the squeeze out to level it.
sprue-goo.diy gap filler: Dissolve chopped plastic frame in plastic glue for overnight to two days into a thick filler paste.
sprue-goo.melted plastic frame paste: That is sprue goo: it glues and fills gaps in one go, on plastic only.
sprue-goo.gaps on a model after gluing: Run plain thin glue along hairline gaps, or fill wider gaps with plastic frame paste and level it with thin glue.
sprue-goo.homemade filler: See: plastic frame dissolved in plastic glue makes a gap filling paste for plastic models.
sprue-goo.what to do with leftover sprue: Chop it into a bottle of plastic glue and leave it overnight to two days to make a gap filling paste.

stippling-to-blend.stippling: Dab many tiny dots of thin paint with the brush tip instead of strokes, so the eye blends them into a smooth fade.
stippling-to-blend.stipple blend: Dab dots of thin, wicked paint densest where a colour is strongest and sparser towards the previous one.
stippling-to-blend.blend with tiny dots: Wick thin paint off on tissue and dab the tip over and over; packed close, the dots read as a smooth fade.
stippling-to-blend.hide rough layer steps: Stipple each colour into its neighbour from both sides, densest near its own band, so the dots disguise the lines.
stippling-to-blend.stippling technique: Touch the brush tip to the surface over and over, using thin, well wicked paint, letting each pass dry.
stippling-to-blend.stipple a gradient: Dab small steps of mixed colour, densest where each is strongest and spaced out towards the previous one.
stippling-to-blend.dab paint instead of strokes: Stipple thin dots instead of brush strokes, densest where each colour is strongest.
stippling-to-blend.stippling looks spotty: Use small steps between colours and let each pass dry; stipple the previous mix back over a spot that is too light.
stippling-to-blend.texture blend for skin: Stipple tiny dots of thin paint to build a smooth fade without brush strokes.
stippling-to-blend.smooth out blotchy blends: Stipple thin colour into each neighbouring band from both sides so the dots disguise the lines.

superglue-problems.glued my fingers together: Do not pull; dab on an acetone based nail polish remover, wait for it to loosen, then peel gently.
superglue-problems.superglue wont set: Usually too much glue or a loose fit; use less and get the parts closer together. Very dry air also slows it.
superglue-problems.glue stays wet and tacky: Too much glue or a loose fit keeps it wet; use less, close the gap, or use an accelerator spray to set it instantly.
superglue-problems.how do i get superglue off skin: Do not pull; dab on acetone based nail polish remover, wait for it to loosen, then peel gently.
superglue-problems.glue stuck to my tweezers: Clean it off with a cotton bud and a little acetone, keeping the acetone well away from painted surfaces.
superglue-problems.thick or thin superglue: Use thick or gel superglue on cork, wood, paper and other porous materials; thin soaks in before it can bond.
superglue-problems.superglue on resin wont hold: Use less glue and a tighter fit, as too much glue or a loose fit keeps it wet; an accelerator sets it instantly.
superglue-problems.acetone for superglue: Yes: acetone frees glued fingers and cleans tools, but keep it well away from paint, as it strips it.
superglue-problems.glue went everywhere: Clean tools with a cotton bud and a little acetone, and free skin with acetone nail polish remover; never pull.
superglue-problems.super glue not drying: Use less glue and get the parts closer together; superglue needs a little moisture, so very dry air slows it.

texture-before-priming.texture paste before priming: Dab crackle or texture paste into the recesses before priming, smooth its edges, and let it dry fully before priming.
texture-before-priming.crackle paste: Dab it into recesses and round pipes before priming for crusty corrosion, using the tip of an old brush.
texture-before-priming.crusty corrosion: Dab crackle or texture paste where rust and grime gather before priming; washes and drybrushing pick it out.
texture-before-priming.texture before primer: Yes: dab texture paste into recesses before priming; the primer then seals it in.
texture-before-priming.hide glue spills: Dab crackle or texture paste over a messy glue drip before priming; it hides it without sanding.
texture-before-priming.rusty grime in recesses: Dab crackle or texture paste into recesses and round pipes before priming, then wash and drybrush it.
texture-before-priming.corrosion texture on pipes: Dab a little crackle or texture paste round the pipes before priming, smoothing the edges with a damp brush.
texture-before-priming.can i texture before priming: Yes: dab texture paste on, let it dry fully, then prime; the primer seals the texture in.
texture-before-priming.crackle before prime: Dab crackle into recesses with an old brush tip, feather the edges with a damp brush, let it dry, then prime.
texture-before-priming.messy glue marks: Dab a little crackle or texture paste over them before priming; it hides the drips and reads as grime.

torn-and-worn-cloth.torn cloth: Paint small dark irregular holes near the bottom edge with a light lip under each, and add broken edge highlights.
torn-and-worn-cloth.ripped cloak: Paint a few small dark brown and black holes near the hem with a light highlight line under each.
torn-and-worn-cloth.frayed hem: Highlight the edge lighter with random small nicks, then paint a few short lines into the fabric for loose threads.
torn-and-worn-cloth.holes in cloth: Paint small irregular dark brown and black shapes, with a line of light highlight just under each for depth.
torn-and-worn-cloth.worn tattered robes: Dab short jagged strokes of lighter colour along the highlights, and add fine crosshatched lines for worn weave.
torn-and-worn-cloth.paint rips in a cloak: Paint small irregular dark holes near the bottom of the cloak, each with a light lip just under it.
torn-and-worn-cloth.battle damaged cloak: Paint dark tears near the bottom edge with light lips, fray the hem, and use jagged broken highlights.
torn-and-worn-cloth.ragged cloth: Paint dark holes with light lips, a nicked hem with loose threads, and short jagged highlights.
torn-and-worn-cloth.paint holes that arent sculpted: Mix dark brown with a little black, paint small irregular holes, and add a light line under each so it reads as depth.
torn-and-worn-cloth.cloak looks too clean: Add wear: small dark holes near the bottom edge, a frayed hem, and jagged highlights instead of clean lines.

two-thin-coats.two thin coats: Two or three thin coats give even colour, sharp detail and no streaks, where one thick coat does not.
two-thin-coats.why thin paint: Thin coats flow into recesses without filling them, so detail stays sharp and there are no streaks or brush marks.
two-thin-coats.paint goes on patchy: Normal on the first thin coat; let it dry fully and add a second, or a third for weak colours like yellow.
two-thin-coats.one thick coat or several thin: Several thin coats; one thick coat drowns detail and leaves streaks and brush marks.
two-thin-coats.how thin should paint be: A drop of water to three or four of paint is a safe start; test a stroke before touching the model.
two-thin-coats.brush strokes showing: Streaks and brush marks almost always mean the paint is too thick; thin it and use two or three coats.
two-thin-coats.my paint looks like jam: That means the paint is too thick; thin it and build the colour in two or three thin coats.
two-thin-coats.detail filled with paint: The paint was too thick or there was too much on the brush; wipe the excess off and use thin coats.
two-thin-coats.first coat looks bad: The first thin coat looks patchy with primer showing; that is normal, so let it dry and add the next.
two-thin-coats.thin your paints meaning: Build colour in two or three thinned coats rather than one thick one, so detail stays sharp.

unique-models-in-a-squad.squad all look the same: Swap heads, change what the hands hold, and turn heads and arms so no two models match.
unique-models-in-a-squad.make each model in a unit unique: Decide what to change on each, then swap heads, hand items and gear, and turn heads and arms.
unique-models-in-a-squad.head swaps: Swap heads between kits: a bare head, a scar or an older face changes character quickly.
unique-models-in-a-squad.how do i stop repeated sculpts looking i: Swap heads and hand items, and turn heads and arms; small angle changes make one sculpt read differently.
unique-models-in-a-squad.vary poses in a squad: Turn heads and arms to follow the action, such as looking down a pointed weapon.
unique-models-in-a-squad.models look like clones: Swap heads and what the hands hold, add gear, and make small pose changes so no two match.
unique-models-in-a-squad.swap weapons between kits: Cut the hand off at the wrist with a sharp knife and glue on a different hand or weapon.
unique-models-in-a-squad.personalise each trooper: Swap heads, hands and gear, turn heads and arms, and hide any cut scars with a pouch.
unique-models-in-a-squad.small conversions for variety: Head swaps, new hand items, gear and small changes to head and arm angles.
unique-models-in-a-squad.five identical soldiers: Swap heads, change what each holds, and turn heads and arms so each reads as a different moment.

varnishing-metallics.matt varnish dulls metal: Varnish before painting the metallics, or brush a thinned metallic or gloss back over the metal afterwards.
varnishing-metallics.varnish dulled my gold: Brush slightly thinned original metallic over the flat central areas once varnished, then a paler metallic on the edges.
varnishing-metallics.metal looks grey after varnish: Brush one coat of thinned original metallic over the flats that catch light, then a paler metallic on top edges.
varnishing-metallics.gloss varnish looks wet: Brush gloss or satin only onto the flat and raised metal surfaces, keeping it out of recesses.
varnishing-metallics.get the shine back after varnish: Brush one coat of thinned original metallic over the flats, or slightly thinned gloss or satin on the metal only.
varnishing-metallics.varnish before metallics: Yes: varnish first, then paint the metallics over the top so they keep their shine.
varnishing-metallics.metallics flat after varnish: Brush thinned original metallic over the flat central areas, then a paler metallic on the top edges.
varnishing-metallics.how do i varnish metallic paint: Varnish first and paint metals on top, or brush gloss or satin onto the metal only afterwards.
varnishing-metallics.varnish ruined my silver: Brush one coat of thinned silver over the lit flats, then a paler metallic on top edges and a few fresh chips.
varnishing-metallics.restore shine on metal: Brush thinned original metallic over the lit flats after varnishing, or thinned gloss or satin on the metal only.

warm-cool-shadows-highlights.warm and cool colours: Give shadows and highlights opposite temperatures in one area, such as a warm brown shade under cool blue grey highlights.
warm-cool-shadows-highlights.warm highlights cool shadows: Shade blue with purple and highlight with pale yellow green, or keep red highlights towards orange with cool shadows.
warm-cool-shadows-highlights.colour temperature on miniatures: Make one of light and shadow warm and the other cool; it adds contrast without adding brightness.
warm-cool-shadows-highlights.more contrast without making it brighter: Make the shadows and highlights opposite temperatures, one warm and one cool, for extra contrast.
warm-cool-shadows-highlights.should shadows be cool: Often, but either way works; one pair is warm pale highlights over deep violet shadows, flipped for cold scenes.
warm-cool-shadows-highlights.warm shadows with cool light: Wash dark brown or warm flesh red into the recesses of blue grey armour, then highlight lighter grey blue and off white.
warm-cool-shadows-highlights.temperature contrast: Contrast from warm against cool: give shadows and highlights opposite temperatures within one area.
warm-cool-shadows-highlights.how do i use warm and cool colours: Decide where the light comes from, keep warm tones facing it and cool tones only in the deepest shadows opposite.
warm-cool-shadows-highlights.highlight colour too similar to shadow: Push them apart by temperature: make one warm and the other cool, which adds contrast without extra brightness.
warm-cool-shadows-highlights.make a cloak pop with temperature: Use a warm pale skin like highlight over a deep violet shadow, or flip it for cold scenes.

weathered-chrome.weathered chrome: Spray mirror chrome over gloss black, keep some panels clean, and grime the rest with black then warm brown one coat paints.
weathered-chrome.mirror chrome on a vehicle: Airbrush mirror finish chrome over a smooth gloss black base for a mirror finish.
weathered-chrome.dirty chrome: Layer black and then warm brown one coat paints over the chrome, keeping a few panels bright.
weathered-chrome.rusty chrome bumpers: Add thinned red brown rust round rivets and where moisture would collect, over grimed chrome.
weathered-chrome.how do i get a chrome finish: Lay a smooth gloss black base, then airbrush mirror chrome over it, or brush liquid chrome quickly.
weathered-chrome.chrome looks too clean: Layer black and then warm brown one coat paints over most of the metal, leaving just a few panels bright.
weathered-chrome.grimy chrome car: Layer black and warm brown one coat paints over the chrome, then add red brown rust where moisture collects.
weathered-chrome.chrome needs gloss black: Yes: a smooth gloss black base, or gloss varnish over black, makes the chrome more mirror like.
weathered-chrome.post apocalyptic chrome: Chrome over gloss black, a few bright panels, black and warm brown grime and red brown rust round the rivets.
weathered-chrome.airbrush mirror chrome: Spray it over a smooth gloss black base, thin chrome inks with lacquer thinner if needed, and let it cure about two days.

wet-blending.wet blending: Lay two colours side by side on the model and mix the join while both are still wet for a fast gradient.
wet-blending.blend two colours on the model: Paint each colour up to the middle, then work the join with quick strokes while both are wet.
wet-blending.fast gradient on a cloak: Wet blend: paint dark and light colours side by side and soften the join while wet, then refine with glazes.
wet-blending.how do i wet blend: Base the area, lay two creamy colours side by side, wipe the brush on a damp towel and work the join while wet.
wet-blending.wet blending looks spotty: Spotty blends come from blending onto bare primer or black; base coat the area solidly first.
wet-blending.blend while both paints are wet: Paint both colours side by side, then soften the join with quick strokes until it starts to drag.
wet-blending.paint dries before blending: Add a little retarder or glaze medium rather than extra water, and work one small area at a time.
wet-blending.wet blend on black primer: Base coat the area solidly first in a tone of the colour; blending onto black looks spotty.
wet-blending.creamy paint for blending: Use creamy, well pigmented paint at about base coat consistency, with retarder or glaze medium rather than water.
wet-blending.smooth blend fast: Wet blend two colours side by side on the model, then refine with layers or glazes.

what-to-upgrade-first.what should i upgrade first: Light first, then a good detail brush, a wet palette, magnification, and an airbrush later.
what-to-upgrade-first.is an airbrush worth it: For most people later, once brushwork is steady; it speeds priming and fades but needs a compressor, cleaning and practice.
what-to-upgrade-first.better brushes or better light: Light first: a bright daylight lamp shows true colour and detail and helps more than any brush.
what-to-upgrade-first.do i need a wet palette: It is the third upgrade, after light and a good brush: paint stays workable for hours, thins evenly and wastes less.
what-to-upgrade-first.magnifier for painting: Head magnifiers or a lens lamp help tired eyes; they come after light, a good brush and a wet palette.
what-to-upgrade-first.next tool to get: Whatever holds you back now; usually a bright daylight lamp first, then a good detail brush.
what-to-upgrade-first.upgrade my painting setup: Light first, then one good detail brush, a wet palette, magnification and comfort, then an airbrush.
what-to-upgrade-first.improve my hobby kit: Upgrade what holds you back: light, a good detail brush, a wet palette, then magnification and comfort.
what-to-upgrade-first.worth getting a good brush: Yes: one quality brush with a sharp point that holds its shape makes eyes and edges far easier.
what-to-upgrade-first.what tools make the biggest difference: A bright daylight lamp first, then a good detail brush, then a wet palette.

worn-leather.worn leather: Use ragged highlights, fine cracks and scratches on worn edges, and a slight sheen left in the creases.
worn-leather.old leather: Dark brown base, chunky mid brown highlights, stippled shadows, fine scratches on worn edges, and a sheen in the creases.
worn-leather.cracked leather: Paint fine cracks and nicks in a lighter tone round worn edges and folds, and run a dark sheened wash into the cracks.
worn-leather.leather straps: Paint fine scratches and nicks along the strap edges, with short marks across where it bends.
worn-leather.how do i paint leather: Base dark brown, blend up to chunky mid brown, then add fine scratches and cracks on worn edges and folds.
worn-leather.weathered leather jacket: Highlight in ragged strokes, put scratches on edges and elbows, and leave a sheen in the creases with matt cloth nearby.
worn-leather.leather boots look plastic: Keep the brightest marks to a few lit spots, and matt the nearby cloth so only the creases keep a sheen.
worn-leather.scuffed leather belt: Scratch nicks along the belt edges in a lighter tone, with a thin dark line beside each scratch to look cut in.
worn-leather.make leather look used: Add ragged highlights, fine scratches at edges and folds, and pale beige grey dots on the most worn spots.
worn-leather.aged leather texture: Stipple dark brown and black into the shadows for texture, then add fine scratches and cracks on worn edges.

bright-green-sand.old school green base: Glue fine sand on, soak it with very watery bright green, drybrush bright yellow over the grains, then paint the rim green.
bright-green-sand.retro bright green bases: Sand soaked in thin bright green, a light bright yellow drybrush on the grains, and a smooth bright mid green rim.
bright-green-sand.how to do classic green grass bases: Glue on sand, flood it with watery bright green so every grain takes it, then flick bright yellow over the tops once dry.
bright-green-sand.sand base painted green and drybrushed y: Let the glued sand sit an hour, soak in very thin green, drybrush yellow in light flicks, and give the rim smooth green coats.
bright-green-sand.make my bases look like 90s models: For that retro look, soak sanded bases in inky bright green, drybrush bright yellow across the grains and paint the rim green.
bright-green-sand.nostalgic grass green basing: Bright green soaked into glued sand, a light yellow drybrush across the grain tops, and a matching green rim.
bright-green-sand.quick green flock look without flock: Sand soaked in bright green and drybrushed yellow gives a grassy look with no fine scatter at all.
bright-green-sand.simple green base for old models: Glue on fine sand, soak it in watery bright green, then drybrush yellow lightly and paint the rim the same green.
bright-green-sand.green sand base with yellow drybrush: Soak the sand with very thin bright green, let it dry, then flick bright yellow across the grains, steering round the feet.
bright-green-sand.what colour were old style bases: Old style bases were bright green sand drybrushed with bright yellow, with a bright mid green rim.

dry-mud-ground.quick easy base: Spread mud texture paste, drybrush a light earth colour, paint the rim dark brown and add a few small clumps of grass fibres.
dry-mud-ground.dry mud base: Apply mud texture paste, drybrush it light earth, push pigment into the dips, then paint the rim and add small grass clumps.
dry-mud-ground.simple dirt base with grass: Texture paste, a light earth drybrush, a dark brown rim, then a few dots of glue dipped in grass fibres.
dry-mud-ground.how to do a basic texture paste base: Spread the paste front and back, work it round the feet with a wet brush, then drybrush it light earth once dry.
dry-mud-ground.drybrush texture paste: Once the paste is dry, drybrush a light earth colour over it. Wash it dark mud brown first only if it dried flat in colour.
dry-mud-ground.brown ground basing for beginners: Texture paste drybrushed a light earth, pigment in the hollows, a neat dark brown rim and a few clumps of grass fibres.
dry-mud-ground.texture paint looks crusty: Thin the texture paste a little if it looks crusty, and work it round the feet with a wet brush before it dries.
dry-mud-ground.fast basing for a whole army: Mud texture paste with a single light earth drybrush and a dark rim is quick, then add a few small grass clumps.
dry-mud-ground.dusty dirt ground: Drybrush the paste light earth, push light earth pigment into the hollows and wipe the high points so dust sits in the dips.
dry-mud-ground.what is the easiest way to base models: Spread mud texture paste, drybrush it a light earth colour, paint the rim and finish with a few small grass fibre clumps.

meadow-and-flowers.grassy base with flowers: Stain glued sand brown, drybrush pale bone, then layer shrub, flower and grass tufts with grass fibre patches between.
meadow-and-flowers.how do i make a green meadow base: Glue sand, flood thin brown and drybrush pale bone, paint the rim, then add tufts, flowers and patches of grass fibres.
meadow-and-flowers.flower tufts on bases: Glue tufts from low to high: shrubs first, flowers overlapping them, then grass tufts in the gaps.
meadow-and-flowers.spring field basing: Sand stained brown and drybrushed bone, then layered shrubs, flowers and grass tufts with grass fibre patches.
meadow-and-flowers.grass base looks fake: Add a few dried real grass stems and stipple red and green pigment on the bare ground so it looks less uniform.
meadow-and-flowers.sand then static grass on a base: Glue sand down, flood it with thin brown, drybrush pale bone and paint the rim, then dab glue and press grass fibres on.
meadow-and-flowers.lush green grassland base: Layer shrub, flower and grass tufts over stained sand, then fill patches with grass fibres and a few real grass stems.
meadow-and-flowers.how to layer tufts and flowers: Layer tufts low to high, starting with shrubs, then overlapping flowers, then grass in the gaps.
meadow-and-flowers.base for an elf or wood themed army: See: this entry's meadow of layered shrub, flower and grass tufts over stained sand suits a green woodland look.
meadow-and-flowers.pretty summery base: Stained sand with layered shrubs, flowers and grass tufts and patches of grass fibres gives a bright summery meadow.

resin-ice.deep frozen lake base: Stick a plastic mirror on the base, cover it with clear resin, tint it in thin blue and blue black glazes, then add cracks.
resin-ice.clear resin ice base: Mirror cut to the base under a thin layer of clear UV resin, tinted with light blue glazes and finished with cracks.
resin-ice.how do i make realistic ice with depth: Put a plastic mirror under clear resin and glaze thin blue over it in light layers so the shine shows through for depth.
resin-ice.mirror under resin for ice: Stick a thin plastic mirror to the base, spread resin to the edge and cure it, so the tint on top seems to have depth.
resin-ice.cracked ice effect: Brush gloss on and work a wet brush over it so it dries cracked, then drag folded sandpaper across for scratches.
resin-ice.frozen water on a base: Resin over a mirror, tinted in thin blue glazes with darker blue black patches, then cracked gloss and snow at the edges.
resin-ice.ice with dark deep water underneath: Glaze deep blue black in one area only, over the paler blue, to suggest deep water under the ice.
resin-ice.epoxy resin frozen pond: See: this entry uses clear UV curing resin over a mirror, tinted with thin blue glazes and cracked gloss on top.
resin-ice.make ice look thick and see through: A mirror under clear resin with tint built in light passes keeps the ice see through, so it reads as thick.
resin-ice.cracks in resin ice: Brush gloss over the resin, work a wet brush through it so it dries cracked, then scratch it with folded sandpaper.

static-grass.static grass: Dot glue in patches on a dry painted base, dip it in a tub of grass fibres and flick the underside to lift the fibres.
static-grass.how to apply static grass: Dot glue in patches, leaving bare ground between, dip the base in the grass tub and flick underneath.
static-grass.grass falls over flat: Pull a dabbed clump away with tweezers while the glue is wet, or hold a charged balloon just above it to lift the fibres.
static-grass.flock basing: Layer it: fine scatter first as low texture, then grass fibres, then a few tufts for bigger clumps.
static-grass.grassy base: Dip glued patches in grass fibres, then layer fine scatter under it and add a few tufts, leaving bare ground between.
static-grass.my static grass wont stand up: Flick the underside after dipping, or hold a charged balloon just above the wet glue to make the fibres stand.
static-grass.moss on a base: Mix fine scatter with plenty of white glue, a drop of dark green and a little water, then dab and press it where moss grows.
static-grass.balloon static grass trick: Charge a balloon on a wool jumper and hold it just above the fresh grass so the fibres lift upright.
static-grass.how to make grass stand upright: Dab a clump on wet glue with tweezers and pull away, or hold a charged balloon just above it.
static-grass.long grass clumps on a base: Dab a clump of grass fibres on wet glue with tweezers and pull it away to leave taller grass standing.

wet-muddy-ground.muddy base: Spread mud thickly round the feet, stab and flick it onto boots, then keep raised mud matt and gloss the dips.
wet-muddy-ground.how do i make wet mud: Spread thick mud paste, paint it dark brown, drybrush khaki, wash green brown, then gloss only the hollows.
wet-muddy-ground.mud splashed up the boots: Thin the mud with water and stab it onto the boots, or flick it from a stiff brush with a toothpick.
wet-muddy-ground.puddles on a base: Gloss varnish only the dips and lowest mud so it reads as standing water, leaving raised mud matt.
wet-muddy-ground.glossy wet mud look: Leave raised mud matt and lighter, then gloss the dips and lowest mud so it looks fresh and wet.
wet-muddy-ground.churned up mud for trench models: Spread mud thickly with mounds and ruts, press in footprints, and brush thinned mud over tufts so they look trampled.
wet-muddy-ground.mud spatter on a tank: Thin the mud with water and flick it from a stiff short brush with a toothpick for spatter.
wet-muddy-ground.flick mud with a toothbrush: Load a stiff short brush with thinned mud and drag a toothpick across it to flick spatter.
wet-muddy-ground.boggy swamp ground: Thick dark mud with a green brown wash, trampled tufts, and gloss in the low wet hollows suits boggy ground.
wet-muddy-ground.make mud look wet and shiny: Gloss varnish the hollows and wettest low mud, leaving the raised areas matt and lighter for contrast.

black-bodysuit.black undersuit: Base an off black, wash black all over, repaint the flat panels off black, then edge in dark grey with light grey corners.
black-bodysuit.how to paint a black bodysuit: Two thin off black coats, a black wash, off black back on the flat panels, then dark grey edges and light grey corners.
black-bodysuit.black body glove: Base off black, wash black, tidy the flat panels in off black, then edge dark grey with light grey only on sharp corners.
black-bodysuit.black rubber suit highlights: Edge every line in dark grey and touch light grey only on the sharpest corners, after repainting the panels off black.
black-bodysuit.edge highlight black: Edge black in dark grey on all edges, then add a light grey touch only on the sharp corners.
black-bodysuit.make black clothing not look flat: Wash an off black base with black, repaint the flat panels to kill the wash sheen, then pick out edges in grey.
black-bodysuit.black catsuit: Off black base, black wash, off black back on the panels, then dark grey edges and light grey only on sharp corners.
black-bodysuit.dark undersuit under armour: Base off black, black wash with pools lifted off raised parts, off black on panels, then dark grey edge highlights.
black-bodysuit.grey edges on black: Dark grey on every edge, with a light grey touch only on the sharpest corners, keeps black looking black.
black-bodysuit.black wash over off black: Wash off black with black all over, lifting pools off raised parts, then repaint flat panels off black to remove the sheen.

blue-energy-glow.blue glow: Drybrush mid blue around the source, glaze thin mid blue over the lit area, then drybrush ice blue and edge in pale blue.
blue-energy-glow.glowing power sword: White undercoat the blade, drybrush mid blue, glaze it thinly, then add light ice blue and a bright pale blue edge.
blue-energy-glow.lightning blue sword: Over a white undercoat, drybrush mid blue, glaze thin blue, drybrush light ice blue and edge sharp lines pale blue.
blue-energy-glow.energy blade: Paint the blade over white, drybrush and glaze mid blue, then lift the edges with light ice blue and bright pale blue.
blue-energy-glow.blue magic glow effect: Drybrush mid blue subtly around the source, glaze it thin over nearby areas, then ice blue and pale blue on the nearest edges.
blue-energy-glow.blue magic hands: Drybrush mid blue around the hands, glaze it thinly over the lit area, then drybrush ice blue on the nearest edges.
blue-energy-glow.how to make something glow blue: Undercoat the source white, drybrush mid blue around it, glaze thin blue over nearby areas and edge the closest parts pale.
blue-energy-glow.electric blue blade: Over white, drybrush and glaze mid blue, then drybrush light ice blue and edge the sharpest lines in bright pale blue.
blue-energy-glow.cold blue light around a spell: Drybrush mid blue softly around the spell, glaze thin blue over lit surfaces, then ice blue on the edges closest to it.
blue-energy-glow.glowing weapon: Undercoat the weapon white, drybrush and glaze mid blue, then light ice blue and a bright pale blue on the sharp edges.

bright-pink-armour.how do i paint bright pink: Base a light saturated pink in thin coats, shade magenta into recesses, deep magenta in the deepest, then pale pink edges.
bright-pink-armour.pink armour: Light saturated pink base, magenta shade in recesses, deep magenta in the deepest, and pale warm pink edges.
bright-pink-armour.bubblegum pink: Paint light saturated pink first, shade into recesses with magenta then deep magenta, and edge with pale warm pink.
bright-pink-armour.pink over black primer is patchy: Over black, use three or four thin coats of light pink, each dry before the next, until it is smooth.
bright-pink-armour.shading pink armour: Thin magenta into all the recesses, then a narrower band inside it, and deep magenta only in the very deepest.
bright-pink-armour.hot pink armour plates: Base a light saturated pink, shade magenta and deep magenta into recesses, then pale pink edges and ivory dots.
bright-pink-armour.pink looks chalky: See: this recipe paints pink in thin coats until smooth and shades into recesses with magenta for depth.
bright-pink-armour.saturated pink plates: Base light saturated pink, shade with magenta then deep magenta, edge in pale warm pink with ivory dots on high points.
bright-pink-armour.pink army scheme: See: this recipe's light pink base shaded magenta and edged pale warm pink would suit a whole army.
bright-pink-armour.neon pink armour: Light saturated pink base, magenta and deep magenta shading in the recesses, and pale warm pink edges.

cool-bone.cold bone colour: Base a dark red grey, layer warm bone and ivory, then edge with ivory mixed with a little pale green grey.
cool-bone.grey bone: Start dark red grey, build up warm bone and ivory, and finish edges in a cold off white.
cool-bone.how to paint bone that is not yellow: Start from a dark red grey rather than brown, layer bone and ivory, and tip it with a cold off white.
cool-bone.pale bone skulls: Dark red grey base, warm bone then ivory on raised parts, and cold off white on the very tips.
cool-bone.cool off white bone: Layer warm bone and ivory over a dark red grey, then edge with ivory and a little pale green grey.
cool-bone.bone with reddish shadows: Base a dark red grey darker than you expect, then layer warm bone, ivory and a cold off white over it.
cool-bone.horns and skulls bone: Dark red grey base, warm bone layers covering less each time, ivory on the tops, cold off white tips.
cool-bone.bleached bone: Build ivory up in half steps over warm bone and a dark red grey, then cold off white on the tips and edges.
cool-bone.bone armour cool tone: Dark red grey base, warm bone and ivory layers, then a cold off white edge for a cool tone.
cool-bone.ivory with grey shading: Base a dark red grey, layer warm bone and ivory in half steps, then edge in cold off white.

desert-spot-camo.desert camo: Base sandy tan, add loose mid brown patches, scatter sparse near black spots, then a pale cream crescent over each.
desert-spot-camo.camouflage on a tank: Sandy tan base, loose rounded brown patches, sparse near black spots, and a pale cream crescent over each spot.
desert-spot-camo.spotted camouflage: Sandy tan base, rounded mid brown blobs, small near black spots, then a pale cream crescent on each spot.
desert-spot-camo.sand camo pattern: Base sandy tan, layer loose mid brown patches, scatter near black spots and edge each with a pale cream crescent.
desert-spot-camo.tan camo with brown spots: Sandy tan base with loose mid brown patches, a few near black spots, and pale cream crescents.
desert-spot-camo.how to paint camo on a vehicle: Base sandy tan, paint loose mid brown patches, scatter small near black spots, then highlight with pale cream.
desert-spot-camo.leopard spot camo: Scatter small near black spots over tan and brown, keep them sparse, and add a pale cream crescent leaving a dark sliver.
desert-spot-camo.desert vehicle paint scheme: Sandy tan base, loose rounded brown patches, sparse near black spots, and pale cream crescents and edges.
desert-spot-camo.camo spots by hand: Paint small near black spots over both colours, then a pale cream crescent over each, leaving a sliver of dark.
desert-spot-camo.camoflage: Base sandy tan, add loose mid brown patches and sparse near black spots, then pale cream crescents and edges.

glowing-screens.how do i paint a screen: Fill it dark green, add a bright green L in one lower corner, a pale lime line inside that, and a white dot opposite.
glowing-screens.glowing monitor: Dark green fill, a bright green crescent in one corner, pale lime deeper in, and a white reflection dot opposite.
glowing-screens.computer screen on a tank: Dark green fill, bright green L in a lower corner, pale lime tucked into it, white dot opposite, then gloss.
glowing-screens.glowing display panel: Fill dark green, add bright green and pale lime into one corner, then a white dot opposite.
glowing-screens.screen reflection: Add one white dot in the corner opposite the glow, and gloss varnish to make it look like glass.
glowing-screens.tiny screens on sci fi models: Fill each screen dark green, add a thin bright green L and pale lime line in one corner, and a white dot opposite.
glowing-screens.make a screen look lit: Light one corner: dark green fill, a bright green L there, pale lime deeper in, and a white dot in the opposite corner.
glowing-screens.tablet screen on a model: Dark green fill, a bright green and pale lime glow in one lower corner, a white glint opposite and a gloss coat.
glowing-screens.green glowing screen: Base dark green, glow one corner with bright green and pale lime, then a white reflection dot and gloss.
glowing-screens.control panel glow: Dark green fill, bright green and pale lime in one corner, a white dot opposite as a reflection.

grey-armour.grey armour: Base mid grey, wash black, layer clean grey back on panels, then edge light grey with paler corners and scratches.
grey-armour.blue grey armor: Same as grey: blue grey base, black wash, clean blue grey on panels, then light grey edges and a few scratches.
grey-armour.how to paint grey power armour: Mid grey base, black wash, mid grey back on flat panels, light grey edges, then paler corners and small scratches.
grey-armour.grey armour looks boring: Edge every line in light grey, go paler on the sharpest corners, and add a few small scratches for interest.
