grey-armour.grimy grey armour: Use a brown wash instead of black over the mid grey for a warmer, grimy grey.
grey-armour.light grey edge highlights: Edge every line in light grey after the panels are layered, then paler grey on the sharpest corners.
grey-armour.gunmetal grey plates: See: this recipe is a mid grey washed black and edged light grey, not a metallic gunmetal.
grey-armour.washed grey plates: Wash mid grey black all over, then layer clean mid grey back onto the flat panels, skipping the recesses.
grey-armour.battleship grey: Mid grey base, black wash, clean grey back on the panels and light grey edges.
grey-armour.cold blue grey armour panels: Blue grey base, black wash, clean blue grey back on the panels, then light grey and paler edges.

ink-shaded-silver.silver: Base mid silver, glaze thin black ink into the darkest spots, then edge bright silver and glaze it on the brightest spots.
ink-shaded-silver.shading silver: Glaze very thin black ink over many coats onto mid silver, pulling it towards the darkest spots.
ink-shaded-silver.metal looks flat: Darken it with thin black ink glazes in the dark spots, then sharp bright silver edges for contrast.
ink-shaded-silver.black ink on silver: Glaze black ink very thin over many coats, pulling it towards the darkest spots on the silver.
ink-shaded-silver.steel armour: Mid silver base, thin black ink glazes in the dark areas, then bright silver edges and spot glazes.
ink-shaded-silver.how to make silver look shiny: Shade with thin black ink, edge with narrow bright silver lines, then glaze watery bright silver on the brightest spots.
ink-shaded-silver.why is my metal so flat: Flat metal lacks contrast: darken it with thin black ink glazes and add sharp bright silver edges.
ink-shaded-silver.silver blade: Mid silver blade, thin black ink pulled to the darkest spots, narrow bright silver edges and bright spots.
ink-shaded-silver.chrome looking metal: Push contrast: black ink glazes in the darks, bright silver edge lines, and watery bright silver on the brightest spots.
ink-shaded-silver.metal sword: Mid silver base, black ink glazes for shade, narrow bright silver on the edges and the brightest spots.

olive-green-skin.orc skin: Base dark olive, wash dark green into recesses, layer yellow green on muscle tops, glaze purple red in the deepest shadows.
olive-green-skin.how do i paint green skin: Dark olive base, dark green wash, yellow green on the muscle tops, then a thin purple red glaze in the deepest shadows.
olive-green-skin.olive green flesh: Dark olive base, dark green wash into the recesses, yellow green layered onto the tops of the muscles.
olive-green-skin.goblin skin: Dark olive base, dark green wash, yellow green on smaller areas at the tops, and a thin purple red glaze in the shadows.
olive-green-skin.green skin highlights: Mix yellow green into the olive, then pure, on smaller areas at the top of each muscle.
olive-green-skin.brute skin green: Dark olive base, dark green wash, yellow green highlights and a thin purple red glaze in the shadows.
olive-green-skin.purple shadows on green skin: Glaze a very thin purple red in the deepest shadows. It sets off the yellow green highlights.
olive-green-skin.earthy green muscles: Dark olive base, dark green wash between muscles, yellow green on the tops, and a purple red glaze in the darks.
olive-green-skin.ogre green skin: Dark olive base, dark green wash, yellow green highlights and purple red in the deepest shadows.
olive-green-skin.how to shade green skin: Work a dark green wash thinned with medium between the muscles, then a very thin purple red glaze in the deepest parts.

pale-tent-cloth.canvas tent: Base dark ivory, shade khaki then dark brown in the folds, restore ivory on flats, and edge pale ivory.
pale-tent-cloth.off white banner: Dark ivory base, khaki and dark brown shading in the creases, then pale ivory on the edges and fold peaks.
pale-tent-cloth.how to paint canvas: Block in dark ivory, shade creases khaki and deepest folds dark brown, restore the flats and edge pale ivory.
pale-tent-cloth.dirty white cloth: Dark ivory base, khaki brown in the creases, dark brown in the deepest folds, pale ivory edges.
pale-tent-cloth.ivory fabric: Dark ivory base, khaki shading, dark brown deep folds, dark ivory back on flats, pale ivory edges.
pale-tent-cloth.grubby canvas sacks: Dark ivory base, khaki then dark brown in the folds, ivory back on flats and pale ivory edges.
pale-tent-cloth.sail cloth: Dark ivory base, khaki and dark brown in the folds, then pale ivory on the edges and peaks.
pale-tent-cloth.pale cloth with grime: Dark ivory base, khaki shade in creases, dark brown in the deepest folds, pale ivory edges. It suits grime.
pale-tent-cloth.rough canvas texture: Block it in dark ivory with an old brush, shade with khaki and dark brown, and edge in pale ivory.
pale-tent-cloth.khaki shading on white cloth: Thin khaki brown into the creases, then dark brown in only the deepest folds, over a dark ivory base.

plasma-coils.plasma coils: Fill the coils off white, cover with bright green contrast, highlight curves pale green, then a thin green airbrush tint.
plasma-coils.glowing coils: Off white base, bright green contrast, pale green on the curves, and a thin green spray onto nearby metal.
plasma-coils.plasma gun: Off white coils, bright green contrast, pale green where they curve, and a light green tint sprayed over.
plasma-coils.glowing cables: Off white base, bright green contrast darker at the coil ends, and pale green on the curves.
plasma-coils.how to make coils glow: Fill neatly off white, cover with bright green contrast, then pale green highlights where the coils curve.
plasma-coils.energy coils: Off white base, bright green contrast, pale green on the curves, and a thin green airbrush tint.
plasma-coils.make the gun look lit from inside: Spray a very thin green tint over the coils so overspray on nearby metal adds to the glow.
plasma-coils.plasma glow: Off white coils, bright green contrast, pale green highlights and a thin green tint sprayed over.
plasma-coils.blue plasma coil: See: this recipe uses green over off white, with pale green highlights and a thin green spray.
plasma-coils.glowing vents on a gun: See: this recipe glows coils with off white, bright green contrast and a thin green tint sprayed nearby.

red-glowing-eyes.red glowing eyes: Base deep red, layer bright red then orange towards the centre, add a pale yellow core and white dot, then glaze red around.
red-glowing-eyes.how do i make eyes glow red: Deep red, bright red, then orange towards the centre with a pale yellow core and white dot, plus a thin red glaze below.
red-glowing-eyes.red lenses: Deep red base with a dark rim, bright red over it, orange in the centre, a pale yellow core and a white dot.
red-glowing-eyes.red eye lenses on helmet: Deep red with a dark rim, bright red, orange to the centre, pale yellow core, white dot and a thin red glow.
red-glowing-eyes.glowing red visor: Deep red base, bright red and orange towards the centre, pale yellow core, then glaze thin red over the area.
red-glowing-eyes.red eye glow effect: Glaze very thin red from below the eye up into it to cast a soft glow.
red-glowing-eyes.evil red eyes: Deep red base, bright red then orange to the centre, pale yellow core and white dot, with a thin red glaze.
red-glowing-eyes.red lens with white dot: Layer deep red, bright red and orange towards the centre, then a pale yellow core and one white dot.
red-glowing-eyes.robot red eyes: Deep red with a dark rim, bright red, orange centre, pale yellow core and white dot.
red-glowing-eyes.demon eyes glowing: Deep red, bright red, orange, a pale yellow core and white dot, then a thin red glaze below for the glow.

clay-roof-tiles.roof tiles: Base mid brown, dab orange brown glaze in random patches, wash dark brown all over, then add red brown pigment dust.
clay-roof-tiles.terracotta roof: Mid brown base, orange brown patches, a dark brown wash over everything and red brown dust in the gaps.
clay-roof-tiles.how to paint a clay roof: Mid brown base, random orange brown glaze patches, a dark brown wash and red brown dust wiped back.
clay-roof-tiles.orange tiled roof: Mid brown base, orange brown patches dabbed randomly, a dark brown wash and red brown dust in the gaps.
clay-roof-tiles.old roof tiles weathered: Mid brown base, orange brown patches, a dark brown wash all over, then pigment dust left in the gaps.
clay-roof-tiles.pigment dust on roof: Flow on runny red brown pigment, leave it for hours, then wipe it back so dust stays in the gaps.
clay-roof-tiles.ruined house roof colour: Mid brown, orange brown patches, a dark brown wash and red brown dust in the gaps for old tiles.
clay-roof-tiles.make tiles look varied: Dab orange brown glaze, thinned about one to ten, in random patches so the tiles vary.
clay-roof-tiles.red tile roof: Mid brown base, orange brown patches, a dark brown wash and red brown dust in the gaps.
clay-roof-tiles.clay tiles recipe: Mid brown base, orange brown glaze patches, a dark brown wash all over, and red brown dust in the gaps.

warm-skin-from-dark-brown.warm skin: Base dark brown, layer in more warm flesh each time, add ivory on the top points, then glaze muted blue under cheeks.
warm-skin-from-dark-brown.skin from brown: Base dark brown, mix in more warm flesh each layer covering less, then ivory on nose, brow and chin.
warm-skin-from-dark-brown.smooth skin: Mix flesh into dark brown in layers, each covering a little less, then ivory on the top points and a muted blue glaze.
warm-skin-from-dark-brown.how to paint skin: Dark brown base, warm flesh layers covering less each time, pale ivory flesh on top points, muted blue glaze in shadows.
warm-skin-from-dark-brown.flesh tone layering: Add more flesh to dark brown in each layer, covering less of brow, cheeks and nose, then ivory on the highest points.
warm-skin-from-dark-brown.skin blending: Mix warm flesh into dark brown step by step, then a very thin muted blue glaze under cheekbones and jaw.
warm-skin-from-dark-brown.tan skin: Dark brown base, layers with more warm flesh each time, and pale ivory flesh only on the top points.
warm-skin-from-dark-brown.healthy skin tone: Dark brown base with warm flesh layered in, ivory on top points, and a thin muted blue glaze under the jaw.
warm-skin-from-dark-brown.sun tanned skin: Dark brown base, warm flesh layers, ivory only on nose, brow and chin, and a muted blue glaze in shadows.
warm-skin-from-dark-brown.skin looks chalky: See: this recipe keeps skin warm by mixing flesh into dark brown and saving ivory for the very top points.

yellow-glowing-lenses.yellow lenses: Black lens, deep orange leaving a black ring, bright yellow towards the inner corner, then a white dot reflection.
yellow-glowing-lenses.glowing yellow eyes: Black, then deep orange with a black ring, bright yellow to the inner corner with a touch of white, then a white dot.
yellow-glowing-lenses.how do i paint yellow lenses: Base the lens black, cover with deep orange leaving a thin black ring, add bright yellow inward, then a white dot.
yellow-glowing-lenses.yellow eye glow: Black base, deep orange, bright yellow towards the inner corner, and a tiny white dot on the outer corner.
yellow-glowing-lenses.amber lenses: Black base, deep orange with a black ring, bright yellow and white towards the inner corner, a white reflection dot.
yellow-glowing-lenses.small yellow gems: Black base, deep orange leaving a black ring, bright yellow inward, then a tiny white glint.
yellow-glowing-lenses.lens glow white dot: Put one tiny white dot on the outer corner as a reflection, opposite the bright yellow.
yellow-glowing-lenses.yellow visor: Black base, deep orange with a thin black ring, bright yellow towards the inner corner, white dot.
yellow-glowing-lenses.helmet eyes yellow: Paint lens and socket black first, then deep orange, bright yellow inward and a tiny white dot.
yellow-glowing-lenses.bright yellow lens: Black, deep orange leaving a ring, bright yellow with a touch of white towards the inner corner, a white dot.

airbrush-deep-clean.airbrush spitting: Spitting that a flush will not fix calls for a strip down: clean the nozzle, check the needle for a bent tip, then oil and rebuild.
airbrush-deep-clean.airbrush clogged: The nozzle causes most clogs. Take the needle out, soak the metal nozzle in cleaner and clear it gently with a reamer.
airbrush-deep-clean.how to strip and clean an airbrush: Remove the needle first, unscrew caps and nozzle, soak only metal parts, scrub and pipe clean, then dry, oil and rebuild.
airbrush-deep-clean.airbrush stops spraying: If air still comes out but paint does not, strip it down and clear the nozzle, the usual cause, with a reamer or needle tool.
airbrush-deep-clean.bubbles in the airbrush cup: Bubbles pushing back into the cup mean a strip down: clean the nozzle and caps, then rebuild with the parts finger tight.
airbrush-deep-clean.clean airbrush nozzle: Soak the bare metal nozzle in cleaner, then clear it with a reamer twisted gently. Check the hole is a perfect circle.
airbrush-deep-clean.airbrush pulsing: Pulsing that a flush does not cure means a strip down: clean the nozzle, check the needle, then lubricate and rebuild.
airbrush-deep-clean.airbrush blocked dried paint: Soak the metal nozzle and caps in cleaner, scrub the cup, pipe clean the body and clear the nozzle gently with a reamer.
airbrush-deep-clean.soak airbrush parts: Soak only the bare metal nozzle and cap parts in cleaner for a few minutes, keeping seals and plastic out.
airbrush-deep-clean.airbrush not spraying but air comes out: That usually means a clogged nozzle. Strip it down, soak and ream the nozzle gently, and replace it if the hole is split.

airbrush-trigger-control.trigger control: Press down for air first, then ease back for paint. Stop paint first, then air, with your finger set back on the trigger.
airbrush-trigger-control.dual action: On a dual action airbrush, pressing down gives air and pulling back opens the needle; the further back, the more paint.
airbrush-trigger-control.how to hold an airbrush: Hold it like a pen, with the pad of your index finger on top of the trigger a little back from the front edge.
airbrush-trigger-control.airbrush spits: Spitting often comes from stopping air and paint together, leaving a droplet on the needle. Stop paint first, then air.
airbrush-trigger-control.air first then paint: Air first blows out debris, and stopping paint before air clears the tip so no droplet spits next time.
airbrush-trigger-control.single action vs dual action: Single action cannot meter paint separately, so it is a poor choice for models; dual action lets you control the flow.
airbrush-trigger-control.airbrush beginner: Set the trigger limiter so you cannot flood the model, and practise dots, lines and fades on paper first.
airbrush-trigger-control.fine lines with an airbrush: Move close, keep the air on and tap the trigger lightly, pulling back only a fraction for small, fine marks.
airbrush-trigger-control.airbrush splatters: Splatter usually means too much paint or a droplet left on the needle. Stop paint before air, and use less paint.
airbrush-trigger-control.how to use an airbrush: Air on before paint, paint off before air, steady pressure, and many light passes. Practise on paper first.

army-conversion-theme.converting a whole army: Set a short list of shared features, such as one helmet style, and repeat small touches and base features across every model.
army-conversion-theme.themed army conversions: Write down a few shared build rules, mark rank with added extras, and finish every base with the same signature features.
army-conversion-theme.how do i make a mixed army look the same: Give every model a few shared features, paint everything in one palette, and use the same signature details on every base.
army-conversion-theme.kitbash army theme: Decide shared features before building, use heads you really like, and add small repeated touches across the whole force.
army-conversion-theme.converted force looks messy: Write down shared build rules, use one palette down to small details, and repeat the same base features to tie it together.
army-conversion-theme.conversion rules for an army: Choose a few features every model shares, such as one helmet or hood style, and write the rules down before building.
army-conversion-theme.making leaders stand out: Mark rank with extras that build up: tabards, then pelts, banners and fancier helmets for leaders.
army-conversion-theme.army from different kits: Use a few kits from the same range that share joints, and vary armour, weapons and shields to fit how each group lives.
army-conversion-theme.unified look across a collection: Repeat a few shared features, one palette and the same signature base details across every model.
army-conversion-theme.custom themed warband: Pick shared heads and gear, mark rank with added extras, repeat small touches, and give every base the same features.

basing-glue-and-tools.what glue for sand on bases: White PVA glue is the main choice for sand. Thin it until it flows off the brush without running, then dip the base.
basing-glue-and-tools.pva for basing: PVA is the main basing glue for sand and loose cover. It dries clear and stays slightly flexible.
basing-glue-and-tools.sand keeps falling off the base: Lock it in by misting watered PVA or brushing gloss varnish over the dry sand before priming and drybrushing.
basing-glue-and-tools.how thin should pva be: Thin it a drop of water at a time until it flows off the brush without running, about like melted ice cream.
basing-glue-and-tools.glue for cork and rocks: PVA suits cork and small grit; use thin super glue for rocks on single bases and two part epoxy for heavy rocks.
basing-glue-and-tools.tools for basing: PVA glue, a small spatula for texture paste, super glue for rocks, and two part epoxy for heavy or large pieces.
basing-glue-and-tools.spreading texture paste: Use a small spatula instead of a brush. It loads more easily and spares your brushes.
basing-glue-and-tools.best glue to stick gravel: PVA suits grit and loose cover. Build deep texture in layers, each dry first, and lock it in before drybrushing.
basing-glue-and-tools.super glue or pva for bases: PVA for sand and loose cover, super glue for quick fixes or handled tufts. Super glue can leave a white bloom.
basing-glue-and-tools.basing kit essentials: PVA glue, thin and gel super glue, two part epoxy for heavy parts, sand in mixed sizes and a spatula for paste.

blending-colour-choice.which colours blend well: Colours of the same hue, or ones similar in strength and brightness, blend smoothly. Opposites go muddy unless glazed.
blending-colour-choice.blend went muddy: Opposite colours mix to a muddy middle when wet blended. Glaze the transition instead, or use simpler colours.
blending-colour-choice.blending two different colours: Adjust one colour until both are close in brightness first, then let the first run past the join and layer the second over.
blending-colour-choice.why does my blend look dirty: Mixed pigments can fight and go grey or brown. Use single pigment paints where the blend must stay clean.
blending-colour-choice.blending opposite colours: Wet blending opposites gives a muddy middle, so glaze the transition instead of mixing them on the model.
blending-colour-choice.blending red into green: See: opposite colours like these go muddy when wet blended, so this entry suggests glazing the transition.
blending-colour-choice.smooth blend between hues: Bring the two hues close in brightness, let the first run past the join, then layer barely thinned second colour over it.
blending-colour-choice.colours that mix nicely for a gradient: Same hue colours at different strengths, or similarly muted hues, blend smoothly into a gradient.
blending-colour-choice.blending colours goes grey: Greying means the pigments are fighting. Use paints made from a single pigment where the blend must stay clean.
blending-colour-choice.can i blend purple into yellow: See: blending clashing colours, which this entry says to bring closer in brightness first or glaze between.

brush-and-airbrush.airbrush and brush together: Brush the light and shadow first, spray thinned colours lightly to smooth the joins, then finish edges and texture by hand.
brush-and-airbrush.should i airbrush or brush: Use the airbrush for smooth gradients, soft blends and filters, and the brush for placing light, edges and fine detail.
brush-and-airbrush.airbrush looks too soft: Sketch light and shadow by brush first, and only spray thin, close passes to soften the joins, not cover them.
brush-and-airbrush.combining airbrush with brush highlights: Paint brushed highlights a bit larger and brighter, then spray very thin colours close and light along the joins.
brush-and-airbrush.airbrush for gradients brush for edges: Yes: brush the highlights, spray thinned colours lightly over the joins to smooth them, then redo edges by hand.
brush-and-airbrush.model looks obviously airbrushed: Spraying alone from the start often looks soft with light in the wrong place. Sketch light and shadow by brush first.
brush-and-airbrush.airbrush filters over brushwork: A thin filter sprayed over the whole area ties it together, though it shifts the colour a little.
brush-and-airbrush.when to use the airbrush: Use it for smooth gradients, soft transitions, filters and quick even base coats, before the fine brush work.
brush-and-airbrush.mixing brush painting and airbrush: Brush the light and shadow, spray thin passes to smooth the joins, then finish edges, texture and details by hand.
brush-and-airbrush.airbrush workflow: Airbrush stages first, so overspray gets painted over, then brush the highlights, edges, textures and details.

building-ruined-walls.ruined walls: Plan the break from the top down and around doors and windows, show bricks or rebar at the edge, and pile rubble below.
building-ruined-walls.how to make ruins: Draw the break line, cut walls from foam board or card, expose bricks at the break and pile rubble where it fell.
building-ruined-walls.battle damaged building: Break walls from the top and around windows, leave corners tallest, and add exposed bricks, rebar and rubble at the foot.
building-ruined-walls.broken wall terrain: Plan the break line, cut or snap the edge so it looks shattered, and show bricks or stones along it.
building-ruined-walls.rubble piles: Pile rubble against the foot of walls and under holes, mixing large chunks, mid pieces and fine grit fixed with thin glue.
building-ruined-walls.bombed out house: Break walls from the top down and around doors and windows, add sagging floors with ragged holes, then pile rubble below.
building-ruined-walls.ruined floor tiles: Score tiles into card or plastic sheet, break holes with ragged edges and let joists stick out underneath.
building-ruined-walls.make a wall look blown apart: Snip plastic walls roughly, then snap small bits off with pliers so the edge looks shattered, not sliced.
building-ruined-walls.scratch built ruins from foam board: Draw the break line, cut the foam board, add foam or card bricks along the break and wire rebar in concrete edges.
building-ruined-walls.where to put rubble: Where it would fall: against the foot of walls and under holes in walls and floors.

cast-shadows.cast shadows: Paint the dark shape one part throws onto another, mapped with a one direction white spray or copied from a lit photo.
cast-shadows.shadow of arm on chest: Spray white from one direction or photograph the model under a lamp, then fill the arm's shadow with dark local colour.
cast-shadows.shadow from a beard: Map where the beard blocks the light, then fill that shape with a dark version of the body colour, edge slightly soft.
cast-shadows.how to paint a shadow on the model: Map it with a one direction spray or a lit photo, then fill the shape with dark local colour, softening its edge slightly.
cast-shadows.advanced lighting shadows: Cast shadows show where one part blocks the light. Map them from a one direction spray or a lit photo, then paint them.
cast-shadows.zenithal for shadows: Prime black and spray thin white from one fixed direction only; the areas overhangs shield stay black as your shadow map.
cast-shadows.realistic shadow shapes: Copy them from a photo of the model lit by a lamp, or from a one direction white spray over black primer.
cast-shadows.dramatic light from one side: Spray white from one side only, or light it with a lamp and photograph it, then paint the shadows to match.
cast-shadows.painting where one part blocks light: Fill the shadow shape with a dark version of the local colour, keeping small lit details sharp and the edge slightly soft.
cast-shadows.cast shadow under a hat brim: Map the brim's shadow with a one direction spray or lit photo, then fill it with a dark version of the face colour.

choosing-army-colours.how do i pick colours for my army: Pick a main, a secondary and one spot colour from an idea you like, keep the rest neutral, and test on one model.
choosing-army-colours.army colour scheme ideas: Start from an idea, such as an insect, bird, flag or film, often one simple contrast, then pick main, secondary and spot.
choosing-army-colours.choosing a colour scheme: Choose a main, a secondary and one spot colour on every model, with neutrals elsewhere, then prove it on a test model.
choosing-army-colours.what colours go together: Strong pairings such as yellow and black read well. Try the colour opposite your main colour as a spot colour.
choosing-army-colours.custom paint scheme: Start from an idea, keep it to a main, a secondary and a spot colour, and test it on one model before committing.
choosing-army-colours.spot colour: One accent colour that appears on every model. Try the colour opposite your main colour on the wheel.
choosing-army-colours.test model for scheme: Paint the most complicated model start to finish, write down every step, and drop anything slow or that fails.
choosing-army-colours.army colors: Pick a main colour, a secondary for trim and one spot colour on every model, and keep everything else neutral.
choosing-army-colours.main colour and secondary colour: The main colour covers big surfaces, the secondary covers cloth or trim, and neutrals fill the rest.
choosing-army-colours.colour palette for warband: A main, a secondary and a spot colour kept on every model, with neutrals like grey, brown and metal for the rest.

clear-plastic-parts.clear canopy fogged: Super glue fumes leave a white frost inside clear plastic that cannot be cleaned off. Use a tiny bit of PVA instead.
clear-plastic-parts.super glue fogging clear parts: Its fumes frost clear plastic permanently. Fix clear parts with a tiny amount of white PVA in the back corners.
clear-plastic-parts.gluing a cockpit canopy: Glue it last, with a tiny amount of white PVA in the back corners. It dries clear and matt, and excess wipes off.
clear-plastic-parts.painting clear plastic: Leave clear parts unvarnished, use inks and thin glazes on effect parts, and scuff or film frames so paint grips.
clear-plastic-parts.visor glue: Use a tiny amount of white PVA glue in the back corners. It sets slowly but dries clear and matt.
clear-plastic-parts.clear parts frosted: That frost is from super glue fumes or varnish, and cannot be cleaned off. Use PVA and mask clear parts when varnishing.
clear-plastic-parts.how to glue windows: Glue windows with a small amount of white PVA after painting is done; avoid super glue and plastic glue.
clear-plastic-parts.clear flying base painting: See: the entry covers clear effect parts, which take a light satin varnish as primer and thin glazes over it.
clear-plastic-parts.paint wont stick to clear plastic: Scuff frame lines with a fine abrasive, or brush on a thinned coat and wipe it off so the film gives grip.
clear-plastic-parts.transparent parts: Fit them last with PVA, do not varnish them, and paint clear effect parts with inks and thin glazes.

colour-variety-in-one-colour.flat colour looks boring: Paint loose patches of other hues underneath, then glaze the intended colour thinly over the top so it reads with depth.
colour-variety-in-one-colour.make red more interesting: Underpaint loose greens, pinks, oranges or purples, then glaze thin red over so it still reads red but with depth.
colour-variety-in-one-colour.colour variety: Layer several hues underneath, then glaze the final colour over in thin coats so the area stays rich, not flat.
colour-variety-in-one-colour.rich colours: Place varied hues loosely under the final colour, then glaze it over thinly so they show through.
colour-variety-in-one-colour.add other hues under a colour: Paint greens, pinks, oranges or purples loosely where they suit the form, then glaze the main colour over thinly.
colour-variety-in-one-colour.colour looks flat and lifeless: Underpaint a range of hues, then glaze the colour over thinly. Keep the glaze thin so the colours beneath stay.
colour-variety-in-one-colour.painterly colour shifts: Paint varied hues underneath and glaze the intended colour over thinly; real materials are never one flat colour.
colour-variety-in-one-colour.single colour cloak looks dull: Underpaint the cloak with loose patches of other hues, then glaze the cloak colour thinly over the top.
colour-variety-in-one-colour.underpainting: Paint a range of hues loosely under the area, then glaze the intended colour over in thin coats.
colour-variety-in-one-colour.color variation in one area: Lay down a range of hues, then glaze the intended colour thinly over them, so the area keeps variety.

consistent-bases.bases look different across army: Write down your base materials and colours, use the same ones every time, and paint every rim the same colour.
consistent-bases.matching bases: Use the same materials and colours on every base, vary rock and tuft placement, and paint every rim alike.
consistent-bases.how do i keep my bases consistent: Record your texture, rocks, tufts and rim colour, reuse them each time, and carry the ground colour onto the feet.
consistent-bases.same base for whole army: Base a batch in one go with the same materials, but cluster rocks and tufts unevenly so they are not identical.
consistent-bases.bases painted months apart: Written notes on materials and colours let you match them later, and an identical rim colour ties them together.
consistent-bases.base recipe: Write down the texture, rocks, rubble, tufts and rim colour you use, and repeat them on every base.
consistent-bases.uniform basing: Same materials and colours on every base, same rim colour, but vary rocks, tufts and dust so each looks natural.
consistent-bases.tie models together with bases: Carry a hint of the ground onto the feet and lower parts, such as snow or mud, and keep the rim colour the same.
consistent-bases.mud on feet to match base: Add dust or mud on the lower legs and carry a hint of the ground colour onto them so models look like they stand there.
consistent-bases.basing consistency: Note your materials and colours, use them every time, paint all rims the same, and tie models in with ground on their feet.

creature-eyes.monster eyes: Keep them bright and glossy: a coloured eye shaded to the rim, or white under clear gloss colour, with a tiny white dot.
creature-eyes.how to paint animal eyes: Block in a strong colour leaving a dark rim, shade the edge, add a pupil and a tiny white dot, then gloss varnish it.
creature-eyes.yellow beast eyes: Strong yellow over a light undercoat with a dark rim, orange round the edge, white towards the middle, then a white dot.
creature-eyes.glossy eyes: Gloss varnish the eyes if the rest of the model is matt. A dab of gloss over pure black looks wet and glassy.
creature-eyes.dragon eye: Yellow shaded orange at the edge and white in the centre, a thin black slit pupil, a white dot, and gloss to finish.
creature-eyes.cat like eyes: Paint the eye yellow with an orange edge, then add one thin, straight vertical black line as a slit pupil.
creature-eyes.creature eye gloss: Gloss varnish the eyes if the model is matt, or paint white and add two coats of a clear glossy colour.
creature-eyes.amber eyes: Strong yellow with a thin dark rim, orange round the edge blended to white in the middle, and a tiny white dot.
creature-eyes.make eyes look wet: Add a tiny white dot in one corner, and dab gloss varnish over them. Gloss over flat black looks glassy.
creature-eyes.evil glowing creature eyes: Paint them white, then two coats of a clear glossy red, green or blue. The white underneath makes them glow.

damp-patches-and-drips.make cloth look wet: Paint wet areas a step or two darker and gloss them, darkest at the hem and fading upwards.
damp-patches-and-drips.water stains on a model: Paint a ragged dusty off white line along the top of a darker patch as a dried tide mark.
damp-patches-and-drips.drips of water: Run thin streaks down from edges, rivets and seams in a darker, cooler tint, softening the top with a damp brush.
damp-patches-and-drips.damp patches: Make the area a step or two darker than the surface, then put satin or gloss varnish over it.
damp-patches-and-drips.soaked hem of a robe: Glaze thin dark brown from the hem upwards, darkest at the bottom, then gloss it.
damp-patches-and-drips.wet boots from walking in water: Darken boots and lower legs from the bottom up with a thin dark brown glaze, then gloss it.
damp-patches-and-drips.how do i make a model look like it came: See: wet effects, where patches go darker and glossy, drips run straight down and gloss drops hang at low points.
damp-patches-and-drips.dripping wet look: Darken and gloss the wet areas, run drip streaks from edges, and dot gloss drops on the lowest points.
damp-patches-and-drips.water droplets with gloss: Dot gloss varnish or clear resin on the lowest points, such as under a chin or hem, building them up slowly.
damp-patches-and-drips.dark shiny wet patches: Use the same colour one or two steps darker, with satin or gloss varnish over the top.

disposing-of-paint-water.can i pour paint water down the sink: Many do, with plenty of running water, but some areas ask you not to. Settling it and binning the dried sludge is kinder.
disposing-of-paint-water.getting rid of rinse water: Leave it in a jar a day or two, pour off the clear water, let the sludge dry and scrape it into household waste.
disposing-of-paint-water.disposing of white spirit: Never pour it down a drain. Let solids settle, reuse the clear part, and take the rest to a hazardous waste site.
disposing-of-paint-water.resin waste disposal: Never pour it down a drain. Cure dirty liquid in sunlight or under a lamp until the resin sets, then filter it.
disposing-of-paint-water.dirty brush water: Let it settle in a jar, pour off the clear water and put the dried sludge in the bin. Check your local rules.
disposing-of-paint-water.is paint water bad for drains: It holds only a little acrylic, but settling it and binning the dried sludge is kinder to drains.
disposing-of-paint-water.what to do with used thinners: See: oil and enamel thinners, which this entry says to settle, reuse the clear part and take to a hazardous waste site.
disposing-of-paint-water.isopropyl waste: See: resin rinse, which this entry says to leave in sunlight or under a lamp until the resin sets, never down a drain.
disposing-of-paint-water.3d print resin cleanup: Cure dirty liquid, failed prints, supports and wet paper towels in sunlight or under a lamp until hard. Wear gloves.
disposing-of-paint-water.safe disposal of acrylic paint: Let rinse water settle, pour off the clear part, and bin the dried sludge, or soak larger amounts into cat litter to dry.

drybrushing-cloth.drybrush a cloak: Use a big soft brush kept faintly damp, wipe off on card, test on your thumb, and stipple then flick over the folds.
drybrushing-cloth.drybrushing robes: Drybrush heavy folds with a large soft brush in light passes, two or three colours each a touch lighter.
drybrushing-cloth.fast cloak highlights: Drybrush with a big soft brush in two or three lightening passes, then highlight the top edges by hand.
drybrushing-cloth.folded cloth drybrush: Stipple onto raised folds and flick along sharp creases with a big, faintly damp soft brush, lightening each pass.
drybrushing-cloth.drybrush streaky: Streaks mean too much paint or too small a brush. Use a big soft brush and wipe more paint off before you start.
drybrushing-cloth.soft brush for drybrushing: Use a medium or large soft round brush, even on a small cloak. A small brush leaves streaks.
drybrushing-cloth.how to highlight a cloak quickly: Drybrush it early with a big soft brush in two or three lighter passes, then wash the cloth to tie them together.
drybrushing-cloth.dry brushing fabric: Use a big, faintly damp soft brush, wipe it on coated card, and stipple onto raised folds in light, lightening passes.
drybrushing-cloth.robes with lots of folds: Heavily folded cloth drybrushes well. Use a big soft brush and build two or three slightly lighter passes.
drybrushing-cloth.big cape highlights: Use a large soft brush, light passes in lightening colours, then a soft pale colour or hand painted top edges.

dynamic-posing.dynamic pose: Oppose arms and legs, lean the body into the move, turn the head to the action, and try it with sticky tack first.
dynamic-posing.how to pose a model: Decide the mood, oppose arms and legs, lean it into the move, and test poses with sticky tack before gluing.
dynamic-posing.model looks stiff: Lean it slightly into the movement, swing arms opposite the legs and turn the head towards the action.
dynamic-posing.action pose for a conversion: Cut off the locating nubs so joints turn, then mock up with sticky tack and lean the body into the move.
dynamic-posing.heroic pose: Pick head, pose and extras to suit the mood, oppose arms and legs, and lean the body into the movement.
dynamic-posing.mock up a pose with sticky tack: Join parts with small blobs of sticky tack, try poses on the base, check front and side, then glue the ones you keep.
dynamic-posing.where to put the arms: When a leg is back, bring the arm on that side forward, and the other way round.
dynamic-posing.make the model look like it is moving: Oppose arms and legs, lean the whole model into the movement and tilt the head to follow that line.
dynamic-posing.pose a model before gluing: Dry fit parts with sticky tack, try several heads and arms, check front and side, then glue and build from there.
dynamic-posing.leaning into the charge: Lean the whole model into the move, slightly off balance, and tilt the head to follow that line.

fabric-textures.cloth texture: Add sparse fine cross hatching or tiny stitch marks with each highlight, only on the lit areas.
fabric-textures.how do i make cloth look like wool: Base a little darker than the midtone, then paint rows of tiny angled V strokes like knitted stitches.
fabric-textures.crosshatching on fabric: Paint a few short fine lines one way, turn the model, add a few the other way, and repeat with each highlight.
fabric-textures.tweed pattern: See: busy flecked fabric, which this entry makes by sponging a lighter tone of the same colour, then highlighting folds.
fabric-textures.stitches on clothing: Paint rows of tiny angled V strokes like stitches, and short evenly spaced vertical lines for ribbed cuffs.
fabric-textures.linen texture on a robe: Thin a highlight colour and paint sparse short lines one way, then the other, repeating with each highlight.
fabric-textures.hessian sacking: Use short broken strokes or dabs for highlights instead of smooth layers. The gaps read as a rough weave.
fabric-textures.knitted jumper texture: Paint rows of tiny angled V stitches over a darker base, then repaint some in lighter mixes, covering fewer each time.
fabric-textures.cloak looks plastic: Add texture where light hits: fine cross hatching, broken highlight strokes or tiny stitches so it reads as cloth.
fabric-textures.fabric looks like skin: Texture makes cloth read differently from skin. Add fine hatching or stitch marks on the lit areas.

filament-3d-prints.3d printed terrain: Filament suits big terrain. Glue the parts, fill seams with putty, then hide layer lines with filler primer or thin epoxy.
filament-3d-prints.layer lines on prints: Coat with thick filler primer, dry, sand and repeat, or brush very thin two part epoxy into every recess to level them.
filament-3d-prints.hide print lines: Build up and sand thick filler primer until the lines go, or brush on a thin coat of epoxy resin, which levels itself.
filament-3d-prints.filament printer terrain: Filament suits large terrain and is easy with little smell. Use supports under overhangs and finer layers for looks.
filament-3d-prints.fdm terrain: Clean off supports, glue with super glue, fill seams with putty that grips plastic, then filler prime or epoxy the lines.
filament-3d-prints.resin or filament for terrain: Filament suits big terrain; resin gives finer detail but has a small build area and is messy in bulk.
filament-3d-prints.filler primer for prints: Coat, dry and sand, repeating until layer lines are gone. Keep it off fine detail, which it buries.
filament-3d-prints.prepping 3d prints: Remove supports, scrape rough spots, dry fit and glue, fill seams with putty, then hide layer lines before priming.
filament-3d-prints.printed buildings: Check the scale, print with supports, glue and fill seams, smooth layer lines, then prime and paint like your figures.
filament-3d-prints.pla terrain painting: Smooth the layer lines, prime, and paint with the same acrylics as your figures so it matches them on the table.

fix-airbrush-bubbling.airbrush bubbling: Air is leaking backwards at the nozzle. Tighten the nozzle and cap until snug, reseat the needle, and test with water.
fix-airbrush-bubbling.bubbles in the paint cup: Air is escaping back at the nozzle joint or a blockage. Snug up the nozzle and cap, then test with plain water.
fix-airbrush-bubbling.airbrush foaming at the tip: Foam at the front is the same backward leak, often after cleaning. Do up the front cap and nozzle until snug.
fix-airbrush-bubbling.air coming back into the cup: Air is leaking back at the nozzle. Tighten it until snug and add a thin film of petroleum jelly round a seated nozzle.
fix-airbrush-bubbling.nozzle leaking air: Tighten the nozzle and cap until snug, and on seated nozzles brush a thin film of petroleum jelly round the base.
fix-airbrush-bubbling.airbrush blowing back: Tighten the nozzle and cap, check the needle is fully seated, then test with water. If it persists, deep clean it.
fix-airbrush-bubbling.bubbles after cleaning my airbrush: A cap or nozzle was probably not fully done up. Tighten both until snug with the wrench and test with water.
fix-airbrush-bubbling.airbrush gurgling: That is air leaking back into the cup. Snug up the nozzle and cap, reseat the needle, then test with plain water.
fix-airbrush-bubbling.air leak at nozzle: Tighten the nozzle until snug, without overtightening, and seal a seated nozzle base with a thin film of petroleum jelly.
fix-airbrush-bubbling.why does my airbrush bubble: Air is leaking backwards, usually at the nozzle joint or from a blockage. Reseat and seal the nozzle, then test.

fix-frosted-varnish.varnish went white: Moisture got trapped as it dried. Leave it a day, then a thin coat of trusted varnish in dry weather often clears it.
fix-frosted-varnish.model frosted after varnish: Leave it about 24 hours, then spray or brush another thin coat in good conditions. The fresh layer often clears the haze.
fix-frosted-varnish.cloudy varnish: Cloudiness usually comes from damp air, a poorly shaken can, heavy coats or spraying from too far away.
fix-frosted-varnish.varnish fogging: Fogging is trapped moisture. Spray only on a dry, mild day, after the paint has fully dried, in thin even passes.
fix-frosted-varnish.matt spray left white haze: Leave it a day, then add a thin coat of a varnish you trust in good conditions, and touch up white spots with paint.
fix-frosted-varnish.varnish frosting humidity: Spray below about 50 percent humidity, on a dry mild day, and avoid cold, damp or very hot conditions.
fix-frosted-varnish.fix frosted model: Leave it 24 hours and recoat thinly in dry conditions. If that fails, a thin olive oil coat wiped off can lift it.
fix-frosted-varnish.why did my varnish go milky: Damp air trapped moisture under it, or the can was not shaken enough. Spray thin passes on a dry day.
fix-frosted-varnish.spray varnish chalky: From too far away the varnish part dries in the air and lands grainy. Spray thin passes from about 15 to 30 cm.
fix-frosted-varnish.varnish dusty white: Usually trapped moisture or an unshaken can. Shake it a full minute and spray on a dry day, then recoat to rescue it.

fix-thick-varnish-or-primer.primer too thick: Stop and let it cure a full day, as it shrinks. Wick out wet pools and strip the model if detail is buried all over.
fix-thick-varnish-or-primer.varnish filled the detail: Let it cure a full day, then work the dried varnish out of recesses with a stiff fine brush and a little water.
fix-thick-varnish-or-primer.lost detail after spraying: Let it cure, as some detail often returns. If thick coats have buried it all over, strip and prime again.
fix-thick-varnish-or-primer.primer pooling in recesses: While still wet, wick pools out of recesses with a clean damp brush and tilt the model so the excess runs off.
fix-thick-varnish-or-primer.too much varnish: Stop adding coats and let it dry a full day. Work small filled recesses out with a stiff fine brush and thinner.
fix-thick-varnish-or-primer.clogged detail: Let it cure, then work a few filled recesses clear with a stiff fine brush and a drop of water, a little at a time.
fix-thick-varnish-or-primer.thick spray coat: Spray light misty passes from about 20 to 30 cm, letting each dry. If detail is buried everywhere, strip and redo it.
fix-thick-varnish-or-primer.should i strip it: Yes, if thick coats have buried detail all over. Strip, wash, dry, then prime and paint again.
fix-thick-varnish-or-primer.varnish pools: While wet, wick pools out with a clean damp brush. Once dry, work them out with a stiff fine brush and a little water.
fix-thick-varnish-or-primer.detail gone after primer: Wait a full day, since primer shrinks as it cures. If detail is still buried all over, strip it and prime again.

fluorescent-paints.fluorescent paint: Paint the area solid white first, then build three or four barely thinned coats of the fluorescent colour over it.
fluorescent-paints.neon paint: Fluorescent colours only glow over solid white. Paint the source white and glaze or spray the colour over it.
fluorescent-paints.uv paint: Fluorescents light up under ultraviolet light, but they need a solid white undercoat to glow brightly.
fluorescent-paints.fluorescent over black does nothing: They are very translucent, so over black they do almost nothing. Paint the area solid white first.
fluorescent-paints.fluorescent looks patchy: Over light grey they look patchy. Undercoat solid white, then build three or four coats, each dry first.
fluorescent-paints.neon colours: Use them as a small accent over solid white: orange for fire, green for toxic glow, pink for magic.
fluorescent-paints.fluoro paint tips: Shake hard, use clean water, paint over solid white, and build three or four barely diluted coats.
fluorescent-paints.blacklight paint: Fluorescents light up under ultraviolet light. Paint them over solid white for the strongest glow.
fluorescent-paints.does fluorescent paint need white: Yes. They are very translucent and only glow over a solid, opaque white undercoat.
fluorescent-paints.super bright glow: Alternate thin white and fluorescent layers over solid white for a stronger glow, and keep it as a small accent.

freehand-painting.freehand: Break the design into simple shapes, place it from the centre, paint it roughly, then cut back with the background colour.
freehand-painting.how do i paint a design on a banner: Paint it before gluing on, mark the centre and work outwards, then tidy the edges with the background colour.
freehand-painting.shield designs: Sketch the design at size on paper, mark the centre, place it faintly, then block in and cut back with the background.
freehand-painting.painting patterns by hand: Break patterns into lines and shapes, place them faintly first, then go bolder and tidy with the background colour.
freehand-painting.freehand tips: Paint on a smooth base coat before shading, start thin, and fix wobbles with the background colour.
freehand-painting.symbol on a cloak: Follow the folds and hems, mark the centre, place it faintly in a colour near the cloak's, then block in and tidy.
freehand-painting.free hand painting: Thin paint to flow, use a sharp size 1 or 2 upright in short strokes, and start with thin lines.
freehand-painting.checkerboard pattern: See: freehand basics in this entry: plan simple shapes, place them from the centre and tidy with the background colour.
freehand-painting.logo on a tank: Mark the centre, place it faintly, block it in roughly, and carve the shape clean with the base colour.
freehand-painting.fixing wobbly freehand: Paint the background colour back into the edges, or hide wobbly spots under a few chips.

glazing-for-smooth-gradients.glazing: Build colour with many thin, nearly dry glazes, each stopping a little short of the last, letting each dry fully.
glazing-for-smooth-gradients.smooth gradients: Plan the brightest and darkest points, then layer thin glazes that each cover less area, drying fully between them.
glazing-for-smooth-gradients.how to glaze: Wick most of the glaze off the brush, stroke so each pass stops short of the last, and let every layer dry fully.
glazing-for-smooth-gradients.glazing with thin paint: Thin glazes build a smooth, steerable gradient. Expect to see almost nothing at first, and let each layer dry.
glazing-for-smooth-gradients.smooth transitions: Glaze dark up into the light, then thin light back down, and use a milk thin base colour glaze to blend the steps.
glazing-for-smooth-gradients.wash pools unevenly: On big panels, use many thin glazes instead of a flooded wash. They build smoother and do not pool.
glazing-for-smooth-gradients.glaze shadows: Glaze dark over less and less area towards the deepest point; switch to a deeper colour if it will not get dark enough.
glazing-for-smooth-gradients.deep shadows smooth: Build shadows with many thin glazes, each covering less area, and use a deeper glaze colour for the darkest point.
glazing-for-smooth-gradients.build colour slowly: Use many thin glazes, each stopping short of the last. After five passes the strong end carries five times the colour.
glazing-for-smooth-gradients.glazes too wet: Blotches mean the brush was too wet or the mix too thick. Wick off almost all the glaze and add more thin coats.

glowing-magic-terrain.glowing runes: Base the runes bright warm ivory, tint with strong magenta, then layer hot pink, fluorescent pink and an ivory mix centre.
glowing-magic-terrain.magic glow: Warm ivory base, a strong tint into recesses, then opaque and fluorescent layers brightest in the centres.
glowing-magic-terrain.glowing terrain: Base glowing parts warm ivory, then strong tints and fluorescent top layers, and mist thin ink in patches across the piece.
glowing-magic-terrain.spell effect: Warm ivory base, a strong tint, then brighter opaque and fluorescent layers in the centres where light is strongest.
glowing-magic-terrain.pink magic: Warm ivory base, a one coat magenta, then hot pink, fluorescent pink, and fluorescent with ivory in the centres.
glowing-magic-terrain.glowing crystals: Base the crystals warm ivory, then tint, layer up brighter, and finish with a fluorescent top layer in the centres.
glowing-magic-terrain.magic portal: Shade the recesses dark, paint patches of two opposite colours side by side, soften the joins and add bright dots.
glowing-magic-terrain.arcane glow on scenery: Mist thin ink in the glow colour in patches and under overhangs so the light seems to come from the piece itself.
glowing-magic-terrain.glowing magic looks dull: Strong colours turn dull over a dark base. Base the glow warm ivory first, and pick a colour opposite the surroundings.
glowing-magic-terrain.bright magic effect: Base it warm ivory, layer strong and fluorescent colours, and choose a glow opposite the surroundings on the colour wheel.

graphic-painting-style.box art style: Prime black, push bold light and shadow, blend smooth gradients on panels, and finish with neat thin edge highlights.
graphic-painting-style.graphic style painting: Bold light and shadow, smooth gradients on panels and crisp edge lines give a clean, illustrated look.
graphic-painting-style.high contrast clean style: Push contrast further than feels natural, blend smooth panel gradients and add neat edge highlights everywhere.
graphic-painting-style.comic book style: See: this entry's bold, graphic style, with strong contrast, smooth panel gradients and crisp edge highlights.
graphic-painting-style.how do i get a crisp illustrated look: Prime black, choose a focal point, blend smooth gradients on flat panels and edge every panel with a thin highlight.
graphic-painting-style.painting like the box art: Prime black, be brave with contrast, blend smooth panel gradients, edge every panel and paint details cleanly.
graphic-painting-style.bold light and shadow: Prime black, mark light and dark blocks, blend between them, and be braver with contrast than feels natural.
graphic-painting-style.model looks flat at arm's length: Timid contrast reads as flat from arm's length. Push light and shadow harder, especially at the focal point.
graphic-painting-style.cartoon style painting: See: this entry's clean graphic style, built on bold contrast, smooth gradients and crisp edge lines.
graphic-painting-style.clean studio style: Prime black, push contrast, blend smooth panel gradients, edge highlight neatly, and finish details completely.

hazard-stripes.hazard stripes: Paint the band yellow first, mark stripes with pencil or tape, then black over it at one even width and angle.
hazard-stripes.yellow and black stripes: Yellow first over a white or grey undercoat, then black stripes over it. Black covers yellow in one coat.
hazard-stripes.warning stripes on a tank: Yellow band first, stripes marked with pencil or tape at about 45 degrees, then black dabbed in at even widths.
hazard-stripes.how to paint chevrons: Paint yellow, mark the angled stripes with pencil or thin tape, then fill black with stripes as wide as the gaps.
hazard-stripes.even stripes: Lay three tape strips side by side and pull out the middle one for even gaps, then dab black on lightly.
hazard-stripes.stripes on a vehicle: Paint yellow first, then mark the stripes with thin tape at about 45 degrees and dab or sponge the black on.
hazard-stripes.hazard marking on doors: Paint the band yellow, mark stripes with pencil or tape, and black them in at the same width and angle.
hazard-stripes.tape for stripes: Lay thin tape at about 45 degrees, dab or sponge the black on with little paint so it does not creep under.
hazard-stripes.yellow black hazard: Paint yellow, then black at one width and angle. Over black, use dull orange ochre edged with golden yellow.
hazard-stripes.stripes keep wobbling: Use thin, free flowing black, pick one comfortable angle, and fix slips by cutting back in with yellow.

highlighting-warm-metals.highlight gold: Use a pale, slightly muted gold rather than silver, on the sharpest edges first, then glazed thinly over brighter flats.
highlighting-warm-metals.highlighting bronze: Highlight bronze with a pale gold, not silver, after a warm brown wash and gold layered back on the flats.
highlighting-warm-metals.copper highlights: Use pale gold for metallic copper. On painted copper, build lights with orange then warm yellow, white only last.
highlighting-warm-metals.silver on gold looks wrong: Silver is shiny but looks out of place. Use a pale gold, or step towards silver in mixes on smaller areas.
highlighting-warm-metals.brass highlight: Use a pale gold highlight rather than silver, edging the sharpest points first.
highlighting-warm-metals.how to highlight gold: Base warm mid gold, wash warm brown, layer gold back on flats, then edge the sharpest points in pale gold.
highlighting-warm-metals.warm metals: Shade gold, bronze and copper with warm brown, and highlight them with a pale gold rather than silver.
highlighting-warm-metals.bronze armour: Warm mid gold base, a warm brown or red brown wash, then pale gold highlights on the sharpest edges.
highlighting-warm-metals.copper pipes: Shade with a warm brown wash, then highlight with pale gold. On painted copper, use orange and warm yellow.
highlighting-warm-metals.gold edge highlight colour: A pale, slightly muted gold. Keep pure silver only for the last tiny edges and dots if you want extra shine.

how-long-painting-takes.how long does it take to paint a model: Roughly: 20 to 60 minutes for quick tabletop, 2 to 4 hours for good tabletop, and 10 to 30 hours or more for display.
how-long-painting-takes.am i painting too slow: Probably not. Beginners often take twice as long as these rough guides, and that is normal.
how-long-painting-takes.how long per mini: Roughly 20 to 60 minutes quick, 2 to 4 hours for good tabletop, and 10 to 30 hours or more for display.
how-long-painting-takes.time to paint one figure: A quick tabletop figure takes 20 to 60 minutes, good tabletop about 2 to 4 hours, display 10 to 30 hours or more.
how-long-painting-takes.painting takes forever: Drying time adds up, so 3 hours of work can take two or three evenings. Batch painting cuts quick models down.
how-long-painting-takes.how many hours for display: Display standard is about 10 to 30 hours or more for one figure. Busts and big display pieces can pass 40.
how-long-painting-takes.tabletop painting time: Quick tabletop is 20 to 60 minutes per model, or 15 to 30 in a batch. Good tabletop is about 2 to 4 hours.
how-long-painting-takes.how fast should i paint: There is no set pace. Time yourself on one model, then decide where to save time and where to spend it.
how-long-painting-takes.beginner painting speed: Beginners often take twice as long as the rough guides, and that is normal.
how-long-painting-takes.hours per model: About 20 to 60 minutes for quick tabletop, 2 to 4 hours for good tabletop, 10 to 30 or more for display.

judging-colours-in-context.colours look wrong: A colour looks different against primer than on the finished model. Block in the neighbouring colours before judging it.
judging-colours-in-context.colour looked fine until finished: It was judged against bare primer. Rough in the colours that touch an area early, so you see it in context.
judging-colours-in-context.judging skin tone on primer: Pale skin next to pale primer is hard to judge. Block in the hair, cloth and armour around the face first.
judging-colours-in-context.block in colours first: Block each main area in fairly thick until no primer shows, then decide what needs more warmth or contrast.
judging-colours-in-context.colour changes next to others: Colours change against their neighbours, so rough in the touching colours early before you finish any area.
judging-colours-in-context.paint looks different on the model: Primer changes how a colour reads. Block in all the main colours first, then judge and refine.
judging-colours-in-context.colours dont work together: Block everything in first, squint to check it reads, then adjust warmth, contrast or saturation while changes are quick.
judging-colours-in-context.hard to tell if colour is right: Rough in the colours around it first. A colour seen against primer looks different from the finished model.
judging-colours-in-context.skin looks pale against primer: Primer makes it hard to judge. Block in the hair, cloth and armour around the face, then judge the skin.
judging-colours-in-context.check colours together: Block in all the main colours roughly until no primer shows, then squint at the model and adjust.

layered-chips.deep chips: Sponge a pale chip, then fill a smaller dark centre inside it so a pale rim shows as primer around bare material.
layered-chips.chips showing primer: Fill pale chips with a smaller dark grey, dark brown or red primer colour centre, leaving a pale rim showing.
layered-chips.battle damage chips: Sponge pale chips where damage makes sense, then add dark or metal centres inside some, smaller so a pale rim shows.
layered-chips.chipping layers: Paint a pale chip, then a smaller dark or metal centre inside it, and a thin highlight along some lower edges.
layered-chips.bare metal chips: Dot dark steel along the chip edge and bright silver only at the hardest point of impact.
layered-chips.paint chips with metal centre: Paint a pale chip, then fill the middle with a smaller dark steel centre and bright silver at the hardest impact.
layered-chips.realistic chipping: Chip where damage makes sense, vary shapes, give some a dark centre with a pale rim, and keep scratches fine and few.
layered-chips.chips look like spots: Vary their shapes with a brush, give some dark centres inside pale rims, and highlight the lower edge of a few.
layered-chips.sponge chips pale ring: Sponge a pale mix of the armour colour, then fill the middle of some chips with a smaller dark centre.
layered-chips.heavy damage: For dents, paint a fairly straight light line, then a bigger uneven dark shape just above it.

lips-and-makeup.lips: Paint thin red following their shape, highlight the bottom lip with a pink mix, and add a tiny pale reflection point.
lips-and-makeup.how do i paint lips: Thin red on both lips, a red and pale yellow pink on the bottom lip, then a tiny pale dot. Keep the top lip darker.
lips-and-makeup.makeup on a face: After the skin is done, add thin glazes: red on lips, a cool tone on lids and soft pink under the cheekbones.
lips-and-makeup.eyeshadow: Glaze a cool turquoise or blue mixed with skin thinly on the lids, blending up towards the brow.
lips-and-makeup.blush on cheeks: Glaze a soft pink mixed from pink and skin tone under the cheekbones. Test it on a patch of skin colour first.
lips-and-makeup.lipstick: Thin red on both lips following their shape, a pinker highlight on the bottom lip and a tiny pale reflection.
lips-and-makeup.female face painting: Paint the skin first, then add thin red lips, a cool glaze on the lids and soft pink on the cheeks. Less is more.
lips-and-makeup.face looks lifeless: Small touches of colour on lips, eyelids and under the cheekbones add life. Paint them thinly over finished skin.
lips-and-makeup.red lips too bright: Mix the lip colour with skin tone, tint only the lower lip, or use a thinned bright red so it stays close to the skin.
lips-and-makeup.rosy cheeks: Glaze a soft pink mixed from pink and skin tone on the upper cheeks towards the front of the face.

marking-leaders-and-ranks.make leader stand out: Give leaders more accent colour, tint one shared detail like a plume or sash, and add upgrade parts or a fancier base.
marking-leaders-and-ranks.sergeant markings: Pick one fixed spot, such as a knee pad or helmet, and a simple rule like a stripe or a different helmet colour.
marking-leaders-and-ranks.squad leader colours: Give leaders more of your accent colour and extra edge highlights on it, and troops only small touches.
marking-leaders-and-ranks.show rank on models: Use the amount of accent colour, one marked detail, a fixed marking spot, or drab to bright clothing for rank.
marking-leaders-and-ranks.character stand out from troops: Reverse the scheme on the leader, swapping light and dark areas, and add swapped parts from the spares box.
marking-leaders-and-ranks.unit champion: Tint a small shared detail such as a plume in the accent colour, and give it more accent colour overall.
marking-leaders-and-ranks.officer details: Give officers trims, simple freehand patterns, more accent colour and a more detailed base.
marking-leaders-and-ranks.different leader base: Save detailed bases for leaders, and give the rest a simpler version in the same colours.
marking-leaders-and-ranks.accent colour for leaders: Give leaders more of the accent colour, with extra edge highlights on it, and troops only small touches.
marking-leaders-and-ranks.tell leaders apart: Mark one fixed detail in the accent colour, use more accent on leaders, or reverse their scheme.

metallic-paint-handling.glitter in my paint: Metallic flakes linger in water and brushes. Use a separate rinse pot and brushes for metallics.
metallic-paint-handling.metallic flakes in my wash: Flakes in a wash come from shared rinse water or brushes. Keep a separate pot and brushes for metallics.
metallic-paint-handling.metallic paint separates: Some separate on a wet palette within minutes. Use a dry palette or glazed tile and stir the puddle often.
metallic-paint-handling.separate brushes for metallics: Yes. Flakes lodge in the bristles and wear brushes out, so use separate, older soft synthetic brushes.
metallic-paint-handling.should i thin metallic paint: Only a little, with a drop of water to about the feel of milk. Too much water breaks up the flakes.
metallic-paint-handling.sparkly haze on matt colours: That haze comes from metallic flakes in rinse water or brushes. Change the water or use a separate pot.
metallic-paint-handling.separate water pot for metallics: Yes, or change the water before going back to other colours, as the flakes linger and show as glitter.
metallic-paint-handling.metallic paint tips: Shake well, thin only a little, build two or three thin coats, and keep separate water and brushes.
metallic-paint-handling.silver specks in my black: Flakes carried in shared water or brushes. Use a separate pot and brushes, and clean the palette after.
metallic-paint-handling.metallic splitting on wet palette: Move them to a dry palette or glazed tile and stir the puddle often.
metallic-paint-handling.How do I paint silver and gold metal?: See: handling metallics: shake well, thin a little, build thin coats, shade with a darker wash and highlight lighter.

mixing-skin-tones.mixing skin colours: Mix a red, a yellow, a blue and an off white. Orange plus off white gives a light warm skin; red and blue give deep brown.
mixing-skin-tones.how do i mix flesh tones: Mix a little red into a lot of yellow for orange, then add off white for a light, warm skin.
mixing-skin-tones.skin tone from primary colours: Red into yellow gives orange, plus off white for light skin. Red plus blue gives a deep brown for dark skin.
mixing-skin-tones.dark skin tone: Mix red and blue to a deep brown, then lift with off white for cool or add orange for a warmer dark brown.
mixing-skin-tones.pale skin: See: pale, delicate skin, which this entry makes by mixing a light cool blue into flesh, up to about four parts in ten.
mixing-skin-tones.skin looks orange: Mix in a light cool blue, up to about four parts in ten for pale skin. Switch to white once highlights look blue.
mixing-skin-tones.sickly skin: Add a touch of blue to cool it and let the yellow dominate.
mixing-skin-tones.realistic skin colours: Mix from red, yellow, blue and off white, mute bright flesh with grey, and match tones to the light.
mixing-skin-tones.brown skin mix: Combine red and blue brown with the orange and white mix, then nudge it warmer with orange or cooler with off white.
mixing-skin-tones.choosing skin colour: Match the light: warm sun means ochre and orange midtones, cold light means pink midtones and blue shadows.

moulds-and-casting.make moulds: Carve a stamp from cured putty on a block, or paint latex onto a rock and peel it off to make a reusable mould.
moulds-and-casting.silicone mould: Seal the masters, space them in a taped card box, pour slow curing silicone, then cast resin copies. Avoid undercuts.
moulds-and-casting.press mould: Spread epoxy putty on a wooden block, let it cure, carve a pattern, then press it into fresh putty on a base.
moulds-and-casting.casting bases: Cast flat backed plaster rocks from a latex mould, or cast resin inserts from silicone moulds of textured discs.
moulds-and-casting.repeat textures: Use a carved press stamp or a silicone or latex mould, so one master supplies textures for a whole army.
moulds-and-casting.stamp for bases: Carve a pattern into cured putty on a wooden block, then press it into fresh putty on each base. It lasts for years.
moulds-and-casting.copy base toppers: Build textures on thin plastic discs, mould them in slow curing silicone in a card box, and cast resin copies.
moulds-and-casting.texture stamp: Carve a pattern into cured epoxy putty on a small wooden block with a fine tool, then press it into fresh putty.
moulds-and-casting.green stuff mould: Epoxy putty pressed into a mould of reusable hot water moulding plastic cures in up to 8 hours and peels out.
moulds-and-casting.cast resin bits: Pour slow curing silicone over sealed masters in a card box, then cast resin. Heavily filled resin sands easily but is brittle.

nmm-cold-light.nmm in blue light: Mix a dark blue grey with the light colour for shadows, work up to blue green, and add a little pale yellow for top glints.
nmm-cold-light.non metallic metal moonlight: Shift the painted metal towards the cold light colour, keeping about a fifth of it even in the brightest dots.
nmm-cold-light.nmm at night: See: painted metal in cold light, shifting it towards blue green with pale yellow only for the top glints.
nmm-cold-light.blue nmm: Shadows of dark blue grey mixed with the light colour, working up to pure blue green and pale yellow for top glints.
nmm-cold-light.nmm with osl: Shift painted metal towards the glow colour, and line its highlights up with the lit areas on nearby armour and cloth.
nmm-cold-light.painted metal in green light: Mix the shadows from dark blue grey and the green light colour, work up to it, and add pale yellow for top glints.
nmm-cold-light.nmm turquoise: Shadows of dark blue grey with blue green, working up to pure blue green, with pale yellow for the top glints.
nmm-cold-light.how to do nmm in coloured lighting: Shift the metal towards the light colour, add pale yellow for top glints, and keep warmth on sides facing a warmer light.
nmm-cold-light.cold light painted steel: Mix dark blue grey with the cold light colour, work up towards it, and keep about a fifth of it in the brightest glints.
nmm-cold-light.nmm under a glowing source: Shift the metal towards the glow's colour and line its highlights up with the lit areas nearby.

oil-paints-on-models.oil paints: Oils go over dry acrylics. Thin with odourless mineral spirits, let them cure fully, seal with matt varnish, then go on.
oil-paints-on-models.how do i use oils on miniatures: Work oils over dry primed acrylics, thinned with mineral spirits. Blend and wipe back, cure, seal matt, then edge in acrylic.
oil-paints-on-models.oil wash: Thin oils with odourless mineral spirits. A gloss surface helps them run into recesses, and they stay wet for hours.
oil-paints-on-models.oils over acrylic: Oils work over acrylics dried about half an hour. Dry acrylic is not harmed unless you scrub it.
oil-paints-on-models.odourless mineral spirits: Use them to thin oils and clean the brush, not water, with a window open and low odour spirit.
oil-paints-on-models.oil paint dry time: Usually a day or more to cure. Thin layers dry faster than thick, and earth browns faster than greens and blues.
oil-paints-on-models.oil paint panel line: A gloss surface helps oil washes run into recesses, and you can wipe the excess back for hours.
oil-paints-on-models.oil weathering: See: oils over acrylics, which stay wet for hours so you can blend and wipe them back with a sponge.
oil-paints-on-models.blending with oils: Oils stay wet for hours, so blend and wipe them back long after acrylics would dry. They suit smooth skin.
oil-paints-on-models.oil paint on plastic: Always prime. Thin oil on unprimed plastic can damage it, while dry acrylic over primer is not harmed.

osl-colour-choice.which colour glows best: Cyan, turquoise, yellow, orange and green glow easily. Plain blue needs so much white it goes chalky.
osl-colour-choice.blue glow looks chalky: Blue needs lots of white for a bright core and goes chalky. Use cyan or turquoise, which stay saturated.
osl-colour-choice.what colour for object source lighting: Cyan, turquoise, yellow, orange or green, which reach a light core without losing saturation.
osl-colour-choice.my glow looks pale and washed out: Too much white washes it out. Choose a naturally lighter colour, and start the ramp from a deeper neighbour.
osl-colour-choice.cyan or blue for a glow: Cyan. It is naturally lighter than plain blue, so it needs less white and stays saturated.
osl-colour-choice.turquoise magic glow: Turquoise works well: it is naturally light, so it needs little white and stays saturated.
osl-colour-choice.green glow effect: Green glows easily. Use a pale yellow as the bright core and start the ramp from a deeper blue green.
osl-colour-choice.orange or yellow lantern glow: Both glow easily. Use a pale yellow as the core and start a yellow glow from orange or red at the edge.
osl-colour-choice.glow colour choice: Pick a naturally light colour like cyan, turquoise, yellow, orange or green, contrasting with what it lights.
osl-colour-choice.why does adding white kill my glow: White makes saturated colours pale and chalky. Pick a naturally lighter hue so it needs less white.

paint-beading-on-primer.paint beading: Slick primer makes paint bead. Work it in, let a thin coat dry and add another, or brush a grippy layer over first.
paint-beading-on-primer.wash beading up: Wash the whole model first, or brush over the spot a few times to break the surface. It takes better the second time.
paint-beading-on-primer.paint wont stick to primer: Let the first thin coat dry and add another. Paint grips much better the second time.
paint-beading-on-primer.paint slides off: Wipe it off with a tissue or fingertip and reapply, or brush it over a few times. It usually grips on the second go.
paint-beading-on-primer.slick primer: Smooth primer makes paint bead. Build thin coats, or wash the whole model first so later coats stick.
paint-beading-on-primer.metallic spray primer repels paint: Brush one thin coat of a matching metallic over the whole model first so washes and base coats can grip.
paint-beading-on-primer.contrast beading on primer: Brush over the spot a few times to break the surface, or wash the whole model first so later coats stick.
paint-beading-on-primer.patchy wash on smooth primer: Brush it over the spot a few times, or wipe it off and reapply. The area usually takes paint the second time.
paint-beading-on-primer.paint pulls into droplets: Thin paint pulls into beads on slick primer. Let the first coat dry and add another, or work it in with the brush.
paint-beading-on-primer.primer too smooth: Add a second thin coat once the first is dry, and build weak colours in several thin coats.

paint-pot-care.paint drying out: Wipe the rim and lid groove clean, shut lids straight away, and keep paints upright somewhere cool and dry.
paint-pot-care.how do i stop paint drying in the pot: Wipe dried paint from the rim so the lid seals, shut it as soon as you have taken paint, and keep it cool.
paint-pot-care.paint pot lid won't close: Dried paint in the rim stops it sealing. Wipe the rim and lid groove with a damp cotton bud.
paint-pot-care.flip top pots: Open tall pots with two hands while steady on the table, or use a stand that holds them.
paint-pot-care.knocked over a paint pot: Act fast. Scoop small spills on hard surfaces back into the pot, and blot wash spills before they dry.
paint-pot-care.dried paint in rim: Wipe the rim and lid groove with a damp cotton bud at the end of each session.
paint-pot-care.keep paints fresh: Shut lids tight straight away, keep rims clean, and keep pots upright somewhere cool and dry, out of sun.
paint-pot-care.paint pot spilled: Scoop small spills on hard surfaces back into the pot, and blot wash spills with tissue before they dry.
paint-pot-care.paint gone thick: Add a few drops of water and shake again. A small glass bead or steel ball helps it mix.
paint-pot-care.storing paint: Upright, somewhere cool and dry with lids shut tight. Avoid freezing, direct sun and hot cars.

painting-black.painting black: Prime black, base in a very dark grey or blue, run thinned black into the recesses, and give each material its own look.
painting-black.black looks flat: Pure black leaves nowhere darker to go. Base a very dark grey or blue and run thinned black into the recesses as shadow.
painting-black.how do i highlight black: Highlight with greys suited to the material: soft warm greys on cloth, up to mid grey on leather, near white on armour.
painting-black.black armour: Hard armour takes the biggest range: bluish greys up to near white on the sharpest spots only.
painting-black.black cloth vs black leather: Keep cloth dark with small, soft, warm grey highlights. Leather has a slight sheen and takes highlights up to a mid grey.
painting-black.make black look interesting: Lean soft parts warm and hard parts cool, give each material its own highlights, and add one spot colour.
painting-black.black highlights look grey: If highlights went too bright, a black wash settles them, but do not wash dry brushed black fur or cloth.
painting-black.black hair or fur: Drybrush heavily with very dark grey, then lighter greys on the edges only, and do not wash it afterwards.
painting-black.should i prime black for black areas: Yes. A black undercoat does most of the work, and a heavy dark blue grey drybrush over it can be enough.
painting-black.warm brown in black shadows: Drop a heavily thinned dark brown low in the recesses. Mix brown paint with clear medium so it dries matt.

painting-competitions.painting competition: Judges want clean basics, strong contrast and a clear focal point. Pick your neatest model and read the rules first.
painting-competitions.enter a contest: Read the rules on categories, base size and whether it must be new, then enter your neatest, clearest model.
painting-competitions.judging criteria: First how the piece reads from a distance, then clean basics up close, then blends, light, faces, materials and freehand.
painting-competitions.how to enter a competition: Read the rules first, check categories, base size and eligibility, photograph the model, and carry it in a foam box.
painting-competitions.painting contest: Judges look for clean basics, strong contrast and a focal point. A simple model done cleanly beats an ambitious one.
painting-competitions.competition rules: Check categories, base size limits, whether it must be your own work, and whether it must be new.
painting-competitions.competition categories: Usually single figure, large model, group or unit, diorama, bust, and sometimes a youth or first timer class.
painting-competitions.first competition: Pick your neatest model, remove every mould line, check the rules, and ask the judges what held it back afterwards.
painting-competitions.what judges look for: Clean basics: no mould lines, gaps, bare primer or dust, clean edges between colours, strong lights and darks, one focal point.
painting-competitions.which model should i enter: Your neatest one. A simple model done cleanly beats an ambitious one done badly.

painting-fire.fire: Paint flames from the inside out: white and pale yellow at the core and base, through orange, to near black at the tips.
