airbrush-highlights.sharpen airbrush highlights by brush: Once other colours are blocked in, add a paler touch on the highest points and a few sharp reflections by brush, blended with thin glazes.
airbrush-highlights.mix shadow mid and light for airbrush: Darken the base with a deeper version of the colour or a grey rather than pure black, then mix a mid tone and a warm off white light tone.

airbrushed-cloth.airbrush a cloak: Pre shade black then white from the light's direction, spray thinned cloak colour in light layers, add darker shadows from a low angle, then sharpen by brush.
airbrushed-cloth.smooth blend on a big cloak: Use an airbrush: pre shade dark with white from above, then spray thin cloth colour so the pre shade shows through as smooth shadow and highlight.
airbrushed-cloth.how do i airbrush cloth: Pre shade dark and white from above, spray thin cloth colour, spray a darker mix into the shadows from a low angle, then push contrast by brush.
airbrushed-cloth.cloak blending is streaky: Large flat cloth is hard to blend by brush, as each stopped stroke leaves a break; an airbrush gives smooth transitions from the start.
airbrushed-cloth.airbrushing robes: Pre shade, spray the thinned cloth colour in light layers, spray darker into the folds from a low steep angle, and finish highlights by brush.
airbrushed-cloth.big flat cloth hard to blend: An airbrush suits it: pre shade, thin the colour about two parts thinner to one paint, spray light layers, and sharpen contrast by brush after.
airbrushed-cloth.airbrush shadows on fabric: Spray a darker mix or a complementary colour into the shadows at a low, steep angle so it lands only on the shadowed sides of the folds.
airbrushed-cloth.smooth fade on a cape: Pre shade so only upward facing folds are light, then spray thinned cape colour in light layers; it gives smooth transitions from the start.
airbrushed-cloth.preshade cloak airbrush: Spray black or dark grey overall, then white from the light direction so only upward folds catch it, and check the placement before colour.
airbrushed-cloth.airbrush capes: Pre shade, spray the thinned cloth colour in light layers, mist darker shadows into the folds, then tidy and sharpen the highlights.

asking-for-critique.how to ask for feedback on my painting: Ask a narrow question with a sharp front and side photo, say what you were aiming for, then pick one or two points to test.
asking-for-critique.critique: Ask something narrow, such as whether the highlights read at arm's length, show good photos, and look for points several people repeat.
asking-for-critique.what should i improve on this mini: Ask a narrow question about the area you are unsure of, with sharp photos and your goal stated, then fix whatever several people repeat.
asking-for-critique.nobody gives useful feedback: Ask a narrow question instead of what do you think, and say your goal and experience; vague questions mostly get praise or noise.
asking-for-critique.harsh comments on my paint job: Read them as notes on the model, not on you; wait a day before replying if one stings, and weigh who is talking.
asking-for-critique.how to take photos for feedback: Take a sharp photo from the front and one from the side or back, in bright even light on a plain background.
asking-for-critique.is this good enough: Judge it against your own goal: say whether you aimed for quick tabletop or a slow display piece, and ask a narrow question.
asking-for-critique.rate my paint job: Ask a narrow question with good photos and your goal; a one word rating is worth less than someone who explains why.
asking-for-critique.too much conflicting advice: Look for repeats and fix what several people mention first; weigh people who explain why, and ignore taste remarks on a deliberate scheme.
asking-for-critique.how do i use feedback to get better: Pick one or two repeated points, test them on a spare model or a small area, and take before and after photos to check.

batch-assembly.build a unit faster: Build the same model several times in a row, doing one step across all of them: clip, clean, then glue each part in turn.
batch-assembly.how do i assemble lots of models quickly: Open every frame at once, clip the same part from all of them, clean them all, then glue them all, step by step.
batch-assembly.batch building: Batch build: do each step across every copy at once, with parts for each model kept in a separate tray or cup.
batch-assembly.assembly line for a squad: Clip the same part from every frame, clean them all, glue them all, keeping each model's parts in its own tray or pile.
batch-assembly.building the same kit ten times: Do one step across all ten copies at a time, and for variety move each pair of arms to a different body on the second set.
batch-assembly.speed up assembling an army: Batch the same step across all copies, use good cutters and a sanding stick, and plan building as its own stage.
batch-assembly.which models should i build first: Start with the simple, common models; they teach you the kit before the big centrepieces.
batch-assembly.assembling a whole unit at once: Open every frame at once and do one step across all the models: clip, clean, then glue, keeping parts sorted per model.
batch-assembly.production line building: Repeat one step across every copy of the same model, kept in separate trays so options do not get mixed up.
batch-assembly.tips for building a new army: Start with simple common models, batch build them step by step, and plan sub assemblies so you leave the same parts off each one.

blending-methods.which blending method: Wet blending is fastest, stippling is quick and textured, and layering with glazes is slowest but most controlled.
blending-methods.wet blending vs layering: Wet blending merges colours while both are wet and is very quick but hard to place; layering with glazes is slower but more controlled.
blending-methods.how do i blend acrylics: Use translucent paint or layers close in value, and pick one method, such as glazing, wet blending or stippling, and practise it.
blending-methods.smooth blends: Use thin, translucent layers close in value, and mix a midway colour where a step is a big jump.
blending-methods.stippling vs glazing: Stippling builds a blend quickly from small dabs and can add texture; glazing is slower but gives the most control.
blending-methods.best way to blend for beginners: Layering with glazes is the most reliable place to start: slower, but with the most control and fewest accidents.
blending-methods.why cant i blend paint: Acrylic dries fast and hard, which works against blending; use translucent paint, close steps, and expect to go back and forth.
blending-methods.blend dries too fast: That is normal for acrylic; work with it using thin glazes or close layers, a wet palette, and a fresh mix for each step.
blending-methods.blending techniques explained: Wet blending merges wet paints, feathering and loaded brush blending are close relatives, stippling uses dabs, and glazing builds thin layers.
blending-methods.layering or wet blend: Wet blend for speed on skin, cloth and fire; layer with glazes for control on metal, faces and small precise areas.

brush-care.brush lost its point: Paint dried in the metal collar splays the bristles; reshape the tip with soap left in overnight, or retire it to rough jobs.
brush-care.how to clean brushes: Rinse often, never leave it bristles down in water, then after a session lather with brush soap in cool water and reshape the tip.
brush-care.brush bristles splaying out: Usually dried paint in the collar; load only the front half, drag rather than push, and deep clean with isopropyl alcohol and soap.
brush-care.paint in the ferrule: Acrylic dried in the collar does not soften again; deep clean with isopropyl alcohol and soap, and load only the front half from now on.
brush-care.dont leave brushes in water: Never leave a brush standing bristles down in water; rinse often and clean by pulling the bristles upward against the side of the pot.
brush-care.brush soap: Lather in cool or lukewarm water, work it gently toward the collar, rinse until clear, reshape the tip, and dry it flat.
brush-care.make my brushes last longer: Keep paint out of the collar, rinse often, never stand it in water, and clean with brush soap after each session.
brush-care.brush hairs curling: Dip just the bristles in water off the boil for a moment, shape the point, then rinse cool; it often springs back.
brush-care.ruined my good brush: Leave soap in it overnight with the tip shaped and wash it out next day; this can bring back a brush that looks ruined.
brush-care.how do i fix a frayed brush tip: Dip the bristles briefly in water off the boil, shape the point, rinse cool, and trim stray hairs with a sharp blade.

building-your-first-kit.first model kit: Read the instructions first, clip parts with care, scrape mould lines and glue with a light touch of plastic glue.
building-your-first-kit.how do i build a plastic kit: Read the instructions, clip parts a short way from the model, trim nubs, scrape mould lines, dry fit, then glue sparingly.
building-your-first-kit.assembling my first miniature: Read the steps, clip and trim each part, scrape mould lines with the back of the blade, dry fit, then glue with a light touch.
building-your-first-kit.beginner model building: Read the instructions, clip and clean each part, dry fit, use plastic glue sparingly, and give each joint a minute.
building-your-first-kit.read instructions first: Read them before cutting anything and decide on head or weapon options, then tick each step off in pencil as you go.
building-your-first-kit.plastic glue on a kit: Use it sparingly on one side, press together and hold about ten seconds; too much squeezes out and blurs detail.
building-your-first-kit.remove mould lines: Scrape them off with the back edge of a hobby knife blade; they are hard to see now but obvious once painted.
building-your-first-kit.how to put together a model: Follow the instructions in order: clip, trim, scrape mould lines, dry fit, glue sparingly, then glue the feet to the base.
building-your-first-kit.never built a kit before: Read the instructions, work on a cloth, clip parts carefully, scrape mould lines, dry fit, and glue with a light touch.
building-your-first-kit.what order to build parts: Follow the instruction steps in order, setting aside only the frames each stage uses and sorting parts into small piles.
building-your-first-kit.How do I build a kit and clean up mould: Clip, trim the nub, scrape mould lines with the blade's back edge, dry fit, glue sparingly, then fill any gap with a little putty.

changing-detail-with-paint.fix a badly sculpted eye with paint: Paint a thin dark line where you want the eye line, highlight just beside it, and cover the old detail with the surrounding colour.
changing-detail-with-paint.move a detail with paint: On shallow sculpts, paint a dark line for the new edge, highlight beside it, and paint over the original detail so it fades away.
changing-detail-with-paint.eyes too big: See: changing a detail with paint, where a shallow eye can be moved slightly with a new dark line, a highlight and paint over the old one.
changing-detail-with-paint.sculpt detail is too shallow: Fake the detail with paint: a thin dark line where you want it, a highlight just above or beside it, and the old detail painted over.
changing-detail-with-paint.fake an edge with paint: Paint a thin dark line for the edge, then highlight just above it so the eye reads it as a raised rim.
changing-detail-with-paint.paint a new eye line: Paint a thin dark line where you want the eye line, highlight just beside it, and fade the old one with the surrounding colour.
changing-detail-with-paint.detail in the wrong place: If it is shallow, paint new shadows and highlights where you want it and cover the original with the surrounding colour.
changing-detail-with-paint.can i change the face with paint: Only slightly, and only where the sculpted detail is very shallow; check it at arm's length before committing.
changing-detail-with-paint.cheat a fold with shading: Paint a thin dark line where you want the fold, highlight just above it, and paint over the original with the surrounding colour.
changing-detail-with-paint.soft detail fix with paint: Paint new shadows and highlights where you want the detail, cover the old one, and check it at arm's length; it is risky.

choosing-brushes.what brushes do i actually need: A few cheap brushes plus one or two good ones: a round size 0 to 2 detail brush and a larger size 4 to 8 synthetic for base coats and washes.
choosing-brushes.best brush size for details: A round brush with a sharp tip and a fat belly, around size 0 to 2, does most detail work, including edge highlights and eyes.
choosing-brushes.is a tiny brush better: No: a size 0 to 2 round with a fat belly holds more paint and still keeps a sharp tip for detail.
choosing-brushes.size 0 or 000: A size 0 to 2 round with a sharp tip and fat belly does most work; compare the actual brush, as sizes vary between makers.
choosing-brushes.brush for edge highlights: A round pointed size 0 to 2 that springs back to a sharp tip and has a fat belly handles edge highlights.
choosing-brushes.round brush with a good point: Choose a plain round watercolour style brush that springs back to a sharp, even tip after each stroke and holds paint in a fat belly.
choosing-brushes.cheap vs expensive brushes: A cheap brush with a good tip is fine for tabletop; for fine detail a mid priced natural hair brush is a big step up.
choosing-brushes.which brush for eyes: A round size 0 to 2 with a sharp tip handles eyes; short haired brushes snap back well for eyes but hold less paint.
choosing-brushes.synthetic or natural hair: Synthetics are cheap but curl and wear quickly; natural hair holds more paint, keeps a firm point and lasts longer.
choosing-brushes.beginner brush set what do i need: A round size 0 to 2 detail brush, a cheap size 4 to 8 synthetic for base coats and washes, and old ones for drybrushing and glue.

clippers-and-clipping.clippers: Choose cutters with one flat face and jaws that meet exactly; a cheap flat backed pair is fine to start with.
clippers-and-clipping.how do i cut parts off the sprue: Use cutters, not a knife: cut a little away from the part, then close in with the flat face towards it, and scrape the nub flush.
clippers-and-clipping.best sprue cutters: Flat faced cutters with jaws that meet exactly; keep a very sharp thin pair for small parts and a cheaper pair for thick frames.
clippers-and-clipping.nubs left on parts: Scrape them away with light strokes of a craft knife pulled towards you, then finish with a fine file or sanding stick.
clippers-and-clipping.clipping parts cleanly: Cut in two stages, a little away first, then close in flat face to the part, thinnest join first and chunkiest last.
clippers-and-clipping.flat cutters vs wire cutters: Flat faced cutters leave a clean cut; curved or bevelled wire cutters leave a rough one.
clippers-and-clipping.cut marks on my model: Leave a small nub so you do not bite into detail, then scrape it flush with light knife strokes and a fine file.
clippers-and-clipping.remove part from frame: Clip through the frame a little away from the part, then close in with the flat face towards it, cutting the thinnest join first.
clippers-and-clipping.sprue nubs: Scrape the nub away with light, repeated knife strokes pulled towards you, then smooth with a fine file or sanding stick.
clippers-and-clipping.white stress marks from cutting: Use a very sharp thin bladed cutter and cut a little away first; a cleaner cut stresses the plastic less, so it whitens less.

colour-wheel-harmonies.colour wheel: Use complementary, triad or split complementary sets, or a gamut mask, to decide which colours go in a scheme.
colour-wheel-harmonies.complementary colours: Two colours opposite each other on the wheel, which make each other look more vivid.
colour-wheel-harmonies.what colours go together: Opposites on the wheel make each other vivid, neighbours are calm, and triads or split complementaries give balanced contrast.
colour-wheel-harmonies.colour scheme ideas: Turn a triad or split complementary guide around the wheel until you find a set you like, then let one colour dominate.
colour-wheel-harmonies.triad colour scheme: Three evenly spaced colours, such as green, orange and purple; let one dominate and use the others as small pops.
colour-wheel-harmonies.split complementary: One colour plus the two either side of its opposite, which gives strong contrast with less tension.
colour-wheel-harmonies.gamut mask: A shape such as a triangle laid over the wheel; its corners are your colours, and anything mixable from them plus black and white is allowed.
colour-wheel-harmonies.picking a colour scheme: Pick a harmony on the wheel, mix the colours on the palette first, then let one colour dominate and scatter the others in small pops.
colour-wheel-harmonies.colour theory for miniatures: Use complementary, triad or split complementary harmonies, let one colour dominate, and scatter each pop colour in two to four places.
colour-wheel-harmonies.color wheel: Red, yellow and blue mix into orange, green and violet; opposites boost each other and neighbours sit calmly together.

contrast-before-smoothness.model looks flat even with smooth blends: Contrast does more than smoothness: set stronger lights and darks first, then smooth the joins only as much as you need.
contrast-before-smoothness.my blends are smooth but boring: Push the values harder: jump to a clearly lighter highlight, push key points like the face nearly to white, and add crisp edges.
contrast-before-smoothness.should i focus on smooth blending: Set strong contrast first; strong lights and darks with rough blends beat smooth blends with weak contrast.
contrast-before-smoothness.jump straight to a bright highlight: Yes: paint the base, then a clearly lighter highlight on the brightest areas, then a midtone only over the join.
contrast-before-smoothness.contrast or smoothness first: Contrast first, with bold strokes, then smooth the transitions only as much as you need.
contrast-before-smoothness.bold highlights rough blends: That works: set strong lights and darks with confident strokes first, then mix a midtone for the joins.
contrast-before-smoothness.too many close layers: Jump straight from the base to a clearly lighter highlight, then paint a covering midtone only over the join.
contrast-before-smoothness.how to get more contrast: Jump to a clearly lighter highlight, push key points like the face nearly to white, and add crisp edge highlights.
contrast-before-smoothness.my model has no pop: Strengthen the contrast: brighter highlights, near white on the focal points, a little bounce light, and crisp edges.
contrast-before-smoothness.paint is smooth but lifeless: Push the lights and darks further apart; strong values even trick the eye into reading a surface as smooth.

crisp-armour-method.clean armour: Base each panel a mid tone, shade only the recesses, then add two or three fine edge highlights, each brighter and finer.
crisp-armour-method.recess shade and edge highlight: Run darker shade only into creases and panel joins, tidy spills with the base, then add two or three increasingly fine edge highlights.
crisp-armour-method.how do i get crisp armour: Base two thin mid tone coats, shade only the recesses, tidy spills with the base, then add finer and brighter edge highlights.
crisp-armour-method.panel lining armour: Run one or two darker shades into the creases and panel joins only, keeping them off the flat surfaces.
crisp-armour-method.sharp clean power armor: Base a mid tone, shade only the recesses, tidy with the base colour, then edge highlight two or three times.
crisp-armour-method.armour looks messy: Shade only the recesses, tidy spills with the base colour, and finish one colour fully before starting the next.
crisp-armour-method.shade only the recesses: Run the darker shade into creases and panel joins, keeping it off flat surfaces, and tidy any spill with the base.
crisp-armour-method.edge highlight armour: Two or three edge highlights, each brighter and finer than the last, with the final one only on the very top points.
crisp-armour-method.neat armour finish: Shade just the recesses, tidy with the base, edge highlight in two or three finer steps, and paint trim last.
crisp-armour-method.clean panels with fine edges: Mid tone base, recess shade only, then two or three edge highlights that get brighter and finer each time.

decanting-paint-to-droppers.move paint into dropper bottles: Sit a small funnel in each empty bottle, pour the pot paint in, scrape the rest in with a damp brush, add a mixing ball, then cap it.
decanting-paint-to-droppers.decanting paint: Pour pot paint into dropper bottles through a small funnel, add a mixing ball, and clean the funnel straight away.
decanting-paint-to-droppers.pot paint to dropper: Add two or three drops of flow improver to thick paint, pour it through a small funnel into the bottle, and drop in a mixing ball.
decanting-paint-to-droppers.transfer paint to bottles: Tape the empty bottles down, pour through a small funnel in each neck, scrape the pot in with a damp flat brush, then add a mixing ball.
decanting-paint-to-droppers.funnel for paint: A small steel icing nozzle or tiny plastic funnel sits in the neck; the small gap around it lets air out.
decanting-paint-to-droppers.mixing ball in dropper: Drop a non rusting mixing ball into each bottle so the paint mixes easily when shaken.
decanting-paint-to-droppers.paint pots drying out: Move them into dropper bottles, which keep paint from drying out and are easier to dose from.
decanting-paint-to-droppers.dropper bottle conversion: Pour through a small funnel, add a mixing ball, press the dropper tip in lightly, then screw the cap on to push it home.
decanting-paint-to-droppers.refill dropper bottles: See: moving paint into dropper bottles, which covers filling empty bottles through a small funnel.
decanting-paint-to-droppers.how to pour paint into a dropper: Sit a small funnel in the neck, pour straight in, scrape the pot with a damp flat brush, then press the tip in and cap it.

drilling-gun-barrels.drill out gun barrels: Start a centred pilot hole with a knife tip, then drill straight and gently with a small bit in a hand pin vice.
drilling-gun-barrels.hollow out a rifle muzzle: Twist a knife tip into the centre of the muzzle for a pilot hole, check it is central, then drill gently with a pin vice.
drilling-gun-barrels.my drill hole went off centre: Turn the knife's cutting edge towards the side that needs enlarging and twist in small steps, or nudge the next drill turns to the middle.
drilling-gun-barrels.pin vice for barrels: Use a small bit in a hand pin vice rather than a power drill, with very light pressure, checking it stays central.
drilling-gun-barrels.how do i drill a tiny barrel straight: Use a pin vice with light pressure, check from one side, then turn the model a quarter turn and check again.
drilling-gun-barrels.drill bit keeps snapping: Use very light pressure in a hand pin vice, stop shallow on thin barrels, and back the bit out slowly.
drilling-gun-barrels.make guns look like they can fire: Drill out the barrels with a pin vice; forward facing guns repay the effort most, as solid barrels pointing at the viewer look odd.
drilling-gun-barrels.pilot hole with a knife tip: Rest a sharp knife tip on the centre of the muzzle, hold it upright and twist; a pin pressed into the centre also works.
drilling-gun-barrels.hollow barrel ends on a tank: Start a centred pilot hole, drill gently with a pin vice, widen the mouth with a larger bit, and clear shavings and burrs.
drilling-gun-barrels.solid barrels look fake: Drill them out with a pin vice after a centred pilot hole; solid barrels pointing at the viewer look odd.

drybrushing-edges.drybrush edges: Wipe nearly all paint off the brush and stroke across the edge in one direction so only the sharp edges catch it.
drybrushing-edges.edge highlight with drybrush: Load the highlight, wipe nearly all off until the brush feels cool, test on the palette edge, then stroke across the edges.
drybrushing-edges.quick edge highlights: Drybrush them: a nearly empty brush catches only sharp edges, much faster than painting lines by hand.
drybrushing-edges.worn edges fast: A nearly empty drybrush stroked across edges gives a used, weathered look much faster than hand lining.
drybrushing-edges.cant paint straight edge lines: Drybrush them with a nearly empty brush, then add a few hand lines only on the most prominent edges.
drybrushing-edges.drybrushing instead of lining: Drybrushing is faster and looks worn; hand lines look crisp and new, so pick the look you want.
drybrushing-edges.shaky edge highlights: Swap to drybrushing: wipe the brush nearly dry and stroke across the edge so only it catches paint.
drybrushing-edges.lazy edge highlighting: Drybrush the edges with almost no paint, stroking in one direction, then change direction for the opposite edges.
drybrushing-edges.weathered edge highlights: Drybrush the edges with a nearly dry brush; it looks used and weathered, unlike crisp hand painted lines.
drybrushing-edges.fast edges on vehicles: Drybrush the edges with almost no paint, then add a few hand lines on the most prominent edges to sharpen the result.

edge-highlight-brush-strokes.edge highlighting: Drag the side of the brush tip along sharp edges and pull the point along blunt or awkward ones, turning the part to suit.
edge-highlight-brush-strokes.how do i edge highlight: Lay the side of the bristles near the tip along the edge at about 45 degrees and sweep once; the edge itself guides the paint.
edge-highlight-brush-strokes.edge highlights wobbly: Use the side of the tip so the edge guides the paint, turn the model rather than your wrist, and straighten any wobble with the colour underneath.
edge-highlight-brush-strokes.side of the brush edge highlight: Lay the side of the bristles near the tip along the edge at about 45 degrees, avoiding the fat part near the collar.
edge-highlight-brush-strokes.paint thin lines on edges: Thin the paint only lightly, blot the brush on paper towel before every stroke, and drag the side of the tip along the edge.
edge-highlight-brush-strokes.edge highlight tips: Blot before every stroke, reload often, use the side of the tip, and turn the model so each edge comes to your best stroke.
edge-highlight-brush-strokes.edge highlights too thick: Blot the brush before every stroke and reload often; once paint dries on the tip you press harder and the line thickens.
edge-highlight-brush-strokes.highlight sharp edges: Lay the side of the bristles near the tip along the edge and sweep once; only the very edge picks up paint.
edge-highlight-brush-strokes.line highlights: Use the side of the tip on sharp edges and pull the point along rounded ones, with a brighter second line inside the first.
edge-highlight-brush-strokes.edge highlight armour: Drag the side of the tip along sharp armour edges, pull the point along rounded ones, and tidy wobbles with the colour underneath.

face-highlight-placement.where do i highlight a face: Gather light on the brow, nose, cheekbones, upper lip and chin, and keep shadows soft where the face is soft.
face-highlight-placement.face looks flat: Focus light on the brow ridge, nose, cheekbone tops, chin and upper lip, building each highlight smaller than the last.
face-highlight-placement.highlight the nose and cheekbones: Highlight the bridge and tip of the nose and the tops of the cheekbones; a reversed L on each cheek reads well.
face-highlight-placement.where do shadows go on a face: Shade along the hairline, around the eyes and nose; keep the brow shadow soft and avoid heavy shade under the eyes.
face-highlight-placement.faces look weird and lumpy: Avoid hard dark lines beside the nose and mouth and heavy shade under the eyes, and keep shallow dips like under the cheekbones lightly shaded.
face-highlight-placement.which parts of the face catch light: The brow ridge, nose bridge and tip, cheekbone tops, chin and upper lip, forming a double T, plus small upward faces like the eyelids.
face-highlight-placement.face shading placement: Deep recesses keep more of the earlier colour, shallow ones are mostly covered; keep under eye and brow shadows soft.
face-highlight-placement.light the face from above: See: where to highlight a face, which covers checking a primed face under a single lamp to see what catches the light.
face-highlight-placement.highlights on a chin and brow: Highlight the brow ridge with the forehead light just above the brows, and the chin; a stronger jaw and chin highlight looks heroic.
face-highlight-placement.how to make a face look three dimensiona: Build thin highlights on the brow, nose, cheekbones, upper lip and chin, each smaller than the last, with the far side kept darker.

finding-reflections.where does the light go: Prime a part satin black or metallic, turn it under a lamp, and copy where the light lands as your highlight guide.
finding-reflections.where to put highlights on shiny parts: Look at a satin black or silver primed part under one lamp: round shapes get strong spots and sharp edges thin bright lines.
finding-reflections.reflections on armour: Prime satin black or silver, shine a lamp from your light direction, and photograph where the shine lands to copy it.
finding-reflections.find highlight placement: Turn a satin or metallic primed part under a lamp and photograph where the light lands as a highlight guide.
finding-reflections.use a lamp to see highlights: Shine one lamp from your light direction at a satin black or silver part and turn it to the main viewing angles.
finding-reflections.satin black primer reference: Satin black shows where light naturally lands, which a matte primer or top down white spray does not.
finding-reflections.where to paint shine: On the spots where light lands on a satin primed part, and along the edges that catch the most light.
finding-reflections.nmm reflection placement: Copy where light lands on a satin black or silver part under a lamp; bright spots sit right beside near black.
finding-reflections.highlight map: Photograph a satin primed part under a lamp from the front and back, and raise the photo contrast to read bright and dark areas.
finding-reflections.how do i see where light lands: Prime satin black or silver, light it with one lamp from your chosen direction, and turn the part to see where the shine falls.

fix-airbrush-spidering.airbrush spider webbing: Spider webbing means paint too thin for the pressure; add a little paint, lower the pressure, move further away or pull the trigger back less.
fix-airbrush-spidering.airbrush spidering: Paint too runny for the pressure, or the brush too close; add a little paint, lower the pressure or move slightly further away.
fix-airbrush-spidering.airbrush speckling: Speckling means paint too thick, pressure too low, or paint dried on the needle tip; thin it to milk and wipe the tip.
fix-airbrush-spidering.airbrush spits: Spitting usually means paint too thick or dried on the needle tip; thin it to the feel of milk and wipe the tip with cleaner.
fix-airbrush-spidering.paint spatters from airbrush: Spattering means paint too thick, pressure too low or a dried needle tip; thin it to milk, wipe the tip, then raise pressure a little.
fix-airbrush-spidering.grainy airbrush finish: Thick paint or spraying from too far away dries it in the air; thin a little more and move closer.
fix-airbrush-spidering.airbrush too close: Too close with runny paint gives spider webbing; move slightly further away, lower the pressure, or set the trigger stop for close work.
fix-airbrush-spidering.airbrush pressure problems: Too much pressure on runny paint gives spider webbing; too little on thick paint gives speckling, so match pressure to the mix.
fix-airbrush-spidering.airbrush paint runs in lines: That is spider webbing: paint too thin for the pressure, so add a little paint, lower the pressure or move back.
fix-airbrush-spidering.spidering: Spidering means paint too runny for the pressure or the brush too close; add paint, lower pressure, or ease off the trigger.

fix-glow-effects.my glow doesnt glow: A glow reads only if it is lighter than its surroundings and fades slowly; darken the rest of the model or brighten the source.
fix-glow-effects.osl not working: Make the lit area visibly lighter than its surroundings, build a long fade with many thin glazes, and check a greyscale photo.
fix-glow-effects.glow looks like coloured paint: A glow is about light, not colour: the lit area must be lighter than its surroundings, so check a greyscale photo.
fix-glow-effects.glow looks darker than the rest: Adding strong hue often darkens it; the source must be the lightest value, so darken the rest or knock back nearby highlights.
fix-glow-effects.how do i make a glow brighter: Often darken the rest of the model rather than brightening the glow, and deepen shadows on surfaces shielded from it.
fix-glow-effects.overdone glow: Glaze the outer edge back with the base or a mid tone, and keep the strongest light close to the source.
fix-glow-effects.light effect not reading from a distance: Make the source the lightest value, darken surrounding areas, and judge it at arm's length under room light.
fix-glow-effects.glow too strong how to tone down: Glaze the outer edge back with the base or a mid tone and keep the strongest light close to the source.
fix-glow-effects.candle effect not showing: A candle barely shows in daylight; darken the rest of the model so the lit area is clearly the lightest value.
fix-glow-effects.object source lighting looks wrong: Check the source is the lightest value, build a long fade with thin glazes, and paint planes facing the source in the glow colour.

fix-too-bright-highlights.highlight too bright: Glaze the colour from the step before back over the over bright highlight, let it dry, then redo it smaller.
fix-too-bright-highlights.overdid the highlight: Thin the previous colour into a very wet glaze, pull it over the highlight, then redo the highlight in a smaller area.
fix-too-bright-highlights.how do i tone down highlights: Glaze the base or previous colour thinly over them, let it dry, repeat if needed, then redo the highlight smaller.
fix-too-bright-highlights.highlights too stark: Glaze the previous colour back over them; if a whole garment looks stark, brush on a dark wash weakened with matt medium.
fix-too-bright-highlights.skin highlights too white: Glaze the base or previous skin colour over them very thinly, then repaint a smaller highlight; pale paints act fast.
fix-too-bright-highlights.fix harsh highlights: Glaze the previous colour back over the harsh step to tone it down and smooth the join, then redo it smaller.
fix-too-bright-highlights.too much contrast highlight: Glaze the previous colour back over the highlight, and if contrast faded, push the darkest areas back before repainting the brightest points.
fix-too-bright-highlights.glaze over highlight: Thin the base or previous colour into a very wet glaze, test it on your nail, and pull it lightly over the over bright area.
fix-too-bright-highlights.highlights stand out too much: Glaze the step before back over them, then redo smaller; for a whole stark garment, brush on a dark wash mixed with matt medium.
fix-too-bright-highlights.jumped too bright: Glaze the previous colour over it to tone it down, let it dry before judging, then redo the highlight in a smaller area.

flying-stands.flying stand: Make a strong, removable join between flyer and stand with magnets or a pin, and use heavier, sturdier stands for big models.
flying-stands.flying base snaps: The small peg snaps or pulls out, so swap it for magnets or a pin before painting.
flying-stands.magnetise flying stand: Fill the base's peg hole with putty, glue a magnet on, glue another on the rod top and one in the model, checking polarity first.
flying-stands.flyer falls off stand: Replace the small peg with a magnet or pin join set in putty so the model is held firmly but can still lift off.
flying-stands.stronger flying stand: Use a heavy base and a metal rod, pin or magnetise the join, and for a scenic stand glue the rod into a rock or ruin.
flying-stands.clear stand peg broke: Cut the peg off and swap to magnets or a pin; a magnet or pin join lifts off so the model travels flat.
flying-stands.dragon flying base: Large flyers need a heavy base, such as two layers of thin plywood with the grain crossing, holding a metal rod.
flying-stands.pin model to flight stand: Drill a socket in the underside, glue stiff wire across it, and rest an angled rod top against the wire.
flying-stands.scenic flying base: Glue a metal rod into a hole drilled in a rock, ruin or printed piece, and drill the model's hole at an angle so it banks.
flying-stands.removable flying stand: A magnet or pin join lifts off, so the model travels flat and can go on the table without its stand.

freehand-patterns.freehand stripes: Mark out stripes with thin guide lines, use a hem or panel edge as a guide, pull every stripe towards you, then shade the pattern as one surface.
freehand-patterns.checks on a cloak: Paint one thin line down the middle and one across, halve each part until the squares are right, then fill alternate squares.
freehand-patterns.checkerboard pattern: Halve the area with thin guide lines until the squares are the right size, fill alternate squares, then shade it all as one surface.
freehand-patterns.chevrons on a shield: Paint thin guide lines, thicken them over a couple of coats, and break shield markings into triangles, mirroring one side.
freehand-patterns.stripes on a tabard: Use a hem or panel rim as the guide, let the brush width set the stripe thickness, follow the folds, and work top to bottom.
freehand-patterns.how do i paint squares on cloth: Mark thin guide lines down the middle and across, halve them until the squares fit, fill alternate ones, and let them follow the folds.
freehand-patterns.guide lines for freehand: Paint thin lines down the middle and across, then halve each part again; for chevrons, thicken the guide lines over a couple of coats.
freehand-patterns.my stripes look wobbly: Hold the model at one fixed angle, pull every stripe towards you, and trim wobbly lines back with the other colour.
freehand-patterns.checkered banner: Mark out with thin guide lines, fill alternate squares, then glaze dark into the folds and light on raised areas across every colour.
freehand-patterns.pattern following the folds: Let stripes follow the folds and small motifs disappear into deep folds, then shade the whole pattern as one surface.

glazing-to-shift-colour.glazing to change colour: A thin transparent glaze over a finished area can warm, deepen, saturate or fix its colour while keeping the shading underneath.
glazing-to-shift-colour.how do i warm up a colour with a glaze: Glaze a thin warm colour such as orange, red or a warm tan over it; the shading underneath carries through.
glazing-to-shift-colour.colour came out wrong, can i fix it with: Yes: a thin glaze can fix a colour that drifted while keeping the shading, so it rarely needs stripping.
glazing-to-shift-colour.red looks too orange after painting: See: shifting a colour with a glaze, which fixes drifted colours while keeping the shading, such as a bright red over a dull red.
glazing-to-shift-colour.deepen a colour but keep the shading: Glaze a transparent paint of the deeper colour over it; ink, one coat paint or a well thinned wash keeps the shading underneath.
glazing-to-shift-colour.tint a finished area: Brush a transparent glaze over it, stroking from highlight to shadow, and let each pass dry before the next.
glazing-to-shift-colour.make colours more saturated: Give the area one all over glaze of a rich colour, or push a thinned vivid paint of the same hue into the shadows only.
glazing-to-shift-colour.glaze over a cloak: Brush a transparent one coat paint or thin glaze over the finished cloth; the shading underneath carries through.
glazing-to-shift-colour.thin ink over finished paint: Yes: ink is transparent, so a thin coat shifts the colour while keeping the shading, though it knocks back the brightest highlights.
glazing-to-shift-colour.should i use a wash or ink to glaze: Either works; thinned washes are the most forgiving to start with, and inks and one coat paints need thinning well.

glowing-orbs.glowing orb: Paint it white, layer a vivid colour until opaque, place the glow low and towards the middle, add a thin rim band, then a small white reflection.
glowing-orbs.crystal ball glow: Base white, layer a vivid colour, put the main glow low and towards the centre, a thinner band along the lower rim, and a white reflection.
glowing-orbs.how to paint a glowing sphere: White base, vivid colour layered opaque, the main glow low and central, a thin lower rim band, then a small white reflection facing the light.
glowing-orbs.magic orb on a staff: White, then a vivid colour; on a carved orb paint dark red brown on the raised parts so the bright grooves look lit from within.
glowing-orbs.make an orb look lit from inside: Keep the bright colour in the grooves by painting the raised parts dark red brown, or on a smooth orb place the glow low and central.
glowing-orbs.glowing globe: Place the main glow low and towards the middle rather than against the edge, add a thinner rim band below, and a white reflection last.
glowing-orbs.orb looks flat: Move the glow low and towards the middle, add a thinner band of light along the lower rim, and a small white reflection facing the light.
glowing-orbs.power orb glow: Paint white past the orb, cover with an opaque wash of the glow colour, build white back towards the centre, and catch nearby edges.
glowing-orbs.sphere glow effect: White base, a vivid colour on top, the glow placed low and central, a thin lower rim band, and a white reflection on the lit side.
glowing-orbs.energy ball: Paint white a little past the orb, wash it in the glow colour, then build white back in smaller layers towards the centre.

green-skin.green skin: Wash down from a bright green base, or layer up from a dark one, and add a warm pink touch on the nose, lips, ears and knuckles.
green-skin.how do i paint green skin: Bright base over white, a green shade cut with medium, the base repainted on top; or dark green over black, layered up paler.
green-skin.orc skin: Either wash a bright base and repaint the tops, or base dark green and highlight paler, then add pink to nose, ears and knuckles.
green-skin.goblin skin: Base bright green over white, wash with green shade cut half with medium, repaint the upper surfaces, and add a little pink.
green-skin.troll skin: Dark green one coat paint over grey, a green wash to even it, bright green on brows, knuckles and sinews, and red in the deepest spots.
green-skin.bright green flesh: Start over white or light grey, mixing a little high coverage green into the bright one, then shade with a green wash cut with medium.
green-skin.dark green skin: Base two coats of drab dark green over black, then highlight paler over most of the area and smaller passes on the tops.
green-skin.green skin looks plastic: Avoid a toy like pure bright green; a slightly drab or blue tinted mid tone looks more serious, with pink on the nose and ears.
green-skin.shading green skin: Mix green shade into the base a little at a time and push darker mixes into the recesses, or glaze thin red into the deepest spots.
green-skin.green skin over black wont cover: Bright greens cover badly over black; start over white or light grey, or use a drab dark green base over black instead.

head-swaps.head swap: Pick a head that fits the neck, trim it to sit at a natural height, and hide the join with a tiny ball of epoxy putty.
head-swaps.how do i swap heads: Choose a head whose neck width fits, trim the peg or socket for a natural height, and press it into a small ball of putty.
head-swaps.putting a different head on a model: Test fit spare heads with a little tack, trim the neck so it sits at a believable height, and fill the gap with a tiny ball of putty.
head-swaps.head looks stuck on: Neck width matters most; a head that does not fit the joint looks stuck on, so trim it lower and fill the gap with putty.
head-swaps.hide the neck join: Press a tiny ball of epoxy putty where the neck meets the body, push the head in, and smooth it with a wetted fine tool.
head-swaps.kitbash heads: Test spare heads of roughly the right scale with tack at different angles; neck width matters most.
head-swaps.head too high on neck: Trim the neck peg or socket, and the back of the head if needed, until it sits at a believable height.
head-swaps.converting with spare heads: Gather spare heads of the right scale, check neck width, trim to height, and hide the join with a small ball of putty.
head-swaps.putty to fill neck gap: Roll a very small ball of epoxy putty, press it at the neck, push the head in so it fills the gap, and smooth it with a wet tool.
head-swaps.which spare head fits: Pick the one whose neck width fits the joint; a slightly smaller head makes the body look larger.

highlights-by-shape.where to put highlights: Treat each part as a sphere, box or cylinder, and give its highlight the same shape as the surface it sits on.
highlights-by-shape.highlight placement: Work out whether each part is a sphere, box or cylinder and follow that shape's rule for where the light goes.
highlights-by-shape.how do i highlight a sphere: Paint a round highlight towards the top that softens into shadow, with a faint reflected light underneath.
highlights-by-shape.highlighting shoulder pads: A round pad is a sphere: a round patch of light towards the top, not a stripe, fading to shadow with faint reflected light below.
highlights-by-shape.highlight a cylinder: Run a stripe of light down the side facing the light and a weaker one down the opposite side, with shadow between.
highlights-by-shape.where does light hit: Top faces are brightest, sides are midtone and undersides darkest; spheres get a round patch and cylinders a stripe.
highlights-by-shape.highlights look wrong: Match the highlight to the shape: round patches on spheres, stripes on cylinders, bright tops and edges on boxes.
highlights-by-shape.basic shapes highlighting: Spheres get a round highlight near the top, boxes a bright top face, and cylinders a stripe down the lit side.
highlights-by-shape.how to highlight a helmet: On a round helmet, paint rings that shrink towards the crown and add a line along the lower edge.
highlights-by-shape.knee pad highlight: A knee pad is a sphere: a round highlight towards the top that softens into shadow, with faint reflected light below.

hue-shifting.hue shifting: Shade and highlight with different hues, not just darker and lighter, such as a deep cool shadow rising to a warm pale highlight.
hue-shifting.shadows a different colour: Use a different hue for shadows, such as blue or purple, as long as the value is right; check it in a greyscale photo.
hue-shifting.dont just add black to shade: Shade with a deeper, cooler version of the hue instead; steps containing black go dull.
hue-shifting.highlights with yellow: Lighten towards a warm pale yellow, and for greens use a yellowish bone or yellow rather than white, which turns them chalky.
hue-shifting.colour ramp from cool to warm: Go from a deep cool colour to a warm pale one in about three steps, with the colours set in a row on the palette.
hue-shifting.richer colour shading: Use different hues for shadows and highlights, like brown shaded pinky purple and lit warm yellow, keeping the values right.
hue-shifting.red shaded with purple: See: changing hue from shadow to highlight, which pairs cool shadows with warm highlights rather than red with purple specifically.
hue-shifting.why do my colours look dull: Shading with black dulls colours; shade towards a cooler hue and highlight towards a warmer one instead.
hue-shifting.shift hue in the highlights: Highlight towards a warm pale colour such as yellow while shading towards blue or purple, keeping it subtle.
hue-shifting.more interesting shadows: Shade towards blue or purple rather than black, keeping the value right, and highlight towards yellow.

keeping-colours-bright.colours look dull: Start with saturated colours over a pale undercoat, shade each colour with its own family, and avoid heavy dark all over washes.
keeping-colours-bright.keep colours bright: Start a little brighter than you want over a pale undercoat, shade each colour with its own family, and skip heavy dark washes.
keeping-colours-bright.wash made my model dull: A heavy all over wash darkens everything evenly; layer the base back over the raised areas, leaving wash only in the shadows.
keeping-colours-bright.saturated colours: Pick saturated starting colours a little brighter than the goal, over a pale undercoat, and shade with washes of the same family.
keeping-colours-bright.how do i keep colours vibrant: Use saturated paints over a pale undercoat, shade with same colour washes cut with medium, and push the final highlights hard.
keeping-colours-bright.colours go muddy: Many dark paints contain black and muddy a colour; shade with a richer, deeper version of the same hue instead.
keeping-colours-bright.yellow looks dirty: Shade yellow with a warm yellow tint rather than black, keep black washes for metal, and start over a pale undercoat.
keeping-colours-bright.vivid paint job: Saturated colours over a pale undercoat, own colour shading, no heavy dark washes, and very bright final highlights.
keeping-colours-bright.dark wash ruined colour: Layer the base colour back over the raised areas, leaving the wash only in the shadows, then highlight upwards.
keeping-colours-bright.bright colourful model: Start bright over a pale undercoat, shade each colour with its own family, and push the last highlights hard.

layering.layering: Stack lighter, smaller and thinner layers over a darker base coat to build highlights, with no washes or blending needed.
layering.how do i layer paint: Base a shadow tone, then a midtone over about 90 percent, then about 30 percent, then 10 percent, each thinner and lighter.
layering.layering highlights: Paint each lighter layer over a smaller area towards the top of each form, thinned until slightly see through.
layering.build up highlights in layers: Over a darker base, layer a midtone on most of the area, then lighter tones on about 30 and 10 percent of it.
layering.layers look stripey: Visible steps can be glazed later: finish with a few very thin glazes over the rough steps, and use thinner later layers.
layering.layering for beginners: Learn it first: base a shadow tone, then midtone on most of the area and smaller lighter layers on top, each thinned with water.
layering.model looks pale after highlighting: Base in a shadow tone darker than the main colour; basing in the main colour and working up makes the model look pale.
layering.what is layering: Stacking lighter, smaller and thinner layers over a base coat to build highlights, with no washes or blending.
layering.highlight without blending: Layer it: each lighter tone over a smaller area, thinned slightly see through, then glaze any rough steps afterwards.
layering.lighter thinner layers: Thin later layers about one part water to one of paint, cover a smaller area each time, and judge them once dry.
layering.What is layering and how do I do it?: Layering stacks lighter, smaller layers over a darker base: midtone on most of the area, then about 30 and 10 percent.

loaded-brush-blending.loaded brush blending: Load the brush with thinned main colour, blot it, touch the tip in a thicker highlight, and drag away from the brightest point.
loaded-brush-blending.two colours on one brush: Carry the thinned main colour in the brush and a thicker highlight on the tip, and the blend happens on the model in one stroke.
loaded-brush-blending.blend in one stroke: Use loaded brush blending: thinned main colour in the brush, thick highlight on the tip, one smooth stroke from the brightest point.
loaded-brush-blending.brush tip in highlight colour: Touch just the very tip into a thicker highlight colour, place it on the brightest point, and drag the stroke away.
loaded-brush-blending.quick gradient on a cloak: Load a thinned cloak colour, tip it with a thicker highlight, and pull one smooth stroke from the brightest point.
loaded-brush-blending.loaded brush technique: Load the thinned main colour, blot it, tip into a thicker highlight, and drag one smooth stroke away from the brightest point.
loaded-brush-blending.tip loading: Loaded brush blending: a modest load of thinned main colour with just the tip dipped in a thicker second colour.
loaded-brush-blending.one stroke blend: Place the tipped brush on the brightest point and drag away in one smooth pass, then reload; scrubbing leaves jagged lines.
loaded-brush-blending.dark and light on one brush: Load the darker colour, blot it, dip only the tip in the lighter one, and pull a single stroke from the bright point.
loaded-brush-blending.fast blend for cloth: Thinned main colour in the brush, thick highlight on the tip, one smooth pass per stroke, then a thin glaze over the join.

masking-tape-stripes.masking stripes: Lay low tack tape strips with a spacer strip for parallel edges, brush only along the gap, and peel when touch dry.
masking-tape-stripes.straight stripes on a tank: Mask with thin low tack tape lined up with panel edges, brush only along the gap, peel when touch dry, and hide bleed as chips.
masking-tape-stripes.masking tape painting: Use thin low tack hobby tape over fully cured paint, press the edges down with a fingernail, and peel when touch dry.
masking-tape-stripes.tape lifted my paint: Tape lifts paint that has not gripped; let it cure fully, test a hidden spot, and reduce the tack by sticking tape to cloth first.
masking-tape-stripes.paint bled under tape: Some bleed is normal; tidy it with the base colour or sponge the base along the edge so it reads as chips.
masking-tape-stripes.paint circles with a mask: Stick a round token or coin on with reusable putty and sponge around it, or cut a hole in a piece of tape.
masking-tape-stripes.half and half colour split: Tape along a panel edge, paint one side, then peel when touch dry; masks work best on flat surfaces.
masking-tape-stripes.hazard stripes with tape: Butt tape strips against a spacer strip for parallel stripes, brush only along the gaps, and peel when touch dry.
masking-tape-stripes.low tack tape: Thin, low tack hobby masking tape; household tape is stiff, lets paint creep under and can rip paint off.
masking-tape-stripes.how do i mask a model: Tape over fully cured paint, press the edges down, brush only along the gap, and peel when the paint is touch dry.

metallic-trim.metallic trim: Block in trim neatly, wash it in light level coats, and highlight it fast with the side of the brush.
metallic-trim.gold trim: Block in the gold, wash it in two light level coats, then drag bright gold along it with the side of the brush.
metallic-trim.silver trim on armour: Block in, wash in two light coats with the model level, then drag bright silver along the edges with the side of the brush.
metallic-trim.trim is messy: Paint the trim first, then fill the panels; painting a flat colour up to a raised edge is easier than a neat metal line.
metallic-trim.paint armour trim neatly: Rough in the trim first and fill the panels after, using a mid size pointed brush, light pressure and two thin coats.
metallic-trim.edges of armour gold: Block in, wash, then drag bright gold along the edge with the side of a lightly loaded brush at about 45 degrees.
metallic-trim.trim highlight: Drag the side of a lightly loaded brush along the trim at about 45 degrees; it catches only the edges.
metallic-trim.trim slips onto armour: Wipe big slips away while wet with a clean damp brush, or paint the trim before the panels so the panels cover slips.
metallic-trim.should i paint trim first or last: Often first: rough in and wash the trim, change your water, then fill the panels, as flat colour up to an edge is easier.
metallic-trim.shoulder pad trim: Block in the metal, wash it level in light coats, highlight with the side of the brush, then fill the pad.

mixing-your-own-wash.make my own wash: Thin any paint with acrylic medium, plus a drop of flow improver, to make a wash in exactly the colour you need.
mixing-your-own-wash.mix a custom shade colour: Put about five drops of medium on the palette, pull in one or two related colours until the tint looks right, and count the drops.
mixing-your-own-wash.diy wash recipe: Roughly equal paint and medium makes a strong wash; more medium turns it into a glaze. A drop of flow improver helps.
mixing-your-own-wash.wash in exactly the colour i want: Thin that colour with medium until it flows; any paint thinned this way becomes a wash.
mixing-your-own-wash.thin regular paint into a wash: Thin it with acrylic medium, water or both; medium dries smoother with fewer tide marks.
mixing-your-own-wash.what do i thin a wash with: Medium is the better base; water alone lets the pigment split and spread unevenly.
mixing-your-own-wash.water or medium for a wash: Medium is better: it keeps pigment bound and dries smoothly, while water alone lets it split and spread unevenly.
mixing-your-own-wash.homemade wash separates: Water alone lets the pigment split; use medium as the base instead, so it stays bound and dries smoothly.
mixing-your-own-wash.can any paint be a wash: Yes: a wash is just paint with less pigment and more water and binder, so any paint thinned with medium works.
mixing-your-own-wash.purple wash from normal paint: Thin a purple paint with medium on the palette until the tint looks right; a drop of flow improver helps it run.

mounting-on-plinths.mount on a plinth: Glue the model on, press epoxy putty around its old base edge and smooth it into the plinth top, or use magnets to keep it removable.
mounting-on-plinths.display base for a model: Keep the plinth simple so the model stays the focus, with the head over the centre, and blend its base in with putty.
mounting-on-plinths.how do i put a model on a plinth: Glue it on, smooth epoxy putty over the old base edge into the plinth, texture it, and paint the ground as one area.
mounting-on-plinths.plinth with magnets: Glue a small magnet under the playing base and set a matching magnet or metal disc flush in the plinth top.
mounting-on-plinths.lift off model for gaming: Glue a magnet under its playing base and set a matching magnet or metal disc flush into the plinth top.
mounting-on-plinths.blend base into plinth: Press epoxy putty around the old base edge, smooth it into the plinth, texture it and paint the whole ground as one.
mounting-on-plinths.plinth putty: Smooth epoxy putty around the model's old base edge into the plinth top, then texture it to match the ground.
mounting-on-plinths.centre the model on plinth: Placing the head over the centre of the plinth usually looks balanced; pin a test hole first.
mounting-on-plinths.display plinth ideas: Keep it simple, or for height glue a trimmed kit base at an angle with rocks and rubble built underneath.
mounting-on-plinths.pinning to a plinth: Pin a test hole first to see where the model will stand, then glue it on and blend the join with putty.

nmm-finishing.nmm: Finish painted metal with graded edge highlights, a few white glints, gloss black shadows and a dim bounce light.
nmm-finishing.nmm edges: Paint each edge one value step above the brightest part of its plate, palest on upward edges, a step lower on downward ones.
nmm-finishing.nmm glints: Stipple tiny dots of the palest tone on the brightest points, then a pinpoint of white in each; keep them few and irregular.
nmm-finishing.how do i finish nmm: Add graded edge highlights, a few white glints, gloss black ink in the darkest areas, and a dim bounce light stopped at the midtone.
nmm-finishing.painted metal shine: Graded edges, a few small white glints on the brightest points, and thinned black ink glazed into the darkest areas for contrast.
nmm-finishing.nmm looks flat: Push contrast: edges a step above each plate, white glints, gloss black ink in the darkest areas, and a cool bounce light below.
nmm-finishing.non metallic metal reflections: Bounce light sits on the side facing the ground, stopped at the midtone and finished pale blue, with a dark band before the main light.
nmm-finishing.nmm highlights: Paint each edge a step brighter than its plate, palest on upward edges, fading towards the ends, and dimmer lower down.
nmm-finishing.non metalic metal: See: finishing painted metal, which covers graded edges, white glints, gloss shadows and bounce light.
nmm-finishing.where to put glints on painted metal: On the brightest points, such as the tip of a blade: tiny pale dots with a pinpoint of white in the centre of each.

oil-pin-wash.oil wash: Gloss varnish first, run thinned dark oil into the recesses only, lift strays with a damp brush after 20 to 30 minutes, then matte varnish.
oil-pin-wash.pin wash: Touch thinned oil into the recesses over a gloss coat; capillary action carries it along the lines and leaves the flats clean.
oil-pin-wash.panel lines with oil paint: Gloss varnish, then touch thinned dark oil into the panel lines and let capillary action carry it along.
oil-pin-wash.thinned oils in recesses: Thin a near black oil with odourless mineral spirits until it runs, and touch the brush tip only into the recesses.
oil-pin-wash.clean recess lining on a tank: Gloss varnish, touch thinned dark brown or greenish grey oil into panel lines and round rivets, then lift strays with damp spirits.
oil-pin-wash.oil wash over gloss varnish: Use an acrylic gloss underneath so the wash slides instead of soaking in; never over an enamel based gloss.
oil-pin-wash.enamel wash: Never put an oil wash over an enamel based gloss; the spirit melts it and the wash fuses in for good.
oil-pin-wash.wash staining the flat panels: The surface was not sealed; gloss varnish first, and lift stray marks across the recess with a just damp brush.
oil-pin-wash.odourless spirits wash: Thin a near black oil with odourless mineral spirits until it runs, over acrylic gloss, mixing only a little at a time.
oil-pin-wash.pinwash panel lines: Over gloss, touch thinned oil into the lines, wait 20 to 30 minutes, wipe across the recess with damp spirits, then matte varnish.

osl-methods.osl: Build a glow by drybrushing out from the source, by many thin glazes, or by a pale mix tinted with a filter.
osl-methods.object source lighting: Drybrush out from the source, glaze many thin layers tighter to the source each time, or build a pale mix and filter it.
osl-methods.glow effect: Drybrush the glow colour out from the source, glaze it thin to smooth it, then add lighter tones and a pale centre.
osl-methods.how do i paint glow: Drybrush it out from the source, glaze it thinly, or build pale highlights and glaze a transparent colour over them.
osl-methods.drybrush glow: Base a mid glow tone, drybrush it over raised areas near the source, glaze about one to five, then drybrush lighter tones nearer the source.
osl-methods.glow with glazes: Thin the colour about ten to one, start each stroke away from the source and end on it, and repeat many times once dry.
osl-methods.filter glow: Highlight with pale yellow mixed into each base colour, then glaze or spray a transparent colour such as orange over it.
osl-methods.light from a lantern: Drybrush or glaze the glow colour outward from the lantern, heaviest near it, then add sharp highlights on nearby edges.
osl-methods.osl techniques: Three methods: drybrushing out from the source, many thin glazes, or a pale mix tinted with a filter.
osl-methods.glowing light on armour: Drybrush or glaze the glow colour onto the armour nearest the source, then catch edges facing the light with sharp highlights.

paint-consistency-by-technique.how thin should paint be: From straight out of the pot to about half water for base coats, less for edge highlights, and up to nine water to one paint for glazes.
paint-consistency-by-technique.paint consistency: Each technique wants its own thickness, from nearly dry for drybrushing to mostly water for glazes and washes.
paint-consistency-by-technique.thinning ratio: Base coats up to about half water, glazes up to about nine water to one paint, and drybrushing barely any water.
paint-consistency-by-technique.how much water: Add it a drop at a time and test: scratchy lines mean too thick, paint flooding off the brush means too thin.
paint-consistency-by-technique.consistency for glazes: Glazes are over half water, up to about nine parts water to one of paint, almost tinted water.
paint-consistency-by-technique.drybrushing consistency: Barely any water: keep the brush just damp and wipe most of the paint off before you start.
paint-consistency-by-technique.what consistency for washes: Thin washes and shades as much as you like, as long as some colour remains.
paint-consistency-by-technique.base coat consistency: Like thin cream or full fat milk: thin enough to level flat, thick enough to cover in two or three coats.
paint-consistency-by-technique.thin paints: Add water a drop at a time and test on the palette; strongly pigmented colours need more thinning than weak ones.
paint-consistency-by-technique.paint thickness for layers: From pot thickness to about half water, like thin cream or full fat milk, getting less watery for the final small highlights.

paint-swatch-cards.swatch cards: Swatch every paint on primed textured plastic card to see its true dried colour, coverage and finish.
paint-swatch-cards.paint swatches: Paint a block of squares per paint on primed card, adding a coat to each in turn, and note the name and coat count.
paint-swatch-cards.make a colour chart of my paints: Swatch every paint on primed plastic card, labelled with a waterproof pen and grouped by colour family.
paint-swatch-cards.paint looks different from the pot: Dried paint often looks different from the pot; a swatch on primed card shows its real colour, finish and coverage.
paint-swatch-cards.keep track of my paint collection: Swatch every paint as soon as you get it on primed card, with its name and coat count, grouped by colour family.
paint-swatch-cards.see the dried colour: Paint a swatch on primed textured card; dried paint often looks quite different from the pot.
paint-swatch-cards.which paints do i own: Keep swatch sheets of every paint, with names written beside each block, grouped by colour family.
paint-swatch-cards.swatch over textured card: Textured card shows how paint behaves over raised and recessed surfaces; avoid paper, which soaks paint up.
paint-swatch-cards.colour reference for planning: Keep swatch sheets grouped by colour family and lay candidate swatches side by side when planning a scheme.
paint-swatch-cards.plan a colour scheme with swatches: Lay candidate swatches side by side to compare colours and contrast before painting anything.

painting-black-armour.black armour: Black cannot be shaded, so build up cool blue grey highlights, strongest at the top of each part, plus soft reflections on curves.
painting-black-armour.how do i highlight black: Build blue grey highlights round the panels, then lighter ones inside, then pale grey on top edges, mixing white into the blue black.
painting-black-armour.black armour looks flat: Add soft patches of light on domes and curved plates, not just edge lines, and make highlights strongest at the top of each part.
painting-black-armour.highlight black armor with grey: Highlight with blue greys, from a chunky dark one round the panels to pale grey on top edges, mixing white into the blue black.
painting-black-armour.can you wash black armour: No: a wash cannot darken black and can leave a patchy sheen, so work only with lighter colours.
painting-black-armour.black power armour: Build cool blue grey highlights strongest at the top of each part, plus soft light patches on curved plates.
painting-black-armour.reflections on black plate: Mix grey half and half with glaze medium, build a soft patch in two thin coats, then a smaller lighter patch inside.
painting-black-armour.black armor patchy sheen: Paint a thinned coat of your black over the primer first; blacks differ in sheen and touch ups show as patches.
painting-black-armour.paint black over black primer: Yes: paint a thinned coat of your black anyway, as blacks differ in sheen and touch ups would show against primer.
painting-black-armour.black looks grey after highlighting: Highlights covered too much; glaze or wash very thin black over it, twice in the shadows, to pull it back.

painting-cracks.paint cracks: Paint a thin wandering dark line, a thin light line just below it, and tiny light dots on the sharpest raised points.
painting-cracks.fake cracks with paint: A dark wandering line with a light line just under it, plus a few uneven bright points on the raised peaks, reads as a real crack.
painting-cracks.cracked stone: Paint a thin branching dark line, run a light line just beneath it, and add uneven bright dots where the edge sticks up.
painting-cracks.how do i paint a crack: Paint a thin, wandering dark line that branches, then a thin light line just below it to show the lower edge catching light.
painting-cracks.painted cracks look fake: Add a thin light line just below the dark one and keep the bright points uneven so they do not look like a printed pattern.
painting-cracks.freehand cracks on rock: Paint a wandering, branching dark line, a light line just under it, and tiny uneven light dots on the sharpest points.
painting-cracks.cracked skin: See: painting cracks, a dark wandering line with a light line under it and bright points, shown on general surfaces rather than skin.
painting-cracks.cracks on armour: A thin wandering dark line, a light line just under it for the lit lower edge, and tiny bright dots on the sharpest points.
painting-cracks.battle damage cracks: Paint a dark wandering line that branches, a light line just below, and a few uneven bright dots on the raised edges.
painting-cracks.crack lines on a statue: Thin wandering dark lines that branch, a light line under each, and tiny uneven bright dots on the sharpest points.

painting-from-reference.use reference photos: Look up photos of the real material or effect before you paint it, and keep the picture in view while you work.
painting-from-reference.paint from reference: Find photos of the real thing first, study the lights and darks, and keep the reference right behind the model as you paint.
painting-from-reference.how do i paint burnt wood: Look at reference of burnt wood and glowing coals first, and match its lights and darks before worrying about exact hue.
painting-from-reference.make materials look realistic: Paint from photos of the real material, getting the lights and darks right first; the exact hue matters less.
painting-from-reference.look at the real thing first: Yes: guessing usually goes wrong, so study where light falls, its colour and how it fades in real photos.
painting-from-reference.reference pictures while painting: Keep the reference right behind the model, ideally printed, so checking it takes only a glance.
painting-from-reference.my effects look fake: Compare the model with photos of the real thing and look for differences in contrast, colour or where the light sits.
painting-from-reference.copy real life colours: Match the lights and darks in your reference first, and check colours against more than one source.
painting-from-reference.what does rust really look like: See: painting from reference, which says to look at photos of real rust rather than guessing before painting it.
painting-from-reference.study photos before painting: Before painting, study where the light falls, what colour it is, how it fades, and how much is dark, mid and bright.

painting-horns.horns: Base dark warm brown, paint fine growth lines in lighter browns, then bone, cream and white towards the light end.
painting-horns.how do i paint horns: Base very dark warm brown, then mid brown, then fine lines in lighter tones up to bone and white, each closer to the tip.
painting-horns.goat horns on a beastman: Dark warm brown base, fine lighter growth lines building to bone and white at the tips, and dark glaze into the cracks.
painting-horns.demon horns: Base dark warm brown, paint fine lighter lines along the horn up to pale cream and white, with a white dot on the point.
painting-horns.ram horns with ridges: Paint fine lines along the horn in lighter tones, pulled out into the darker areas, then glaze dark brown into the cracks.
painting-horns.growth lines on horns: Paint fine lines along the horn with the brush tip in lighter tones, each set inside the last and closer to the light end.
painting-horns.bone coloured horns: Keep them a different tone from nearby bone, such as a darker brown or grey lifted to pale grey green, so they read separately.
painting-horns.what colour are horns: Usually a very dark warm brown building to bone and white at the tips, kept a different tone from nearby bone.
painting-horns.horns dark at base light at tip: Base bone, then coat thinned see through brown over two thirds from the root, with two more coats each stopping shorter.
painting-horns.bull horns look plain: Add fine lighter growth lines, a pale streak along one edge for shine, or thin dark stripes from root to tip for bands.

painting-on-the-sprue.painting on the sprue: Tiny figures joined to the frame only at their feet are often faster painted before clipping off; larger models are better built first.
painting-on-the-sprue.paint before clipping: Yes for very small figures attached at the feet; clean mould lines, prime, paint in a production line, then clip and touch up.
painting-on-the-sprue.should i paint on the frame: Usually build first, but very small figures attached only at the feet are easier to paint while still on the frame.
painting-on-the-sprue.tiny figures on sprue: Clean the mould lines, cut the frame into small pieces grouped by colour, prime, paint, then clip off and touch up.
painting-on-the-sprue.paint before assembly: Usually build first; tiny figures and small add ons are the exception, and large pieces like a big beast are better assembled.
painting-on-the-sprue.paint on sprue: For tiny figures attached at the feet, clean mould lines, cut the frame into small pieces and paint one colour across all of them.
painting-on-the-sprue.small minis still attached: Paint them on the frame, turning the piece to reach each part, then clip off, trim feed marks and touch up the bare spots.
painting-on-the-sprue.paint models on runners: Small figures attached at the feet paint well on the frame; glue painted parts with super glue, not plastic glue.
painting-on-the-sprue.leave them on the sprue: Leave tiny figures attached only at the feet on the frame for painting, cut into small pieces that are easy to hold.
painting-on-the-sprue.tiny models hard to hold: Leave tiny figures on the frame, cut into small pieces that are easy to hold, and paint them before clipping off.

painting-scales.paint scales: Drybrush scales up in lighter, gentler steps with pale tips, and keep the gaps dark or dusty so each scale stands out.
painting-scales.dragon scales: Drybrush the base generously, then lighter tones with lighter touches, a flick of the palest on the tips, and keep gaps dark.
painting-scales.scaly skin: Drybrush in lighter, gentler steps with pale tips, keeping the gaps dark or dusty so each scale stands out.
painting-scales.lizard scales: Drybrush the base colour, then lighter tones with a lighter touch each time, finishing with a flick of the palest on the tips.
painting-scales.snake scales: Drybrush up in lighter, gentler steps, finishing with a light flick of the palest tone on the scale tips.
painting-scales.drybrush scales: Start with a generous circular overbrush of the base, then lighter tones with a lighter touch, using a clean dry brush each time.
painting-scales.scales look flat: Push the drybrush steps lighter with pale tips, keep the gaps dark, and plan the light so upper surfaces catch the most.
painting-scales.scales not standing out: Keep the gaps dark or dusty and the tips light; after a wash, do not press hard or you push paint back into the recesses.
painting-scales.fish scales: Drybrush them up in lighter steps with pale tips, keeping the gaps between them dark so each scale stands out.
painting-scales.scaled hide on a monster: Drybrush up in lighter steps with pale tips, and run a pale wash or pigment into the gaps for dusty scales.

painting-soft-faces.female faces: Keep shading and highlights subtle and thin, with no hard lines; heavy shadows and bright highlights quickly look harsh.
painting-soft-faces.how do i paint a woman's face: Start pale with thin pinkish flesh, shade with thin warm tones in small amounts, and highlight with very thin pale glazes.
painting-soft-faces.young face looks old: Strong highlights and heavy shading age a face; keep both thin and subtle, with one soft highlight on small heads.
painting-soft-faces.soft faces: Thin pale pinkish flesh, light warm shading in small amounts, soft pale yellow and cream highlights, and no hard lines.
painting-soft-faces.face looks harsh: Shading or highlights too strong; keep them thin and subtle, and judge at arm's length, as close photos look harsher.
painting-soft-faces.child face miniature: See: soft, youthful and feminine faces, which covers keeping shading and highlights thin so young faces stay soft.
painting-soft-faces.feminine face shading: Shade with thin warm flesh washes in small amounts at the hairline, eyes, nose and mouth, and avoid hard lines.
painting-soft-faces.too much shading on a face: Use smaller amounts of thinned warm shade each time, and work back and forth with highlights so it does not drift dark.
painting-soft-faces.subtle face highlights: Use thin glazes of pale flesh with pale yellow, then cream, and only a very thin white on the highest points.
painting-soft-faces.pretty face miniature: Pale, slightly pink flesh in thin coats, subtle warm shading, soft yellow and cream highlights, and a glazed reddish lower lip.

painting-vehicles-by-brush.paint a tank without an airbrush: No airbrush needed: spray prime in the main colour, shade each panel darker towards one end, layer back up with a large brush, then edge and chip.
painting-vehicles-by-brush.brush paint vehicles: Paint panel by panel: prime in the main colour, shade towards one end, layer up with a large brush, edge highlight, then chip and weather.
painting-vehicles-by-brush.big kit by brush: Spray prime in the main colour to save brush time, then shade, layer up one panel at a time, edge highlight and chip.
painting-vehicles-by-brush.how do i paint a tank: Prime in the main colour, shade each panel towards one end, layer back up, add crisp top edge highlights, then metallics and chipping.
painting-vehicles-by-brush.large models by hand: Spray prime in the main colour, then work one panel at a time with a large brush so coats stay smooth.
painting-vehicles-by-brush.vehicle panels look streaky: Work one panel at a time with a large brush, or use soft drybrushing in several steps from the panel centres outwards.
