painting-vehicles-by-brush.no airbrush tank: Prime in the main colour, shade panels darker at one end, layer up, edge highlight, then chip edges and low areas.
painting-vehicles-by-brush.paint a truck: See: brush painting vehicles and large kits, which covers any vehicle panel by panel: prime, shade, layer, edge and chip.
painting-vehicles-by-brush.brush painting big flat panels: Use a large brush one panel at a time, or wash the recesses and drybrush the base in small circles to soften wash marks.
painting-vehicles-by-brush.chipping and edge highlights on a tank: Crisp edge highlights in the brightest tone along top edges, then chips on edges, corners and low areas, sponged on big areas.

panel-gradients.shade armour panels: Darken the lower part of each plate with a quick wet blend, then run thinned black into the deepest recesses.
panel-gradients.panel gradient: Paint most of the panel in the main colour, add dark at the bottom while wet and brush it up, then repeat once dry to smooth it.
panel-gradients.plate armour shading: Darken the lower part of each plate with a wet blend or thin glazes, line the deepest recesses, then edge highlight in stages.
panel-gradients.wet blend panels: Paint the panel leaving the bottom edge, add a little black or dark shade there while wet, and brush back and forth to blend.
panel-gradients.darken the bottom of each panel: Wet blend dark into the bottom while the colour is wet, or glaze a thin darker tone over the lower part in two or three passes.
panel-gradients.vehicle panels look flat: A simple light to dark fade from top to bottom reads well on big flat panels.
panel-gradients.armour plates: Darken the lower part of each plate, line the deepest recesses with thinned black, and edge highlight in stages.
panel-gradients.panel blend: Paint the panel in the main colour, work dark into the bottom while wet, and repeat once dry to smooth streaks.
panel-gradients.shading big flat plates: A simple light to dark fade from top to bottom reads well; build it with thin darker glazes or extra wash pushed downward.
panel-gradients.how do i shade a panel: Darken the lower part of the plate with a quick wet blend or thin glazes, then line the deepest recesses with thinned black.

pinning-parts.pinning: Drill matching holes and glue in short lengths of wire with super glue so joints on heavy or handled parts will not break.
pinning-parts.how do i pin a model: Drill into one part, glue in wire, trim it, dab paint on the ends to mark the other part, drill there, test fit and super glue.
pinning-parts.arm snapped off at the shoulder: Pin it: drill a hole in each side, glue in a short wire, and fix it with super glue; two pins stop it twisting.
pinning-parts.heavy metal part keeps falling off: Pin it with wire in drilled holes; glue alone rarely holds heavy metal arms and weapons for long.
pinning-parts.drill a hole and glue in wire: Drill a bit the same size as the wire or slightly bigger, glue the wire in with super glue, then mark and drill the other part.
pinning-parts.should i pin resin models: Yes: pinning strengthens joints on metal and resin models; use super glue, not plastic glue, for resin.
pinning-parts.broken ankle on a miniature: Drill into the leg and foot, glue in a short wire pin with super glue, and let it cure fully before handling.
pinning-parts.model on one foot keeps breaking: Pin the joint with wire glued into drilled holes; pinning suits models standing on one foot.
pinning-parts.glue alone wont hold: Drill matching holes and glue in a wire pin; two pins stop a joint from twisting and falling off.
pinning-parts.paperclip pin: Paper clip wire or brass rod both work; cut it with rough old cutters, not your good ones.

poor-coverage-paints.paint does not cover: Use an opaque light undercoat and more thin coats, not thicker paint; acrylic is partly see through, especially bright colours.
poor-coverage-paints.patchy base coat: Thin coats over a light grey or white primer, three or four for weak colours, letting each dry fully before the next.
poor-coverage-paints.streaky base coat: Keep it thinned and add more coats, letting each dry; going back over wet paint drags it and builds texture.
poor-coverage-paints.red covers badly: Undercoat with a dense strong orange first, then red usually covers in about two coats.
poor-coverage-paints.yellow patchy: Undercoat with a pale stone or cream, then yellow covers in one or two more coats; keep it thinned.
poor-coverage-paints.see through paint: Acrylic is partly see through, especially bright colours; use a light undercoat and several thin coats.
poor-coverage-paints.how many coats: Over a good light undercoat, red takes about two coats and yellow a couple more; weak colours over black need far more.
poor-coverage-paints.paint looks murky over black: One coat over black always looks patchy or murky; use a light undercoat and more thin coats.
poor-coverage-paints.green wont cover: Keep it thinned with a drop of flow improver, use a light undercoat, and apply three or four coats.
poor-coverage-paints.should i use thicker paint to cover: No: thick paint leaves brush marks and hides detail; use a lighter undercoat and more thin coats.
poor-coverage-paints.Why is my base coat streaky and patchy?: Acrylic is partly see through, so one coat looks patchy; use a light undercoat and several thin coats, each left to dry.

pressing-texture-into-putty.press chainmail into green stuff: Let the putty firm up 20 to 40 minutes, keep tools wet, and press rows of rings with a thin hollow tube, offsetting each row.
pressing-texture-into-putty.sculpt scales into putty: Press the end of a cut tube or pen nib at a slight angle, from the bottom up so each row overlaps the one below.
pressing-texture-into-putty.rivets in putty: Press a thin tube for a ring, or roll tiny balls of putty and press them on with a wet tool, spaced with marked tape.
pressing-texture-into-putty.putty sticks to my tools: Keep tools and fingers wet with water or a thin smear of petroleum jelly, and let the putty firm up first.
pressing-texture-into-putty.stamp repeating patterns into putty: Sculpt one good strip, press it into reusable mould putty, and use the mould as a stamp.
pressing-texture-into-putty.make scales with a small tube: Press the end of a cut tube at a slight angle, working from the bottom up so each row overlaps the one below.
pressing-texture-into-putty.when is putty ready to texture: After mixing, wait 20 to 40 minutes until it holds a mark but no longer sticks.
pressing-texture-into-putty.fill a gap with chainmail texture: Press rows of rings with a thin hollow tube, offset by half a ring, and blend the patch edges in before it cures.
pressing-texture-into-putty.sculpt rows of scales: Work from the bottom up with a cut tube or pen nib, overlapping each row, smaller near joints and edges.
pressing-texture-into-putty.green stuff too soft to hold detail: Let it firm up for 20 to 40 minutes after mixing; too soft and the pattern smears.

quick-tabletop-method.quick tabletop standard: Prime light, block in every colour, wash once, tidy the raised areas with the base colours, then add optional highlights.
quick-tabletop-method.base wash and tidy: Block in every colour, wash once by colour, then repaint the base on raised areas, skipping the recesses.
quick-tabletop-method.fastest way to paint an army: Prime light, base coat everything, wash once, tidy or drybrush, then highlight top edges if you want.
quick-tabletop-method.tabletop ready quickly: Base, wash once, tidy with the base colours on raised areas, and the model is ready for the table.
quick-tabletop-method.how do i paint quickly: Prime light, block in every colour a little lighter than you want, wash once, then tidy the raised areas.
quick-tabletop-method.painting board game pieces: The base, wash and tidy method suits board game pieces: block in, wash once, then repaint the raised areas.
quick-tabletop-method.rpg heroes in an evening: Prime light, block in all colours, wash once, tidy raised areas, and stop there or add a light edge highlight.
quick-tabletop-method.simple routine for troops: Block in every colour, wash once, then tidy or drybrush the raised areas, painting details after any drybrushing.
quick-tabletop-method.base coat then wash: Yes: block in every colour a little lighter, wash once, then tidy the raised and flat areas with the base colours.
quick-tabletop-method.too slow at painting squads: Use base, wash and tidy: prime light, block in everything, wash once, tidy the raised areas, and stop when ready.

removing-sculpted-details.remove sculpted detail: Clip off the bulk, shave down in thin slivers with a fresh blade, scrape and sand smooth, then fill any holes left behind.
removing-sculpted-details.shave off detail: Shave a thin sliver at a time with a fresh blade braced against your thumb, then scrape upright near the surface.
removing-sculpted-details.remove a badge: Clip the bulk off with flat cutters, shave down in thin layers, scrape with the blade upright, then sand smooth.
removing-sculpted-details.sand smooth: Finish with a file or fine wet sandpaper around 800 to 1000, then brush thin plastic glue over it to melt away fuzz.
removing-sculpted-details.how do i remove icons from armour: Clip off the bulk, shave in thin slivers, scrape following the curve, sand with fine wet paper, and fill engraved symbols with putty.
removing-sculpted-details.clip off detail: Clip the bulk off with flat faced cutters, staying clear of the surface you want to keep, then shave and scrape down.
removing-sculpted-details.scrape off sculpted emblem: Shave it down in thin slivers with a fresh blade, scrape upright following the curve, then sand and fill any dips.
removing-sculpted-details.remove details for freehand: Clip, shave, scrape and sand the detail away, ideally before gluing halves together; a smooth surface takes freehand well.
removing-sculpted-details.fill holes after removing: Push in sandable two part putty or water based filler, wipe it level, and sand with a hard backed stick.
removing-sculpted-details.smooth surface for transfers: Clip, shave, scrape and sand the detail off, fill any dips, and sand smooth with fine wet paper; a smooth surface takes transfers.

resin-water-effects.resin water: Choose the resin for the depth, paint everything underneath first, tape the edges, tint sparingly, then leave it at least 48 hours.
resin-water-effects.pour water effects on a base: Paint the base first, wrap tape round the edge, pour the right resin for the depth, lift bubbles, and leave it alone to cure.
resin-water-effects.river base: Paint the riverbed first, wall the edges with tape or card, pour two part epoxy for depth, and tint with just a drop of ink.
resin-water-effects.clear resin pond: For deeper water use two part clear epoxy, which shrinks less; mix more than you need and stir slowly to avoid bubbles.
resin-water-effects.resin shrank and left a dip: One part water resin shrinks and leaves a dip; pour several thin layers, or use two part epoxy, which shrinks much less.
resin-water-effects.two part epoxy water: Two part epoxy shrinks much less and suits deeper pours; mix more than you need so the ratio is easier to hit.
resin-water-effects.resin leaking out the edges: Wrap at least three tight layers of tape round the base edge, or build a card wall sealed outside with hot glue.
resin-water-effects.how do i tint resin water: Use a single drop of transparent ink in a lot of resin; too much kills the depth.
resin-water-effects.puddle effect on base: One part water resin or gel, or UV curing resin built in thin layers, suits small shallow puddles.
resin-water-effects.bubbles in my resin water: Stir slowly to avoid bubbles, then lift any that rise out with a skewer straight after pouring.

scratch-built-terrain.scratch build terrain: Plan from reference, build from plastic card with braced walls on a rigid base, then detail it with spare parts.
scratch-built-terrain.how do i make a building from scratch: Gather reference, cut plastic card walls against a steel ruler, brace them inside with strips, and work from big shapes to details.
scratch-built-terrain.plastic sheet buildings: Cut walls by scoring and snapping against a steel ruler, keep them square with angle guides and inner strips, and add detail.
scratch-built-terrain.make my own terrain: Start simple with rocks, hills and standing stones, using rigid insulation foam, card or plastic card as the core.
scratch-built-terrain.diy ruined house: Plan it from reference, cut and brace plastic card walls on a rigid base, then add spare parts and daily clutter.
scratch-built-terrain.cheap terrain from plastic card: Cardboard and foam board make cheap cores, clad in plastic card where weak, with walls braced by plastic strips.
scratch-built-terrain.walls keep bending and warping: Use angle guides at joints and plastic strips inside to keep walls straight, and give the piece a rigid base.
scratch-built-terrain.what terrain should i scratch build firs: Start simple: rocks, hills and standing stones forgive wobbly cuts and need few tools.
scratch-built-terrain.detail a building with spare bits: Add spare kit parts, wire cables, tiny rivets and daily clutter like stacked logs or a ladder, but know when to stop.
scratch-built-terrain.plan a terrain piece from reference: Gather reference, give the building a purpose, then work from big shapes to medium ones and details, checking the whole.

selective-gloss.gloss eyes: A thick blob of gloss on a black eye stays put and shines sharply; brush it on as the very last step.
selective-gloss.matt vs gloss: Gloss makes things look wet or polished, matt suits cloth, skin and fur, and mixing them lets materials read differently.
selective-gloss.make gems shiny: Brush thinned gloss on gems as the last step, so no later matt coat dulls it; it also deepens the colour.
selective-gloss.how do i make something look wet: Brush thinned gloss over it as the last step; gloss makes things look wet or polished.
selective-gloss.gloss on blood: Brush gloss over fresh blood as the last step so it looks wet.
selective-gloss.satin finish on armour: Satin gives a soft sheen that suits slightly polished armour; brush it on chosen parts after a matt coat.
selective-gloss.should the whole model be matt: Varnish it all matt first for an even base, then brush gloss or satin on chosen parts such as eyes and boots.
selective-gloss.shiny leather with varnish: Satin over leather gives a soft sheen; matt black leather looks like cloth until satin goes over it.
selective-gloss.wet look slime: Brush thinned gloss over the slime as the last step; it makes things look wet and deepens the colour.
selective-gloss.same colour different materials: Give them different finishes: gloss on polished or wet parts, satin on leather, matt on cloth, and they read differently.

sketchy-painting-style.sketchy style: Build highlights from thin scratchy lines over a coloured primer left showing as the deepest shadow.
sketchy-painting-style.gritty painting style: Prime warm dark or black, leave it in the shadows, and highlight with many thin, loose scratchy lines where light hits.
sketchy-painting-style.scratchy line highlights: Thin the paint a little more than usual, graze the surface with the tip, and stack lighter scratches over smaller areas.
sketchy-painting-style.grimdark look: For a grimier mood, layer brown, rust and dust washes over a simple base and highlight, and keep metals high contrast.
sketchy-painting-style.rough painterly style: Highlight with thin scratchy lines that follow the form, over a primer left showing, and let the brush marks show.
sketchy-painting-style.leave the primer showing: Never fully cover the primer; leave it in the shadows and paint around it, which unifies the model and saves shading.
sketchy-painting-style.comic book style mini: See: gritty, sketchy style, which uses scratchy lines and bold brightness jumps over a coloured primer.
sketchy-painting-style.sketch style highlights: Stack many thin scratchy lines where light hits, then a lighter colour over a smaller area, following each surface's form.
sketchy-painting-style.loose gritty finish: Use a slightly bigger brush held further back, thin paint, and fast scratchy strokes, with a time limit to keep it rough.
sketchy-painting-style.paint like a sketch: Prime dark, keep the primer as shadow, and build highlights from thin, loose lines that follow the form.

snow-on-models.snow on boots: Dab off white onto boots and kit with a small piece of foam, mostly wiped off, where snow would clump first.
snow-on-models.how do i paint snow on a model: Stipple or sponge off white or very pale grey onto boots, hems and calves, then the tops of shoulders, helmets and packs.
snow-on-models.winter whitewash on a tank: Seal the base with satin, apply a thin uneven water washable white, then rub some off with a damp brush once dry.
snow-on-models.snow stuck to armour: Dab off white with a foam stub on the tops of shoulders, helmets and packs, where snow would settle.
snow-on-models.sponge on snow: Roll packing foam into a stub, load it with off white, dab most off, and stab lightly where snow would clump.
snow-on-models.patchy winter camo: Stab white onto the armour with an almost dry small soft brush, building an uneven speckle.
snow-on-models.snowy cloak hem: Sponge off white lightly around the coat hem, where snow clumps first, using a foam stub mostly wiped off.
snow-on-models.make it look like its been in snow: Sponge off white on boots, hems and the tops of kit, use snow paste on the base, and add cold blue grey tones.
snow-on-models.whitewash vehicles: Seal with satin, apply a thin uneven washable white, then rub areas back with a damp brush and clear markings.
snow-on-models.snow looks too white: Use an off white or very pale grey instead; it looks more natural than pure white.

sponge-gradients.gradient with a makeup sponge: Cover the model in the shadow colour, then dab lighter colours from above with a fine makeup sponge, each over a smaller area.
sponge-gradients.sponge instead of airbrush: Yes: a fine pored cone makeup sponge dabs soft gradients cheaply, though curvy, intricate models are faster with an airbrush.
sponge-gradients.how do i get a smooth fade without an ai: Dab it with a fine makeup sponge: shadow colour all over, then lighter colours from above, each over a smaller area once dry.
sponge-gradients.sponge blending: Touch the sponge to water, thin the paint slightly, and dab colours close in brightness, letting each layer dry first.
sponge-gradients.cheap airbrush alternative: A fine pored makeup sponge dabs smooth gradients and fades as a cheap alternative.
sponge-gradients.smooth fade on a cloak: Cover it in the shadow colour, dab the main colour on from above, then lighter colours over smaller areas, and finish edges by brush.
sponge-gradients.sponge stipple gradient: Dab with a fine pored cone makeup sponge, colours close in brightness, each layer dry before the next.
sponge-gradients.dabbing paint with a sponge: Thin the paint slightly, dampen the sponge, dab most off, and let each layer dry, as the sponge lifts wet paint.
sponge-gradients.sky gradient: See: gradients with a makeup sponge, which dabs smooth fades from shadow to brightest colour over any surface.
sponge-gradients.foam speckles too coarse: Use a fine pored cone makeup sponge instead; coarse packing foam leaves an obvious speckle.

stamping-designs.stamp designs onto shields: Spread paint over an etched plate, scrape the surplus off, pick the design up with a silicone stamp, and press it straight onto the shield.
stamping-designs.nail art stamps on models: Nail art or hobby stamping kits work: etched plate, flat scraper and soft silicone stamp, pressed onto a painted, dry area.
stamping-designs.stamp heraldry: Use an etched plate and silicone stamp: paint the design, scrape it, pick it up with the stamp and press it on fast.
stamping-designs.print an emblem on armour: Stamp it: fill the etched design with paint, scrape off the surplus, pick it up with a silicone stamp and press it on.
stamping-designs.stamping plate and silicone stamp: Etched plates hold the design, a scraper clears the surplus, and the soft silicone stamp lifts it onto the model.
stamping-designs.repeat the same symbol on a squad: Use a stamping plate and silicone stamp to print the same emblem on each model, tidying gaps by hand.
stamping-designs.stamp rings on a shield: Dip the end of a clear plastic brush cover in paint and press it on, turning it and pressing again for a full ring.
stamping-designs.neat symbols without freehand: Stamp them with an etched plate and silicone stamp, or press rings with a paint dipped brush cover.
stamping-designs.stamped pattern smudged: Work fast, as acrylic dries on the stamp in seconds, then fill gaps by hand and sponge the base colour again over smudges.
stamping-designs.heraldry without freehand: Print it with an etched plate and silicone stamp, fill gaps by hand, then paint a bright colour over a white print.

streaking-grime-and-rust.rust streaks: Pull thinned rust washes straight down from rivets and trim in several thin passes, strongest at the source and feathered at the end.
streaking-grime-and-rust.how do i paint rain streaks: Thin a dark warm brown until inky, pull lines straight down and parallel, and soften the ends with a clean damp brush.
streaking-grime-and-rust.streaking grime on a tank: Pull thin brown streaks straight down from rivets, vents and trim, build them in several passes, and feather the ends.
streaking-grime-and-rust.rust running down from rivets: Paint a ring round the rivet, pull a thin line straight down, soften the end with a damp brush, then add orange brown and ochre.
streaking-grime-and-rust.vertical dirt streaks: Thin a dark warm brown until inky, pull it straight down, and feather the end with a clean damp brush.
streaking-grime-and-rust.streaks look too blobby: The paint is not thinned enough; thin it until inky or mix with glaze medium, and build streaks in several thin passes.
streaking-grime-and-rust.water stains on armour: Pull thinned streaks straight down from fittings and trim, in a tone that contrasts with the base, and feather the ends.
streaking-grime-and-rust.rust drips from bolts: Ring the bolt with thinned brown, pull a line straight down, feather the end, then thinner orange brown and tiny ochre dots.
streaking-grime-and-rust.weathering streaks on vehicles: Streak thinned browns straight down from rivets, vents and trim, varying length and strength, matched to show on the base.
streaking-grime-and-rust.feather the end of a streak: Soften the end with a clean damp brush, rinsing often; enamel or oil streaking paints give more working time.

tabletop-vs-display-standard.tabletop standard: Every area painted with its own clear colour, a wash and simple highlight for depth, and a finished base with a neat rim.
tabletop-vs-display-standard.what is tabletop standard: No bare primer or plastic showing, each area its own colour, basic shading and highlights, and a textured base with a neat rim.
tabletop-vs-display-standard.display standard: Display adds believable blends, crisp small details, often freehand or texture effects, and a built base that gives context.
tabletop-vs-display-standard.good enough for the table: When every area is painted, shaded, highlighted and based, so it reads well at arm's length, it is tabletop standard.
tabletop-vs-display-standard.how good is good enough: Tabletop standard: every area painted with its own colour, basic depth, and a finished base, reading well at arm's length.
tabletop-vs-display-standard.display quality vs gaming: Gaming needs every area painted, shaded and based; display adds smooth blends, crisp details and a story base.
tabletop-vs-display-standard.competition level painting: See: tabletop versus display level, where display adds believable blends, crisp details, freehand and a story base.
tabletop-vs-display-standard.what does battle ready mean: See: tabletop standard, every area painted, shaded, highlighted and based so it reads well at arm's length.
tabletop-vs-display-standard.is my model finished enough: If nothing bare shows, each area has its own colour with basic depth, and the base is done, it is tabletop standard.
tabletop-vs-display-standard.difference between tabletop and display: Tabletop is fully painted, shaded and based to read at arm's length; display adds smooth blends, crisp detail and a story base.

thatched-roofs.thatched roof: Soak fake fur in watered PVA, comb it downwards, glue it to the roof, let it dry hard, then paint and drybrush it.
thatched-roofs.fake fur thatch: Fake fur with a longish pile, soaked in PVA and water and combed downwards, dries hard into convincing thatch.
thatched-roofs.straw roof for a cottage: Glue PVA soaked fake fur combed downwards onto the roof, then base mid brown and drybrush straw yellow and pale cream.
thatched-roofs.how do i make thatch: Cut fake fur to each panel, soak it in PVA and water, comb it downwards, glue it on, and let it dry hard.
thatched-roofs.teddy bear fur roof: Fake fur with a longish pile works: soak it in watered PVA and comb it downwards so it lies like straw.
thatched-roofs.medieval village roofs: Fake fur soaked in watered PVA and combed downwards, then painted mid brown with straw yellow and cream drybrushes.
thatched-roofs.thatch terrain: Soak fake fur in watered PVA, comb it down, glue it on, then paint mid brown with straw yellow and pale cream drybrushes.
thatched-roofs.comb fur for thatch: Comb the soaked pile downwards with an old comb so it lies like straw, then glue it to the roof.
thatched-roofs.pva soaked fur: Soak the fur until wet right through in PVA and water, comb it down, glue it on, and let it dry hard overnight.
thatched-roofs.thatch looks fluffy: Soak it right through in PVA and water, comb it down so it lies like straw, and trim straggly ends once stiff.

toy-soldier-style.toy soldier style: Simple bright red, blue, black and white, neat clean edges, and only gentle highlights for a clean, classic look.
toy-soldier-style.classic toy soldier look: Strong simple colours with clean edges, light shading and subtle highlights, plus an optional gloss varnish.
toy-soldier-style.gloss toy soldier paint: Paint bold simple colours with subtle highlights, then add a gloss varnish at the end for the old toy look.
toy-soldier-style.simple bright red coats: Base a clear red coat neatly, shade lightly, and layer a slightly brighter red on the raised areas only.
toy-soldier-style.old fashioned soldier painting: See: classic toy soldier style, with a red coat, blue cuffs, black hat and boots, white belts and gentle highlights.
toy-soldier-style.how do i paint like a tin soldier: Base bold red, blue, black and white neatly, keep highlights subtle so the colours stay flat, and finish in gloss.
toy-soldier-style.nutcracker style figure: See: classic toy soldier style, bold simple colours with neat edges, gentle highlights and an optional gloss varnish.
toy-soldier-style.clean simple uniforms: Base each colour neatly and fully; clean edges between colours matter more than shading here.
toy-soldier-style.red coat blue cuffs: A clear red coat with blue cuffs and facings, black hat and boots, white belts, subtle highlights; swap colours for a rival side.
toy-soldier-style.retro toy look: Bright reds, blues, black and white, neat edges, gentle highlights, a light blush on faces, and gloss varnish to finish.

types-of-contrast.types of contrast: Contrast is any difference: light and dark, hue, temperature, saturation, shape or texture, and each helps a model read.
types-of-contrast.model needs more contrast: Make the highlights brighter, the shadows darker, or both; value contrast matters most.
types-of-contrast.value contrast: Light next to dark; it matters most, and a bright line beside a dark one makes detail jump out.
types-of-contrast.what does contrast mean in painting: Any difference, in light and dark, hue, warm and cool, saturation, shape or texture, that helps parts read apart.
types-of-contrast.temperature contrast: Warm next to cool makes the warm look warmer and the cool cooler.
types-of-contrast.saturation contrast: One strong colour among greys or muted tones stands out strongly.
types-of-contrast.light and dark contrast: Value contrast: a bright highlight next to deep shadow, which makes detail jump out and looks brighter than it is.
types-of-contrast.texture contrast: Rough dusty surfaces against clean shiny ones, soft faces against hard armour, or matt black beside gloss black.
types-of-contrast.why does my model not read: Turn a photo black and white; if parts do not separate, widen the gap between light and dark.
types-of-contrast.detail does not pop: Put a bright line beside a dark one; small markings need strong value contrast with what is under them.

using-inks.using inks: Inks are thin, strongly coloured and see through, so they tint what is underneath rather than cover it; thin them a lot.
using-inks.ink vs paint: Paint is solid pigment that hides the undercoat; many inks are dyes that stay see through however many coats you add.
using-inks.what are inks for: Tinting undercoats and textures, glazing, home made washes, boosting weak colours, and tinting metal or clear effects.
using-inks.ink too strong: A little goes a long way; thin it a lot with water or medium, and test on a spare piece first.
using-inks.how much to thin ink: Usually thin it a lot with water or medium, as ink is very strongly coloured; test the strength on a spare piece.
using-inks.inks are see through: Many inks are dyes that stay see through however many coats you add, so they tint rather than cover.
using-inks.ink over white undercoat: Over a white or zenithal undercoat, ink gives strong colour while the light and dark below still show through.
using-inks.inks for beginners: Thin them a lot, test on a spare piece first, and use them to tint an undercoat or as glazes and washes.
using-inks.ink wont cover: That is how most inks work: they stay see through; some are made semi opaque or opaque if you need cover.
using-inks.tint with ink: Thin ink heavily and glaze it over the area, or over a zenithal undercoat, so the light and dark below show through.

varying-browns-and-leathers.too much brown: Separate leathers, straps and pouches by value and warmth, often by tinting one mid brown, so they do not merge.
varying-browns-and-leathers.leather straps blend together: Put light next to dark, never two dark or two pale leathers side by side, and vary warmth between red and olive browns.
varying-browns-and-leathers.different browns on one model: Tint one mid brown with a little white, yellow, red, green, black or ivory for each item; the shared base keeps harmony.
varying-browns-and-leathers.how do i tell leathers apart: Separate by value first, light next to dark, then by warmth, starting one from red brown and another from olive brown.
varying-browns-and-leathers.pouches and belts all same colour: Pouches and belts are often canvas or webbing, so they need not be brown; black or olive green can work beside red armour.
varying-browns-and-leathers.brown model looks dull: Separate the browns by value and warmth so straps, pouches and boots do not merge into one dull brown mass.
varying-browns-and-leathers.vary leather colours: Mix one mid brown with a little white, yellow, red, green, black or ivory for each item, and keep light next to dark.
varying-browns-and-leathers.warm and cool brown: Start one leather from a red brown and another from a greenish olive brown, highlighting one yellowish and one pale tan.
varying-browns-and-leathers.boots and belts: Give boots and belts different values, light next to dark, and run one dark brown wash only into the recesses and joins.
varying-browns-and-leathers.leather looks muddy: Change direction rather than stacking coats; a red brown shade can rescue a pale leather that looks flat.

wash-vs-contrast-paint.wash or contrast paint: A wash shades colours you have already painted; a one coat paint colours and shades in one step.
wash-vs-contrast-paint.difference between wash and contrast: A wash sits in recesses over existing colours; a one coat paint does base colour and shading together.
wash-vs-contrast-paint.should i use contrast or a shade: Use a shade to keep colours you already painted; use a one coat paint over a light undercoat to colour and shade at once.
wash-vs-contrast-paint.when to use a one coat paint: For base colour and shading in one step over white, light grey or zenithal prime, with consistent results for batch painting.
wash-vs-contrast-paint.contrast over metallics: A wash keeps metallics shiny; one coat paints that do not settle into a pale layer in the pot also let metallics shine through.
wash-vs-contrast-paint.contrast instead of base coat and wash: Yes: a one coat paint does base and shading together, best over white, light grey or a zenithal prime.
wash-vs-contrast-paint.do contrast paints replace washes: No: a wash shades over finished colours and keeps them; a one coat paint over base coats can darken them a lot.
wash-vs-contrast-paint.shade vs contrast: A shade tints recesses over existing colours; a one coat paint is base colour and shading together.
wash-vs-contrast-paint.which is faster wash or contrast: A one coat paint does base and shade in one step, so it saves a stage; add an opaque edge highlight after.
wash-vs-contrast-paint.washing vs one coat paints: A wash shades existing colours lightly; a one coat paint colours and shades at once but can darken base coats a lot.

weathering-basics.weathering basics: Weathering shows age and use with wear, rust, grime and dust, placed where it would really happen.
weathering-basics.where should weathering go: On edges, corners, feet, hands, hatches and other spots that get touched or knocked; placement matters more than quantity.
weathering-basics.weathering vs battle damage: Weathering shows time and exposure, like rust and grime; battle damage shows impacts, like chips, gouges and scorch marks.
weathering-basics.make a vehicle look old and used: Chip edges, run rust streaks from rivets, put grime in recesses, and dust and mud on tracks and lower areas.
weathering-basics.model looks too clean: Add a little weathering where it would really happen: chipped edges, grime in recesses, and dust on lower parts.
weathering-basics.wear and tear on armour: Add chips and scratches on edges, corners and spots that get knocked, building a little at a time.
weathering-basics.how do i start weathering: Decide the model's story first, then build a little at a time and check from arm's length.
weathering-basics.grime dust and wear: Grime goes in recesses and low areas, dust and mud on lower legs and bases, and wear on edges and corners.
weathering-basics.how much weathering is too much: Build a little at a time, check at arm's length, and keep one level across a group; it is easy to add and hard to remove.
weathering-basics.make it look like it has been through a: A veteran gets both weathering and battle damage: wear, rust and grime plus chips, gouges, scratches and scorch marks.

wet-blending-large-areas.wet blending: Base a mid tone, then pull a shadow and highlight in while wet with a large brush laid close to flat.
wet-blending-large-areas.how do i wet blend a cloak: Base a strong mid tone, put shadow into the recesses while wet and brush it along the folds, then the reverse for highlights.
wet-blending-large-areas.blend while the paint is wet: Lay the mid tone beside a recess, add shadow into it while wet, and brush along the fold into the mid tone.
wet-blending-large-areas.smooth blend on big cloth: Use a large brush laid on its side, a strong mid tone base, and shadow and highlight steps pulled in while wet.
wet-blending-large-areas.wet blending skin: Mix shadow and highlight steps on a wet palette, pull them into a wet mid tone, and work one section at a time quickly.
wet-blending-large-areas.paint dries too fast to blend: Use the paint barely thinned, as thicker paint stays wet longer, and work one section at a time quickly.
wet-blending-large-areas.big brush blending: Use a large, full bellied brush, size 8 or even a flat, laid close to flat to blend with its side.
wet-blending-large-areas.blend a large area quickly: Use a large brush, barely thinned paint and a mid tone with shadow and highlight pulled in wet, one section at a time.
wet-blending-large-areas.wet blend tips: Use a big brush laid flat, barely thinned paint, and expect the first pass to look streaky; let it dry and repeat.
wet-blending-large-areas.streaky blending on a cape: The first pass often looks streaky; let it dry fully and repeat on top, then glaze the main colour to smooth it.

where-chips-go.where do chips go: On edges, corners and parts that get hit or move, mostly small chips with a few larger ones.
where-chips-go.chip placement: Follow each edge with small fine chips, then a few larger ones, concentrated where things get knocked.
where-chips-go.where to put scratches: Put scratches on moving parts and fronts as parallel lines, keeping their direction the same on flat panels.
where-chips-go.battle damage placement: Lower legs, hands, feet, knees, forward facing plates, weapon heads and shoulder edges, where things get knocked.
where-chips-go.chipping looks random: Keep chips mostly on edges and where things get knocked, and leave quiet areas like inner legs nearly clean.
where-chips-go.too many chips: Keep most chips small, add one or two at a time on big panels, and judge before adding more.
where-chips-go.realistic wear and tear: Look at photos of worn vehicles and tools, then place small chips on edges and corners and scrape scratches the same way.
where-chips-go.scratches on a tank: Keep scratch direction the same on flat panels so it reads as a scrape, with the odd diagonal across.
where-chips-go.where would paint wear off: On edges, corners and anything sticking out, plus hatches, doors, hinges and metal rubbing on metal.
where-chips-go.chips on armour edges: Small fine chips roughly following each edge, a few larger ones, and some with a dark chip inside the light one.

wounds-and-gore.paint wounds: Wash deep red into the cut, darken the deepest parts, highlight raw flesh red to pink to cream, and add glossy blood last.
wounds-and-gore.gore and guts: Base guts deep red, wash dark brown, and finish with a glossy blood effect; add gore slowly and stop early.
wounds-and-gore.severed limb stump: Base a pale flesh, flood with clear red mixed with a dark wash, then a thick coat of plain clear red for a wet shine.
wounds-and-gore.open wound: Wash deep red into the wound, then black into the deepest parts, highlight brighter red to pink, and glaze purple round it.
wounds-and-gore.raw flesh colour: Highlight raised flesh with a brighter red, then a pink, and a pale cream on the sharpest corners.
wounds-and-gore.bloody cut on skin: Paint thin red slashes for small cuts, then glaze purple round them and a stronger pink right at the edges.
wounds-and-gore.how do i paint guts: Base a deep red, wash dark brown so they sit apart from the skin, then finish with a glossy blood effect.
wounds-and-gore.make a wound look deep: Wash deep red into it, then add a little black and wash only the deepest parts once dry.
wounds-and-gore.glossy gory injury: Varnish matt or satin first, then add glossy blood effect last so it stays wet looking.
wounds-and-gore.inside of a mouth red: Wash a slightly thinned deep red into the inside of the mouth, then darken only the deepest parts with a little black.

coloured-liquid-pools.pool of blood on a base: Paint the hollow, glaze it deep red so it deepens away from the edge, then pour clear gloss tinted with a drop of red ink in thin layers.
coloured-liquid-pools.how do i make a slime puddle: Paint the hollow dark, then pour clear gloss with a very small drop of ink stirred in, in thin layers, as it shrinks while drying.
coloured-liquid-pools.glowing ooze on a base: Base the hollow bright yellow, glaze lime green darker towards the middle, then pour tinted clear gloss so it looks lit from within.
coloured-liquid-pools.toxic sludge pool: Paint the hollow dark for murky sludge, glaze it with ink, pour tinted clear gloss in thin layers and drop in tiny beads as bubbles.
coloured-liquid-pools.blood puddle looks flat not wet: Glaze the bed deeper in the middle and lighter at the edges, then top it with thin layers of thick clear gloss or resin.
coloured-liquid-pools.make goo look glossy and deep: Glaze the pool bed darker in the middle, then pour thick clear gloss or resin with a tiny drop of ink, in thin layers.
coloured-liquid-pools.radioactive green pool on base: Base the hollow bright yellow, glaze lime green over it, darker towards the middle, and pour green tinted clear gloss on top.
coloured-liquid-pools.colored liquid in the hollows of a base: Paint the hollow, glaze it with ink, then pour thick clear gloss tinted with a very small drop of ink, in thin layers.
coloured-liquid-pools.gore pool for a monster base: Glaze deep red over a pale bed so it deepens away from the edge, pour red tinted clear gloss, and set dead tufts round the rim.
coloured-liquid-pools.glowing acid puddle: Base bright yellow, glaze lime green over it, pour tinted clear gloss, then dot a brighter tint round the bubbles once cured.

dusty-wasteland.dry dusty base: Spread texture paste, wash it rust brown, drybrush bone over the grit, then dab on earth pigment and add a few dry tufts.
dusty-wasteland.desert wasteland base: Texture paste washed rust or brown, drybrushed bone, dusted with dark, mid and light pigment, and dry beige tufts placed at random.
dusty-wasteland.how do i make a dusty dirt base: Wash texture paste with thinned rust brown, drybrush bone over the grit, then dab on pigment, mostly dark, and fix it with water.
dusty-wasteland.rusty brown ground for post apocalyptic: Wash the texture with a thinned rust brown, dot dark brown into it while wet to mottle the ground, then drybrush bone.
dusty-wasteland.dead dry tufts on a cracked earth base: Stick a few dry beige tufts on at random, not in rows, once the ground is washed, drybrushed and dusted with pigment.
dusty-wasteland.base looks too clean, want it dusty: Dab earth pigment over it, mostly dark, less mid and a touch of light, carry it up the feet and fix it with a little water.
dusty-wasteland.weathering powder on bases: Use pigment in a dark, mid and light tone, mostly dark, carry it up the feet and fix it in place with a little water.
dusty-wasteland.arid ground basing: Texture paste with a rust brown wash, a bone drybrush on the raised grit, dusty tan pigment, and a few dry beige tufts.
dusty-wasteland.wash on texture paste dries shiny: Stir two drops of matt varnish into the thinned wash so it dries flat, and seal the finished base with matt varnish.
dusty-wasteland.barren dusty earth for a tank: Texture paste washed rust brown, drybrushed bone, or dark grey for a sooty, burnt look, then dusted with earth pigment.

pale-stone-ground.light sandy base: Base earth brown, drybrush sandy stone then a strong ivory, sponge grime on the edges, and wash with thinned brown oil paint.
pale-stone-ground.pale dusty ground: Build from brown up to ivory, brighter than feels right, wash with thinned oil paint, and dust the feet with light pigment to match.
pale-stone-ground.desert stone base colours: An earth brown base, sandy stone and ivory drybrushes, greenish brown grime on the edges, and a warm brown wash.
pale-stone-ground.how to paint a light coloured base: Build from brown through lighter browns to ivory, brighter than feels right, because the wash afterwards tones it down.
pale-stone-ground.dusty feet to match the base: Run pigment mixed with water round the feet and dry it, then dab dry pigment on the feet and lower legs so both share the same dust.
pale-stone-ground.bright beige rocks: Drybrush sandy stone then a strong ivory, and after the oil wash, wipe back with clean spirits where the stone should be brightest.
pale-stone-ground.grimy edges on a sand base: Sponge a dark greenish brown grime onto the edges of the base only, after the lighter drybrushes.
pale-stone-ground.dry dusty ground basing: Stone built up to ivory, grimy sponged edges, a thinned oil wash wiped back, then light pigment round and on the feet.
pale-stone-ground.my base looks too dark and dull: Drybrush up to ivory, brighter than feels right, and wipe the oil wash back with clean spirits where the stone should be brightest.
pale-stone-ground.bleached stone base recipe: Base earth brown, drybrush sandy stone then ivory, sponge greenish brown on the edges, then a warm brown wash wiped back on highlights.

sandbags-and-low-walls.sandbags: Cut a thin, flattened strip of putty into small rectangles, lay them overlapping like bricks, sag each one and mark seams with a knife.
sandbags-and-low-walls.how to sculpt sandbags with green stuff: Roll two part epoxy putty into a thin strip, flatten it, cut small rectangles, lay them like bricks and press seams in with a knife edge.
sandbags-and-low-walls.low stone wall on a base: Clear the front of the base and stack small rounded stones or fine gravel into a low wall with dots of super glue.
sandbags-and-low-walls.trench base with sandbags: Glue a low stone wall at the front, lay putty sandbags over it like bricks, then paint the stones dark brown and the bags pale olive.
sandbags-and-low-walls.defensive wall on a base: Glue small stones into a low wall, then lay putty sandbags over it, overlapping like bricks and pressed so each one sags.
sandbags-and-low-walls.make sandbags from putty: Roll and flatten a thin putty strip, cut small rectangles, press each so it sags, mark seams with a knife edge and pinch the corners.
sandbags-and-low-walls.small cover wall for a base: Stack small stones into a low wall with super glue and lay putty sandbags over it, then paint the stones and bags as separate steps.
sandbags-and-low-walls.trench warfare style base: A low wall of glued stones topped with putty sandbags, painted dark brown and light brown for stone, pale olive and khaki for the bags.
sandbags-and-low-walls.stacked stone wall: Stack small rounded stones with dots of super glue, base them dark brown and give two light brown drybrush passes.
sandbags-and-low-walls.sandbag wall at the front of the base: Clear the front, glue a low stone wall, lay putty bags over it like bricks, then wash dark brown between the bags to outline them.

texture-paint-bases.quickest way to base a model: Spread gritty texture paint from the middle out to the feet with an old brush, wipe the feet clean, paint the rim and add a tuft.
texture-paint-bases.texture paint how thick: Spread it about 1 to 2 mm thick so it suits the scale, and wipe any off the feet with a clean damp brush.
texture-paint-bases.gritty paste for bases: Blob it in the middle, spread it to the feet with an old flat brush, press in grit while it is wet, and let it air dry.
texture-paint-bases.easy beginner basing: Texture paste spread 1 to 2 mm thick, a warm brown wash if flat, a light earth drybrush, a near black rim and a tuft or two.
texture-paint-bases.how do i use texture paint on a base: Blob it in the middle, spread it to the feet with an old brush or spatula, wipe the feet with a damp brush and let it air dry.
texture-paint-bases.base colour to contrast with the model: Use a light ground for a dark model and a dark ground for a light one.
texture-paint-bases.ground paste looks too thick: Keep it about 1 to 2 mm thick so it suits the scale, spreading it out from a central blob with an old flat brush or spatula.
texture-paint-bases.what colour should my base be: Pick a ground that contrasts with the model: light ground for a dark model, dark ground for a light one.
texture-paint-bases.cheap fast bases for an army: A large tub of artist's texture paste spread with an old brush, a quick drybrush, a near black rim and a tuft or two.
texture-paint-bases.spreading texture paste around feet: Spread it out from a blob in the middle to the feet, then wipe any off the feet with a clean damp brush.

worn-grass-pitch.sports pitch base: Crackle paste mixed with grit, washed beige brown and drybrushed, tufts in two shades, and a masked, sponged white line.
worn-grass-pitch.cracked dry earth base: Paint the base first, spread crackle mixed with a little gritty paste, let it dry, then wash beige brown and drybrush the raised chunks.
worn-grass-pitch.faded white lines on base: Mask a line and sponge or stipple thick white along it, so it reads as a broken, patchy line rather than a solid stripe.
worn-grass-pitch.make a base look like a football field: Cracked earth with tufts in two shades or grass fibres trimmed flat, then a masked, stippled white line that looks worn.
worn-grass-pitch.playing field basing: Short turf from grass fibres trimmed flat, or tufts in two shades, over washed crackle paste, with a worn white marking.
worn-grass-pitch.crackle paste dry ground: Paint the base first so cracks do not show bare black, mix crackle with a little gritty paste, and let it dry fully.
worn-grass-pitch.worn out grass with lines: Press on tufts in two shades with their tops pointing different ways, then stipple a broken white line along masking tape.
worn-grass-pitch.pitch markings on a base: Mask a line, then sponge or stipple thick chalky white along it for a broken, worn marking.
worn-grass-pitch.parched cracked mud: Crackle paste with a little grit, washed beige brown into the cracks and drybrushed dry tan on the raised chunks only.
worn-grass-pitch.sports team themed bases: See: this entry's worn pitch base, with cracked earth, tufts in two shades and faded white lines like a playing field.

black-fur.black fur: Over black, drybrush very dark grey, then dark grey, then mid grey on the most raised tufts, with an optional faint bone on the tips.
black-fur.drybrush black fur: Start fairly heavy with very dark grey over black, then lighter with dark grey, then a very light mid grey on the raised tufts.
black-fur.dark wolf pelt: Build up grey drybrushes from very dark to mid over a black undercoat, then a faint warm bone touch on the tips.
black-fur.black hair on a model: Drybrush greys over black, each lighter in tone and pressure, and keep it subtle so it still reads as black.
black-fur.black fur cloak: Black undercoat, then dry brushes of very dark grey, dark grey and a very light mid grey on the most raised tufts.
black-fur.how to highlight black fur: Use grey drybrushes, each lighter in tone and pressure, ending with mid grey only on the most raised tufts.
black-fur.black fur looks flat: Build texture with lighter grey drybrushes in turn, then add a faint warm bone on the tips so the black does not look cold.
black-fur.black bear fur: Drybrush very dark grey heavily over black, then dark grey and mid grey with lighter pressure, finishing with a faint bone tip.
black-fur.dark furry pelt: Over a black undercoat, drybrush very dark grey, dark grey, then mid grey on the raised tufts only.
black-fur.black dog or wolf fur: Three grey drybrushes over black, very dark, dark and mid, each lighter, plus a faint bone on the tips so it is not cold.

blue-tinted-steel.blue steel armour: Base dark silver, glaze silver mixed with blue ink low on each panel, wash blue black in the recesses, then edge in bright silver.
blue-tinted-steel.how do i get cool silver armour: Add a touch of blue to the silver base, glaze blue ink tinted silver low on each panel, and shade with a blue black wash.
blue-tinted-steel.silver armour with blue ink: Mix a little blue ink into the silver and glaze it low on each panel, adding more ink each pass.
blue-tinted-steel.knight armour looks too plain silver: Glaze blue tinted silver low on each panel, shade the recesses blue black, then pick the edges out in bright silver.
blue-tinted-steel.tinting metallic paint blue: Mix a little blue ink into the silver, adding more ink with each glaze pass.
blue-tinted-steel.cold steel plate: Dark silver with a touch of blue, blue ink glazes low on the panels, a blue black shade, and bright silver edges.
blue-tinted-steel.blue shaded silver: Shade the recesses with a black wash with a little blue in it; a purple or turquoise tint also works.
blue-tinted-steel.shiny blued metal: Dark silver, blue ink glazes, a blue black shade, then a thin bright silver edge or a light buffed dry brush.
blue-tinted-steel.glazing ink over silver: Glaze silver with a little blue ink mixed in low on each panel, in two coats, adding more ink each pass.
blue-tinted-steel.paladin armour metal: Base dark silver, glaze it blue with ink low on the panels, shade blue black, and edge highlight bright silver.

bright-yellow-armour.yellow armour: Base a rich yellow in thin coats over bone or white, glaze orange brown low on each panel, line warm brown in gaps, and edge pale yellow.
bright-yellow-armour.punchy yellow armor: Three thin coats of rich yellow over a pale primer, warm orange brown glazes low on the panels, and fine pale yellow edges.
bright-yellow-armour.shading yellow without it going green: Shade with warm browns: glaze an orange brown down each panel and line a warm dark brown into gaps and rivets only.
bright-yellow-armour.yellow over black primer: Over black, start with a yellow orange before the rich yellow coats; bone or white primer makes it easier.
bright-yellow-armour.how to get a strong yellow: Use a pale primer such as bone or white and build the rich yellow up in three thin coats.
bright-yellow-armour.yellow armour looks dirty: Never wash it all over: line the warm dark brown only into panel gaps and rivets, and glaze the orange brown low on each panel.
bright-yellow-armour.warm brown shading on yellow: Glaze an orange brown down the lower part of each panel, darker lower still, and line a warm dark brown into gaps and rivets.
bright-yellow-armour.bright yellow tank: Rich yellow over a pale primer, orange brown glazed low on each panel, warm brown lined into gaps and rivets, pale yellow on the edges.
bright-yellow-armour.yellow plates recipe: Base a rich yellow, glaze orange brown low on each plate, line warm dark brown into the gaps, then edge pale yellow.
bright-yellow-armour.yellow wont cover: Prime bone or white and use three thin coats; over black, start with a yellow orange first.

dark-brown-skin.dark skin: Base a warm brown, shade deep brown in the creases, layer up with bone or tan mixed in, then glaze thinned dark brown over all the skin.
dark-brown-skin.black skin tone: A warm brown base with a little red, deep brown shading, thin bone toned highlights, and a half water dark brown glaze to tie it together.
dark-brown-skin.how to paint dark skin: Base mid brown with a little red, shade brown and black in the deep creases, layer bone or tan into the base, then glaze dark brown.
dark-brown-skin.brown skin recipe: Base a warm brown, shade a deep brown, layer a light warm brown on the raised areas, then glaze a thinned dark brown over all of it.
dark-brown-skin.darker skin tones: Start from a warm mid brown with a little red, shade with brown and black, and highlight by adding bone or tan in thin steps.
dark-brown-skin.dark skin looks grey and ashy: Keep it warm: add a little red to the brown base, and glaze half water dark brown over all the skin after highlighting.
dark-brown-skin.highlight dark skin: Add bone or tan to the base in thin steps on the forehead, cheeks, nose, ears and knuckles, then re touch the top tips after the glaze.
dark-brown-skin.deep brown skin face: Shade brown and black round the eyes and under the brow, highlight forehead, cheeks and nose with bone toned brown, then glaze dark brown.
dark-brown-skin.warm dark skin: Mix mid brown with a little red, about three to one, for the base, and highlight with bone or tan added in thin steps.
dark-brown-skin.how to paint african skin tones: A warm brown base with a little red, deep brown shading, bone or tan highlights in thin steps, and an all over dark brown glaze.

exposed-muscle.raw meat: Base a deep dull red, wash dark violet brown, paint thin pinkish red fibre lines, then glaze a wet gloss blood red over the top.
exposed-muscle.how do i paint flayed skin: Deep dull red base, a dark violet brown wash, parallel fibre lines in red then red with warm grey, and a gloss blood glaze.
exposed-muscle.exposed muscle: Base a deep dull red, wash all over in dark violet brown, add thin parallel fibre lines, and finish with a thinned gloss blood effect.
exposed-muscle.gore and raw flesh: Deep dull red washed dark violet brown, pinkish red fibre lines, and a wet blood gloss glaze with the darkest gaps relined.
exposed-muscle.red muscle fibres: Paint thin parallel lines, red then red with warm grey, each set shorter than the last.
exposed-muscle.skinless zombie: Base the muscle a deep dull red, wash dark violet brown, line in pinkish fibres, then glaze a thinned gloss blood over it.
exposed-muscle.wet bloody muscle: Glaze a thinned gloss blood effect over the finished muscle, then reline the darkest gaps.
exposed-muscle.meat looks too bright red: Avoid a bright red: a dull deep red base reads more like meat, washed all over with a dark violet brown.
exposed-muscle.painting guts and sinew: See: this entry covers raw muscle, a dull red base, violet brown wash, fibre lines and a gloss blood glaze.
exposed-muscle.horror model with flesh showing: For exposed flesh, base dull deep red, wash dark violet brown, line fibres in pinkish red, and glaze wet gloss blood.

gold-armour.gold armour: Base warm gold, wash chestnut brown, repaint the flat panels bright gold short of the recesses, then edge pale silvery gold.
gold-armour.metallic gold trim: Warm gold base, a chestnut brown wash, bright gold layered back on, and gold mixed with a little silver on the crisp edges.
gold-armour.how do i paint gold: Base warm gold, wash all over with warm chestnut brown, layer bright gold on the flats, then edge with gold plus a little silver.
gold-armour.gold looks flat: Wash it warm chestnut brown, add a thin purple in the deepest recesses, and edge with a pale silvery gold.
gold-armour.gold with brown wash: Wash warm chestnut brown all over, lifting pools from flat panels, then repaint the panels bright gold short of the recesses.
gold-armour.shiny gold edges: Mix gold with a little silver and run it along the crisp edges with the side of the brush.
gold-armour.golden armor recipe: Warm gold, a chestnut brown wash, a bright gold layer on the panels, and pale silvery gold edges.
gold-armour.make gold look rich: A warm chestnut brown wash over warm gold, with a thin purple in the deepest recesses for added depth.
gold-armour.gold trim on armour: Base warm gold, wash chestnut brown, layer or drybrush bright gold, then edge with gold mixed with a little silver.
gold-armour.purple wash in gold recesses: After the chestnut brown wash, a thin purple in the deepest recesses adds depth to the gold.

grey-stone-detail.grey stone: Base a mid grey, shade a brown black into the recesses, layer up to light grey, then edge off white on the sharpest edges.
grey-stone-detail.stone statue: Neutral mid grey base, a dark brown and black shade in the recesses, light grey layered up in steps, and off white edges.
grey-stone-detail.carved stone details: Base mid grey, shade the carving with dark brown mixed into a black shade, then layer light grey and edge off white.
grey-stone-detail.stone icons: Mid grey base, brown black shade into the recesses, light grey layers in steps, off white on the very sharpest edges.
grey-stone-detail.how to paint stone on a model: Base an even mid grey, shade brown black, mix light grey into the base in steps up to pure light grey, then edge off white.
grey-stone-detail.stone looks too flat: Shade the recesses with dark brown mixed with a black shade, then layer up in steps to light grey and edge off white.
grey-stone-detail.gray stone: Base a neutral mid grey, shade with a brown black, layer to light grey and finish with off white edges.
grey-stone-detail.small stone details: Mid grey, a brown black shade, light grey layered up in steps, and light grey with white on the sharpest edges.
grey-stone-detail.cold grey rock: A cool neutral mid grey base, a brown black shade, light grey layers and an off white edge highlight.
grey-stone-detail.stone skull ornament: Base mid grey, shade brown black into the recesses, layer light grey, then off white on the very sharpest edges.

light-rust.a little bit of rust: Wash a thinned rust orange only into a few cracks and round rivets; on kept armour less is more.
light-rust.subtle rust on armour: Over finished silver, wash rust orange thinned with medium into just a few cracks and round rivets.
light-rust.how do i add light rust: Thin a rust orange wash with medium and run it only into a few cracks and round the rivets.
light-rust.rust in the cracks: Thin a rust orange wash with medium and place it only into a few cracks and round rivets.
light-rust.slightly weathered silver armour: Silver primer, a dark brown grey wash, gunmetal on raised areas, a silver dry brush, then a little rust orange in the cracks.
light-rust.not too much rust: Keep the rust orange wash to a few cracks and rivets only; on well kept armour less is more.
light-rust.well kept metal with hint of rust: Silver, a dark brown grey wash, gunmetal and silver highlights, then rust orange thinned with medium in just a few cracks.
light-rust.rusty joints: Pick joints out in black over the silver, wash dark brown grey, then put thinned rust orange into a few cracks and round rivets.
light-rust.rust wash on silver: Thin a rust orange with medium and use it only in a few cracks and round rivets, after the metal is highlighted.
light-rust.light weathering on metal: Wash the silver dark brown grey so recesses are dark and matt, highlight with gunmetal and silver, then add rust only in a few cracks.

olive-uniform-cloth.olive drab: Base dark olive green, layer olive on the creases and raised folds, mid olive on smaller areas, then pale olive on the edges.
olive-uniform-cloth.army green uniform: Mix two greens with a little black for the base, layer up with less black, then add white in two steps for the edges.
olive-uniform-cloth.how to paint military uniform: Base dark olive, layer olive and mid olive on the raised folds, and highlight knees, shoulders and collars with pale olive.
olive-uniform-cloth.modern soldier fatigues: Dark olive green base, olive and mid olive layers on the folds, and a pale olive edge on knees, shoulders and collars.
olive-uniform-cloth.olive green cloth: Base dark olive green, layer olive green then mid olive on smaller areas of each fold, then edge pale olive.
olive-uniform-cloth.military green clothes: Dark olive base with a little black, lighter olive layers on the folds, and white added in two steps for the top edges.
olive-uniform-cloth.khaki green trousers: Base dark olive, layer olive on the creases, mid olive on smaller areas, then pale olive on the knees.
olive-uniform-cloth.ww2 uniform green: Mix two greens with a little black, layer up by dropping the black, then add white in two steps for strong contrast on the edges.
olive-uniform-cloth.drab green jacket: Dark olive green base, olive and mid olive layers on the folds, and pale olive on shoulders and collars.
olive-uniform-cloth.olive fatigues highlights: Add white to the olive in two steps for knees, shoulders and collars; strong contrast reads well.

pale-sickly-skin.pale skin: Base a pale pinkish bone in thin coats, wash warm chestnut, layer light pinkish bone on raised areas, then near white on the crests.
pale-sickly-skin.sickly skin: Pale pinkish bone, a warm chestnut wash, lighter bone layers, then a very thin sickly green glaze round eyes, mouth and knuckles.
pale-sickly-skin.zombie skin: Base pale pinkish bone, wash chestnut, layer up lighter, then glaze a thin sickly green or purple round the eyes, mouth and knuckles.
pale-sickly-skin.vampire skin: Pale pinkish bone with a warm chestnut wash, lighter bone layers to near white on the crests, and a faint purple or pink flush.
pale-sickly-skin.undead flesh: A pale pinkish bone base, a warm chestnut wash, light bone highlights, and a very thin sickly green glaze on the eyes and mouth.
pale-sickly-skin.ghoul skin: Base pale pinkish bone, wash warm chestnut, highlight light bone, then glaze sickly green thinly round the eyes, mouth and knuckles.
pale-sickly-skin.corpse skin: Pale pinkish bone, a chestnut wash for the creases, light bone layers, and a very thin green, purple or yellow glaze.
pale-sickly-skin.plague victim skin: Pale bone base, a warm chestnut wash, light bone highlights, and a very thin sickly green or yellow glaze round eyes and mouth.
pale-sickly-skin.unhealthy looking skin: Glaze a very thin sickly green round the eyes, mouth and knuckles over pale bone skin; purple or yellow also work.
pale-sickly-skin.clammy pale flesh: Smooth thin coats of pale pinkish bone, a warm chestnut wash, light bone layers and near white on the crests.

polished-brass.brass: Base brass neatly, shade with a warm brown wash, line dark brown into the deepest recesses, then edge brass with some silver.
polished-brass.how do i paint brass: Brass base, a warm brown wash over the whole area, dark brown with black in the deepest recesses, and brass mixed with silver on edges.
polished-brass.shell casings: Paint them brass, wash warm brown, line the deepest recesses dark brown, then edge with brass and silver and dot silver on the corners.
polished-brass.bullet casings: Brass base, a warm brown shade, dark brown in the deepest recesses, and pale brass edges with tiny silver dots on the corners.
polished-brass.brass trim: Base brass neatly on the trim, wash warm brown, line dark brown in the recesses, and edge pale brass with tiny silver dots on rivets.
polished-brass.small gold details: See: this entry does warm brass for small trims, a brass base, warm brown wash, dark brown lining and pale brass edges.
polished-brass.brass on guns: Paint the details brass, shade warm brown then dark brown in the deepest recesses, and edge with brass mixed with some silver.
polished-brass.shiny brass highlights: Mix some silver into the brass for the edges, then add tiny silver dots on rivets and corners.
polished-brass.bronze trim: See: this entry covers brass trim, a brass base, warm brown wash, dark brown recesses and pale brass edges.
polished-brass.brass wash brown: Use a brown wash or thinned brown over the whole brass area, then a dark brown with black only in the deepest recesses.

red-warning-light.red light: Block in dark red, layer bright red in the middle with orange near the front, then glaze thin reds around it so the glow fades out.
red-warning-light.little red lights: Dark red base, bright red in the middle, orange near the front, dark red at the rim, then very thin red glazes around them.
red-warning-light.how to paint a glowing button: Block it in dark red, layer bright red to orange, then glaze very thin dark red around it and bright red closer in, feathered out.
red-warning-light.warning lamp on a vehicle: Dark red base, a bright red to orange gradient in the lamp, and thin red glazes on the surface around it for a soft glow.
red-warning-light.small dials: Block them in dark red, layer bright red in the middle with orange near the front, keeping dark red at the rim.
red-warning-light.red bulb glow: Glaze very thin dark red around the light, feathered out with a damp brush, then bright red closer in so the glow fades outwards.
red-warning-light.tiny light glow on armour: Glaze a very thin dark red around the light and feather it with a clean damp brush, then a thin bright red closer to the light.
red-warning-light.red led effect: Dark red base, bright red in the centre, orange near the front, and a soft red glaze glow feathered onto the surface around it.
red-warning-light.glowing red lamp: Layer the lamp dark red to bright red to orange, then glaze thin reds around it, stronger closer to the lamp.
red-warning-light.control panel lights: Block each light in dark red, add bright red and orange in the middle, and glaze a faint red glow around them.

turquoise-armour.turquoise: Base blue green, drybrush pale turquoise all over, wash deep green in two coats, then soft drybrush light turquoise on the edges.
turquoise-armour.teal armour: Blue green base, a pale turquoise drybrush all over, two deep green washes cut with medium, and a soft light turquoise drybrush.
turquoise-armour.sea green armour: Base a blue green, drybrush pale turquoise everywhere, wash it deep green a section at a time, then catch the edges with light turquoise.
turquoise-armour.aqua armour: Blue green, then a pale turquoise drybrush, two deep green washes, and a very soft light turquoise drybrush across the edges.
turquoise-armour.how to paint turquoise: Base blue green, drybrush pale turquoise all over, wash two coats of green shade with a little medium, then drybrush light turquoise.
turquoise-armour.cyan armour: Base a blue green, drybrush pale turquoise, wash deep green twice, and roll a soft light turquoise drybrush across the edges.
turquoise-armour.pastel teal looks chalky: It looks pastel after the pale drybrush; two coats of deep green wash cut with a little medium bring the colour back.
turquoise-armour.drybrush armour turquoise: Drybrush pale turquoise over every surface of a blue green base, wash deep green, then drybrush light turquoise very softly.
turquoise-armour.teal armor: Blue green base, pale turquoise drybrush, two coats of deep green wash, then a soft light turquoise drybrush on the edges.
turquoise-armour.blue green armour: Base blue green, drybrush pale turquoise all over, wash deep green section by section, and finish with a soft light turquoise drybrush.

white-and-grey-hair.white hair: Base blue grey, layer up by mixing in off white, covering less each time, then off white on the top clumps and a thin white halo on the crown.
white-and-grey-hair.grey hair: Base a blue grey, then layer lighter greys by mixing in off white in steps, covering less each time.
white-and-grey-hair.how do i paint an old man's beard: Blue grey base, lighter grey layers in strands, off white on the highest clumps only, highlighting clumps rather than single hairs.
white-and-grey-hair.grey beard: Base two coats of blue grey, then layer lighter grey in steps and off white on the highest clumps.
white-and-grey-hair.white beard looks flat: Use a darker shadow underneath: blue grey, or a warm red grey for more contrast, then build up to off white on the clumps.
white-and-grey-hair.silver hair: Blue grey base, lighter grey layers mixed with off white, off white on the top clumps, and a little thinned white on the crown.
white-and-grey-hair.old wizard hair: Base blue grey, layer lighter grey in strands, then off white on the highest clumps, with a small thinned white halo on the crown.
white-and-grey-hair.strands of white hair: Layer lighter greys in strands, covering less each time, and highlight clumps rather than single hairs.
white-and-grey-hair.grey to white hair highlights: Mix off white into the blue grey base in steps, covering less each time, ending with off white on the top clumps.
white-and-grey-hair.dwarf white beard: Base blue grey or a warm red grey, layer lighter greys mixed with off white, then off white on the highest clumps.

accent-colour.my model looks boring: Add one colour not yet on it, ideally opposite the main colour on the colour wheel, in small spots near the face.
accent-colour.spot colour: One small contrasting colour, on a gem, lens or stripe, painted with extra care, gives the eye a resting point.
accent-colour.accent color: Pick one colour from the far side of the colour wheel, use it in small spots, strongest on the upper half, and echo it two or three times.
accent-colour.what colour should i add: One that is not yet on the model, ideally from the far side of the colour wheel from the main colour.
accent-colour.model looks unfinished: A small patch of one contrasting colour, such as a red sash on a grey figure, gives the eye a resting point and makes it look finished.
accent-colour.add a pop of colour: Use one contrasting colour in small amounts, a gem, lens or stripe, with its strongest spot near the face or head.
accent-colour.everything is brown and grey: Add one colour that is not yet on the model, like a red sash on a grey figure, in a few small, well painted spots.
accent-colour.how do i make a plain model more interes: Add a small accent in one colour opposite the main colour, placed near the face, then echo it two or three times around the model.
accent-colour.contrasting colour for details: Use one colour from the far side of the colour wheel on a gem, lens or stripe, with more care and saturation than the big areas.
accent-colour.complementary colour accent: Pick the colour opposite the main colour on the wheel, use it sparingly near the head, and echo it in a rough triangle.

airbrush-masking.masking: Spray the lighter or smaller area first, cover it with tape, putty or liquid mask, then spray thin dry coats so the new colour stops cleanly.
airbrush-masking.masking tape: Lay low tack tape in small strips up to where the colour should stop, burnish the edges with a fingernail, and peel slowly at a low angle.
airbrush-masking.liquid mask: Lay it on with some body using a sponge or soaped old brush, test it on a hidden spot, and peel it soon after spraying.
airbrush-masking.two colours with an airbrush: Spray the lighter or smaller colour first, let it dry, mask it with tape or putty, then spray the second colour in thin dry coats.
airbrush-masking.clean line with an airbrush: Burnish low tack tape down well, or trim it along a panel line, and spray thin, slightly dry coats at low pressure.
airbrush-masking.overspray: Cover the rest of the model with putty or cling film, and spray thin coats aimed at the open area.
airbrush-masking.mask off: Cover finished areas with tape, low tack putty or liquid mask, sealing every edge, then spray thin, slightly dry coats.
airbrush-masking.sticky putty masking: Press low tack reusable putty onto curves, seal every edge with the side of a brush, and do not leave it on overnight.
airbrush-masking.how to airbrush stripes: Tape both sides of a band and spray between them in thin, slightly dry coats.
airbrush-masking.paint bleeding under tape: Wet coats creep under the mask: spray thin, slightly dry coats at low pressure and burnish the tape edges down.

airbrushed-metal.airbrush metallic: Over black, spray a mid steel all over, a thin dark blue black from below, then bright silver from above.
airbrushed-metal.quick shaded metal with airbrush: Mid steel all over, very thin dark passes from underneath, then bright silver sprayed from above; no all over wash needed.
airbrushed-metal.airbrushing silver: Spray bright silver from above, anywhere from straight down to about 45 degrees, over a mid steel base and a dark underside.
airbrushed-metal.metal looks glittery: Use metallics with a fine flake; they spray best and avoid a glittery look.
airbrushed-metal.steel gradient airbrush: Mid steel all over, a thin dark blue black sprayed from below, then bright silver from above so upper surfaces catch the light.
airbrushed-metal.airbrush tank metal: Mid steel over black, a dark tone from below, bright silver from above, and a slightly thicker black on exhausts and barrels.
airbrushed-metal.spraying metallics: Spray smooth coats over a black primer and choose metallics with a fine flake, which spray best.
airbrushed-metal.dark from below light from above metal: Spray mid steel all over, then several very thin dark passes from underneath and bright silver from above.
airbrushed-metal.fast metal on vehicles: Mid steel, a thin dark tone from below and bright silver from above, then a dark wash only in the upper panel lines.
airbrushed-metal.airbrush silver armour: Spray mid steel over black, a thin dark blue black from below, bright silver from above, then brush a few top edge highlights.

avoiding-pure-white.should i use pure white: Only for the very last small highlight, roughly the top tenth, and tiny glints like an eye catchlight or a gem hotspot.
avoiding-pure-white.white looks too stark: Use near whites such as off white greys, creams or pale tints, and save pure white for the smallest final highlight.
avoiding-pure-white.white highlights chalky: White paint is coarse and goes on chalky; lift colours with a pale yellow, ivory or pale skin tone instead of white.
avoiding-pure-white.off white instead of white: Yes, near whites read as white next to darker colours, look less stark and leave pure white free for the last highlight.
avoiding-pure-white.final highlight colour: Pure white only on the top tenth of edges and glints; a very light grey with a touch of white suits corner dots on dark colours.
avoiding-pure-white.when to use white: For the very last small highlight on edges and top surfaces and for tiny glints such as an eye catchlight.
avoiding-pure-white.too much white: Mixing white in greys a colour and makes skin chalky; highlight with pale yellow or ivory and keep the brightest layers very small.
avoiding-pure-white.white paint patchy: White paint is coarse and tends to go on patchy; base white panels in a very light grey instead.
avoiding-pure-white.near white highlight: Use off white greys, creams or pale tints of blue, green or pink; ivory or bone for warm light, pale blue for snow.
avoiding-pure-white.white looks fake: Almost nothing real is pure white; use near whites suited to the light, and keep pure white for the smallest final touch.

batch-painting.batch painting: Do each step on every model in a small group before starting the next, largest areas first, with three to ten models per batch.
batch-painting.how to paint a whole army fast: Prime and base the main colour across the whole army, then split into small batches, plan about five colours, and keep strong contrast.
batch-painting.paint lots of models at once: Line them up and do each step on every model before the next, so by the last one the first is dry.
batch-painting.how many models should i batch: Three to ten similar models suits most people, fewer for very detailed ones; fifteen or more tends to feel endless.
batch-painting.painting a squad together: Do each step across the whole squad before the next, base everything that shares a wash and wash it all at once, and paint the leader separately.
batch-painting.assembly line painting: Line the models up and work along the row, one step on every model, head to feet, checking for missed areas after each colour.
batch-painting.speed up painting a horde: Keep batches small, use about five colours, skip detailed eyes on rank and file, and use the biggest brush that keeps a good point.
batch-painting.painting 20 models feels endless: Split the batch: run two or three small batches side by side, paint a leader between them, and set a steady target like a unit a week.
batch-painting.paint the leader separately: Yes. Paint leaders on their own, spending extra time there and on faces, where the eye goes.
batch-painting.paint one colour on every model then the: Yes, do each step on every model before starting the next, largest areas first, so the first model is dry by the time you finish.

blending-tiny-areas.blending small areas: Mix one or two colours halfway between the layers and paint them over the join, each a little smaller than the last.
