blending-tiny-areas.how do i blend on tiny parts: Paint in between mixes over the join at normal consistency, each smaller than the one before; two or three steps usually read as a blend.
blending-tiny-areas.blending fingers: There is rarely room to glaze fingers, so paint one or two halfway mixes over the join between layers, each a little smaller.
blending-tiny-areas.no room to glaze: Paint in between colour mixes over the join at covering consistency instead, adding steps until it looks smooth from normal distance.
blending-tiny-areas.smoothing steps on straps: Mix a colour halfway between the two layers and paint it over the join, then another smaller step if needed.
blending-tiny-areas.blending on small plates: Mix one or two midway colours on the palette and paint them over the join, each a little smaller, until the change looks smooth.
blending-tiny-areas.layers look stripey on small bits: Add in between mixes over each join until it looks smooth from normal viewing distance; two or three steps usually read as a blend.
blending-tiny-areas.mixing midtones: Mix one or two colours halfway between the two layers on the palette, then paint them over the join at normal consistency.
blending-tiny-areas.smooth transitions on tiny details: Paint halfway mixes over the join, each a little smaller than the last, or glaze with very thin paint and a small brush.
blending-tiny-areas.can't blend small areas: Use in between mixes painted over the join, each a little smaller; at that size two or three steps read as a blend.

brush-coat-over-primer.touch ups dont match spray: Spray and pot paint dry with different sheen; brush one or two thin coats of the matching paint over the sprayed colour first.
brush-coat-over-primer.brushed coat over coloured primer: Brush one or two thin coats of the matching paint over the main areas, and every later touch up blends in.
brush-coat-over-primer.patches show after fixing mistakes: Sprayed and pot colours differ in sheen and texture; give the spray a brushed coat of the pot colour and fix slips with that pot.
brush-coat-over-primer.spray and pot colour look different: They dry with a different sheen and texture; brush one or two thin coats of the pot colour over the sprayed areas.
brush-coat-over-primer.sheen differs on touch ups: Brush a thin coat of the matching paint over the sprayed colour, then use that same pot for all later clean up.
brush-coat-over-primer.do i need to brush over colour primer: If you will touch up, yes: one or two thin brushed coats of the matching paint stop later fixes from showing.
brush-coat-over-primer.colour primer then brush: Yes, brush one or two thin coats of the matching paint over the main areas so later touch ups blend in.
brush-coat-over-primer.fixing spray primer slips: Brush a coat of the matching pot colour over the spray first, then paint slips back over invisibly with that same pot.
brush-coat-over-primer.mismatched patches after tidying: The spray and pot colour have different sheen; brush the pot colour over the sprayed areas so fixes match.
brush-coat-over-primer.why do my corrections show: Pot paint dries with a different sheen to spray; give the model a brushed coat of the same pot colour you use for corrections.

bullet-holes-and-impacts.bullet holes: Paint a short dark brown streak ending in a larger round chip, dot a mid grey then lighter grey in its centre, and the highlight below.
bullet-holes-and-impacts.battle damage: See: this entry covers bullet strikes, a dark brown streak and chip with grey at the centre and a highlight on the lower edge.
bullet-holes-and-impacts.impact marks on armour: A dark brown chip with mid grey in the middle and lighter grey at the very centre, plus the armour highlight dotted along its lower edge.
bullet-holes-and-impacts.shot marks on a tank: Paint a short dark brown streak ending in a round chip, add grey at its centre, and keep strikes few and on the front.
bullet-holes-and-impacts.bullet strikes: A short dark brown streak for the path, ending in a larger chip, with grey layered at the centre and the highlight on the lower edge.
bullet-holes-and-impacts.how to paint dents: Dot the armour's highlight colour along the lower edge of a dark brown chip so it reads as a dent catching light.
bullet-holes-and-impacts.damage from gunfire: Brown streak and chip, mid grey then light grey at the centre, highlight under it; keep strikes few and where shots would land.
bullet-holes-and-impacts.ricochet marks: Paint a short dark brown streak for the path of the shot, ending in a larger roughly round chip where it struck.
bullet-holes-and-impacts.laser burn marks on armour: See: this entry covers bullet strikes, painted as a dark brown streak and chip with greys in the centre for depth.
bullet-holes-and-impacts.make armour look shot up: Add a few streaks and chips where shots would land, such as the front, layered brown, mid grey and light grey so they read deep.

cheap-basing-materials.cheap basing materials: Garden grit and sand, found dirt, tea leaves, twigs, sanded tile grout, cork, chopped old sprue and small coins all work.
cheap-basing-materials.free basing stuff: Sand, dirt and small stones from outside are free; bake them at about 175 C for half an hour first.
cheap-basing-materials.what can i use for basing: Garden grit, sand, pebbles, tea leaves for leaf litter, cork for rock faces, twigs for logs and chopped sprue for rubble.
cheap-basing-materials.garden sand for bases: Sieve it into grades, bake found sand at about 175 C for half an hour, and run a magnet through it if your models use magnets.
cheap-basing-materials.tea leaves as leaves on a base: Dried tea leaves pass for leaf litter; glue them down and prime the base with everything else.
cheap-basing-materials.basing on a budget: Bags of garden grit and sand last years, found sand is free once baked, and tea leaves, cork and old sprue cost almost nothing.
cheap-basing-materials.household items for bases: Tea leaves for leaf litter, coffee grounds sealed with varnish for soil, sanded tile grout, torn cork for rock, and coffee stirrers for planks.
cheap-basing-materials.kitty litter basing: See: this entry lists garden grit, sand, tumbled glass, tea leaves, grout, cork, twigs and sprue as cheap basing.
cheap-basing-materials.cork and grit basing: Torn cork makes rock faces and garden grit sieved into grades adds texture; glue it all down, then prime the whole base.
cheap-basing-materials.twigs as tree branches: Small twigs make fallen logs: bake them on a low heat for a long time to dry them, then place them at varied angles.

choosing-glue.which glue should i use: Plastic glue for plastic to plastic, super glue for resin, metal, mixed materials and quick fixes, epoxy for heavy parts.
choosing-glue.plastic glue or super glue: Plastic glue welds bare plastic permanently; super glue suits resin, metal, mixed materials, painted parts or poses you may redo.
choosing-glue.glue for resin: Super glue; wash the resin in warm soapy water first, as plastic glue will not bond it.
choosing-glue.glue for metal models: Super glue, as plastic glue will not bond metal; use two part epoxy for heavy or stressed parts.
choosing-glue.plastic cement: It melts bare plastic parts together; thin cement wicks into a held seam, and thicker cement in a needle bottle gives time to line up.
choosing-glue.superglue not holding: Wash resin in warm soapy water first, scrape off old glue before refitting, and use epoxy for heavy or stressed parts.
choosing-glue.polystyrene cement: Plastic cement melts bare plastic parts together, so scrape off primer or paint first; bigger contact areas make stronger joins.
choosing-glue.glue for mixed materials: Super glue works on resin, metal, plastic and mixed materials; gel gives time to adjust on upright joins.
choosing-glue.best glue for miniatures: Plastic glue for a permanent plastic weld, super glue for resin, metal and mixed parts, epoxy for heavy parts, PVA for basing.
choosing-glue.why wont my glue stick: Plastic glue only works on bare plastic, not resin, metal, primer or paint; use super glue there, and wash resin first.

cold-light-scenes.moonlight: Light from one direction, a cold pale blue highlight on every material, low saturation, darker shadows and midtones kept warm.
cold-light-scenes.night scene: Darken shadows and midtones, highlight every material with the same cold turquoise or pale blue, and keep colours low in saturation.
cold-light-scenes.how to paint a model at night: Push the shadows darker, then highlight everything with one mid value turquoise or pale blue instead of white, from one direction.
cold-light-scenes.cold light: Highlight every material with the same cold colour, such as turquoise or pale pastel blue, so it reads as one light.
cold-light-scenes.blue highlights instead of white: A highlight only has to be lighter than its surroundings; darken the range so a mid value blue reads as bright.
cold-light-scenes.moonlit diorama: Zenithal prime from the moon's direction, paint the face first as a guide, highlight in cold pale blue and keep shadows warm.
cold-light-scenes.make it look like night time: Lower the whole value range, highlight with a cold turquoise or blue, and work violet or purple into deep black shadows.
cold-light-scenes.winter cold lighting: Highlight every material with the same cold pale blue or turquoise and keep saturation low, with warm violet tinted shadows.
cold-light-scenes.turquoise highlights: Use one mid value turquoise on every material after pushing the shadows and midtones darker, so it reads as bright light.
cold-light-scenes.night time lighting effect: One light direction, cold pale blue highlights, low saturation, and warm shadows with violet and a touch of red.

coloured-undercoats.coloured primer: Prime, then spray or brush one dark colour over the whole model, warm darks under warm colours and cool darks under blues and steel.
coloured-undercoats.what colour undercoat: Match the scheme: a warm dark like red brown under warm colours and gold, a cool dark like deep blue under blues and steel.
coloured-undercoats.undershading: Put one dark colour under everything, add a lighter colour from above for light, then build each area up leaving the dark in recesses.
coloured-undercoats.should i prime black or white: Black and white suit cool colours but can flatten warm ones like red and yellow; a coloured undercoat gives a shared shadow.
coloured-undercoats.red undercoat for warm colours: Yes, use warm darks such as a red brown or deep red under warm colours and gold, then a warm flesh from above.
coloured-undercoats.colored primer: Spray or brush one dark colour over the primer, such as navy or deep red, so every later colour shares the same shadow.
coloured-undercoats.prime model blue: A deep blue undercoat suits blues and steel; add a pale blue from above for a cold mood.
coloured-undercoats.shadow colour under everything: Spray or brush one dark colour over the whole model, then leave it showing in the deepest recesses as you build each area up.
coloured-undercoats.dark undercoat for warm colours: Use a warm dark such as a red brown or deep red, as black can flatten warm colours like red and yellow.
coloured-undercoats.primer for red: Black can flatten red; a warm dark undercoat such as a red brown or deep red gives it richer shadows.

contrast-medium.contrast medium: Medium thins one coat paint but keeps its flow and grip; start about half paint, half medium, in two thin coats.
contrast-medium.thinning contrast paint: Thin with medium, about half and half, or two parts paint to one for stronger colour, and give two thin coats.
contrast-medium.contrast too dark: Start thinner with medium; if it dries too dark, paint over it with a matching opaque colour rather than adding more.
contrast-medium.water or medium for contrast: Medium gives an even tint, even on smooth metal; water suits pushing deeper colour into folds and feathering it out.
contrast-medium.contrast paint pooling: Thin it with medium so it grips without pooling as badly, and lift pools with the belly of a clean, damp brush.
contrast-medium.softer shading with one coat paints: Mix one coat paint with medium for a softer, lighter colour that hides brush mistakes better than the neat paint.
contrast-medium.diluting speed paints: Dilute one coat paints with medium, starting around half and half; over white, go as far as one part paint to six or eight.
contrast-medium.contrast medium ratio: About half paint, half medium, or two to one for stronger colour; over white or very pale bases, up to one to six or eight.
contrast-medium.make contrast lighter: Add more medium, as far as one part paint to six or eight over a white or very pale base, and test on one section first.
contrast-medium.streaky contrast: Cover the whole area so there are no gaps, which leave hard lines, and shake and mix the pot well before use.

cube-and-eye-monsters.clear cube monster: Wash it, paint anything trapped inside first in muted colours, then tint with thinned glossy green or blue green ink in thin coats.
cube-and-eye-monsters.floating eye monster: Make the big eye the brightest, glossiest point: pale yellow white, a strong iris, black pupil, gloss only the eye, and a contrasting body.
cube-and-eye-monsters.how to paint a see through jelly monster: Tint the clear part with thinned glossy ink in thin coats, adding more low down and in the corners where the jelly is deepest.
cube-and-eye-monsters.clear plastic monster went cloudy: Thick coats go cloudy; build the tint up in thin coats of thinned glossy ink instead.
cube-and-eye-monsters.tint clear resin green: Wash it in warm soapy water, then tint with thinned glossy slime green ink, building up in thin coats.
cube-and-eye-monsters.transparent cube with stuff inside: Paint the trapped bones, helmet or coins first in muted colours, then tint the cube with thinned glossy ink in thin coats.
cube-and-eye-monsters.big eye monster with eye stalks: Paint the stalk eyes as a set with the same iris colour as the big eye, but smaller and duller, so the big eye still leads.
cube-and-eye-monsters.make a giant eye look wet: Paint the white pale yellow white shaded pink near the lids, add a strong iris and black pupil, then gloss only the eye.
cube-and-eye-monsters.slime cube: Tint clear plastic with thinned glossy slime green ink; on an opaque cube, base mid green, darken low and centre, and gloss varnish it.
cube-and-eye-monsters.how to paint transparent models: Wash in warm soapy water, then build up thinned glossy ink in thin coats, as thick coats go cloudy.

designing-a-base.how do i make a good base: Use the right size, fit the ground to the model's story, build big to small, mix textures, and keep detail away from the rim.
designing-a-base.what size base should i use: The standard base or one or two sizes up; stand big figures on it first, as an overhanging one often looks better a size up.
designing-a-base.base hides the model: Raise the back so the whole figure shows, keep large features away from the front, and treat the base as a frame.
designing-a-base.base looks empty: Too big looks empty without something worth looking at; add one or two well chosen items, or drop to a smaller size.
designing-a-base.base design tips: Place the figure a little off centre, build from big rocks down to fine sand, mix textures, and half bury small extras.
designing-a-base.display plinth ideas: Round plinths suit all round viewing and square ones fix a front view; one or two well chosen items is often enough.
designing-a-base.square or round base: Round suits all round viewing, square fixes a front view.
designing-a-base.base too busy: Treat it as a frame: one or two well chosen items is often enough, with limited colours and soil showing between tufts.
designing-a-base.telling a story with the base: Fit the ground to the model, like snow for a figure in furs, and think of a tiny story of what happened there to pick the bits.
designing-a-base.how big should a display base be: The standard size or one or two sizes up; too big looks empty and too small leaves no room.
designing-a-base.How do I make a simple base?: If unsure, a mid brown earth works with almost any colour; add one or two well chosen items and a few uneven tufts.

drop-blending.blending layers: Thin the lighter colour to a watery mix, wick most off the brush, and drag a small drop from the dark layer to end right on the join.
drop-blending.smooth blend with thin paint: Use roughly six parts water to four of paint, wick the excess onto a damp tissue, and repeat passes until the edge vanishes.
drop-blending.hide the edge of a layer: Drag a small drop of thinned lighter paint from the darker side, ending the stroke on the join, and repeat after it dries.
drop-blending.how to blend on a mini: Thin the lighter colour right down, wick most of it off, and pull a small drop from the dark layer to the join, a few times over.
drop-blending.watery paint blending: Roughly six parts water to four of paint; erring thin only means more passes, erring thick gives coverage, not a blend.
drop-blending.soft fade between two colours: Drag a small drop of thinned lighter paint from the darker colour towards the join, let it dry, and repeat until the edge vanishes.
drop-blending.blend highlights smoothly: Use small steps in brightness and drag thinned drops of each across its join, as one big jump is far harder to blend.
drop-blending.joins between layers show: Thin the lighter layer to a watery mix and drag a small drop across the join, ending on it, a few times until it disappears.
drop-blending.glaze blending: Thin to about six parts water to four of paint, keep only a small drop in the brush, and pull from dark to light, ending on the join.
drop-blending.feathering paint: Start the stroke on the darker layer with a small drop of thin paint and end it on the join, where most pigment is left.

drybrushing-large-areas.drybrushing large areas: Use a big, soft fluffy brush, wipe nearly all the paint off, and work many light passes outwards from where the light is strongest.
drybrushing-large-areas.big soft drybrush: A large, fluffy brush leaves a smoother, more even dusting than a small stiff one; soft round blush brushes work well.
drybrushing-large-areas.makeup brush for drybrushing: Yes, soft round makeup brushes made for blush work well, giving a smoother, more even dusting on large areas.
drybrushing-large-areas.drybrush a gradient: Work from where the light is strongest outwards, adding each lighter colour over a smaller area and going back and forth to balance it.
drybrushing-large-areas.drybrush instead of airbrush: A big soft brush in many light passes builds a gradient that can look close to airbrushing on a smooth vehicle.
drybrushing-large-areas.drybrushing looks chalky and scratchy: Use a soft fluffy brush, load very little paint and wipe nearly all of it off; too much paint is the main thing that goes wrong.
drybrushing-large-areas.smooth drybrushing on flat panels: Go from the top down with a soft brush, twenty or more light strokes per area, refreshing it on a damp pad instead of taking more paint.
drybrushing-large-areas.drybrush a glow: Work the light colour in from where the glow should be strongest, spreading outwards, each lighter mix over a smaller area.
drybrushing-large-areas.drybrush a whole tank: Start with the base mixed half and half with a lighter colour; it catches rivets, panel lines and edges by itself.
drybrushing-large-areas.dry brushing big flat surfaces: Use a large soft brush with almost no paint, many light strokes from the top down, and a firm small brush for the final crisp highlight.

edge-highlighting.edge highlights: Paint a thin line clearly brighter than the base along raised edges, after any wash, with a size 1 to 3 brush and little paint on the tip.
edge-highlighting.how do i do edge highlighting: Thin paint slightly, take most off on tissue, brace your wrists, practise swings, then skim the edge lightly, turning the model.
edge-highlighting.shaky lines on edges: Brace your wrists on the table and your hands against each other, make practice swings just above the edge, and turn the model, not your hand.
edge-highlighting.edge highlight colour: Clearly brighter than the base: half base and half a lighter colour first, then the lighter colour alone; on red, a pale orange.
edge-highlighting.thin lines along armour edges: Use a size 1 to 3 with a good point, touch the loaded brush on tissue until the tip carries little, and skim the edge lightly.
edge-highlighting.model looks flat after wash: Edge highlight it: a fine, lighter line along raised edges brings back the contrast a dark wash dulls.
edge-highlighting.edge highlight too thick: You are likely carrying too much paint: touch the loaded brush on tissue until the tip carries little, and skim the edge lightly.
edge-highlighting.how to paint thin lines: Thin paint to layer consistency, use a pointed size 1 to 3, take the excess off on tissue, brace your hands and skim lightly.
edge-highlighting.edge highlightng: Paint a fine, lighter line along raised edges so each shape reads clearly, using slightly thinned paint and a braced hand.
edge-highlighting.tank edges: Paint a fine line brighter than the base along every raised edge, and add a paler dot on the sharpest corners for extra punch.
edge-highlighting.How do I paint thin edge highlights?: Slightly thinned paint, a size 1 to 3 brush with little on the tip, braced wrists, and a light skim along the edge as you turn the model.

faces-with-contrast-paints.faces with contrast: Over a pale primer, tint the skin with a thinned pale flesh one coat paint, shade down selectively, then layer and glaze highlights back.
faces-with-contrast-paints.skin with one coat paints: Tint all the skin with pale flesh thinned half and half, push less thinned coats into recesses, then a darker tone more selectively.
faces-with-contrast-paints.easy face painting: Over bone primer, thin pale flesh one coat paint to tint the skin, shade down into recesses, then layer pale skin back on the high points.
faces-with-contrast-paints.contrast skin: Over bone or off white, brush a light tint of thinned pale flesh one coat paint over all the skin without letting it pool, then shade down.
faces-with-contrast-paints.speed paint faces: Shade down from a pale primer with thinned one coat flesh paints, then layer pale skin on forehead, nose, cheekbones and chin.
faces-with-contrast-paints.face over bone primer: Thin pale flesh one coat paint half and half with water to tint, shade the recesses with it less thinned, then add a darker flesh.
faces-with-contrast-paints.how to paint a face quickly: Tint, then shade down with thinned one coat flesh paints over a pale primer, add a warm brown in the deepest spots, and layer highlights.
faces-with-contrast-paints.shade down from light face: Start from a pale primer, tint the skin, then put less thinned and darker flesh tones into ever smaller recesses.
faces-with-contrast-paints.flesh contrast thinned: About half and half with water, plus a touch of clear medium if you have it, brushed lightly over all the skin without pooling.
faces-with-contrast-paints.beginner face method: Bone primer, a thinned pale flesh tint, the same less thinned in recesses, a darker flesh and brown deeper, then pale skin highlights.

finding-time-to-paint.no time to paint: Use short, regular sessions with a set stopping time; fifteen minutes is enough for a base coat, a wash or one detail.
finding-time-to-paint.painting with kids around: Pick a routine you can keep, like an early hour or once the house is quiet, and leave the desk ready so you can start at once.
finding-time-to-paint.short painting sessions: Leave the desk ready, with models on handles and the next paints set out, so you can start at once and use small windows.
finding-time-to-paint.busy schedule hobby: Regular short sessions get more done than waiting for a free weekend; set a stopping time before you start.
finding-time-to-paint.painting routine: Pick one you can keep, such as an hour early in the morning or a short session once the house is quiet.
finding-time-to-paint.what can i do in 15 minutes: Fifteen minutes is enough for a base coat, a wash or one detail.
finding-time-to-paint.how to fit painting in: Use small windows and a routine you can keep, with the desk set up so you can start at once.
finding-time-to-paint.painting after work: Set a stopping time first, pick a simple task you enjoy when energy is low, and use a bright task lamp at night.
finding-time-to-paint.never have time for the hobby: Short regular sessions beat waiting for a free weekend; even fifteen minutes covers a base coat or a wash.
finding-time-to-paint.how often should i paint: Regularly, in short sessions you can keep up, rather than marathon nights or waiting for a free weekend.

fix-airbrush-spitting.airbrush spitting: Usually water from the air line: drain the moisture trap, lower the pressure a little, and then check the nozzle and needle for dried paint.
fix-airbrush-spitting.airbrush spatter: Check the air first for water or an uneven supply, then the needle tip and nozzle for dried paint, and thin the paint more.
fix-airbrush-spitting.airbrush pulsing: Pulsing means the air supply is not steady; a compressor with an air tank and a proper regulator smooths it out.
fix-airbrush-spitting.water drops coming out of airbrush: Compressed air drops water as it cools; fit a moisture trap, drain it often with its bleed valve, and lower the pressure a little.
fix-airbrush-spitting.moisture trap: It sits between compressor and hose and catches water; drain it often with its bleed valve and replace worn filters.
fix-airbrush-spitting.airbrush sputters: Thick or old paint makes it sputter: thin it more or mix a fresh batch, and check the nozzle for dried paint.
fix-airbrush-spitting.uneven airbrush flow: Check the air supply is steady, then clean dried paint off the needle tip and nozzle and tighten nozzle, cap and needle chuck.
fix-airbrush-spitting.airbrush splatters paint: Drain water from the moisture trap, check for a part clog at the needle tip and nozzle, and thin thick or old paint.
fix-airbrush-spitting.compressor pulsing: A compressor without a tank gives an uneven supply; one with an air tank and a proper regulator smooths it out.
fix-airbrush-spitting.airbrush keeps spitting: Drain the moisture trap often, lower the pressure a little, and make sure the nozzle, cap and needle chuck are tight and clean.

fix-harsh-faces.face looks old: Very dark creases and bright ridges age a face; keep wrinkles only slightly darker than the skin around them.
fix-harsh-faces.face too harsh: Glaze midtone skin over the deepest lines to pull them back, and keep the darkest accents to a few places like the eye sockets.
fix-harsh-faces.wrinkles too dark: Keep wrinkles only slightly darker than the surrounding skin, and glaze midtone skin over lines that are already too deep.
fix-harsh-faces.face looks angry: Deep dark recesses and bright ridges make a face look hard and severe; glaze midtone skin over the deepest lines to soften it.
fix-harsh-faces.young face painting: Do not shade creases like armour panel lines; keep them only slightly darker than the skin and keep the brightest highlights small.
fix-harsh-faces.softer face: Glaze shadow, midtone and highlight back and forth until it softens, keeping the brightest highlights small on nose, cheekbones and brow.
fix-harsh-faces.face looks dirty: See: this entry covers harsh faces; glaze midtone skin over the deepest lines and keep dark accents to a few places.
fix-harsh-faces.too much contrast on face: Keep the darkest accents to the sides of the nose, eye sockets and under the lip, and glaze midtone over other deep lines.
fix-harsh-faces.female face looks old: Keep wrinkles only slightly darker than the skin, glaze midtone over deep lines, and keep the brightest highlights small.
fix-harsh-faces.face shading too strong: Glaze midtone skin over the deepest lines, and judge the face only once the rest of the skin and nearby areas have colour.

fix-transfer-problems.decal silvering: Greyish patches and a clear edge mean trapped air over a matt or rough surface: gloss varnish first and trim the film close.
fix-transfer-problems.transfers wrinkle: Press a very sharp blade tip into the fold without sawing, let the cut edges sink into the softener, and nudge them flat while wet.
fix-transfer-problems.decal tears: It was forced off the paper: wait until it slides off on its own, and use only very light brush pressure once softener is on.
fix-transfer-problems.decal bubbling: Press out bubbles while the softener is still working, or roll a damp cotton bud gently over them.
fix-transfer-problems.decal curling up in water: Leave it in a little longer until it relaxes, or ease it flat with a damp brush.
fix-transfer-problems.visible clear film on decal: Gloss varnish underneath and trim the film close to the design; if the edge still shows after sealing, add more matt.
fix-transfer-problems.decal problems: Most come from a rough surface, a rushed soak, too much blotting or matt varnish straight on top; gloss under it prevents most.
fix-transfer-problems.torn transfer: Do not force it off the paper; wait until it slides, keep it slightly damp, and never scrub once softener is on.
fix-transfer-problems.decal wont stick: Lay it on gloss varnish, keep it slightly damp so it can slide, and use softener in small amounts to settle it.
fix-transfer-problems.transfer went cloudy under matt varnish: Matt straight onto a freshly softened transfer can frost white; seal it with gloss or satin first, then matt later.

focal-points.focal point: Pick one or two key areas, give them the most saturated colours and sharpest highlights, and let the rest darken and calm down.
focal-points.how do i make the face stand out: Make it lighter than the rest of the skin, keep the brightest values high on the model, and add small bright detail near it.
focal-points.draw the eye: Put the brightest, sharpest highlights and most saturated colour at the focus, and keep the lower body darker so the eye drifts up.
focal-points.model looks busy: High contrast everywhere looks busy; save it for the focus and give minor details one or two clear highlights at most.
focal-points.where to put the brightest highlights: High on the model, around the head and chest, at the one or two areas people should look at first.
focal-points.everything is same brightness: Let colours darken and calm away from the focus, keep lower body and limbs darker, and make the face lighter than the other skin.
focal-points.make the character stand out: Use the brightest highlights and most saturated colour on the face, or a cool face on a warm model, and tame anything competing.
focal-points.contrast on the face: Give the face the sharpest highlights and most saturated colour, and keep other areas, including bone and skulls, more muted.
focal-points.model lacks a focus: Decide one or two areas from what the model is about, and give them the strongest colour and highlights, no more than two.
focal-points.focus point on a display model: Pick one or two areas, push saturation and sharp highlights there, keep the lower body darker, and check the balance at the end.

freehand-symbols.freehand: Paint at the base coat stage with slightly thinned paint, start from a centre line, grow shapes a little at a time and trim with the background.
freehand-symbols.painting symbols: Find the centre, paint a line down the middle, add crossing lines through it, fill between, then thicken lines once the shape is right.
freehand-symbols.heraldry: Treat white and yellow as metals and red, blue and black as colours, and put a metal on a colour or a colour on a metal.
freehand-symbols.freehand shield design: Dot the exact centre first, as lines drift on a curved plate, then build the design outwards from a centre line and crossing lines.
freehand-symbols.painting icons: Draw it on paper first, then on the model build it from a centre line with thinned paint, slightly big, and trim back with the base colour.
freehand-symbols.how to paint a logo by hand: Sketch it on paper, mark key points with dots on the model, join them with smooth lines in thinned paint, then fill and trim.
freehand-symbols.symmetry in freehand: Find the centre from a straight edge, paint one line down the middle, then crossing lines and diagonals through that same centre.
freehand-symbols.shield emblem freehand: Place a dot in the exact centre, paint a centre line and a crossing line, build the shape out from them, then outline it last.
freehand-symbols.simple shapes freehand: An eight pointed star is four lines, a diamond joins the tips of a cross, and a skull is a circle, an oval and a slanted box.
freehand-symbols.banner symbols: Find the centre from the straight top edge, paint a line down the middle following the cloth, and build the symbol out from it.

gloss-coat-before-washing.gloss before wash: Yes: over gloss or satin the wash slides into recesses and panel lines, and spills wipe off flat areas without a mark.
gloss-coat-before-washing.wash staining flat areas: On matt paint a wash soaks in; varnish gloss first, touch the wash into recesses only, and wipe spills with a damp cotton bud.
gloss-coat-before-washing.wash tide marks: Gloss varnish the base colours first, keep the wash to recesses and panel lines, and wipe spills one section at a time before they dry.
gloss-coat-before-washing.varnish before washing: Brush one thin coat of gloss, or spray it thinned to about milk, one or two coats at most, and let it dry fully first.
gloss-coat-before-washing.wash on gloss: Touch it into recesses and panel lines only and let it run along by itself; wipe spills off the gloss with a damp bud.
gloss-coat-before-washing.panel lining: Over gloss varnish, touch a wash a little darker than the area into the panel lines and let it run along them by itself.
gloss-coat-before-washing.wash stains everything: Seal the paint with gloss or satin first so the wash slides into recesses, and keep it off broad flat areas.
gloss-coat-before-washing.satin varnish before a wash: Yes, satin works: a paint that dries satin, or matt and gloss varnish mixed, lets the wash flow into recesses too.
gloss-coat-before-washing.do i gloss before a wash: For a clean recess wash, yes: gloss lets it run into lines and spills wipe off; finish with matt or satin afterwards.
gloss-coat-before-washing.wash left rings: Over matt paint a wash soaks and stains; gloss first, and lift any pooling by dampening and wiping gently.

glowing-runes.glowing runes: Paint the stone dark, run thinned white into the lines, add a strong see through colour in thin coats, then glaze the glow outwards.
glowing-runes.how do i make runes glow: Dark stone around them, a white underlayer in the lines, a strong see through tint on top, and glazes fading into the stone.
glowing-runes.glowing symbols on stone: A glow only reads in shadow: paint the stone dark, underlay the carving in white, tint it, then glaze the colour fading into the stone.
glowing-runes.magic runes: Thinned white with a touch of yellow in the carved lines, two thin coats of a strong see through colour, then a fluorescent retrace.
glowing-runes.rune glow on armour: Paint the armour dark first, underlay the runes white, tint them, glaze outwards, and skip edge highlights on that panel.
glowing-runes.glowing carved lines: Over gloss, brush a pale blue and white gouache mix into the grooves, wipe the surface clean, then seal with matt varnish.
glowing-runes.engraved runes on a sword: Run thinned white into the engraving, glaze a strong see through colour over it, and tidy between the lines with the dark colour.
glowing-runes.blue glowing runes: Over gloss, brush a pale blue and white gouache mix into the grooves, wipe the surface with a damp brush, and seal with matt.
glowing-runes.runestone: Paint the stone dark and wash it to mark the carving, underlay white, tint, glaze outwards, and put the palest mix deepest in the groove.
glowing-runes.glowing writing: The lettering must be the brightest thing nearby: white under a strong tint, a glazed fade, then a fluorescent retrace on the lines.

greyscale-underpainting.greyscale underpainting: Set light and shade in greys or white first, bolder than feels right, then cover each area with a see through colour.
greyscale-underpainting.zenithal then contrast: Spray white from about 45 degrees above over black, then tint with saturated, lighter one coat paints, lightest colours first.
greyscale-underpainting.grisaille: Paint the light and shade in greys first, then glaze or tint colour over it so the shading shows through.
greyscale-underpainting.paint light and shadow in grey first: Yes, then add see through colour on top; make the greys bolder than feels right, as colour cuts the contrast.
greyscale-underpainting.white over black primer from above: Spray white from about 45 degrees above, turning the model, so the tops catch light like sunlight.
greyscale-underpainting.colour over grey: Use see through colours, one coat paints, inks or glazes, in saturated, lighter tints, working from lightest to darkest.
greyscale-underpainting.value sketch before colour: Set the light and shade in greys first, bolder than feels right, then tint over it so it shows through as shading.
greyscale-underpainting.sketch style undercoat: See: this entry's greyscale underpainting, light and shade set in grey or white first, then see through colour on top.
greyscale-underpainting.glazing colour over greyscale: Pick saturated, lighter tints, as dark shading paints pool and browns turn muddy, and let each grey stage dry first.

hiding-transfer-film.decal shine: Brush thinned matt varnish over the dry transfer and its edges in two or three thin coats, blotting any that pools.
hiding-transfer-film.make transfers look painted on: Apply over gloss, matt varnish over it, then glaze the lower part darker and add fine chips and grime across it.
hiding-transfer-film.decal edge visible: Thin matt varnish in two or three coats settles around the film edge and hides it; varnish the whole panel to match.
hiding-transfer-film.hide decal film: Lay it on gloss so it sits flat, then two or three thin coats of matt varnish or matt medium over it and its edges.
hiding-transfer-film.weathering decals: Apply them before washes and weathering, then glaze the lower part darker and add fine chips and grime across them.
hiding-transfer-film.shiny decal edges: Brush thinned matt varnish over the edges in thin coats, then varnish the whole panel in the same sheen.
hiding-transfer-film.decals stand out too much: Glaze very thin black or shade over the lower part so it darkens with the panel, and add a little chipping and grime.
hiding-transfer-film.chip decals: Paint fine chips over it or scratch them with a needle tip once it is sealed; they also hide any wrinkles.
hiding-transfer-film.matt varnish over decals: Two or three thin coats of thinned matt over the dry transfer with a soft brush, as a thick coat can dry milky.
hiding-transfer-film.decals look stuck on: Varnish over the film so washes do not outline it, then shade the lower part and add fine chips so it looks painted on.

hobby-burnout.hobby burnout: Take a break without guilt, paint one model just for fun, and keep quick one sitting models to hand.
hobby-burnout.lost motivation to paint: Finish a simple model in one sitting, or look through your unpainted models until one sparks an idea.
hobby-burnout.don't feel like painting: Taking a break is fine; when you return, pick a quick model and start with the part that drew you to it.
hobby-burnout.bored of painting my army: Swap between a quick batch and one slow display piece, vary tones across the group, and set a lower standard so it gets finished.
hobby-burnout.painting slump: Keep a box of simple one sitting models, or a spare model just for experiments; finishing something lifts motivation.
hobby-burnout.motivation: It comes and goes for everyone; finishing a quick one off model or painting something just for fun helps bring it back.
hobby-burnout.hate my painting: If an area will not come right, stop for the day and rest; a few glazes with fresh eyes next session often fix it.
hobby-burnout.how do i get back into painting: Pick a model that builds quickly, get colour on at once with shadow from below and light from above, and follow what catches your eye.
hobby-burnout.taking a break from painting: Taking a break is fine and motivation comes and goes for everyone; come back with a quick, simple model.
hobby-burnout.tired of painting the horde: Set a lower standard on purpose, spend time on parts you enjoy, and break dull jobs into short sessions with music or audiobooks.

hue-value-saturation.what is value: Value is how light or dark a colour is; a pale pink is high value, a deep wine red low, and a black and white photo shows it alone.
hue-value-saturation.hue value saturation: Hue is the colour family, value how light or dark it is, and saturation how intense; each can change on its own.
hue-value-saturation.colour theory basics: Every colour has a hue, a value and a saturation; contrast between colours can come from any of the three.
hue-value-saturation.what does saturation mean: How intense or pure a colour is: neon green is highly saturated, a grey hardly at all.
hue-value-saturation.light and dark colours: That is value; it does most of the work of light and shadow on a model.
hue-value-saturation.colour intensity: That is saturation; paint straight from the pot is usually at its most saturated, and mixing in other colours tends to dull it.
hue-value-saturation.value in painting: Value is how light or dark a colour is, and it does most of the work of light and shadow on a model.
hue-value-saturation.desaturate a colour: Add a touch of the opposite colour, a grey or an earthy brown; adding white also lowers saturation as it raises value.
hue-value-saturation.why does my model lack contrast: Check value: put the strongest value contrast and most saturated colour on the focal point; a black and white photo shows value alone.
hue-value-saturation.colour terms explained: Hue is the colour family, value is lightness, saturation is intensity, and contrast is how different two colours are.

keeping-solvents-safe.how do i get rid of old white spirit: Never pour it down a drain; take it to your local recycling or waste centre as household hazardous waste.
keeping-solvents-safe.where to keep thinners: Sealed in the labelled original container, somewhere cool, dry and dark, up high or locked away, far from heaters and flames.
keeping-solvents-safe.can i pour solvent down the sink: No. Never pour solvent or stripper down a sink, drain or toilet; take it to a waste centre as household hazardous waste.
keeping-solvents-safe.paint stripper disposal: Let it settle, pour the clear part back for reuse, dry the sludge in an open tub outside, then take it to a hazardous waste site.
keeping-solvents-safe.safe bottle for decanted thinner: Use a glass or solvent safe bottle, label it with what it is, and never reuse a drinks bottle.
keeping-solvents-safe.hazardous waste tip for solvents: Take used solvent and dried sludge to your local recycling or waste centre as household hazardous waste, checking local rules first.
keeping-solvents-safe.throw away used isopropyl alcohol: Do not pour it down a drain; take it to your local waste centre as household hazardous waste, checking local rules.
keeping-solvents-safe.keep solvents away from kids: Keep them up high or in a locked cupboard, lids tight, away from food and drink, and never in a drinks bottle.
keeping-solvents-safe.dirty thinner what do i do with it: Let it settle and pour the clear part back for reuse, dry out the sludge outside, and take the waste to a hazardous waste site.
keeping-solvents-safe.keeping brush cleaner in the garage: Keep it sealed and labelled somewhere cool, dry and dark, away from heaters, flames and the boiler, ideally locked or up high.

leave-room-for-highlights.nowhere to go with highlights: Choose a base or mid tone dark enough that a brighter highlight is still left to reach, such as a deeper orange or a cool off white.
leave-room-for-highlights.base colour too bright: Start from a deeper version of the colour, so there is still a much brighter tone left for edges and peaks.
leave-room-for-highlights.pure white base: There is nothing brighter to highlight it with; start from a cool off white and keep pure white for the sharpest edges.
leave-room-for-highlights.can't highlight white: Base a cool off white instead, such as a thinned blue grey over pale grey primer tidied with off white, and save pure white for edges.
leave-room-for-highlights.highlights going bone: Your brightest orange or yellow is the base; start from a deeper version so highlights have room above it.
leave-room-for-highlights.yellow too bright to highlight: Start from a deeper yellow so a much brighter tone is left for the edges, and prime white or bone underneath.
leave-room-for-highlights.no brighter colour for highlights: Pick a darker base or mid tone; it is the jump up to a much brighter tone on edges that makes a colour read.
leave-room-for-highlights.what base colour to choose: One dark enough to leave a brighter highlight above it, but not so dark that edge highlights have nothing to work against.
leave-room-for-highlights.start darker for highlights: Yes, start from a deeper version of the colour so the jump up to a much brighter tone on edges and peaks still reads.
leave-room-for-highlights.highlights look chalky: See: start from a deeper base so highlights stay in the colour instead of drifting pale, and try base and highlights on a spare piece.

loading-the-brush.how much paint on the brush: Load the bristles about half full, then roll off the excess on a damp towel so the brush comes to a sharp point.
loading-the-brush.loading a brush: Dip only the tip, load about half the bristles, then roll and drag it on a slightly damp towel to remove excess and reform the point.
loading-the-brush.brush wont point: Roll and drag it on a slightly damp paper towel, or twist it on the palette, to take off excess and reform the point.
loading-the-brush.paint in the ferrule: Load only about half the bristles and keep paint well away from the metal collar, or it dries there and the brush splays.
loading-the-brush.brush splits: Keep paint away from the metal collar and keep the towel damp, as a dry one sucks the brush dry and splays the tip.
loading-the-brush.too much paint on brush: Roll the brush on a slightly damp towel before touching the model; a loaded brush floods detail or leaves a raised blob.
loading-the-brush.brush tip: Roll it on a damp towel to reform the point, then test on your thumb or a spare base for tiny dots and fine lines.
loading-the-brush.wipe excess paint: Roll and drag the brush on a slightly damp paper towel or tissue, holding it there longer to wick off more.
loading-the-brush.damp brush: Rinse and blot it so it is damp, not wet, before loading, and keep your wiping towel damp too.
loading-the-brush.brush keeps flicking paint: If it drags or bends and you press, stop, rinse, reload and test again; small brushes dry quickly in a warm room.

matching-squad-markings.squad markings: Decide and write down the system, mark the same spot on every model, and paint each step across the squad in turn.
matching-squad-markings.unit numbers on shoulder pads: Mark the spot on each pad, build each digit from plain straight strokes, tidy with the background colour, and keep digits the same size.
matching-squad-markings.make markings match across a squad: Paint them as a batch, base shape on all, then outline, then highlight, and mix plenty of each colour in a sealed bottle.
matching-squad-markings.paint numbers on every model: Build each digit from plain straight strokes, keep every digit the same height and width, and tidy edges with the background.
matching-squad-markings.leader helmet stripe: Write it into the squad's marking system first, such as a stripe on the leader's helmet, then paint it with the batch.
matching-squad-markings.keep markings in the same place: Mark the same spot on every model with a light pencil dot or a dot of thinned paint before painting.
matching-squad-markings.consistent squad identification: Decide the system first, write it down, and paint every step on every model in turn so colours and line weight match.
matching-squad-markings.how to paint unit markings: Plan the system, mark each spot, then do base shape, outline and highlight on every model in turn.
matching-squad-markings.markings look different on each model: Paint them as a batch, step by step on every model, from one mixed colour, then line the squad up and fix any that stand out.
matching-squad-markings.plan squad colours and symbols: Write the system down first, what goes where and what changes per model, such as a number on the left shoulder.

metallic-undercoats.what primer under metallics: A smooth one, ideally satin under metal areas; black suits thin silver and a brown suits gold, bronze and copper.
metallic-undercoats.metallic looks dull: Metallics need a smooth surface; a very matt primer scatters light. Expect the first coat to look dull until the dark is hidden.
metallic-undercoats.undercoat for gold: A brown, such as a mid brown, makes gold look richer and cover in fewer coats; yellow under it looks poor.
metallic-undercoats.black under silver: For thin coats, silver looks most like silver over black; a glossy black looks noticeably shinier than a flat one.
metallic-undercoats.brown under copper: Yes, a reddish brown under copper makes it look richer and cover in fewer coats.
metallic-undercoats.metallic paint not shiny: Use a smooth, satin or glossy undercoat, since matt primer scatters light, and do not over thin, which makes flakes blotchy.
metallic-undercoats.base for metallic paint: Black under silver, a brown under gold and bronze, and a reddish brown under copper; under two solid coats any primer is fine.
metallic-undercoats.red under gold: A brown such as a mid brown suits gold, and a reddish brown suits copper; yellow under most metals looks poor.
metallic-undercoats.gloss primer under metal: A satin primer under metal helps, and a glossy black under a thin metal coat looks noticeably shinier than flat black.
metallic-undercoats.metal shows mould lines: Metal shows every mould line and scratch, so clean the parts up carefully before priming.

modelled-battle-damage.bullet holes: Drill shallow craters with small bits in a hand drill, in a few sizes, then paint them thinned black inside with a chip colour under the rim.
modelled-battle-damage.battle damage modelling: Before priming, drill shallow holes, carve pits with a twisted knife tip, nibble edges with clippers and tear thin plastic back.
modelled-battle-damage.drill holes in armour: Use small bits in a hand drill in a few sizes for different weapons; a short row reads as a burst of fire.
modelled-battle-damage.cracks in armour: Press a knife tip in and twist to carve a shallow pit, then scribe a few short lines out from it in an uneven star.
modelled-battle-damage.damaged vehicle: One to three big hits is usually plenty: drill or carve them, bend mudguards with smooth plier jaws, and damage one side more.
modelled-battle-damage.carve damage: Twist a knife tip into the armour for a shallow pit, scribe short uneven lines from it, and brush thin plastic glue over to melt shavings.
modelled-battle-damage.torn metal: Make lots of small nibbles with clippers inside a hatch, then bend and tear part of it back.
modelled-battle-damage.make it look shot up: Drill shallow holes in a short row, carve a few pits, and paint them black inside with a chip colour and a grey centre.
modelled-battle-damage.blast marks: After painting a hole, add a fine armour highlight round its outer edge and stipple a little black around it for scorching.
modelled-battle-damage.damaged armour plates: Drill or carve a few hits, take small bites from the edges with clippers, and scar the surface with a ball burr where shots did not punch through.

mouths-and-tongues.mouth: Base it light grey, tint with a purple pink one coat paint, re highlight with grey, then glaze the purple pink back over.
mouths-and-tongues.tongue: Light grey base, purple pink one coat tint, grey on the tip and ridges, a thin glaze back over, and gloss varnish to look wet.
mouths-and-tongues.gums: Base them light grey with the teeth, tint with a purple pink one coat paint, highlight the ridges grey, and glaze back over.
mouths-and-tongues.inside of the mouth: Tint a pale grey base with purple pink, and keep the back of the throat darkest with a touch of deep red or purple.
mouths-and-tongues.monster mouth: Grey base, purple pink tint, grey highlights on ridges and bumps, a thin glaze back, a dark throat and gloss on the tongue.
mouths-and-tongues.teeth and gums: Base the gums light grey at the same time as the teeth, then tint the gums with a purple pink one coat paint.
mouths-and-tongues.wet looking mouth: A dab of gloss varnish on the tongue makes it look wet, and a single pale pink dot where it is wettest.
mouths-and-tongues.open mouth roaring: Keep the back of the throat darkest, with a touch of deep red or purple, so the mouth has depth, and gloss the tongue.
mouths-and-tongues.how to paint a mouth: Light grey base, purple pink one coat tint, grey highlights on tip and ridges, a glaze back over, darkest at the throat.
mouths-and-tongues.tongue colour: A purple pink over light grey, or over a dark base, deep red then bright pink and light pink on top.

nmm-gold.nmm gold: Place light as for steel, carry the colour in rich browns and ochres through the midtones, keep shadows dark and edges pale yellow.
nmm-gold.non metallic metal gold: Use the same light rules as steel but run the midtones through browns, ochres and olive greens, ending in pale yellow edges.
nmm-gold.how do i paint nmm gold: Quick version: dirty yellow base, thinned brown wash in the hollows, then three smaller highlights with white and a little blue.
nmm-gold.nmm bronze: Mix steps from dark brown through orange to a pale peach, placing the light exactly as for steel.
nmm-gold.nmm copper: Mix steps from dark brown through orange to a pale peach; a few warm gold accents nearby make it read as a different metal.
nmm-gold.gold without metallics: Paint it with steel's light placement, carrying the colour in browns, ochres and olive greens, with pale yellow edges and dots.
nmm-gold.warm gold or cool gold: Warm runs from deep red brown through warm yellow brown to warm yellow; cool runs from black through a muted yellow.
nmm-gold.non metallic gold reflections: Add smaller secondary reflections split from the main shine by shadow, glaze them thin orange, and set a small dark spot before each ends.
nmm-gold.gold looks yellow not gold: A very thin blue or green glaze before the last highlights calms it, and glaze a yellow brown through the middle.
nmm-gold.painted gold reflections: With each brighter mix, highlight edges, then the main reflection, then detail tips, following each curve with your strokes.

oil-streaking.oil streaks: Over gloss, dab neat oil where grime gathers, then pull it straight down with a brush barely damp with spirit, dense at the top and fading.
oil-streaking.weathering with oil paints: Work over gloss, dab small amounts of oil on rivets, recesses and panel tops, and pull them into streaks with a lightly damp brush.
oil-streaking.grime streaks on a tank: Dab dark brown oil along panel tops and under rivets and chips, pull it down with a damp brush, and soften the edges with a dry one.
oil-streaking.how do i make streaks run down armour: Dab neat oil at the top, press a brush with a little spirit on it gently into the dab and pull straight down so it fades lower.
oil-streaking.rust staining with oils: Once the first streaks are dry, add an orange brown as fresher rust, especially round pistons, joints and moving parts.
oil-streaking.dirty vehicle look: Oil streaks from rivets, recesses and panel tops, fresher orange brown rust round joints, and blended brown or red oil round hatches.
oil-streaking.oils over gloss varnish: Yes, gloss lets the oil move easily and protects the paint if you need to wipe back with a bud and a little thinner.
oil-streaking.rain marks on a hull: Dot oil a shade lighter and a shade darker than the panel, then pull them down with a just damp flat brush into soft vertical streaks.
oil-streaking.oil paint drying too slow: Leave the oils on card for a while first to draw out excess oil, so they dry faster and handle better.
oil-streaking.staining under rivets: Dab a little neat dark brown oil on each rivet, then pull it straight down with a barely damp brush so it fades lower down.

osl-planning.osl: Decide where the glow lands before painting, keep those areas dark, test with a small coloured light, then block it in roughly first.
osl-planning.object source lighting: Only surfaces facing the source get light; plan it with a small coloured torch, keep a dark scheme, and fade the glow outwards.
osl-planning.how do i plan a glow: Hold a small coloured torch where the glowing object is in a dim room and photograph which surfaces catch the light.
osl-planning.light source on a model: Only surfaces facing the source catch it; hold the model so the source lines up with your eye, and light the surfaces you see.
osl-planning.lantern glow: Test with a small torch at the lantern, keep nearby areas dark, then paint bright only where light hits hardest and fade outwards.
osl-planning.osl tips for beginners: Use a dark overall scheme, a base that contrasts with the light, test with a small torch, and block it in roughly before smoothing.
osl-planning.where does the glow go: Only on surfaces facing the source; the far side stays in shadow, and one part can shade another, such as an arm over the chest.
osl-planning.osl lamp: Light only the surfaces facing the lamp, keep a dark band between top lit areas and the glow, and fade weaker mixes outwards.
osl-planning.osl looks wrong: Tone down the top light and keep a dark band before the glow, then hold the model away, squint, and adjust with shadow glazes.
osl-planning.test glow with a small light: Hold a small coloured torch or light strip at the source in a dim room and take photos to see what it lights and how far.

paint-dries-darker.paint dries darker: Acrylics usually dry a little darker and duller than they look wet, so judge a colour only once it is fully dry.
paint-dries-darker.colour changes when dry: Acrylic darkens and dulls slightly as it dries, most of all whites and pale colours, so let each layer dry before judging.
paint-dries-darker.why does paint look different dry: Acrylic darkens and dulls slightly as it dries, and thinned paint looks solid wet but dries far more see through.
paint-dries-darker.highlight looks too bright wet: It often ends up just right once dry; let it dry fully and check with fresh eyes before changing it.
paint-dries-darker.paint dries duller: Acrylic dulls and darkens slightly as it dries; judge only when dry, and test new paints on a spare piece first.
paint-dries-darker.white dries grey: White and pale colours show the drying shift most; let it dry fully and check again the next day before adding more.
paint-dries-darker.mixed colour doesn't match dry: Acrylic dries a little darker and duller than it looks wet; test the mix on a spare piece and judge it once dry.
paint-dries-darker.paint darker after drying: That is normal for acrylic; if it ends up too bright instead, a thin glaze of a darker version knocks it back.
paint-dries-darker.acrylic colour shift: Acrylics dry slightly darker and duller, whites most; thinned paint, red especially, dries far more see through.
paint-dries-darker.wet vs dry paint: Wet paint looks lighter, brighter and more solid than it dries, so let each layer dry fully before deciding on another coat.

paint-transparency.is this paint see through: Spread a little thinly over black: if the black still shows, it is transparent, which is a property, not a fault.
paint-transparency.paint coverage test: Paint a black and white test strip, spread the paint thinly over both, and see if the black shows through.
paint-transparency.which of my paints cover well: Test each over a black stripe on a white tile; those that hide the black are opaque, and paints with a lot of white cover well.
paint-transparency.opaque or transparent paint: Opaque suits early coats, clean mixes and crisp final dots; transparent suits glazing and subtle blends over a light undercoat.
paint-transparency.test strip over black and white: Spread paint thinly over the black to check coverage, and over the white to see if it glows, which is ideal for glazing.
paint-transparency.why does this colour need five coats: Clean, pure colours cover poorly; weak or transparent paints need more thin coats, each left to dry first.
paint-transparency.transparent colours for glazing: Brush a little over white: one that glows bright like a highlighter pen is ideal for glazing over a light undercoat.
paint-transparency.paint lets primer show through: It is a transparent paint; give it more thin coats, letting each dry, rather than one thick coat that softens detail.
paint-transparency.check paint opacity: Spread it thinly over a stripe of black on a white tile; if the black shows, the paint is transparent.
paint-transparency.how well does a paint cover: Test it thinly over black and white side by side; paints with a lot of white cover well, clean pure colours poorly.

painting-black-cloth.black cloth: Base off black, shade with a dark brown wash, then build brownish greys gradually on the crease tops, covering less each time.
painting-black-cloth.charcoal cloth: Off black base, a brown wash, then highlights starting at two parts black to one dark or brownish grey, adding grey each stage.
painting-black-cloth.black robes: Base off black, wash dark brown, layer brownish greys up the folds, and finish with a sharper grey on hems and fold tops.
painting-black-cloth.highlight black cloth: Start with two parts black to one brownish grey on raised folds, add more grey each stage, and end with a sparing pale blue grey.
painting-black-cloth.black coat: Off black base, dark brown wash, gradual grey highlights on the folds, and a mid or pale blue grey only on hems and shoulders.
painting-black-cloth.black clothing: Base an off black so it still reads as black, shade dark brown, and build greys gradually so transitions stay soft.
painting-black-cloth.black uniform: Off black, a dark brown wash for a worn look, gradual brownish grey highlights, kept very matt, plus an accent colour.
painting-black-cloth.off black: Base in off black rather than pure black; it still reads as black but leaves room for darker shading.
painting-black-cloth.dark cloth: Base off black, shade with brown, then build brownish greys on crease tops, covering smaller areas with each lighter mix.
painting-black-cloth.black cloak looks grey: Glaze thin black over the cloth and re touch only the top highlights, keeping the brightest grey to hems and crisp fold tops.

painting-crystals.crystals: Base a deep dark version of the colour, keep each facet dark at the top and bright at the bottom, glaze it smooth, then add fine scratches and dots.
painting-crystals.how do i paint crystals: Dark at the top of each facet, bright at the bottom, every dark next to a light, smoothed with thin glazes and edged pale blue white.
painting-crystals.gems: See: this entry covers crystals, dark at the top of each facet and bright at the bottom, with a tiny bright dot in shadow.
painting-crystals.magic crystal: Over a light undercoat, base a deep colour, light the bottom of each facet, glaze smooth, then glaze thin fluorescent colour over it.
painting-crystals.ice crystals: Base a deep dark version of the colour over a light undercoat, keep facets dark at top and bright at bottom, and edge in pale blue white.
painting-crystals.crystal looks flat: Put every dark area next to a light one, let facets facing the light go almost white, and edge every ridge with the side of the brush.
painting-crystals.glowing crystals: Use a light undercoat, as many greens and blues will not glow over black, then glaze heavily thinned fluorescent colour over it all.
painting-crystals.transparent crystal effect: Reverse normal lighting: dark at the top of each facet and bright at the bottom, like light passing through.
painting-crystals.gemstone: See: this entry covers crystals; each facet goes dark at the top, bright at the bottom, with a tiny gloss white dot in shadow.
painting-crystals.crystal faceting: Each facet is dark at the top and bright at the bottom, every dark area beside a light one, with a thin pale edge on every ridge.

painting-fur.painting fur: Plan the light first, drybrush or wash the texture, then build tufts with lines or blends, darker underneath and on the lower legs.
painting-fur.fur looks fake: Do not take every tuft to the brightest colour; use warm khaki or bone tones rather than plain light grey, and follow how the hair grows.
painting-fur.wolf fur: Over dark brown, drybrush mid brown, then lighter brown, then flick a pale bone onto the most raised tips, darker underneath.
painting-fur.how to paint animal fur: Treat it as a few big shapes lit from above, drybrush or line the texture, and keep chest, belly and lower legs duller.
painting-fur.fur texture with lines: Use thin paint and a pointed brush, start moving before the tip lands, flick off so strokes taper, and follow the hair's growth.
painting-fur.drybrush fur: Over dark brown, drybrush mid brown lightly all over, a lighter brown more lightly, then a pale colour on the most raised tips.
painting-fur.beast hide fur: Plan big light shapes, drybrush browns up to a warm bone on raised tips, and keep chest, under the arms and lower legs darker.
painting-fur.fur cloak trim: A quick grey pelt: grey at the edges and tan brown in the middle, a very thin black wash, then a pale blue grey drybrush.
painting-fur.werewolf fur colours: A dark brown base drybrushed mid and lighter brown with warm khaki or bone tips, or dark brown lines with warm bone added.
painting-fur.fur looks fuzzy and messy: Base slowly with slightly thinner paint so it settles in the grooves, and soften harsh steps with a glaze of the previous colour.

painting-in-sub-assemblies.sub assemblies: Leave parts that block your brush unglued, paint them on holders, then assemble, scrape the contact points and tidy the joins.
painting-in-sub-assemblies.paint before gluing: Yes for parts that block the brush, such as shields, riders or sealed in pilots; glue where detail flows across a join.
painting-in-sub-assemblies.assemble after painting: Scrape paint and old glue off the contact points first, and use super glue where paint remains, as plastic glue needs bare plastic.
painting-in-sub-assemblies.hard to reach areas: Dry fit first and ask if you could reach every visible detail once glued; leave the blocking parts off and paint them separately.
painting-in-sub-assemblies.rider and mount separate: Yes, riders on mounts are a common blocker; paint the rider on a short pin pushed into a cork, then join them.
painting-in-sub-assemblies.shield across chest: Leave it off, paint it on a handle, then scrape the contact point clean and glue it on at the end.
painting-in-sub-assemblies.paint in parts: Split into a few groups, such as body with backpack, arms with weapons and the head, as too many loose bits stops models getting finished.
painting-in-sub-assemblies.should i glue before painting: For a quick batch, build it whole with only the head or rider loose; for a model painted to your best, split it.
painting-in-sub-assemblies.cant reach behind the shield: Leave the shield unglued, paint it on a holder, and glue it on after painting with super glue where paint remains.
painting-in-sub-assemblies.paint it in pieces: Keep only blocking parts loose, fix them to handles with a dot of super glue, then assemble and shade the new joins with a glaze.

painting-orange.how do i paint orange: Start from a deeper orange over white or pale primer, highlight by mixing in yellow, and finish the highest points in pure yellow.
painting-orange.orange looks pastel when i highlight it: White makes orange pastel and dull; highlight by mixing in yellow instead.
painting-orange.highlighting orange: Mix an in between orange yellow first for a small step, then finish the highest points in pure yellow.
painting-orange.orange goes dull when i add white: Highlight with yellow instead of white, and only add a little white to the yellow at the end on hard or metallic looking parts.
painting-orange.bright orange armour: Deeper orange over white primer, an orange yellow layer, pure yellow on the top points, and a touch of white in the yellow for shine.
painting-orange.what colour do i highlight orange with: Yellow: an in between orange yellow first, then pure yellow on the highest points.
painting-orange.orange cloak: Base a deeper orange over pale primer, layer an orange yellow, then pure yellow on the highest folds.
painting-orange.keep orange vibrant: Highlight towards yellow rather than white, and prime white or pale, as orange loses punch over dark.
painting-orange.orange layers look chalky: That is white in the mix; highlight by mixing yellow into the orange instead.
painting-orange.flame orange plates: Lay a one coat orange mixed with an ordinary orange over white primer, then highlight up through orange yellow to pure yellow.

painting-scars.scars: On finished skin, run thin dark red into the cut, darken its deepest part, and highlight the raised edges with a pale pinkish skin tone.
painting-scars.how to paint a scar: Thin dark red in the cut, a touch of black in the deepest part, and pale, slightly pink skin on the raised lips either side.
painting-scars.battle scar on face: Finish the face first, paint the cut dark red and darker in its depth, highlight the lips pale pink, and keep skin highlights around it.
painting-scars.scar tissue: Highlight the raised lips either side of the cut with a paler skin tone with a little pink; on a big scar the lower lip may be enough.
painting-scars.facial scar: Dark red into the cut, darkened with black in the deepest part, pale pinkish raised edges, and a faint red glaze if it is fresh.
painting-scars.pink scar edges: Use a paler skin tone with a little pink in it on the raised lips either side of the cut.
painting-scars.sculpted scar: Run very thin dark red into the cut, then red with black in its deepest part, and highlight the raised lips pale pink.
painting-scars.freehand scar: Paint a thin narrow diamond of mid skin with a little pinkish red, then a fine pale line along its centre.
painting-scars.scar across the eye: Leave the pupil off and paint the eye plain off white so it looks blinded.
painting-scars.realistic scar: Keep the skin highlights around it, add a dark groove and pale pinkish edges, and a faint red glaze only if it is fresh.

painting-stitching.stitches: Run thinned black or dark brown around them, touch each stitch with a sandy khaki or bone, then dot the top with that colour plus white.
painting-stitching.stitching on leather: Outline the stitches in thinned dark brown or black, dab each with light khaki or bone, then add a tiny paler dot on top.
painting-stitching.how to paint stitching: Dark line around the stitches, a sandy light colour touched onto each with the tip, then a tiny highlight with white added.
painting-stitching.seams on a coat: Run a thinned dark line around the stitches to separate them, then dab each stitch with a light sandy colour.
painting-stitching.stitched leather belt: Outline the stitches thinned black or dark brown, tap each with bone, and dot the tops with bone plus white.
painting-stitching.sewn patches on clothes: Separate the stitches with a dark line, dab each in a light khaki or bone colour, and highlight their tops with a little white added.
painting-stitching.stitches on a teddy bear or doll: Where none are sculpted, paint a dark seam line, short dark bars across it with end dots, then a thin pale line down each bar.
painting-stitching.stitches look messy: Touch each stitch with the brush tip rather than dragging a line, and tidy smudges with the dark line colour once dry.
painting-stitching.highlight stitches: Add white to the sandy stitch colour and dot the top of each stitch, along with your other final highlights.
painting-stitching.thread on cloth: Paint a dark line around the thread, a light sandy or bone colour on each stitch, and a tiny paler dot on top.

painting-verdigris.verdigris: Over finished metal, wash thinned jade green into recesses, add brighter turquoise on part of it, then pale blue green in the deepest spots.
painting-verdigris.green patina on bronze: Thin a deep jade green about four parts water to one, touch it into recesses, then build brighter turquoise and pale blue green.
painting-verdigris.how do i paint verdigris: Wash thinned mid green into the recesses, go over part of it in brighter turquoise, and dab pale blue green into the deepest spots.
painting-verdigris.copper corrosion: Copper turns blue green; even an ultra thin turquoise glaze in the deepest shadows makes it read as copper.
painting-verdigris.brass turning green: Wash a dark brown black over the brass, then build patchy green and turquoise round rivets, dents and recesses where water sits.
painting-verdigris.turquoise crust on old metal: Dab pale blue green into the deepest spots, with a touch of light flesh tone mixed in for a chalky crust.
painting-verdigris.oxidised bronze statue: Stipple greens from deep to pale over smaller areas each time, then pull thin pale streaks down from cracks as runoff.
painting-verdigris.aged copper look: Wash thinned green into the recesses, add patchy turquoise, and re brighten raised details so they stand clear of the green.
painting-verdigris.weathered bronze armour: Patchy green and turquoise thickest round rivets and recesses, kept off spots that would be rubbed clean, with bright metal edges.
painting-verdigris.verdigis on a bell: Build patchy green to turquoise to pale blue green where water would sit, and pull thin pale runoff streaks down, working top to bottom.

panel-lining.panel lining: Over gloss varnish, touch a dark wash, ink or thinned one coat paint into the panel lines and let it run along them.
panel-lining.panel lines on a tank: Gloss first, run an enamel or oil wash into the lines and round rivets, then clean the excess with a brush damp with white spirit.
panel-lining.how do i do panel lines: Gloss varnish first, then touch a lightly loaded brush of dark wash into the groove and let it run; keep the model level.
panel-lining.pin wash: Over varnish, run an enamel wash into recesses and round rivets, leave it 30 to 60 minutes, then clean up with a spirit damp brush.
panel-lining.dark lines in vehicle panels: Use ink or a thinned one coat paint, which stay dark when thin, flowed along the groove over a gloss coat.
panel-lining.panel line wash spreads everywhere: Gloss first, or brush clean water into the line so the groove stays wet, then touch the wash in lightly rather than dragging.
panel-lining.ink in the panel gaps: Ink holds a fine point and stays dark; touch it into the gap with a lightly loaded brush and let it run along.
panel-lining.plates dont stand apart: Line the gaps with a dark wash or ink, then add edge highlights; a bright edge looks brighter next to a dark line.
panel-lining.thinned black goes chalky in lines: Thinned black acrylic tends to come out grey; use ink or a thinned one coat paint, which stay dark when thin.
panel-lining.panel lining a spaceship: Gloss varnish, then a dark wash tinted with the base colour run into each line, done before the edge highlights.

pinning-to-bases.pinning: Drill the feet, push in short pins to mark the base, drill the marks, then glue longer pins into the feet with thick super glue.
pinning-to-bases.pin model to base: Mark the base by pressing the model on with short pins in the feet, drill the marks, and glue longer pins into the feet only.
pinning-to-bases.heavy model falls off base: Heavy metal and large models need pins, or the joint snaps when handled; glue pins into the feet and drill the base to match.
pinning-to-bases.metal model snaps off base: Pin it: drill each foot slowly and straight, glue in pins with thick super glue, and drill matching holes in the base.
pinning-to-bases.how to pin feet: Start a hole under the foot with a knife tip, check the angle against the leg, then drill slowly and straight.
pinning-to-bases.pin vice for bases: Start each hole with a knife tip, check the angle against the leg, then drill slowly and straight into the foot.
pinning-to-bases.remove cast on base: Cut it away carefully with pliers, knife and file, without nicking the feet.
pinning-to-bases.model keeps breaking off its base: Pin it, using thicker wire for a model handled a lot, and let the glue cure fully before handling.
pinning-to-bases.brass rod into the feet: Glue the pins into the feet only with thick super glue; thicker wire lets you bend the model slightly to adjust the angle.
pinning-to-bases.attach model to a scenic base: Dab paint on each foot and press it in place to mark the spots, then pin, fill gaps with epoxy putty and carve it to match.

porcelain-and-doll-faces.porcelain face: Base a pale off white, keep shadows soft, light and cool, paint flat doll features, add a crack or two, and gloss only the face and hands.
porcelain-and-doll-faces.doll face: Pale off white skin with soft cool shadows, round rosy cheek glazes, thin dark lashes, small deep rose lips and glossy glassy eyes.
porcelain-and-doll-faces.how do i paint a porcelain mask: Base pale off white, shade only softly in pale blue grey, add a wandering dark grey crack with a pale edge, then gloss it.
porcelain-and-doll-faces.cracked porcelain: Paint a thin dark grey line that wanders and branches, with a fine pale line along one side as if light catches the broken edge.
porcelain-and-doll-faces.china doll look: Very little shading, pale off white skin, flat stylised features with rosy cheeks, and gloss on the face and hands only.
porcelain-and-doll-faces.creepy doll miniature: Pale glossy porcelain skin, slightly large glassy eyes, flat painted features, and cracks or a dull chipped patch to sell the material.
porcelain-and-doll-faces.glossy white face: Base pale off white with soft cool shadows, then gloss varnish the face and hands only, keeping clothes and hair matt.
porcelain-and-doll-faces.ceramic face: Pale off white with soft cool blue grey shadows; for a chip, paint a matt warm off white patch outlined in a fine dark line.
porcelain-and-doll-faces.pale smooth face with no shading: Keep shadow to the eye sockets, under the nose and along the jaw, in a soft pale blue grey blended with thin glazes.
porcelain-and-doll-faces.painted on doll eyes: Paint them a little large: iris, black pupil and a white dot, then gloss the eye alone so it looks like glass.

progress-photo-records.progress photos: Photograph every model the same way each time, same spot, lamps, background and distance, at each stage of painting.
progress-photo-records.how to photograph my models: Use a plain grey or white background, the same lamps and distance, filters off, and tap and hold to lock focus and brightness.
