progress-photo-records.before and after pictures: Take a quick photo at each stage, built, primed, base coats, shading, highlights, base done, with the same setup every time.
progress-photo-records.track my painting improvement: Every few months, put a new model next to an old one, on the desk and in a photo side by side.
progress-photo-records.consistent photo setup: Mark camera and model positions with tape, keep the same lamps and background, and shoot front, three quarter and back in order.
progress-photo-records.photos look different every time: Use the same spot, lamps, background and distance, turn off filters, and lock focus and brightness by tapping and holding.
progress-photo-records.same lighting for photos: Use the same lamps in the same spot every time, and mark the camera and model positions with tape on the desk.
progress-photo-records.compare old and new models: Put them side by side on the desk and in a photo every few months, and keep a few early models as they are.
progress-photo-records.record my progress: Photograph each stage the same way, name files by date and model, keep a folder per model or month, and back them up off the phone.
progress-photo-records.grey background for mini photos: Use the same plain grey or white background every time so old and new photos compare fairly.

raised-ground-on-bases.uneven ground: Glue the model a little high on a trimmed support, then fill round it with glue and fine earth, adding a second layer near the feet.
raised-ground-on-bases.raise model on base: Trim the moulded support and glue it slightly high, or glue flat slate or cork under the soles for a bigger lift.
raised-ground-on-bases.model on a slope: Dry fit slate under it to find an angle where every foot touches, then press warmed epoxy putty where the feet need raising.
raised-ground-on-bases.base with height: Glue flat slate or cork under the soles, fix it to the base so the feet sit properly, then build rough ground up round it.
raised-ground-on-bases.built up ground: Glue and sprinkle fine earth round the model in two layers, with loose stones settling at the bottom of any slope.
raised-ground-on-bases.keep the moulded support: Yes, keep part of it under thin push fit legs, cut it down, glue the model slightly high and hide it with earth.
raised-ground-on-bases.thin legs hard to pin: Keep part of the moulded support under the feet, glue the model slightly high, and build ground up to hide it.
raised-ground-on-bases.model sinking into base: Glue it slightly above the base on its trimmed support or on slate or cork, then build the ground up round the feet.
raised-ground-on-bases.rocky raised base: Glue flat slate or cork under the soles, push slate chips into warmed putty at random, and seal with spray varnish once dry.
raised-ground-on-bases.glue model higher: Cut the support down and glue the model slightly above the base surface, then fill round it with glue and fine earth.

repainting-toys-and-figures.repainting toys: Clean it well, prime thinly over the old paint with a water based primer, then rebuild colour in two or three thin coats.
repainting-toys-and-figures.repaint an action figure: Wash it in warm soapy water, brush one or two thin primer coats over the factory paint, and repaint, starting with the face.
repainting-toys-and-figures.prepainted figure looks cheap: Factory paint is often thick and fills detail; clean it, prime thinly over it, and repaint the face and head first.
repainting-toys-and-figures.how do i repaint a board game figure: Wash off oils, brush thin water based surface primer over the factory paint, then build colour in thin coats.
repainting-toys-and-figures.repaint a statue: Clean it, prime thinly over the existing paint rather than stripping, and rebuild colour in thin, water thinned acrylic coats.
repainting-toys-and-figures.factory paint hides detail: Factory paint is often thick; a careful repaint in thin coats over a thin primer can bring the sculpt back.
repainting-toys-and-figures.can i prime over existing paint: Yes, priming over factory paint is usually better than stripping, which is slow and can pit soft plastic and vinyl.
repainting-toys-and-figures.repaint a collectible figure: Gather several reference pictures, clean it well, prime thinly over the old paint, and repaint in thin coats.
repainting-toys-and-figures.thick factory paint: Prime over it thinly rather than stripping; sanding is only needed if you want a model grade surface.
repainting-toys-and-figures.repaint vinyl figure: Prime thinly over the paint, as harsh solvents can pit vinyl; pressed together vinyl parts pull apart with firm, steady force.

reusing-old-sprue.leftover sprue: It becomes stretched rod, spikes, girders, terrain bits, filler and helpers like painting handles, since it is the same plastic as the kit.
reusing-old-sprue.what to do with spare sprue: Make cables, spikes, walls, girders, tank traps, pipes, painting handles, brush racks, or dissolve it in plastic glue as filler.
reusing-old-sprue.sprue as plastic rod: It glues, carves, sands and primes like any kit part; stretch it over a low flame for thin rod, cables or aerials.
reusing-old-sprue.make spikes from sprue: Slice long thin triangles off a rod and scrape them smooth for quick spikes on armour or hulls.
reusing-old-sprue.stretched sprue: Turn a straight length above a candle, never in it, until soft, pull the ends apart gently, and lay it flat to cool.
reusing-old-sprue.sprue as gap filler: Dissolve chopped sprue in plastic glue to make a filler of the same plastic as the model, with good airflow.
reusing-old-sprue.terrain bits from sprue: Glue lengths into low walls, fences and girders, cross them into tank traps, and cut round sections into pipes.
reusing-old-sprue.recycle plastic frame: Use it as rod, spikes, terrain, filler, painting handles or a practice panel; it glues with plastic glue like any part.
reusing-old-sprue.girders from sprue: Glue long straight lengths behind card walls as girders, or into low walls and fences.
reusing-old-sprue.dont throw away sprue: Keep a box of offcuts: long straight lengths, round sections and junctions all have uses as rod, terrain and helpers.

sculpting-anatomy.sculpting proportions: Measure the whole figure from one unit, the head width, about five eye widths, and check landmarks after every pose change.
sculpting-anatomy.how many heads tall is a figure: The classic eight heads is idealised; most people are nearer seven, and counting heads only works for a figure standing straight.
sculpting-anatomy.sculpt a human figure: Use the head width as a unit along each limb, block the skull as a ball with the face added, and build muscles from small putty pieces.
sculpting-anatomy.face proportions for sculpting: Split the face from hairline to chin into thirds; eye sockets sit just under the top line and the mouth halfway down the lower third.
sculpting-anatomy.sculpting muscles: Build them from small putty pieces shaped like each muscle, placed from reference, blended with rubber tipped shapers.
sculpting-anatomy.anatomy for sculptors: Learn a few measurements by heart, based on head width, so anatomy runs like a checklist and you can focus on pose.
sculpting-anatomy.my sculpt looks wrong: Check landmarks against the head width unit, such as two units for the upper arm and three for the thigh, after every pose change.
sculpting-anatomy.where do the eyes go on a sculpted head: Press the sockets in just under the top line when the face is split into thirds, starting large as smoothing shrinks them.
sculpting-anatomy.heroic scale proportions: See: this entry measures by head width rather than counting heads, and notes the classic eight heads is idealised.
sculpting-anatomy.body measurements for sculpting: Using the head width as a unit: upper arm two units, forearm two, thigh three to mid knee, shin three, foot half a unit tall.

shading-metallics.shading metallics: Darken with washes, ink glazes or dark paint mixed into the metal, then re layer the original metallic on raised parts.
shading-metallics.how do i shade metal: A wash in the recesses on textured metal, or dark paint mixed into the metallic blended wet on smooth plates, then shine back on top.
shading-metallics.washing metallic paint: Washes suit textured metal like mail; on large smooth plates they bead or dry patchy, so thin matt paint works better there.
shading-metallics.ink on metallic: Thin dark ink can go into the deepest corners after mixing dark paint into the metallic for the shadows.
shading-metallics.wash beading on metal: On smooth plates and blades washes bead; use thin matt paint, or mix dark paint into the metallic and blend while wet.
shading-metallics.darken silver: Mix black or a dark paint into the silver, up to half and half, for the shadows; blue black suits steel.
shading-metallics.shading gold: Use warm brown shades, or a little copper in the gold, then a thin purple only in the deepest recesses after the wash.
shading-metallics.metal looks flat: Re layer the original metallic slightly thinned on raised parts, then one sharp edge highlight of bright silver.
shading-metallics.wash went patchy on a sword blade: Washes dry patchy on smooth blades; use thin matt paint, or brush a wash on and scrub it off the raised areas while wet.
shading-metallics.shade metallic armour: Wash recesses or blend dark mixed into the metallic, keep shadows on the same side of every shape, then bright silver edges.

skill-roadmap.what should i learn next: Add one new skill per model, moving on when your current stage feels routine, such as edge highlights, then glazing, then wet blending.
skill-roadmap.skill progression: Tidy base coats, wash and drybrush; then layered and edge highlights; then glazing and value; then wet blending; then display work.
skill-roadmap.how do i get better at painting: Add one new skill per model, try it on one area or a test model first, and move on when the current stage feels routine.
skill-roadmap.learning path for painting: Base coat, wash and drybrush first; then highlights and faces; then glazing and colour schemes; then wet blending; then display work.
skill-roadmap.next technique to learn: Move on when the current stage feels routine, not perfect, and try one new skill per model on one area first.
skill-roadmap.stuck at tabletop standard: Work on control: two or three highlight steps, glazing to soften them, one accent colour, and checking value from arm's length.
skill-roadmap.beginner to advanced: Tidy and finished first, then basic highlights, then control with glazing, then depth with wet blending, then display work.
skill-roadmap.what order to learn skills: Prep, priming, thinning and base coats, then highlights, then glazing, then wet blending and freehand, then display techniques.
skill-roadmap.how to improve each model: Add one new skill per model and try it on one area first; a test model or spare part keeps mistakes off the good figure.
skill-roadmap.plateaued at painting: Pick the next stage's skill, such as glazing or wet blending, and add just one per model; most people hop between stages.

soften-harsh-transitions.stripy blend: Paint a halfway mix over the join, then thin passes of the darker colour pulled from the line into the shadow, letting each dry.
soften-harsh-transitions.stepped blend: Mix the two colours half and half and paint that first, then glaze thin passes of the darker colour over the line several times.
soften-harsh-transitions.harsh transitions: Thin the darker colour to a tint, start just over the line and pull into the shadow, let it dry, repeat, then do the same with the lighter.
soften-harsh-transitions.my layers are visible: Some steps are normal; glaze the midtone thinly over the whole area to restore saturation and mask many lines.
soften-harsh-transitions.blend looks stripy: Glaze the main colour once over the whole area, then again where the steps meet, then sharpen the brightest point.
soften-harsh-transitions.fix stepped layering: Add a halfway mix over each step, then glaze thin passes of the darker colour over the line, letting each dry fully.
soften-harsh-transitions.mix a halfway colour: If a jump looks stark, mix the two colours half and half and paint that before the next step.
soften-harsh-transitions.glaze to smooth a blend: Thin with water, glaze medium or matt varnish, take almost all off the brush, and pull from just over the line into the shadow.
soften-harsh-transitions.banding in my highlights: Glaze the main colour over the whole area, then where steps meet; over highlight slightly first, as the glaze tones it down.
soften-harsh-transitions.how to make transitions smoother: Use halfway mixes and thin glazes pulled across the line, let each dry, or stipple the lighter colour over the border.

sponging-texture.sponging: Dab paint with a scrap of foam, loaded lightly and mostly dabbed off on a towel, for mottled skin, texture, quick metal or chips.
sponging-texture.sponge weathering: Sponge browns and oranges over metal for rust, or dab the sponge on armour edges for chips.
sponging-texture.how do i sponge paint: Load a little slightly thinned paint, dab most of it off on a towel, then dab gently; raised parts pick up more.
sponging-texture.foam chipping: Dab a lightly loaded scrap of foam on armour edges to make chips.
sponging-texture.mottled skin with a sponge: Dab the skin tone gently with a lightly loaded sponge, then glaze thinly with the same colour to blend the dabs in.
sponging-texture.speckled texture: Dab paint with a scrap of foam loaded lightly; stippling with an old brush tip gives a similar texture with more control.
sponging-texture.sponge metal over black: Prime black, sponge a darker silver fairly heavily leaving some black, then a brighter silver lightly on raised areas.
sponging-texture.blister foam: Twist a small piece of packing foam into a plastic brush sleeve or cap so a little sticks out, or hold a scrap in tweezers.
sponging-texture.sponge technique: Load a little paint, dab most off on a towel as with drybrushing, then dab the area; raised parts catch more and read as highlights.
sponging-texture.chipping with sponge: Dab a lightly loaded foam scrap on the armour edges to make chips.

starter-sets-vs-separate-paints.starter set or separate paints: A starter set is a quick, simple start; picking paints one by one costs more at first but wastes less.
starter-sets-vs-separate-paints.paint set worth it: Count the colours you would really use and check it has a good white, black, brown, metal and wash; once you own a few paints, sets bring doubles.
starter-sets-vs-separate-paints.what paints to get first: Start from the scheme you want to paint and list only the colours it needs, or a broad core set built for mixing.
starter-sets-vs-separate-paints.beginner paint set: Check it has a white and black that cover well, a brown, a metal and a wash; plan on a better brush than the one included.
starter-sets-vs-separate-paints.individual paints vs set: Single pots take more thought but every one earns its place; after the first few paints they are almost always better value.
starter-sets-vs-separate-paints.starter box worth it: It removes the guesswork and gets you painting the same day, but often holds colours you will never use and a basic brush.
starter-sets-vs-separate-paints.first paints: A broad set of core colours, ideally strong primaries with black and white for mixing, then single pots per project.
starter-sets-vs-separate-paints.which colours to start with: A white and a black that cover well, a brown, a metal and a wash, plus the colours your chosen scheme needs.
starter-sets-vs-separate-paints.how many paints do i need: Only what your scheme needs: list its colours, or start with a core set and add single pots as each project needs them.
starter-sets-vs-separate-paints.starting paint collection: Start with a broad core set, ideally one built for mixing, then add single pots as each new project needs them.

streaky-rotten-textures.rotten armour: Base mid olive, then wet blend thinned lighter olive and grey brown in streaks along the part, with dark brown lining the deeper streaks.
streaky-rotten-textures.streaky texture: Lay a thin coat of the base, then pull streaks of the other colours through it while wet, always along the length of the part.
streaky-rotten-textures.water stained cloth: Wet blend drab olive and grey brown streaks down the cloth, then drag a thin yellow brown wash down from the top.
streaky-rotten-textures.rotting effect: Wet blend a few drab colours, olive, lighter olive and grey brown, in streaks along the part, one small area at a time.
streaky-rotten-textures.decayed look: Streak drab olives and grey brown wet into each other, add darker olive in places, and highlight rips with light olive and bone.
streaky-rotten-textures.streaks of grime on armour: Pull wet streaks of lighter olive and grey brown through a thin base coat, up and down on legs and shields, across on arms.
streaky-rotten-textures.rotten cloth: Wet blend olive streaks down the cloth, finish with a thin yellow brown wash from the top and dark brown stippled at the hem.
streaky-rotten-textures.putrid diseased armour: Mid olive base with wet streaks of lighter olive and grey brown, darker olive in places, and thin dark brown in deep streaks.
streaky-rotten-textures.wet blend streaks: Keep thinned colours wet on a wet palette, lay a thin base coat, and pull the others through it in streaks along the part.
streaky-rotten-textures.make metal look rotten and stained: See: this entry streaks drab olive and grey brown wet along the part, with light olive and bone on edges and rips.

taking-apart-old-models.how do i take apart a glued model: Cut plastic glue joints along the seam with a fine razor saw; freeze superglue joints for a few hours, then twist or tap them apart.
taking-apart-old-models.remove old superglue: A few hours in the freezer then a firm twist, or a soak in strong isopropyl alcohol or stripper, especially on metal.
taking-apart-old-models.freeze model to break glue: A few hours in the freezer, then a firm twist or a tap with a blade along the seam, often pops a superglue joint.
taking-apart-old-models.dismantle an old model: Cut plastic glue seams, freeze or soak superglue joints, pull pins with pliers, then pick out old putty working edge inward.
taking-apart-old-models.break glue joints: Superglue is brittle, so freeze and twist it; plastic glue joints rarely come apart cleanly, so cut along the seam instead.
taking-apart-old-models.rebuild second hand models: Separate the joints, pick out old putty and glue, soak off old white glue and sand, clean, and dry every part before regluing.
taking-apart-old-models.plastic glue welded parts: Plastic glue melts parts together, so cut along the seam with a fine razor saw or sharp blade, and expect to fill a little.
taking-apart-old-models.cut apart glued parts: Cut along the seam with a fine razor saw or a sharp blade rather than pulling, then fill and tidy afterwards.
taking-apart-old-models.pick out old putty: Soak in stripper to loosen it, then pick it out with a dental pick or blade, working from the edge inward.
taking-apart-old-models.undo a gluing mistake: Freeze a superglue joint for a few hours and twist it apart; cut a plastic glue joint along the seam with a fine saw.

thinning-paint.thin your paints: Thin on the palette, not in the pot, adding water a drop at a time until it flows like thin cream or milk but still has strong colour.
thinning-paint.how thin should paint be: Like thin cream or full fat milk: it flows off the brush and covers without brush marks, but does not run into recesses like a wash.
thinning-paint.paint too thick: Pull some aside on the palette with a damp brush and add water a drop at a time; thick paint goes lumpy and fills detail.
thinning-paint.paint consistency: Thin cream or full fat milk, flowing off the brush without running; test a stroke on the palette or your thumb.
thinning-paint.milk consistency: It flows off the brush, covers without brush marks and does not run into recesses; there is no fixed ratio.
thinning-paint.lumpy paint: It is too thick; add water a drop at a time on the palette, and never go back over a coat while it is drying.
thinning-paint.brush marks showing: Thin the paint until it flows like milk, spread it out across the surface, and use two or three thin coats.
thinning-paint.how much water to add: No fixed ratio; add a drop at a time until it flows like thin cream, and add paint if you overdo it.
thinning-paint.paint fills detail: Thin it and spread it out across the surface; paint left in a pile fills the recesses.
thinning-paint.two thin coats: Yes, two or three thin coats, each left to dry, give a smooth finish and keep detail crisp.
thinning-paint.How thin should my paint be?: Like thin cream or full fat milk: it flows off the brush, covers without brush marks, and does not run like a wash.

transporting-models.transport models: Glue strong magnets under each base and carry them on a metal baking tray in a lidded plastic tub.
transporting-models.carry case: A lidded tub with a metal tray in the bottom and magnets under the bases, or a case with removable steel shelves.
transporting-models.magnets under bases: Glue strong magnets under each base and line a box or tin with a metal tray or thin steel sheet; models stop shifting.
transporting-models.foam tray damage: Models shift in foam, snapping spiky parts and rubbing edges to primer; magnets under the bases on a steel tray avoid both.
transporting-models.carrying models to a game: Magnetise the bases and put them on a metal tray in a lidded tub; trays with handles lift straight out.
transporting-models.travel with miniatures: Magnets under the bases on a steel lined box, tacky putty for grip on bumpy trips, and foam for tall or fragile models.
transporting-models.cheap model case: A lidded plastic tub with a metal baking tray in the bottom, plus strong magnets glued under each base.
transporting-models.transporting minis safely: Magnets on a steel tray stop models shifting; use cut foam for tall or fragile ones and soft fabric on case walls.
transporting-models.paint rubbing off in foam: Models shift in foam trays and rub raised edges; magnets under bases on a metal tray, or clip cases that grip only the base, avoid it.
transporting-models.models break in transport: Spiky parts snap when models shift; magnetise the bases on a steel tray, and use deep cut foam for tall or fragile models.

ultrasonic-cleaner.ultrasonic cleaner: Fill it to the line with fresh tap water, hang parts in a basket off the floor, and never fill a standard unit with alcohol.
ultrasonic-cleaner.how do i use an ultrasonic cleaner: Fresh tap water to the maker's line, parts in a basket with liquid under and around them, not overcrowded, warm water for grease.
ultrasonic-cleaner.deep clean airbrush parts: Hang them in a basket in water and run it for about 15 minutes per run; warm water shifts oil and grease better.
ultrasonic-cleaner.clean dried paint off palette: An ultrasonic cleaner with water soaks dried paint off ceramic palettes; finish stubborn residue with warm soapy water and a soft brush.
ultrasonic-cleaner.remove mould release from new figures: An ultrasonic cleaner with water lifts mould release and grime; a drop of soap can help, and warm water shifts grease better.
ultrasonic-cleaner.can i put alcohol in ultrasonic cleaner: Not in a standard unit; the tank warms and the fumes can catch. Units rated for flammable liquids exist.
ultrasonic-cleaner.ultrasonic cleaner for stripping: It helps strip old paint; use a stripping liquid that is safe for the plastic and safe to warm.
ultrasonic-cleaner.cleaning sculpting tools: An ultrasonic cleaner with fresh water deep cleans sculpting tools; hang them in a basket off the tank floor.
ultrasonic-cleaner.what liquid in ultrasonic cleaner: Fresh tap water, perhaps with a drop of soap; never isopropyl alcohol or other flammable liquids in a standard unit.
ultrasonic-cleaner.sonic cleaner for minis: It shakes mould release and grime off new figures in water; use a basket and empty and rinse the tank often.

using-real-objects.real objects in a diorama: Cut them cleanly where they meet the scene, harden anything soft, glue moving parts, then repaint everything so it matches.
using-real-objects.paintbrush as part of the scene: Soak the bristles in super glue to set them solid, cut it cleanly where it meets the scene, then prime and repaint it.
using-real-objects.everyday items in display: Brushes, cutters, pots or a cutting mat can join a scene; cut, harden and fix them, then repaint them with everything else.
using-real-objects.display ideas: See: this entry covers building real objects such as brushes, pots or a cutting mat into a painted display scene.
using-real-objects.giant scale scene: Cut real items like brushes or pots into the scene and repaint them, even if they already look right, so they share the finish.
using-real-objects.cutting mat in diorama: Repaint it, and measure and paint its grid and any labels carefully by hand; that neat detail sells the effect.
using-real-objects.mixed media display: Prime real objects and the model together and repaint everything, so the whole scene reads as one painted world.
using-real-objects.real world objects: Cut them cleanly, harden soft parts, glue moving parts, then prime and repaint them to match the painted scene.
using-real-objects.diorama props: Brush tip covers make pipes, bent paperclips twisted metal, stripped wire cables and tea leaves coarse ground, fixed with thin super glue.
using-real-objects.tiny person on a real paint pot: Cut the pot cleanly where it meets the scene, glue any moving parts, then prime and repaint it, copying its labels carefully.

varying-colours-across-a-unit.varied unit: Pick four or five colours and combine them differently on each figure, so the unit looks natural but still belongs together.
varying-colours-across-a-unit.different colours on each model: Use a short shared palette and move the colours around per figure, such as a black hood on one and a red hood on the next.
varying-colours-across-a-unit.uniform variation: Keep one shade colour on every coat and vary only the highlight colour or how far you take it, with about one in five older.
varying-colours-across-a-unit.unit variety: Aim between the extremes: a short list of colours mixed differently per figure, with most kit one colour and one or two changed.
varying-colours-across-a-unit.horse colours for cavalry: Group coats into light, mid and dark; in a unit of six, three in your easiest colour, two in a second and one in a third.
varying-colours-across-a-unit.natural looking unit: Spread a short list of colours across the unit in different combinations, and do not repeat a pattern on neighbouring figures.
varying-colours-across-a-unit.mix colours across unit: Choose four or five colours you find easy and combine them differently on jackets, trousers and gear for each figure.
varying-colours-across-a-unit.ragtag militia: Mix freely: legs in different colours, a stripe down one side, split garments or contrasting trim, and some iron, some bronze helmets.
varying-colours-across-a-unit.irregular troops clothing: Mix colours freely, such as hose with each leg different or a contrasting trim, without repeating patterns on neighbours.
varying-colours-across-a-unit.avoid every model looking identical: Move a shared set of colours around on repeated sculpts, and vary metals and a little kit on one or two figures.

wash-vs-glaze.wash vs glaze: A wash runs into recesses from a loaded brush; a glaze has most liquid wicked off so it stays on the surface and tints it.
wash-vs-glaze.difference between wash and glaze: Both are mostly water; a wash goes on from a loaded brush to run into cracks, a glaze is wicked off to sit on the surface.
wash-vs-glaze.what is a glaze: Thin paint with most of the liquid wicked off the brush, so it sits on the surface and tints the colour underneath.
wash-vs-glaze.what is a wash: Thin paint applied straight from a loaded brush so it breaks surface tension and runs into cracks.
wash-vs-glaze.should i wash or glaze: Glaze when a wash would spoil the finish, such as on metal, which a wash can dull, or for cleaner dark shading.
wash-vs-glaze.how do i apply a wash: Apply it straight from a loaded brush so it breaks surface tension and runs into the cracks.
wash-vs-glaze.wash running into recesses: That is what a wash does, applied from a loaded brush; wick most off the brush instead if you want it to stay on the surface.
wash-vs-glaze.glaze stays on surface: Yes, wick most of the liquid off first so it sits on the surface, and build it in several thin passes.
wash-vs-glaze.shade or tint: A wash shades by running into recesses; a very thin glaze tints, shifting the colour underneath without hiding it.
wash-vs-glaze.same paint for wash and glaze: Yes, thin a wash about three parts medium to one to glaze shadowed parts, then run it neat into the recesses once dry.

weathering-buildings.weathering buildings: Place weathering where weather really leaves it: rain streaks from sills and gutters, damp and moss low down, soot above openings.
weathering-buildings.how to weather terrain: Shift tones with blended oils, add green damp low on walls, a pigment wash on tiles, rain streaks, soot and edge highlights.
weathering-buildings.damp stains on walls: Add a green oil low on stone walls and at the foot of corners, or a thin green filter near the ground.
weathering-buildings.soot on walls: Drybrush or airbrush soot above windows, doors and chimneys.
weathering-buildings.moss on a roof: Add a green oil on the roof tiles, then dust a few tiles with green pigment for moss.
weathering-buildings.dirty walls: Wash lower walls with light and dark brown pigments in white spirit, then lift the excess off raised areas with a cotton bud.
weathering-buildings.aged buildings: Damp stains and moss low down, rain streaks from sills and gutters, soot above openings, and dust gathered in corners.
weathering-buildings.where does weathering go: Rain runs from roof edges, sills and gutters, damp rises from the ground, and dust and mud gather low down and in corners.
weathering-buildings.rain streaks from gutters: Run thin dark streaks down from sills, gutters and broken edges.
weathering-buildings.make a house look old: Shift tones with oils, add green damp low down and on tiles, rain streaks from gutters, soot above windows, and a pigment wash.

wet-in-wet-blending.wet in wet: Wet the area with water or medium, then touch thin paint in with the brush tip and let it spread and soften on its own.
wet-in-wet-blending.watercolour technique: Wet the surface first and let thin paint diffuse into it, guiding the spread with a clean damp brush tip.
wet-in-wet-blending.wet surface first: Wet it evenly with clean water, maybe a little medium or retarder, so it is wet but not running or pooling.
wet-in-wet-blending.diffuse paint: Touch slightly thinned paint into an evenly wet area; the pigment spreads by itself, and thinner paint travels further.
wet-in-wet-blending.soft blend: Wet the area, touch in thin paint and let it soften on its own, watching the edge of the wet area for hard lines.
wet-in-wet-blending.blend with water: Wet the area with clean water first, then touch in slightly thinned paint and guide its spread with a clean damp brush.
wet-in-wet-blending.watercolor style: Wet the area first, touch in thin paint and let it spread, working one section at a time and letting each dry.
wet-in-wet-blending.retarder blending: Add a little medium or retarder to the water you wet the area with, then touch in thin paint and let it diffuse.
wet-in-wet-blending.paint spreading on wet surface: That is wet in wet: thinner paint travels further, and you guide it with the tip of a clean damp brush.
wet-in-wet-blending.difference from wet blending: Wet blending pushes two wet paints together; wet in wet wets the surface first and lets thin paint diffuse into it.

where-highlights-go.where to highlight: On the tops of shapes and anything that sticks out, brighter higher up, from one chosen light direction.
where-highlights-go.highlight placement: Look straight down on the model: whatever you see gets the first highlight, and each lighter layer is the same shape, smaller.
where-highlights-go.how do i know where highlights go: Hold the primed model under a single lamp, turn it slowly, and highlight where the glare lands, or zenithal spray white from above.
where-highlights-go.light direction: Pick one, usually above and slightly to one side, and leave the side facing away in the darker tone.
where-highlights-go.where do highlights go: Upward facing surfaces and parts protruding towards the viewer, pushed to the top of each part, brightest near the face.
where-highlights-go.where to highlight a cloak: At the top of each fold where it meets the material above, brighter higher up, with sharp folds getting a hard dark line.
where-highlights-go.top down highlights: Look straight down on the model; everything you can see gets the first highlight, each lighter layer smaller.
where-highlights-go.highlight shapes: Treat each part separately and push its highlight to the top; arms are cylinders, heads spheres, brightest facing the light.
where-highlights-go.highlights look random: Choose one light direction, highlight the top of each part, not the middle or bottom, and use duller values lower down.
where-highlights-go.light source from above: Highlight upward facing surfaces and protruding parts, with the brightest values on the top tenth near the face.

yellow-armour.yellow armour: Prime white or bone, base a rich yellow in three or four thin coats, shade gently down with warm oranges and browns, edge very pale yellow.
yellow-armour.painting yellow: Change your water, prime white or bone, build a smooth solid base in thin coats, and shade more than you highlight.
yellow-armour.yellow over white primer: Base a rich yellow in three or four thin coats over clean white, each fully dry, or one heavy coat of one coat yellow.
yellow-armour.yellow looks patchy: Use three or four thin coats over white or bone, or drybrush a matching opaque yellow over blotchy one coat yellow.
yellow-armour.shading yellow: Glaze an orange yellow down the lower part of each panel, then darker warm mixes lower each time, over a gloss coat.
yellow-armour.yellow armor: White or bone primer, rich yellow in thin coats, orange and warm brown glazes low on the panels, and pale yellow edges.
yellow-armour.yellow shows dirty water: Change your water first, as yellow shows every bit of dirt.
yellow-armour.yellow needs loads of coats: Yellow covers badly; prime white or bone and use three or four thin coats, each fully dry.
yellow-armour.yellow goes green when shaded: Shade with warm oranges and browns: an orange yellow glaze low on each panel, and warm mid brown only in the panel lines.
yellow-armour.how do i paint smooth yellow: Thin coats over white or bone, each fully dry, then glaze the base yellow back over messy shading or tide marks.
